And if that [experiencer-nature] arises, then it too has origination — so how is it not accepted that <s>Ātman</s> has origination? Thus again,

body.text: anutpannaṃ hi tannāsti ka icchedbhavituṃ tadā /
body.translated_text: 'For when that has not arisen, it does not exist — who then would wish to come into being?'

body.text: ityāyātam //
body.translated_text: This is arrived at. //

body.text: aparamapi dūṣaṇamatrāha-
body.translated_text: He states yet another fault here —

body.text: viṣayavyāpṛtatvācca niroddhumapi nehate // Bca_6.28 //
body.translated_text: And because of being engaged with sense-objects, it does not even wish to cease. // Bca_6.28 //

body.text: yadyapyasau pradhānopahitaviṣayopabhogāya pravartata itīṣyate, tadā prāgapravṛttasya paścātpravṛttirna yujyate / atha kathaṃcit pravartate, tadāpi viṣaye vyāpṛtasya nivṛttirna syāt / etadevāha- niroddhumapi nehate / viṣayopabhogānnivartitumapi notsahate, tadā tasya tatsvabhāvatvāt, tasya ca nityatayā anivṛtteḥ / nivṛttau vā anityatvaprasaṅgāt / naiyāyikādīnāmātmano vyapadeśo nityatvāt //
body.translated_text: Even if it is accepted that it operates for the enjoyment of sense-objects presented by <s>Pradhāna</s>, then for one not previously engaged, subsequent engagement is not logical. And if somehow it does engage, then for one engaged in sense-objects, cessation would not occur. This is exactly what is said — 'it does not even wish to cease' — to cease from the enjoyment of sense-objects, it is not able, since at that time it is of that nature, and since that [nature] is permanent, there is no cessation. Or else, if there were cessation, the absurd consequence of impermanence [would follow]. The designation of <s>Ātman</s> by the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others [is given] because of permanence. //

body.text: viśeṣamapi tasyāha-
body.translated_text: He states a particular [quality] of that [Ātman] as well —

body.text: nityo hyacetanaścātmā vyomavat sphuṭamakriyaḥ /
body.translated_text: For <s>Ātman</s> is permanent and non-sentient — clearly inactive, like space.

body.text: acaitanyaṃ sāṃkhyādiha viśeṣaḥ / anyatra samānatā / tatra nityaḥ pūrvāparakālayorekasvabhāvaḥ / acetanaśca acitsvabhāvaḥ / jaḍa ityarthaḥ / anyacaitanyayogāccetayate / vyomavad vyāpī / ata eva sphuṭaṃ vyaktamakriyaḥ / yadāha-
body.translated_text: 'Non-sentient' — [according to] the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> and such — this is the distinguishing [feature]. Otherwise there is similarity [with other schools]. There, 'permanent' — of one nature in earlier and later times. 'Non-sentient' — of non-conscious nature; the meaning is 'inert.' It cognizes through the conjunction of another's consciousness. 'Like space' — all-pervading. Therefore 'clearly' — manifestly — 'inactive.' As is said —

children.translated_text: 'Others here maintain <s>Ātman</s> as the substratum of desire and such,
inherently non-conscious, permanent, and likewise all-pervading; //

body.text:
śubhāśubhānāṃ kartāraṃ karmaṇāṃ tatphalasya ca /
bhoktāraṃ cetanāyogāccetanaṃ na svarūpataḥ //
body.translated_text:
the agent of good and bad <s>karmas</s>, and the experiencer of their fruits;
sentient through the conjunction of consciousness, not by its own nature.' //

body.text: tattvasaṃgraha-171-72
body.translated_text: <s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 171-72

body.text:
tathā ca akiṃcitkara evāsau, kvacidapi kārye 'nupayogāt / atha aparasahakāripratyayasaṃnidhau niṣkriyasyāpi tasya kriyā[bhyu]pagamyate / yaduktam-
jñānayatnādisaṃbandhaḥ kartṛtvaṃ tasya bhaṇyate / iti /
body.translated_text:
Thus it is entirely ineffective, being of no use in any effect whatsoever. If however, even for that inactive one, activity is accepted in the presence of other cooperating conditions — as is said:
'The connection with knowledge, effort, and such is declared to be its agency' — thus.

body.text: atrāha-
body.translated_text: To this he says —

body.text: pratyayāntarasaṅge 'pi nirvikārasya kā kriyā // Bca_6.29 //
body.translated_text: Even in connection with other conditions, what action is there for what is unchanging? // Bca_6.29 //

body.text: jñānayatnādipratyayāntarasaṃparke 'pi nityatvānnirvikārasya pūrvasvabhāvādapracyutasyātmanaḥ kā kriyā? naiva kriyā yujyate //
body.translated_text: Even in contact with other conditions such as knowledge and effort, what action is there for <s>Ātman</s> which, being permanent, is unchanging — not departed from its prior nature? No action whatsoever is justified. //

children.text: yaḥ pūrvavat kriyākāle kriyāyāstena kiṃ kṛtam /
children.translated_text: If [<s>Ātman</s>] at the time of action is the same as before, what has action accomplished?
If 'it is [Ātman's] action' is the connection, what is the basis for that? // Bca_6.30 //

body.text: yathā pūrvamakriyākāle tathākriyākāle 'pi yaḥ, tena kārakasvabhāvavikalena kriyāyāḥ kiṃ kṛtam, yena pratyayāntarasaṅge tasya kriyā vyavasthāpyeta? api ca / ubhayasaṃbandhābhāvāt tasya ātmanaḥ kriyeyamiti saṃbandhe katarattadanyanimittam? naivāsti kiṃcit //
body.translated_text: If [<s>Ātman</s>] at the time of action is just as it was before, at the time of non-action, then what has action accomplished for it, which is devoid of agent-nature, such that one could establish its action through connection with other conditions? Moreover — since there is no connection between the two, if [one says] 'this is the action of <s>Ātman</s>' — what is the other ground for that connection? There is none whatsoever. //

body.text: vistareṇa cātmano nirākariṣyamāṇatvāt [9.58-60] īśvarasya ca [9.119-126], na svatantraḥ kaścidapi saṃbhavati / evamasvātantryaṃ sarvatra prasādhyopasaṃharannāha-
body.translated_text: Since <s>Ātman</s> will be refuted at length [9.58-60] and <s>Īśvara</s> (God) as well [9.119-126], no one independent is possible. Thus, establishing the absence of independence in all things, he concludes —

children.text: evaṃ paravaśaṃ sarvaṃ yadvaśaṃ so 'pi cāvaśaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus everything is dependent on another; and that on which it depends is also powerless.
When things are thus inert like magical creations, at what should one be angry? // Bca_6.31 //

body.text: evamuktanayena paravaśaṃ parāyattaṃ sarvaṃ bāhyādhyātmikaṃ vastujātam / tarhi yadvaśe tadaparāyattaṃ bhaviṣyatīti cet, na / yadvaśaṃ so 'pi cāvaśaḥ svahetuparatantraḥ / evaṃ sa heturapi svahetorityanādisaṃsāraparaṃparāyāṃ na svavaśitā kvacidapi saṃbhavati / ato nirvyāpārāḥ sarvadharmā iti / kaḥ kasmai druhyati paramārthataḥ yenāparādhini kvacit kasyacidaparādhe tasya dveṣo yuktaḥ / idamevāha- nirmāṇavat sarvavyāpārakalpanāvigamāt, aceṣṭeṣu nirīheṣu sarvadharmeṣu evaṃ satsu kva kupyatām? na yujyate prekṣāvatāṃ kvacidapi kopa iti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: By the method thus stated, all external and internal things are dependent on others, subject to others' control. If then what they are subject to would itself be independent — no. That which they are subject to is also not independent, being dependent on its own causes. Thus that cause too [depends] on its own cause, and so in the beginningless succession of <s>saṃsāra</s>, self-mastery is nowhere to be found. Therefore all <s>dharmas</s> are without activity. Who ultimately harms whom, such that toward some offender, in some offense, hatred would be justified? This is what he says — like a magical creation, because all conceptualization of activity is eliminated; when all <s>dharmas</s> are thus without volition, without desire — this being so, at whom should one be angry? Anger is not appropriate for the discerning, ever — this is the meaning.

body.text: syādetat- evaṃ hi ekaṃ samarthayato dvitīyaṃ vighaṭate ityāśaṅkayannāha-
body.translated_text: One might object: when establishing one [position] in this way, a second [principle] is undermined — anticipating this objection, he says —

body.text: vāraṇāpi na yuktaivaṃ kaḥ kiṃ vārayatīti cet /
body.translated_text: Even prevention is not justified thus — if one asks, 'Who prevents what?'

body.text: samarthitanyāyenaiva vāraṇāpi nivartanamapi nirmāṇavadaceṣṭeṣu bhāveṣu na yuktā / evamiti yadā kiṃcidapi svatantraṃ na dṛśyate, sarvaṃ pratyayasāmagrīṃ pratītya jāyate, tadā vāraṇāpi na
body.translated_text: By the very principle established, even prevention — cessation too — is not justified when things are without volition, like magical creations. 'Thus' — when nothing whatsoever is seen to be independent, when everything arises dependent on the assemblage of conditions, then even prevention is not

body.text: yuktā / yadi vā- maivam, tathāpi kathaṃ na yuktā? ko vārayati, svatantraḥ kartā kiṃ niṣedhyaṃ svatantrapravṛttaṃ vārayatīti cet / ayamabhiprāyaḥ- na hi samāne 'pi nyāye kvacit pravṛttiḥ sāmānyatvāt / tasmādyuktametat- vāraṇā na yukteti //
body.translated_text: justified. Or alternatively: let it not be so; even then, how is it not justified? Who prevents — what independent agent prevents what independently occurring [activity]? — if one asks thus. This is the intention: for given the same principle, activity [would apply] everywhere due to its generality. Therefore this is correct: prevention is not justified.

body.text: yadyevaṃ manyase, atrottaramāha-
body.translated_text: If you think thus, he states the reply here —

body.text: yuktā pratītyatā yasmādduḥkhasyoparatirmatā // Bca_6.32 //
body.translated_text: Prevention is justified, since the cessation of suffering is accepted as dependent [on conditions]. // <s>Bca</s> 6.32 //

body.text: yuktā vāraṇā, kutaḥ? pratītyatā, idaṃ pratītyedamutpadyate iti pratītyasamutpannatā yasmādasti nirvyāpāreṣvapi bhāveṣu, ato vāraṇā yuktā, tato na vyāghātaḥ / etaduktaṃ bhavati- yadyapi nirvyāpārāḥ sarvadharmāḥ, tathāpi pratītyasamutpādavaśāt pāratantryamupadarśitam- evaṃ paravaśaṃ sarvam [6. 31] ityādivacanāt / tataḥ avidyādipratyayabalāduttarottaraḥ kāryapravāhaḥ saṃskārādirūpaḥ pravartate, pūrvapūrvanivṛttau nivartate / etacca uttaratra [9. 75] vistareṇa pratipādayiṣyate / tasmādduḥkhasya saṃsārasya uparatirnivṛttirabhimatā / ato dveṣādipāpapravṛttivāraṇā saṃgacchate / tāṃ pratītya tathāvidhamabhyudayaniḥśreyasasvabhāvaṃ phalamutpadyate //
body.translated_text: Prevention is justified. Why? Because of dependent arising — 'dependent on this, that arises' — such dependently arisen nature exists even in things without activity; therefore prevention is justified, and there is no contradiction. What is meant is this: although all <s>dharmas</s> are without activity, nevertheless through the force of dependent arising, their dependent nature has been shown — by the statement 'all is subject to others' [6.31] and so forth. Therefore, through the force of conditions such as <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and the rest, the successive stream of effects in the form of <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations) and so on proceeds; upon the cessation of the preceding [conditions], it ceases. And this will be explained in detail later [9.75]. Therefore the cessation — the stopping — of suffering, of <s>saṃsāra</s>, is accepted. Thus the prevention of engagement in evil such as hatred and so on is coherent. Dependent on that [prevention], a result of such a nature — consisting of prosperity and the highest good — arises.

body.text: sāṃprataṃ prakṛtameva yojayannāha-
body.translated_text: Now, connecting with the main topic itself, he says —

children.translated_text: Therefore, having seen even an enemy or a friend acting wrongly,

children.text: īdṛśāḥ pratyayā asyetyevaṃ matvā sukhī bhavet // Bca_6.33 //
children.translated_text: thinking 'such are the conditions of this one,' one should be happy. // <s>Bca</s> 6.33 //

body.text: yasmāt pratītyajaṃ sarvam, tasmādamitretaraṃ [amitramitaraṃ ca] apakāriṇaṃ pratītya sukhamevālambanīyam / kutaḥ? īdṛśā apakārakaraṇaśīlahetavaḥ asya amitrasya itarasya vā, iti evaṃ niścitya sukhī bhavet, daurmanasyaṃ na kurvīta //
body.translated_text: Since everything is born from conditions, therefore toward an enemy or the other [i.e., a friend] who acts harmfully, one should resort only to happiness. Why? 'Such' — causes whose nature is to produce harm — belong to 'this' enemy or the other; thus having determined, one should be happy, and should not produce despondency.

body.text: kiṃ ca / duḥkhopanipātena cittakṣobhe 'pi na duḥkhasya nivṛttirastītyupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, showing that even when the mind is disturbed by the onset of suffering, there is no cessation of suffering [through anger], he says —

children.text: yadi tu svecchayā siddhiḥ sarveṣāmeva dehinām /
children.translated_text: If success were achieved by the mere wish of all embodied beings,

children.text: na bhavetkasyacidduḥkhaṃ na duḥkhaṃ kaścidicchati // Bca_6.34 //
children.translated_text: no one would have suffering, for no one wishes for suffering. // <s>Bca</s> 6.34 //

body.text: na hi ātmecchāmātreṇa anavimataṃ nivartate, abhimataṃ copatiṣṭhate hetumantareṇa / tathātve sa ti na bhavet kasyacit sattvasya duḥkham / kimiti? na duḥkhamātmanaḥ kaścidicchati / svasukhābhilāṣiṇa eva hi sarvasattvāḥ //
body.translated_text: For what is undesired does not cease by mere self-wish alone, nor does what is desired come about, without a [separate] cause. If it were so, no sentient being would have suffering. Why? No one wishes suffering for oneself. For all sentient beings desire only their own happiness.

body.text: duḥkhādhivāsanākṣāntimabhidhāya idānīṃ parāpakāramarṣaṇakṣāntimupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Having described the patience of enduring suffering, he now shows the patience of tolerating others' harm, saying —

children.translated_text: Through carelessness, they harm themselves with thorns and such;
through anger, by cutting off food and such; through desire for what is hard to obtain. // <s>Bca</s> 6.35 //
By hanging, by falling from heights, by consuming poison and unwholesome things,
some kill themselves, and by engaging in non-meritorious conduct. // <s>Bca</s> 6.36 //
When thus, being subject to <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), they destroy even their own dear self,

children.text: tadaiṣāṃ parakāyeṣu parihāraḥ kathaṃ bhavet // Bca_6.37 //
children.translated_text: how could there be restraint in these [beings] toward others' bodies? // <s>Bca</s> 6.37 //

body.text: asamīkṣitakāritā pramādaḥ / svayameva svakāyaṃ kaṇṭakakhāṇukaṭhallapāṣāṇaśarkarādibhirdurgamārgeṣu karmapravṛttāḥ kaṇṭakāstaraṇaśayanādibhirvā bādhante / tathā bhojanapānaparihārādibhiḥ / kimiti? kopāt agamyaparadāradhanādi labdhumicchayā vā //
body.translated_text: 'Carelessness' is acting without consideration. They harm their own body with thorns, stumps, rough stones, pebbles, and such on difficult paths while engaged in activity, or by sleeping on beds of thorns and the like. Likewise by abstaining from food and drink and such. Why? Through anger, or through the desire to obtain forbidden things such as others' wives and wealth.

body.text: udbandhanamūrdhvalambanam / prapātaḥ prapatanaṃ parvatādeḥ / jalāgnipraveśādibhiḥ, viṣāpathyādibhakṣaṇaiḥ, atyāhārātipānādibhiḥ, nighnanti mārayanti kecinmohapuruṣā ātmānaṃ svakāyam / paravadhādibhiḥ, apuṇyācaraṇena ca / paravadhābhiprāyāḥ saṃgrāmādiṣvakuśalakriyayā ca //
body.translated_text: 'Hanging' is suspending oneself from above. 'Falling' is throwing oneself from mountains and such. By entering water, fire, and such; by consuming poison and unwholesome things; by excessive eating and excessive drinking and such — some deluded persons kill themselves, their own body. By killing others and such — through non-meritorious conduct. Those intent on killing others, through unskillful action in battles and such.

body.text: yadaivamuktakrameṇa kleśavaśyatvāt kleśaparatantratvāt ete sattvā ātmānamapi priyaṃ vallabhaṃ ghnanti pīḍayanti, tadā eṣāṃ parakāyeṣu paraśarīreṣu apakāraviratiḥ kathaṃ syāt?
body.translated_text: When in the manner thus stated, due to being subject to <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), due to being dependent on afflictions, these beings destroy, torment even their own dear, beloved self — then how could there be cessation of harm toward others' bodies, toward others' persons?

body.text: itthaṃ ca kṛpāpātramevaite, na dveṣasthānamityāha-
body.translated_text: And thus, these beings are objects of compassion, not grounds for hatred — he says —

children.translated_text: When these [beings], maddened by <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), engage in self-destruction,

children.text: na kevalaṃ dayā nāsti krodha utpadyate katham // Bca_6.38 //
children.translated_text: not only is there no compassion — how can anger arise? // <s>Bca</s> 6.38 //

body.text: piśācairiva grasteṣu eṣu apakārakāriṣu uktanayena pravṛtteṣu ātmaghātane parāpakāradvāreṇa vā na kevalaṃ na tāvat kṛpā nāsti, audāsīnyamapi sādhūnāṃ tatrāyuktam / dveṣa utpadyate kathaṃ kṛpāsthāneṣviti viparyayo mahān //
body.translated_text: When these harm-doers, as if seized by demons, engage in self-destruction in the manner described — or through harming others — not only should compassion not be absent, but even indifference is improper for the virtuous in such cases. How can hatred arise toward those who are objects of compassion? — this would be a great perversion.

body.text: evamapi svacittaṃ nivārayedityāha-
body.translated_text: Even so, one should restrain one's own mind — he says —

children.translated_text: If it is the nature of the childish to cause harm to others,

children.text: teṣu kopo na yukto me yathāgnau dahanātmake // Bca_6.39 //
children.translated_text: anger toward them is no more justified for me than toward fire, whose nature is to burn. // <s>Bca</s> 6.39 //

body.text: tathā hi vikalpadvayamatra / bālānāṃ pṛthagjanānāṃ yadi etādṛśa eva svabhāvaḥ paropadravakāritā nāma, tadā na khalu svabhāvāḥ paryanuyogamarhanti- kimiti parāpakāraṃ kurvanti te? iti paribhāvya teṣu dveṣo na yukto me / tadyathā agnau dahanasvabhāve dāhakaraṇāt / anyathā tadabhāve tatsvabhāvatāhāniprasaṅgāt //
body.translated_text: For here there are two alternatives. If such is indeed the nature of the childish — of ordinary beings — namely causing harm to others, then surely natures do not deserve reproach — [thinking] 'Why do they harm others?' — and so hatred toward them is not justified for me. Just as toward fire, whose nature is to burn, [one does not get angry] for its causing burning. Otherwise, in the absence of that [nature], the absurd consequence would follow that it is not their nature.

body.text: dvitīyaṃ vikalpamadhikṛtyāha-
body.translated_text: Regarding the second alternative, he says —

children.translated_text: If, however, this fault is adventitious, and beings are gentle by nature,
even so, that anger is unjustified — like [being angry at] pungent smoke in the sky. // <s>Bca</s> 6.40 //

body.text: atha doṣo 'yamāgantuḥ anya eva na tatsvabhāvabhūtaḥ / sattvāḥ punaḥ prakṛtiprabhāsvaracittasaṃtānatayā peśalā akuṭilasvabhāvāḥ / doṣā hi duṣṭasvabhāvāḥ, na tatsvabhāvāḥ sattvāḥ / tathāpi ayuktasteṣu sattveṣu peśalasvabhāveṣu kopaḥ / kasminniva? kaṭudhūmo yathā iva ambare / na hi kaṭutā nāma nirmalasyākāśasya svabhāvaḥ, api tu dhūmasya / ataśca taddoṣeṇa dhūma eva doṣo yujyate, nākāśe prakṛtipariśuddhe / tasmāddoṣeṣveva kopo yujyate na sattveṣu /
body.translated_text: If, however, this fault is adventitious — something other, not belonging to their nature — and beings, by virtue of their mind-streams being luminous by nature, are gentle, of uncrooked nature — for the faults are of corrupt nature, not the nature of beings — even so, anger toward those beings of gentle nature is unjustified. Toward what then? Like pungent smoke in the sky. For pungency is not the nature of the pure sky, but of the smoke. Therefore, through the fault of that [smoke], the smoke alone deserves blame, not the sky, which is pure by nature. Therefore anger is justified only toward the faults, not toward the beings.

body.text: api ca / yadeva hi pradhānaṃ duḥkhakāraṇam, tatra yukto bhavet kopo nāpradhāne ityāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, anger would be appropriate toward the primary cause of suffering, not toward what is secondary — he says —

children.text: mukhyaṃ daṇḍādikaṃ hitvā prerake yadi kupyate /
children.translated_text: If, setting aside the primary [cause] — the stick and such — one becomes angry at the instigator,

children.text: dveṣeṇa preritaḥ so 'pi dveṣe dveṣo 'stu me varam // Bca_6.41 //
children.translated_text: he too is impelled by hatred; let my hatred rather be toward hatred itself. // <s>Bca</s> 6.41 //

body.text: kāye hi daṇḍaprahārādabhāvitacittasya duḥkhaṃ samutpadyate / tato daṇḍa eva mukhyaṃ duḥkhakāraṇamiti tatraiva kopo yuktaḥ / atha parapreritasya daṇḍasya ko doṣaḥ? tena preraka eva dveṣyo bhavati / evaṃ tarhi dveṣeṇa so 'pi daṇḍaprerakaḥ prerita iti dveṣe dveṣo mama yukto na prerake //
body.translated_text: For when one whose mind is unguarded receives a blow from a stick upon the body, suffering arises. Therefore the stick alone is the primary cause of suffering, and anger is justified only toward that. But what fault belongs to the stick, which is impelled by another? Therefore only the instigator should be hated. But then, since that instigator of the stick is also impelled by hatred, hatred toward hatred is justified for me, not toward the instigator.

body.text: api ca / nādattaṃ kiṃcidupabhujyate sukhaṃ vā duḥkhaṃ vā / iti vicintya parāpakāre 'pi na tatra cittaṃ pradūṣayedityāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, nothing — whether pleasure or suffering — is experienced without having been [previously] given [by oneself]. Reflecting thus, even when harmed by others, one should not corrupt the mind — he says —

children.translated_text: I too have previously inflicted just such suffering upon beings;
therefore this is fitting for me — [I] who have caused harm to beings. // <s>Bca</s> 6.42 //

body.text: pūrvaṃ janmāntare mayāpi sattvānāmevaṃvidhaiva pīḍā kṛtā yasmāt, ṛṇapariśodhananyāyena ucitameva mamaitat parāpakārakāriṇaḥ / tatkarmaphalaparipākāditi bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: Since previously, in other lives, I too inflicted just such torment upon beings, by the principle of repaying a debt, this is indeed fitting for me from those who cause harm. The meaning is: through the ripening of the fruit of that <s>karma</s>.

body.text: yadyasya kāraṇaṃ tasmādetadutpadyate nānyasmāditi parāmṛśya parāpakāraṃ marṣayedityupadaśaryannāha-
body.translated_text: Instructing that one should endure others' harm by reflecting that 'this arises from this cause and not from another,' he says —

children.text: tacchasraṃ mama kāyaśca dvayaṃ duḥkhasya kāraṇam /
children.translated_text: His weapon and my body — both are causes of suffering;

children.text: tena śasraṃ mayā kāyo gṛhītaḥ kutra kupyate // Bca_6.43 //
children.translated_text: he has taken up the weapon, I the body — toward whom should one be angry? // <s>Bca</s> 6.43 //

body.text: avikalakāraṇasāmagrī hi sarvakāryasya kāraṇamiti pramāṇapariniścitam / sā cātra tathāvidhā vidyate / tathāhi tasyāpakāriṇaḥ śastraṃ khaṅgādi mama kāyaśca, etaddvayaṃ sāmagrīrūpaṃ duḥkhasya kāraṇam / iti samarthakāraṇasadbhāve 'pi kāryaṃ kathaṃ notpadyeta? anyathā tattasya kāraṇameva na syāt / tato 'nyadapi, tat utpādayogaḥ? [=tatsāmagrīto 'nyadapi kāraṇaṃ syāt, tataḥ..........] tasmādyādi kāraṇopanāyake kupyate, tadā svātmanyapi kopo yuktaḥ / yataḥ svayamapi duḥkhakāraṇaṃ vahatyupanayati ca bhavān / ātmanyakope paratrāpi na yukta iti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: For it is established by valid cognition that the complete assemblage of causes is the cause of every effect; and such [an assemblage] exists here. For the weapon — the sword and such — of that aggressor, and my body: this pair, in the form of an assemblage, is the cause of suffering. Thus, given the existence of a sufficient cause, how could the effect not arise? Otherwise, that would simply not be its cause. And from something other than that [assemblage], would there be production? Therefore, if one becomes angry at one who brings a cause [of suffering], then anger toward oneself too is justified, since one also bears and brings the cause of suffering. The meaning is: if anger toward oneself is not [accepted], then toward another it is also not justified.

body.text: prakārāntareṇoktamevārthaṃ spaṣṭayannāha-
body.translated_text: Clarifying the same meaning in another way, he says —

children.translated_text: This boil in the shape of a body, unable to bear contact, has been taken up;

children.text: tṛṣṇāndhena mayā tatra vyathāyāṃ kutra kupyate // Bca_6.44 //
children.translated_text: blinded by craving, I — toward whom should one be angry when there is pain? // <s>Bca</s> 6.44 //

body.text: śarīrākṛtirayaṃ pakvagaṇḍo mayā gṛhītaḥ / sarvaduḥkhahetutvāt sarvopamardasahaḥ / ākoṭanatāḍanādibhirapyabhedyatvāt / duḥkhaparihārāya sukhaprāptaye ca yā tṛṣṇā abhilāṣaḥ, tadandhena pihitaprajñālocanena tasyāṃ vyathāyāṃ satyāṃ kutra kupyate? na hi gaṇḍasya kuḍyādisaṃparkaje duḥkhe kvacidvivekataḥ kopo yuktaḥ //
body.translated_text: This body-shaped ripe boil has been taken up by me — being the cause of all suffering, it is subject to every kind of affliction; because it cannot be split even by striking, beating, and such. Blinded by craving — by desire — with the eye of wisdom covered over, when that pain exists, toward whom should one be angry? For surely, in the suffering of a boil arising from contact with a wall and such, anger toward anything is not justified from the standpoint of discernment.

body.text: api ca / yaḥ kāryeṇānarthī, tena tatkāraṇameva parihartavyaṃ bhavet / ahaṃ tu viparyastamatiriti vimarśamupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, one who does not desire an effect should avoid its very cause; but I am of perverted understanding — showing this reflection, he says —

children.translated_text: I do not wish for suffering, yet foolishly I wish for the cause of suffering;
when suffering comes through my own fault, why be angry at another? // <s>Bca</s> 6.45 //

body.text: duḥkhaṃ daṇḍādyabhighātajaṃ necchāmi / tasya punaḥ kāraṇaṃ śarīraṃ pratyapakāriṇaṃ cecchāmi / bāliśa iti bāladharmo viparyāsaḥ / tasmātkāraṇāt svakāye yadduḥkhaṃ tat svāparādhāgatameva / iti kasmādanyatra tatsahakārimātre kupyate?
body.translated_text: I do not wish for suffering born from the blow of a stick and such; yet I desire its cause — the body — and the disposition to retaliate. 'Foolish' — the perversity characteristic of the childish. Therefore, the suffering in one's own body has come about through one's own fault. So why be angry at another, who is merely a contributing factor?

body.text: ātmavadhāya svayaṃ saṃskṛtaśastrasyaiva anyatra mama kopo na yukta ityāha-
body.translated_text: Showing that anger toward what was fashioned by oneself for one's own destruction is not justified toward another, he says —

children.translated_text: Just as the sword-leaf forest, just as the birds of hell —

children.text: matkarmajanitā eva tathedaṃ kutra kupyate // Bca_6.46 //
children.translated_text: these are generated by my own <s>karma</s> alone; toward whom then should one be angry? // <s>Bca</s> 6.46 //

body.text: asipatravanaṃ narakasamudbhavam / asaya eva patrāṇyasyeti kṛtvā / asigrahaṇaṃ prādhānyāt / anyadapi śastraṃ nārakaduḥkhaheturyantraṃ ca / vane tasminnivāsino gṛdhrolūkavāyasādayaḥ pakṣiṇo yathā matkarmajanitā eva duḥkhahetavo bhavanti / nānyadatra duḥkhakāraṇamasti / tathā idamapi paraśastrādikaṃ duḥkhaheturmatkarmajanitameva, iti kutra kupyate?
body.translated_text: The <s>Asipatravana</s> (Sword-leaf Forest) arises in hell — because swords themselves are its leaves, thus the name. The word 'sword' is used as representative; other weapons and instruments too are causes of hellish suffering. The birds dwelling in that forest — vultures, owls, crows, and such — just as they are produced by my own <s>karma</s>, they become causes of suffering. There is no other cause of suffering there. Likewise, this too — the suffering caused by the weapons and such of others — is produced by my own <s>karma</s> alone. So at whom does one become angry?

body.text: itthamapi viparyāsa evāyamityupadarśayitumāha-
body.translated_text: To show that even in this way, this is indeed a distortion, he says —

children.translated_text: Impelled by my own <s>karma</s>, those who harm me have arisen;

children.text: yena yāsyanti narakānmayaivāmī hatā nanu // Bca_6.47 //
children.translated_text: since by this they will go to the hells, is it not I who have destroyed them? // Bca_6.47 //

body.text: yena madīyena karmaṇā coditāḥ preritā eva mayi pūrvakṛtāpakāre apakāriṇo jātāḥ santo narakān yāsyanti, tena mayaivāmī apakāriṇo hatā nanu / svacittaṃ saṃbodhayati- na amībhirahaṃ hataḥ / ayamabhiprāyaḥ- yadi nākariṣyamahamīdṛśaṃ karma, tadā ete 'pi nāpakāriṇo 'bhaviṣyanniti matkṛtenaiva karmaṇā apakāriṇo bhavanti //
body.translated_text: Impelled — urged — by my own <s>karma</s>, those who harm me, [retaliating against] my previously committed offenses, having arisen and being such, will go to the hells; therefore is it not I indeed who have destroyed these harmers? He addresses his own mind: it is not they who have destroyed me. This is the intent: if I had not performed such <s>karma</s>, then these too would not have become harmers — thus it is by <s>karma</s> done by me alone that they become harmers.

body.text: upakāriṣveva mohādapakāribuddhirmameti kārikādvayena darśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Showing through two verses that one who is actually a benefactor is, through delusion, perceived as a harmer, he says —

children.text: etānāśritya me pāpaṃ kṣīyate kṣamato bahu /
children.translated_text: Relying on these [harmers], my evil is greatly diminished through patience;

children.text: māmāśritya tu yāntyete narakān dīrghavedanān // Bca_6.48 //
children.translated_text: but relying on me, they go to the hells of long-lasting pain. // Bca_6.48 //
It is I who harm them, and they who benefit me;
why, having reversed things, do you, O wicked mind, become angry? // Bca_6.49 //

body.text: etānapakāriṇa āśritya nimittīkṛtya mama pāpaṃ pūrvajanmakṛtaparāpakārajanitaṃ kṣīyate tadduḥkhānubhavanavipākena kṣayaṃ yāti / kṣamataḥ kṣāntimālambamānasya / bahu anekaparyāyeṇa kṛtam / māmāśritya matkarmacoditāḥ evamapyapakāraṃ kṛtvā punarete narakān tīvravedanān duḥsahaduḥkhānubhavān yānti / ata uktakrameṇa ahameva apakārī eṣāmityādi subodham //
body.translated_text: Relying on — taking as the occasion — these harmers, my evil — produced by harming others in previous lives — is diminished, goes to exhaustion through the ripening of experiencing that suffering. 'Through patience' — for one who relies on forbearance. 'Greatly' — [evil] committed in many ways. 'Relying on me' — impelled by my <s>karma</s>; even after having thus committed harm, these again go to the hells of intense pain, of unbearable suffering. Therefore, in the manner stated, 'it is I who harm them' — and so forth — this is easily understood.

body.text: nanu yadyapakārī bhavān, tarhi bhavata eva narakagamanamucitam, na tveṣāmityāha-
body.translated_text: Now, if you are the harmer, then it is appropriate for you yourself to go to hell, not for them — to this he says —

children.translated_text: If through the virtue of my intention I do not go to the hells,

children.text: eṣāmatra kimāyātaṃ yadyātmā rakṣito mayā // Bca_6.50 //
children.translated_text: what advantage is there for them if I protect myself? // Bca_6.50 //

body.text: yā pratyapakāranivṛttiniṣṭhā etanmamāśayamāhātmyaṃ narakagatinivṛttihetuḥ / narakān na yāmi tadātmāśayamāhātmyabalena / na tu punareṣāṃ durāśayatayā narakeṣu mamāpatanamiti bhāvaḥ / etadevāha- eṣāmityādinā / ayamatra samudāyārthaḥ- yadyahamapakārī sannapi kenacidupāyakauśalena narakān na yāmi, tadaiṣāmu[ma?]pakāriṇāṃ kimāyātam, kimapakṣīyate? kā kṣatirityarthaḥ / mayā tāvadekena rakṣitā na bhavantāmanye, rakṣita ātmā ca bhavet / na caitāvatā kiṃcideṣāṃ nyūnādhikaṃ guṇadoṣeṣu syāt //
body.translated_text: The greatness of intention that culminates in desisting from retaliation — this is the cause of the cessation of going to hell. I do not go to the hells by the power of that greatness of my own intention — but not because of their malicious intention do I not fall into the hells: this is the meaning. He states this very point with 'for them' and so forth. Here the combined meaning is: if I, though being a harmer, by some skillful means do not go to the hells, then what advantage have these harmers gained, what has diminished [for them]? What loss is there? — this is the meaning. By me alone being protected, not you others, my self alone would be protected. And even so, nothing in their virtues or faults would be increased or diminished.

body.text: nanu yadi nāma evam, tathāpi bhavato 'pi na yuktamātmarakṣaṇamupakārikṛtajñatayā ityāśaṅkayāha-
body.translated_text: Now, even if this is so, still it is not appropriate for you to protect yourself, out of gratitude to benefactors — anticipating this objection, he says —

children.text: atha pratyapakārī syāṃ tathāpyete na rakṣitāḥ /
children.translated_text: If I were to retaliate, even so they would not be protected;

children.text: hīyate cāpi me caryā tasmānnaṣṭāstapasvinaḥ // Bca_6.51 //
children.translated_text: and my conduct too would be impaired — therefore those wretched ones are lost. // Bca_6.51 //

body.text: yadi daṇḍādighātaṃ kurvatsu pratyapakārī bhaveyam, tathāpi ete rakṣitā na bhavanti / na kaścideṣāṃ pratīkāro narakagamanādiṣu kṛtaḥ syāt / pratyuta tāḍitenāpi mayā na pratitāḍitavyam / tathā sarvasattveṣu na maitracittaṃ mayā niści[kṣepta?]tavyam / antaśo na dagdhasthūṇāyāmapi pratighacittamutpādayitavyam / ityāderbodhisattvacaryāyā mama hānireva syāt / tasmādetarhi pratīkāropāyābhāvāttapasvino varākā rakśitumaśakyatvānnaṣṭā durgatipatitā eva / ityupekṣyante tāvadidānīm / paścāttadupāyamadhigamya tatkariṣyāmi yathaiṣāṃ duḥkhamaṇumātrakamapi na syāt //
body.translated_text: If, when they inflict blows with sticks and such, I were to retaliate, even so they would not be protected — no remedy for them in going to hell and such would have been accomplished. On the contrary, even when struck, I should not strike back. Likewise, I should not cast away my loving mind toward all beings. At the very least, I should not generate a mind of hostility even toward a burnt post — and so forth. Thus my <s>Bodhisattva</s> conduct would only be impaired. Therefore, since there is no means of remedy at this time, these wretched unfortunate ones, unable to be saved, are lost — fallen into lower realms. Thus they are left aside for now. Later, having attained the means, I shall do what ensures that not even the slightest suffering befalls them.

body.text: tadevaṃ parāpakāramarṣaṇakṣāntiṃ pratipādya adhunā dharmanidhyānakṣāntimupadarśayitumāha-
body.translated_text: Having thus established the patience of enduring harm from others, now to demonstrate the patience of contemplating <s>dharma</s>, he says —

children.translated_text: The mind, being immaterial, cannot be destroyed by anyone anywhere;
but through attachment to the body, the mind is afflicted by suffering. // Bca_6.52 //

body.text: dvividhaṃ duḥkhamavicārato bādhakamupajāyate kāyikaṃ mānasikaṃ ceti / tatra manasi na kaściddaṇḍādikaṃ dātuṃ śaktaḥ, amūrtatvānmanasaḥ / iti tadudbhavaṃ duḥkhaṃ paramārthato na saṃbhavati / kalpanākṛtaṃ tu daurmanasyādikaṃ vidyate / etadeva darśayati śarīretyādinā / mamedaṃ śarīramiti vikalpābhyāsavāsanāvaśāt kāyaduḥkhena cittaṃ vihanyate //
body.translated_text: Two kinds of suffering arise as afflictions when not examined: physical and mental. There, no one is able to inflict blows and such upon the mind, because of the mind's immateriality. Therefore suffering arising from it does not ultimately occur. But conceptually constructed [suffering] such as mental distress exists. He shows this very point with 'body' and so forth. Through the force of habitual tendencies from the repeated conceptualization 'this body is mine,' the mind is distressed by bodily suffering.

body.text: tatrāpi pratiniyatameva duḥkhakāraṇamityāha-
body.translated_text: Even there, the cause of suffering is specifically determined — he says —

children.translated_text: Contempt, harsh words, and disrepute — this group

children.text: kāyaṃ na bādhate tena cetaḥ kasmātprakupyasi // Bca_6.53 //
children.translated_text: does not harm the body; why then, O mind, do you become angry? // Bca_6.53 //

body.text: nyakkārādigaṇaḥ samūhaḥ kāyasya duḥkhaheturna bhavati / na hi kāyasyāyaṃ kaṃcidupaghātaṃ karotīti yena, tena cetaḥ kasmāddhetoḥ prakupyasi?
body.translated_text: The group — the collection — of contempt and such does not become a cause of suffering for the body. For this does not inflict any injury on the body, so why, for what reason, does the mind become angry?

body.text: athāpi syāt- yadi nāma nyakkārādayaḥ kāyasya bādhakā na bhavanti, tathāpi tacchrutvā mayi lokānāmaprasannaṃ cittamutpadyate, iti mayā neṣyate ityāśaṅkayāha-
body.translated_text: One might think: even if contempt and such do not harm the body, still, upon hearing them, an unfavorable attitude toward me arises in people, and this is undesirable to me — anticipating this objection, he says —

children.text: mayyaprasādo yo 'nyeṣāṃ sa māṃ kiṃ bhakṣayiṣyati /
children.translated_text: The displeasure of others toward me — will it devour me,

children.text: iha janmāntare vāpi yenāsau me 'nabhīpsitaḥ // Bca_6.54 //
children.translated_text: in this life or in another, such that it is undesirable to me? // Bca_6.54 //

body.text: bhavatu nāma evam, tathāpi vicāraṇīyameva / mayi nyakkārādiśravaṇād yo 'yamaprasādo janānām, sa kiṃ māṃ bhakṣayiṣyati ihaloke paraloka vā, yenāsau lokāprasādo mamāpriyaḥ, iti vicārya na kartavyo 'trābhiniveśaḥ //
body.translated_text: Let it be so; still, it must be examined. This displeasure of people arising from hearing contempt and such directed at me — will it devour me in this world or the next, such that this displeasure of people is disagreeable to me? Having reflected thus, one should not form attachment in this matter.

body.text: asti vā atrābhiniveśakāraṇaṃ lābhavighāto nāmetyāha-
body.translated_text: Or is there a reason for attachment in this, namely the obstruction of gain? — he says —

children.translated_text: If it is undesirable to me because it obstructs gain,

children.text: naṅkṣyatīhaiva me lābhaḥ pāpaṃ tu sthāsyati dhruvam // Bca_6.55 //
children.translated_text: my gain will perish right here, but the evil will surely remain. // Bca_6.55 //

body.text: tathāhi nyakkārādiśravaṇādaprasādo lokānām, tasmācca lābhopanāmanavaimukhyam / tato 'sau nyakkārādigaṇo mamāniṣṭa iti cet, tadayuktam / naṅkṣyati vinaśvaradharmatayā apagamiṣyati / ihaiva pratiniyataireva dinairmama lābhaḥ / na tu paralokānubandhī bhaviṣyati / tannimittaṃ nyakkārādikartṛṣu krudhyato yatpāpaṃ tadeva paraṃ sthāsyati paralokānubandhi bhaviṣyati / dhruvamiti aparimukte tatphale tasyāvināśāt //
body.translated_text: For indeed, from hearing contempt and such there is displeasure of people, and from that an aversion to offering gifts. If therefore this group of contempt and such is undesirable to me — that is wrong. 'Will perish' — by its nature of being perishable, it will pass away. Right here — within a determinate number of days — my gain [will perish]. It will not follow me to the next life. But the evil of becoming angry at those who inflict contempt and such — that alone will remain, will follow to the next life. 'Surely' — because of the inescapability of its fruit, being its non-release.

body.text: idamapi cātrālocanīyam-
body.translated_text: This too should be considered here —

children.translated_text: Better for me to die today than to live long through wrong livelihood;

children.text: yasmācciramapi sthitvā mṛtyuduḥkhaṃ tadeva me // Bca_6.56 //
children.translated_text: for even after living long, the suffering of death is the same for me. // Bca_6.56 //

body.text: idameva varaṃ śreṣṭhaṃ yallābhābhāvādasminnevāhani me maraṇamastu, na tu punaḥ parāpakāradvāreṇa lābhapratilambhānmithyājīvitaṃ ciraṃ dīrghakālam / kutaḥ? yasmādvahutarakālamapi jīvitvā maraṇāntaṃ hi jīvitam ityavaśyaṃbhāvino mṛtyorduḥkhaṃ tadeva mama / yatpaścādvarṣaśatātyaye bhaviṣyati, tadevedānīṃ mama mriyamāṇasya iti cirajīviteṣvaviśeṣaḥ //
body.translated_text: This alone is better, preferable: that due to the absence of gain, let death come to me on this very day, rather than living long — for a long time — through wrong livelihood by means of retaliating against others' offenses in order to obtain gain. Why? Because even after living for a very long time, since 'life ends in death,' and death is inevitable, the suffering of death is the same for me. What will occur after the passage of a hundred years — that very same [suffering] is mine now as I die. Thus there is no difference in [the case of] long lives.

body.text: ito 'pyaviśeṣa eveti ślokadvayena darśayannāha-
body.translated_text: There is no difference from this perspective either — showing through two verses, he says —

children.text: svapne varṣaśataṃ saukhyaṃ bhuktvā yaśca vibudhyate /
children.translated_text: One who enjoys happiness in a dream for a hundred years and then awakens,

children.text: muhūrtamaparo yaśca sukhī bhūtvā vibudhyate // Bca_6.57 //
children.translated_text: and another who, having been happy for a moment, then awakens — // Bca_6.57 //
does not the happiness cease for both upon awakening?
The same simile [applies] at the time of death to the long-lived and the short-lived. // Bca_6.58 //

body.text: yathā kaścitsvapnopalabdhaṃ varṣaśataṃ sukhamupabhujya vibudhyate, anyaḥ punaḥ kṣaṇamātram / sa tāvanmātreṇa sukhinamātmānaṃ manyate / anayordvayorapi svapnopalabdhopabhuktasukhayoḥ prativibuddhayoḥ satoḥ tadupalabdhaṃ vinaṣṭaṃ sukhaṃ na nivartate, jāgradavasthāyāṃ nānuvartate, smaraṇamātrāvaśeṣatvāt / saivopamā svapnopalabdhasukhayoriva puruṣayormṛtyukāle maraṇasamaye cirajīvino 'lpajīvinaśca / nanu nivartate saukhyamiti svārthe 'pyaṇ / ityalaṃ mithyājīvitena //
body.translated_text: Just as someone, having enjoyed happiness obtained in a dream for a hundred years, awakens, while another [enjoys] for only a moment — he considers himself happy with just that much — for both of these, upon awakening, the happiness obtained in the dream does not return, does not continue in the waking state, since only a memory remains. The same simile [applies]: just as for the two men with dream-obtained happiness, so at the time of death, at the moment of dying, for the long-lived and the short-lived. 'Does not the happiness cease' — the reflexive suffix is used in its own sense. Thus, enough with wrong livelihood!

body.text: asmādapi lābhālābhayorna kaścidviśeṣa ityupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Showing that even from this [perspective] there is no difference between gain and non-gain, he says —

children.text: labdhvāpi ca bahūṃllābhān ciraṃ bhuktvā sukhānyapi /
children.translated_text: Even having obtained many gains and having enjoyed pleasures for a long time,

children.text: riktahastaśca nagraśca yāsyāmi muṣito yathā // Bca_6.59 //
children.translated_text: I shall go empty-handed and naked, as if robbed. // Bca_6.59 //

body.text: pracurataralābhān labdhvāpi samāsādya, cirakālamupabhujya sukhānyapi, punarmṛtyumadhigamya riktahastaśca tucchahastaḥ / na tasmāllābhādīṣadapi pātheyaṃ gṛhītam / nāpi sukhāt kiṃcit pariśiṣṭamavasthitam / kaṭisūtrakamātramapi na pariśeṣitamiti nagnaśca cauraiḥ parimuṣita iva asmāllokātparaṃ lokaṃ yāsyāmi //
body.translated_text: Even having obtained — having acquired — very abundant gains, and having enjoyed pleasures for a long time, then upon reaching death, empty-handed — with vacant hands; not even the slightest provision has been taken from those gains; nor has any remnant of happiness remained; not even as much as a waist-cord has been left — and naked, as if robbed by thieves, I shall go from this world to the next.

body.text: syādetat- astyeva viśeṣo lābhasya cīvarādīnāmanupaghātādāyuḥsaṃskārāṇāmupastambhācciratarakālaṃ jīvitaṃ syāt / tataśca pūrvakṛtapāpasya vidūṣaṇāsamudācārādinā parikṣayaṃ śikṣāsaṃvaraparirakṣaṇena bodhicittasevanādinā ca kuśalapakṣasya ca vṛddhiṃ kuryām / yaduktam-
body.translated_text: One might say: there is indeed an advantage to gain, for through the non-destruction of requisites such as robes and so forth, and through the support of life-sustaining forces, one could live for a longer time. And thereby I could accomplish the exhaustion of previously committed evil through the practice of censure and such, and the increase of the wholesome side through guarding the training-vow, cultivating <s>bodhicitta</s>, and such. As stated —

body.text: yāvacciraṃ jīvati dharmacārī tāvatprasūte kuśalapravāham //
body.translated_text: 'As long as one who practices <s>dharma</s> lives, so long does one produce a stream of virtue.'

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: ato lābhāntarāyakāriṇi yukta eva pradveṣa ityāśaṅkayannāha-
body.translated_text: Therefore, hatred toward one who obstructs gain is indeed justified — anticipating this objection, he says —

body.text: pāpakṣayaṃ ca puṇyaṃ ca lābhājjīvan karomi cet /
body.translated_text: If, living from gain, I accomplish the exhaustion of evil and merit —

body.text: lābhāduktakrameṇa jīvan dhriyamāṇaḥ pāpakṣayaṃ ca puṇyaṃ ca karomītyādi manyase / nanu etaditaḥ samadhikaṃ doṣamapaśyatā abhidhīyata ityāha-
body.translated_text: 'Living from gain' — being sustained — 'I accomplish the exhaustion of evil and merit' — thus you think. But surely this is stated by one who sees an even greater fault herein — he says —

body.text: puṇyakṣayaśca pāpaṃ ca lābhārthaṃ krudhyato nanu // Bca_6.60 //
body.translated_text: is there not exhaustion of merit and evil for one who becomes angry for the sake of gain? // Bca_6.60 //

body.text: lābhārthaṃ lābhanimittaṃ tadantarāyakāriṇi dveṣaṃ kurvataḥ sukṛtakṣaya evopajāyate / yaduktam- sarvametatsucaritam [6.1] ityādinā / ayaṃ tu viśeṣaḥ- akṣāntisamudbhavasya pāpasya rāśirabhivardhate //
body.translated_text: For one who, for the sake of gain — on account of gain — generates hatred toward one who obstructs it, the exhaustion of merit alone arises. As stated: 'All this good conduct' [6.1] and so forth. But here is the distinction: the mass of evil born from impatience increases.

body.text: athāpi syāt- yathākathaṃcit tāvaccirakālaṃ lābhājjīvitaṃ syāt / tāvataiva naḥ prayojanamityāha-
body.translated_text: One might further think: in any case, let there be a long life from gain; that alone is our purpose — to this he says —

children.translated_text: If the very purpose for which I live is itself destroyed,
what is the use of that life which only produces evil? // Bca_6.61 //

body.text: na khalu bodhisattvasya itarasattvavajjīvitaṃ niṣprayojanamevābhilaṣitam, kiṃ tarhi saṃbhārābhisaṃvardhanārthaṃ pāpakṣayārthaṃ ca / tad yadi sukṛtakṣayanimittameva tat syāt, tadā kiṃ tena tādṛśena jīvitenāpi kevalāśubhakarmakaraṇaśīlena? ninditameva taditi bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: A <s>Bodhisattva</s> does not desire life purposelessly like other beings; rather, it is for the purpose of increasing the accumulations and exhausting evil. If that [life] were to become the very cause of exhausting merit, then what use is such a life that is habitually engaged only in unwholesome action? Such [a life] is indeed to be condemned — this is the meaning.

body.text: syādetat- na lābhāntarāyakāritayā mamāvarṇavādini pratighacittamutpadyate, kiṃ tu guṇapracchādanādikarmaṇā, duḥkhahetutvādityāha-
body.translated_text: One might say: it is not because of obstructing gain that a mind of hostility arises toward one who speaks ill of me, but rather because of the act of concealing [my] virtues and such, since it is a cause of suffering — to this he says —

children.translated_text: If [you say] hatred toward one who speaks ill of you destroys [his merit and harms] beings,

children.text: parāyaśaskare 'pyevaṃ kopaste kiṃ na jāyate // Bca_6.62 //
children.translated_text: why does your anger not likewise arise toward one who disgraces another? // Bca_6.62 //

body.text: ayaśobhidhāyini yo 'yaṃ bhavato vidveṣaḥ, so 'varṇavādī doṣāviṣkaraṇādguṇapracchādanācca tvāṃ nāśayati / iti matvā cedyadi tannimittakaḥ / athavā / sattvān lokānnāśayati / avarṇavādena mayi nigrāhayati / svayamaprasannacittasteṣāmapi cittamaprasādayatītyarthaḥ / iti avarṇavādini dveṣaścet, ucyate / tadā yo 'pi pareṣāmanyasattvānāmayaśaḥ prakāśayati, tatrāpi kopaste kiṃ na jāyate? so 'pi ca avarṇavādī sattvānnāśayati / tadasminnapi yuktarūpa eva kopaḥ //
body.translated_text: This hostility of yours, which speaks of disrepute — the one who speaks ill, by revealing faults and concealing virtues, destroys you — if, having thought thus, [your hatred] is caused by that. Or alternatively: he destroys beings, people, through speaking ill. By speaking ill of me, he causes [others] to reject me. Being himself of displeased mind, he causes their minds also to be displeased — this is the meaning. If there is hatred toward one who speaks ill, it is said: then does your anger not also arise toward one who reveals the disrepute of other beings? For he too, speaking ill, destroys beings. Therefore, anger would be entirely justified toward him as well.

body.text: atrottaramāśaṅkayannāha-
body.translated_text: Anticipating an objection to this, he says:

body.text: parāyattāprasādatvādaprasādiṣu te kṣamā /
body.translated_text: Since displeasure depends on others, you are patient toward those who are displeased;

body.text: pareṣu anyeṣu sattveṣu āyatta āśrito 'prasādo 'sya / anyasattvān viṣayīkṛtya samutpanna iti / tasya bhāvastattvaṃ tasmāt / parāśritāprasādattvādaprasādiṣu aprasannacitteṣu avarṇavādiṣu tava kṣamā kṣāntirūtpadyate / ātmacittameva pṛcchati / atrāha-
body.translated_text: The displeasure of others depends on, relies upon, other beings — it arises having taken other beings as its object. The state of that is its nature; therefore, 'since displeasure depends on others,' toward those who are displeased — those of displeased minds, those who speak ill — your patience, your <s>kṣānti</s> (forbearance), arises. He questions his own mind. To this he says:

body.text: kleśotpādaparāyatte kṣamā nāvarṇavādini // Bca_6.63 //
body.translated_text: Why is there no patience toward one who speaks ill, who is subject to the arising of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions)? // Bca_6.63 //

body.text: yadi yaḥ parāyattāprasādaḥ tatra kṣamā bhavato bhavati, tadā svasminnavarṇavādini kiṃ na kṣamā? kiṃrūpe? kleśotpādanaparāyatte kleśānāmutpādaparatantre / parāyattāprasādatvaṃ kṣamāhetuḥ tulyamubhayatrāpi ityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: If you have patience toward one whose displeasure depends on others, then why is there no patience toward one who speaks ill of you? Of what kind? One who is subject to the arising of <s>kleśas</s> — one who is dependent on the production of afflictions. The fact that displeasure depends on others is equally the cause of patience in both cases — this is the meaning.

body.text: pratimādyupaghātakāriṣu śraddhāvaśādapi pratighacittaṃ notpādayitavyamityāha-
body.translated_text: Even toward those who damage images and such, one should not produce a mind of hostility, even out of the force of faith — he says:

children.translated_text: Toward those who destroy or revile images, <s>stūpas</s>, and the true <s>Dharma</s>,

children.text: na yujyate mama dveṣo buddhādīnāṃ na hi vyathā // Bca_6.64 //
children.translated_text: my hatred is not justified, for the <s>Buddhas</s> and others have no distress. // Bca_6.64 //

body.text: nāśakā vikopayitāraḥ / ākrośakā doṣabuddhayā vairūpyābhidhāyinaḥ / teṣu na yukto mama dveṣaḥ / kutaḥ? yasmādbuddhādīnāṃ bodhisattvāryaśrāvakapratyekabuddhānāṃ vitathābhiniveśaprasūtātmagrāhanivṛtterabhiṣvaṅgābhāvānna vyathā cittapīḍālakṣaṇaṃ daurmanasyaṃ nāsti / iti bhāvaḥ / ataḥ pratimāvināśakeṣu dveṣacittaṃ notpādayitavyam / tathā viruddhadharmakāriṣu karuṇaiva tu yujyate teṣu sādhūnām / anyathā tatra viśeṣābhāvāt pāpameva kevalamupajāyate / yadi punardharmato nivārayituṃ śakyate, tadā na doṣaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Destroyers' are those who damage. 'Revilers' are those who, with the perception of faults, speak of deformities. Toward them my hatred is not justified. Why? Because for the <s>Buddhas</s> and others — <s>Bodhisattvas</s>, noble <s>Śrāvakas</s>, and <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s> — since the self-grasping born from false attachment has ceased and there is no clinging, there is no distress — no mental anguish characterized by mental affliction. This is the meaning. Therefore, toward those who destroy images, a mind of hatred should not be produced. Likewise, toward those who act contrary to the <s>Dharma</s>, compassion alone is appropriate from the virtuous. Otherwise, in the absence of any distinction in that regard, only evil would arise. If, however, it is possible to restrain them through the <s>Dharma</s>, then there is no fault.

body.text: yadapi ca dharmakāmatayā gurumātāpitrādyupaghātakāriṣu dveṣacittamutpadyate, tadapi vinivāryamevetyāha-
body.translated_text: And even the mind of hatred that arises from love of the <s>Dharma</s> toward those who harm one's teacher, mother, father, and such — even that should be restrained — he says:

children.translated_text: Toward those who harm one's teacher, blood-relatives, and dear ones,
seeing the arising from conditions as before, one should restrain anger. // Bca_6.65 //

body.text: guravo dharmamārgopadeṣṭāro 'kuśalapakṣanivartayitāraḥ / sālohitāḥ sodarāḥ / anye 'pi jñātisagotrabāndhavādayaḥ / teṣāmapakāriṣu / tathā priyāṇāṃ premasthānānāṃ cāpakāriṣu kopaṃ nivārayediti saṃbandhaḥ / katham? pūrvavatpratyayotpādaṃ dṛṣṭvā / yaduktam- ye kecidaparādhāśca ityādinā / ataḥ sarve 'pyamī pūrvakarmopajanitameva phalamupabhuñjate / nātra kaścit pratīkāraheturasti / tadanena yathā aparasamaye devagurudvijātimātāpitṛprabhṛtīnāmarthe pāpaṃ kurvato 'pi na doṣa iti matam, na tathā ihābhimatamityuktaṃ bhavati //
body.translated_text: Teachers are those who instruct in the path of <s>Dharma</s> and turn one away from the unwholesome. 'Blood-relatives' (<s>sālohita</s>) are those of the same womb. And others such as kinsmen, clansmen, and relations. Toward those who harm them; and likewise toward those who harm one's dear ones — the objects of love — one should restrain anger: this is the connection. How? 'Seeing the arising from conditions as before' — as was stated: 'Whatever offenses there are...' and so forth. Therefore, all these [beings] are experiencing only the fruit produced by prior <s>karma</s>. There is no cause for retaliation here. By this it is stated that the view held by some — that even when committing evil for the sake of deities, teachers, twice-born, mothers, fathers, and such, there is no fault — is not the view accepted here.

body.text: kiṃ ca / idamapi vastutattvaṃ manasi kurvatā na sattveṣu cittaṃ dūṣayitavyamityāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, keeping in mind even the true nature of reality, one should not corrupt the mind toward beings — he says:

children.translated_text: Suffering for embodied beings is certain, whether caused by the sentient or the insentient;

children.text: sā vyathā cetane dṛṣṭā kṣamasvaināṃ vyathāmataḥ // Bca_6.66 //
children.translated_text: that suffering is observed in the sentient [body] — therefore endure this suffering. // Bca_6.66 //

body.text: samastakāryasya anvayavyatirekābhyāṃ janakatvenāvadhāritaṃ sāmagrīlakṣaṇaṃ kāraṇam / sā ca sāmagrī vastudharmatayā kācit kvacit samarthasvabhāvā / tatra cetanena kṛtā hastapādādiprahāreṇa / acetanena daṇḍaśastrarogādinā / tatrāpi cetanāvadvayāpāro 'styeva / sākṣāt pāraṃparyakṛtastu viśeṣaḥ / svayameva yadṛcchayā vā loṣṭakuḍyādyabhighātajanitā vā dehināṃ śarīriṇāṃ niyatā vyathā niyamena samutpadyate / nānyadito vyathākāraṇamasti / sā caivaṃ dvividhakāraṇasāmagrīprasūtāpi cetane savijñānake kāye dṛṣṭā pramāṇapariniścitā / atastadeva tadutpattisthānaṃ nānyat / acetane / vedanāyogāt / tato yad yasyotpattisthānaṃ tat tatraiva bhavati nānyatra, yathā paṅke paṅkajaṃ na sthale / ataḥ asmānyāyāt kṣamasva sahasva enāmanantarakathitobhayarūpāṃ vyathām //
body.translated_text: The cause, characterized as an assemblage, has been ascertained as the producer of every effect through the methods of agreement and difference. And that assemblage, by the nature of things, has a certain capacity somewhere regarding something. Therein, [suffering] caused by the sentient is through blows of hands, feet, and such; by the insentient, through sticks, weapons, diseases, and such. Even in the latter case, there is indeed the operation of a sentient being — the distinction is between direct and indirect causation. [Suffering] generated spontaneously, by chance, or produced by impact with clods, walls, and such — suffering for embodied beings, for those with bodies, is certain — it arises by necessity. There is no other cause of suffering. And that [suffering], though born from the assemblage of these two kinds of causes, is observed — ascertained by valid cognition — in the sentient, in the body possessed of consciousness. Therefore, that alone is its locus of arising, not anything else — not in the insentient, due to the impossibility of sensation. Therefore, that which is the locus of arising of something exists only there, not elsewhere — just as a lotus [arises] in mud, not on dry ground. Therefore, by this reasoning, endure — bear with — this suffering of both kinds just described.

children.text: tadānīmubhayorapi sādhāraṇadūṣaṇatayā kvacidapi kopo na yukta iti kathayitumāha-
children.translated_text: In order to say that since the fault is common to both [parties], anger toward either is not justified, he says:
Some offend out of delusion; others, deluded, become angry;

children.text: brūmaḥ kameṣu nirdoṣaṃ kaṃ vā brūmo 'parādhinam // Bca_6.67 //
children.translated_text: whom among these shall we call faultless, and whom shall we call the offender? // Bca_6.67 //

body.text: ātmātmīyagrāhābhiniveśaviparyāsādeke kecidaparādhyanti daṇḍādinā / samākrośādi vā vadantaḥ sadoṣamātmānaṃ kurvanti / anye punastadaparādhena kupyanti / vimohitā mohādeva svakṛtakarmaphalasaṃbandhamananusaranto 'vidyāvaraṇāt, pratitāḍanākrośādikamārabhante / itthaṃ brūmaḥ- kam eṣu kleśarākṣasāveśavaśīkṛteṣu nirdoṣam, kaṃ vā brūmo 'parādhinam? ubhayeṣāmapi sādhāraṇadoṣatvāt //
body.translated_text: Some, due to the perversion of grasping at self and what belongs to self, offend through blows with sticks and such, or by uttering abuse and such make themselves faulty. Others in turn become angry at that offense. Deluded — through delusion itself, through the obscuration of ignorance, not following the connection between one's own <s>karma</s> and its fruit — they undertake retaliation through striking, abuse, and such. Thus we ask: whom among these, who are under the power of possession by the demon of afflictions, shall we call faultless, and whom shall we call the offender? Since the fault is common to both.

body.text: idamapi ca ātmagatameva cintayatā pratighacittaṃ nivartayitavyamityāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, even this — reflecting on what pertains to oneself — one should restrain the mind of hostility, he says:

children.text: kasmādevaṃ kṛtaṃ pūrvaṃ yenaivaṃ bādhyase paraiḥ /
children.translated_text: Why was this done previously, such that you are now harmed by others?
All are subject to <s>karma</s> — who am I to alter this? // Bca_6.68 //

body.text: kasmātkāraṇāt kimityevam etatphalaṃ hetukarma kṛtam / yeneti lokoktireṣā yadityasyārthe / yadevam / yadi vā yena karmasāmarthyena hetunā / ākrośabandhanatāḍanādibhiḥ bādhyase pīḍyase parairanyaiḥ / nanu yadi nāma evam, tathāpi pratīkāro yukta ityāha- sarva ityādi / sarve duḥkhahetavaḥ karmapratyayopajanitapravṛttayaḥ iti ko 'hamatra anyathākṛtau tatphalanivartanāya? na kaścit / phaladānonmukhasya karmaṇaḥ kenacinnivartayitumaśakyatvāt //
body.translated_text: For what reason — why — was this causal <s>karma</s> whose fruit is thus done? 'By which' — this is a colloquial expression in the sense of 'that.' That is, in this way. Or alternatively, by which power of <s>karma</s> — by which cause — you are harmed, afflicted by others. But even if this is so, surely retaliation is justified — to this he says: 'All' and so forth. All causes of suffering have their activity produced by <s>karma</s> and conditions — so who am I to alter that — to avert its fruit? No one. Because <s>karma</s> that is ready to yield its fruit cannot be averted by anyone.

body.text: idaṃ punaratra yuktarūpamityāha-
body.translated_text: What is appropriate here, then — he says:

children.text: evaṃ buddhvā tu puṇyeṣu tathā yatnaṃ karomyaham /
children.translated_text: Having understood thus, I shall make effort toward merit,

children.text: yena sarve bhaviṣyanti maitracittāḥ parasparam // Bca_6.69 //
children.translated_text: so that all will become of loving mind toward one another. // Bca_6.69 //

body.text: ete sattvāḥ karmakleśaparāyattāḥ parasparamasamañjasakarmakāriṇo nivartayitumaśakyā iti / evaṃ buddhvā jñātvā punaḥ puṇyeṣu kuśaleṣu karmasu tathā yatnaṃ karomyaham, tena prakāreṇa vīryaṃ samārabhe, yena tathāvidhaṃ sāmarthyaṃ pratilabhya sanmārge pravartitāḥ santaḥ sarve maitracittā hitasukhavidhānatatparāḥ parasparamanyonyaṃ bhaviṣyanti //
body.translated_text: These beings, subject to <s>karma</s> and <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), performing improper actions toward one another, cannot be restrained. Having understood this, having known it, I shall then make effort toward meritorious, wholesome <s>karmas</s> — in that manner I shall arouse vigor — so that, having attained such capacity and having been set upon the right path, all will become of loving mind — devoted to providing benefit and happiness — toward one another.

body.text: drohacittaṃ vinivartya priyavastūpaghātakāriṇi laukikodāharaṇena dveṣaṃ nivartayediti ślokadvayamupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Having turned away the mind of malice, in order to avert hatred toward that which damages what is dear, he presents two verses by way of a worldly illustration, saying:

children.translated_text: Just as when a house is burning, fire, having gone to another house,
is [about to] catch upon grass and such where it would adhere — that [fuel] is pulled out and removed.
Likewise, when the mind is burned by the fire of hatred due to attachment,
at that very moment that [attachment] should be relinquished, from fear of conflagration of the substance of merit. // Bca_6.71 //

body.text: ekasmin gṛhe 'gninā dahyamāne yathā tasmād gṛhādanyad gṛhaṃ gṛhāntaraṃ gatvā / agniryatra tṛṇakāṣṭhādau sajjate lagati, tadantargatamanyadapi vastu mā dhākṣīditi śaṅkayā tadākṛṣyāpanīyate, pṛthak kṛtvā nirdhāryate, iti dṛṣṭakramaṃ prakṛte 'pi yojayannāha / evamuktodāharaṇanyāyena cittaṃ mano yasya vastuna āsaṅgādāsakto dahyate paritapyate dveṣavahninā pratighānalena tadāsaṅgasthānaṃ vastu tatkṣaṇaṃ na kālāntarapalimbena parityājyaṃ tatrābhiniveśaḥ parihartavyaḥ / kiṃ kāraṇam? puṇyasyātmā śarīram / puṇyaskandha iti yāvat / tasya uktakrameṇa uddāhaḥ parikṣayo mā bhūt / anyathā gṛhāntargatapadārthavat pradveṣavahniḥ tamapi dahet //
body.translated_text: When one house is being burned by fire, just as from that house, having gone to another house — a different dwelling — the fire, where it catches upon grass, wood, and such — where it adheres — that [fuel], and also other things inside it, fearing lest it too be consumed, is pulled out and removed — separated and taken out. Applying this observed sequence to the present case as well, he says: in the same manner, by the principle of the illustration just stated, when the mind — the mental [faculty] — due to attachment to some object, is burned — tormented — by the fire of hatred, by the flame of hostility, then that object of attachment should be relinquished at that very moment — not by procrastinating to another time — the fixation upon it should be abandoned. For what reason? The body — the substance — of merit, the mass of merit: lest there be its conflagration, its destruction, in the manner described. Otherwise, like objects inside a house, the fire of enmity would burn even that.

body.text: api ca / lābha evāyaṃ labdhaḥ, yanmanuṣyaduḥkhairnarakaphalaṃ karma vipacyate iti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, this is actually a gain obtained — that hellish <s>karma</s> ripens through human suffering — establishing this, he says:

children.translated_text: If one condemned to death is freed by having a hand cut off — is that not fortunate?
If one is freed from the hells through human sufferings — is that not fortunate? // Bca_6.72 //

body.text: yo hi māraṇamarhati, sa yadi hastamātraṃ chittvā mucyate, tadā na kācit kṣatirasya / pratyuta labdhalābhamātmānaṃ manyate atyalpamidaṃ maraṇaduḥkhāt karacchedanaduḥkhamiti / tathā yo 'pi manuṣyaduḥkhaṃ tāḍanabandhanatiraskārādikṛtamanubhūya narakaduḥkhādvimukto bhavati, tasyāpi na kiṃcidapacīyate / na kiṃcididaṃ duḥkhaṃ narakaduḥkhāt, sukhameva tat / tato yadi vicakṣaṇaḥ syāt, tadā saumanasyamevātra yuktamasya //
body.translated_text: For one who deserves death, if he is freed by cutting off merely a hand, then there is no loss for him. On the contrary, he considers himself as having gained a profit — 'this suffering of having a hand cut off is very slight compared to the suffering of death.' Likewise, one who, having experienced human suffering — beatings, bondage, humiliation, and such — is freed from the suffering of the hells, for him too nothing is diminished. This suffering is nothing compared to hellish suffering — it is actually happiness. Therefore, if one is discerning, cheerfulness alone is appropriate here.

body.text: athāpi syāt- na mayā svalpamātre 'pi duḥkhe kṣamā kartuṃ śakyata iti, atrāha-
body.translated_text: But one might say: I cannot endure even the slightest suffering — to this he says:

children.translated_text: If even this much suffering today cannot be endured,
then why is anger — the cause of hellish torment — not restrained? // Bca_6.73 //

body.text: khaṭacapeṭaloṣṭādiprahārakṛtamīṣanmātramapi duḥkhamidānīṃ soḍhuṃ marṣituṃ na pāryate na śakyate / tadatra bhavantaṃ pṛcchāmaḥ- yadi evameva, tadayaṃ nārakaduḥkhasaṃvartanīyaḥ krodhaḥ kopaḥ kasmātkāraṇānna vāryate? ayameva hi atitarāṃ narakeṣu duḥkhadāyaka iti duḥkhabhīrūṇāmeva krodhaṃ nivartayituṃ yuktaṃ syāt //
body.translated_text: The suffering caused by blows with boards, slaps, clods, and such — suffering that is merely slight — cannot now be endured or tolerated. Then we ask you this: if indeed it is so, then why is this anger — this rage, which leads to hellish suffering — not restrained? For this very [anger] is what causes suffering excessively in the hells. Therefore, it would be proper for those who fear suffering to restrain anger.

body.text: kiṃ ca / yadyapi soḍhuṃ na śakyate, tathāpi taddhetukakarmasaṃbhavādanicchato 'pi duḥkhamāpatiṣyati bhavataḥ / na ca kiṃcitphalamutpatsyate / marṣaṇāt punastasya mahārthalābho bhaviṣyatīti vṛttadvayena śikṣayitumāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, even if it cannot be endured, suffering will befall you even unwillingly due to the <s>karma</s> caused by it, and no fruit [of benefit] will arise [from anger]. But from forbearance, a great gain will come — instructing through two verses, he says:

body.text: kopārthamevamevāhaṃ narakeṣu sahasraśaḥ /
body.translated_text: For the sake of anger, in just this way, I have been made to suffer in the hells thousands of times,

body.text: kārito 'smi na cātmārthaḥ parārtho vā kṛto mayā // Bca_6.74 //
body.translated_text: yet I have accomplished neither my own purpose nor the purpose of others. // Bca_6.74 //

children.text: na cedaṃ tādṛśaṃ duḥkhaṃ mahārthaṃ ca kariṣyati /
children.translated_text: This [present suffering] is not of such [magnitude], and it will accomplish a great purpose;
in suffering that removes the suffering of the world, joy alone is appropriate here. // Bca_6.75 //

body.text: kopanimittameva / evameva niṣphalameva / narakeṣu saṃjīvādiṣu / sahasraśaḥ anekavāram / ahaṃ kāritaḥ chedanabhedanapāṭanādikāraṇābhiḥ pīḍitaḥ / evaṃ duḥkhamanubhavatāpi mayā na ca naiva ātmārthaḥ dṛṣṭādṛṣṭaphalasādhanaḥ kṛto niṣpāditaḥ / parasya anyasya vā arthaḥ sukhavidhānalakṣaṇaḥ / iti niṣprayojanameva nārakaduḥkhasahasraśaḥ paribhavo jātaḥ / tadadyāpi na tathaiva mamāsahiṣṇutā yuktetyāha- idaṃ duḥkhaṃ naiva tādṛśaṃ yādṛśaṃ narakasamudbhavam / atha ca mahārthaṃ sarvasattvahitasukhavidhānabhūtaṃ buddhatvaṃ sādhayiṣyati / ato jagato duḥkhahare trijagatparyāpannasarvasattvaduḥkhapraśamanakare duḥkhe prītirevātra yujyate nāruciriti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: the very cause of anger — just so, fruitlessly — in the hells such as <s>Saṃjīva</s> and the rest — thousands of times, repeatedly — I have been subjected to torment by causes such as cutting, splitting, tearing, and so on. Even while experiencing such suffering, neither my own purpose — the accomplishment of visible and invisible fruits — has been fulfilled, nor the purpose of another — characterized by the provision of happiness. Thus the thousandfold suffering of hell was produced entirely without purpose. Therefore even now my intolerance should not be the same — he says: this suffering is not at all like that which arises in hell; moreover, it will accomplish a great purpose — <s>Buddhahood</s> (awakening), which consists in providing benefit and happiness to all beings. Therefore, in this suffering that removes the suffering of the world — that pacifies the suffering of all beings within the three worlds — delight alone is fitting here, not aversion. This is the meaning.

body.text: paraguṇaśravaṇerṣyāmalaprakṣālanāyāha-
body.translated_text: For the purpose of washing away the stain of envy upon hearing of others' virtues, he says —

children.translated_text: If others have obtained the joy and happiness of praising one rich in virtues,

children.text: manastvamapi taṃ stutvā kasmādevaṃ na hṛṣyasi // Bca_6.76 //
children.translated_text: O mind, why do you not likewise rejoice by praising him? // <s>Bca</s> 6.76 //

body.text: guṇādhikaṃ stutvā yadi prītisukhaṃ kaiścit prāptam, tadā he manaḥ tvamapi tadguṇasaṃvarṇanena kimiti harṣasukhaṃ nānubhavasi? kimakāṇḍameva tadīrṣyānalajvālāyāmātmasaṃtānamindhanīkaroṣi?
body.translated_text: If some have obtained the joy and happiness of praising one endowed with superior virtues, then O mind, why do you too not experience the happiness of delight through extolling those virtues? Why do you without cause make your own mental continuum fuel for the flame of envy?

body.text: nanu sarvasukhamāsaṅgātmatayā niṣiddhameva sevitum / tataḥ ahaṃ sarvasukhavaimukhyādidamapi nopādade / vakṣyati hi-
body.translated_text: [Objection:] All happiness, being of the nature of attachment, is indeed prohibited to pursue. Therefore, out of aversion to all happiness, I do not take up even this. For it will be said [later] —

children.text: yatra yatra ratiṃ yāti manaḥ sukhavimohitam /
children.translated_text: 'Wherever the mind, deluded by pleasure, goes in pursuit of delight,
from that very [source], suffering multiplied a thousandfold arises and presents itself.'

body.text:
iti /
[bodhi. 8.18]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Bodhi</s>. 8.18]

body.text: āha-
body.translated_text: He replies —

children.text: idaṃ ca te hṛṣṭisukhaṃ niravadyaṃ sukhodayam /
children.translated_text: This joy-happiness of yours is blameless, a source of happiness;

children.text: na vāritaṃ ca guṇibhiḥ parāvarjanamuttamam // Bca_6.77 //
children.translated_text: it is not prohibited by the virtuous, and is the supreme means of winning over others. // <s>Bca</s> 6.77 //

body.text: na hi sarvaṃ hṛṣṭisukhamapākṛtam, api tu yat sāvadyamakuśalahetuḥ / idaṃ ca paraguṇāśrayaṃ hṛṣṭisukhaṃ niravadyaṃ tava, na ca akuśalahetuḥ / ataḥ sukhodayaṃ sukhasyodayo 'smāditi kṛtvā / ata eva na vāritaṃ ca guṇibhirbhagavacchāsanavidhijñaiḥ / ayamaparo 'sya guṇaḥ, yat parāvarjanamuttamaṃ paraguṇeṣu prītyā / guṇeṣu evamayaṃ matsarīti manyamānā anye 'pi sattvā āvarjitā bhavanti, ato yuktamevātra prītisukhamupādātum //
body.translated_text: Not all joy-happiness is rejected, but only that which is blameworthy and a cause of the unwholesome. This joy-happiness of yours, based on others' virtues, is blameless and not a cause of the unwholesome. Therefore it is 'a source of happiness' — because happiness arises from it. For this very reason it is not prohibited by the virtuous — by those who know the prescriptions of the Blessed One's teaching. This is another merit of it: it is the supreme means of winning over others through delight in their virtues. Thinking 'this one is free from envy regarding [our] virtues,' other beings too become favorably disposed. Therefore it is indeed appropriate to embrace this joy-happiness.

body.text: syādetat- na paraguṇeṣu akṣamā kācinmama / kiṃ tarhi tāvattasyaiva sukhametaditi mayā soḍhumaśakyamiti / atrāha-
body.translated_text: [Objection:] I have no intolerance whatever of others' virtues. Rather, I simply cannot bear that this is happiness for him alone. To this he replies —

children.text: tasyaiva sukhamityevaṃ tavedaṃ yadi na priyam /
children.translated_text: If 'this is happiness for him alone' is not pleasing to you,
then by ceasing to give wages and such, both visible and invisible [fruits] would be destroyed. // <s>Bca</s> 6.78 //

body.text: tasyaiva stutikartuḥ sukhamiti evamanenābhiprāyeṇa bhavato yadi idaṃ paraguṇastutipratisamudbhavaṃ sukhaṃ na priyam, tadā atisaṃkaṭe patito 'si / katham? bhṛtidānādivirateḥ / yadapi ca bhavataḥ svātmasukhanimittaṃ svabhṛtyādiṣu bhṛtidānaṃ karmamūlyadānam, tathā upakārakāriṇi pratyupakārakaraṇam / ityāderviratervaimukhyāt, tadapi na kartavyameva syāt parasukhavidveṣiṇā / yatastenāpi tasya sukhameva saṃpatsyate / tato dṛṣṭamaihikaṃ phalam, adṛṣṭaṃ pāralaukikam / ubhayamapi hataṃ bhavet parasukhasaṃpadamarṣiṇā //
body.translated_text: 'This is happiness for the praiser alone' — if with this intention this happiness arising from the praise of others' virtues is not pleasing to you, then you have fallen into extreme difficulty. How? By ceasing to give wages and such: whatever giving of wages — payment for labor — you do to your own servants and so on for the sake of your own happiness, and likewise performing reciprocal services for those who have helped you — from the aversion to all such [activities], even that should not be done by one who is hostile to others' happiness, since through that too, happiness will accrue to them. Thus both the visible fruit — pertaining to this life — and the invisible — pertaining to the next life — would be destroyed by one who cannot bear others' attainment of happiness.

body.text: kiṃ ca / mithyottaramevedaṃ bhavata iti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, showing that this is indeed a false reply of yours, he says —

children.translated_text: When your own virtues are being extolled, you wish happiness even for the other [who praises];
when another's virtues are being extolled, you do not wish happiness even for yourself. // <s>Bca</s> 6.79 //

body.text: yadi kaścidbhavato guṇamudīrayati, tadā tasya parasyāniṣṭamapi saukhyamicchasi / atha paraguṇānanuvarṇayati, tadā punarīrṣyāśalyavitudyamānamānasaḥ / svasaukhyamapi necchasi / āstāṃ tāvat parasaukhyamityapiśabdaḥ / tasmāt parasukhasaṃpadīrṣyaiva bhavataḥ, na stāvakasukhāsahiṣṇutā //
body.translated_text: If someone proclaims your virtue, then you desire even the unwelcome happiness of that other person [the praiser]. But when someone praises another's virtues, then again, with your mind pierced by the thorn of envy, you do not wish happiness even for yourself — let alone others' happiness, as indicated by the word 'even.' Therefore it is envy alone at others' attainment of happiness that is yours, not intolerance of the praiser's happiness.

body.text: yaduktam-
body.translated_text: What was said —

body.text:
tasyaiva sukhamityevaṃ tavedaṃ yadi na priyam /
iti /
[bodhi. 6.78]
body.translated_text: 'If "this is happiness for him alone" is not pleasing to you' — thus. [<s>Bodhi</s>. 6.78]

body.text: tatra viśeṣeṇa dūṣaṇamāha-
body.translated_text: Regarding that, he states a particular censure —

children.translated_text: Having generated <s>bodhicitta</s> with the wish for the happiness of all beings,
why are you now angry at beings who have themselves obtained happiness? // <s>Bca</s> 6.80 //

body.text: idamatigarhitameva viśeṣeṇa samutpāditabodhicittasya, yat parasukhasaṃpadasahiṣṇutā nāma / yataḥ sarvasattvāḥ triadhātukāntaścarāḥ samastasukhasaṃpattisaṃtarpitā buddhatvamadhigamya mayā kartavyāḥ iti manasikāreṇa bodhicittamutpādyate / tadutpādya kasmāt sattveṣu kupyate? adya idānīm / kiṃbhūteṣu prasādasthāneṣu? svacittamabhiprasādya svayamātmanaiva prāptasukheṣu / iti akaraṇīyameva tat parasukhavaimukhyacittaṃ bodhisattvasyeti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: This is especially reprehensible for one who has generated <s>bodhicitta</s> — namely, intolerance of others' attainment of happiness. For <s>bodhicitta</s> is generated with the mental resolve: 'I shall bring all beings dwelling within the three realms to <s>Buddhahood</s>, satisfying them with the complete attainment of happiness.' Having generated that [<s>bodhicitta</s>], why is one angry at beings? 'Now' — at this present time. At those in what condition? At those who are grounds for faith — who have obtained happiness by themselves, through their own [merit]. Thus, that attitude of aversion to others' happiness is entirely unfitting for a <s>Bodhisattva</s> — this is the meaning.

body.text: yaḥ punarutpāditabodhicitto 'pi parasya lābhasatkārasaṃpattimabhisamīkṣya tadīrṣyākaṣāyitahṛdayaḥ tenaiva śokena dahyate, tasya paribhāṣaṇārthamāha-
body.translated_text: For one who, even having generated <s>bodhicitta</s>, upon observing another's gain, honor, and prosperity, with a heart stained by envy toward that, is burned by that very grief — for the purpose of rebuking such a one, he says —

children.translated_text: You profess to wish <s>Buddhahood</s> — worshipped by the three worlds — for beings;

children.text: satkāramitvaraṃ dṛṣṭvā teṣāṃ kiṃ paridahyase // Bca_6.81 //
children.translated_text: seeing their paltry honor, why are you consumed [with envy]? // <s>Bca</s> 6.81 //

body.text: athavā syādetat- na khalu mayā tatsukhameva na mṛṣyate, kiṃ tarhi tadudbhāvitānyaguṇaśravaṇābhiprasannamānasaiḥ teṣāmupanāmitaṃ lābhasatkāramityatrāha- trailokyetyādi / trayo lokāeva kāmarūpārūpyadhātulakṣaṇāḥ lokaprasiddhayā vā svargādisvabhāvāḥ trailokyam, tatsamudāyo vā / tasya pūjāmarhatīti pūjyamabhyarcanīyam / anena sarvātiśāyitvaṃ pratipāditam / tathābhūtaṃ buddhatvaṃ sattvānāṃ kila vāñchasi / kiletyanena viparyayaṃ dṛṣṭvā aruciṃ prakāśayati / satkāra mityupalakṣaṇam / lābhamapi / śeṣaṃ subodham //
body.translated_text: Or alternatively, one might say: it is not that I cannot bear that happiness itself; rather, [I cannot bear] the gain and honor offered to them by those whose minds are favorably disposed through hearing of the virtues produced by that [person]. To this he says: 'the three worlds' and so forth. The three worlds are characterized as the desire, form, and formless realms, or by worldly convention as heaven and such; 'the three worlds' is their totality. What is 'worthy of worship' by that [totality] means worthy of veneration. By this, supreme excellence is conveyed. You profess to wish such <s>Buddhahood</s> for beings — the word 'profess' (<s>kila</s>) expresses distaste upon seeing the contradiction. 'Honor' is indicative [of gain also]. The rest is easily understood.

body.text: lābhamabhisaṃdhāyāha-
body.translated_text: With regard to gain, he says —
