Thus, by the principle of the [example of] taste and the eye as stated, even when encountering hardship, one should not come under the power of afflictions.

body.text: ityuktena prabandhena sthāmabalaṃ vidhāya ratibalamāvedayitumāha-
body.translated_text: Having established the strength of firmness through the series thus stated, to teach the strength of delight, he says —

children.translated_text: Whatever action one undertakes, one should become absorbed in that action,
addicted to that action, insatiable — like one desiring the pleasure of a game's reward. // <s>Bca</s> 7.62 //

body.text: karma saṃbhāranibandhanaṃ dhyānādhyayanādilakṣaṇaṃ yadevāpadyate, kramakaraṇayogenāpatitaṃ bhavet, tasminneva karmaṇi vyasanī bhavet tatkriyārasanimagnacittaḥ / tatkarmaśauṇḍaḥ tatpravṛttilampaṭaḥ / atṛptātmā punaḥpunarabhilāṣayuktaḥ / ka iva? krīḍāphalasukhepsuvat dyūtādikrīḍāyā yatphalaṃ sukhaṃ tadāptumicchuriva //
body.translated_text: The action connected with the accumulations [of merit and wisdom] — characterized by meditation, study, and such — whatever [action] 'one undertakes,' comes to be undertaken through the sequential method of practice — in that very action one should become absorbed, with the mind immersed in the relish of performing it. 'Addicted to that action' — passionate about engaging in it. 'Insatiable' — endowed with desire again and again. Like whom? Like one desiring the pleasure that is the reward of a game — like one wishing to obtain the pleasure that is the fruit of games such as gambling and the like.

body.text: ito 'pi vicārayatā karmaṇi ratirutpādayitavyetyupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Showing moreover that by one who reflects, delight in action should be generated, he says —

children.text: sukhārtha kriyate karma tathāpi syānna vā sukham /
children.translated_text: Action is done for the sake of happiness, yet that happiness may or may not come;

children.text: karmaiva tu sukhaṃ yasya niṣkarmā sa sukhī katham // Bca_7.63 //
children.translated_text: but for one whose happiness is action itself, how can he be happy without action? // Bca_7.63 //

body.text: sarvaireva karmaphalasukhalipsayā karma kriyate / anyathā tatra pravṛttirna syāt / tathāpi evaṃ cetasā pravṛttāvapi kasyacit karmaṇo 'bhivāñchitaphalaṃ syāt, kasyacit punarna syāt / niṣphalārambhasyāpi saṃbhavāt / tathāpi karmārambhāt punaḥ phalasaṃbhāvanayā naiva nivartate
body.translated_text: By everyone, action is performed out of desire for the happiness that is the fruit of action; otherwise there would be no engagement in it. Yet even when one engages with such an intention, for some actions the desired fruit may come, for others it may not, since even fruitless undertakings are possible. Nevertheless, even so, by the expectation of fruit from undertaking action, people never desist.

body.text: janaḥ / yasya punaḥ karmaiva sukham, na taduttaramaparasukhābhilāṣaḥ, sa niṣkarmā karmavirahitaḥ kathaṃ sukhī syāt? na kathaṃcidityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: But one for whom action itself is happiness, who has no further desire for any other happiness beyond that — how could he be happy without action, devoid of action? Not in any way — this is the meaning.

body.text: idamapi bhāvayatā karmaṇyabhiniveṣṭavyamityāha-
body.translated_text: Reflecting on this too, one should be devoted to action — he says —

children.translated_text: There is no satisfaction from sensual pleasures in <s>saṃsāra</s>, which are like honey on a razor's edge;
how then could there be satisfaction from the nectar of merit, which is sweet in its ripening and auspicious? // Bca_7.64 //

body.text: rūpādiviṣayaiḥ / saṃsāra iti saṃsarati punaḥ punaḥ / abhūtairatṛptiḥ anāpyāyanam / kiṃbhūtaiḥ? kṣuradhārāmadhūpamaiḥ kṣuradhārāyāṃ yanmadhu madhurasaṃ yadāsvādya tṛṣṇāvaśājjihvocchedanottarakālaṃ duḥkhamupajāyate, tenopamā upamānaṃ yādṛśaṃ yeṣāṃ te / āpātamātramādhurye 'pi pariṇatiduḥkhena kaṭukarasattvātteṣāmityabhiprāyaḥ / puṇyānyeva amṛtānīva, taiḥ kathaṃ tṛptirastu? kiṃviśiṣṭaiḥ? vipākamadhurairabhyudayaphalasukhahetutayā pariṇāmena madhurarasatvāt / paramasukhajanakaiḥ śivaiḥ kalyāṇakāribhirniḥśreyasāvāhakatayā / ajarāmaraphaladānaparatvāt sarvaduḥkhanirvartakairityarthaḥ / ata eva puṇyāmṛtairityatra hetupadametat //
body.translated_text: From objects such as form and so forth. 'In <s>saṃsāra</s>' — one transmigrates again and again. From unreal [pleasures] there is no satisfaction, no fulfillment. Of what kind? 'Like honey on a razor's edge' — the honey, the sweet substance on a razor's edge, upon tasting which, through the force of craving, after the cutting of the tongue, suffering arises — the simile, the comparison, is of such a nature for those [sensual pleasures]. The intent is: though sweet at first contact, they are of bitter essence through the suffering of transformation. 'The nectars of merit' — merits that are like nectar — from those, how could there be satisfaction? Of what kind? 'Sweet in their ripening' — being of sweet essence in their maturation, through being causes of the happiness that is the fruit of prosperity. 'Auspicious' — productive of good, through bringing about the highest good. Since they bestow the fruit of agelessness and immortality, they remove all suffering — this is the meaning. Hence, in 'the nectar of merit,' this is an expression indicating the reason.

body.text: tasmādityupasaṃhāreṇa punaḥ karmābhirāmaṃ draḍhayannāha-
body.translated_text: With the concluding 'therefore,' again reinforcing the delight in action, he says —

children.translated_text: Therefore, even at the conclusion of an action, one should plunge into the next action,

children.text: yathā madhyāhnasaṃtapta ādau prāptasarāḥ karī // Bca_7.65 //
children.translated_text: just as an elephant scorched by the midday [sun], upon first reaching a lake, [plunges in]. // Bca_7.65 //

body.text: tasya ārabdhasya karmaṇaḥ avasāne 'pi nimajjet, tadabhiniveśarasanimagna eva vimuñcet / kathamiva? yathā grīṣmasamaye madhyaṃdinavartini sūrye sarvato jalamalabhamānaśca ātāpatāpito hastī paramābhiniveśasaṃyuktaḥ atiśayavadāhlādakāriśītalajalaparipūritaṃ hadamāsādya prathamato nimajjati tathā iti samudāyārthaḥ / prāptaṃ saro yena sa tathā / paścātkarmadhārayaḥ / ādāvityasya nimajjatītyanena saṃbandhaḥ //
body.translated_text: Even at the conclusion of that commenced action, one should plunge — immersed in the savor of devotion to it, one should let go [only to begin anew]. How so? Just as an elephant in the summer season, when the sun is at midday, unable to find water anywhere, scorched by the heat, with supreme devotion reaching a pool filled with exceedingly refreshing cool water, first plunges in — thus is the combined meaning. 'Having reached a lake' — one who has reached a lake, thus [the compound]. The latter is a <s>karmadhāraya</s> compound. 'First' connects with 'plunges.'

body.text: idānīṃ ratibalaṃ vyākhyāya muktibalaṃ vyākhyātumāha-
body.translated_text: Having now explained the power of delight, he says, in order to explain the power of relinquishment —

children.translated_text: When there is a subsequent diminishing of strength, one should set aside [the task] in order to do it again;
and when it is well completed, one should leave it, with the desire for what comes next and next. // Bca_7.66 //

body.text: ārabdhakarmaniṣpādane sāmarthyakṣayamātmano 'vagamya sāmarthyapratilambhe sati punaḥ kariṣyāmi ityabhiprāyeṇa tāvatkālaṃ parityajet muñcet / na tāvatāsya vikṣepaḥ syāt / anyathā tathāpi tadaparityāge 'narthasamāveśa eva syāt / yadāpi suniṣpannaṃ tadārabdhaṃ karma bhavet, tadāpi moktavyam / anyathā svarasavāhitayāpi tasmin pravṛtte punarvyāpārādvikṣepa eva syāt / tasmādaparāparaviśeṣākāṅkṣayā tanmuñcet parityajet / etena yaduktaṃ prākpūrvaṃ samīkṣya sāmagrīm [7.47] ityādi, tasyotsargasyāyamapavāda uktaḥ //
body.translated_text: Understanding one's own depletion of capacity in accomplishing the commenced task, with the intention 'I shall do it again when capacity is regained,' one should set aside, should leave [the task] for that period. Thereby there would be no distraction for him. Otherwise, even so, in not relinquishing it, there would only be an incursion of harm. Even when that commenced task has been well accomplished, it should be released. Otherwise, even if one proceeds in it carried by momentum, there would be distraction due to further engagement. Therefore, with the desire for one distinction after another, one should leave it, should relinquish it. By this, what was stated earlier — 'having first examined the resources' [7.47] and so forth — this exception to that rule has been stated.

body.text: tadevamavāntaraviśeṣopadarśanena balavyūhaṃ sarvathābhidhāya prathamoddeśapratipāditamapi punaśchandādigaṇe [7.16] kathitaṃ tātparyaṃ vyācakṣāṇa āha-
body.translated_text: Having thus thoroughly set forth the deployment of strength through showing particular distinctions, explaining the purport stated [earlier] in the group [beginning with] 'zeal' and so forth [7.16], which was set forth in the first exposition, he says —

body.text: kleśaprahārān saṃrakṣet kleśāṃśca prahareddṛḍham /
body.translated_text: One should guard against the blows of the defilements, and strike the defilements firmly,

body.text: khaṅgayuddhamivāpannaḥ śikṣitenāriṇā saha // Bca_7.67 //
body.translated_text: as one who has engaged in sword-battle with a trained enemy. // Bca_7.67 //

body.text: kleśānāṃ prahārān upaghātān saṃrakṣet nivārayet / yathā teṣāṃ praharo na prabhavatītyarthaḥ / kleśān punaḥ praharet nihanyāt / dṛḍhaṃ gāḍhaprahāreṇa / yathā punaravakāśaṃ na labheran / atra nidarśanamāha- yathā śikṣitena śastravidyākauśalasamanvāgatena śatruṇā saha nipuṇataraḥ khaṅgena saṃgrāmayan tamabhibhavati, na ca tenābhibhūta iti //
body.translated_text: One should guard against — should ward off — the blows, the injuries, of the defilements, so that their blows do not prevail — this is the meaning. And one should strike — should destroy — the defilements. 'Firmly' — with a strong blow, so that they do not again find an opening. Here he gives an illustration: just as one who battles with a sword against a trained enemy endowed with skill in the science of weapons, being more skilled, overcomes him and is not overcome by him.

body.text: tathā tatretyādinā punastātparyaṃ śikṣayitumāha-
body.translated_text: Then, with 'there' and so forth, teaching the purport again, he says —

children.translated_text: There, just as one would quickly pick up a sword that has fallen, in fear,

children.text: smṛtikhaṅgaṃ tathā bhraṣṭaṃ gṛhṇīyānnarakān smaran // Bca_7.68 //
children.translated_text: so too, one should pick up the sword of mindfulness when it has fallen, remembering the hells. // Bca_7.68 //

body.text: tatra tasmin khaṅgayuddhe yathā khaṅgaṃ hastāt kathaṃcit vicalitaṃ punaḥ saṃvṛtya gṛhṇīyāt samayaḥ, mā māmayaṃ chalamanupraviśya śatrurvadhīt / tvaranniti śīghrameva / na kālapratilambeneti yāvat / tathā tadvadeva smṛtipramoṣe / smṛtireva khaṅga iva kleśaśatruvijayāya / taṃ bhraṣṭamapagataṃ gṛhṇīyāt āmukhīkuryāt / narakān rauravādīn smaran / skhalite sati tadduḥkhabhāgitāṃ manasikurvan //
body.translated_text: 'There' — in that sword-battle, just as one would retrieve a sword that has somehow slipped from the hand — the thought being 'lest this enemy, finding an opening, slay me' — 'quickly' means immediately, without delay in time — so too, likewise, when mindfulness is lost: mindfulness itself is like a sword for conquering the enemy of defilements. When it has 'fallen' — departed — one should pick it up, should take it up again, remembering the hells — <s>Raurava</s> and such — reflecting, in the event of a lapse, on the state of being subject to that suffering.

body.text: nanu sūkṣmakleśasamudācāre 'pi kā kṣatiḥ yena tatra upekṣā na kriyate ityatrāha-
body.translated_text: Now, even in the case of a subtle arising of defilements, what harm is there that one should not be indifferent? To this he says —

children.translated_text: Just as poison, reaching the blood, spreads through the body,
so too a fault, finding an opening, spreads through the mind. // Bca_7.69 //

body.text: aṇumātrasyāpi doṣasya avakāśo na dātavyaḥ / anyathā tanmātrasyāpyanupraveśe citte tatprasarāvarodhasya kartumaśakyatvāt / yathā hi svalpavraṇe 'pi rudhirasaṃparkavato viṣasya śarīre / tasmādaṇumātrakleśaprahāranivāraṇe 'pi tātparyaṃ kuryāt //
body.translated_text: Not even the slightest opening should be given to a fault. Otherwise, even with the entry of just that much into the mind, it becomes impossible to arrest its spread. Just as [it is] with poison that has come into contact with blood, even through a small wound, in the body. Therefore, one should apply oneself earnestly even in warding off the blows of the slightest defilement.

body.text: punaranyathā tātparyaṃ dṛḍhīkurvannāha-
body.translated_text: Again, reinforcing the earnestness in another way, he says —

children.translated_text: Just as an oil-pot bearer, watched over by sword-wielding [guards],
[fears] death should he stumble — so too should the practitioner of vows be intent. // Bca_7.70 //

body.text: yathā kaścit puruṣaścaṇḍanṛpājñayā tailaparipūrṇapātramādāya picchalasaṃkrameṇa asihastai rājapuruṣaiḥ bindumātratailabhraṃśe 'pi adyaiva tvāṃ prāṇairviyojayiṣyāma iti bruvāṇairadhiṣṭhito gacchan yadi mamātra kathaṃcit skhalitaṃ syāt, tadā nūnamamī māṃ vyāpādayeyuriti maraṇabhayāttatparo bhavati, tathā vratī gṛhītasaṃvaraḥ prakṛtaskhalite narakādiduḥkhatrāsāt tadanavakāśāya tatparaḥ syāt yatnavān bhavet //
body.translated_text: Just as a certain person, by the command of a wrathful king, having taken a pot filled with oil, [crossing] on a slippery bridge, watched over by king's officers with swords in hand, saying 'even if a single drop of oil spills, we shall this very day separate you from your life' — going thus, [thinking] 'if I should somehow stumble here, then surely these will kill me' — out of fear of death becomes intent [on his task] — so too the practitioner of vows, one who has undertaken the precepts, at a lapse in the subject [of practice], out of fear of the suffering of hell and such, should be intent — should be diligent — on preventing any opening for that.

body.text: uktamupasaṃhṛtya darśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Summarizing what has been stated, he shows —

children.translated_text: Therefore, just as one rises quickly when a snake falls into one's lap,
so too, when drowsiness and laziness approach, one should quickly counteract them. // Bca_7.71 //

body.text: yata evam, tasmādutsaṅgage kroḍagate sarpe āśīviṣe yathā tvaritamevottiṣṭhati- mā māmayamahirdakṣīt, tathaiva nidrālasyāgame middhastyānaprādurbhāve pratikurvīta tatpratipakṣānityatādibhāvanaya pratīkāraṃ kuryāt //
body.translated_text: Since this is so, therefore, just as when a snake — a venomous serpent — has fallen into one's lap, one rises quickly — 'lest this snake bite me' — so too, when drowsiness and laziness approach — when torpor and sluggishness manifest — one should counteract them — one should apply the remedy through the cultivation of impermanence and such, which are their antidotes.

body.text: asya caivaṃ yatnavato 'pi kathaṃcit kiṃcit skhalitaṃ śūraskhalitanyāyena syāt / tadā pratīkāraṃ kṛtvā punaryatnavān bhavet / ityupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: And even for one thus diligent, some lapse might occur in the manner of a hero's stumble. Then, having applied the remedy, one should again be diligent — showing this, he says —

children.translated_text: At each and every lapse, having thoroughly reproached [oneself], one should reflect:

children.text: kathaṃ karomi yenedaṃ punarme na bhavediti // Bca_7.72 //
children.translated_text: 'What should I do so that this does not happen to me again?' // Bca_7.72 //

body.text: smṛtipramoṣe sati ekaikasmin pratyekaṃ chale skhalite kathaṃcit kleśānāmanupraveśe sati paritapya adhyāśayena manastāpaṃ kṛtsna vicintayet- aho bata jānanneva skhalito 'smi, tatkena prakāreṇātra pratividhānaṃ karomi yena punaridaṃ chalaṃ na syāt? ityevaṃ dṛḍhasamārambhaṃ samādāya viharet / na tu punaḥ śithilaḥ syāditi bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: When there is a loss of mindfulness, at each and every — at each individual — lapse, stumble, when the defilements have somehow entered, having reproached [oneself] — having produced mental anguish through aspiration — one should thoroughly reflect: 'Alas, knowing full well, I have stumbled! By what means then do I apply the remedy here so that this lapse does not occur again?' Undertaking firm resolve in this way, one should abide. One should not be lax — this is the meaning.

body.text: ata eva vivekakāmānāṃ pratiṣiddhamapyanujānannāha-
body.translated_text: For this very reason, even permitting what is otherwise prohibited for those desiring solitude, he says —

body.text: saṃsargaṃ karma vā prāptamicchedetena hetunā /
body.translated_text: One should desire association or [remedial] action that has arisen, for this very reason.

body.text: ācāryopādhyāyatadanyasabrahmacāriprabhṛtibhiḥ bahuśrutaiḥ tripiṭakavedibhiḥ kaukṛtyavinodanakuśalaiḥ saha saṃsargaṃ samavadhānamicchedāśaṃset / tanniśrita eva tiṣṭhedityabhiprāyaḥ / karma vā prāptaṃ tadavavādānuśāsanīlakṣaṇam, āpattisamuddharaṇam, tairdaṇḍakarmapraṇayanaṃ vā samutpannamicchet / etena hetunā teṣāmavatārasaṃrakṣaṇābhiprāyeṇa / etadevāha-
body.translated_text: One should desire, should wish for, association — the company — with teachers, preceptors, and other fellow practitioners, those who are learned, who know the three baskets [of scripture], who are skilled in dispelling remorse. The intent is: one should remain relying on them. Or one should desire the action that has arisen — characterized by their admonition and instruction, the extraction from transgression, or the disciplinary action imposed by them. 'For this very reason' — with the intent of guarding against the entry of those [defilements]. He states this very point —

body.text: kathaṃ nāmāsvavasthāsu smṛtyabhyāso bhavediti // Bca_7.73 //
body.translated_text: 'How may the practice of mindfulness come about in these situations?' // Bca_7.73 //

body.text: kena vidhinā nāma āsu avasthāsu kleśāvatāradaśāsu smṛtyabhyāso bhavet, ayatnata evālambanāt saṃpramoṣo na syāt, ityanena abhiprāyeṇa / ayaṃ samudāyārthaḥ- kalyāṇamitrasaṃnidhānāt tadavavādānuśāsanītaḥ tadācārasaṃdarśanācca sadā smṛtisaṃprajanyavihāriṇaḥ kleśā nāvatāraṃ labhante / tato 'sya avirodhata eva utsāho vardhata iti yuktam /
body.translated_text: 'By what method may the practice of mindfulness come about in these situations — these states where defilements find entry — so that effortlessly, through [constant] apprehension, the loss [of mindfulness] would not occur?' — with this intent. The combined meaning is: through the proximity of a spiritual friend, through their admonition and instruction, and through observing their conduct, for one who always abides in mindfulness and introspective awareness, the defilements do not find entry. Therefore, it is fitting that for such a one, zeal increases without obstruction.

body.text: sadā kalyāṇamitraṃ ca jīvitārthe 'pi na tyajet /

children.translated_text: — thus. [Bca_5.102]

body.translated_text: 'One should never abandon the spiritual friend, even at the cost of one's life'

body.text: tathā-
body.translated_text: Likewise —

children.translated_text: 'For the fortunate who act with respect, even out of awe, toward the preceptor's instruction,
mindfulness arises easily from dwelling with the teacher.'

body.text: iti // [bodhi. 5.30]
body.translated_text: — thus. [Bca_5.30]

body.text: adhunā tātparyamupadarśya ātmavidheyatāmupadarśayitumāha-
body.translated_text: Now, having shown the purport, in order to show self-mastery, he says —

children.translated_text: One should make oneself light, remembering the teaching on heedfulness,

children.text: karmāgamādyathā pūrvaṃ sajjaḥ sarvatra vartate // Bca_7.74 //
children.translated_text: so that one stands ready in everything, even before the approach of action. // Bca_7.74 //

body.text: sarvakarmaṇyamātmānaṃ kāyavākcittalakṣaṇaṃ tathā kuryāt, utsāhābhyāsādāyattiṃ nayedityarthaḥ / yathā karmāgamāt karmārambhāt pūrvaṃ prāgeva sajjaḥ āyattīkṛtaḥ sudāntāśvavat tanmārganirīkṣaṇāsīna iva karmaṇi pravartate //
body.translated_text: One should make oneself — characterized by body, speech, and mind — serviceable for all action; the meaning is: through the practice of zeal, one should bring [oneself] under control. Just as, even before the approach of action — before the commencement of action — [one who is] already ready, brought under control, like a well-trained horse, sitting as if watching for that path, one engages in action.

body.text: uktamevārthamudāharaṇena vyaktīkurvannāha-
body.translated_text: Clarifying the stated meaning with an illustration, he says —

children.translated_text: Just as a piece of cotton is subject to the coming and going of the wind,
so too one should be subject to zeal — and thus <s>ṛddhi</s> (supernatural power) prospers. // Bca_7.75 //

body.text: tūlakaṃ karpāsādisamudbhūtaṃ yathā vāyorgamane ca āgamane ca vaśamāyattam, tathā tadvadeva utsāhavaśaṃ yāyāt vīryavaśavartī bhavet / evamabhyāsaparāyaṇasya ṛddhiśca ākāśagamanādilakṣaṇā samṛdhyati saṃpadyate //
body.translated_text: A piece of cotton — arisen from cotton plants and such — just as it is subject to, dependent on, the wind in its coming and going, so too likewise one should be subject to zeal, should be under the control of effort. For one thus devoted to practice, <s>ṛddhi</s> — characterized by traversing the sky and such — prospers, is accomplished.

body.text: parātmasamatāparātmaparivartane punaḥ ubhayatrāpi upayukte iti dhyānaparicchede eva vyākhyeye //
body.translated_text: The exchange of self and other and equality of self and other, moreover, since both are applicable, are to be explained in the chapter on meditation itself.

body.text: iti prajñākaramativiracitāyāṃ bodhicaryāvatārapañjikāyāṃ vīryapāramitā nāma saptamaḥ paricchedaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus concludes the seventh chapter, called 'The Perfection of Effort,' in the <s>Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā</s> composed by <s>Prajñākaramati</s>.

body.text: 8. dhyānapāramitā nāma aṣṭamaḥ paricchedaḥ /
body.translated_text: 8. The eighth chapter, called 'The Perfection of Meditation.'

body.text: tadevaṃ kṣānteranantaraṃ vīryamabhidhāya yaduktam-
body.translated_text: Having thus set forth effort immediately after patience, as stated —

children.translated_text: 'Then one should resort to the forest;
one should apply oneself to concentration, and should cultivate the contemplation of the unattractive and such.'

body.text: śikṣā. sa. kārikā-20
body.translated_text: <s>Śikṣāsamuccaya</s> verse 20

body.text: iti, tad vardhayitvaivamityādinā pratipādayitumupakramate-
body.translated_text: — that, he undertakes to set forth with 'having increased' and so forth —

body.text: vardhayitvaivamutsāhaṃ samādhau sthāpayenmanaḥ /
body.translated_text: Having thus increased one's zeal, one should establish the mind in <s>samādhi</s> (concentration).

body.text: evamuktapratipakṣasya āsevanādinā vipakṣamunmūlya vīryaṃ vardhayitvā anābhogavāhitayā sthirīkṛtya samādhau samādhāne cittaikāgratāyāṃ sthāpayenmanaḥ, tatra niveśayet / āropayediti yāvat / kimarthamityāha-
body.translated_text: Having thus uprooted the opposing forces through the practice and so on of the remedies described, having increased <s>vīrya</s> (effort) and stabilized it through effortless flow, one should place the mind in <s>samādhi</s> — in concentration, in one-pointedness of mind — one should settle it there, one should establish it. To what purpose? He says —

body.text: vikṣiptacittastu naraḥ kleśadaṃṣṭrāntare sthitaḥ // Bca_8.1 //
body.translated_text: For a person whose mind is distracted stands between the fangs of the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). // <s>Bca</s> 8.1 //

body.text: turiti hetau / yasmāt samādhānamantareṇa vikṣiptacittaḥ asamāhitacittasamudācāraḥ vīryavānapi naraḥ puruṣaḥ kleśānāṃ rākṣasānāmiva daṃṣṭrāntare madhye sthitaḥ, kavalīkṛta eva tairāste / tasmāt //
body.translated_text: The particle 'tu' is in the sense of reason. Since, without concentration, a person whose mind is distracted — whose mental activity is unconcentrated — even if he is diligent, stands between the fangs of the <s>kleśas</s>, as if between the fangs of <s>rākṣasas</s> (demons); he remains as if swallowed by them. Therefore —

body.text: tatra tāvat samādhivipakṣaṃ nirākartuṃ pīṭhikābandhaṃ racayannāha-
body.translated_text: Now, in order to remove the obstacles to <s>samādhi</s>, he constructs the preliminary foundation, saying —

children.translated_text: Through the solitude of body and mind, distraction does not arise;
therefore, abandoning the world, one should forsake discursive thoughts. // <s>Bca</s> 8.2 //

body.text: kāyaviveko janasaṃparkavivarjanatā / cittavivekaḥ kāmādivitarkavivarjanatā / iti / kāyacittayorviveke nirāsaṅgatayā vikṣepasya tayorunnatatāyāḥ / ālambanāpratiṣṭhānasyeti yāvat / na saṃbhavaḥ na prādurbhāvaḥ / yata evam, tasmāllokaṃ svajanabāndhavādilakṣaṇaṃ parityajya vihāya pūrvaṃ vitarkāścittavikṣepahetūn parivarjayet parityajet //
body.translated_text: Solitude of body is the avoidance of contact with people. Solitude of mind is the avoidance of discursive thoughts about sensual pleasures and such. Thus, when there is solitude of body and mind, through freedom from attachment, distraction — the agitation of those [body and mind] — that is, the non-establishment upon an object — does not arise, does not manifest. Since this is so, therefore, abandoning the world — characterized by one's own relatives, kinsmen, and such — having forsaken it, one should first forsake discursive thoughts, the causes of mental distraction.

body.text: tatra lokāparityāgahetuṃ tāvannirākartumupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Now, in order to remove the cause of not abandoning the world, he shows —

children.text: snehānna tyajyate loko lābhādiṣu ca tṛṣṇayā /
children.translated_text: The world is not abandoned due to affection and due to craving for gain and such;
therefore, in order to abandon these, the wise person should reflect as follows. // <s>Bca</s> 8.3 //

body.text: ātmātmīyagrahapravartito 'bhiṣvaṅgaḥ snehaḥ / tasmānna tyajyate lokaḥ / lābhādiṣu ca tṛṣṇayā / ādiśabdāt satkārayaśaḥślokādayaḥ parigṛhyante / teṣu tṛṣṇayā pralobhena / cakārānna tyajyate loke iti samuccīyate / yata etatkāraṇamaparityāgasya, tasmādetasya snehasya lobhādīnāṃ vā / yadi vā lokasya parityāganimittaṃ vidvān vicakṣaṇaḥ / evamiti vakṣyamāṇaṃ vibhāvayet //
body.translated_text: Affection is attachment driven by the grasping of self and what belongs to self. Because of that, the world is not abandoned. And due to craving for gain and such — by the word 'and such,' honor, fame, renown, and so forth are included — due to craving for these, due to avarice. By the conjunction 'and,' 'is not abandoned' is connected also to 'in the world.' Since this is the cause of non-abandonment, therefore, for the abandonment of this affection and avarice and such — or alternatively, the wise, discerning person should reflect on the cause for abandoning the world — 'thus' refers to what will be stated.

body.text: tadevāha-
body.translated_text: That [reflection] he states —

children.translated_text: Knowing that one endowed with <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) together with <s>śamatha</s> (tranquility) accomplishes the destruction of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions),

children.text: śamathaḥ prathamaṃ gaveṣaṇīyaḥ sa ca loke nirapekṣayābhiratyā // Bca_8.4 //
children.translated_text: <s>śamatha</s> should first be sought, and that is [achieved] through indifference toward delight in the world. // <s>Bca</s> 8.4 //

body.text: śamathaḥ cittaikāgratālakṣaṇaḥ samādhiḥ / tena suyukta iti apoddhṛtya ihāpi yojanīyam / yadi vā hetvarthe tṛtīyā / śamathena hetunā vipaśyanāsuyuktaḥ / sahārthe vā / śamathena sārdhaṃ vipaśyanāsuyukta iti / vipaśyanā yathābhūtatattvaparijñānasvabhāvā prajñā / tayā suyuktaḥ / yuganaddhavāhimārgayogena kurute kleśānāṃ vināśaṃ prahāṇamityevamavetya jñātvā kleśavimumukṣuṇā śamathaḥ prathamamādau gaveṣaṇīyaḥ / utpādya ityarthaḥ / tadanantaraṃ vipaśyanā /
body.translated_text: <s>Śamatha</s> (tranquility) is <s>samādhi</s> characterized by one-pointedness of mind. 'Well-endowed with that' — this should be construed also here by separating it out. Or alternatively, the instrumental is in the sense of cause: 'well-endowed with <s>vipaśyanā</s> by means of <s>śamatha</s> as cause.' Or in the sense of accompaniment: 'well-endowed with <s>vipaśyanā</s> together with <s>śamatha</s>.' <s>Vipaśyanā</s> (insight) is <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom) whose nature is the comprehension of reality as it truly is. 'Well-endowed' with that. Through the practice of the path of the unified pair (<s>yuganaddha</s>), knowing that the destruction — the abandonment — of <s>kleśas</s> is accomplished, one who desires liberation from <s>kleśas</s> should first, at the beginning, seek <s>śamatha</s> — generate it, this is the meaning. After that, <s>vipaśyanā</s>.

children.translated_text: 'One who is concentrated knows things as they truly are,' said the <s>Muni</s>;
'and the mind should not waver from tranquility, through the cessation of external activity.'

body.text: iti / [śikṣā. sa. kārikā-9]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Śikṣāsamuccaya</s> verse 9]

body.text: sa ca śamathaḥ loke lokaviṣaye nirapekṣayā abhiratyā / abhiratiṃ pariharata eva utpadyate nānyathā //
body.translated_text: And that <s>śamatha</s> arises through indifference — the giving up of delight — toward the world, toward worldly objects; it does not arise otherwise.

body.text: tāmeva abhiratinirapekṣatāmuttaraprabandhena darśayitumāha-
body.translated_text: In order to show that very indifference to delight in the subsequent passages, he says —

children.translated_text: What being, itself impermanent, can deserve affection for impermanent things,

children.text: yena janmasahasrāṇi draṣṭavyo na punaḥ priyaḥ // Bca_8.5 //
children.translated_text: by whom the beloved will not be seen again for thousands of births? // <s>Bca</s> 8.5 //

body.text: kasya sacetanasya svayameva anityasya anityeṣu putradārādiṣu sneho bhavitumarhati yujyate / kena hetunā? yena kāraṇena janmanāṃ sahasrāṇi anekāni janmāni aparyantasaṃsāre saṃsaratā kadācidapi draṣṭavyo na punaḥ priyaḥ / prīṇātīti priya ucyate //
body.translated_text: What sentient being, itself impermanent, can deserve — can justify — affection for impermanent things such as children, wife, and so on? For what reason? Because while wandering in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s> for thousands of births — for innumerable births — the beloved will never again be seen. 'Beloved' — one who pleases is called the beloved.

body.text: tadapi ca asminnāsti ityāha-
body.translated_text: And even that [pleasure of seeing] does not exist in this [situation] — he says —

children.text: apaśyannaratiṃ yāti samāghau na ca tiṣṭhati /
children.translated_text: Not seeing [the beloved], one falls into unhappiness and cannot abide in concentration;

children.text: na ca tṛpyati dṛṣṭvāpi pūrvavadbādhyate tṛṣā // Bca_8.6 //
children.translated_text: nor is one satisfied even upon seeing [the beloved] — as before, one is tormented by craving. // <s>Bca</s> 8.6 //

body.text: yadā tāvanna paśyati tam, tadā ayamaratimadhṛtiṃ yāti / tenaiva asaumanasyena samākulitacittatvāt samādhau na ca tiṣṭhati, naiva sthito bhavati / tamavalambitumaśakta ityarthaḥ / atha yadāpi priyadarśanamasya jāyate, tadāpi na ca tṛpyati / dṛṣṭvāpi punaradhikataraṃ bādhyate tṛṣā / taddarśanābhilāṣeṇa pūrvavat adarśanakāla iva pīḍyate //
body.translated_text: When one does not see that [beloved], one falls into unhappiness, into despondency. Because the mind is agitated by that very mental suffering, one cannot abide in <s>samādhi</s>, one simply does not remain established. One is unable to hold onto it — this is the meaning. And even when the seeing of the beloved occurs, one is not satisfied. Having seen, one is tormented all the more by craving — by the longing for seeing the beloved, one is afflicted just as before, as in the time of not seeing.

body.text: api ca / sarvānarthanidānaṃ priyasaṃgatikaraṇamityupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, showing that association with the beloved is the root of all calamity, he says —

children.translated_text: One does not see things as they truly are, one falls away from spiritual urgency,
and one is burned by that grief — through the longing for union with the beloved. // <s>Bca</s> 8.7 //

body.text: yathābhūtaviparītaṃ doṣaguṇānna paśyati na jānāti / priyasaṃgamakāṅkṣayā tenaiva mohena saṃvegādavahīyate bhraṣṭo bhavati / tathā tenaiva abhiṣvaṅgeṇa dahyate tena śokena muhūrtamapi vicchede / tathā tena śokena dahyate paritapyate tenaiva manastāpena / priyasaṃgamakāṅkṣayā priyasya saṃgamaḥ saṃprayogaḥ, tasminnākāṅkṣā tṛṣṇā, tayā hetubhūtayā, punaruttarottaramadhikādhikaprārthanayā //
body.translated_text: One does not see, does not know, the faults and virtues that are contrary to [seeing] things as they truly are. Through that very delusion, through the longing for union with the beloved, one falls away from spiritual urgency, becomes deprived of it. Likewise, through that very attachment, one is burned by that grief — at even a moment's separation. Thus, one is burned, scorched by that very mental anguish, that very torment of mind — through the longing for union with the beloved. The union, the coming together with the beloved — longing for that, craving, which is the cause — through ever-increasing, escalating desire.

body.text: ito 'pyanarthahetureva tatsaṃgatirityāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, that association is nothing but a cause of calamity — he says —

body.text: taccintayā mudhā yāti hrasvamāyurmuhurmuhuḥ /
body.translated_text: Through thinking of that [beloved], the brief life passes away uselessly, again and again.

body.text: tasya priyasya tatsaṃgamasya vā cintayā tadguṇānāṃ sadā paribhāvanayā / kathaṃ nāma mamāsya priyasaṃgamasya vicchittirmā bhūditi tallīnacittatayā vā / niṣphalameva āyuḥsaṃskārāḥ pratikṣaṇaṃ kṣīyante / na ca kvacidapi kuśalakarmaṇi samupayujyante iti bhāvaḥ / na ca yadarthamāyuḥ kśayamupanīyate tanmitraṃ sthiramityata āha-
body.translated_text: Through thinking of that beloved, or of that union — through the constant contemplation of that one's virtues; or through having a mind absorbed in [the thought]: 'How can there be no interruption of my union with the beloved?' — the life-forces are exhausted moment by moment to no avail. And they are never applied to any wholesome action — this is the meaning. And the friend for whose sake one's life is led to exhaustion is not permanent — therefore he says —

body.text: aśāsvatena dharmeṇa dharmo bhraśyati śāśvataḥ // Bca_8.8 //
body.translated_text: Through an impermanent <s>dharma</s>, the permanent <s>Dharma</s> is ruined. // <s>Bca</s> 8.8 //

body.text: avaśyaṃ bhaṅguratayā anavasthānādasthāvareṇa mitreṇa hetunā dharmo bhraśyati parihīyate śāśvato dīrghakālāvasthāyī saṃbhārāntargamāt phalamahattvācca //
body.translated_text: Through a friend who is necessarily unstable — who does not remain due to being perishable — through this cause, the permanent <s>Dharma</s> — lasting for a long time — is ruined, is impaired, since [the opportunity for] the accumulations has passed, and the fruit is great.

body.text: syādetat- avaśyaṃ hi kiṃcittatsaṃgamāddhitasukhanibandhanaṃ prāpyate / tatkimiti sarvathā tanniṣidhyata ityatrāha-
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Surely something beneficial and conducive to happiness is obtained from that association. So why is it entirely prohibited? To this he says —

children.translated_text: One who acts in common with the childish surely goes to lower realms;

children.text: neṣyate viṣabhāgaśca kiṃ prāptaṃ bālasaṃgamāt // Bca_8.9 //
children.translated_text: and if one is dissimilar, one is hated — what is gained from the company of the childish? // <s>Bca</s> 8.9 //

body.text: nāpi tatsaṃgamādanarthamantareṇa kiṃcidaparamiha labhyate / tathā hi bālaiḥ pṛthagjanaiḥ saha sabhāgacaritaḥ samānaśīlaḥ niyatamavaśyaṃ yāti durgatim, tatkarmasadṛśasamācaraṇat, āryadharmabahirbhāvācca / atha āryadharmānuvartanāt tato 'sadṛśakarmakārī syāt, tadā neṣyate dviṣyate visabhāgaśceti asamānacaritaḥ / bālairiti saṃbandhaḥ / atra kartari tṛtīyā / iti ubhayalokabādhanāt kiṃ prāptamadhigataṃ hitasukhanimittaṃ bālasaṃgamāt? naiva kiṃcidityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: Nor is anything other than calamity obtained from that association. For one who acts in common with the childish — with ordinary persons — whose conduct is similar, surely goes to lower realms, due to engaging in conduct similar to their <s>karma</s>, and due to being outside the noble <s>Dharma</s>. But if, through following the noble <s>Dharma</s>, one were to act dissimilarly to them in <s>karma</s>, then one is hated — one is disliked, being of dissimilar conduct. 'By the childish' is the connection. Here the instrumental is in the agentive sense. Thus, since there is harm in both ways, what is gained — what benefit or happiness — from the company of the childish? Nothing at all — this is the meaning.

body.text: na ca anukūlacaritairapi ātmasātkartuṃ śakyā ityāha-
body.translated_text: Nor can they be won over even by acting agreeably — he says —

children.translated_text: In an instant they become friends; in an instant they become enemies;
they become angry even at occasions for pleasure — ordinary persons are hard to please. // <s>Bca</s> 8.10 //

body.text: kṣaṇamātreṇa suhṛdo mitrāṇi bhavanti kiṃcit svaprayojanamuddiśya, kṣaṇādeva ca viṣamābhiprāyatvāt kiṃcinnimittamālambya ta eva ripavaḥ śatravo bhavanti / na ca nimittamapyeṣāṃ niyatam, yat kadācittoṣasthāne prītiviṣaye viparyāsavaśāt prakupyanti / iti durārādhā duḥkhenārādhayituṃ śakyāḥ pṛthagjanāḥ anāryāḥ //
body.translated_text: In a mere instant they become friends, companions, with some personal interest in view; and in an instant, due to having contrary intentions, seizing upon some pretext, those very ones become enemies, adversaries. And their pretexts are not even consistent, for sometimes they become angry even at occasions for pleasure — at objects of delight — due to the force of perversity. Thus ordinary persons, the ignoble, are hard to please — difficult to satisfy.

body.text: aparamapi bāladharmaṃ tadvivarjanārthamupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Showing yet another characteristic of the childish, for the purpose of avoiding them, he says —

children.text: hitamuktāḥ prakupyanti vārayanti ca māṃ hitāt /
children.translated_text: Spoken to for their benefit, they become angry and turn me away from what is beneficial;

children.text: atha na śrūyate teṣāṃ kupitā yānti durgatim // Bca_8.11 //
children.translated_text: and if their [words] are not heeded, they go to lower realms out of anger. // <s>Bca</s> 8.11 //

body.text: idaṃ karaṇīyam, idamakaraṇīyam, ityuktāḥ abhihitāḥ prakupyanti vidviṣanti, na punastaduktaṃ hitamiti gṛhṇanti / pratyuta vārayanti ca māṃ hitāt, kiṃ tava anena kevalaprayāsaphalānuṣṭhāneneti tatra pravṛttaṃ māṃ niṣedhayanti tataḥ / atha na śrūyate teṣāṃ bālānām / vacanamiti śeṣaḥ / yadi tadvacanamavagamya hite pravṛttiḥ kriyate, tadā kupitā asmadvacanānnāyaṃ nivartate iti tasmin hitakarmakāriṇi kopaṃ kṛtvā tatkarmapreritā durgatiṃ prayānti //
body.translated_text: 'This should be done, this should not be done' — having been told, having been advised thus, they become angry, they become hostile; they do not accept what was spoken as beneficial. On the contrary, they turn me away from what is beneficial — 'What is the use for you of this practice whose fruit is merely toil?' — thus they obstruct me, who am engaged in that, from it. And if the words of those childish persons are not heeded — 'words' is to be supplied. If, understanding their words [as wrong], one engages in beneficial activity, then, angered — [thinking] 'this one does not turn away at our word' — having become angry at that doer of beneficial action, driven by that <s>karma</s>, they go to lower realms.

body.text: imaṃ ca bāladharmamaparaṃ tadvivekāya bhāvayedityupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Showing another characteristic of the childish, to be contemplated for the purpose of solitude from them, he says —

children.translated_text: Envy toward superiors, rivalry with equals, arrogance toward inferiors, intoxication from praise,
and hostility from censure — when would benefit ever come from the childish? // <s>Bca</s> 8.12 //

body.text: ātmano vidyākuladhanādibhirutkṛṣṭāduttamādīrṣyā parasaṃpattyasahanatā jāyate / arthātteṣveva / ātmanā samāt tulyād dvandvo vivādaḥ / ātmano hīnādadhamānmānaḥ, ahamitaḥ śreṣṭha ityabhimananāt / stutermadaḥ sadasatāṃ tadguṇānāmākhyānādahaṃ mahīyānityāropādavalepaḥ / avarṇādātmano doṣakīrtanaśravaṇād dveṣaśca / arthādavarṇavādini / ityevaṃ kadā kasmin kāle bāladdhitaṃ bhavet? na kadācidityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: Toward one superior in learning, family, wealth, and such — envy arises, intolerance of another's prosperity — that is, toward those very [superior persons]. Toward one equal to oneself — rivalry, quarreling. Toward one inferior, lower than oneself — arrogance, from the conceit 'I am superior to this one.' From praise — intoxication, haughtiness arising from the proclamation of one's qualities whether real or imagined, [thinking] 'I am great.' From censure — from hearing one's faults proclaimed — anger; that is, toward the one who speaks ill. Thus, when — at what time — would benefit ever come from the childish? Never — this is the meaning.

body.text: ito 'pi bālān parihṛtya viharediti pratipādayitumāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, to demonstrate that one should dwell having avoided the childish, he says —

children.translated_text: Self-aggrandizement, disparagement of others, conversation delighting in <s>saṃsāra</s> —
such and similar unwholesome things inevitably [arise] from one childish person to another. // <s>Bca</s> 8.13 //

body.text: ekasya bālasya aparasmādbālāt ityevamādi kiṃcidaśubhamakuśalamavaśyaṃ niyamena jāyate / kiṃ tat? ātmana utkarṣaḥ prakarṣaḥ śrutajñānādipraśaṃsayā / pareṣāmavarṇo doṣaprakāśanaṃ śrutādipracchādanam / yā saṃsāre ratirabhirāmaḥ tasyāḥ saṃkathā saṃvarṇanam, kāmaguṇānāṃ saṃpramodanāt / ityādi evaṃprakāram //
body.translated_text: From one childish person in relation to another childish person, such and similar unwholesome, unskillful things inevitably, without fail, arise. What are they? Self-aggrandizement — exaltation of oneself through praising one's own learning, knowledge, and such. Disparagement of others — exposing others' faults, concealing their learning and such. The conversation — the glorification — of delight in <s>saṃsāra</s>, through the extolling of sensual pleasures. 'Such and similar' — of this kind.

body.text: evaṃ tasyāpi tatsaṅgāttenānarthasamāgamaḥ /
body.translated_text: Thus, from that association, there is for this one too an encounter with calamity.

body.text: aparasyāpi tatsaṅgāt dvitīyasya saṅgāt kiṃcidaśubhamavaśyaṃ syāt / yena evam, tena kāraṇena anarthasya akalyāṇasya samāgamaḥ saṃprāptireva ayaṃ bālasamāgama / ata āryadharmānuśikṣaṇārtham-
body.translated_text: From the association of the other one too — of the second — some unwholesome thing will inevitably arise. Since this is so — for this reason — this encounter with the childish is an encounter with calamity, with what is unwholesome. Therefore, for the purpose of training in the noble <s>Dharma</s> —

body.text: ekākī vihariṣyāmi sukhamakliṣṭamānasaḥ // Bca_8.14 //
body.translated_text: I shall dwell alone, happily, with unafflicted mind. // <s>Bca</s> 8.14 //

body.text: bālajanasaṃgamaviyuktaḥ advitīyaḥ vihariṣyāmi / tadvivekāt sukham / kriyāviśeṣaṇametat / katham? akliṣṭamānasa iti tatsaṃparkavivarjanāt tatkṛtasaṃkleśābhāvāt / pūrvasmin hetupadametat / yadi vā / sukhaṃ kāyikam / akliṣṭamānasa iti mānasam //
body.translated_text: Separated from the company of childish people, alone, without a second, I shall dwell. 'Happily' — through solitude from them. This qualifies the action. How? 'With unafflicted mind' — because through the avoidance of contact with them, the affliction caused by them is absent. This is the causal clause of the preceding [statement]. Or alternatively: 'happily' refers to the physical; 'with unafflicted mind' refers to the mental.

body.text: tasmādvālajanasaṃparkajaduḥkhaparijihīrṣuṇā tatsaṃgatirna kāryeti kathayitumāha-
body.translated_text: Therefore, for one who wishes to avoid the suffering arising from contact with childish people, one should not keep their company — saying this, he says —

children.translated_text: One should flee far from the childish; when encountered, one should please them with courtesies,
not through the ties of close association, but rather like an impartial good person. // <s>Bca</s> 8.15 //

body.text: bālāt sarvato dūramārāt palāyeta apasaret, yathā taiḥ saha kācidapi saṃgatirna syāt / atha kathaṃciddaivayogādbhavet, tadā prāptaṃ militamārādhayet ārāgayet / priyaiḥ prītikarairupacāraiḥ / ārādhayannapi na saṃstavānubandhena na paricayāsattikaraṇābhiprāyeṇa / yadi vā, na saṃstavānunayena, kiṃ tarhi pratighānunayavarjanādudāsīnasādhuvat sadācāramadhyasthajanavat //
body.translated_text: One should flee far away from the childish, departing from a distance, so that no contact with them whatsoever might occur. If, however, by some stroke of fate it should occur, then one should please — gratify — the one encountered with agreeable, pleasing courtesies. Yet even while pleasing them, not with the intention of forming intimacy — not with the purpose of creating attachment through familiarity. Or alternatively, not with flattering deference, but rather like an indifferent virtuous person, like a well-mannered neutral bystander — [avoiding] the deference of hostility.

body.text: idamaparaṃ sādhujanasamācāraṃ śikṣayitumāha-
body.translated_text: He says this further, to teach the conduct of the virtuous:

children.translated_text: Taking only what is needed for the <s>Dharma</s>, like a bee [takes] honey from a flower,
I shall dwell everywhere as if a stranger, without intimacy. // Bca_8.16 //

body.text: dharmāyedaṃ dharmārtham, tadeva kevalaṃ tanmātram / tadādāya gṛhītvā / sārādānaṃ kṛtvetyarthaḥ / bhṛṅgavat cañcarīkavat / madhu makarandam / yadi vā / dharma eva arthaḥ prayojanamasya cīvarapiṇḍapātāderiti vigrahaḥ / bālasaṃparkavimukhaḥ apūrva iva navacandropamaḥ sarvatra deśe sthāne vā vihariṣyāmi / asaṃstutaḥ aparicitaḥ / tannivāsijanaiḥ pratyāsattirahita ityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'For the sake of <s>Dharma</s>' — this is for the <s>Dharma</s>; that alone, nothing else, is 'mere' — only that. Having taken that — having extracted the essence, is the meaning. Like a bee — like a <s>bhṛṅga</s>. 'Honey' is nectar. Or alternatively: the <s>Dharma</s> itself is the purpose of robes, alms-food, and such — this is the analysis of the compound. Averse to association with the childish, as if a stranger — like a new moon — I shall dwell everywhere, in every country or place. 'Without intimacy' — unfamiliar; meaning without closeness to the residents of that place.

body.text: tadevaṃ priyasaṃgatikāraṇaṃ snehamapākṛtya sāṃprataṃ lābhāditṛṣṇā lokāparityāgakāraṇaṃ parihartavyetyupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Having thus set aside affection — the cause of attachment to dear companions — he now shows that craving for gain and such, which causes non-renunciation of the world, should be abandoned, saying:

children.translated_text: 'I have gains, I am honored, and many desire me' —
for a mortal, from the arrival of death, fear arises from such [thinking]. // Bca_8.17 //

body.text: lābho vidyate 'syeti cīvarapiṇḍapātādilābhayogāllābhī ca aham / satkṛtaśca pūjito janaiḥ / icchanti abhilaṣanti bahavaśca aneke mām / bahujanasaṃmato 'hamityarthaḥ / ityevaṃ cintayataḥ evaṃ martyasya manuṣyasya maraṇājjāyate bhayam / kiṃbhūtāt? saṃprāptāt acintitopasthitāt //
body.translated_text: 'One who has gain' — gain exists for him — through being endowed with gains of robes, alms-food, and such; 'and I am honored' — worshipped by people. 'Many desire me' — many, numerous people long for me; meaning, 'I am esteemed by the multitude.' For one thinking thus — for such a mortal, a human being — from death, fear arises. Of what kind? 'Arrived' — having come without being anticipated.

children.text: yatra yatra ratiṃ yāti manaḥ sukhavimohitam /
children.translated_text: Whatever the mind, deluded by pleasure, takes delight in,
that very thing, multiplied a thousandfold, becomes suffering and presents itself. // Bca_8.18 //
Therefore, the wise one should not desire that; for from desire, fear arises.

children.text: svayameva ca yātyetadvairyaṃ kṛtvā pratīkṣatām // Bca_8.19 //
children.translated_text: And this [gain] goes away of its own accord — having made firm [resolve], let one watch. // Bca_8.19 //
Many have been gainful, and many have been famous;

children.text: saha lābhayaśobhiste na jñātāḥ kka gatā iti // Bca_8.20 //
children.translated_text: together with their gain and fame, they are not known — where have they gone? // Bca_8.20 //
Others despise me — why should I rejoice when praised?

children.text: māmevānye praśaṃsanti kiṃ viṣīdāmi ninditaḥ // Bca_8.21 //
children.translated_text: Others praise me — why should I be despondent when blamed? // Bca_8.21 //
Beings are of diverse dispositions — even the <s>Jinas</s> could not satisfy them;
how much less an ignorant one like me — therefore, what use is concern for the world? // Bca_8.22 //

body.text: * * * * * * iti sarvadā avaśyaṃbhāvimaraṇamanasikārāt kiṃ lokasya bālajanasya cintayā caritaparibhāvanayā? na kiṃcit prayojanam, anupādeyatvāditi bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: * * * * * * Thus, from the constant reflection on the certainty of death, what use is concern for — reflection on the conduct of — the childish folk of the world? There is no purpose, since they are not worth accepting — this is the meaning.

body.text: itthamapi bālajanasaṃgatirduḥkhaheturevetyāha-
body.translated_text: Even in this way, association with the childish is nothing but a cause of suffering — he says:

children.translated_text: They blame one who is without gain, and disparage one who has gain;

children.text: prakṛtyā duḥkhasaṃvāsaiḥ kathaṃ tairjāyate ratiḥ // Bca_8.23 //
children.translated_text: how can delight arise from those whose companionship is by nature painful? // Bca_8.23 //

body.text: nindanti kutsayanti alābhinaṃ lābhavirahitaṃ sattvam / akṛtapuṇyo 'yaṃ varākaḥ, yena ayaṃ piṇḍapātādimātrakamapi naiva aparikleśena prāpnotīti / lābhinaṃ punaravadhyāyanti prasannairdāyakadānapatibhiścīvarādipradānaiḥ pūjitam / kuhanādibhirapi dāyakadānapatīn prasādyacīvarādilābhamāsādayati / anyathā kimanyasya tathāvidhā guṇā na santi, yena ayameva varaṃ labhate nāparaḥ, iti asmiṃścittamaprasādayanti, vacanaṃ caivamudgiranti / iti ubhayathāpi tebhyo na cetasi śāntirasti / tadevaṃ prakṛtyā svabhāvena duḥkhahetutvāt duḥkhaṃ saṃvāso yeṣāṃ bālānāṃ te tathā / taistathāvidhaiḥ saha saṃvasataḥ kathaṃ jāyate ratiḥ? naivetyarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: They blame — censure — a being who is without gain, devoid of material possessions: 'This wretched one has done no merit, which is why he cannot obtain even mere alms-food without hardship.' But they disparage even one who has gain — one who is honored by faithful donors and patrons through offerings of robes and such: 'He obtains gains of robes and such by winning over donors and patrons through hypocrisy and such means. Otherwise, why does he alone receive the best and not another, since no such qualities exist in him?' — thus they make their minds displeased toward him and utter such speech. Therefore in both cases there is no peace of mind from them. Thus, since by nature — by their very essence — they are causes of suffering, those childish ones for whom companionship is suffering are such. How can delight arise from dwelling together with such [people]? It does not — this is the meaning.

body.text: [na ca bālo dṛḍhasuhṛdbhavati / yasmānna bāla ityāha-
body.translated_text: [Nor is the childish one a steadfast friend. Since the childish one is not — he says:

children.translated_text: 'The childish one is no one's friend' — thus it is declared by the <s>Tathāgatas</s>;

children.text: na svārthena vinā prītiryasmādvālasya jāyate // Bca_8.24 //
children.translated_text: for the affection of the childish does not arise apart from self-interest. // Bca_8.24 //
The affection that arises through the door of self-interest — that is self-interested affection alone;

children.text: dravyanāśe yathodvegaḥ sukhahānikṛto hi saḥ // Bca_8.25 //
children.translated_text: just as the distress at the loss of wealth is caused by the loss of happiness. // Bca_8.25 //

body.text: mitramiti suhṛt / uktaṃ tathāgatenetyāgameṣu uktam / kasmāt? yasmāt svaprayojanena vinā bālasya na karhicidapi prītirjāyate / tasmāt tadabhāve viparyayaḥ / tadapi bālasaṃvāse satyapi na nirdiṣṭam (?) tatra maitrīkṛtenāpi pṛthagjanasya prītiraśakyā //
body.translated_text: 'Friend' means a well-wisher. 'Declared by the <s>Tathāgata</s>' — stated in the scriptures. Why? Because the affection of the childish never arises apart from self-interest. Therefore, in its absence, the opposite [occurs]. Even in the case of association with the childish, this has not been explicitly indicated (?); therein, even affection motivated by friendliness is impossible for an ordinary being.

body.text: evaṃ sati tatsaṃvāsodbhūtadoṣaparihārārthaṃ sukhena] saumanasyena ca vihārāya vivekakāmena mayā araṇyaniṣevaṇāya yatitavyamiti tadanuśaṃsāṃ darśayannāha-
body.translated_text: This being so, for the purpose of avoiding the faults arising from association with them and for dwelling in happiness] and cheerfulness, one who desires solitude should exert oneself for the practice of dwelling in the forest — showing its benefits, he says:

body.text: nāvadhyāyanti taravo na cārādhyāḥ prayatnataḥ

children.text: kadā taiḥ sukhasaṃvāsaiḥ saha vāso bhavenmama // Bca_8.26 //
children.translated_text: when will I dwell together with those whose companionship is happy? // Bca_8.26 //

body.translated_text: Trees do not disparage, nor must they be propitiated with effort —

body.text: taravo vṛkṣāḥ nāvadhyāyanti, na ca ārādhyāḥ ārādhayitavyāḥ prayatnata iti / tadanukūlasamācaraṇena araṇyādiṣu vasatā viṣamābhiprāyarahitatvāt / iti kadā taistarubhiḥ saha vāso bhavenmama? kibhūtaiḥ sukhasaṃvāsairityāśaṃsati / sukhahetutvāt sukhamiti pūrvavat //
body.translated_text: Trees — forest trees — do not disparage, and they need not be propitiated — need not be gratified — with effort; that is, through acting in accordance with their wishes, since for one dwelling in forests and such, there is no crooked intent. Thus, when will I dwell together with those trees? Of what kind? Those whose companionship is happy — he yearns. 'Happy' because they are causes of happiness — as before.

body.text: punarekākitāvihāre 'bhiratimāha-
body.translated_text: Again, he expresses his delight in solitary dwelling:

children.translated_text: Having stayed in an empty temple, at the root of a tree, or in caves,
when shall I go without concern, not looking back? // Bca_8.27 //

body.text: śūnyadevakule janasaṃkīrṇatārahite sthitvā nivasya rātrimekāmuṣitvā dve vā, yathābhilāṣaṃ vṛkṣamūle vṛkṣasyādhastāt / parvatādiṣu guhyapradeśā guhāḥ, tatra vā / anapekṣaḥ kadā yāsyāmi? āsaṅgasthānasya kasyacidabhāvāt / ata eva pṛṣṭhato 'navalokayan paścādanirvṛterabhāvāt //
body.translated_text: Having stayed — having dwelt — in an empty temple, free from the crowding of people, for one night or two, as one wishes; at the root of a tree — beneath a tree; caves are hidden places in mountains and such — or there. Without concern — when shall I go? Due to the absence of any place of attachment. For this very reason, not looking back — because there is no dissatisfaction upon departure.

body.text: punaranyathā prāha-
body.translated_text: He speaks again in another way:

children.translated_text: In these regions, vast by nature,
when shall I dwell, wandering freely, without a fixed abode? // Bca_8.28 //

body.text: kenacidvirodhakāriṇā purvamasvīkṛteṣu / vistīrṇeṣu vipuleṣu saumanasyakāriṣu / svabhāvataḥ svayameva tathāvidheṣu, na kṛtrimatayā / vihariṣyāmyahaṃ kadā ityāśāste / evaṃ viharato yatsukhaṃ tadupadarśayannāha- svacchanda cārī na paratantravṛttiḥ / anilayaḥ na vidyate nilayaḥ ālayaḥ nirāsaṅgatayā yasyeti anilayaḥ, kvacidapi svīkārābhāvāt / tathābhūtaḥ pratibaddho na kasyacit / śeṣaḥ subodhaḥ //
body.translated_text: Not previously claimed by anyone hostile. 'Vast' — expansive, producing cheerfulness. 'By nature' — naturally such, not artificially [made]. 'When shall I dwell' — he yearns. Showing the happiness of one dwelling thus, he says: wandering freely — not dependent on others in conduct. 'Without a fixed abode' — no abode, no dwelling exists, due to non-attachment: such is one who has no home, because of the absence of appropriation anywhere. Being thus, one is bound to no one. The rest is easily understood.

body.text: punarevamalpecchatayā āśaṃsanīyamityādarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Again, showing that this is to be wished for through having few wants, he says:

children.translated_text: With possessions consisting of merely an earthen bowl, wearing a robe useless to thieves,
when shall I dwell fearlessly, not guarding [my] body? // Bca_8.29 //

body.text: mṛtpātraṃ muṇmayaṃ bhikṣābhājanam, tadeva kevalaṃ tanmātraṃ vibhavo dhanaṃ yasyeti / tathā caurāṇāmasaṃbhogyaṃ pāṃsukūlāmbarakṛtatvādaparibhogyam / anupayuktamiti yāvat / tādṛśaṃ cīvaraṃ vāso yasya sa tathā / etaddvayamapi parairahāryam / ata eva nirbhayaḥ kāyajīvitanirapekṣatayā ca / tadeva darśayati- kāyamagopayanniti / bāhyādhyātmikasya parigrahāgrahasyābhāvāt asaṃrakṣayan //
body.translated_text: An earthen bowl — a begging vessel made of clay — that alone, nothing else, is 'mere' — constituting [his] sole wealth, possessions. And a robe that cannot be enjoyed by thieves — that cannot be used — because it is made of cast-off rags; meaning it is of no use [to them]. Such a robe, garment, belongs to him who is thus. Both of these cannot be taken by others. For this very reason, fearless — and through indifference toward body and life. That very [point] he shows: 'not guarding the body' — because of the absence of grasping at external and internal possessions, not protecting [it].

body.text: iyamanityatā ca āsaṅgaparityāgasya kāraṇaṃ sarvadā sevitavyeti vṛttatritayenopadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: And this impermanence should always be cultivated as the reason for abandoning attachment — showing this through three verses, he says:

children.translated_text: Having gone to the charnel ground, my body's own ground, together with other skeletons,
when shall I compare my own body, subject to decay, [with them]? // Bca_8.30 //

children.text: ayameva hi kāyo me evaṃ pūtirbhaviṣyati /
children.translated_text: For this very body of mine will become thus putrid,
such that even jackals would not approach nearby because of its stench. // Bca_8.31 //
Even the bone fragments born together with this single body

children.text: pṛthak pṛthaggamiṣyanti kimutānyaḥ priyo janaḥ // Bca_8.32 //
children.translated_text: will go their separate ways — how much more so another dear person! // Bca_8.32 //

body.text: kāyabhūmiṃ nijāmiti śmaśānabhūmim, ciramapi sthitvā tatparyavasānatvāccharīrasya / kaṅkālairaparairiti pūrvamṛtānāmasthibhiḥ pañjaraiḥ / śatanaṃ pūtibhāvaḥ, taddharmiṇaṃ tatsvabhāvam / tāmeva tulanāṃ kathayati- ayameva hītyādinā / evamiti aparakaṅkālagalitaśarīrasādṛśyamucyate / pūtiḥ kutsito bhaviṣyati / kīdṛśa ityāha- śṛgālā ityādi / atidurgandhatayā tadāhāraparāyaṇānāṃ gomāyūnāmapi duḥsaha iti / itthamapi priyasya saṃgatiranityetyāha- asyaikasyāpītyādi / asya upāttasyaikasya ekatvena kalpitasyāpi kāyasya / sahajāḥ kāyena sahajātāḥ asthikhaṇḍakāḥ pṛthak pṛthagbhaviṣyanti / visaṃyuktā bhaviṣyantītyarthaḥ / kimutānyaḥ priyo janaḥ pṛthag na bhaviṣyati, yaḥ sarvadā visaṃyukta evāste //
body.translated_text: 'My body's own ground' — the cremation ground, because it is the final destination of the body even after long [life]. 'With other skeletons' — with the bone-cages of those previously deceased. '<s>Śatana</s>' means putrefaction; 'subject to that' means having that as its nature. He states that very comparison: 'For this very [body]' and so forth. 'Thus' refers to the resemblance to other skeletons' decomposed bodies. '[It] will become putrid' — loathsome. Of what kind? — he says: 'even jackals' and so forth. Due to its extreme foulness, it is unbearable even for jackals, who are devoted to such food. Even so, the companionship of the beloved is impermanent — he says: 'even [the bones] of this single [body]' and so forth. Of this appropriated body, conceived of as one, even the bone fragments — born together with the body — will go their separate ways. They will become disjoined — this is the meaning. How much more will another dear person not go separately — one who is already always disjoined!

body.text: syādetat- sukhaduḥkhasahāyāḥ sadā mamaite putradārādayaḥ / tadeṣu yukta evānunayaḥ kartumityāha-
body.translated_text: One might say: these sons, wives, and such are always my companions in happiness and suffering — therefore devotion toward them is indeed justified. To this he says:

children.text: eka utpadyate janturmriyate caika eva hi /
children.translated_text: A being is born alone, and dies alone indeed;
no other has a share in that suffering — what use are dear ones who create obstacles? // Bca_8.33 //

body.text: janmamaraṇayorna kaścit kasyacidduḥkhasaṃbhāgī syāt / antarāle ca svakarmopahitameva sukhaduḥkhamupabhuñjate sarve / ato 'bhimānamātramevaitat / yato nānyasya tadātmano vyatiriktasya tadvayathābhāgaḥ / tasyānunayakāriṇo vyathā, tasyā bhāgaḥ pratyaṃśo jāyate, tasya sā, tenaiva tasyāḥ saṃvedyamānatvāt / ato na kiṃcit prayojanaṃ priyaiḥ kuśalapakṣavighātakāribhiḥ //
body.translated_text: In birth and death, no one is a sharer in anyone's suffering. And in the interval, all experience only the happiness and suffering produced by their own <s>karma</s>. Therefore this [attachment] is mere conceit. Since no other — distinct from oneself — has a share of that suffering: the suffering of the one who expresses devotion, a share — a portion — of that arises for him, it belongs to him, since it is experienced by him alone. Therefore there is no purpose in dear ones who create obstacles to the wholesome side.

body.text: paramārthato na kasyacit kenacit saṃgatirastītyupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Showing that ultimately no one has any [real] companionship with anyone, he says:

children.translated_text: Just as for one who has set out on a journey, there is the taking up of a temporary lodging,
so too for one traveling through existence, there is the taking up of lodging in a birth. // Bca_8.34 //

body.text: mārgaprasthitasya kāṃciddiśaṃ gantumudyatasya yathā aparairadhvagaiḥ saha ekasminnāvāse kvacinmaṇḍapādau vā āvāsaparigraho bhavati, tathā saṃsāre 'pi karmāyattagateḥ saṃsarato jñātisagotrasālohitādibhirekasmin janmani āvāsaparigraho jāyate / punarapi tatparityajya kvacidekākitayā yāti / na ca tatra kecitsahāyāstamanugacchanti / ato na kenacit kasyacidvāstavī saṃgatiḥ saṃbhavati / tasmānnānarthasahasropanetrīṃ svayamupakalpya kenacit saṃgatiṃ kuryāt //
body.translated_text: For one who has set out on a road — one preparing to travel in some direction — just as there is the taking up of lodging with other travelers in some shelter or pavilion, so too in <s>saṃsāra</s>, for one transmigrating whose destination is determined by <s>karma</s>, together with kinsmen, clansmen, and blood-relatives, there is the taking up of lodging in a single birth. Then again, abandoning them, one goes somewhere alone. And no companions follow him there. Therefore no real companionship with anyone is possible. Hence one should not, by fashioning for oneself a companionship that leads to thousands of misfortunes, form attachments with anyone.

body.text: tadevamabhidhāya saṃgatidoṣam, ekākitāyāḥ punarime guṇā iti vṛttatritayenopadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Having thus described the faults of companionship, he shows through three verses that solitude has these virtues, saying:

children.translated_text: Before one is carried out by four men,

children.text: āśocyamāno lokena tāvadeva vanaṃ vrajet // Bca_8.35 //
children.translated_text: while the world still mourns — let one go to the forest then and there. // Bca_8.35 //
Through absence of both intimacy and enmity, alone in body,

children.text: pūrvameva mṛto loke mriyamāṇo na śocati // Bca_8.36 //
children.translated_text: already dead to the world, when dying one does not grieve. // Bca_8.36 //
And no one standing nearby, grieving, causes distress.

children.text: buddhādyanusmṛtiṃ cāsya vikṣipanti na kecana // Bca_8.37 //
children.translated_text: and no one disturbs his recollection of the <s>Buddha</s> and such. // Bca_8.37 //

body.text: avaśyamanicchannapi idānīṃ jīvadavasthāyāṃ maraṇamupagato balāttyājayitavyo [gṛhāvāsaḥ / tasmādevaṃ svayaṃ jīvanneva tyaktumarhati / tata iti gṛhāt /] āśocyamānaḥ hā vatsetyādivilāpavacanaiḥ paridevyamānaḥ lokena bandhuprabhṛtinā tāvadeva tataḥ pūrvameva vanaṃ vrajet / kaḥ punaratra guṇaviśeṣa ityāha- asaṃstavetyādi / anunayapratighābhāvāt mriyamāṇo na śocati, śokopajanitaduḥkhabhāgī na bhavati / kutaḥ? pūrvameva mṛto loke / yadaiva gṛhānniṣkrāntaḥ, tadaiva svajanabāndhavādau lokaviṣaye / ayamaparo guṇastasyetyāha- na cāntikacarā ityādi / antikacarāḥ samīpavartino jñātisagotrādayastadviyogāturāḥ śocantaḥ śokamupajanayantaḥ na ca naiva kurvate vyathām, ātmanaḥ kāyamanasoḥ pīḍām / yadi vā / teṣāṃ śokaṃ paśyato mriyamāṇasya manastāpam / na kevalamayameva guṇaḥ, api tu buddhādyanusmṛtiṃ ādiśabdāddharmādyanusmṛtim,tattvālambanamanaskāraṃ vā / asyeti janasaṃparkavivekacāriṇo maraṇasamaye //
body.translated_text: Inevitably, even unwillingly, at the time of death one will be forcibly made to abandon [household life]. Therefore one should voluntarily abandon it while still living. 'From there' — from the house. Being lamented — with wailing words such as 'Alas, dear one!' — mourned by the world, by relatives and such — [instead] one should go to the forest even before that. What then is the particular virtue in this? — he says: 'without familiarity' and so forth. Due to the absence of affection and aversion, the dying one does not grieve; one does not become a partaker of suffering produced by grief. Why? Because one has already died to the world; from the very moment one went forth from the household, [one is dead] to one's own people and relatives and such in the worldly domain. This is yet another virtue — he says: 'nor do those dwelling near' and so forth. Those dwelling near — relatives, clansmen, and such — being stricken with grief at separation from him, do not cause him — and they certainly do not — distress, torment of body and mind. Or alternatively: the mental anguish of the dying one who sees their grief. Not only this virtue, but also: the recollection of the <s>Buddha</s> and such — by the word 'such,' the recollection of the <s>Dharma</s> and such, or meditative attention with reality as its object. 'His' — of one who dwells in seclusion from contact with people, at the time of death. //

body.text: tasmādityādinā upasaṃharati-
body.translated_text: With 'therefore' and so forth, he concludes —

children.translated_text: Therefore, solitude — delightful, effortless, auspicious in its arising,
the pacifier of all distraction — should be cultivated by me always. // Bca_8.38 //

body.text: ekākitā anāsaṅgavihāritā / ramyā sukhahetutvāt / nirāyāsā duḥkhavipakṣatvāt / śivodayā niḥśreyasāvāhakatvāt / sarvavikṣepaśamanī sarvavikṣepasya kāyavāṅmānasikasya durācārasya śamanī nivartanī samādhānahetutvāt / sevitavyā mayā sadeti / atraiva abhiniveśena āsaṅgaḥ kārya ityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Solitude' — dwelling without attachment. 'Delightful' — because it is a cause of happiness. 'Effortless' — because it is opposed to suffering. 'Auspicious in its arising' — because it brings about the highest good. 'Pacifier of all distraction' — the calmer, the averter of all distraction — physical, verbal, and mental misconduct — because it is the cause of mental composure. 'Should be cultivated by me always': the meaning is that attachment should be directed here alone, with resolve. //

body.text: tadevaṃ janasaṃparkavivarjanāt kāyavivekaṃ pratipādya cittavivekaṃ pratipādayitumāha-
body.translated_text: Having thus established physical seclusion through the avoidance of contact with people, to teach mental seclusion, he says —

children.translated_text: Freed from all other thoughts, with mind single-pointedly [focused] on my own mind,

children.text: samādhānāya cittasya prayatiṣye damāya ca // Bca_8.39 //
children.translated_text: I shall strive for the composure of the mind and for its restraint. // Bca_8.39 //

body.text: sarvā yā anyacintā asadvitarkasvabhāvāḥ, tābhirnirmuktaḥ, tadvirahitaḥ / svacittaikāgramānasaḥ svacittameva ekamagraṃ pradhānaṃ yasmin mānase manasikāre tat tathoktam, tādṛśaṃ mānasaṃ yasya sa tathā / svacittaṃ vā ekāgramekāyattaṃ tatpracāravyavalokanatatparaṃ niyatālambanapratibaddhaṃ vā mānasaṃ yasyeti samāsaḥ / tathābhūtaḥ samādhānāya cittasya śamathāya prayatiṣye, tatparāyaṇo bhaviṣyāmi / tadekāgratāyāṃ niyojayiṣyāmītyarthaḥ / damāya ceti punaḥpunastatraivālambane niyojanāya, bahirvikṣepanivāraṇāya vā //
body.translated_text: 'All other thoughts' — those of the nature of unwholesome conceptualizations — freed from them, that is, devoid of them. 'With mind single-pointedly on my own mind' — the mental attention in which one's own mind alone is the single, principal [object] — that is what is thus called; one whose mental [disposition] is such, he is thus. Or alternatively: the compound [means] one whose mental attention is single-pointedly devoted to one's own mind — intent upon observing its movements, or bound to a fixed object. Being thus, 'for the composure of the mind' — for <s>śamatha</s> (tranquility) — I shall strive; I shall become devoted to it. The meaning is: I shall engage it in that single-pointedness. 'And for restraint' — for repeatedly directing it back to that very object, or for the prevention of outward distraction. //

body.text: tatra cittasamādhānasya vipakṣatvāt kāmavitarkaṃ nivārayitumāha-
body.translated_text: Therein, to ward off thoughts of desire, which are opposed to mental composure, he says —

children.text: kāmā hyanarthajanakā iha loke paratra ca /
children.translated_text: For desires are generators of harm, in this world and in the next;
in this world through imprisonment, killing, and dismemberment; and in the hells and such in the next. // Bca_8.40 //

body.text: aprahīṇabhavasaṃyojanaiḥ kamanīyatayā adhyavasitatvāt kāmā rūpādayo viṣayā ucyante / hiśabdo yasmādarthe / tasmādudvijya kāmebhyaḥ [8.85] iti vakṣyamāṇena saṃbandhaḥ / te ca sevyamānā anarthajanakā a........ yadarthaṃ dūtadūtīnāṃ kṛtāñjaliranekadhā /

children.text: na ca pāpamakīrtirvā yadarthaṃ gaṇitā purā // Bca_8.41 //
children.translated_text: and neither sin nor infamy was formerly considered [a deterrent] for whose sake. // Bca_8.41 //

body.translated_text: For those who have not abandoned the fetters of existence, sense-objects — forms and such — are called 'desires' (<s>kāma</s>) because they are determined to be desirable. The word 'for' (<s>hi</s>) is in the sense of 'because.' The connection is with the statement to come: 'therefore, being repelled by desires' [8.85]. And these, when indulged in, are generators of harm... For whose sake, with folded hands in many ways, to messengers male and female;

children.translated_text: And one has even cast oneself into danger, and wealth has been squandered.
Those very [limbs] which, embraced, produced the highest bliss — // Bca_8.42 //
those are nothing but bones, no different [from other bones], ownerless, belonging to no one;

children.text: prakāmaṃ saṃpariṣvajya kiṃ na gacchasi nirvṛtim // Bca_8.43 //
children.translated_text: embracing them to your heart's content, why do you not go to [the same] bliss? // Bca_8.43 //
That face which had to be lifted up with effort, drawn downward by modesty,

children.text: purā dṛṣṭamadṛṣṭaṃ vā mukhaṃ jālikayāvṛtam // Bca_8.44 //
children.translated_text: which was formerly seen or unseen, veiled by a covering — // Bca_8.44 //
that very face, as if those unable to bear your torment [are now revealing it],
is now laid bare by vultures — look! Why do you now flee? // Bca_8.45 //
That which was guarded even from the glances of others' eyes —

children.text: tadadya bhakṣitaṃ yāvat kimīrṣyālo na rakṣasi // Bca_8.46 //
children.translated_text: now that it is being devoured, why do you not guard it, jealous one? // Bca_8.46 //
Seeing this heap of flesh being devoured by vultures and others,
the food of others is being worshipped with garlands, sandalwood, and ornaments? // Bca_8.47 //

body.text: ........rūpaḥ / pūjyate tvayā stragādibhiḥ / tairgṛdhrairanyaiśca gomāyuprabhṛtibhirmāṃsocchrayaṃ māṃsapuñjamimaṃ bhakṣitaṃ bībhatsaṃ dṛṣṭvā kimīrṣyālo na rakṣasīti yojayitavyam / kimidānīṃ palāyase iti vā vyavahitena saṃbandhaḥ //
body.translated_text: ...of such form. It is worshipped by you with garlands and such. Having seen that heap of flesh — this mound of flesh — being devoured by vultures and others such as jackals and the like, the repulsive [sight] — 'Why do you, jealous one, not guard it?' — this is how it should be construed. Or alternatively, the connection is with the separated [phrase]: 'Why do you now flee?' //

body.text: nanu idamapi praṣṭavyo bhavānityāha-
body.translated_text: Surely this too you should be asked — he says —

body.text: niścalādapi te trāsaḥ kaṅkālādevamīkṣitāt /
body.translated_text: You are frightened even by a motionless skeleton thus seen;

body.text: niścalādapi kāṣṭhaloṣṭhasamānāt tava trāso jāyate iti kākkā pṛcchati / kaṅkālāt asthipañjarāt / evamapi bībhatsarūpāt īkṣitāt dṛṣṭāt yadi vā evaṃ trāsaḥ / yaddūrādapi dūrataraṃ palāyase iti yojanīyam / yadevaṃ calataḥ kathaṃ na trāsa ityāha-
body.translated_text: Even from a motionless [skeleton], equal to a piece of wood or a clod of earth, fear arises in you — [the author] asks mockingly. From a skeleton — from a cage of bones. 'Thus' — even from one of such repulsive form, when seen — if fear [arises]. The construal should be: you flee even farther away. If this is so from the motionless, how is there no fear from the moving? — he says —

body.text: vetāleneva kenāpi cālyamānādbhayaṃ na kim // Bca_8.48 //
body.translated_text: why is there no fear of one being moved about as if by a zombie? // Bca_8.48 //

body.text: bhūtagraheṇa cālyamānāt jīvataścalataḥ kiṃ na bhayaṃ bhavati? tasmādatiśayena bhayaṃ yuktamityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: From one being moved about by a spirit-possession — from a living, moving [body] — why is there no fear? Therefore, fear is all the more justified — this is the meaning. //

body.text: evaṃ tāvajjugupsanīyatāṃ pratipādya punaranyathā pratipādayitumāha-
body.translated_text: Having thus established [the body's] repulsive nature, to demonstrate [it] in yet another way, he says —

children.translated_text: From the same food, saliva and excrement are produced;

children.text: tatrāmedhyamaniṣṭaṃ te lālāpānaṃ kathaṃ priyam // Bca_8.49 //
children.translated_text: when excrement is disliked by you, how is the drinking of saliva dear? // Bca_8.49 //

body.text: yo hi nāma mohāvṛtaviveko rāgaviṣamūrcchitacaitanyaḥ, tasya atikamanīyatayā kāminīvadanamadhupānabuddhayā tanmukhavigalallālāpānābhilāṣiṇaḥ / paryanuyogamāha- ekameva kāraṇaṃ dvayorapyāhārapānasvabhāvāt / tatra tayormadhye amedhyaṃ purīṣamapriyaṃ bhavataḥ / lālāyāḥ śleṣmaṇaḥ pānaṃ kathaṃ priyam? kena prakāreṇa tatrābhiratirnānyatra? dvayorapi yukteti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: For one whose discernment is covered by delusion, whose consciousness is poisoned by passion — with the notion of drinking honey from the mouth of a beloved woman, desiring to drink the saliva dripping from her mouth — he poses a reproach: the cause of both [saliva and excrement] is one and the same, being of the nature of food and drink. Between those two, excrement — feces — is disliked by you. Then how is the drinking of saliva — of phlegm — dear? By what means is there delight in the one but not the other? The purport is: both are alike. //

body.text: athāpi syāt- yadyapi dvayorapi kāraṇamabhinnam, tathāpi tasminnatidurgandhatayā vaimukhyam, itarasmiṃstu tadabhāvātprītiriti / tadetadapi na samyagabhidhānamityupapādayannāha-
body.translated_text: But one might say: even though the cause of both is the same, still, because the one [excrement] is extremely foul-smelling, there is aversion toward it, while toward the other [saliva], because of the absence of that [foul smell], there is delight. That this is not a sound argument either — establishing this, he says —

children.translated_text: Those lustful ones do not delight in cushions filled with cotton, [which are] soft to the touch;
'They do not emit a foul smell' — [thinking thus,] they are deluded by impurity. // Bca_8.50 //

body.text: kārpāsāditūlaparipūritairmasūrakādibhirūpadhānaiḥ sukumārasparśaiḥ kāmino na ramante, na dhṛtimadhivāsayanti / kutaḥ? daurgandhyamaśuciniṣyandaṃ na muñcantīti kṛtvā aśuciparipūrite strīkalevare eva ramante / etadapi kutaḥ? kāminaḥ kāmasukhābhilāṣiṇaḥ amedhyamohitā yataḥ / hetupadametat / amedhyaviṣaye amedhyena vā mohitāḥ / aśucau śuciviparyāsāt tatraiva atiśayavatīmabhiratimanubhavanti //
body.translated_text: In cushions — such as <s>masūraka</s> and others — filled with cotton from cotton-plants and such, of delicate touch, the lustful ones do not delight, do not find contentment. Why? Because [those cushions] do not discharge foulness — the flow of impurities — thinking thus, they delight only in the body of a woman, which is filled with impurities. And why is this? Because they are lustful — desiring sensual pleasure — deluded by impurity. This is the causal statement. Deluded regarding the impure object, or deluded by the impure [itself] — through the perversion of [seeing] the pure in the impure, they experience surpassing delight in that very [impure body]. //

body.text: syādetat- yadi nāma aśucitvamamedhye strīkalevare ca sādhāraṇam, tathāpi tadekatra vivṛtamanyatra pracchāditam / atastadanyaparihāreṇa asminnabhiṣvaṅgaḥ ityatrāha-
body.translated_text: One might say: even if impurity is common to both the impure [excrement] and the female body, still, in one case it is exposed while in the other it is concealed. Therefore, avoiding the one, there is attachment to the other — to this he says —

children.translated_text: If this passion [exists] even when [the body is] covered, why is the uncovered [body] not pleasing?

children.text: na cetprayojanaṃ tena kasmācchannaṃ vimṛdyate // Bca_8.51 //
children.translated_text: If there is no use for the uncovered, why do you caress the covered? // Bca_8.51 //

body.text: yasminnamedhyasvabhāve pracchāditarūpe / adṛṣṭe 'pīti yāvat / etādṛśo 'bhiṣvaṅgaḥ, tadacchannaṃ dṛśyatāṃ gatamatiśayena prītikaramupajāyate ityucitam / tat kimiti tathābhūtamapriyaṃ bhavataḥ? atha tathābhūte sarvathā vaimukhyameva te nācchannena kiṃcit prayojanaṃ tavāsti / yadyevam, tarhi kasmāddhetoḥ channaṃ viśeṣeṇa mṛdyate, tadanyaparihāreṇa tasyaiva ghaṭanāya yatnaḥ kriyate?
