body.translated_text: 'In what is of impure nature, in covered form' — even when unseen, so to speak. If such attachment [exists], then when it is uncovered — brought to view — it is fitting that delight should arise all the more. So why is it displeasing to you when in such a state? If, however, there is complete aversion toward the uncovered, and the uncovered is of no use to you — if this is so, then for what reason is the covered caressed with particular attention — why is effort made to obtain that very thing, while avoiding the other?

body.text: api ca / idamapi praṣṭavyastvam- kiṃ bhavānaśucivirāgo na veti / atra prathamaṃ vikalpamadhikṛtyāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, you should also be asked this: are you averse to the impure or not? Regarding the first alternative, he says —

body.text: yadi te nāśucau rāgaḥ kasmādāliṅgase 'param /
body.translated_text: If you have no passion for the impure, why do you embrace another —

body.text: yadi bhavataḥ aśucau na rāgaḥ, na sarvathā āsaṅgo 'sti, tarhi kasmādāliṅgase apara manyam? kiṃ tadityāha-
body.translated_text: If you have no passion for the impure, if there is no attachment whatsoever, then why do you embrace the other? What is it? — he says —

body.text: māṃsakardamasaṃliptaṃ snāyubaddhāsthipañjaram // Bca_8.52 //
body.translated_text: a cage of bones bound with sinews, plastered with the mud of flesh? // Bca_8.52 //

body.text: māṃsameva kardama iva lepanasādharmyāt, tena liptamupadigdham / kimevaṃbhūtamiti cet, snāyubaddhāsthipañjaram, snāyvābaddhaṃ saṅgīkṛtam, āyattīkṛtam asthipañjaram asthisaṃkalam / anyathā khaṇḍaśo viśakalitaṃ syāt, iti virāgaviṣayatāmasya darśayati // atha śucau rāga iti dvitīyo vikalpaḥ svīkriyate, tatrāha- svamevetyādi / athavā / anyathāvatāryateyaduktaṃ pareṇa- channe carmādinā rāgo bhavati nācchanne / tatrāha- yadītyādi / yadi tena hetunā carmādinā pihitatvāditi kṛtvā aśucau rāgo bhavati bhavataḥ, tadā kasmādāliṅgase paramanyadīyaṃ pañjaram / anyat pūrvavat //
body.translated_text: 'Flesh itself is like mud' — by the similarity of being a plaster; 'plastered' means smeared with it. If asked 'what is this?' — a cage of bones bound with sinews — bound, held together, made dependent by sinews — a skeleton, a chain of bones. Otherwise it would disintegrate into pieces — thus he shows this to be a proper object of dispassion. // If the second alternative is accepted — that there is passion for the pure — to that he says: 'your own' and so forth. Or alternatively, the opponent's statement is redirected: what the other said — 'there is passion when covered by skin and such, not when uncovered.' To that he says: 'if' and so forth. If for that reason — because it is concealed by skin and such — you have passion for the impure, then why do you embrace the other — another's skeleton? The rest is as before. //

body.text: kiṃ tarhi samucitamatretyāha-
body.translated_text: What then is appropriate here? — he says —

children.translated_text: You yourself have abundant impurity; practice contentment with that alone.
O devourer of filth, forget the other sack of excrement! // Bca_8.53 //

body.text: svameva ātmanaiva bahutaramaśucilālāsiṅghāṇamastaluṅgamūtrapurīṣādi tavāsti, tenaivāśucinā saṃtoṣaṃ kuruṣva / tato 'pyameghyabhastrāṃ purīṣaprasevikām aparāmanyāṃ strīśarīrasvabhāvām / gūthaghasmara purīṣabhakṣaṇaśīla vismara, tatra manasikāraṃ mā kārṣīḥ //
body.translated_text: You yourself — your own [body] — has abundant impurity: saliva, nasal mucus, brain matter, urine, feces, and such. Practice contentment — be satisfied — with that very impurity. Beyond that, another sack of excrement — another vessel of feces — of the nature of the female body: O devourer of filth — O habitual eater of feces — forget [her]; do not direct your attention there! //

body.text: māṃsapriyo 'hamityādinā punaranyathā parihāramāha-
body.translated_text: With 'I am fond of flesh' and such, he presents a refutation in yet another way —

children.translated_text: If you [think] 'I am fond of flesh,' and wish to see and touch it,

children.text: acetanaṃ svabhāvena māṃsaṃ tvaṃ kathamicchasi // Bca_8.54 //
children.translated_text: how can you desire flesh, which by nature is non-sentient? // Bca_8.54 //

body.text: māṃsaṃ priyaṃ yasya / eṣo 'haṃ māṃsapriyaḥ / asya asthipañjarasya / yadi vā / māṃsasya priyo māṃsapriyo 'hamasyeti pūrvavat / māṃsapriyo 'hamasya priya iti yāvat / sāpekṣatve 'pi samāso gamakatvāt / ityevaṃ tatpralobhāt pratyupakāradhiyā vā draṣṭuṃ spraṣṭuṃ ca vāñchasi, darśanaṃ sparśanaṃ ca abhilaṣasi / atrāha- acetanaṃ caitanyaśūnyaṃ mṛtpiṇḍaprāyam / svabhāvena prakṛtyā / na tu punaryathāpare varṇayanti- caitanyayogādacetanamapi cetanamabhidhīyate / tādṛśaṃ māṃsaṃ tvamacetanasvabhāvaṃ kāmukaḥ san kathamicchasi? taddṛṣṭau ca mṛtpiṇḍe 'pi syāt / tathā ca sati bhavānapi na cetanaḥ syāt //
body.translated_text: 'Fond of flesh' — one to whom flesh is dear. 'This is I — the one fond of flesh.' 'Of this' — of this skeleton. Or alternatively: 'dear to flesh — fond of flesh — I am of this' — as before. 'Fond of flesh' — 'I am dear to this' — thus far. Even with dependence [between terms], the compound is [acceptable] because it conveys the meaning. Thus, from the enticement of that, or from the thought of reciprocating, one wishes to see and touch — one desires seeing and touching. To this he says: 'non-sentient' — devoid of consciousness, like a lump of clay. 'By nature' — by its own essence. Not, however, as others describe it: 'even the non-sentient is called sentient through conjunction with consciousness.' Such flesh, being non-sentient by nature — how do you, being lustful, desire it? For if that [were valid], then there would be [desire] for a lump of clay too. And if so, you too would not be sentient. //

body.text: asti tatra citsvabhāvaṃ cittam, tena tadicchāmīti cedāha-
body.translated_text: If one says: there is consciousness there — the mind, of the nature of awareness — and it is that I desire — to this he says —

children.text: yadicchasi na taccittaṃ draṣṭuṃ spraṣṭuṃ ca śakyate /
children.translated_text: That mind which you desire cannot be seen or touched;

children.text: yacca śakyaṃ na tadvetti kiṃ tadāliṅgase mudhā // Bca_8.55 //
children.translated_text: and that which can [be seen and touched] does not know [anything] — why do you embrace it in vain? // Bca_8.55 //

body.text: yaccittaṃ citsvabhāvamicchasi, tadarūpitvāt draṣṭuṃ na śakyate / yacca māṃsādisvabhāvaṃ kalevaraṃ draṣṭuṃ spraṣṭuṃ ca śakyate, na tadvetti, na jānāti, acetanatvāt / ataḥ kimiti
body.translated_text: The mind that you consider to be of the nature of consciousness — because it is formless, it cannot be seen. And the body that is of the nature of flesh and such — which can be seen and touched — it does not know, does not cognize, being insentient. Therefore, why do you

body.text: tadacetanamāliṅgase āśliṣyasi? mudheti niṣphalam / naiva āliṅgitumucitamiti bhāvaḥ / anyathā loṣṭhādyāliṅganaprasaṅgaḥ //
body.translated_text: embrace, cling to, that insentient [body]? 'In vain' — fruitlessly. The meaning is: it is not at all appropriate to embrace it. Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of embracing clods of earth and such.

body.text: kiṃ ca / idamapyatigarhitamityādarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, showing that this too is extremely reprehensible, he says —

children.translated_text: That you do not know another's body to be made of impurities is not surprising;

children.text: svāmedhyamayameva tvaṃ taṃ nāvaiṣīti vismayaḥ // Bca_8.56 //
children.translated_text: but that you do not recognize your own [body] as made of impurities — that is astonishing! // <s>Bca</s> 8.56 //

body.text: anyasya kāyaṃ yadamedhyamayaṃ na vetsi, tanna kiṃcidāścaryam / yuktameva tadavedanam, parasaṃtānasyātmanā vyavahitatvāt / idaṃ punaratiśayenāścaryasthānam, yat svasyātmano 'medhyamayaṃ tvaṃ taṃ kāyaṃ nāvaiṣi nāvagacchasi //
body.translated_text: That you do not know another's body to be made of impurities — that is no wonder at all. Such ignorance is quite justified, since another's continuum is separated from oneself. But this is a matter of supreme wonder: that you do not know, do not realize, your own body to be made of impurities!

body.text: idānīṃ śāstrakārastaṃ saṃvejayannāha-
body.translated_text: Now the author of the treatise, admonishing him, says —

children.translated_text: Having set aside the young lotus, opened by the cloudless sun's rays,
for one whose mind is addicted to impurity, what delight is there in a cage of excrement? // <s>Bca</s> 8.57 //

body.text: vighanārkāśubhirvikacaṃ vikasitam / tādṛśaṃ taruṇapaṅkajam / abhinavasaroruhaṃ hitvā amedhyābhiniviṣṭacittasya kā ratirgūthapañjare / na yukteti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Opened by the cloudless sun's rays' — bloomed. Such a young lotus — a fresh water-lily — having abandoned [that], for one whose mind is fixated on impurities, what delight is there in a cage of excrement? The meaning is: it is not appropriate.

body.text: punaranyathā prāha-
body.translated_text: He states [the matter] yet another way —

children.translated_text: If you do not wish to touch earth and such smeared with impurities,
how do you wish to touch the body, from which that [impurity] has issued? // <s>Bca</s> 8.58 //

body.text: ādiśabdādvastrādi / aśucimrakṣitatvāt / yadi spraṣṭuṃ na vāñchasi / yataḥ kāyāttadamedhyaṃ nirgataṃ niryātam, taṃ kāyaṃ kathamicchasi spraṣṭum?
body.translated_text: The word 'and such' [includes] cloth and the like — smeared, stained with impurities. If you do not wish to touch [them] — since that impurity has issued, has come forth, from the body — how do you wish to touch that body?

body.text: athāpi syāt- nāyamupālambho mama yuktarūpaḥ, yato na me kaścidabhiniveśo 'medhye ityatrāha-
body.translated_text: But one might say: 'This reproach is not justified in my case, since I have no attachment to impurities.' To this he says —

children.text: yadi te nāśucau rāgaḥ kasmādāliṅgase param /
children.translated_text: If you have no desire for the impure, why do you embrace another
who was born in a field of impurity, whose seed is that [impurity], and who is nourished by it? // <s>Bca</s> 8.59 //

body.text: amedhyakṣetraṃ māturjaṭharam, anekāśucisthānatvāt, tatra saṃbhūtaṃ samutpannaṃ tadbījam, tadeva amedhyaṃ mātāpitṛśukraśoṇitasvabhāvaṃ bījaṃ yasya tattathoktam / tena vardhitamiti tena amedhyena mātṛpītāśitasya vāntakalpasya rasena vardhitaṃ garbhasthitamupabṛṃhitam / bahirnirgatamapi svayamaśitapītaparipākāśucirasena / kasmādāliṅgase paramiti saṃbandhaḥ / paraṃ strīkalevaram / ityupālambho 'styeva bhavataḥ //
body.translated_text: 'The field of impurity' is the mother's womb, being a site of many impurities. 'Born there' — produced there. 'Whose seed is that' — that very impurity, the seed being of the nature of the father's semen and the mother's blood — such is what is meant. 'Nourished by it' — nourished, sustained in the womb by that impurity — the nutritive essence of what the mother has eaten and drunk, which is like vomit. Even after emerging [from the womb], [the body is nourished] by the impure essence of the digestion of one's own food and drink. 'Why do you embrace another?' — this is the connection. 'Another' — a woman's body. Thus the reproach does indeed apply to you.

body.text: atha aśucirāgo 'hamiti pakṣasvīkāraḥ, tathāpi upālambhastadavastha evetyāha-
body.translated_text: If one accepts the position 'I do have desire for the impure,' even so the reproach remains just the same — he says —

children.translated_text: You do not desire the impure worm, born from impurity, because of its smallness;
yet you desire the body, made of much impurity and also born from impurity! // <s>Bca</s> 8.60 //

body.text: purīṣādyaśucisaṃbhūtaṃ kṛmiṃ prāṇakajātaṃ na vāñchasi / kāyaṃ punarmātṛgrāmasya bahutarāśucisvabhāvamaśucisaṃbhūtamapi pūrvakrameṇa icchasi //
body.translated_text: You do not desire a worm — a type of creature — born from impurity such as excrement and such. Yet you desire the body of a woman, which is of the nature of even more impurity and is also born from impurity in the manner described before.

body.text: athāpi syāt- kimatrottaraṃ vaktavyam? yato 'hamapi yādṛśaḥ, tādṛśaṃ tasyāḥ śarīram, tena aśucernāśucisaṃparko doṣaḥ, yādṛśo yakṣastādṛśo balirapītyāha-
body.translated_text: But one might say: 'What answer need be given here? Since I too am of such a nature, her body is also of such a nature; therefore there is no fault in the contact of the impure with the impure — as the saying goes: as the demon, so the offering.' To this he says —

children.translated_text: Not only do you not feel disgust at your own impure nature,
but you, glutton for excrement, desire others — vessels of impurity! // <s>Bca</s> 8.61 //

body.text: ayamiha mahāmohasya prabhāvaḥ, yadātmagatameva tāvadaśucisvabhāvaṃ na vigarhasi / pratyuta aparānaśucikumbhānabhilaṣasi, iti dhik parāmarśavikalatā / gūthaghasmareti tiraskāravacanena tasyaiva saṃbodhanam //
body.translated_text: This here is the power of great delusion: that you do not even abhor your own impure nature. On the contrary, you desire others — vessels of impurity. Alas, what a failure of discernment! '<s>Gūthaghasmara</s>' (glutton for excrement) — with this term of reproach, he addresses that very person.

body.text: idānīṃ sākṣātkṛtya aśucisvabhāvatāṃ pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Now, directly demonstrating the impure nature, he says —

children.translated_text: Even camphor and such pleasant things, or rice, food, and condiments,
once placed in the mouth and expelled, the very ground is considered impure. // <s>Bca</s> 8.62 //

body.text: evaṃ śucipavitravastunyapi yadekadeśaniṣyandasaṃparkādapavitrasvabhāvatāṃ vrajanti / āsatāṃ tāvattāni vastūni, tatsaṃsargādbhūmirapi śucisvabhāvā aśucitvaṃ yāti //
body.translated_text: Thus even pure and clean substances, through contact with the flow of a part [of the body], become of impure nature. Setting aside those substances themselves — even the ground, which is of pure nature, becomes impure from contact with them.

children.translated_text: If you do not accept this impurity even though it is directly perceived,

children.text: śmaśāne patitān ghorān kāyān paśyāparānapi // Bca_8.63 //
children.translated_text: look at the dreadful bodies of others fallen in the charnel ground! // <s>Bca</s> 8.63 //

body.text: evaṃ tāvadadhyakṣasiddho 'yaṃ vyavahāraḥ, tathāpi yadi nādhimucyase, na saṃpratyeṣi / dṛṣṭvāpi na śraddadhāsi ityarthaḥ / tadā śmaśāne pūtinivāse kāyān paśya / kiṃbhūtān? ghorāniti / vikhāditakavinīlakavipūyakādisvabhāvatayā bībhatsān bhayaṃkarān vā aparāniti ato 'dhikān //
body.translated_text: Thus far this is a matter established by direct perception; yet if you do not accept it, do not acknowledge it — the meaning is: even having seen, you do not believe — then look at the bodies in the charnel ground, the abode of putrefaction. Of what kind? 'Dreadful' — repulsive and frightening due to being eaten by [animals], being bluish-black, being putrid and such. 'Others' — even more [dreadful] than that.

body.text: kiṃ ca / prakṛtyā vikṛta evāyaṃ kāyo nābhiratisthānaṃ yujyate ityupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, showing that this body is by nature deformed and not a suitable object of delight, he says —

children.translated_text: Since, when the skin is torn off, great fear arises,

children.text: kathaṃ jñātvāpi tatraiva punarutpadyate ratiḥ // Bca_8.64 //
children.translated_text: how, knowing this, can delight arise again in that very [body]? // <s>Bca</s> 8.64 //

body.text: utpāṭite viyojite / yasmāditi kāyāt / trāso jāyate mahān- kimetaditi / evaṃ tatsvabhāvaṃ viditvāpi kathaṃ tasminneva sthāne bhayasthānatvena ekadā pratipanne punaranyadā jāyate ratirabhiṣvaṅgaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Torn off' — separated. 'Since' — from the body. Great terror arises — 'what is this?' Thus, even having known its true nature, how can delight, attachment, arise again in that very place — in what was once recognized as a source of fear?

body.text: syādetat- yadi nāma aśucisvabhāvatā kāyasya adhyakṣasiddhā, tathāpi candanādisurabhivastūpalipto 'sau kamanīyo bhavati ityatrāha-
body.translated_text: One might say: even if the impure nature of the body is established by direct perception, still, when anointed with fragrant substances such as sandalwood, it becomes attractive. To this he says —

children.translated_text: The fragrance applied to the body is from sandalwood alone, not from anything else;
why are you attracted to something else by a fragrance that belongs to another? // <s>Bca</s> 8.65 //

body.text: śarīre niveśito 'pyasau gandhaḥ candanādiprasūtaḥ, yadvaśātkāye kamanīyabuddhirupajāyate / candanādeva kevalāt / nānyataḥ iti kāyāt / ataḥ kasmāt parakīyena gandhena candanasamudbhūtena anyatra yasyāsau gandho na bhavati, atra abhiratiḥ kriyate?
body.translated_text: The fragrance applied to the body is produced from sandalwood and such — on account of which the notion of attractiveness arises regarding the body. From sandalwood alone — exclusively. 'Not from anything else' — not from the body. Therefore, why is attraction made toward something else — this [body] to which that fragrance does not belong — by a fragrance belonging to another, originating from sandalwood?

body.text: api ca / candanādisaṃskāro 'pi kevalātmopaghātāya vartate, na hitāyeti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, showing that even the adornment with sandalwood and such serves only for one's own destruction, not for benefit, he says —

children.translated_text: If, due to its natural foul smell, desire does not arise in this [body], is that not auspicious?
Why does the world, fond of harm, anoint it with fragrance? // <s>Bca</s> 8.66 //

body.text: svabhāvadaurgandhyāt sahajātpūtigandhavahatvāt / atreti kāye / yadi rāgo notpadyate, tadā śivaṃ nanu kalyāṇameva syāt / evaṃ guṇasaṃbhave 'pi kiṃ kāraṇamanarthapriyo lokaḥ taṃ kāyaṃ gandhenānulimpati? sarvathā na yuktametadityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Due to its natural foul smell' — due to its innate quality of emitting a putrid odor. 'In this' — in the body. If desire does not arise, then 'is it not auspicious?' — it would indeed be beneficial. Yet even when such a benefit would arise, why does the world, fond of harm, anoint that body with fragrance? The meaning is: this is in no way justified.

body.text: na cāsya saṃskārasahasratve 'pi svabhāvānyathātvamastītyāha-
body.translated_text: And even with a thousand adornments, the body's nature does not change — he says —

body.text: kāyasyātra kimāyātaṃ sugandhi yadi candanam /
body.translated_text: If it is the sandalwood that is fragrant, what has come to the body from that?

body.text: kāyasya svabhāvadurgandhasya kimāyātam, kiṃ bhūtam? na kiṃcit / sugandhi yadi candanam / śobhano gandho 'syeti bahuvrīhisamāsāntādin / tathāpi tasya na svabhāvapracyutirastīti bhāvaḥ / atha tadvaśāt tasmin kamanīyatāmupādāya abhiratirutpadyate ityatrāha-
body.translated_text: What has come to the body — which is by nature foul-smelling — what has changed? Nothing. 'If the sandalwood is fragrant' — [a compound] ending in a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> meaning 'that of which the fragrance is good.' Even so, the point is: there is no loss of its [the body's] own nature. But if, on account of that [fragrance], one adopts attractiveness in it and delight arises — to this he says —

body.text: anyadīyena gandhena kasmādanyatra rajyate // Bca_8.67 //
body.translated_text: Why is one attracted to something else by a fragrance belonging to another? // <s>Bca</s> 8.67 //

body.text: evaṃ ca na vicakṣaṇatā syādityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus it would not be discernment — this is the meaning.

body.text: keśādisaṃskāradvāreṇāpi anarthaheturevāyaṃ kāya iti ślokadvayenopadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Showing through two verses that this body is a cause of harm even through the adornment of hair and such, he says —

children.translated_text: If, with long hair and nails, with teeth stained and pale,
bearing a coating of filth, naked — the body is frightful by nature; // <s>Bca</s> 8.68 //
why is it adorned with effort, like a weapon for self-destruction?
The earth is filled with madmen striving to delude themselves! // <s>Bca</s> 8.69 //

body.text: dīrghaiḥ sahajāvasthitaiḥ / acchinnairityarthaḥ / dantairdaśanaiḥ samalapāṇḍuraiḥ dantadhāvanakramukādibhirasaṃskṛtaiḥ / malapaṅkadharaḥ mala eva paṅkaḥ kardamaḥ, taṃ dhārayatīti tathā, snānābhyañjanādivirahāt / nagna iti vastraviviktatvāt yathājāta ivāvasthitaḥ / tathābhūtaḥ san / yadi kāyaḥ prakṛtyā bhīṣaṇaḥ pretānāmiva svabhāvena bhayaṃkaraḥ / sa evaṃbhūtaḥ kimiti saṃskriyate? yatnāditi keśanakhādiracanāviśeṣaiḥ, dantadhāvanatāmbūlādibhiḥ, snānābhyañjanānulepanādibhiḥ, vastrādibhirvā / kimiva? ātmaghātāya śastravat / ātmano vadhārthaṃ khaṅgādiryathā saṃskriyate tadvat / ityeṣāṃ mohavaśīkṛtaṃ viceṣṭitaṃ paridevayannāha- ātmetyādi / ātmanaiva saṃcintya ātmano vyāmohamutpādayituṃ yatnavadbhiḥ unmattairasvasthacittaiḥ / evaṃ ca viparītakarmānuṣṭhānānnaite varākāḥ sacetasa iti khedaṃ karoti śāsrakāraḥ / na cātra kaścidātmajño dṛśyata iti unmattairākulā samākīrṇā mahī pṛthivīti //
body.translated_text: 'Long' — in their natural state, uncut — this is the meaning. 'Teeth' — 'stained and pale' — unadorned with tooth-cleaning [implements], betel nut, and such. 'Bearing a coating of filth' — filth itself is the mud, the grime — one who bears that, from the absence of bathing, oiling, and such. 'Naked' — devoid of clothing, as if in one's natural state. Being thus, if the body is by nature frightful — like ghosts, naturally terrifying — then why is such a body adorned? 'With effort' — through special arrangements of hair, nails, and such; through tooth-cleaning, betel, and such; through bathing, oiling, anointing, and such; or through clothing and such. Like what? 'Like a weapon for self-destruction' — just as a sword and such is polished for the purpose of killing oneself. Thus lamenting the conduct of those controlled by delusion, he says 'The earth…' and so forth. By oneself, deliberately, striving to produce delusion in oneself — by madmen, those of unsound mind. And thus, through the performance of contrary actions, the author of the treatise expresses sorrow [that] these wretches are not in their right minds. And no one here is seen who knows the self — thus the earth is filled, overrun, with madmen.

body.text: prāsaṅgikaṃ parisamāpya prakṛtamanubandhannāha-
body.translated_text: Having completed the digression, resuming the topic at hand, he says —

children.text: kaṅkālān katicidṛṣṭvā śmaśāne kila te ghṛṇā /
children.translated_text: Having seen a few skeletons in the charnel ground, you indeed feel revulsion;
yet you delight in the village-charnel-ground, crowded with walking skeletons! // <s>Bca</s> 8.70 //

body.text: śavānāmasthipañjarān katicit pratiniyatān / etaduktaṃ bhavati- carmaṇyutpāṭite [8. 64] ityādikamuktvā yaduktaṃ kathaṃ jñātvāpītyādi, tatra parasyottaram- na śmaśānagatakalevarasādṛśyamasya, yena tasminneva atrāpi ratirna syāt, kiṃ tarhi śmaśāne tasya ghṛṇāsthānatvāt / nātreti atra abhidheyakaṅkālānityādi / grāmaśmaśāne / iti / naivātra kaścidviśeṣo 'sti / tadeva śarīraṃ śmaśāne ghṛṇāsthānagrāme vā abhiratisthānamiti kākvā brūte / naitadvicakṣaṇadhiyāṃ samāyuktamiti bhāvaḥ / calatkaṅkālasaṃkule ityanena etaddarśayati- etāvāṃstu viśeṣaḥ / na ca anena viśeṣeṇāśucisvabhāvatā ghṛṇāheturnivartate, yena pravṛttiriyaṃ syāditi / saṃkula iti samākīrṇe //
body.translated_text: 'Bone-frameworks of corpses' — a specific number [of them]. What is stated here is this: having said 'when the skin is torn off' [8.64] and such, and having said 'how, knowing this?' and so forth — the opponent's reply [would be]: 'This [living body] is not like the bodies found in the charnel ground, such that there would be no delight here as there is [no delight] there; rather, in the charnel ground, that is the basis for revulsion, not here.' [The answer:] the skeletons referred to here — and so forth — 'in the village-charnel-ground.' There is indeed no distinction at all. That the very same body is a source of revulsion in the charnel ground but a source of delight in the village — he says with irony. The point is: this is not appropriate for those of discerning intellect. By the phrase 'crowded with walking skeletons,' this is shown: only this much difference [exists — they are walking]. And this difference does not remove the impure nature that is the cause of revulsion, such that this [attraction] would be justified. 'Crowded' means filled.

body.text: bhavatu nāma īdṛśamaśucisvabhāvamapi sūkarāṇāmiva abhiratisthānam / tathā ca evaṃ vidhamapi draviṇavikalasya naitat sulabhamityupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Granted, such a thing of impure nature may indeed be a source of delight even for pigs. And furthermore, showing that even such a thing is not easily obtained by one lacking wealth, he says —

children.translated_text: Thus even this impure [body] is not obtained without a price;
for its sake there is the toil of earning, and suffering in the hells and such. // <s>Bca</s> 8.71 //

body.text: vinā mūlyaṃ dravyamantareṇa na labhyate na prāpyate / atastadarthinā prathamato dhanameva arjanīyam / tadarjanena āyāsāt kṛṣivāṇijyasevādisamāśrayeṇa pariśramādihaiva duḥkhamupajāyate, adharmeṇa copārjanānnarakādiṣu, iti ubhayaloke 'narthahetureva tadarjanam / nāpi tatsukhaprāptirasti //
body.translated_text: 'Without a price' — without wealth — it is not obtained, not acquired. Therefore, one who desires it must first earn wealth itself. Through the toil of earning that — through resorting to farming, trade, service, and such — suffering arises even here in this life, and through wrongful earning, in the hells and such. Thus in both worlds, that earning is nothing but a cause of harm. Nor is there any attainment of happiness from it.

body.text: duḥkhameva tu kevalaṃ tadarjaneneti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Showing that earning brings nothing but suffering, he says —

children.translated_text: A child has no capacity to earn; how then is youth happy?

children.text: yātyarjanena tāruṇyaṃ vṛddhaḥ kāmaiḥ karoti kim // Bca_8.72 //
children.translated_text: Youth passes in earning; what can an old person do with pleasures? // <s>Bca</s> 8.72 //

body.text: bālāvasthāvasthitasya na dhanopārjanaśaktirasti, bālatvādeva / kena dhanena prakāreṇa vā asau bālo yauvane yuvāvasthāyāṃ sukhī syāt? dhanavikalatvānna kvacidityarthaḥ / yadapi kasyacit pitṛpitāmahopārjitadhanena yauvane sukhitvaṃ dṛśyate, tadapi pratiniyatasyaiva na sarvasya / na cāpi pūrvoktaduḥkhadvayādvimucyate 'sau / ato dhanārjanamupādeyamādau sukhasādhanopāyatvāt / tadarjayata eva galitavayaso na kaścidupayogo viṣayairiti //
body.translated_text: For one situated in childhood, there is no capacity to earn wealth — precisely because of being a child. By what wealth or by what means would that child be happy in youth, in the state of being young? The meaning is: nowhere, due to lack of wealth. And even the happiness seen in some during youth through wealth earned by fathers and grandfathers — that too belongs to a particular [few], not to all. Nor is such a person freed from the two kinds of suffering mentioned earlier. Therefore, earning wealth must be undertaken first, as a means of attaining happiness. But by the time one has earned it, one's youth has passed and there is no use for sense-pleasures.

body.text: athāpi syāt- tadarjayatāpi kāmasukhamanubhūyata eva, ityatrāha-
body.translated_text: But one might say: even while earning, sense-pleasure is experienced. To this he says —

children.translated_text: Some wretched desire-seekers, exhausted by their day-long labors,

children.text: gṛhamāgatya sāyāhne śerate sma mṛtā iva // Bca_8.73 //
children.translated_text: come home in the evening and lie down like the dead. // <s>Bca</s> 8.73 //

body.text: ye kecit kutsitakāmākṣiptacetasaḥ kāṣṭhatṛṇapatrādyāharaṇabhṛtikarmakriyālakṣaṇairdinaparyantavyāpāraiḥ parikhinnakāyamanaso nirutsukāḥ, astaṃ gate savitari svagṛhamāgatya gāḍhamiddhākrāntatvāt mṛtakalpāḥ śerate sma svapanti / prabhāte punarutthāya tatraiva nīcakarmaṇi yujyante / smaśabdo 'tra vākyālaṃkāre atītārthāviṣayatvāt / evamāyuḥsaṃskārān kecit kukāminaḥ kṣapayanti, na ca kāmasukhāsvādamupalabhante /
body.translated_text: Some whose minds are seized by base desires — exhausted in body and mind from day-long labors characterized by fetching wood, grass, leaves, and such, or by hired labor — dispirited, when the sun has set, come to their own homes and, being deeply overcome by torpor, lie down as if dead. And rising again at dawn, they engage in the very same menial work. The word '<s>sma</s>' here is [used as] an ornament of expression, not being restricted to a past meaning. Thus some wretched desire-seekers waste away their life-forces, yet do not obtain even a taste of sensual pleasure.

body.text: parasevakānadhikṛtyāha-
body.translated_text: Speaking with reference to servants of others, he says —

children.translated_text: Others, afflicted by the suffering of hardship in foreign lands, on military campaigns,
do not see their children and wives for years, those who desire them. // <s>Bca</s> 8.74 //

body.text: apare pūrvakāmikebhyo 'nye kukāminaḥ sevakā ityarthaḥ / te daṇḍayātrādibhiḥ, daṇḍaḥ paracakravijayāya yātrā prayāṇam, pararāṣṭradravyagrahaṇāya vā yātrā, tadādiryeṣāṃ deśāntarapreṣaṇādīnām, taiḥ pravāso deśāntaragamanam, tena kleśaḥ pariśramaḥ, tena duḥkhitāḥ pīḍitāḥ / sarvadā tathābhūtāḥ / vatsarairapi anekavarṣātyaye 'pi putrān dārāṃśca nekṣante na paśyanti / tadarthina iti taiḥ putradārādibhirarthinaḥ tadabhilāṣukāḥ / tadarthameva parasevādisvīkārādityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Others' — different from the previously mentioned desire-seekers — are wretched servants, this is the meaning. They [suffer] from military campaigns and such — a 'campaign' (<s>daṇḍayātrā</s>) is a march for conquering an enemy's forces, or a march for seizing the wealth of another's kingdom — the word 'and such' [includes] being dispatched to other lands, and so forth. Through these, living abroad — going to other lands — is the hardship, the toil — by which they are afflicted, tormented. Always being in such a state, they do not see — do not behold — their children and wives even for years, even after the passing of many years. 'Those who desire them' — those who long for their children, wives, and such. The meaning is: it is for their sake alone that they have accepted service of others and such.

body.text: aho bata amīṣāṃ niṣphalamanuṣṭhānamiti śocayannāha-
body.translated_text: Alas, how fruitless is the endeavor of these people! Lamenting thus, he says —

children.translated_text: That very thing for whose sake the self has been sold by those deluded by desire

children.text: tanna prāptaṃ mudhaivāyurnītaṃ tu parakarmaṇā // Bca_8.75 //
children.translated_text: has not been obtained; life has been spent in vain, in service to another. // <s>Bca</s> 8.75 //

body.text: yadarthaṃ sukhapratilambhanimittaṃ vikrītaḥ paradāsīkṛtaḥ ātmā kāmaviḍambitaiḥ tanna prāptam, taditi sukhaṃ na prāptaṃ na pratilabdham / āyuḥsaṃskārā eva hi kevalamanarthakaṃ parakarmānuṣṭhānena kṣayamupanītāḥ / na sādhukarmaṇi kvacidapi yojitā iti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'For the sake of which' — for the purpose of obtaining happiness — the self has been 'sold,' made into another's slave — by those deceived by desire — that has not been obtained — 'that' meaning happiness — has not been obtained, not gained. For the life-forces have merely been brought to exhaustion pointlessly through the performance of others' work. The meaning is: they have never been directed toward virtuous action.

body.text: sukhalipsayā pravṛttānāṃ pratyuta duḥkhamevāpatitameṣāmityupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Showing that for those who act out of desire for happiness, what befalls them is only suffering, he says —

children.translated_text: The wives of others — those who have sold their own persons,
who are always engaged in carrying out errands — give birth in forests, in thickets, and such. // <s>Bca</s> 8.76 //

body.text: sukhabubhukṣayā vikrītaḥ parāyattīkṛtaḥ svātmabhāva svakāyo yaiste tathā, teṣām / anyeṣāṃ sevakānāmityarthaḥ / ata eva sadā preṣaṇakaraṇaśīlānām / anyeṣāmapareṣāṃ prabhuprayojanena gacchatām / mārga eva prasūyante striyaḥ / aṭavīviṭapādiṣu / ādiśabdāt parvatanitagbanadīkūlādiṣu kaṣṭasthāneṣu //
body.translated_text: 'Those whose own person — their own body — has been sold,' made subject to another, out of a hunger for happiness — of such [people]. 'Others' means servants — this is the meaning. And for this very reason, of those who are always engaged in carrying out errands — of others, of different [servants] going [somewhere] on their master's business — their wives give birth right on the road, in forests, in thickets, and such. The word 'and such' [includes] difficult places such as mountain slopes, valleys, riverbanks, and so forth.

body.text: ayamaparo viparyāsasteṣāmiti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Showing yet another perversity of theirs, he says —

children.translated_text: They enter battle, where life is in doubt, in order to live;

children.text: mānārthaṃ dāsatāṃ yānti mūḍhāḥ kāmaviḍambitāḥ // Bca_8.77 //
children.translated_text: for the sake of honor, they go into slavery — the fools, deceived by desire! // <s>Bca</s> 8.77 //

body.text: vikrītasvātmabhāvāḥ saṃgrāmaṃ caturdantasaṃghaṭṭaṃ praviśanti / kiṃbhūtaṃ jīvitasaṃdeham? tatra praviṣṭasya jīvitaṃ syādvā na veti jīvitasya saṃdeho 'sminniti kṛtvā / jīvitumiti jīvanārtham / atra pratilabdhairlābhairjīvikāṃ kalpayiṣyāma iti matvetyarthaḥ / mānārthaṃ dāsatāṃ yānti, balavatā kenacidabhibhūtāḥ svamānoddharaṇārtham / aṅgulīcchedavelāgrahaṇasvīkārāt / mūḍhā mohāndhīkṛtavivekacakṣuṣaḥ / ke te? kāmabiḍambitāḥ kāmāya kāmena vā viḍambitāstiraskṛtāḥ //
body.translated_text: Those who have sold their own persons enter battle — the clash of four-fold armies. Of what kind? 'Where life is in doubt' — for one who has entered there, it is uncertain whether one will live or not — thus it is [a situation] of doubt regarding life. 'In order to live' — for the sake of livelihood. The meaning is: thinking 'with the gains obtained here, we shall make a living.' 'For the sake of honor, they go into slavery' — overcome by someone more powerful, for the sake of preserving their own honor — through accepting seizure of fingers, frontier-posts, and such. 'Fools' — those whose eye of discernment has been blinded by delusion. Who are they? 'Deceived by desire' — deceived, humiliated, by desire or for the sake of desire.

body.text: ihaiva janmani kāmāsaktacetasāṃ yadduḥkhaṃ dṛśyate tatkathayannāha-
body.translated_text: Describing the suffering that is seen even in this very life for those whose minds are attached to sense-pleasures, he says —

children.translated_text: Some desire-seekers are cut to pieces, others impaled on stakes;
they are seen being burned and being killed with spears. // <s>Bca</s> 8.78 //

body.text: paradāradhanāpaharaṇādeḥ // śeṣaḥ subodhaḥ //
body.translated_text: Because of stealing others' wives, wealth, and such. The rest is easily understood.

body.text: kiṃ ca / ayaṃ sukhasādhanatvena upādīyamāno 'pi ca anarthaparaṃparāprasūtiheturevārthaḥ iti kathayannāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, showing that wealth, even when adopted as a means of happiness, is nothing but a cause of an unending series of misfortunes, he says —

children.translated_text: Know wealth to be an endless misfortune through the anguish of earning, guarding, and losing;
for those whose minds are attached to wealth, due to their preoccupation, there is no opportunity for release from the suffering of existence. // <s>Bca</s> 8.79 //

body.text: arjanamanutpannasyotpādanaṃ duḥkham / upārjitasyāpi jalānalādibhyaḥ pañcapratyavāyebhyaḥ paripālanaṃ kaṣṭataram / tathā rakṣitasyāpi kathaṃcit taskarādibhirnāśādviṣādo daurmanasyaṃ paritāpaheturanarthaḥ / tadevamanarthaparaṃparānidānatvāt kāraṇe kāryopacārādartha evānartha uktaḥ / ityevamarjanādibhiḥ sarvadā vyākulatvāt dhanāsaktacetasāṃ kṣaṇamapi samādhānānavakāśatvāt nāvasaraḥ saṃsārāśṛ[śri?]tajātyādiduḥkhanirmokṣāya sadā tadgatamanasikāraireva āyuḥrāṇāṃ kṣapaṇāt //
body.translated_text: 'Earning' — producing what has not yet arisen — is suffering. Even what has been earned — its protection from water, fire, and such — the five calamities — is even more difficult. And the despondency, the mental distress, from the loss of what was guarded — somehow, through thieves and such — is a cause of torment, a misfortune. Thus, since it is the root cause of an unending series of misfortunes, wealth itself is called a 'misfortune' by attributing the effect [misfortune] to the cause [wealth]. Therefore, because of being always disturbed by earning and such, for those whose minds are attached to wealth, since there is not even a moment's opportunity for mental composure, there is no occasion for release from the suffering of birth, and such, which belongs to <s>saṃsāra</s> — since [their] lifespans are exhausted entirely through mental preoccupation with that alone.

body.text: sarvametadupasaṃhṛtya kāmāsaṅgaparityāgāya saṃvegakathayā protsāhayati evamityādinā-
body.translated_text: Summarizing all of this and encouraging renunciation of attachment to sense-pleasures through a discourse that inspires disenchantment, he says with 'thus' and so forth —

children.translated_text: Thus the disadvantages are many for desire-seekers, and the taste is slight,
like the grasp of a morsel of grass by a beast pulling a cart. // <s>Bca</s> 8.80 //

body.text: evamityuktaprakāraparāmarśe / ādīnavo 'narthaḥ / bhūyānanekaprakāraḥ / na cātra sukhotpādavārtāpyasti / yadapi viparyāsāt kathaṃcit sukhamiti pratibhāsate, tadapi na kiṃcit / gurutarabhārākramaṇapariklāntavapuṣaḥ paśoriva ghāsalavagrāsagrahaṇam //
body.translated_text: 'Thus' refers to the manner described. 'Disadvantage' is misfortune. 'Many' — of numerous kinds. And here there is not even a mention of the arising of happiness. Whatever, through perversity, somehow appears as happiness — even that is nothing — like the grasping of a morsel of grass by a beast exhausted from treading under a very heavy load.

children.translated_text: For the sake of that mere taste [of pleasure], which is not difficult to obtain even for a beast,
this precious opportunity of a [human] moment, so difficult to obtain, has been destroyed — ruined by fate. // <s>Bca</s> 8.81 //

body.text: tasyaivaṃbhūtasya atitucchasya sukhāsvādaleśasya paśorapi sādhāraṇāsyārthe tasya nimittam / iyaṃ kṣaṇasaṃpat aṣṭākṣaṇavinirmuktā hatā vināśitā / vṛthā kṛtetyarthaḥ / kiṃviśiṣṭā sudurlabhā vyākhyātā / kena daivahatena / daivaṃ purātanaṃ karma, tena hatā / hitāhitaparijñāne viparyastamatiḥ kṛtaḥ / vimohita ityarthaḥ / vastutastu tiraskāravacanametat / bhāgavihīna evamucyate //
body.translated_text: 'Of that' — of such a trivial, most insignificant taste of pleasure — which is common even to a beast — 'for the sake of' — on account of. 'This precious opportunity of a moment' — free from the eight unfavorable conditions — has been 'destroyed,' annihilated — the meaning is: wasted. Of what kind? 'So difficult to obtain' — as has been explained. By whom? 'Ruined by fate' — '<s>daiva</s>' is former <s>karma</s>; by that, one is 'ruined' — made to have perverted understanding regarding the discernment of what is beneficial and harmful — the meaning is: deluded. But in reality, this is a term of reproach — one who is bereft of fortune is spoken of thus.

body.text: avaśyaṃ ganturityādinā ślokadvayena viparyāsarūpatāmeva pratipādayati-
body.translated_text: With two verses beginning with 'must certainly depart,' he demonstrates the very nature of perversity —

children.translated_text: For this body, which must certainly depart, which is insignificant,

children.text: kāyasyārthe kṛto yo 'yaṃ sarvakālaṃ pariśramaḥ // Bca_8.82 //
children.translated_text: which plunges into the hells and such — this toil has been undertaken at all times. // <s>Bca</s> 8.82 //

body.text: avaśyaṃ ganturiti anityatayā asthirasvabhāvasya / alpasya lokottarakāyamapekṣya atidūraṃ niṣkṛṣṭasya / narakādiprapātina iti aparimitaduḥkhabhāginaḥ / svasukhotpādane 'pyasamarthasyetyarthaḥ / kāyasya ātmaśarīrasyārthe sukhotpādanāya yo 'yaṃ narakādiduḥkhamavigaṇayya kṛtaḥ sarvakālaṃ saṃsārasya pūrvasyāṃ koṭau pariśramaḥ prayāsaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Must certainly depart' — being of an impermanent, unstable nature. 'Insignificant' — vastly inferior in comparison with the supramundane body. 'Which plunges into the hells and such' — which partakes of immeasurable suffering — the meaning is: which is incapable even of producing its own happiness. 'For the sake of the body' — one's own physical person — 'for the sake of producing happiness' — this toil, this exertion, has been undertaken 'at all times' — since the beginning of <s>saṃsāra</s> — disregarding the suffering of the hells and such.

body.text: tataḥ koṭiśatenāpi śramabhāgena buddhatā /
body.translated_text: With even a hundred-millionth fraction of that effort, <s>Buddhahood</s> [could be attained];

body.text: tatastasmāt pariśramāt koṭiśatenāpi pariśramabhāgena aṃśena buddhatvaṃ syāt, tadapekṣayā atyalpīyasā āyāsabalena buddhatvaṃ syāt / tathāpi tadarthaṃ mandabuddhayo notsahanta ityarthaḥ / atha bodhicaryāyāmapi carataḥ anekaduṣkaraśatasamārambhādatiśayabadduḥkhasahasramutpadyata evetyāha-
body.translated_text: 'From that' — from that toil — with even a hundred-millionth 'fraction,' portion, of the effort, <s>Buddhahood</s> could be attained — that is, with an extremely small amount of exertion compared to that, <s>Buddhahood</s> could be attained. Yet even for that purpose, those of dull intellect do not make the effort — this is the meaning. But if even while engaged in the <s>Bodhisattva</s> practice, great suffering arises from undertaking hundreds of difficult deeds — he says —

body.text: caryāduḥkhānmahadduḥkhaṃ sā ca bodhirna kāminām // Bca_8.83 //
body.translated_text: the suffering of the [<s>Bodhisattva</s>] practice is [far] exceeded [by this]; yet that awakening does not come to the desire-seekers. // <s>Bca</s> 8.83 //

body.text: caryāduḥkhamapekṣya idameva mahadduḥkhaṃ yatkāmārthe caratāṃ saṃsāre teṣāmavīcyādinarakapatanāt, pāratantryeṇa dīrghakālamanubhavanācca / na tu bodhisattvānāṃ pratiniyatakālaṃ svecchayā tadanubhavatām / tadevaṃ duḥkhamanubhavatāmapi kāmārthe kāmināṃ sā ca bodhirna bhavati, yā bodhisattvānāṃ parārthe duḥkhamanubhavatāmityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: Compared to the suffering of the [<s>Bodhisattva</s>] practice, this very suffering is greater — that which befalls those who pursue sense-pleasures in <s>saṃsāra</s>, through falling into the hells of <s>Avīci</s> and such, and through enduring [it] for a long time in servitude. But for <s>Bodhisattvas</s>, [it is] for a limited time and experienced willingly. Thus, even though those who pursue sense-pleasures undergo such suffering, that awakening does not come to them — which does come to <s>Bodhisattvas</s> who undergo suffering for the sake of others — this is the meaning.

body.text: punarviśeṣeṇa kāmanidānaduḥkhaṃ pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Demonstrating yet more emphatically the suffering caused by sense-pleasures, he says —

children.text: na śastraṃ na viṣaṃ nāgnirna prapāto na vairiṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: Neither weapons, nor poison, nor fire, nor precipices, nor enemies
bear comparison with sense-pleasures, when one recalls the suffering of the hells and such. // <s>Bca</s> 8.84 //

body.text: amī śastrādayo duḥkhajanakatvena prasiddhā na sādṛśyaṃ bhajante prati kāmānām / kasmāt? narakādidurgatiduḥkhasya āgamāt pratipannasya smaraṇāt smaraṇenāmukhīkaraṇāt / śastrādayo hi niyatakālaṃ maraṇamātraduḥkhadāyakāḥ, kāmāstu dīrghakālikatīvranarakādiduḥkhahetava iti kīdṛśī tairupamā bhavet?
body.translated_text: These — weapons and such — well-known as producers of suffering, do not bear resemblance to sense-pleasures. Why? Because of the remembrance — the bringing to mind — of the suffering of the hells and other lower realms, as learned from scripture. For weapons and such inflict suffering only for a limited time, and only the suffering of death; but sense-pleasures are causes of intense suffering in the hells and such for a long duration — so what comparison could there be with those?

body.text: tadevaṃ kāyavivekānantaraṃ cittavivekaṃ pratipādya prakṛte yojayitumāha-
body.translated_text: Having thus taught the seclusion of mind following the seclusion of body, to apply it to the topic at hand, he says —

body.text: evamudvijya kāmebhyo viveke janayedratim /
body.translated_text: Thus being repelled by sense-pleasures, one should generate delight in solitude.

body.text: kāmebhyo bhayahetubhyaḥ / evamuktakrameṇa udvijya saṃtrāsaṃ kṛtvā pūrvoktaviveke ratimabhiratimutpādayet / kutra sthitvā tatrāha-
body.translated_text: 'By sense-pleasures' — causes of fear. Thus, in the manner stated, having been repelled, having generated alarm, one should produce delight, fondness, in the previously described solitude. Situated where? There he says —

body.text: kalahāyāsaśūnyāsu śāntāsu vanabhūmiṣu // Bca_8.85 //
body.translated_text: In forest grounds, peaceful, free from quarrels and weariness. // <s>Bca</s> 8.85 //

body.text: pratidvandvināmabhāvāt kalahāyāsaśūnyāstāḥ, vyālamṛgasarīsṛpataskarādivirahācca ramyāḥ //
body.translated_text: Due to the absence of adversaries, they are free from quarrels and weariness; and due to the absence of wild animals, serpents, thieves, and such, they are delightful.

body.text: tatrānuśaṃsāmāha-
body.translated_text: There, he states the benefits —

children.translated_text: The fortunate ones stroll on lovely expanses of stone, vast as palaces, cooled by the rays of the moon like sandalwood,

children.text: niḥśabdasaumyavanamārutavījyamānaiḥ caṃkramyate parahitāya vicintyate ca // Bca_8.86 //
children.translated_text: fanned by the silent, gentle forest breezes, contemplating the welfare of others. // <s>Bca</s> 8.86 //

body.text: dhanyaiḥ sukṛtibhiḥ / śaśāṅkasya candramasaḥ karā raśmaya eva śuklatāśaityasādharmyāccandanānīva, taiḥ śītalāni yāni ślātalāni teṣu caṃkramyata iti saṃbandhaḥ / kiṃviśiṣṭeṣu? prakṛtyaiva śucipavitreṣu karkaśādidoṣarahiteṣu ca / harmyavipuleṣu dhavalagṛhavadvistīrṇeṣu / kīdṛśaiḥ sadbhiścaṃkramyate? niḥśabdaiḥ pratikūlaśabdavirahitaiḥ / saumyairanutkaṭaiḥ / sukhasaṃsparśairityarthaḥ / vanamārutaiḥ vanapavanaiḥ / vījyamānāḥ taiścaṃkramyata iti parāvṛttyā punaḥ punarmandaṃ bhramyate / na kevalaṃ caṃkramyate, kiṃ tu parahitāya sattvānāṃ sukhotpādanāya vicintyate / sarvametadayatnasiddhaṃ yoginām, kāmināṃ tu prayatnasādhyam / tadanena aiśvaryasukhādviśiṣyate vivekasukhamityupadarśitaṃ bhavati //
body.translated_text: 'The fortunate ones' — those of good merit. The rays of the moon — its beams — being like sandalwood due to their similarity in whiteness and coolness — 'cooled by those' — on those cool [surfaces] they stroll — this is the connection. Of what kind? By nature pure and clean, free from faults such as roughness and such. 'Vast as palaces' — as spacious as white mansions. By what kind of persons is the strolling done? 'Silent' — free from unpleasant sounds. 'Gentle' — not intense. The meaning is: of pleasant touch. 'By forest breezes' — forest winds. 'Fanned' — by those [breezes], they stroll — that is, they walk back and forth again and again, slowly. Not only do they stroll, but they 'contemplate the welfare of others' — the production of happiness for beings. All this is accomplished effortlessly for <s>yogins</s>, but only with effort for desire-seekers. By this, it is shown that the happiness of solitude surpasses the happiness of sovereignty and such.

body.text: idamaparamasādhāraṇaṃ sukhaṃ vivekavihāriṇa ityupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Showing yet another uncommon happiness of one who dwells in solitude, he says —

children.text: vihṛtya yatra kvacidiṣṭakālaṃ śūnyālaye vṛkṣatale guhāsu /
children.translated_text: Having dwelt as long as one wishes, wherever one wishes — in empty dwellings, under trees, in caves —
Free from the weariness of guarding possessions, one moves about unconcerned, as one wishes. // <s>Bca</s> 8.87 //

body.text: subodham //
body.translated_text: This is easily understood.

body.text: svacchandacārītyādinā kathitamevārthaṃ vyaktīkaroti-
body.translated_text: By 'one who roams at will' and so forth, he makes clear the meaning already stated —

children.translated_text: One who roams at will, whose abode is unbound, attached to no one —
the happiness of contentment that he enjoys is hard to find even for <s>Indra</s>. // <s>Bca</s> 8.88 //

body.text: svasyātmanaḥ chando 'bhilāṣaḥ, tena carituṃ śīlamasyeti / svecchācārītyarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'One's own' — of oneself — 'wish' — desire; one whose nature is to move by that [wish] — meaning: one who acts according to one's own will.

body.text: iti vivekaguṇānabhidhāya prakṛtamabhidhitsurāha-
body.translated_text: Having thus described the virtues of solitude, intending to state the main subject, he says —

children.translated_text: By contemplating the virtues of solitude through these and other aspects,

children.text: upaśāntavitarkaḥ san bodhicittaṃ tu bhāvayet // Bca_8.89 //
children.translated_text: having stilled discursive thoughts, one should cultivate <s>bodhicitta</s>. // <s>Bca</s> 8.89 //

body.text: evamiti pūrvoktaiḥ / ādiśabdādanyairapi evaṃvidhairākāraiḥ / vivekasya kāyikacaitasikasya guṇānāṃ bhāvanāt, iti hi sarvasukhasaṃpattiheturviveka iti cetasi punaḥ punarāmukhīkaraṇāddhetoḥ upaśānto vitarkaḥ asanmanasikāro yasya saḥ / tathābhūtaḥ san bodhicittaṃ tu bhāvayet / evaṃ pariśuddhe cetasi bhāvyamānaṃ bodhicittaṃ prakarṣapadamadhirohatīti viśeṣaṃ tuśabdena darśayati //
body.translated_text: 'Thus' — by the previously described [aspects]. By the word 'and such,' by other such aspects as well. Through the contemplation of the virtues of solitude — physical and mental. Since solitude is the cause of all attainments of happiness — through the repeated turning of the mind toward this: this is the cause. One whose discursive thoughts — unwholesome mental engagements — have been stilled; being in such a state, one should cultivate <s>bodhicitta</s>. The word 'tu' (but/indeed) shows the distinction: when cultivated in a thus-purified mind, <s>bodhicitta</s> ascends to the pinnacle of excellence.

body.text: tatra yāvadekatvaṃ pareṣu nātmanā kriyate, na tāvat parahitasukhāya samyak cittaṃ calati, ātmagrāhasya ātmanyeva viśeṣeṇa pravṛtteḥ / ato 'sya nivṛttaye-
body.translated_text: Now, as long as one does not establish oneness with others through oneself, one's mind does not properly move toward the benefit and happiness of others, since the grasping of self is specifically directed toward oneself alone. Therefore, for its cessation —

body.text: parātmasamatāmādau bhāvayedevamādarāt /
body.translated_text: One should first cultivate the equality of self and other, diligently, as follows.

body.text: ādau prathamataḥ / paścāt parātmaparivartanamiti bhāvaḥ / evamiti vakṣyamāṇanītyā / ādarāditi mahatābhiniveśena / tasyā evākāraṃ darśayati-
body.translated_text: 'First' — at the beginning. Afterward, the exchange of self and other — this is the implication. 'As follows' — by the method to be stated. 'Diligently' — with great commitment. He shows the form of that [practice] —

body.text: samaduḥkhasukhāḥ sarve pālanīyā mayātmavat // Bca_8.90 //
body.translated_text: All beings are equal in suffering and happiness, and should be protected by me as myself. // <s>Bca</s> 8.90 //

body.text: matto nāmīṣāṃ kaścidviśeṣo 'sti / ato yathā mama duḥkhaṃ bādhakaṃ tathā eṣāmapi / yathā mama sukhamanugrāhakaṃ tathā eṣāmapi / iti tulyaduḥkhasukhāḥ sarve prāṇino bhavanti / tasmāt pālanīyā mayātmavat / yathā ātmā duḥkhādduḥkhahetorvā samudbhiyate, tathā anyepi sattvāḥ samuddharaṇīyāḥ / yathā ātmā sarvathā sukhīkartumiṣyate, tathā anye 'pīti paripālanīyā ātmavat //
body.translated_text: There is no distinction whatsoever between me and these others. Therefore, just as suffering is harmful to me, so it is to them; just as happiness is beneficial to me, so it is to them. Thus all living beings are equal in suffering and happiness. Therefore they should be protected by me as myself. Just as I myself am to be rescued from suffering and the causes of suffering, so too should other beings be rescued. Just as I myself am desired to be made happy in every way, so too should others be cared for, as oneself.

body.text: nanu kathamātmanā anekaprakāragatibhedabhinnānāṃ sattvānāmekatvaṃ setsyati, abhinnasukhaduḥkhasvabhāvatvaṃ ca katham? ityatrāha-
body.translated_text: But how will oneness be established between oneself and beings who are differentiated by many kinds of destinies and divisions? And how [can they be] of undifferentiated nature with respect to happiness and suffering? To this he says —

children.translated_text: Just as the body, though of many parts through the division of hands and such, is to be protected as one,
so too this entire world, though differentiated, is of undifferentiated suffering and happiness — just so. // <s>Bca</s> 8.91 //

body.text: karacaraṇaśiraḥprabhṛtibhedādanekaprakāraḥ kāyo yathikatvenādhyavasitaḥ paripālanīyo bhavati duḥkhanivartanāt sukhopadhānācca, jagatsattvalokaḥ abhinnamekatvenādhyavasitamātmanaḥ paripālanīyaṃ bhavati / abhinnaduḥkhasukhātmakaṃ ca / luptacakāro nirdeśaḥ / tathaiva hastādibhedavadeva sarvamidamiti bahuprakāragatibhedabhinnamapi / ayamabhiprāyaḥ- yathā abhyāsādekatvādhyavasāyo 'smin kāye ekatvamantareṇāpi, tathā anekaprakāre jagatyapīti na kaścidviśeṣaḥ //
body.translated_text: Just as the body, of many parts through the division of hands, feet, head, and so on, being conceived as one, is to be protected — through the removal of suffering and the provision of happiness — so too the world, the realm of beings, being conceived as one with oneself, is to be protected. And [it is] of undifferentiated suffering and happiness — the statement has an elided 'and.' 'Just so' — just as through the division of hands and such — 'this entire' [world], though differentiated by many kinds of destinies and divisions. The intention is: just as through habituation, the conviction of oneness arises in this body even without [actual] oneness, so too in the world of many parts — there is no difference.

body.text: syādetat- yadi bhavatā saha jagadekasvabhāvam, tadā kathamiva bhavato duḥkhamanyasaṃtāneṣu na bādhakaṃ syāt? evaṃ viparyaye 'pi yojyamityāśaṅkayāha-
body.translated_text: One might say: if the world is of one nature with you, then how could your suffering in other mind-streams not be harmful? The same should be applied in the reverse case. Anticipating this, he says —

children.translated_text: Although my suffering does not afflict other bodies,
nevertheless, that suffering is indeed mine — unbearable due to self-love. // <s>Bca</s> 8.92 //

body.text: anyeṣu apareṣu śarīreṣu mama duḥkhaṃ yadi nāma prabādhakaṃ na bhavati, tathāpi tadduḥkhameva mama / kutaḥ? ātmani snehena duḥsahaṃ soḍhumaśakyam / hetupadametat / aṃśena pravṛttāvapi duḥkhasvabhāvatāṃ na muñcatītyarthaḥ / evaṃ viparyayo 'pi vyākhyeyaḥ //
body.translated_text: Even if my suffering is not harmful in other, different bodies, nevertheless that suffering is indeed mine. Why? Because it is unbearable — impossible to endure — due to love for the self. This is the causal clause. Even when engaged only partially, it does not release the nature of suffering — this is the meaning. The reverse [case] should also be explained thus.

children.translated_text: Likewise, although another's suffering is not experienced by me myself,
nevertheless, that suffering belongs to that one — unbearable due to self-love. // <s>Bca</s> 8.93 //

body.text: ataḥ svaparaviśeṣamapāsya duḥkhasvabhāvataiva nivartanahetuḥ / ata āha-
body.translated_text: Therefore, setting aside the distinction between self and other, the nature of suffering alone is the cause for its removal. Therefore he says —

body.text: mayānyaduḥkhaṃ hantavyaṃ duḥkhatvādātmaduḥkhavat / yadyadduḥkhaṃ tattanmayā hantavyam, yathātmaduḥkham / duḥkhaṃ cedamanyasattvaduḥkhamiti svabhāvahetuprayogaḥ / duḥkhasvabhāvatāmātrabhāvinī hantavyatā / na ca asiddhatā hetoḥ, aviśeṣeṇa duḥkhasvabhāvatāyāḥ prasādhitatvāt / na cāpyanaikāntikatā, ātmaduḥkhasyāpi hantavyatā na syādaviśeṣāditi viparyayabādhakam / viruddhatāpyata eva na syāt / tathāyamaparaḥ prayogaḥ-
body.translated_text: Another's suffering should be removed by me, because it is suffering, just like my own suffering. Whatever suffering there is, all that is to be removed by me, just like my own suffering. 'This suffering of other beings is suffering' — this is a natural-reason argument. The quality of being-to-be-removed inheres solely in the nature of being suffering. Nor is the reason unestablished, since the nature of being suffering has been proven without distinction. Nor is there inconclusiveness, since if [the conclusion] did not apply even to one's own suffering without distinction — this serves as a counter-proof by reversal. From this very [argument], there would also be no contradiction. Likewise, here is another argument —

body.text: anugrāhyā mayānye 'pi sattvatvādātmasattvavat // Bca_8.94 //
body.translated_text: Others too should be helped by me, because they are sentient beings, just as my own self is a sentient being. // <s>Bca</s> 8.94 //

body.text: ye sattvāste sarve mayā anugrāhyāḥ, yathā ātmasattvaḥ / sattvāśca anye 'pi prāṇinaḥ iti svabhāvahetureva / sattvātmakatāmātrabhāvini anugrāhyasvabhāvatā atra / ayamapi nāsiddhaḥ, sattvātmakatāyāḥ pakṣe prasiddhatvāt / ātmano 'nugrāhyatābhāvaprasaṅgena anaikāntiko 'pi na syāt / pūrvavanna viruddhaḥ //
body.translated_text: Those who are sentient beings — all of them should be helped by me, just as my own self [is helped]. And others too are living beings — this is indeed a natural-reason [argument]. The quality of being-worthy-of-help inheres solely in the nature of being a sentient being. This too is not unestablished, since the nature of being a sentient being is well-known in the thesis. Through the absurd consequence of one's own self not being worthy of help, it would also not be inconclusive. As before, it is not contradictory.

body.text: nanu asti viśeṣo 'nyasmādātmani sukhābhiniveśo nāma / tathā tato 'yamanaikāntiko heturiti / atrāha-
body.translated_text: But there is a distinction: there is a special clinging to happiness in the self as opposed to others. Therefore this reason would be inconclusive — to this he says —

children.text: yadā mama pareṣāṃ ca tulyameva sukhaṃ priyam /
children.translated_text: When happiness is equally dear to me and to others,

children.text: tadātmanaḥ ko viśeṣo yenātraiva sukhodyama // Bca_8.95 //
children.translated_text: then what special quality does the self have, that the effort for happiness is directed only here? // <s>Bca</s> 8.95 //

body.text: tulyameva samameva sukhaṃ priyamiṣṭam / tadātmanaḥ parasmāt ko viśeṣaḥ? naiva kaścit yena tatraiva ātmanyeva sukhotpādanāya tātparyaṃ na parasminnityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: Happiness is equally — identically — dear, desired. Then what distinction does the self have from another? None whatsoever — such that the intent for producing happiness is directed only toward the self and not toward the other. This is the meaning.

body.text: prathame hetāvanaikāntikatāṃ pariharannāha-
body.translated_text: Removing the inconclusiveness in the first argument, he says —

children.text: yadā mama pareṣāṃ ca bhayaṃ duḥkhaṃ ca na priyam /
children.translated_text: When fear and suffering are equally unwanted for me and for others,

children.text: tadātmanaḥ ko viśeṣo yattaṃ rakṣāmi netaram // Bca_8.96 //
children.translated_text: then what special quality does the self have, that I protect it and not the other? // <s>Bca</s> 8.96 //

body.text: bhayamiti duḥkhahetuḥ / netaramiti nānyam //
body.translated_text: 'Fear' is the cause of suffering. 'Not the other' means not another.

body.text: syādetat- yadi nāma duḥkhātmakatā na viśiṣyate, tathāpi yasya duḥkhena bādhā syāt, sa eva rakṣitumucito nānya ityāha-
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Even if the nature of being suffering is not distinct, still, only the one who is afflicted by that suffering is fit to be protected, not another — to this he says —

children.text: tadduḥkhena na me bādhetyato yadi na rakṣyate /
children.translated_text: 'His suffering does not afflict me' — if for that reason he is not protected,
the suffering of the future body does not afflict me [now] either — then by what [reasoning] is it protected? // <s>Bca</s> 8.97 //

body.text: tasya parasya duḥkhena mama bādhā pīḍā nāstītyato 'smāt kāraṇād yadi na rakṣyate 'nyaḥ, tadā aparamidaṃ vyāhataṃ syāt / yato nāgāminaḥ kāyasya paralokabhāvino narakādijātasya duḥkhātmakasya [duḥkhānme] tasyopāttasya kāyasya kācidbādhā saṃbhavati, tasya anyatvāt / iti lokoktau, tasmādarthe vā / yata evam, tasmāt kenābhiprāyeṇa asau rakṣyate? kāya iti prakṛtatvāt pāpānnivartanāt kuśale pravartanācca //
body.translated_text: If the other person is not protected because 'his suffering does not cause me pain' — for this reason — then there would be another absurd consequence. Since no pain from the sufferings of the future body — which will come to exist in the next life, born in hell and such, of the nature of suffering — [no pain] of that assumed body exists [for me now], that [body] being other. Thus, in common parlance, or for this purpose: since this is so, therefore by what intention is that [future body] protected? That is, through turning away from evil and engaging in the wholesome — since the body is the [implicit] subject.

body.text: athāpi syāt- ahameka eva sarvadā, tenātra bhinnatvaṃ nāsti śarīrayoḥ / nāyaṃ doṣa ityatrāha-
body.translated_text: One might say: I am one and the same at all times; therefore there is no duality between the bodies. This is not a fault — to this he says —

body.text: ahameva tadāpīti mithyeyaṃ parikalpanā /
body.translated_text: 'I myself [exist] even then' — this is a false conceptualization.

body.text: ātmano nirākariṣyamāṇatvāt nirastatvācca leśataḥ tatko 'yamahaṃpratyayasya viṣayo bhaviṣyati? tasmādahaṃpratyayaviṣayasya kasyacidekasyābhāvānmithyeyaṃ parikalpanā adhyavasāyaḥ /
body.translated_text: Since the self will be refuted and has already been partially refuted — what then will be the object of the I-notion? Therefore, since there is no single entity that is the object of the I-notion, this conceptualization — this conviction — is false.

body.text: ahameva tadāpīti / bhavāntare 'pi / māyopamapañcopādānaskandhamātrālambanatvādasya / itīdamapi adhyavasāyavaśāducyate, na tu punarasya vastutaḥ kiṃcidālambanamasti, vikalpātmakatvāt //
body.translated_text: 'I myself [exist] even then' — even in a future existence. Because it has as its object merely the five <s>upādānaskandhas</s> (appropriation-aggregates), which are like an illusion. And 'thus' too is stated by force of convention, for in reality this [I-notion] has no object whatsoever, being of the nature of conceptualization.

body.text: kutaḥ punariyaṃ mithyākalpanetyāha-
body.translated_text: Why then is this a false conceptualization? He says —

body.text: anya eva mṛto yasmādanya eva prajāyate // Bca_8.98 //
body.translated_text: Because the one who dies is indeed different, and the one who is born is indeed different. // <s>Bca</s> 8.98 //

body.text: yadā nātmādiḥ kaścidekaḥ paralokagāmī saṃbhavati, skandhamātrameva kevalam, tadā na khalu yadeva skandhapañcakamiha vinaśyati, tadeva punarapyutpadyate paraloke, api tu apūrvameva pūrvanivṛttau tatra idaṃpratyayatāviśiṣṭaṃ kleśakarmābhisaṃskṛtamantarābhavasaṃtatyā samutpadyate / tasmādanādisaṃsārapravṛttavitathavikalpābhyāsavāsanāvaśādahaṃpratyayo vitatha eva upajāyate //
body.translated_text: When no self or similar single entity that transmigrates to the next world exists — when there are merely the aggregates alone — then surely the very group of five aggregates that perishes here does not arise again in the next world; rather, an entirely new [set], distinct from the previous [set] upon its cessation, characterized by being conditioned by this [previous set], fashioned by <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) and <s>karma</s>, arises there through the continuity of the intermediate existence. Therefore, the I-notion arises as entirely false, through the force of the habitual tendencies of false conceptualization that has been operating since beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>.

body.text: kiṃ ca / idamaparaṃ tatra bādhakamityāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, here is another objection against that [view] — he says —

children.text: yadi tasyaiva yadduḥkhaṃ rakṣyaṃ tasyaiva tanmatam /
children.translated_text: If [only] the one whose suffering it is should be protected — this is accepted as [applying to] that one alone —

children.text: pādaduḥkhaṃ na hastasya kasmāttattena rakṣyate // Bca_8.99 //
children.translated_text: [then] the suffering of the foot does not belong to the hand — why is it protected by the hand? // <s>Bca</s> 8.99 //

body.text: āstāṃ tāvad yadāgāmikāyaduḥkharakṣārthaṃ na yatitavyam / iha ekasminnapi kāye pratyaṅgabhedādbhinnaṃ duḥkham / tato yadā anyadduḥkhamanyasya rakṣituṃ na yujyate, tadā kathaṃ pādādau prahāraṃ patantaṃ dṛṣṭvā hastaṃ prasārya rakṣyate? anyatvāviśeṣānna yuktametadityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: Setting aside for now the argument that one need not strive to protect against the suffering of the future body — even in this single body, suffering is differentiated through the division of limbs. So when it is not justified to protect the suffering of one [part] by another, then how is it that when a blow is seen falling on the foot and such, the hand is extended to protect it? Since there is no difference in otherness — this is not justified. This is the meaning.

body.text: atha-
body.translated_text: But —

body.text: ayuktamapi cedetadahaṃkārātpravartate

children.translated_text: what is unjustified — whether one's own or another's — should be eliminated as far as possible. // <s>Bca</s> 8.100 //

body.translated_text: Even if this is unjustified and proceeds from the sense of 'I,'

body.text: ahaṃkāro 'smin kāye ahamityātmagrahādātmano 'bhāve 'pi / pravartate jāyate pādādau rakṣaṇamanasikāraḥ / naitat sādhu / yato yadayuktaṃ yuktyā saṃgataṃ na bhavati, tannivartyamapasāryaṃ svakīyaṃ parakīyaṃ ca yathābalaṃ yathāsāmarthyam / śaktivaikalyādeva tadupekṣitumucitamiti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: The sense of 'I' — the grasping of self as 'I am this body' — even though the self does not exist. The mental engagement of protection toward the foot and such arises, proceeds. This is not good. Because what is unjustified — what is not in accord with reason — that should be eliminated, removed — whether one's own or another's — as far as possible, as far as one is able. Only due to the deficiency of power is it appropriate to disregard that — this is the meaning.

body.text: syādetat- yadi nāma ātmādirnāsti, tathāpi saṃtāno nāma ekaḥ saṃbhavati, tathā bahūnāṃ karacaraṇādīnāṃ samudāyaḥ śarīramekam / tadetaddvayaṃ yathāsaṃbhavamihaloke paraloke ca ātmaduḥkhāpaharaṇāderniyāmakaṃ bhaviṣyati / tato 'yamaviśeṣādityasiddho hetuḥ, pūrvaśca anaikāntika ityāśaṅkayāha-
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Even if the self and such do not exist, still there is a single thing called a 'continuum,' and likewise the aggregation of many [parts] such as hands, feet, and such is a single body. These two, as applicable here in this world and in the next, would serve as the determinant for the removal of one's own suffering and such. Therefore, the [argument from] 'no distinction' has an unestablished reason, and the earlier [argument] is inconclusive. Anticipating this, he says —

children.translated_text: The continuum and the aggregate are false, like a row, an army, and such.

children.text: yasya duḥkhaṃ sa nāstyasmātkasya tatsvaṃ bhaviṣyati // Bca_8.101 //
children.translated_text: The one whose suffering it is does not exist — therefore, to whom will that [suffering] belong as its own? // <s>Bca</s> 8.101 //

body.text: saṃtāno nāma na kaścidekaḥ paramārthasan saṃbhavati / kiṃ tarhi kāryakāraṇabhāvapravṛttakṣaṇaparaṃparāpravāharūpa evāyam, tato vyatiriktasyānupalambhāt / tasmādeteṣāmeva kṣaṇānāmekapadena pratipādanāya saṃketo kṛto buddhairvyavahārārthaṃ saṃtāna iti / iti prajñaptisanneva ayam / tena atrābhiniveśo na kāryaḥ / anyathā ātmanā kimaparāddhaṃ yenāsau na svīkriyate / evaṃ samudāyo 'pi na samudāyibhyo vastusan eko vidyate, tasya tebhyaḥ pṛthaganupalabdheḥ?
body.translated_text: No single thing called a 'continuum' exists in the ultimate sense. Rather, it is nothing but the flow of a succession of moments operating in the mode of cause and effect, since nothing apart from that is apprehended. Therefore, for the purpose of designating these very moments with a single term, the convention 'continuum' has been made by the wise for the sake of practical usage. Thus this is a mere designation. Therefore one should not cling to it. Otherwise, what wrong has the self done that it should not be accepted? Likewise, the 'aggregate' too does not exist as a single real thing apart from its constituents, since it is not apprehended separately from them.

body.text: tattvānyatvavikalpastu asya avayavivicāreṇaiva gata iti neha pratāyate / tataśca ayamapi saṃvṛtisanneva pūrvavat / anayoryathāsaṃkhyamudāharaṇamāha paṅktisenādivaditi / paṅkivat saṃtānaḥ, senādivat samudāyaḥ / ādiśabdānmālāvanādayo gṛhyante / yathā anekeṣāṃ pipīlikādīnāṃ pūrvāparabhāvena vyavasthitānāṃ svarūpamantareṇa paṅktirnāsti straksūtravadekāḥ, yathā ca hastyaśvapadātiprabhṛtibhyo militebhyo vyatiriktā nānyā senā kācidekā tatrāsti, tathā samudāyo 'pi / etacca anyatra [9.73] vistareṇa vicāritamiti neha vicāryate / tasmādvastusadālambanābhāvānmṛṣāyaṃ pratyayaḥ / artho vā, vicārāsahatvāt / evamātmādeḥ svāminaḥ kasyacidabhāvād yasya saṃbandhi duḥkhaṃ sa nāsti / ataḥ kasya tadduḥkhaṃ svātmīyaṃ bhaviṣyati? naiva kasyacidityarthaḥ / nanu yadi ātmādirnāsti, tadā kathamayaṃ dṛṣṭānto bhaviṣyati ātmavaditi ātmasattvavaditi ca? satyametat / kiṃ tu nedaṃ vyasanitayā sādhanamabhidhīyate, kiṃ tarhi parasya ātmagrahābhiniveśanivāraṇāya / tadyadi parasya nivṛtta eva ātmagrahābhiniveśaḥ, tadā na kiṃcit prayojanamanumānaprayogasya / atha na nivṛttaḥ, tadā tadabhiprāyeṇaiva svaparavibhāgaṃ kṛtvā tatpratyāyanārthaṃ sādhanaṃ dṛṣṭāntaścocyate, iti na dṛṣṭāntasyāsiddhirvyavahārapravartanāya / kiṃ ca / idamupāttapañcaskandhamātramabhisaṃdhāya dṛṣṭānte dīyamāne na kācit kṣatiḥ, atraiva ātmaśabdasya pravṛtteriti //
body.translated_text: The conceptual analysis of identity and difference with regard to this has already been dealt with through the investigation of the possessor of parts, and so is not elaborated here. Accordingly, this too exists merely conventionally, as before. He gives examples for each respectively, saying 'like a row, an army, and such.' A continuum is like a row; an aggregate is like an army and such. By the word 'such,' garlands, forests, and the like are included. Just as, for many ants and such arranged in sequence, apart from their individual forms there is no one thing called a 'row' like a thread of a garland, and just as apart from elephants, horses, foot-soldiers, and others assembled together there is no other single entity called an 'army' existing there — so too with an aggregate. And this has been investigated at length elsewhere [9.73], so it is not examined here. Therefore, due to the absence of a substantially real referent, this cognition is false. Or rather, the object [is false], because it cannot withstand analysis. Thus, since no owner such as a self and so forth exists, to whom suffering belongs — that [owner] does not exist. Therefore, whose suffering will it be, as one's own? Of no one whatsoever — this is the meaning. But if a self and such do not exist, then how will this example apply — 'like the self,' and 'like a sentient being'? This is true. However, this proof is not stated out of dogmatism; rather, it is for the purpose of removing the opponent's clinging to the apprehension of self. If the opponent's clinging to the apprehension of self has already ceased, then there is no purpose whatsoever for the application of an inference. But if it has not ceased, then, in accordance with that [opponent's] own view, making the distinction of self and other, the proof and the example are stated for the purpose of convincing that [opponent] — so there is no invalidity of the example for the functioning of conventional discourse. Moreover, if the example is given with reference merely to this — the appropriated five aggregates — there is no fault whatsoever, since the word 'self' applies precisely to this. //

body.text: idānīṃ prakṛtamupasaṃharannāha-
body.translated_text: Now, concluding the main topic, he says —

children.translated_text: All sufferings without distinction are ownerless;
they are to be warded off simply because they are suffering — what is the basis for any restriction? // Bca_8.102 //

body.text: na vidyante svāmino yeṣāmuktakrameṇeti vigrahaḥ / amamāni na kasyacitpratibaddhāni ityarthaḥ / kutaḥ? kiṃ kānicideva? na / sarvāṇyevāviśeṣataḥ / na kvacit kasyacit svāmitvamasti, viśeṣābhāvāt / duḥkhatvādeva svaparāvibhāgaṃ kṛtvā vāryāṇi niṣedhyāni bhavanti / nānyannimittamasti tatra ātmīyatvādi / tenāyaṃ niyamaḥ kiṃkṛtaḥ, kena viśeṣeṇa kṛtaḥ? yena svakīyāni ca vāryāṇi na parakīyānīti / evaṃ duḥkhatvāditi heturanaikāntiko na bhavatīti samarthitam //
body.translated_text: 'Those of which there are no owners' — in the manner stated — this is the analysis. 'Without possessors' — not bound to anyone — this is the meaning. Why? Are only some [ownerless]? No. 'All without distinction.' There is no ownership by anyone anywhere, due to the absence of any distinction. 'Simply because they are suffering' — without making the division of self and other — they 'are to be warded off,' are to be prevented. There is no other ground such as 'being one's own' and so forth. Therefore, 'what is the basis for this restriction?' — by what distinguishing feature is it made — that one's own [sufferings] are to be warded off but not others'? Thus it has been demonstrated that the reason 'because they are suffering' is not inconclusive. //

body.text: nanu yadi duḥkhī nāma na kaścit saṃsāre saṃbhavati, tarhi duḥkhamanivāryameva syāt, kṛpāpātrasya duḥkhinaḥ kasyacidabhāvādityāśaṅkamāna āha-
body.translated_text: But if no one called 'a sufferer' is possible in <s>saṃsāra</s>, then suffering would simply not need to be warded off, since there is no one who would be an object of compassion — anticipating this, he says —

children.translated_text: If [you ask] why suffering should be warded off — because this is undisputed by all.

children.text: vāryaṃ cetsarvamapyevaṃ na cedātmāpi sattvavat // Bca_8.103 //
children.translated_text: If it is to be warded off, then all [suffering must be warded off]; if not, then [one's] own [suffering] too, just like [that of] sentient beings. // Bca_8.103 //

body.text: na vāryameva nirātmakatvādeva yadi manyase, tadā na yuktametat / kutaḥ? sarveṣāmavivādādavipratipatteḥ / cārvākasyāpi svaduḥkhaparihāreṇaiveha pravṛtteḥ / na ca teṣāmātmano
body.translated_text: If you think it simply need not be warded off precisely because [beings] are selfless — that is not correct. Why? Because all are in agreement, without dispute. Even the <s>Cārvāka</s> engages [in action] precisely for the avoidance of his own suffering. Nor is there no fault due to their acceptance of a self

body.text: 'bhyupagamādadoṣaḥ, tatsvabhāvasyānupalabdheḥ / na ca abhyupagamamātreṇa tasya sattā prasidhyati tatsādhakapramāṇābhāvāt, bādhakasya ca anekaprakārasyābhidhānāt / evaṃ sati yadi vāryaṃ duḥkham, tadā sarvaṃ vāryam, na cetsarvaṃ vāryam, tadātmāpi / upāttapañcaskandhasvabhāvamapi duḥkhaṃ na vāryam, sarva(ttva?)vadaviśeṣādityupasaṃhāraḥ //
body.translated_text: because that nature [of the self] is not apprehended. Nor is its existence established merely by acceptance, due to the absence of a valid cognition proving it, and because invalidating [cognitions] of many kinds have been stated. This being so, if suffering is to be warded off, then all is to be warded off. If not all is to be warded off, then one's own too — even that which is of the nature of the appropriated five aggregates — need not be warded off, since there is no distinction, just like [the suffering of] sentient beings: this is the conclusion. //

body.text: syādetat- karuṇāparatantratayā paraduḥkhaduḥkhinaḥ sarvaduḥkhāpaharaṇāya yatnaḥ / tadvaraṃ bahuduḥkhanidānaṃ saiva prathamato notpādayituṃ yujyata iti paravacanāvakāśaṃ śaṅkamāna āha-
body.translated_text: One might object: since one who suffers from another's suffering through being governed by compassion [seeks] to remove all suffering, would it not be better first not to generate that very compassion, which is the source of much suffering? — anticipating this opening for the opponent, he says —

body.text: kṛpayā bahu duḥkhaṃ cetkasmādutpadyate balāt /
body.translated_text: If much suffering [arises] through compassion, why is it generated forcibly?

body.text: balāditi prayatnāt / atrottaramāha-
body.translated_text: 'Forcibly' means through effort. To this, the answer is —

body.text: jagadduḥkhaṃ nirūpyedaṃ kṛpāduḥkhaṃ kathaṃ bahu // Bca_8.104 //
body.translated_text: Having considered the suffering of the world, how is the suffering of compassion great? // Bca_8.104 //

body.text: jagato duḥkhaṃ narakādikṛtamanekaprakāraṃ samīkṣya idaṃ kṛpākṛtaṃ duḥkhaṃ kathaṃ bahu? nedaṃ bahu kṛpāduḥkhamiti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: Having considered the suffering of the world — the multifarious suffering produced by the hells and such — how is this suffering produced by compassion great? The purport is: the suffering of compassion is not great. //

body.text: kiṃ ca / aparamidamatrottaramityāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, this is yet another answer — he says —

children.translated_text: If by the suffering of one, the suffering of many ceases,
that suffering should indeed be generated by the compassionate one, for the sake of others and oneself. // Bca_8.105 //

body.text: ekasya puruṣasya duḥkhena bahūnāṃ sattvānāṃ yadi duḥkhaṃ vigacchati nivartate, tadā utpādyameva janayitavyametattādṛśaṃ duḥkham / sadayena kṛpātmakena parasyātmanaśca //
body.translated_text: If by the suffering of one person the suffering of many beings ceases — is averted — then such suffering should indeed be generated, should be produced. By the compassionate one — by one of compassionate nature — for the sake of both others and oneself. //

body.text: utsūtratāmasya pariharannāha-
body.translated_text: Forestalling [the charge of] unscripturalness, he says —

children.translated_text: Therefore <s>Supuṣpacandra</s>, even knowing the danger from the king,

children.text: ātmaduḥkhaṃ na nihataṃ bahūnāṃ duḥkhināṃ vyayāt // Bca_8.106 //
children.translated_text: did not destroy his own suffering, for the sake of the many who suffered. // Bca_8.106 //
