body.translated_text: This pair of truths has been stated. Of these, <s>saṃvṛtisatya</s> is understood as such by those whose minds are stricken by ignorance, since it is of that nature. But <s>paramārthasatya</s> is not known — what is it like, what is its nature, what are its characteristics? Therefore, its own form must be stated — he says: 'Reality is not the domain of the intellect.' 'Of the intellect' — of all cognitions; 'not the domain' — not an object, because it has transcended the domain of all cognitions. It cannot be made an object of any cognition whatsoever — this is the meaning. Then how can its own form be demonstrated? For the reality that is <s>paramārthasatya</s> is of a nature free from all elaboration; therefore, being empty of all qualifying conditions, how could one perceive it through any conceptualization? And that whose own nature has transcended conceptualization is not the domain of words. For words, being born from conceptualization, are unable to operate in what is not the domain of conceptualizing minds.

body.text: tasmāt sakalavikalpābhilāpavikalatvādanāropitamasāṃvṛtamanabhilāpyaṃ paramārthatattvaṃ kathamiva pratipādayituṃ śakyate? tathāpi bhājanaśrotṛjanānugrahārthaṃ parikalpamupādāya saṃvṛtyā nidarśanopadarśanena kiṃcidabhidhīyate //
body.translated_text: Therefore, the reality that is the ultimate — being devoid of all conceptualization and verbal expression, unsuperimposed, unconcealed, inexpressible — how indeed could it be demonstrated? Nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting receptive listeners, relying on fabrication, something is said by means of conventional illustration and example. //

body.text: yathā timiraprabhāvāt taimirikaḥ sarvamākāśadeśaṃ keśoṇḍukamaṇḍitamitastato mukhaṃ vikṣipannapi paśyati / tathā kurvantamavekṣya ataimirikaḥ kimayaṃ karotīti tatsamīpamupasṛtya tadupalabdhakeśapraṇihitalocano 'pi na keśākṛtimupalabhate, nāpi tatkeśādhikaraṇān bhāvābhāvādiviśeṣān parikalpayati / yadā punarasau taimirikaḥ ataimirikāya svābhiprāyaṃ prakāśayati- keśāniha paśyāmīti, tadā tadvikalpāpasāraṇāya tasmai yathābhūtamasau bravīti- nātra keśāḥ santīti / taimirikopalabdhānurodhena pratiṣedhaparameva vacanamāha / na ca tena tathā pratipādayatāpi kasyacit pratiṣedhaḥ kṛto bhavati vidhānaṃ vā / tacca keśānāṃ tattvaṃ yadataimirikaḥ paśyati, tanna taimirikaḥ //
body.translated_text: Just as, through the power of an eye-disease (<s>timira</s>), a person with impaired vision sees the entire expanse of space as adorned with floating hairs, looking here and there. Seeing him doing so, a person without the eye-disease [thinks] 'what is he doing?' and approaching him, even though looking with eyes directed toward the hairs that person perceives, does not apprehend the form of hairs, nor does he fabricate distinctions of existence, non-existence, and such regarding those hairs as substrate. But when that person with the eye-disease discloses his intention to the one without it — 'I see hairs here' — then, in order to dispel his conceptualization, the other tells him the truth: 'There are no hairs here.' He speaks a statement that is solely a negation, in conformity with what the person with the eye-disease perceives. But by speaking thus, he has not actually made any negation of anything, nor any affirmation. And that reality of the hairs which the person without the eye-disease sees — that, the person with the eye-disease does not [see]. //

body.text: evamavidyātimiropaghātādatattvadṛśo bālāḥ yadetat skandhadhātvāyatanādisvarūpamupalabhante, tadeṣāṃ sāṃvṛtaṃ rūpam / tāneva skandhādīn yena svabhāvena nirastasamastāvidyāvāsanā buddhā bhagavantaḥ paśyanti ataimirikopalabdhakeśadarśananyāyena, tadeṣāṃ paramārthasatyamiti / yadāha śāstravit-
body.translated_text: Likewise, the childish who see what is not real, through the affliction of the darkness of ignorance, perceive what is the form of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and such — that is their conventional form. The very same aggregates and such, in the way the Blessed <s>Buddhas</s>, who have eliminated all traces of ignorance, see them — in the manner of the one without the eye-disease seeing the hairs perceived [by the afflicted one] — that is their <s>paramārthasatya</s> (ultimate truth). As the knower of the treatises says —

children.translated_text: 'What is fabricated through the power of the eye-disease — the form of hairs and such — that itself is false;
know that the nature by which one with pure vision sees — that is reality.'

body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Madhyamakāvatāra</s> 6.29]

body.text: iti paramārthato 'vācyamapi paramārthatattvaṃ dṛṣṭāntadvāreṇa saṃvṛtimupādāya kathaṃcit kathitam / na tu tadaśeṣasāṃvṛtavyavahāravirahitasvabhāvaṃ vastuto vaktuṃ śakyate iti / yaduktam-
body.translated_text: Thus, though the ultimate reality is inexpressible from the standpoint of the ultimate, it has been somehow spoken of through the gateway of an illustration, relying on convention. But its nature, being devoid of all conventional discourse, cannot truly be stated. As is said —

children.text: anakṣarasya dharmasya śrutiḥ kā deśanā ca kā /
children.translated_text: 'For a <s>Dharma</s> that is without syllables, what hearing and what teaching can there be?
Yet the meaning — which is without syllables — is heard and taught through superimposition.'

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: tasmādvayavahārasatye eva sthitvā paramārtho deśyate / paramārthadeśanāvagamācca paramārthādhigamo bhavati, tasyāstadupāyatvāt / yaduktaṃ śāstre-
body.translated_text: Therefore, it is only while standing within the truth of conventional discourse that the ultimate is taught. And from the understanding of the teaching of the ultimate, realization of the ultimate occurs, since that [teaching] is the means to it. As is said in the treatise —

children.translated_text: 'Without relying on conventional [truth], the ultimate is not taught;
without realizing the ultimate, <s>nirvāṇa</s> is not attained.'

body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Madhyamakaśāstra</s> 24.10]

body.text: evaṃ paramārthadeśanopāyabhūtā saṃvṛtiḥ, paramārthādhigamaśca upeyabhūta iti / anyathā tasya deśayitumaśakyatvāt / nanu ca tathāvidhamapi tathāvidhabuddhiviṣayaḥ paramārthataḥ kiṃ na bhavatītyatrāha- buddhiḥ saṃvṛtirucyate iti / sarvā hi buddhiḥ ālambananirālambanatayā vikalpasvabhāvā, vikalpaśca sarva eva avidyāsvabhāvaḥ, avastugrāhitvāt / yadāha-
body.translated_text: Thus, convention is the means for teaching the ultimate, and the realization of the ultimate is the goal. Otherwise, it would be impossible to teach it. But surely, could not a cognition of such a kind be an object of ultimate reality from the standpoint of the ultimate? — to this he says: 'The intellect is called <s>saṃvṛti</s> (conventional).' For all intellect, by virtue of having an object that is ultimately without object, is of the nature of conceptualization; and all conceptualization is of the nature of ignorance, because it grasps what is not a real thing. As is said —

body.text:
vikalpaḥ svayamevāyamavidyārūpatāṃ gataḥ /
iti
body.translated_text:
'Conceptualization itself has assumed the form of ignorance.'
Thus.

body.text: avidyā ca saṃvṛtiḥ / iti naiva kācid buddhiḥ pāramārthikarūpagrāhiṇī paramārthato yujyate / anyathā sāṃvṛtabuddhigrāhyatayā paramārtharūpataiva tasya hīyeta, paramārthasya vastutaḥ sāṃvṛtajñānāviṣayatvāt / tatra cedamuktaṃ bhagavatā āryasatyadvayāvatāre-
body.translated_text: And ignorance is <s>saṃvṛti</s> (convention). Therefore, no intellect whatsoever can be a grasper of the ultimate form from the standpoint of the ultimate. Otherwise, by being graspable by conventional intellect, its very nature as ultimate would be undermined, since the ultimate is in reality not the domain of conventional knowledge. In this regard, the Blessed One said in the <s>Āryasatyadvayāvatāra</s> —

body.text: yadi hi devaputra paramārthataḥ paramārthasatyaṃ kāyavāṅyanasāṃ viṣayatāmupagacchet, na tat paramārthasatyamiti saṃkhyāṃ gacchet, saṃvṛtisatyameva tadbhavet / api tu devaputra paramārthasatyaṃ sarvavyavahārasamatikrāntam, nirviśeṣam, asamutpannamaniruddham, abhidheyābhidhānajñeyajñānavigatam, yāvat sarvākāravaropetasarvajñajñānaviṣayabhāvasamatikrāntaṃ paramārthasatyamiti vistaraḥ //
body.translated_text: 'If, O son of the gods, from the standpoint of the ultimate, <s>paramārthasatya</s> were to become an object of body, speech, and mind, it would not be reckoned as <s>paramārthasatya</s>; it would be <s>saṃvṛtisatya</s> alone. However, O son of the gods, <s>paramārthasatya</s> transcends all conventional discourse; it is without distinction; unborn; unceased; free from what is expressed and expression, from what is known and knowledge; up to: <s>paramārthasatya</s> transcends even the domain of omniscient knowledge endowed with all aspects.' Thus in detail. //

body.text: ata eva tadaviṣayaḥ sarvakalpanānāṃ yadbhāvābhāvasvaparabhāvasatyāsatyaśāśvatocchedanityānityasukhaduḥkhaśucyaśucyātmānātmaśūnyāśūnyalakṣyalakṣaṇaikatvānyatvotpādanirodhādayo viśeṣāstattvasya na saṃbhavanti, amīṣāṃ sāṃvṛtadharmatvāt / etaduktaṃ bhagavatā pitāputrasamāgame-
body.translated_text: For this very reason, reality is beyond the domain of all conceptual elaborations — the distinctions such as existence and non-existence, self and other, own-nature and other-nature, true and false, eternal and annihilated, permanent and impermanent, pleasure and suffering, pure and impure, self and non-self, empty and non-empty, characterized and characteristic, unity and multiplicity, arising and cessation, and so forth — [these] do not apply to reality, since they are properties of conventional <s>dharmas</s>. This was stated by the Blessed One in the <s>Pitāputrasamāgama</s> —

body.text: etāvaccaiva jñeyam- yaduta saṃvṛtiḥ paramārthaśca / tacca bhagavatā śūnyataḥ sudṛṣṭaṃ suviditaṃ susākṣātkṛtam / tena sarvajña ityucyate / tatra saṃvṛtirlokapracāratastathāgatena dṛṣṭā / yaḥ punaḥ paramārthaḥ, so 'nabhilāpyaḥ, anājñeyaḥ, aparijñeyaḥ, avijñeyaḥ, adeśitaḥ, aprakāśitaḥ, yāvadakriyaḥ, akaraṇaḥ, yāvanna lābho nālabho na sukhaṃ na duḥkhaṃ na yaśo nāyaśo na rūpaṃ nārūpamityādi //
body.translated_text: 'This much alone is to be known — namely, the conventional and the ultimate. And that has been well seen, well known, well directly realized by the Blessed One from [the perspective of] emptiness. Therefore he is called omniscient. There, the conventional has been seen by the <s>Tathāgata</s> from the standpoint of worldly convention. But the ultimate — that is inexpressible, unknowable, not fully knowable, not cognizable, not taught, not illuminated, and so forth up to: without activity, without doing, and so forth up to: neither gain nor non-gain, neither pleasure nor suffering, neither fame nor infamy, neither form nor formlessness' — and so forth.

body.text: iti pratyastamitasamastasāṃvṛtavastuviśeṣamaśeṣopādhiviviktamuktamanantavastuvistaravyāpijñānālokāvabhāsitāntarātmanā bhagavatā paramārthasatyamiti / tadetadāryāṇāmeva svasaṃvidita svabhāvatayā pratyātmavedyam / atastadevātra pramāṇam / saṃvṛtisatyaṃ tu lokavyavahāramāśritya prakāśitam / tadevaṃ yathāvadvibhāgataḥ satyadvayaparijñānādaviparīto dharmapravicaya upajāyate //
body.translated_text: Thus, ultimate truth [is known] by the Blessed One, in whose inner being all particular conventional things have set, who is free from all adventitious conditions, whose [inner nature] is illuminated by the light of knowledge that pervades the expanse of infinite things. And this is to be personally experienced by the noble ones alone, being of a nature known through their own direct awareness. Therefore, that alone is the valid cognition here. But conventional truth has been revealed in reliance upon worldly convention. Thus, through the correct knowledge of the two truths in their proper distinction, unerring discernment of <s>dharmas</s> arises.

body.text: evaṃ saṃvṛtiparamārthabhedena dvividhaṃ satyaṃ vyavasthāpya tadadhikṛtaśca loko 'pi dvividha evetyupadarśayannāha- tatra loke ityādi-
body.translated_text: Having thus established the twofold truth through the distinction of conventional and ultimate, and showing that the world too, being governed by these, is likewise twofold, he says with 'there, the world' and so forth —

children.text: tatra loko dvidhā dṛṣṭo yogī prākṛtakastathā /
children.translated_text: There, the world is seen to be twofold: the <s>yogin</s> and the ordinary person.

children.text: tatra prākṛtako loko yogilokena bādhyate // Bca_9.3 //
children.translated_text: There, the world of the ordinary person is superseded by the world of the <s>yogin</s>. // <s>Bca</s> 9.3 //

body.text: tatra tayoḥ saṃvṛttiparamārthasatyayoradhikṛtaḥ vyavasthitaḥ / tatsatyapratipatteti yāvat / loko janaḥ / dvidhā dviprakāraḥ saṃvṛtiparamārthasatyavedī / loka iti samudāyavacanam, tena
body.translated_text: 'There' — established with reference to those two — conventional truth and ultimate truth. 'Governed by the understanding of those truths' — this is the implication. 'The world' — people. 'Twofold' — of two kinds — those who know conventional truth and ultimate truth. 'World' is a collective term; therefore

body.text: rāśidvayamityarthaḥ / dṛṣṭa iti pratipannaḥ, yukterāgamācca / kathaṃ kṛtvā dvidhetyāha- yogī prākṛtakastatheti / yogaḥ samādhiḥ sarvadharmānupalambhalakṣaṇaḥ, so 'syāstīti yogī loka ityekaḥ prakāro rāśiḥ / tathā prakṛtiḥ saṃsārapravṛtteḥ kāraṇamavidyā tṛṣṇā, tasyā jāta iti prākṛtaḥ / prākṛta eva prākṛtako loka iti dvitīyaḥ / tatra yogī pradhānatattvamaviparītaṃ paśyati, prākṛtakaśca viparyastaṃ vastutattvaṃ paśyati bhrāntatvāt //
body.translated_text: the meaning is: two groups. 'Seen' means understood — through reasoning and scripture. How is it twofold? He says: 'the <s>yogin</s> and the ordinary person.' '<s>Yoga</s>' is <s>samādhi</s> characterized by the non-apprehension of all <s>dharmas</s>; one who has that is a <s>yogin</s> — the world [of the yogin] — this is one kind, one group. 'Likewise, <s>prakṛti</s>' — the cause of the continuation of <s>saṃsāra</s> — is ignorance and craving; one born from that is '<s>prākṛta</s>' (ordinary). The '<s>prākṛtaka</s>' world itself — this is the second [kind]. There, the <s>yogin</s> sees the primary reality correctly, while the ordinary person sees the nature of things in a perverted way, due to being deluded.

body.text: syādetat- ubhayorapi yathāsvaṃ tattvadarśitvāt kataraḥ punaranayorbhrāntimānastu ya evānyatareṇa bādhyate? kaḥ punaranayoḥ kena bādhyata ityāha- tatretyādi / tatreti saptamyā samudāyanirdeśaḥ, nirdhāraṇe ca saptamī / tatra tayoryogiprākṛtakayorlokayormadhye prākṛtako lokaḥ prākṛtakatvajātyā samudāyānnirdhāryate, nirdhārya ca bādhyate, iti bādhanaṃ vidhīyate / kenetyapekṣāyāmāha- yogilokeneti / yogī eva lokaḥ yogilokaḥ, tena bādhyate iti viparyastamatirvyavasthāpyate / katham? dhīviśeṣeṇeti yojanīyam / na tu yogī prākṛtakena bādhyate //
body.translated_text: One might say: since both see reality according to their own [perspective], which of these two is the deluded one — namely, the one who is superseded by the other? Which of these two is superseded by which? He says with 'there' and so forth. 'There' — the locative indicates the collective; and the locative is used for selection. There, among those two — the <s>yogin</s> world and the ordinary world — the ordinary world is selected from the collective by virtue of the class 'ordinary,' and having been selected, is superseded — thus supersession is prescribed. When asked 'by whom?' he says: 'by the world of the <s>yogin</s>.' The <s>yogin</s> himself is the <s>yogin</s>-world; by that [world] it is superseded — thus the perverted understanding is established. How? It should be construed as: 'through a distinction of intellect.' But the <s>yogin</s> is not superseded by the ordinary person.

body.text: idamihābhimatam- yathā vibhramāhitasadbhāvaṃ timiropahatacakṣuṣaḥ asadbhūtakeśoṇḍukādidarśino jñānaṃ yathāvasthitavastutattvagrāhiṇo 'taimirikajñānena bādhyate, na tathā taimirikajñānena ataimirikajñānaṃ bādhyate, evamavidyāmalatimiradūṣitabuddhicakṣuṣo viparītavastusvarūpagrāhiṇaḥ prākṛtakasya jñānaṃ prajñāsalilakṣālitavigatamalānāsravajñānacakṣuṣaḥ bhāvanijatattvavedinaḥ yogilokasya jñānena bādhyate, na punaritarajñānena yogijñānamiti / tathā coktam-
body.translated_text: This is what is intended here: just as the knowledge of one with eyes impaired by cataracts (<s>timira</s>), who perceives non-existent floating hairs and such whose existence is produced by the error, is superseded by the non-cataract knowledge of one who grasps the true nature of things as they are — but the non-cataract knowledge is not superseded by the cataract knowledge — so the knowledge of the ordinary person, whose eye of intellect is corrupted by the cataract of the stain of ignorance, who grasps the perverted nature of things, is superseded by the knowledge of the <s>yogin</s> world — one who knows the truth born of cultivation, whose eye of uncontaminated knowledge is free from stain, washed with the water of wisdom. But the <s>yogin</s>'s knowledge is not [superseded] by the other's knowledge. And thus it is stated —

children.translated_text: 'The knowledge of those free from cataracts is not superseded by what is perceived by cataract-afflicted eyes;
so the intellect of those stained by impure knowledge is superseded, but not the stainless intellect.'

body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Madhyamakāvatāra</s> 6.27]

body.text: tasmāt prākṛtakajñānameva bhrāntamiti bādhyate //
body.translated_text: Therefore, it is the knowledge of the ordinary person alone that is established as deluded and is superseded.

body.text: atha kiṃ prākṛtā eva bādhyante yogibhiḥ, uta yogino 'pītyāha- bādhyanta ityādi-
body.translated_text: Now, are only the ordinary persons superseded by the <s>yogins</s>, or the <s>yogins</s> too? He says with 'are superseded' and so forth —

body.text: bādhyante dhīviśeṣeṇa yogino 'pyuttarottaraiḥ /
body.translated_text: Even <s>yogins</s> are superseded by successively higher ones, through distinction of intellect.

body.text: yogino 'pi yogibhiraparāparairbādhyante / na kevalaṃ prākṛtakā ityapiśabdārthaḥ / kiṃbhūtaiḥ? uttarottaraiḥ / uttare ca uttare ca uttarottarāḥ, taiḥ / tāratamyabhedāvasthitaguṇaviśeṣapratilambhotkarṣaprāptaiḥ / adhikādhikairityarthaḥ / tadapekṣayā apacitaguṇā adharādhare bādhyante, jñānamāhātmyādibhirabhibhūyante / katham? dhīviśeṣeṇeti / dhiyo jñānasya prajñāyā viśeṣaḥ tattadāvaraṇavigamāt prakarṣaḥ, tena / upalakṣaṇaṃ caitat / dhyānasamādhisamāpattyādiviśeṣeṇāpi / tathā hi- pramuditākhyaprathamabhūmilābhino bodhisattvasya jñānādiguṇāpekṣayā taduttaravimalābhidhānadvitīyabhūmilābhino bodhisattvasya jñānaprabhāvādayo guṇā viśiṣyante / evamanyeṣāmapi
body.translated_text: Even <s>yogins</s> are superseded by <s>yogins</s> — by successively [higher ones]. Not only the ordinary — this is the meaning of the word 'even.' Of what kind? 'Successively higher' — <s>uttara</s> and further <s>uttara</s> are <s>uttarottara</s> — by those. Those who have attained superiority through the acquisition of distinguishing qualities established in graduated levels of excellence — the meaning is: by those who are progressively more [advanced]. Those of lesser qualities in comparison with them are superseded — the lower ones — are overpowered by the greatness of knowledge and such. How? 'Through distinction of intellect' — the distinction, the excellence, of intellect, of knowledge, of wisdom — through the removal of the respective obscurations — by that. And this is illustrative. Also through distinction of <s>dhyāna</s>, <s>samādhi</s>, <s>samāpatti</s>, and such. For a <s>Bodhisattva</s> who has attained the first <s>bhūmi</s> called <s>Pramuditā</s> — the qualities such as knowledge and such of a <s>Bodhisattva</s> who has attained the second <s>bhūmi</s> called <s>Vimalā</s> are superior in comparison with that one's qualities of knowledge and such. Thus for the others too

body.text: uttarottarabhūmilābhināṃ veditavyam / tathā prathamadhyānādilābhināmapi uttarottarairbādhanaṃ yojanīm, yāvat sāsravāṇāmanāsravairiti //
body.translated_text: who attain successively higher <s>bhūmis</s>, this should be understood. Likewise, the supersession of those who have attained the first <s>dhyāna</s> and such by successively higher ones should be construed — up to: the supersession of the contaminated by the uncontaminated.

body.text: syādetat- satyapi yogināṃ dhiyo viśeṣe prākṛtajñānaṃ bhrāntamiti kathamavagamayituṃ śakyata ityāha dṛṣṭāntenobhayeṣṭeneti-
body.translated_text: One might say: even granting the distinction of the <s>yogin</s>'s intellect, how can it be demonstrated that the knowledge of the ordinary person is deluded? He says, with 'by an example accepted by both' —

body.text: dṛṣṭāntenobhayeṣṭena kāryārthamavicārataḥ // Bca_9.4 //
body.translated_text: By an example accepted by both, for the purpose of the goal, without analysis. // <s>Bca</s> 9.4 //

body.text: ubhayeṣāṃ yogiprākṛtakānāmiṣṭaḥ abhimataḥ, tena dṛṣṭāntena nidarśanena / ya eṣa sūtreṣu bhagavatā māyāmarīcigandharvanagarapratibimbādirukto dṛṣṭāntaḥ, sa ca ubhayeṣāmapi niḥsvabhāvatayā prasiddhaḥ / tatsādharmyeṇa sarvadharmāṇāṃ niḥsvabhāvatvapratipādanāt / tathā hi- ye tāvat sarvajanapratipannasvarūpā rūpādayaḥ, te yogināmeva paramārthasatyādhigamānniḥsvabhāvatayā siddhāḥ / ye punarime svapnamāyādiṣu upalabdhāḥ, te prākṛtakānāmapi / atastatra ubhayorapi vipratipatterabhāvāt dṛṣṭāntadharmatā na vihanyate / yeṣāṃ tu mīmāṃsakādīnāṃ deśakālānyathātmakaṃ vastu eva tattathā pratibhāsate iti matam, te 'nyatra nirākṛtā iti na tanmatamiha nirasyate / ye tu svayūthyāḥ cittameva vastusat svapnādiṣu tathā pratibhāsate iti manyante, te 'pi yathāvasaramagrataḥ [9.17-18] svasaṃvedananirākaraṇānnirākariṣyante / yuktisiddhamapi ubhayasiddhameva / atastena dṛṣṭāntena viparītavastusvarūpagrāhitayā prākṛtakajñānaṃ bhrāntamiti vyavasthāpyate / evaṃ yogināmapi yathāsaṃbhavaṃ vaktavyam //
body.translated_text: 'Accepted by both' — by both the <s>yogins</s> and the ordinary persons — 'by that example,' that illustration. The example stated by the Blessed One in the <s>sūtras</s> — such as illusion, mirage, city of <s>gandharvas</s>, reflection, and so forth — that is accepted by both as being devoid of intrinsic nature. Through the analogy with that, the lack of intrinsic nature of all <s>dharmas</s> is demonstrated. For: those things such as form and so forth, whose nature is accepted by all people — they are established as devoid of intrinsic nature only for the <s>yogins</s>, through the realization of ultimate truth. But those that are apprehended in dreams, illusions, and such — they [are accepted as devoid of intrinsic nature] even by the ordinary persons. Therefore, since there is no disagreement between the two regarding those [examples], the analogy between the example and the subject is not vitiated. But those such as the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> and others who hold that the thing itself, being of a different nature [from the example] with respect to place and time, appears in that way — they have been refuted elsewhere, and so their view is not rejected here. And those of our own school who think that mind alone, being a truly existent thing, appears in that way in dreams and such — they too will be refuted below, as occasion arises [9.17-18], through the refutation of self-cognition (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>). What is established by reasoning is also accepted by both. Therefore, by that example, the knowledge of the ordinary person is established as deluded through its grasping the perverted nature of things. Thus for the <s>yogins</s> too, it should be stated as applicable.

body.text: nanu yadi niḥsvabhāvāḥ sarvabhāvā iti vastutattvam, kathaṃ tarhi sarvasattvasamuddharaṇāśayena dānādiṣu saṃbhāraparipūraṇārthaṃ tattvavedināmapi bodhisattvānāṃ pravṛttiḥ? teṣāmapi niḥsvabhāvatvāt, ityata āha- kāryārthamavicārataḥ iti / kāryaṃ sādhyam, upādeyam / phalamucyate / tadarthaṃ tannimittam / avicārataḥ avicāreṇaiva taddhetau pravartanāt / tathābhūteṣvapi tatra idaṃpratyayatāniyamasya vidyamānatvāt na hetuphalabhāvasya virodhaḥ / etaduktaṃ bhavati- yadyapi māyādisvabhāvatayā niḥsvabhāvā dānādayaḥ, tathāpi trikoṭipariśuddhyā sādarādiyogena abhyasyamānāḥ tathābhūtā api paramārthādhigamāya hetubhāvamāpadyante, teṣāṃ tadupāyatvāt, pratītyasamutpādasya ca acintyatvāt / etādṛśādeva hetoretādṛśaṃ phalamadhigamyate, tasya tadupeyatvāt / taduktam-
body.translated_text: But if all things lack intrinsic nature — this being the true nature of things — then how is there activity on the part of <s>Bodhisattvas</s>, who know the truth, for the purpose of fulfilling the accumulations through generosity and such, with the intention of rescuing all beings? Since those too lack intrinsic nature — therefore he says: 'for the purpose of the goal, without analysis.' 'The goal' — what is to be accomplished, what is to be adopted — is called the fruit. 'For its purpose' — on its account. 'Without analysis' — precisely without analysis, through engaging in its cause [without analyzing it]. Since even in things of such a nature, the restriction of conditionality is present, the relationship of cause and effect is not contradicted. What is stated here is this: although generosity and such are devoid of intrinsic nature, being of the nature of illusions and such, nevertheless, when practiced with the purity of the three spheres, with earnest devotion and such, even being of such a nature, they become causes for the realization of ultimate [truth], since they are means to that [realization], and since dependent origination is inconceivable. From just such a cause, just such a fruit is realized, since it is the result to be attained by that [cause]. As stated —

body.text: upāyabhūtaṃ vyavahārasatyamupeyabhūtaṃ paramārthasatyam /

children.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Madhyamakāvatāra</s> 6.80]

body.translated_text: 'Conventional truth is the means; ultimate truth is the goal.'

body.text: avaśyaṃ caitadevam / anyathā mārgābhyāsataḥ samalāvasthāyā nirmalāvasthā, savikalpāvasthāyā nirvikalpāvasthā kathamutpadyeta? tasyāḥ paramārthatastatsvabhāvatvāt / anyatrāpi samānametat / sarvadharmāṇāṃ paramārthato niḥsvabhāvatvāt hetvanurūpaṃ ca sarvatra phalamiṣyate / ataḥ sāṃvṛtādapi niḥsvabhāvāddhetoḥ niḥsvabhāvatādhigama eva phalam, kathamanyathā saṃskṛtādapi
body.translated_text: And this must necessarily be so. Otherwise, how would the stainless state arise from the stained state through the cultivation of the path? How would the non-conceptual state arise from the conceptual state? Since that [stainless state] is ultimately of that [same empty] nature. The same applies elsewhere as well. Since all <s>dharmas</s> are ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature, and since everywhere the fruit is accepted as conforming to the cause — therefore, from a conventional cause too, which is devoid of intrinsic nature, the fruit is precisely the realization of the lack of intrinsic nature. For how else could the unconditioned <s>nirvāṇa</s> be attained from the conditioned

body.text: mārgādaṃsaṃskṛtaṃ nirvāṇamavāpyeta? iti dānādayo vastuto niḥsvabhāvā api paramārthatattvādhigamāya sarvasattveṣu karuṇāyamānairbodhisattvairupādīyante, anyathā paramārthādhigamāyogāt / tato dānādiṣu pravṛttiranivāritā / evamiṣṭāniṣṭaphalaprāptiparihārārthināṃ kuśalākuśalayoḥ pravṛttinivṛttī vaktavye / etat punaḥ paścādvayaktīkariṣyate //
body.translated_text: path? Thus generosity and such, though in reality devoid of intrinsic nature, are adopted by <s>Bodhisattvas</s> who have compassion for all beings, for the sake of realizing ultimate truth — since otherwise the realization of the ultimate would be impossible. Therefore, activity in generosity and such is not prevented. Thus, for those who seek to obtain desired fruits and avoid undesired ones, engagement in the wholesome and cessation from the unwholesome should be stated [as valid]. This will be clarified further below.

body.text: syādetat- yadetanmāyādisamānasvabhāvaṃ vasturūpaṃ yoginaḥ pratipadyante, tadeva yadi prākṛtako 'pi janaḥ pratipadyate, kva tarhi vipratipattirastītyāha lokenetyādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: if even the ordinary person understands that form of things which is of the same nature as illusions and such — which the <s>yogins</s> understand — then where is the disagreement? He says with 'by the world' and so forth —

children.text: lokena bhāvā dṛśyante kalpyante cāpi tattvataḥ /
children.translated_text: Things are seen by the world and are also conceptualized as real;

children.text: na tu māyāvadityatra vivādo yogilokayoḥ // Bca_9.5 //
children.translated_text: but [they are] not [seen] as like an illusion — herein lies the dispute between the <s>yogin</s> and the world. // <s>Bca</s> 9.5 //

body.text: lokena prākṛtakajanena / hetupratyayaṃ pratītya bhavanti svarūpaṃ labhante iti bhāvāḥ / na punaḥ pāramārthikaṃ rūpaṃ nijameṣāmasti, iti bhāvaśabdena niḥsvabhāvatābhidhānaṃ pratīyate / satsvarūpeṇa na kevalaṃ dṛśyante kalpyante cāpi tattvataḥ / yathāpratītasvabhāvenaiva paramārthato 'dhyavasīyante / abhiniviśyante iti yāvat / yadetadasmatpratītigocaro vasturūpam, tadvāstavameve tyabhimananāt / na tu māyāvat, na tu punaryathā yoginā māyeva māyāvat svabhāvaśūnyā dṛśyante, paramārthatastathā pratīyante, ityatrāsmin vivādo vipratipattiryogilokayoḥ yoginā saha lokasyetyarthaḥ / tatpratipanne vastuttattve lokasyāpratipatteḥ lokena saha vā yoginaḥ, tatpratipanne yoginā yathārthatāpratiṣedhāt / ayamabhiprāyaḥ- sarvabhāvānāṃ sāṃvṛtaṃ pāramārthikaṃ ceti rūpadvayamasti, tatra yat sāṃvṛtaṃ tadeva lokena pratīyate, yattu pāramārthikaṃ tad yoginetyuktam / yathā māyākāranirmitahastyādirūpameva mantrādisāmarthyavibhramitalocano janaḥ paśyati, māyā kārastu tatsvabhāvādi nijaṃ tatsvarūpam, evaṃ yogilokayorapi yathāyogaṃ pratipattavyam //
body.translated_text: By the world — by ordinary, common people. 'They come into being' — they obtain their own form — dependent on causes and conditions; these are '<s>bhāvas</s>' (things). But they do not possess a real, ultimate form of their own — thus by the word '<s>bhāva</s>' the designation of lack of intrinsic nature is understood. They are not only 'seen' with a real intrinsic nature, but are also 'conceptualized in truth' — they are determined ultimately to have the very nature in which they appear. They are clung to — this is the full meaning. [Thinking:] 'This form of things that is the object of our cognition is indeed real' — due to such conceit. But not like an illusion; not as a yogin sees things as like an illusion, empty of intrinsic nature — they are not ultimately cognized in that way. Herein lies the 'dispute' — the disagreement — between the yogin and the world, of the world with the yogin: this is the meaning. Because the world does not understand the true nature of things that has been understood [by the yogin]; or because [there is disagreement] of the yogin with the world, since there is no denial of the accuracy of the yogin's understanding of that true nature. The intention is this: all things have two forms — conventional and ultimate. Of these, what is conventional is cognized by the world; what is ultimate is [cognized] by the yogin — thus it is said. Just as an audience whose eyes are confused by the power of mantras and such sees only the form of elephants and such created by a magician, while the magician [sees] their true nature, their own real form — so too between the yogin and the world, this should be understood in accordance with each.

body.text: athāpi syāt- yadetat samastajanasādhāraṇamarthakriyākṣamaṃ pratyakṣapramāṇapratītaṃ vasturūpam, tat kathamapahrotuṃ śakyata iti parasya hṛdayamāśaṅkayāha pratyakṣamapītyādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: how can this form of things — which is common to all people, capable of effective action, and cognized by the valid cognition of direct perception — be denied? Anticipating the opponent's thought, he says 'even direct perception' and so forth —

body.text: pratyakṣamapi rūpādi prasiddhayā na pramāṇataḥ /
body.translated_text: Even form and such, [apprehended by] direct perception, are [established] by convention, not by valid cognition.

body.text: yadapi ca pratyakṣamabhidhīyate rūpādi / ādiśabdena śabdādi vedanādi gṛhyate / tadapi prasiddhayā rūḍhyā lokapravādena na pramāṇataḥ / na pramāṇenādhigataṃ sat pratyakṣaṃ rūpādīti saṃbandhaḥ / sāṃvyavahārikapramāṇatvāt pratyakṣādīnām, tadadhigataṃ sāṃvṛtameva rūpādi / na ca laukikapramāṇasamadhigamyaṃ tāttvikaṃ rūpam, sarvajanānāṃ tattvaveditvaprasaṅgāt / yadāha-
body.translated_text: And what is called direct perception — form and such — by the word 'and such,' sound and such, feeling and such are included — even that is [established] by convention, by established usage, by worldly discourse — not by valid cognition. It is not the case that form and such, having been cognized by valid cognition, are [truly] directly perceived: this is the syntactic connection. Because direct perception and such are valid cognitions only in the conventional sense, what is cognized by them is merely conventional form and such. Nor is the form of things cognized by worldly valid cognition their true form, since there would be the absurd consequence of all people being knowers of reality. As stated —

children.translated_text: 'If what is apprehended by the senses were true [reality],
then the childish would already be knowers of reality — what use then would knowledge of reality serve?'

body.text: iti / [catuḥ 3.18]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Catuḥśataka</s> 3.18]

body.text: tasmāt pratyakṣamapi na pramāṇenādhigatam //
body.translated_text: Therefore, even what is directly perceived is not cognized by [ultimate] valid cognition.

body.text: rūpādi tattvaṃ pratyakṣamapi yadi na pramāṇādhigatam, kathaṃ tatprasiddhiḥ? prasiddhiścet kathaṃ mṛṣetyatrāha aśucyādiṣvityādi-
body.translated_text: If even the reality of form and such, though directly perceived, is not cognized by valid cognition, how is it established? And if it is established, how is it false? To this he says 'in impure things' and so forth —

body.text: aśucyādiṣu śucyādiprasiddhiriva sā mṛṣā // Bca_9.6 //
body.translated_text: That [establishment] is false — like the establishment of purity and such in impure things and such. // <s>Bca</s> 9.6 //

body.text: yathā ca paramārthato 'śucini strīkalevarādau tadāsaktiviparyastacetasāṃ śucibuddhirupajāyate / ādiśabdādanityādau nityādibuddhirgṛhyate / sā ca atasmiṃstadgahānmṛṣā / vitathagrāhiṇītyarthaḥ / tadvadiyaṃ rūpādāvapītyaviśeṣaḥ //
body.translated_text: Just as in a woman's body and such, which is ultimately impure, the perception of purity arises for those whose minds are perverted through attachment to that. By the word 'and such,' the perception of permanence and such in what is impermanent and such is included. And that [perception] is false — because it grasps what is not there as being there. It is an apprehension of what is untrue — this is the meaning. Likewise, even with regard to form and such, this [establishment] is no different.

body.text: yadi na pratyakṣapramāṇāt tatsiddhiḥ, āgamāttarhi bhaviṣyati / tathā hi skandhadhātvāyatanādisvabhāvatayā bhagavatā bhāvāḥ sūtre deśitāḥ, kṣaṇikādisvabhāvatayā ca / tatredamuktaṃ bhagavatā-
body.translated_text: If its establishment is not from the valid cognition of direct perception, then perhaps it will be from scripture. For things have been taught by the Blessed One in the <s>sūtras</s> as being of the nature of aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and such, and as being of momentary nature and such. In that regard, the Blessed One stated —

body.text: sarvaṃ sarvamiti brāhmaṇa yāvadeva pañca skandhāḥ, dvādaśāyatanāni, aṣṭādaśaḥ dhātavaḥ / iti /
body.translated_text: '"Everything, everything" — O <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, this extends only to the five aggregates, the twelve sense-bases, and the eighteen elements.'

body.text: tathā-
body.translated_text: Likewise —

children.translated_text: 'All formations are momentary; how can there be activity for what is unstable?

children.text: bhūtiryaiṣāṃ kriyā saiva kārakaṃ saiva cocyate //
children.translated_text: Their existence is their activity, and that itself is called their agent.'

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: na ca māyādisvabhāvānāṃ kṣaṇikākṣaṇikādidharmatāpratipādanamucitam, niḥsvabhāvānāṃ kasyacit svabhāvasyābhāvāt / tatkathamamī na paramārthasanta ityatrāha lokāvatāraṇetyādi-
body.translated_text: And it is not appropriate to attribute the quality of being momentary or non-momentary and such to things of the nature of illusions and such, since for things devoid of intrinsic nature, no intrinsic nature whatsoever exists. How then are these not ultimately real? To this he says 'for the purpose of leading the world' and so forth —

children.translated_text: Things were taught by the Protector for the purpose of leading the world [to understanding];

children.text: tattvataḥ kṣaṇikā naite saṃvṛtyā cedvirudhyate // Bca_9.7 //
children.translated_text: these are not ultimately momentary — if [you say] conventionally, [that] is contradicted. // <s>Bca</s> 9.7 //

body.text: lokānāṃ bhāvābhiniveśināṃ skandhādideśanāvaineyānāṃ sattvānāmāpātataḥ śūnyatādeśanānadhikṛtānāṃ śūnyatāyāmavatāraṇārthaṃ sukumāropakrameṇa pravartanāya / co hetau / yasmādbhāvāḥ skandhāyatanādilakṣaṇāḥ, vastuto niḥsvabhāvatve 'pi sarvadharmāṇām, nāthena narakādiduḥkhāt sattvān paritrāyamāṇena abhyudayaniḥśreyasasukhaṃ prāpayatā sattvāśayādivedinā buddhena bhagavatā deśitāḥ prakāśitāḥ, na tu paramārthataḥ / tasmānna sūtravirodhaḥ / taduktam-
body.translated_text: For the sake of gradually leading into [the understanding of] emptiness — through a gentle approach — beings who are attached to [the reality of] things, who are amenable to being taught through the teaching of aggregates and such, who are not immediately amenable to the teaching of emptiness. The word 'and' is in the sense of reason. Since things — characterized as aggregates, sense-bases, and such — even though in reality all <s>dharmas</s> are devoid of intrinsic nature, were taught — revealed — by the Protector, who rescues beings from the suffering of hells and such, who brings them to the happiness of prosperity and the highest good, who knows the dispositions and such of beings — by the <s>Buddha</s>, the Blessed One — but not as ultimately [real]. Therefore there is no contradiction with the <s>sūtras</s>. As stated —

children.translated_text: 'Just as the <s>Jinas</s> spoke of "mine" and "I" as the situation required,
so too, as the situation required, they spoke of aggregates, sense-bases, and elements.'

body.text: iti / [yuktiṣaṣṭikā]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Yuktiṣaṣṭikā</s>]

body.text: yadi na paramārthato deśitāḥ, kathaṃ tarhi te kṣaṇikā ityāha- tattvataḥ kṣaṇikā naite iti / tattvataḥ paramārthataḥ niḥsvabhāvatvāt kṣaṇikā api na bhavanti ete ime bhāvāḥ / kśaṇikādideśanā vaineyānāṃ tatsvabhāvatāprakāśanāt / yadi na tattvataḥ kṣaṇikāḥ, kathaṃ
body.translated_text: If they were not taught as ultimately [real], then how are they momentary? He says: 'These are not ultimately momentary.' Ultimately — in the ultimate sense — due to lack of intrinsic nature, these things are not even momentary. The teaching of momentariness and such serves to reveal [the conventional] nature to those who are amenable. If they are not ultimately momentary, how

body.text: tarhi deśanāyāmapi kathitā iti manasi nidhāya [āha] saṃvṛtyā cet [iti]- yadi saṃvṛtyā kṣaṇikā abhidhīyanta ityucyate, ityuttaramāśaṅkaya dūṣayati, tadā virudhyate, saṃvṛtyā kṣaṇikā na paramārthataḥ iti virudhyate na saṃgacchate / akṣaṇikatayā pratīteḥ pratītivirodhaḥ, sāṃvyavahāribhirakṣaṇikatvapratīteḥ na kṣaṇikatvaṃ sāṃvṛtaṃ rūpamiti yāvat //
body.translated_text: then are they spoken of even in the teaching? Keeping this in mind [he says] 'if conventionally' — if it is said that they are called momentary conventionally, anticipating this answer he objects: then it is contradicted — [the claim that] they are momentary conventionally and not ultimately is contradicted, does not hold together. Because of the contradiction with cognition — through the cognition of non-momentariness. Since conventionally-operating people cognize non-momentariness, momentariness is not a conventional form — this is the full meaning.

body.text: etat siddhāntavādī pariharati na doṣo yogisaṃvṛtyeti-
body.translated_text: The proponent of the [Mādhyamika] system resolves this: 'there is no fault, [it is] the yogin's convention' —

children.translated_text: There is no fault, through the yogin's convention; from the world's [standpoint], these are seers of reality;
otherwise there would be the world's invalidation of the determination that a woman is impure. // <s>Bca</s> 9.8 //

body.text: nāyaṃ pratītivirodhalakṣaṇo doṣaḥ / kutaḥ? yogināṃ pudgalanairātmyasamādhilābhināṃ yā saṃvṛtirvyavahāraḥ, tayā kṣaṇikatayā pratīteḥ / ayamabhiprāyaḥ- yadi nāma arvāgdarśanaiḥ kṣaṇikatvaṃ na pratīyate, tathāpi yogivyavahāragocaraḥ / yogivyavahāro 'pi saṃvṛtirūpatāṃ na jahāti, buddhiḥ saṃvṛtirūcyate [9.2] iti vacanāt / na ca pratītibādhitaṃ bādhitameva, tathāvidhāyāḥ pratīterapramāṇatvāt //
body.translated_text: This fault characterized by contradiction with cognition does not apply. Why? Through the convention — the practical discourse — of yogins who have attained the <s>samādhi</s> of the selflessness of persons, [things] are cognized as momentary. The intention is this: even if momentariness is not cognized by those of limited vision, still it is within the domain of yogic discourse. And yogic discourse does not abandon its conventional nature, because of the statement 'the intellect is said to be <s>saṃvṛti</s>' [9.2]. Nor is what is contradicted by [ordinary] cognition [necessarily] invalidated, since such cognition is not a valid [ultimate] cognition.

body.text: kutaḥ punaretat sāṃvṛtamapi kṣaṇikatvādi yogina eva paśyanti nārvāgdarśina ityāha- lokātte tattvadarśina iti / lokādarvācīnadarśanāt sakāśāt te yoginastattvadarśinaḥ atīndriyadarśinaḥ / hetupadametat / yasmāt tattvadarśinaste, tasmāt kṣaṇikatvanairātmyādi lokāpratītamapi pratipadyante / ata eva na teṣāṃ lokapratītibādhā //
body.translated_text: Why then do only the yogins see this — the conventional reality of momentariness and such — and not those of limited vision? He says: 'from the world, these are seers of reality.' 'From the world' — from ordinary, limited vision — those yogins are seers of reality, seers of what transcends the senses. This is the causal clause. Since they are seers of reality, therefore they understand momentariness, selflessness, and such, even though these are not cognized by the world. For this very reason, the world's cognition does not invalidate theirs.

body.text: avaśyaṃ caitadaṅgīkartavyamityāha- anyathetyādi / anyathā yadi caivaṃ na svīkriyate, tadā bhavadabhyupagate 'pi lokabādhā syāt / kutra? aśucistrīnirūpaṇe iti / aśucibhāvanāsamaye aśucīti striyāḥ kāminyā nirūpaṇe vibhāvanāyāṃ lokabādhā syāt, lokapratītena virodho bhavet, lokena śucisvabhāvatayā strīśarīrasyādhyavasānāt / tasmānna lokapratītena yogidarśanabādheti / atra-
body.translated_text: And this must necessarily be accepted — he says 'otherwise' and so forth. Otherwise — if this is not accepted — then even in what you accept, there would be invalidation by the world. Where? 'In the determination that a woman is impure.' At the time of contemplating impurity, in the determination of a woman, an attractive woman, as impure — there would be invalidation by the world, there would be contradiction with worldly cognition, since the world determines a woman's body to be of a pure nature. Therefore, worldly cognition does not invalidate the yogin's vision. Here —

body.text: yathopalabdhaṃ timirekṣaṇānam
body.translated_text: 'What is apprehended by the eyes of those afflicted with an eye-disease'

body.text: ityādinā upacayahetutvena yojanīyam / iti nāgamādapi bhāvānāṃ paramārthataḥ siddhirasti / tasmānmāyāsvapnādisvabhāvāḥ sarvadharmā iti niścitametat //
body.translated_text: — and so forth should be connected as a cause by way of augmentation. Thus, even from scripture, there is no establishment of the ultimate reality of things. Therefore it is established that all <s>dharmas</s> are of the nature of illusion, dream, and such.

body.text: syādetat- yadi sarvavyāpinī māyopamasvabhāvatā, buddho 'pi tarhi māyopamaḥ svapnopamaḥ syāt / uktaṃ caitad bhagavatyām-
body.translated_text: [Objection:] If the nature of being like an illusion is all-pervading, then the <s>Buddha</s> too would be like an illusion, like a dream. And this has been stated in the <s>Bhagavatī</s> [Prajñāpāramitā] —

body.text: evamukte subhūtistān devaputrānetadavocat- māyopamāste devaputrāḥ sattvāḥ / svapnopamāste devaputrāḥ sattvāḥ / iti hi māyā ca sattvāśca advayametadadvaidhīkāram / sarvadharmā api devaputrā māyopamāḥ svapnopamāḥ / strotaāpanno 'pi māyopamaḥ svapnopamaḥ / strotaāpattiphalamapi
body.translated_text: 'Thus addressed, <s>Subhūti</s> said to those <s>devaputras</s>: "Those beings, O <s>devaputras</s>, are like an illusion. Those beings, O <s>devaputras</s>, are like a dream. For illusion and beings — this is non-dual, without division. All <s>dharmas</s> too, O <s>devaputras</s>, are like an illusion, like a dream. A stream-enterer too is like an illusion, like a dream. The fruit of stream-entry too

body.text: māyopamaṃ svapnopamam / evaṃ sakṛdāgāmyapi sakṛdāgāmiphalamapi / anāgāmyapi anāgāmiphalamapi / arhannapi arhattvamapi māyopamaṃ svapnopamam / pratyekabuddho 'pi māyopamaḥ svapnopamaḥ / pratyekabuddhatvamapi māyopamaṃ svapnopamam / samyaksaṃbuddho 'pi māyopamaḥ svapnopamaḥ / samyaksaṃbuddhatvamapi māyopamaṃ svapnopamam / yāvat nirvāṇamapi māyopamaṃ svapnopamam / sacennirvāṇādapi kaścid dharmo viśiṣṭataraḥ syāt, tamapyahaṃ māyopamaṃ svapnopamaṃ vadāmi //
body.translated_text: is like an illusion, like a dream. Likewise a once-returner and the fruit of once-returning; a non-returner and the fruit of non-returning; an <s>Arhat</s> too, and <s>Arhatship</s> too, are like an illusion, like a dream. A <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> too is like an illusion, like a dream. <s>Pratyekabuddhahood</s> too is like an illusion, like a dream. A perfectly awakened <s>Buddha</s> too is like an illusion, like a dream. Perfect <s>Buddhahood</s> too is like an illusion, like a dream. Even <s>nirvāṇa</s> is like an illusion, like a dream. If there were some <s>dharma</s> more exalted even than <s>nirvāṇa</s>, even that I would call like an illusion, like a dream."'

body.text: evaṃ kathaṃ tatra satkārāpakārayoḥ puṇyapāpasamudbhava iti parasyābhiprāyamāśaṅkayannāha māyopamādityādi-
body.translated_text: If so, how then do merit and demerit arise from honoring and dishonoring [the Buddha]? — anticipating the opponent's intention, he says 'from one like an illusion' and so forth —

body.text: māyopamājjinātpuṇyaṃ sadbhāve 'pi kathaṃ yathā /
body.translated_text: How could merit [arise] from a <s>Jina</s> who is like an illusion, in the same way as if [he were] truly existent?

body.text: yadi bhagavānapi māyopamasvabhāvaḥ, tadā māyopamānniḥsvabhāvājjinādbhagavataḥ puṇyaṃ sukṛtaṃ pūjāsatkārapādavandanādibhiḥ kathaṃ yathā kathamiveti manyase? upalakṣaṇaṃ caitat / pāpamapi tadapakāre kathamiti draṣṭavyam / na hi māyākāranirmitapuruṣasatkārāpakārayoḥ puṇyapāpaprasūtiryukteti parasyā bhiprāyaḥ / atra prāguktamevottaram / tathātra parameva paripṛcchati- sadbhāve 'pi kathaṃ yatheti / sadbhāve 'pi paramārthasatyatve 'pi bhagavataḥ kathamiva puṇyam? kathaṃ yathetyubhayatrāpi yojanīyam / ayamabhiprāyaḥ- yathā kasyacit paramārthasato jināt paramārthasat puṇyamupajāyate, tathā anyasya māyopamānmāyopamamevetyāvayorna kaścidviśeṣaḥ, idaṃpratyayatāmātrasyobhayasādhāraṇatvāt / iti yadevottaraṃ bhavatām, tadevāsmākamapi, nātiricyate kiṃcit / na ca yuktisiddhaṃ paramārthasad vastusvarūpaṃ kiṃcidastīti pratipāditam //
body.translated_text: If the Blessed One too is of the nature of being like an illusion, then from the <s>Jina</s>, the Blessed One, who is like an illusion, devoid of intrinsic nature — how, in what way, do you think, does merit — wholesome [karma] — [arise] from worship, honor, prostration, and such? This is indicative; demerit too from dishonoring him should also be considered. For the production of merit and demerit from honoring and dishonoring a person created by a magician is not justified — this is the opponent's intention. Here, the previously stated answer applies. Here the opponent himself further asks: 'even if truly existent, how in the same way?' Even if the Blessed One is truly existent in the ultimate sense — how could there be merit in the same way? 'How in the same way' should be construed in both cases. The intention is this: just as for someone, from an ultimately real <s>Jina</s>, ultimately real merit arises, in the same way for another, from one like an illusion, [merit] is itself like an illusion. Thus there is no distinction between our [positions], since mere conditionality is common to both. Whatever answer is yours is also ours — nothing is added. And it has been demonstrated that no real intrinsic nature of things established by reasoning exists.

body.text: bhavatu nāma māyopamādapi jināt puṇyam / idaṃ tu kathaṃ samādhīyate ityāha yadi māyopama ityādi-
body.translated_text: Granted, merit may arise even from a <s>Jina</s> who is like an illusion. But how is this reconciled? He says 'if like an illusion' and so forth —

body.text: yadi māyopamaḥ sattvaḥ kiṃ punarjāyate mṛtaḥ // Bca_9.9 //
body.translated_text: If a being is like an illusion, why is he born again after dying? // <s>Bca</s> 9.9 //

body.text: athavā anyathāvatāryate- yadi jino 'pi māyopamaḥ, kā vārtā tarhi sāṃsārikeṣu sattveṣu? te 'pi tatheti brūmaḥ / māyopamāste devaputrāḥ sattvāḥ iti vacanāt / evaṃ sati mahān doṣaḥ prasajyate ityāha- yadītyādi / yadi māyopamo māyāsvabhāvasamānadharmaḥ sattvaḥ prāṇī, tadā kiṃ punarjāyate mṛtaḥ? kimiti praśne akṣamāyāṃ vā / kiṃ punarjāyate utpadyate? mṛto nikāyasabhāgatāyāścyutaḥ / kāraṇamatra vaktavyam, naitadyuktamiti vā / nahi māyāpuruṣo vinaṣṭaḥ punarutpadyate / tasmāt paramārthasanto bhāvā ityupagantavyam //
body.translated_text: Or alternatively, [the verse] is introduced differently: if even the <s>Jina</s> is like an illusion, what need to speak of <s>saṃsāric</s> beings? They too are so — we say this. Because of the statement: 'Those beings, O <s>devaputras</s>, are like an illusion.' This being so, a great fault follows — he says 'if' and so forth. If a being — a living creature — is like an illusion, of the same nature as an illusion, then why is he born again after dying? 'Why' — in the sense of a question, or of intolerance. Why is he born — does he arise — again? Having died — having fallen from the class of rebirth-existence. A reason should be stated here; or [the point is:] this is not justified. For an illusory person, once destroyed, does not arise again. Therefore, things must be accepted as ultimately real.

body.text: naitadupagantavyamityāha yāvadityādi-
body.translated_text: This should not be accepted — he says 'as long as' and so forth —

body.text: yāvatpratyayasāmagrī tāvanmāyāpi vartate /
body.translated_text: As long as the assemblage of conditions [persists], even an illusion persists.

body.text: yāvatkālaṃ pratyayānāṃ kāraṇānāṃ mantrauṣadhādīnāṃ sāmagrī samudāyaḥ, samagrāṇi kāraṇāni, tāvatkālaṃ māyāpi vartate, na arvāṅ nivartate, nāpi tataḥ paraṃ pravartate / evaṃ yāvadavidyākarmatṛṣṇāsvabhāvā sāmagrī, tāvat sattvasaṃtānamāyāpi vartate, idaṃpratyayatāyattavṛttitvāt /
body.translated_text: As long as there is the assemblage — the coming together — of conditions, of causes such as mantras, herbs, and such, for that duration even the illusion persists — it does not cease before [that assemblage ends], nor does it continue beyond that. Likewise, as long as there is the assemblage whose nature is ignorance, <s>karma</s>, and craving, the sentient continuum — which is also [like] an illusion — persists, since its activity depends on conditionality.

body.text: yadi na paramārthataḥ sattvo 'sti, kathamāsaṃsāraṃ sattvasaṃtānaḥ pravartate, na tu māyāvadaciraṃ nivartate? uktamatra- yāvatpratyayasāmagrī tāvat pravartate, yasya tu tathā nāsti, sa nānuvartate iti / api ca / na cirakālāvasthitiḥ samyaktvavyavasthānibandhanamityāha dīrghasaṃtāna ityādi-
body.translated_text: If no sentient being exists in the ultimate sense, how does the continuum of beings continue throughout <s>saṃsāra</s>, yet not cease quickly like an illusion? This has been answered here: it continues as long as the assemblage of conditions [persists]; but that for which [conditions] do not exist in that way — it does not continue. Moreover, long duration is not the ground for establishing [something as] real — he says with 'merely through a long continuum' and so forth —

body.text: dīrghasaṃtānamātreṇa kathaṃ sattvo 'sti satyataḥ // Bca_9.10 //
body.translated_text: How does a being exist in truth merely through a long continuum? // <s>Bca</s> 9.10 //

body.text: dīrghaścirakālāvasthitaḥ saṃtānaḥ pravāhaḥ, sa eva kevalastanmātraṃ tena / kathamiti pṛcchati- kena prakāreṇa sattvo 'sti vidyate? satyataḥ paramārthataḥ / etāvāṃstu viśeṣaḥ- yasya hi dīrghakālāvasthitihetupratyayaviśeṣo 'sti, sa dīrghakālamanuvartate / yasya tu tathā nāsti, sa nānuvartate iti / na tu tāvatā samyaṅyithyātvam / tasmānmāyāsvabhāvatve 'pi na punarjanmāsaṃbhavaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Long' — persisting for a long time — is the continuum, the stream; that alone, merely that. By that [mere fact of duration]. 'How' — he asks: in what way does a being exist? 'In truth' — in the ultimate sense. Only this much is the distinction: that which has the specific causes and conditions for long duration — that continues for a long time. But that for which such [causes and conditions] do not exist — it does not continue. But by that much alone, [something's] being real or unreal [is not determined]. Therefore, even though of the nature of an illusion, rebirth is not impossible.

body.text: evaṃ tarhi yathā māyāpuruṣavadhādau na prāṇātipātaḥ, tathā tadaparapuruṣavadhādāvapi na syāt, abhinnasvabhāvatvāt, ityatrāha māyāpuruṣa ityādi-
body.translated_text: If this is so, then just as there is no taking of life in the killing of an illusory person, so too in the killing of another real person there should be none, since their natures are not different. To this he says with 'an illusory person' and so forth —

body.text: māyāpuruṣaghātādau cittābhāvānna pāpakam /
body.translated_text: In the killing and such of an illusory person, there is no evil, because there is no mind.

body.text: māyāpuruṣasya ghātādau māraṇādau / ādiśabdena tasya adattādi gṛhṇataḥ / samāne 'pi niḥsvabhāvatve cittasya vijñānasya māyāpuruṣasaṃtāne 'bhāvāt asattvāt na pāpakaṃ na akuśalamutpadyate prāṇātipātādi / pāpameva pāpakam / svārthe kanvidhānāt / tatrāpi māraṇābhiprāyeṇa prahāraṃ dadato bhavatyeva aśubham, na tu prāṇātipātaḥ / māyāpuruṣādanyatra kathaṃ prāṇātipāta iti cedāha cittamāyetyādi-
body.translated_text: In the killing and such — the slaying and such — of an illusory person. The word 'and such' includes his taking what is not given, and so forth. Even though the lack of intrinsic nature is the same, because of the absence — the non-existence — of mind, of consciousness, in the continuum of the illusory person, no evil — no unwholesome [<s>karma</s>] — arises, such as the taking of life and so forth. '<s>Pāpaka</s>' is '<s>pāpa</s>' itself — the <s>kan</s> suffix being in the sense of the word itself. Even there, for one who strikes with the intention of killing, there is indeed unwholesome [<s>karma</s>], but not the taking of life. How then does the taking of life occur in [the killing of a being] other than an illusory person? He says with 'mind-illusion' and so forth —

body.text: cittamāyāsamete tu pāpapuṇyasamudbhavaḥ // Bca_9.11 //
body.translated_text: But when [a being is] endowed with mind-illusion, the arising of merit and demerit [occurs]. // <s>Bca</s> 9.11 //

body.text: cittameva māyā cittamāyā, tayā samete yukte / māyāsvabhāvena cittena saṃbaddhe ityarthaḥ / tuśabdaḥ pūrvasmādviśeṣārthaḥ / puṇyaṃ ca pāpaṃ ca puṇyapāpe, tayoḥ sukṛtaduṣkṛtayoḥ samudbhavaḥ samutpattiḥ / upakārāpakārayoḥ iti sāmagrīviśeṣāt kāryaviśeṣaḥ / yathā satyapi gomayetarajanmanorvartikayorākārasāmye kāraṇabhedāt svabhāvabhedaḥ / tathā ihāpi noktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ //
body.translated_text: Mind itself is the illusion — 'mind-illusion'; endowed with, connected with, that. The meaning is: connected with a mind that is of the nature of illusion. The word 'but' is for distinguishing from the preceding [case]. Merit and demerit — the arising, the production, of both wholesome and unwholesome [<s>karma</s>] — of benefit and harm — occurs through the specific [nature of] the assemblage of conditions: thus specific effects [arise from] specific [conditions]. Just as, even though the form of a cowdung-beetle and another kind of worm (<s>vartikā</s>) is the same, there is a difference in nature due to the difference in cause — so here too, the fault stated [by the opponent] does not follow.

body.text: yaduktam- cittamāyeti, tat paro vighaṭayannāha mantrādīnāmityādi-
body.translated_text: The opponent, undermining what was said — 'mind-illusion' — says with 'mantras and such' and so forth —

body.text: mantrādīnāmasāmarthyānna māyācittasaṃbhavaḥ /
body.translated_text: Due to the incapacity of mantras and such, there is no arising of mind-illusion.

body.text: mantrādīnām, ādiśabdādauṣadhādīnāṃ cittotpādaṃ prati asāmarthyādavyāpārāt na māyācittasaṃbhavaḥ na māyāsvabhāvaṃ cittaṃ saṃbhavati / yathā paravyāmohanibandhanānāṃ māyākāraprayuktānāṃ mantrādīnāṃ prabhāveṇa hastyādyākāranirvṛttiḥ, na tathā cittasyeti parasya bhāvaḥ / etat pariharannāha sāpi nānāvidhetyādi-
body.translated_text: 'Mantras and such' — by the word 'and such,' herbs and such. Due to the incapacity — the inefficacy — of these regarding the production of mind, there is no arising of mind-illusion — no mind of the nature of illusion comes into being. The opponent's view is: just as through the power of mantras and such employed by a magician for the purpose of deluding others, there arises the appearance of elephants and such, the mind does not [arise] in that way. Resolving this, he says with 'that too is of various kinds' and so forth —

body.text: sāpi nānāvidhā māyā nānāpratyayasaṃbhavā /
body.translated_text: That [illusion] too is of various kinds, arising from various conditions.

body.text: apiśabdo 'vadhāraṇārtho bhinnakramaśca / sā māyā nānāvidhaiva nānāprakāraiva / ata eva nānāpratyayasaṃbhavā nānāpratyayāt anekaprakārakāraṇāt saṃbhava utpādo yasyāḥ sā tathoktā / ayamabhiprāyaḥ- yadi māyā māyeti śabdasāmyamasti, tathāpi na tatkāraṇasyāpyabhedaḥ, māyāsvabhāvatve 'pi kāryasya nānāsvabhāvatvāt / na hi ekasmin kārye kiṃcit kāraṇaṃ dṛṣṭamiti kāryaśabdasāmyāt sarvatra tadeva prakalpayituṃ yujyate, api tu kvacideva kasyacit sāmarthyam, śabdasāmye 'pi svabhāvabhedāt / etadevopadarśayannāha naikasyeti-
body.translated_text: The word 'even' ('api') is for emphasis, and is [placed] in a different order. That illusion is of various kinds indeed — of various types. And for this very reason it arises from various conditions — various causes of many kinds — it is said to have arisen from that; such it is called. This is the intention: even if there is a similarity of the word 'illusion,' there is still no identity of its cause, since even though the effect is of the nature of illusion, [it is] of various natures. For it is not justified, merely because some cause is seen in one effect and there is a similarity of the word 'effect,' to posit that very same [cause] everywhere; rather, the efficacy of a given [cause applies] only in a given [case], since despite the similarity of the word, their natures differ. Showing this very point, he says with 'of no single [condition]' and so forth —

body.text: naikasya sarvasāmarthyaṃ pratyayasyāsti kutracit // Bca_9.12 //
body.translated_text: No single condition has the capacity for everything, anywhere. // <s>Bca</s> 9.12 //

body.text: naikasya kvacidupalabdhasāmarthyasya pratyayasya kāraṇasya hetoḥ sarvasāmarthyaṃ sarvasmin kārye sāmarthyaṃ śaktirasti saṃbhavati / kvacidṛṣṭamiti kṛtvā kutraciditi kasmiṃścit samaye deśe kāle vā dṛṣṭamiṣṭaṃ vā / tataśca kācinmāyā mantrādisāmarthyapratilabdhasvabhāvā, kācit punaranādisaṃsārapravṛttamāhātmyā avidyādiprabhāvapravartitā / tasmānna sarvāsu mantrādisāmarthyamiti / etat sarva lokavyavahārānugataṃ kalpanānirmitaṃ sāṃvṛtaṃ vastutattvamupādaya samutthitaṃ na tu paramārthataḥ / paramārthadaśāyāṃ jananamaraṇotpādanirodhahetuphalabhāvābhāvādikalpanāyā abhāvāt, prakṛtinirvṛtatvāt sarvadharmāṇāmiti //
body.translated_text: No single condition — no cause, no reason — whose capacity has been observed somewhere, has the capacity — the power — for everything, in every effect. 'Observed somewhere' — thus, having been seen or accepted at some time, in some place, or at some occasion. And thus some illusion has obtained its nature through the power of mantras and such, while another operates through the power of beginningless <s>saṃsāric</s> momentum, set in motion by the force of ignorance and such. Therefore, not all [illusions arise through] the power of mantras and such. All this — following worldly convention — is an edifice of conceptual construction, arising in reference to conventional reality. But not in the ultimate sense. In the perspective of the ultimate, there is no [room for] conceptual elaboration of arising and cessation, production and destruction, cause and effect, existence and non-existence, and such — because all <s>dharmas</s> are quiescent by nature.

body.text: etadasahamānaḥ paraḥ punaranyathā prasañjayannāha nirvṛta iti-
body.translated_text: Unable to bear this, the opponent raises a further consequence, saying with 'quiescent' and so forth —

body.text: nirvṛtaḥ paramārthena saṃvṛtyā yadi saṃsaret /
body.translated_text: If [a being] is quiescent in the ultimate sense, yet wanders in <s>saṃsāra</s> conventionally,

body.text: nirvṛtaḥ svabhāvaśūnyatvādutpādanirodharahitaḥ / paramārthena paramārthasatyataḥ prakṛtinirvāṇatayā ādiśāntatvāt / yadi saṃvṛtyā saṃvṛtisatyena kālpanikatvena saṃsaret, jātijarāmaraṇayogī bhavet, tadā ayaṃ mahān virodhaḥ syādityāha buddho 'pi saṃsaredevamityādi-
body.translated_text: 'Quiescent' — devoid of intrinsic nature, hence free from arising and cessation. 'In the ultimate sense' — from the perspective of ultimate truth, by virtue of being quiescent by nature, by virtue of being primordially at peace. If [a being] 'wanders in <s>saṃsāra</s> conventionally' — through conventional truth, through being conceptually constructed — if it were to wander in <s>saṃsāra</s>, would undergo birth, old age, and death — then this would be a great contradiction, he says with 'even the <s>Buddha</s> would wander in <s>saṃsāra</s>' and so forth —

body.text: buddho 'pi saṃsaredevaṃ tataḥ kiṃ bodhicaryayā // Bca_9.13 //
body.translated_text: even the <s>Buddha</s> would wander in <s>saṃsāra</s>; then what is the use of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s practice? // <s>Bca</s> 9.13 //

body.text: evamabhyupagamyamāne buddho 'pi sarvāvaraṇaprahāṇato nirvṛto 'pi saṃsaret janmādibhāg bhavet / yata evam, tataḥ tasmāt kāraṇāt kiṃ bodhicaryayā? bodhaye buddhatvāya caryā karacaraṇaśiraḥpradānādyanekaduṣkaraśatalakṣaṇā, tayā kim? na kiṃcit prayojanam, uktakrameṇa vaiphalyāt / sā hi sarvasāṃsārikadharmanivṛttaye sarvaguṇasamuccayāśritabuddhatvaprāptaye ca samāśrīyate, tathāpi na sāṃsārikadharmanivṛttiścet, kiṃ tatsamāśrayeṇa saṃsādhitamiti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: If this is accepted, then even the <s>Buddha</s> — though quiescent through the abandonment of all obscurations — would wander in <s>saṃsāra</s>, would be subject to birth and such. Since this is so, then from that reason, what is the use of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s practice? The 'practice for awakening' — for <s>Buddhahood</s> — characterized by the giving of hands, feet, head, and such hundreds of difficult deeds — what use is it? None whatsoever, since by the stated reasoning it would be fruitless. For it is undertaken for the cessation of all <s>saṃsāric</s> <s>dharmas</s> and for the attainment of <s>Buddhahood</s> endowed with the accumulation of all qualities; yet if <s>saṃsāric</s> <s>dharmas</s> do not cease even so, what is accomplished by undertaking it? — this is the meaning.

body.text: tat pratyuktameva yāvatpratyayasāmagrītyādinā, punarapi vispaṣṭayannāha pratyayānāmityādi-
body.translated_text: This has already been answered with 'as long as the assemblage of conditions' and so forth; making it clearer again, he says with 'of conditions' and so forth —

children.translated_text: For as long as the conditions are not cut off, even an illusion is not cut off.

children.text: pratyayānāṃ tu vicchedātsaṃvṛtyāpi na saṃbhavaḥ // Bca_9.14 //
children.translated_text: But through the severance of conditions, it does not exist even conventionally. // <s>Bca</s> 9.14 //

body.text: pratyayānāṃ kāraṇānām / anucchede avināśe / hiryasmāt / māyāpi na kevalaṃ saṃsāra iti samuccaye apiśabdaḥ / naivocchidyate na nivartate / pratyayānāṃ kāraṇānāṃ tu
body.translated_text: 'Of conditions' — of causes. 'Not cut off' — not destroyed. 'For' (<s>hi</s>) — because. 'Even an illusion' — the word 'even' is in the sense of inclusion, [meaning:] not only <s>saṃsāra</s>, but even an illusion [is not cut off]. It is never cut off, does not cease. 'But through the severance' — through the cessation — 'of conditions,' of causes

body.text: vicchedāt nivṛtteḥ, saṃvṛttyāpi kālpanikavyavahāreṇāpi na saṃbhavo na saṃsaraṇam / pratyayānāṃ samucchedaḥ punastattvābhyāsādavidyādinirodhakrameṇa veditavyaḥ / tadyathoktamāryaśālistambasūtre-
body.translated_text: — 'even conventionally' — even by conventional discourse — there is 'no existence,' no wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s>. The complete severance of conditions should be understood as [occurring] through the progressive cessation of ignorance and such, by means of the cultivation of reality. As stated in the <s>Āryaśālistambasūtra</s> —

body.text: evamukte maitreyo bodhisattvo mahāsattva āyuṣmantaṃ śāriputrametadavocat- yaduktaṃ bhagavatā dharmasvāminā sarvajñena- yo bhikṣavaḥ pratītyasamutpādaṃ paśyati, sa dharma paśyati / yo dharmaṃ paśyati, sa buddhaṃ paśyati / tatra katamaḥ pratītyasamutpādo nāma? yadidam- avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ / saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam / vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam / nāmarūpapratyayaṃ ṣaḍāyatanam / ṣaḍāyatanapratyayaḥ sparśaḥ / sparśapratyayā vedanā / vedanāpratyayā tṛṣṇā / tṛṣṇāpratyayamupādānam / upādānapratyayo bhavaḥ / bhavapratyayā jātiḥ / jātipratyayā jarāmaraṇaśokaparidevaduḥkhadaurmanasyopāyāsāḥ / evamasya kevalasya mahato duḥkhaskandhasya samudayo bhavati / tatra avidyānirodhāt saṃskārā nirudhyante / peyālaṃ / evamasya kevalasya mahato duḥkhaskandhasya nirodho bhavati / ayamucyate pratītyasamutpādaḥ / peyālaṃ / ya imaṃ pratītyasamutpādaṃ satatasamitaṃ nirjīvaṃ yathāvadaviparītamajātamabhūtamasaṃskṛtamapratighamanālambanaṃ śivamabhayamahāryamavyupaśamasvabhāvaṃ paśyati, sa dharmaṃ paśyati / yastu evaṃ satatasamitaṃ yāvadavyupaśamasvabhāvaṃ dharmaṃ paśyati, so 'nuttaraṃ dharmaśarīraṃ buddhaṃ paśyati / peyālaṃ / tatra avidyā katamā? eteṣāmeva ṣaṇṇāṃ dhātūnāṃ yā ekasaṃjñā piṇḍasaṃjñā nityasaṃjñā dhruvasaṃjñā śāśvatasaṃjñā sukhasaṃjñā ātmasaṃjñā sattvasaṃjñā jīvasaṃjñā jantusaṃjñā manujasaṃjñā mānavasaṃjñā ahaṃkāramamakārasaṃjñā / evamādi vividhamajñānam, iyamucyate 'vidyā / evamavidyāyāṃ satyāṃ viṣayeṣu rāgadveṣamohāḥ pravartante / tatra ye rāgadveṣamohā viṣayeṣu, amī avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārā iutyucyante / vastuprativijñaptirvijñānam / catvāri mahābhūtāni copādāya rūpamaikadhyarūpam / vijñānasahajāścatvāro 'rūpiṇa upādānaskandhā nāma, tannāmarūpam / nāmarūpasaṃniśritāni indriyāṇi ṣaḍāyatanam / trayāṇāṃ dharmāṇāṃ saṃnipātaḥ sparśaḥ / sparśānubhavo vedanā / vedanādhyavasānaṃ tṛṣṇā / tṛṣṇāvaipulyamupādānam / upādānanirjātaṃ punarbhavajanakaṃ karma bhavaḥ / bhavahetukaḥ skandhaprādurbhāvo jātiḥ / jātyabhinirvṛttānāṃ skandhānāṃ paripāko jarā / skandhavināśo maraṇam / mriyamāṇasya saṃmūḍhasya sābhiṣvaṅgasya antardāhaḥ śokaḥ / śokotthalapanaṃ paridevaḥ / pañcavijñānasaṃprayuktamāghātānubhavanaṃ duḥkham / duḥkhamanasikārasaṃprayuktaṃ mānasaṃ duḥkhaṃ daurmanasyam / ye cānye evamādāya upakleśāḥ, ime upāyāsā ityucyante //
body.translated_text: Thus addressed, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> <s>Mahāsattva</s> <s>Maitreya</s> said to the venerable <s>Śāriputra</s>: 'The Blessed One, the Lord of <s>Dharma</s>, the Omniscient One, has said: "He who sees dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>), O monks, sees the <s>Dharma</s>. He who sees the <s>Dharma</s> sees the <s>Buddha</s>." What then is dependent origination? It is this: conditioned by ignorance are the formations (<s>saṃskāras</s>). Conditioned by formations is consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>). Conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form (<s>nāmarūpa</s>). Conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense-bases (<s>ṣaḍāyatana</s>). Conditioned by the six sense-bases is contact (<s>sparśa</s>). Conditioned by contact is feeling (<s>vedanā</s>). Conditioned by feeling is craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>). Conditioned by craving is clinging (<s>upādāna</s>). Conditioned by clinging is becoming (<s>bhava</s>). Conditioned by becoming is birth (<s>jāti</s>). Conditioned by birth are old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and agitation. Thus there is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering. There, through the cessation of ignorance, formations cease. [Abbreviation.] Thus there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering. This is called dependent origination. [Abbreviation.] He who sees this dependent origination as continuous, unbroken, lifeless, as it truly is, unerring, unborn, unactual, unconditioned, unobstructed, without support, peaceful, fearless, unremovable, of the nature of non-cessation — he sees the <s>Dharma</s>. And he who thus sees the <s>Dharma</s> as continuous, unbroken, and so forth up to of the nature of non-cessation — he sees the unsurpassed <s>Dharma</s>-body, the <s>Buddha</s>. [Abbreviation.] What therein is ignorance? With regard to these very six elements, the perception of unity, the perception of a mass, the perception of permanence, the perception of stability, the perception of eternality, the perception of pleasure, the perception of self, the perception of a sentient being, the perception of a living being, the perception of a creature, the perception of a human, the perception of a person, the perception of I-making and mine-making. Thus various kinds of non-knowledge — this is called ignorance. When ignorance is thus present, desire, hatred, and delusion operate with regard to objects. Those desires, hatreds, and delusions regarding objects — these are called formations conditioned by ignorance. The cognition directed toward an object is consciousness. The four great elements and the form depending on them — material form taken as a whole. The four immaterial aggregates of clinging that are co-arisen with consciousness — that is name-and-form. The sense-faculties that depend on name-and-form are the six sense-bases. The conjunction of the three <s>dharmas</s> is contact. The experience of contact is feeling. The adherence to feeling is craving. The proliferation of craving is clinging. The <s>karma</s> produced by clinging that generates renewed existence is becoming. The manifestation of the aggregates caused by becoming is birth. The maturation of the aggregates that have been produced by birth is old age. The destruction of the aggregates is death. The inner burning of one who is dying, deluded, and attached — is grief. The verbal expression arising from grief is lamentation. The experience of affliction associated with the five [sense-]consciousnesses is suffering. The mental suffering associated with the mental attention to suffering is mental distress. And whatever other secondary afflictions arise from these — they are called agitation.'

body.text: tatra mahāndhakārārthena avidyā / abhisaṃskārārthena saṃskārāḥ / viajñānanārthena vijñānam / mananārthena nāmarūpam / āyadvārārthena ṣaḍāyatanam / sparśanārthena sparśaḥ / anubhavanārthena vedanā / paritarṣaṇārthena tṛṣṇā / upādānārthena upādānam / punarbhavajananārthena
body.translated_text: There, ignorance is in the sense of great darkness. Formations are in the sense of fashioning. Consciousness is in the sense of cognizing. Name-and-form is in the sense of ideation. The six sense-bases are in the sense of gateways of entry. Contact is in the sense of touching. Feeling is in the sense of experiencing. Craving is in the sense of thirsting. Clinging is in the sense of grasping. Becoming

body.text: bhavaḥ / skandhaprādurbhāvārthena jātiḥ / skandhaparipākārthena jarā / vināśārthena maraṇam / śocanārthena śokaḥ / vacanaparidevanārthena paridevaḥ / kāyasaṃpīḍanārthena duḥkham / cittasaṃpīḍanārthena daurmanasyam / upakleśārthena upāyāsāḥ / iti vistaraḥ //
body.translated_text: is in the sense of generating renewed existence. Birth is in the sense of the manifestation of the aggregates. Old age is in the sense of the maturation of the aggregates. Death is in the sense of destruction. Grief is in the sense of grieving. Lamentation is in the sense of verbal lamenting. Suffering is in the sense of bodily affliction. Mental distress is in the sense of mental affliction. Agitation is in the sense of secondary affliction. Thus in detail.

body.text: evamupadarśitapratyayānāmanucchede saṃsāro 'vikalaḥ pravartate, dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpādasyaiva saṃsāratvāt / yadāhurācāryapādāḥ-
body.translated_text: When the conditions demonstrated in this way are unbroken, <s>saṃsāra</s> continues without deficiency, since the twelve-linked <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination) itself constitutes <s>saṃsāra</s>. As the Master [<s>Vasubandhu</s>] says —

children.translated_text: 'The continuum, impelled by afflictions and <s>karmas</s>, drawn along sequentially,
goes to the next world again — beginningless is the wheel of existence.'

body.text: sa pratītyasamutpādo dvādaśāṅgastrikāṇḍakaḥ /

children.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Abhidharmakośa</s> 3.19-20]

body.translated_text: 'That dependent origination is of twelve links and three sections.'

body.text: pratyayānāṃ punarucchede sarvathaiva saṃsaraṇaṃ na syāt, kāraṇavaikalyāt / tataśca 'buddho 'pi saṃsaredevam' ityetanna prasajyate iti //
body.translated_text: But when the conditions are broken, transmigration would not occur at all, due to the deficiency of causes. And therefore, the [objection that] 'even a <s>Buddha</s> would continue to transmigrate in this way' does not follow as an absurd consequence. //

body.text: evaṃ tāvat sautrāntikādicodyamudasya yogācāravipratipattinirākaraṇāya tanmatena dūṣaṇamudbhāvayannāha yadā na bhrāntirapītyādi-
body.translated_text: Having thus set aside the objection of the <s>Sautrāntikas</s> and others, in order to refute the disagreement of the <s>Yogācāras</s>, he raises a criticism based on their own position, saying 'when not even error' and so forth —

body.text: yadā na bhrāntirapyasti māyā kenopalabhyate // Bca_9.15 //
body.translated_text: When not even error exists, by what is the illusion perceived? // Bca_9.15 //

body.text: yadā sarvaṃ jagat māyātmakatayā svabhāvaśūnyamupagataṃ madhyamakavādibhiḥ, māyāsvabhāvasaṃvṛtigrāhiṇī buddhirapi bhavatāṃ nāsti bāhyavat, tadā māyā kenopalabhyate, kena pratīyate tadgāhakavastusajjñānamantareṇa? naiva kenacidityarthaḥ / yasya punaḥ svacittameva paramārthasat bāhyarūpatayā bhrāntaṃ tathā pratibhāsate, na tasyāyaṃ doṣa iti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: When the entire world has been accepted by the <s>Mādhyamikas</s> as empty of intrinsic nature through being of the nature of illusion, and the cognition that grasps the convention of the nature of illusion also does not exist for you, just like external [objects] — then by what is the illusion perceived, by what is it cognized, in the absence of any real cognition that grasps it? By nothing whatsoever — this is the meaning. For one who holds that one's own mind alone is ultimately real and appears erroneously in the form of external [objects] — for such a one this fault does not apply: this is the purport. //

body.text: etannirākartumāha yadā māyaivetyādi-
body.translated_text: To refute this, he says 'when the illusion itself' and so forth —

body.text: yadā māyaiva te nāsti tadā kimupalabhyate /
body.translated_text: When even the illusion itself does not exist for you, then what is perceived?

body.text: yadā māyaiva grāhyatayā hastyādyākārapravṛtyā tava vijñānavādino nāsti, cittamātraṃ jagadabhyupagacchanto bahirarthābhāvāt, tadā kimupalabhyate, tadā kimiha pratibhāsate? bahirarthābhāvāddeśādivicchedena pratibhāso na yukta ityarthaḥ / atra parasyābhiprāyamāśaṅkayannāha cittasyaiva sa ityādi-
body.translated_text: When even the illusion itself — as that which is to be grasped, operating in the form of elephants and such — does not exist for you, the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> who, accepting the world as mind-only, [denies] the existence of external objects — then what is perceived, what appears here? Since external objects do not exist, an appearance with spatial and other distinctions is not justified — this is the meaning. Here, anticipating the opponent's view, he says 'it is an aspect of mind itself' and so forth —

body.text: cittasyaiva sa ākāro yadyapyanyo 'sti tattvataḥ // Bca_9.16 //
body.translated_text: Even if it is an aspect of mind itself, it is in reality something other [than the grasping aspect]. // Bca_9.16 //

body.text: uktamatra cittameva bahīrūpatayā bhrāntaṃ hastyādyākāraṃ pratibhāsate iti / uktameva / kiṃ tu yadyapi cittasyaiva jñānasyaiva sa iti deśādivicchedena grāhyatayā pratibhāsamāna ākāro nirbhāsaḥ, anya ityaparaḥ āntarād grāhakāccittākārāt, asti vidyate, tattvato vastutaḥ //
body.translated_text: It has been said here: mind itself, appearing erroneously as external, appears as the form of elephants and such — this has been stated. However, even though it is an aspect of mind itself — of cognition itself — that which appears as to-be-grasped with spatial and other distinctions — 'that' — 'other' — different from the internal grasping aspect of mind — it exists, it is present, in reality — in substance. //

body.text: yadyapītyabhyupagamyoktam, tathāpi naitat saṃgacchata ityāha cittameva yadā māyetyādi-
body.translated_text: Although this was said by way of concession, still it does not hold together — he says 'when mind itself is the illusion' and so forth —

body.text: cittameva yadā māyā tadā kiṃ kena dṛśyate /
body.translated_text: When mind itself is the illusion, then what is seen by what?

body.text: cittameva vijñānameva vedakatayā svīkṛtam, yadā māyā nānyā, na hi vedakacittavyatiriktā kācidanyā māyā nāma, tadātmatayā tasyāstathā pratibhāsopagamāt, tadā kiṃ
body.translated_text: Mind itself — cognition itself — has been accepted as the experiencer. When it is the illusion and nothing other — for there is no illusion whatsoever apart from the experiencer-mind — then, having accepted it as such through its appearing in that way
