body.text: kena dṛśyate, kiṃ kena pratīyate? darśanameva hi kevalamasti na dṛśyam / dṛśyamantareṇa darśanamapi na syāt, dṛśyāpekṣatvāttasya / ato na kenacit kiṃcit dṛśyeta, iti āndhyamaśeṣasya jagataḥ prāptamiti bhāvaḥ / nanu syādevaitat yadi jñānasya ātmasaṃvedanaṃ na syāt, yāvatā svasaṃvedanatayā svarūpaṃ saṃvedayat tadabhinnaṃ māyādipratibhāsamapi vedayet / tathā ca sati na kācit kṣatiḥ / iti vijñānavādino 'bhiprāyamāśaṅkayāha-
body.translated_text: — what is seen by what? What is cognized by what? For only seeing exists, not what is seen. Without what is to be seen, seeing too would not occur, since seeing depends upon what is to be seen. Therefore nothing would be seen by anything — thus the blindness of the entire world would follow: this is the purport. But surely this would follow only if the cognition had no self-cognition; insofar as, through self-awareness, cognizing its own form, it would also cognize the undifferentiated appearance of illusion and such. And if that were so, there would be no fault. Thus, anticipating the <s>Vijñānavādin</s>'s view, he says —

body.text: uktaṃ ca lokanāthena cittaṃ cittaṃ na paśyati /
body.translated_text: And the Lord of the World said: 'Mind does not perceive mind.'

body.text: svabhāvaśūnyameva sarva jagad yadā yuktitaḥ pratipāditam, tadā kaḥ kasya svabhāvo vastutaḥ iti kasya kena vedanaṃ syāt? uktaṃ ca bhagavatā-
body.translated_text: When all the world has been demonstrated to be empty of intrinsic nature through reasoning — then whose intrinsic nature, in reality, could be cognized by what? And the Blessed One said —

body.text: sarvadharmāḥ śūnyāḥ, śūnyatālakṣaṇaṃ cittam / sarvadharmā viviktāḥ, viviktatālakṣaṇaṃ cittam / iti /
body.translated_text: 'All <s>dharmas</s> are empty; the characteristic of emptiness is mind. All <s>dharmas</s> are isolated; the characteristic of isolation is mind.' Thus.

body.text: kiṃ ca / uktaṃ ca kathitaṃ ca lokanāthena lokānāṃ sarvasattvānāṃ nāthena śaraṇyena buddhena bhagavatā / kimuktam? cittaṃ cittaṃ na paśyatīti, cittaṃ svātmānaṃ na jānāti, satyapi vastutve svātmani kāritravirodhāt / kathamiva?
body.translated_text: Moreover, 'it has been said' — 'and stated by the Lord of the World' — by the <s>Buddha</s>, the lord, the refuge of all beings in the world. What was said? 'Mind does not perceive mind' — mind does not know itself; even though it is a real thing, because of the contradiction of action upon itself. How so?

body.text: na cchinatti yathātmānamasidhārā tathā manaḥ // Bca_9.17 //
body.translated_text: Just as the blade of a sword does not cut itself, so too the mind. // Bca_9.17 //

body.text:
yathā sutīkṣṇāpyasidhārā khaṅgadhārā tadanyavadātmānaṃ svakāyaṃ na cchinatti na vighāṭayati, svātmani kriyāvirodhāt, tathā manaḥ / asidhārāvaccittamapi svātmānaṃ na paśyatīti yojyam / tathā hi na tadevaikaṃ jñānaṃ vedyavedakavedanātmasvabhāvatrayaṃ yuktam / ekasya niraṃśasya trisvabhāvatāyogāt / tatredamuktamāryaratnacūḍasūtre-
sa cittaṃ parigaveṣamāṇo nādhyātmaṃ cittaṃ samanupaśyati / na bahirdhā cittaṃ samanupaśyati / na skadheṣu cittaṃ samanupaśyati / na dhātuṣu cittaṃ samanupaśyati / nāyataneṣu cittaṃ samanupaśyati / sa cittamasamanupaśyaṃścittadhārāṃ paryeṣate- kutaścittasyotpattiriti / ālambane sati cittamutpadyate / tat kimanyaccittamanyadālambanam, atha yadevālambanaṃ tadeva cittam? yadi tāvadanyadālambanamanyaccittam, tad dvicittatā bhaviṣyati / atha yadevālambanaṃ tadeva cittam, tat kathaṃ cittaṃ cittaṃ paśyati? na hi cittaṃ cittaṃ samanupaśyati / tadyathā na tasyaiva asidhārayā saiva asiṃdhārā śakyate chettum, na tenaiva aṅgulyagreṇa tadeva aṅgulyagraṃ spraṣṭuṃ śakyate, evameva tenaiva cittena tadeva cittaṃ draṣṭumiti vistaraḥ //
body.translated_text:
Just as even a very sharp sword-blade, a scimitar's edge, does not cut — does not cleave — itself, its own body, like something other [than itself], because of the contradiction of action upon itself — so too the mind. Just as with the blade of a sword, mind too does not perceive itself — this should be construed. For indeed, it is not justified that the same single cognition should have a threefold nature as that which is to be known, the knower, and the knowing. Since a threefold nature is impossible for what is single and without parts. Here the following is stated in the <s>Āryaratnacūḍasūtra</s> —
'He, searching for the mind, does not perceive the mind internally; does not perceive the mind externally; does not perceive the mind in the aggregates; does not perceive the mind in the elements; does not perceive the mind in the sense-bases. Not perceiving the mind, he investigates the stream of mind: "From where is the arising of mind?" When there is an object, mind arises. Is mind one thing and the object another, or is the object itself the mind? If the object is one thing and mind another, then there would be two minds. But if the object itself is the mind, then how does mind perceive mind? For mind does not perceive mind. Just as the blade of a sword cannot cut that very blade, just as the tip of a finger cannot touch that very tip of a finger — so too, by that very mind, that very mind cannot be seen.' Thus in detail. //

body.text: atra cittāmātravādinaḥ svātmani kriyāvirodhaṃ vighaṭayituṃ svapakṣaprasādhanāya dṛṣṭāntamudbhāvayannāha ātmabhāvamityādi-
body.translated_text: Here, the <s>Cittamātravādin</s> (proponent of mind-only), in order to dissolve the contradiction of action upon itself and establish his own position, presents an example, saying 'its own nature' and so forth —

body.text: ātmabhāvaṃ yathā dīpaḥ saṃprakāśayatīti cet /
body.translated_text: If one says: 'Just as a lamp illuminates its own nature' —

body.text: ātmabhāvaṃ svasvarūpaṃ yathā dīpaḥ pradīpaḥ saṃprakāśayati dyotayati / yathā hi kila andhakārāvṛtaghaṭādivastupratipattaye pradīpa upādīyate, na tathā pradīpaprakāśanāya pradīpāntaram, api tu ghaṭādi prakāśayanneva ātmānamapi prakāśayati, tathā prakṛte 'pi svasaṃvedane
body.translated_text: 'Its own nature' — its own form — 'just as a lamp' — a light — 'illuminates,' 'makes visible.' For just as a lamp is employed for the cognition of objects such as pots concealed in darkness, but another lamp is not [needed] for illuminating the lamp, rather, while illuminating the pot and such, it also illuminates itself — so too in the case at hand, regarding self-cognition

body.text: veditavyam / na cāpi kvacidvirodho dṛṣṭa iti sarvatra yojanīyam / tasmāt pradīpavadavirodha eveti cet, yadyevaṃ manyase, tadā naivaṃ vaktavyam / kuta ityāha naivetyādi-
body.translated_text: it should be understood. And no contradiction is seen anywhere — this should be connected throughout. Therefore, just as a lamp [is free from] contradiction — if you think thus, then it should not be said so. Why? — he says 'not at all' and so forth —

body.text: naiva prakāśyate dīpo yasmānna tamasāvṛtaḥ // Bca_9.18 //
body.translated_text: A lamp is not at all illuminated, since it is not concealed by darkness. // Bca_9.18 //

body.text: naiva prakāśyate ghaṭādivannaiva uddayotyate dīpaḥ, yasmānna tamasāvṛtaḥ na andhakārapihitaḥ / vidyamānasyāvaraṇasya apanayanaṃ prakāśanam, tato yuktaṃ ghaṭādīnāṃ prakāśanam, teṣāṃ prāg vidyamānatvāt / naivaṃ pradīpasya, tasya prāgavidyamānatvāt / na ca avidyāmānasya prakāśanaṃ yuktam, asattvāt / tasmānnaiva prakāśyate dīpaḥ / iti visadṛśatvānna pradīpadṛṣṭāntāt sādhyasiddhiḥ //
body.translated_text: A lamp is 'not at all illuminated' — is not at all made visible like a pot and such. Why? Because it is 'not concealed by darkness' — not covered by darkness. 'Illumination' is the removal of an existing obstruction. Therefore, the illumination of pots and such is justified, since they previously exist [in darkness]. Not so for the lamp, since it does not previously exist [in darkness]. And the illumination of what does not exist is not justified, because of its non-existence. Therefore, a lamp is not at all illuminated. Thus, due to dissimilarity, the establishment of the thesis does not follow from the example of the lamp. //

body.text: syādetat- ātmabhāvamityādinā naitadabhidhīyate yadātmānaṃ ghaṭavat tamasāvṛtaṃ prakāśayati dīpaḥ, api tu tatsvabhāvaṃ prati paranirapekṣatāmātramasyābhidhīyate / etadevopadarśayannāha na hītyādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: by 'its own nature' and so forth, it is not being stated that a lamp illuminates itself like a pot concealed by darkness; rather, what is being expressed is merely its independence with respect to another for its own nature. Showing just this, he says 'for indeed' and so forth —

children.translated_text: Indeed, unlike a crystal, a blue thing does not depend on another for its blueness;
likewise, some things are seen to depend on another, and some not to depend [on another]. // Bca_9.19 //

body.text: hiriti yasmāt / yathā sphaṭikopalaḥ svayamanīlaḥ san, nīlatve nīlaguṇotpattinimittamanyamupādhiṃ nīlapatrādisaṃnidhimapekṣate, tathā svayameva yadvastu nīlam, tadapi na nīlatve 'nyamupādhimapekṣate / tathā tena prakāreṇa kiṃcid ghaṭādikaṃ parāpekṣaṃ pradīpādyapekṣaṃ prakāśaṃ dṛśyate, kiṃcit punaḥ pradīpādikamanapekṣaṃ ca svayaṃprakāśātmakaṃ dṛśyate upalabhyate / etāvanmātrameva vivakṣitam //
body.translated_text: 'Indeed' — because. Just as a crystal, itself being non-blue, depends on another condition — the proximity of a blue surface such as a blue cloth and such — for its blueness, for the arising of the quality of blue. But something that is itself blue does not depend on another condition for its blueness. 'Likewise' — in that manner — some thing such as a pot depends on another — depends on a lamp and such — for its manifestation; but some thing, such as a lamp and such, not depending [on another], is seen — is found — as of self-luminous nature. This much alone is intended. //

body.text: evaṃ vijñānavādinā upadarśite viśeṣe siddhāntavādī nīlameva tāvannīlatve paranirapekṣaṃ dṛṣṭāntatvenopadarśitaṃ pratiṣedhayannāha anīlatva ityādi-
body.translated_text: When the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> has presented this distinction, the proponent of the [Mādhyamika] system, refuting the example presented of blue itself being independent of another for its blueness, says 'non-blueness' and so forth —

children.translated_text: In non-blueness, that [thing] is not blue — as it were, what cause of blue is observed?

children.text: nīlameva hi ko nīlaṃ kuryādātmānamātmanā // Bca_9.20 //
children.translated_text: Who indeed could make what is [already] blue, blue by itself? // Bca_9.20 //

body.text: ayamapi na sadṛśo dṛṣṭāntaḥ, yato nīlamapi na nīlatve sphaṭikavannirapekṣam, tadbhāvaṃ prati svahetupratyayāpekṣatvāt / kadā punaridamanapekṣaṃ syāt? yadi tadanīlameva svahetorutpadyeta / punastadbhāve paranirapekṣaṃ svayameva nīlamātmānaṃ kuryāt / na caitadasti / yataḥ anīlatve nīlaguṇarahitatve sati / neti niṣedhayati / taditi nīlābhimataṃ vastu / nīlaṃ nīlaguṇayuktamātmānaṃ svarūpamātmanā svayameva na kuryāt, na kartuṃ śaknoti, pūrvavat svasmin kriyāvirodhāt / tasmānna nīlasyāpi parānapekṣatā nīlatvaṃ prati sphaṭikavat / tathā hi
body.translated_text: This example too is not apt, because even blue is not independent of another for its blueness, like a crystal, since it depends on its own causes and conditions for that state. When would this be independent? If it arose from its own cause as non-blue, and then, in that state, made itself blue independently of another, by itself. But this is not the case. Because 'in non-blueness' — in the state of being devoid of the quality of blue — he negates: 'that' — the entity held to be blue — would not make itself, its own form, blue — endowed with the quality of blue — by itself, is not able to do so, because of the contradiction of action upon itself, as before. Therefore, even blue is not independent of another with respect to its blueness, like a crystal. For indeed

body.text: sphaṭikopalo 'pi vastuto 'vasthitarūpa eva upādhisaṃnidhau na nīloparāgamanubhavati, api tu sarvasvopādānalakṣaṇāt / nīlopādhiviśeṣahakāriṇaśca pūrvasvarasanirodhāt anya eva nīlaguṇoparaktaḥ sphaṭikopala utpadyate iti siddhāntaḥ / tasmāt sādhāraṇamanayostadguṇaṃ prati hetupratyayādhīnatvam / iti prakṛte 'pi sādhye na kaścidviśeṣaḥ //
body.translated_text: even a crystal of a specific established form does not experience the coloring of blue in the proximity of a substrate; rather, from the causal condition of all its contributing factors, and due to the cessation of the preceding moment of its own continuity in the presence of a cooperating particular blue substrate, an entirely new crystal colored with the quality of blue arises — this is the established doctrine. Therefore, the dependence on causes and conditions for that quality is common to both [the crystal and the blue thing]. Thus there is no distinction even in the case at hand. //

body.text: nanu priyamidamanuṣṭhitaṃ priyeṇa yasmāt jaḍasvabhāvavyāvṛttātmatayā svahetupratyayāt utpattireva jñānasya prakāśāntaranirapekṣasya ātmaprakāśatā svasaṃvedanamucyate / etadeva tvayāpi nīlasvarūpaparāmarṣeṇa samarthitam / etāvanmātreṇa pradīpo 'pi dṛṣṭāntīkṛtaḥ / na punarasmābhiḥ karmakartṛkriyābhedena jñānasyātmaprakāśanamiṣyate / ekasya sataḥ karmādisvabhāvatrayasyāyogāt / tanna kriyādibhedena dūṣaṇe 'pi kiṃciddūṣitamasmākaṃ syāt, svahetujanitasyātmaprakāśasyānupaghātāt / iti nātmasaṃvedane pratipāditadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ / taduktam-
body.translated_text: But [the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> objects:] This has been well performed by a dear friend. For the arising from its own causes and conditions of cognition — which is distinguished from what is of inert nature — that itself, of what is independent of another illumination, is called 'self-illumination,' 'self-cognition.' This very [point] has been established by you too through your examination of the nature of blue. This much alone is the basis for the example of the lamp. We do not, however, maintain that cognition illuminates itself through a division of object, agent, and action — since a threefold nature is impossible for what is single. Therefore, even if the criticism is made through the division of action and such, nothing of ours is criticized, since the self-luminosity generated by its own cause remains unharmed. Thus there is no entailment of the faults demonstrated regarding self-cognition. As is said —

children.translated_text: 'Cognition arises as distinct from inert things;
this itself is the self-cognition — its non-inert nature.'
'Its self-cognition is not through the distinction of action and agent,
since a threefold nature is impossible for what is single and without parts.'

body.text: iti / [tattvasaṃgraha-2000-1]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 2000-2001]

body.text: atrocyate- kriyākārakabhedena vyavahāraprasiddhaṃ śabdārthamadhigamya dūṣaṇamuktam, svasaṃvedanaśabdasya tadarthābhidhāyakatvāt / yadi punardoṣabhayāllokaprasiddho 'pi śabdārthaḥ parityajyate, tadā lokata eva bādhā bhavato bhaviṣyati / itthamapi na paramārthataḥ svasaṃvedanasiddhiḥ / tathā hi hetupratyayopajanitasya pratibimbasyeva niḥsvabhāvatvamuktam / tathā ca sutarāṃ na svasaṃvedanaṃ jñānasya, tattvato nijasvabhāvābhāvāt / na ca svabhāvābhāve gaganotpalasya ātmasaṃvedanamucitam / na cāpi jaḍasvabhāvatā madhyamakavādinaṃ prati paramārthataḥ kasyacit siddhā, yena jaḍavyāvṛttamajaḍaṃ svasaṃvedanaṃ syat / tasmādanyāneva vastuvādinaḥ prati yuktametadvaktum / tato niḥsvabhāvatayā na kathaṃcidapi svasaṃvedanasiddhiḥ / etat punaḥ paścāt smṛtyupasthānopadarśanaprastāve [9.24] vistareṇopadarśayiṣyāmaḥ //
body.translated_text: Here it is said: having understood the conventional meaning of words — well-known through the distinction of action and agent — the refutation has been stated, since the word "self-awareness" denotes that very meaning. But if, out of fear of fault, even the conventionally well-known meaning of words is abandoned, then there will be invalidation for you from the world itself. Even thus, there is no ultimate establishment of self-awareness. For indeed, it has been stated that what is produced by causes and conditions, like a reflection, is devoid of intrinsic nature. And all the more so, there is no self-awareness of cognition, since it ultimately lacks its own intrinsic nature. And in the absence of intrinsic nature, self-awareness of a sky-lotus is not justified. Nor is the nature of insentience ultimately established for the <s>Mādhyamika</s>, such that self-awareness — as what is excluded from the insentient, i.e., the non-insentient — would [be established]. Therefore this is proper to say only against the Realists. Hence, through lack of intrinsic nature, the establishment of self-awareness is not possible in any way. We shall demonstrate this further below, in the context of showing the foundations of mindfulness [9.24], in detail.

body.text: sāṃprataṃ pradīpasya svayaṃprakāśatāmabhyupagamya buddheḥ svasaṃvedanamayuktamiti pratipādayannāha dīpa ityādi-
body.translated_text: Now, having accepted the self-illuminating nature of a lamp, he establishes that self-awareness of cognition is unjustified — with "a lamp" and so forth —

children.text: dīpaḥ prakāśata iti jñātvā jñānena kathyate /
children.translated_text: "A lamp illuminates" — this is known and spoken of by means of cognition;

children.text: buddhiḥ prakāśata iti jñātvedaṃ kena kathyate // Bca_9.22 //
children.translated_text: "cognition illuminates" — having known this, by what is it spoken of? // Bca_9.22 //

body.text: bhavatu vā pradīpasya prakāśātmatā, tathāpi na buddhisaṃvedanasādhanaṃ prati sadṛśo dṛṣṭānta iti samudāyārthaḥ / dīpaḥ prakāśata iti ābhāsate prakāśāntaranirapekṣaḥ svayameva, iti jñātvā pratītya jñānena buddhyā kathyate pratipādyate, pradīpasya jñānaviṣayatvāt / buddhirjñānaṃ
body.translated_text: Let the nature of being luminous belong to a lamp; still, it is not a valid example for proving the awareness of cognition — this is the combined meaning. That a lamp illuminates — that it shines, independent of any other light, by itself — this is known, is understood, and is spoken of, is explained, by means of cognition, because the lamp is an object of cognition. But cognition

body.text: prakāśate iti yaducyate, tat punaḥ kena jñānena jñātvā kathyate iti paraṃ pṛcchati / na cātra kiṃcid buddhipratipattinibandhanamastīti asaṃbhāvanāṃ prakāśayati / na tāvat pūrvajñānena tatpratipattiḥ, tatkālamanutpattestasyāsattvāt / nāpi paścātkālabhāvinā tadānīṃ kṣaṇikatayā grāhyasyātītatvāt / na ca tatsamānakālabhāvinā tena tasyānupakārāt / na ca anupakārakasya viṣayabhāvaḥ, nākāraṇaṃ viṣayaḥ iti vacanāt / nāpi svayam, tatraiva vipratipatteḥ / tat kathaṃ tatpratītiriti na vidmaḥ //
body.translated_text: illuminates — when this is said, by what cognition is it known and then spoken of? — thus he asks the opponent. And he reveals the impossibility that there is any basis here for the apprehension of cognition. It is not apprehended by a prior cognition, since that [prior cognition] has not arisen at that time, being non-existent. Nor by a subsequent cognition, since the object to be grasped, being momentary, has passed at that time. Nor by a cognition simultaneous with it, since that [simultaneous cognition] is of no benefit to it. And what is of no benefit does not become an object, as stated: "what is not a cause is not an object." Nor by itself, since there is disagreement about that very point. Thus, how there could be apprehension of it — we do not know.

body.text: itthaṃ sarvathā buddherapratipattau tatsaṃvedanamatīva ayuktamityāha prakāśā vetyādi-
body.translated_text: Since thus in every way there is non-apprehension of cognition, he says that its awareness is extremely unjustified — with "whether luminous" and so forth —

children.text: prakāśā vāprakāśā vā yadā dṛṣṭā na kenacit /
children.translated_text: Whether luminous or non-luminous — since it is seen by no one,
even when spoken of, it is futile, like the grace of a barren woman's daughter. // Bca_9.23 //

body.text: prakāśā vā prakāśātmikā dīpavat / aprakāśā vā aprakāśātmikā ghaṭādivat / parasparasamuccaye vāśabdadvayam / buddhiḥ yadā dṛṣṭā na kenacit, na pratipannā kenacit pratipantrā svayaṃrūpeṇa vā / yadeti padaṃ tadetyākarṣati / tadā vandhyāyā aprasavadharmiṇyāḥ striyā duhitā putrī, tasyā līlā vilāso lalitaṃ tadvat / kathyamānāpi ākhyāyamānāpi sā mudhā / seti buddhiḥ / mudheti niṣphalā / vandhyāduhituravidyamānatayā pratipannatvāt tallīlā sutarāmapratipannetyabhiprāyaḥ / athavā / anutpannāniruddhasvabhāvatayā vandhyāduhitṛsthānīyā buddhiḥ / apratītatatsvabhāvatayā tallīlāvat svasaṃvittiḥ / tadapratīteḥ tasyā api apratītiriti kathyamānāpi yuktirahitena vacanamātreṇa sā svasaṃvittirmudhāḥ, anupādeyatvānniṣprayojanā //
body.translated_text: "Luminous" — of a luminous nature, like a lamp. Or "non-luminous" — of a non-luminous nature, like a pot and such. The two uses of "or" indicate mutual combination. Cognition, "since it is seen by no one" — apprehended by no apprehender, whether by its own form or otherwise. The word "since" draws in "then." Then — like the grace, the playfulness, the charm, of the "daughter" of a "barren woman," one incapable of giving birth — even when spoken of, when being told about, "it" — cognition — is "futile" — fruitless. The intent is: since the barren woman's daughter is known to be non-existent, her grace is all the more unapprehended. Alternatively: cognition, being of an un-arisen and un-ceased nature, occupies the position of the barren woman's daughter. Self-awareness, like her grace, [is futile] because its nature is not apprehended — because of the non-apprehension of that [cognition], there is non-apprehension of this [self-awareness] too. Thus, even when spoken of — through mere words devoid of reasoning — that self-awareness is futile, useless because it cannot be adopted.

body.text: syādevam- yuktiśūnyaṃ vacanamātrametat / yataḥ iyamatra yuktirastītyāha yadi nāstītyādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: this is merely words devoid of reasoning. For there is this reasoning here — he says with "if there is no" and so forth —

body.text: yadi nāsti svasaṃvittirvijñānaṃ smaryate katham /
body.translated_text: If there is no self-awareness, how is consciousness remembered?

body.text: yadi svasaṃvedanaṃ vijñānasya nāsti na vidyate, tadā vijñānaṃ smaryate katham? vijñānasya svasaṃvedanābhāvāduttarakālaṃ smaraṇaṃ na syāt / na hi ananubhūtasmaraṇaṃ yuktam, atiprasaṅgāt / tasmādanubhavaphalasya smaraṇasya uttarakālaṃ darśanāt jñānasaṃvedanamastītyanumīyate iti / naitat sādhanaṃ sādhīyaḥ / yato yadi svasaṃvedanakāryatayā smaraṇaṃ niścitaṃ bhavet, bhaved vahveryathā dhūmaḥ svasaṃvedanasya kāraṇaṃ smṛtiḥ / na ca asiddhe svasaṃvedane pramāṇataḥ, smaraṇasya tatkāryatāgrahaṇamasti / sarvathā ubhayapratipattināntarīyakatvāt kāryakāraṇabhāvapratipatteḥ / na ca cakṣurāderiva vijñānam, adarśane 'pi smaraṇaṃ tatkāryaṃ setsyati, cakṣuṣo hi vyatireke nīlādijñānābhāvato [vyatirekadvāreṇa] tatkāryamanumīyate / smṛtistu jñānasaṃvedanamantareṇāpi bhavatīti pratipādayiṣyāmaḥ, iti svasaṃvedanakāryatāniścayamantareṇa smaraṇasya
body.translated_text: If there is no self-awareness of consciousness — if it does not exist — then how is consciousness remembered? Due to the absence of self-awareness of consciousness, there would be no subsequent recollection. For the recollection of what has not been experienced is not justified, since it would lead to absurd consequences. Therefore, from seeing that recollection — which is the result of experience — occurs subsequently, it is inferred that there is awareness of cognition — thus [argues the opponent]. This proof is not strong. For if recollection were determined to be an effect of self-awareness — as smoke is of fire — then self-awareness would be [proven as] the cause of recollection. But since self-awareness is not established by any valid cognition, there is no ascertainment of recollection's being its effect. Because the ascertainment of causal relation necessarily depends on the ascertainment of both [terms]. Nor is consciousness like the eye and such — [in the case of] the eye, even without [direct] seeing, recollection as its effect will be established, for through the absence of blue-cognition and such in the absence of the eye [i.e., through the method of negative correlation], its being an effect is inferred. But we shall demonstrate that memory arises even without the awareness of cognition — hence, without the determination that [memory] is an effect of self-awareness, since memory [can exist]

body.text: tadvinābhāvānna saṃvedanasiddhiḥ / ataḥ smaraṇamapi jñānatvāt kathaṃ siddhamiti vaktavyam / na ca svayamasiddhaṃ liṅgaṃ jñāpakamanyasya / na ca smaraṇaṃ svasaṃvedanasya pratyakṣatayā grāhakam, tasya tasmādanyatvāt / na ca jñānasya jñānāntaraviṣayatvam, bahirarthavat saṃbandhāsiddhayādidoṣaprasaṅgāt / anyatvāviśeṣāt saṃtānāntarabhāvināpi smaraṇena tasya grahaṇaṃ syāt / atha tena pūrvamananubhūtatvānna smaryata iti cet, ekasaṃtatipatitenāpi na pūrvamanubhūtamiti samānaḥ prasaṅgaḥ //
body.translated_text: without it, there is no establishment of awareness. Therefore, since recollection too is a cognition, it must be asked how it is established. And what is itself unestablished as a sign cannot be an indicator of something else. Nor does recollection grasp self-awareness through direct perception, since it is different from it. Nor is one cognition the object of another cognition, since the fault of the unestablished relation and such would follow, just as with external objects. Because there is no difference in their otherness, recollection belonging to another mental continuum should also grasp it. If [you say] that is not remembered because it was not previously experienced by that [other continuum], the same consequence applies to [recollection] belonging to the same continuum, since it too has not been previously experienced [by it].

body.text: kāryakāraṇabhāvo 'pi na tasya niyāmako yujyate, kāryakāraṇabhāvasyaiva paramārthato 'bhāvāt, satyapi tasmin sarvajñānānāṃ svapratipattiniṣṭhatayā tadgahaṇasyāśakyatvāt / yathāvyavahāramabhyupagame kālpanikatvam, kālpanikatve ca sarvavyavahārāṇāṃ kalpanānirmitatvāt sāṃvṛtatvamiti sādhitaṃ naḥ sādhyam / iti na smṛteḥ svasaṃvedanasiddhiḥ //
body.translated_text: The causal relation too cannot be its determiner, since the causal relation itself is ultimately non-existent; and even if it exists, since the grasping of it is impossible, all cognitions being terminated in their own apprehension [at the moment of arising]. If conventional usage is accepted, it is constructed; and if constructed, all conventions, being fabricated by conceptualization, are conventional — thus our thesis is established. Hence there is no establishment of self-awareness from memory.

body.text: bhavato 'pi kathaṃ tarhi svasaṃvedanābhāve smṛtirityāha anyānubhūta ityādi-
body.translated_text: How then for you too, in the absence of self-awareness, is there memory? — he says with "what is experienced as other" and so forth —

body.text: anyānubhūte saṃbandhāt smṛtirākhuviṣaṃ yathā // Bca_9.24 //
body.translated_text: Through connection with what was experienced as other, memory [arises] — like rat-poison. // Bca_9.24 //

body.text: jñānādanyasmin grāhye vastuni viṣaye 'nubhūte sati jñāne smṛtiḥ smaraṇamupajāyate / nanu anyasminnanubhūte anyatra smaraṇe atiprasaṅgaḥ syādityāha- saṃbandhāditi / viṣaye 'nubhūte tadvijñānasmaraṇaṃ saṃbandhādbhavati / vijñānaṃ hi tadgāhakatayā tatsaṃbaddham, ato vijñānaṃ smaryate, nānyat / satyapi saṃbandhe anyasminnanubhūte anyasya smaraṇe viplutaṃ smaraṇaṃ syāditi cenna, pūrvamanubhūto viṣayaḥ uttarakālamanusmaryamāṇaḥ sa evānubhavaviśiṣṭo 'nusmaryate / tadviśiṣṭasya tasya grahaṇāt / jñānameva ca viṣayānubhavo nānya iti viṣayānubhavasmaraṇāttatsaṃbaddhatayā jñāne smaraṇamabhidhīyate, na tu viṣayarahitaṃ jñānamapi kevalamanusmaryate ityadoṣaḥ //
body.translated_text: When something other than cognition — a graspable object, a sense-object — has been experienced, memory, recollection, arises regarding the cognition. Now, if from something other being experienced, there were recollection of [yet] another [thing], there would be an absurd consequence — to this he says: "through connection." When an object has been experienced, the recollection of that cognition arises through connection. For cognition is connected with that [object] by virtue of being its grasper; therefore cognition is remembered, not something else. If [you say] that even given the connection, when something other has been experienced, the recollection of something else would be a distorted recollection — no, [because] the object that was previously experienced, when subsequently recollected, is recollected as qualified by that very experience. Because what is qualified by that is grasped. And cognition itself is the experience of the object, not anything else — hence from the recollection of the object-experience, through its connection, recollection is said to apply to the cognition; but cognition devoid of an object is not remembered in isolation — hence there is no fault.

body.text: nanu kathamiva jñānasaṃvedanāhitasmṛtivāsanābījamantareṇa smṛtiruttarakālaṃ syādityāhaākhuviṣaṃ yatheti / ākhuviṣaṃ mūṣikaviṣaṃ yathā saṃbandhāt kālāntareṇa jāyate, tathā smṛtirapītyarthaḥ / tathā hi mūṣikaviṣamekasmin kṣaṇe śarīrasaṃkrāntaṃ punaḥ kālāntareṇa meghastanitamadhigamya vināpi svasaṃvedanāhitasmṛtivāsanābījamidaṃpratyayatāmātrāyatavṛttitvāt anyasmin kṣaṇe vikṛtimupayāti, tathā prakṛte 'pi na duṣyatīti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: Now, how could memory arise subsequently without a seed of memory-impression deposited by the awareness of cognition? — he says: "like rat-poison." Rat-poison, the venom of a mouse, just as it arises at a later time through connection [with thunder] — so too memory: this is the meaning. For rat-poison, having entered the body at one moment, then at a later time, upon hearing thunder, even without a seed of memory-impression deposited by self-awareness — simply through its function depending on mere "this-conditionality" — undergoes transformation at another moment. Likewise, in the present case too, there is no fault — this is the meaning.

body.text: punarapi vijñānavādī jñānasaṃvedanasiddhaye prakārāntaramupadarśayitumāha pratyayāntareti-
body.translated_text: Once again, the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> attempts to show another way of establishing the awareness of cognition — with "through another condition" and so forth —

body.text: pratyayāntarayuktasya darśanātsvaṃ prakāśate /
body.translated_text: Through being endowed with another condition, [its own nature] is illuminated from perception.

body.text:
pratyayāntaraṃ kāraṇāntaram [kālāntaram
?] / īkṣaṇikādividyā paracittādijñānābhijñā ca tābhyāṃ yuktasya tatsāmagrīsaṃbaddhasya cittasya darśanāt pratibhāsanāt vijñānasya khaṃ prakāśate svarūpaṃ pratibhāsate / saṃvedanamastīti yāvat / yadi hi tat sarvadā parokṣarūpaṃ kathaṃ kadācit sāmagrīviśeṣādupalabhyeta, tato yathā sāmagrīviśeṣāt paracittamupalabhyate, tathā samanantarālambanādipratyayāt svacittamapyupalabhyate iti bhāvaḥ / etadapi na jñānasaṃvedanasāmarthyamityāha siddhāñjanetyādi-
body.translated_text: "Another condition" — another cause [or: another time]. Clairvoyance such as that of magicians and the supernormal knowledge of others' minds — through being endowed with these, i.e., connected with that particular set of conditions, from the perception — the appearing — of [another's] mind, one's own nature of consciousness is illuminated, appears. That is to say, awareness exists. For if it were always hidden, how could it ever be apprehended through a particular set of conditions? Therefore, just as another's mind is apprehended through a particular set of conditions, so too one's own mind is apprehended through conditions such as the immediately preceding, the object-condition, and such — this is the meaning. Even this does not [prove] the capacity of cognition's awareness — he says with "magical ointment" and so forth —

body.text: siddhāñjanavidherdṛṣṭo ghaṭo naivāñjanaṃ bhavet // Bca_9.25 //
body.translated_text: A pot seen through the application of magical ointment would not itself become the ointment. // Bca_9.25 //

body.text: siddhaṃ ca tadañjanaṃ ca, siddhasya vā añjanam, tasya vidhiḥ vidhānaṃ prayogaḥ, tasmād dṛṣṭaḥ pratītaḥ ghaṭo nidhānādi vā naiva añjanaṃ bhavati / na ca ghaṭādirañjanameva syāt / na yad yasmātpratīyate tadeva tadbhavati / evamīkṣaṇikādividyāsahakāriṇā jñānena paracittaṃ ca ghaṭādivad dṛṣṭamiti naitāvatā tatsaṃvedanaṃ siddhaṃ syāt / tasmānnaitadapi sādhyopayogi sādhanam / nanu yadi jñānamaviditasvarūpaṃ syāt, arthasyāpi pratītirna syāt / avyaktavyaktikatvād jñānasya, na hi arthasya vyaktiḥ / tadapratītau kathamarthasya pratītiḥ? tathā hi svasaṃvedanasya pratiṣedhāt, anyena anyasya grahaṇāyogācca, tadgahaṇābhyupagame ca uttarottarasya apratītasya pratītaye jñānāntarānusaraṇena anavasthāprasaṅgācca na kathaṃcidapi arthasya pratītiriti / tena yaduktam "anyānubhūte" ityādi, tadasaṃgatam, arthasyānubhavābhāvāt //
body.translated_text: "Magical" and "ointment" [form a compound]; or, the ointment of the adept — its "application," method, procedure — "seen" from that, i.e., apprehended — a pot, or a hidden treasure, would not itself become the ointment. Nor would the pot and such simply be the ointment. It is not the case that whatever is apprehended through something thereby becomes that thing. Thus, through cognition assisted by clairvoyance and such, another's mind is seen like a pot — but this much does not establish its [self-]awareness. Therefore, this too is not a proof useful for the thesis. Now, if cognition were of unknown nature, the apprehension of objects too would not occur. Because cognition is of un-manifest manifestation — indeed, objects are not manifested [independently]. In its non-apprehension, how could there be apprehension of objects? For from the denial of self-awareness, and from the impossibility of another grasping another, and if grasping of it [by yet another] is accepted, then from the absurd consequence of infinite regress in pursuing further cognitions to apprehend the unapprehended next [cognition] — in no way whatsoever is there apprehension of objects. Therefore, what was stated — "through what was experienced as other" and so forth — that is incoherent, since there is no experience of objects.

body.text: sarvaścāyaṃ dṛṣṭādivyavahāro loke na syādityāha yathā dṛṣṭamityādi / yaducyate dṛṣṭādivyavahāro na syāditi, sa kiṃ paramārthato na syāt, saṃvṛtyā vā? tatra yadi paramārthato na syādityucyate, tadā priyamidamasmākam / na hi sāṃvṛtasya paramārthacintāyāmavatāro 'sti / atha lokaprasiddhiḥ, tadā-
body.translated_text: And all this worldly discourse of "seeing" and such would not exist — he says with "as seen" and so forth. When it is said that the discourse of "seeing" and such would not exist, is it that it would not exist ultimately, or conventionally? If it is said that it would not exist ultimately, then this is agreeable to us. For what is conventional has no entry into the inquiry of the ultimate. But if [it concerns] worldly convention, then —

body.text: yathā dṛṣṭaṃ śrutaṃ jñātaṃ naiveha pratiṣidhyate /
body.translated_text: What is seen, heard, and known — that is not denied here.

body.text: iti / yathā dṛṣṭamiti cakṣurādivijñānena pratyakṣeṇa pratipannam / śrutamiti parapudgalādāgamācca / jñātamiti trirūpaliṅgajādanumānānniścitam / tadetadiha sarvaṃ vyavahāramāśritya naiva pratiṣidhyate, naiva vāryate / yad yathā lokataḥ pratīyate, tat tathaiva avicāritasvarūpamabhyupagamyate lokaprasiddhitaḥ, na tu punaḥ paramārthataḥ / tena jñānasaṃvedanābhāvādarthānadhigamādayo 'pi doṣāḥ paramārthapakṣavādina iha nāvataranti / yadi tat tathaivābhyupagamyate, kiṃ nāma tarhi pratiṣidhyate ityāha satyata ityādi-
body.translated_text: Thus. 'As seen' — understood through direct perception by visual and other cognitions. 'As heard' — from scripture, from the testimony of other persons. 'As known' — ascertained through inference from a logical mark possessing the three characteristics. All this here is not denied, is not rejected, insofar as it relies upon conventional discourse. Whatever is cognized from the worldly [standpoint] in whatever way — that is accepted just so, its intrinsic nature being unexamined, on the basis of worldly convention; but not, however, in the ultimate sense. Therefore, faults such as the absence of self-cognizing awareness, the non-apprehension of objects, and so forth do not apply to the proponent of the ultimate thesis here. If that is accepted just as it is, then what is it that is denied? He says 'in truth' and so forth —

body.text: satyataḥ kalpanā tvatra duḥkhaheturnivāryate // Bca_9.26 //
body.translated_text: But conceptualization in truth — the cause of suffering — is what is prevented here. // <s>Bca</s> 9.26 //

body.text: satyataḥ paramārthataḥ / kalpanā āropaḥ / tuśabdaḥ punararthe / sā punaratra vicāre siddhānte vā / nivāryate pratiṣidhyate / kutaḥ? duḥkhaheturiti / hetupadametat / duḥkhasya hetuḥ kāraṇaṃ yasmāt, tasmādityarthaḥ / upādānaskandhānāṃ sadasadādikalpanāhitapravṛttihetuta eva ca saṃsāraḥ / saṃsāraśca duḥkhasvabhāvaḥ /
body.translated_text: 'In truth' — in the ultimate sense. 'Conceptualization' — superimposition. The word 'tu' (but) is in the sense of 'again.' That again, 'here' — in this investigation or in this system — 'is prevented,' is denied. Why? 'Because it is the cause of suffering.' This is the causal clause. Because it is the cause, the reason for suffering — therefore: this is the meaning. For <s>saṃsāra</s> exists precisely because conceptualization — the superimposition of real existence, non-existence, and such upon the aggregates of clinging — is the cause that sets it in motion. And <s>saṃsāra</s> is of the nature of suffering.

body.text:
duḥkhaṃ samudayo loko dṛṣṭisthānaṃ bhavaśca te /
[abhi. kośa-1.8]
body.translated_text: 'Suffering, origination, the world, the basis of views, and becoming — all these are yours [O aggregates].'

body.text: iti vacanāt / iti satyataḥ kalpanā duḥkhaheturbhavati / tasmādasatsamāropakalpanābhiniveśapratiṣedhamātramatrābhipretam, na tu vāstavaṃ kiṃcit pratiṣidhyate iti / tadevaṃ svasaṃvedanaṃ jñānasya na kathaṃcidacidapi yujyate / taduktam-
body.translated_text: — from this statement. [<s>Abhidharmakośa</s> 1.8] Thus, conceptualization in truth is a cause of suffering. Therefore, what is intended here is solely the prevention of the clinging to the superimposition of what does not exist in reality — nothing that actually exists is denied. Thus, self-cognizing awareness of cognition is in no way whatsoever justified. As stated —

children.translated_text: 'Mind with the aspect of knower and known was not seen by the <s>Tathāgatas</s>;

children.text: yatra boddhā ca bodhyaṃ ca tatra bodhirna vidyate //
children.translated_text: where there is a knower and something to be known, there awakening does not exist.'

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: yattu kvacid bhagavatā cittamātratāstitvamuktam, tat skandhāyatanādivanneyārthatayeti kathayiṣyate //
body.translated_text: As for the Blessed One's occasional statements about the existence of mere-mind — that, like [the teaching of] aggregates, sense-bases, and such, is of provisional meaning: this will be explained.

body.text: idānīṃ prāsaṅgikaṃ parisamāpya prakṛte yojayannāha cittādanyetyādi-
body.translated_text: Now, having completed the consequentialist [refutation], connecting with the main topic, he says 'other than mind' and so forth —

children.translated_text: If illusion is not other than mind, it is not to be conceived as non-other either.

children.text: vastu cetsā kathaṃ nānyānanyā cennāsti vastutaḥ // Bca_9.27 //
children.translated_text: If it is a real thing, how is it not other? And if non-other, it does not exist as a real thing. // <s>Bca</s> 9.27 //

body.text: tarhi cittādanyā māyā syāt, ananyā vā syāt, ubhayasvabhāvā vā, anubhayasvabhāvā vā, iti catvāro vikalpāḥ / tatra na tāvat prathamapakṣaḥ, cittādanyābhyupagame 'pi cittamātraṃ jagadicchataḥ siddhāntavirodhaḥ syāt / dvitīyapakṣe tu "yadā māyaiva te nāsti" [9.6] ityādinā pratipādita eva doṣaḥ / tṛtīyastu prakāro na saṃgacchate, parasparaviruddhayorekatrābhāvāt / atha caturthī kalpanā, sāpi na saṃgacchate / tāmupādāyocyatecittādanyā na māyā ityanyatvapratiṣedhaḥ / ananyā tarhi, nāpyananyeti tattvasyāpi pratiṣedhaḥ, iti ubhayapakṣapātaścedyadi kalpyate vyavasthāpyate, so 'pi na yuktaḥ, anyonyaparihāravatorekapratiṣedhasya aparavidhināntarīyakatvāt tayorekatrābhāvāt caturthī kalpanā sāpi na saṃghaṭate // api ca / vastu cediti / yadi sā māyā vastusatī kathaṃ nānyā cittādvayatiriktā na bhavati? atha ananyā cet, yadi cittameva māyā, tadā nāsti vastutaḥ, na vidyate paramārthataḥ, tasyāstatsvabhāvatvāt cittameva kevalam ityetat tadevāyātam / yaduktam-
body.translated_text: Then, illusion would either be other than mind, or non-other, or of both natures, or of neither nature — these are the four alternatives. Of these, the first position does not hold, because even if otherness from mind is accepted, there would be contradiction with one's own system for one who maintains that the world is mere mind. In the second position, the very fault established by 'when illusion itself does not exist for you' [9.6] and so forth has already been demonstrated. The third alternative does not work either, since things that are mutually contradictory cannot coexist in one [entity]. And the fourth conception — that too does not work. Taking that up, he says: 'illusion is not other than mind' — this is the denial of otherness. 'Nor non-other' — the denial of that [identity] as well. If it is conceived — if it is established — that there is a lapse into both positions, that too is not justified, since where two [properties] are mutually exclusive, the denial of one necessarily entails the other, and because the two cannot coexist, the fourth conception does not work either. Moreover: 'if it is a real thing' — if that illusion is a real existent thing, how is it not other than mind, not distinct from it? But if non-other — if illusion is just mind itself — then it does not exist as a real thing, it does not exist in the ultimate sense, since it has the nature of that [mind] — mere mind alone: this is precisely what has been arrived at. As stated —

children.text: yadā māyaiva te nāsti tadā kimupalabhyate /
children.translated_text: 'When illusion itself does not exist for you, what then is apprehended?'
Thus.

body.text: adhunā prakṛtaṃ prasādhya upasaṃharannāha asatyapītyādi-
body.translated_text: Now, having established the main point, concluding it, he says 'even though unreal' and so forth —

body.text: asatyapi yathā māyā dṛśyā draṣṭṛ tathā manaḥ /
body.translated_text: Just as illusion, though unreal, is seen — so too the mind, [though unreal,] is a seer.

body.text: asatī upalabhyamānā māyā hastyādivadvastuto 'satsvabhāvā / tādṛśyapi dṛśyā darśanaviṣayā yathā māyā, draṣṭu tathā manaḥ / saiva asatī māyā dṛśyā dṛṣṭāntaḥ, tathā manaḥ paramārthato 'satsvabhāvamapi darśanasamarthaṃ bhaviṣyati / tena "yadā na bhrāntirapyasti" [9.15] ityādi yaduktaṃ pareṇa tat prasādhya upasaṃhāreṇa darśitam / punarapi prakārāntareṇa paramārthasadvijñānasādhanāya paropakramamabhisaṃdhāya āha vastvāśrayaścetyādi-
body.translated_text: Illusion — being apprehended, yet in reality of non-existent intrinsic nature, like elephants and such — even being such, is 'seen,' is an object of seeing. Just as illusion, though unreal, is seen — this is the example — so too the mind. That very unreal illusion is seen — this is the analogy. So too, the mind, though of non-existent intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense, will be capable of seeing. By this, what was stated by the opponent — 'when even confusion does not exist' [9.15] and so forth — has been established and shown by way of conclusion. Once again, with a view to a further attempt by the opponent to prove that consciousness is ultimately real, through a different approach, he says 'if <s>saṃsāra</s> depends on a real substance' and so forth —

body.text: vastvāśrayaścetsaṃsāraḥ so 'nyathākāśavadbhavet // Bca_9.28 //
body.translated_text: If <s>saṃsāra</s> depends on a real substance, it would otherwise be like space. // <s>Bca</s> 9.28 //

body.text: tathāhi- saṃkleśo vyavadānaṃ ca heyopādeyatayā dvayamidaṃ yathāvat pratipattavyam / tatra rāgādimalāvṛtaṃ cittaṃ saṃkliṣṭamityucyate / te ca abhūtasamāropabalotpannatvādāgantukāścittāśritāḥ pravartante / tatprabhūtakarmajanmaparaṃparopanibandhaḥ saṃsāraḥ prajāyate / tadeva cittaṃ paramārthataḥ prakṛtiprabhāsvaramanāgantukamabhūtaparikalpasamutthagrāhyagrāhakādidvayasamāropābhiniveśavāsanāśūnyamadvayasvabhāvamāgantukadoṣavinirmuktamāśrayaparāvṛttervyavadānamityucyate / tadevaṃ
body.translated_text: For affliction and purification — these two, as what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted — must be properly understood. There, the mind, covered by the stains of desire and such, is called 'afflicted.' And those [stains], being produced by the force of false superimposition, are adventitious and operate as dependent on the mind. <s>Saṃsāra</s> arises as bound by the succession of <s>karma</s> and birth originating from that [affliction]. That very mind, in the ultimate sense, being luminous by nature, non-adventitious, empty of the habitual tendencies of clinging to the superimposition of the duality of grasped and grasper and such — which are produced by false conceptualization — of non-dual nature, freed from adventitious faults: [this] is called purification, through the transformation of the basis. Thus

body.text: saṃkleśavyavadānayorvastusamudbhūtacittamantareṇa vyavasthāpanaṃ na ghaṭate iti manyante, saṃsāranirvāṇayościttadharmatvāt / cittameva saṃkliśyate, cittameva vyavadāyate iti vacanāt / tadeva paramataṃ nirūpayati-vastveva vastusadbhūtacittameva āśrayaḥ asyeti vastvāśrayaḥ / cet yadi saṃsāro vyavasthāpyate, tadā saṃsāro 'nyathā bhavet, cittādanyaḥ syāt, vastuno 'nyatve avastu syāt, cittasyaiva ca vastutvāt / kathamiva? ākāśavat gaganamiva / ya eṣa cittāśrayaḥ saṃsāro 'bhidhīyate, sa kiṃ vastu avastu vā? vastvapi cittaṃ tadanyadvā? tatra yadi vastu cittameva, tadā na cittādanyaḥ saṃsārastadāśryaḥ, cittameva saḥ / cittaṃ ca prakṛtiprabhāsvaratayā vyavadānasvabhāvatvānna praheyam / atha cittādanyaḥ, tadā cittavyatiriktasya anyasyābhyupagamāt siddhāntakṣatiḥ / atha avastu, tadā saṃsāro nāma na kiṃcidasti, kharaviṣāṇavat / ata evāha ākāśavat iti / yathā ākāśaṃ prajñaptisanmātramasat, na kvacidarthakriyāyāṃ samartham, tathā saṃsāro bhavataḥ syāt / athavā / ākāśavaditi niḥsvabhāvatvādasmatsiddhāntānupraveśaḥ //
body.translated_text: they [the Vijñānavādins] think that without a real, substantial mind, the establishment of both affliction and purification is not possible, since <s>saṃsāra</s> and <s>nirvāṇa</s> are properties of mind. Because of the statement: 'mind itself is afflicted; mind itself is purified.' He examines that very thesis of the opponent: 'substance' — the really existent mind itself — is the 'basis' (<s>āśraya</s>) — thus it has substance as its basis. If <s>saṃsāra</s> is established [in this way], then <s>saṃsāra</s> would be 'otherwise' — other than mind; being other than the substance [mind], it would be a non-thing, since mind alone is the substance. In what manner? 'Like space' — like the sky. This <s>saṃsāra</s> that is called dependent on mind — is it a substance or a non-substance? Is the substance mind itself or something other? Among these, if the substance is mind itself, then <s>saṃsāra</s>, depending on it, is not other than mind — it is mind itself. And mind, being luminous by nature, being of the nature of purification, is not to be abandoned. But if other than mind, then since something other than mind is being accepted, there is a loss of the system. But if it is a non-substance, then <s>saṃsāra</s> is nothing at all, like a hare's horn. This is why he says 'like space.' Just as space is a mere designation, unreal, nowhere capable of effective action — so would <s>saṃsāra</s> be for you. Or alternatively: 'like space' — because of being devoid of intrinsic nature, this amounts to entering our own system.

body.text: syādetat- yadi nāma avastu, tathāpi vastusadbhūtacittasamāśritatvāt tasya arthakriyāsāmarthyaṃ bhaviṣyatītyāha vastvāśrayeṇetyādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: even if it is a non-substance, still, because it depends on the really existent mind, it will have the capacity for effective action. To this he says 'through a real substance as basis' and so forth —

body.text: vastvāśrayeṇābhāvasya kriyāvattvaṃ kathaṃ bhavet /
body.translated_text: How can a non-existent thing have activity through having a real substance as its basis?

body.text: na asadrūpasya kaścidāśrayo bhavitumarhati, āśrayāśrayibhāvasya kāryakāraṇarūpatvāt / na ca abhāvaḥ kasyacit kāryam, anirvartyaviśeṣatvāt / bhavatu nāma, tathāpi vastvāśrayeṇa vastusadbhūtacittasamāśrayeṇa abhāvasya asadātmakasya kriyāvattvam, arthakriyākāritvaṃ kathaṃ bhavet? na kadācidapi yujyate ityarthaḥ / anyathā tasya bhāvasvabhāvatā syāt / śaktirhi bhāvalakṣaṇam / sarvaśaktiviraho 'bhāvalakṣaṇamiti vacanāt / kimidānīmiti vicāryamāṇamupasthitaṃ bhavata ityāha asatsahāyamityādi-
body.translated_text: No basis can belong to something of unreal nature, since the relation of basis and what depends on it is of the form of cause and effect. Nor is a non-existent thing the effect of anything, since it has no determinable specific character. Granted, even so — how can a non-existent thing, of non-real nature, have activity — the capacity for effective action — through having a real substance as its basis, through depending on a really existent mind? It is never justified — this is the meaning. Otherwise it would have the nature of a real entity, since capacity is the defining mark of a real entity — because of the statement: 'total absence of capacity is the defining mark of a non-entity.' What then has arrived as the result of your analysis? He says 'with an unreal companion' and so forth —

body.text: asatsahāyamekaṃ hi cittamāpadyate tava // Bca_9.29 //
body.translated_text: For, on your view, mind arrives as having only an unreal companion. // <s>Bca</s> 9.29 //

body.text: asannevaḥ abhāvaḥ sahāyo 'syeti asatsahāyam / hiravadhāraṇe / ekamadvitīyameva cittamāpadyate tava cittaikaparamārthavādinaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Unreal' — non-existent, a non-entity — is its companion: thus 'with an unreal companion.' The particle 'hi' is for emphasis. Mind alone, without a second, arrives — for you who maintain that mind alone is ultimately real.

body.text: nanu uktameva- grāhyagrāhakādyākāravinirmuktamadvayalakṣaṇaṃ cittam, iti cittaikatāpratipādane na kiṃcidaniṣṭamasmākam / tadayuktam / saṃkleśasyāpi praheyatayā vastutvamuktam / tat kathaṃ cittamevaikaṃ vastu? astu nāma, tathāpi na bādhakānmuktirityāha grāhyamuktamityādi-
body.translated_text: But we have already said: mind is free from the aspects of grasped and grasper and such, of non-dual character — thus in establishing mind-only there is nothing undesired for us. That is not justified. Since affliction too has been said to be a real thing because it is to be abandoned — how then is mind alone the [sole] real thing? Granted, let it be so; even then, there is no escape from the objection — he says 'when mind is freed from the grasped' and so forth —

body.text: grāhyamuktaṃ yadā cittaṃ tadā sarve tathāgatāḥ /
body.translated_text: When mind is freed from the grasped, then all [beings] are <s>Tathāgatas</s>.

body.text: grāhyamityupalakṣaṇam / grāhakādimuktamapi veditavyam / athavā grāhyādhīnaṃ grāhakatvamiti tadabhāvād grāhakābhāvaḥ / grāhakābhāve ca tadupakalpitasya abhilāpyasyābhāvāt abhilāpasyābhāva ityupadarśayituṃ grāhyamuktamityuktam / grāhyādyākāraviviktamadvayasvabhāvaṃ yadā sarvasya jagataścittam, tadā tasya cittasya sarvasattvasaṃtānāntargatatvāt sarvasaṃsāriṇaḥ sattvāḥ
body.translated_text: 'Grasped' is indicative; it should be understood as freed from the grasper and such as well. Or alternatively, since the grasper is dependent on the grasped, in the absence of the grasped there is no grasper. And in the absence of the grasper, since the expressible that is constructed upon it is absent, expression too is absent — to show this, he said 'freed from the grasped.' When the mind of the entire world is free from aspects such as the grasped, of non-dual nature — then, since that mind is present in the continua of all beings, all <s>saṃsāric</s> beings

body.text: tathāgatā buddhā bhagavantaḥ prāpnuvanti / na kaścit pṛthagjanaḥ syāt / tataśca saṃkleśaprahāṇāryamārgabhāvanāvaiyarthyaprasaṅgaḥ / na caivam / tasmāt satyapi grāhyagrāhakavaidhurye bhāvābhiniveśasya tadavasthatvānna sarvathā saṃkleśaprahāṇamityabhisaṃdhāyāha evaṃ cetyādi-
body.translated_text: would attain [the status of] <s>Tathāgatas</s>, <s>Buddhas</s>, Blessed Ones. No one would be an ordinary person. And consequently, there would be the absurd consequence of the futility of abandoning affliction and cultivating the noble path. But this is not so. Therefore, even though there is separation from grasped and grasper, since clinging to things remains in its [same] state, there is no complete abandonment of affliction in every respect — with this intent he says 'if so' and so forth —

body.text: evaṃ ca ko guṇo labdhaścittamātre 'pi kalpite // Bca_9.30 //
body.translated_text: If so, what benefit is obtained even in conceiving mind-only? // <s>Bca</s> 9.30 //

body.text: evaṃ ceti nipātasamudāyaḥ evaṃ satītyasminnarthe / apyarthe cakāraḥ / evamapi svīkṛte ko guṇo labdhaḥ? naiva kaścit / cittamātre 'pi vijñaptimātratāyāmapi kalpitāyāṃ kalpanayā samāropite, advayatattvaparijñānānvaye 'pi sarvasattvasaṃtāne rāgādīnāṃ paryavasthānāt //
body.translated_text: 'If so' — this combination of particles means 'this being the case.' The particle 'and' is in the sense of 'even.' Even if this is accepted, what benefit is obtained? None whatsoever. Even in conceiving mind-only — even when the doctrine of mere-representation is superimposed through conceptualization — because desire and such continue to afflict the continua of all beings, even when the comprehension of non-dual reality is present.

body.text: nanu etatsamānaṃ niḥsvabhāvavādino bhavato 'pīti samānadūṣaṇatāmāpādayannāha māyopamatve 'pītyādi-
body.translated_text: But this same [objection] applies equally to you who propound the lack of intrinsic nature — thus showing that it is a common fault, he says 'even when the nature of being like an illusion' and so forth —

body.text:
māyopamatve 'pi jñāte kathaṃ kleśo nivartate /
māyopamatve māyāsvabhāvatve 'pi jagato jñāte kathaṃ kleśo nivartate, kathaṃ rāgādigaṇaḥ prahīyate iti pṛcchati / kimatra prahāṇānupapattikāraṇaṃ yat pṛcchasītyāha yadā māyetyādi-
body.translated_text: Even when the nature of being like an illusion is known, how do the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) cease?

body.text: yadā māyāstriyāṃ rāgastatkarturapi jāyate // Bca_9.31 //
body.translated_text: Even when the nature of being like an illusion — the nature of being like a magical creation — of the world is known, how do the <s>kleśas</s> cease, how is the host of desire and such abandoned? — he asks. What is the reason that abandonment is impossible, that you ask this? He says 'when toward an illusory woman' and so forth —

body.text: idamatra prahāṇānupapattibījaṃ dṛśyate- yadā māyāstriyāṃ māyākāravinirmitāyāmabalāyāṃ rāgaḥ saṃraktacittatā jāyate utpadyate / kasya jāyate? tatkarturapi / na kevalaṃ yadvayāmohanāya sā vinirmitā, teṣāmeva jāyate, kiṃ tu tasyā māyāstriyāḥ kartuḥ nirmāturapi jāyate iti apiśabdārthaḥ / yadā hi paracittavibhramasaṃpādanārthaṃ mantrauṣadhisāmarthyavinirmitāṃ sarvāṅgapratyaṅgāvayavalakṣaṇaparipūrṇāmabhinavayauvanaśobhāsaṃpatsamāpannāṃ prasannamanoharavarṇāṃ lāvaṇyātiśayaśālinīm atīva tadākāranirmāṇapravīṇaḥ kaścinmāyākāro janapadakalyāṇīṃ striyamupadarśayati, tadā na tāvat tadanye tāmabhisamīkṣya manmathaśaraprahārāntaravyathitacetaso jāyante, api tu yo 'pi sa tasyāḥ kamanīyakāntisaṃpadaḥ kāmakalākauśalotkaṇṭhitamūrterabhinirmātā, mayā svayameva caiṣā viraciteti tatsvabhāvavicakṣaṇaḥ, so 'pi kāmakalayā paramadaśāmāsādayan na kathaṃcidapi cetaḥ saṃdhārayitumalam, tat kathaṃ māyopamatve 'pi niścite saṃsārasaṃtaticchedaḥ syāt?
body.translated_text: Here, the seed of the impossibility of abandonment is seen as follows: when attachment — the state of an enamored mind — arises toward an illusory woman, one conjured by a magician, who is insubstantial. In whom does it arise? Even in that creator — not only in those for whose delusion she was conjured does it arise, but even in the creator, the fabricator of that illusory woman — this is the meaning of the word 'api' (even). For when some magician, who is extremely skilled in creating such forms, displays to the public a woman beautiful as the fairest of the realm — conjured through the power of mantras and herbs, complete in the features of every limb and minor limb, endowed with the splendor of fresh youth, of pleasing and captivating complexion, excelling in grace — then not only do others, beholding her, become those whose minds are afflicted by the strike of <s>Kāma</s>'s arrows, but even he who is the creator of her lovely, enchanting beauty, of her form fashioned with the skill of the art of desire — even he who is expert in her true nature, [knowing] 'This was fashioned by me myself' — even he, reaching the highest state through the art of desire, is utterly unable to restrain his mind. So how, even when the illusion-like nature [of things] is established, could the severance of the continuity of <s>saṃsāra</s> occur?

body.text: etat parijihīrṣannāha aprahīṇā hi tadityādi-
body.translated_text: Wishing to resolve this, he says 'for the creator's' and so forth:

children.translated_text: For the creator's latent impression of the defilement of the knowable is not abandoned;
therefore, at the time of seeing her, his impression of emptiness is weak. // Bca_9.32 //

body.text: hiryasmādarthe / naitaddūṣaṇamasmākamāsajjate / yasmādaprahīṇā anivṛttā / tatkartuḥ māyāstrīnirmātuḥ / kimaprahīṇā? jñeyasaṃkleśavāsanā jñeyasaṃkleśaḥ sasvabhāvatāsamāropādāsaṅgādiḥ, vastutāsamāropo vā / jñeyāvaraṇaṃ yāvat / tasya vāsanā anādisaṃsārajanmaparaṃparābhyastamithyāvikalpajanitatadvījabhūtacittasaṃtatisaṃskārādhānam, tasyā aprahīṇatvāt / nanu etat
body.translated_text: 'For' (<s>hi</s>) is in the sense of 'because.' This objection does not apply to us. Because the latent impression of the defilement of the knowable — the defilement of the knowable being the superimposition of intrinsic nature and the attachment arising therefrom, or the superimposition of real existence; that is, the obscuration of the knowable — its latent impression, which is the depositing in the mental continuum of seed-like impressions generated by false conceptual constructions cultivated through the beginningless succession of births in <s>saṃsāra</s> — because of its not being abandoned, [this is so]. For the creator — the fabricator of the illusory woman. What is not abandoned? The latent impression of the defilement of the knowable. But surely

body.text: samānaṃ vijñānavādino 'pi pratividhānam / tasyāpi advayatattvasya sattve 'pi āgantukasaṃkleśavāsanāyā aprahīṇatvāt na sarve tathāgatā bhavanti / naitat samānam / yasmādabhāvātmāno malāḥ kāryakalāvikalā nāvaraṇaṃ bhavitumarhanti, ityuktameva / asmākaṃ tu niḥsvabhāvameva janyaṃ janakaṃ ceti na samānam / sā yasmādaprahīṇā, ato 'smāt kāraṇāt / taddṛṣṭikāle, tasyā jñeyasasvabhāvatāyā dṛṣṭiḥ upalabdhiḥ, tasyāḥ kāle / tasyā vā māyāstriyā dṛṣṭikāle upalambhakāle / tasyeti aprahīṇasaṃkleśavāsanasya draṣṭuḥ / durbalā śūnyavāsaneti śūnyasya śūnyatattvasya śūnyatāyā veti vigrahaḥ / chandonurodhād bhāvapratyayasya lopaṃ kṛtvā śūnyeti nirdeśaḥ / vāsanā saṃskārādhānam, sa durbalā sāmarthyavikalā, āropitasya darśanāt / atastadā bhāvavāsanā balavatī //
body.translated_text: the same remedy applies to the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> (mind-only proponent) as well. For even though the non-dual reality exists for him, since the latent impression of adventitious defilement is not abandoned, not all become <s>Tathāgatas</s>. This is not the same. Because impurities of non-existent nature, devoid of the capacity for effects, cannot constitute an obscuration — as has already been stated. But for us, both what is produced and what produces are themselves devoid of intrinsic nature — thus it is not the same. Since that [latent impression] is not abandoned, therefore — for this reason — at the time of seeing that — at the time of the perception of intrinsic nature in the knowable; or at the time of seeing that illusory woman, at the time of perceiving her — 'of him' means of the seer whose defilement-impression is not abandoned — the impression of emptiness is weak. 'Of the empty' — the analysis of the compound is: of the empty, of the empty reality, or of emptiness. Due to metrical requirement, the possessive suffix is elided, yielding the form '<s>śūnya</s>.' The impression — the depositing of <s>saṃskāras</s> — is weak, lacking in power, because of the perception of what is superimposed. Therefore at that time the impression of existence is strong.

body.text: kathaṃ tarhi sā nivartate ityāha śūnyatetyādi-
body.translated_text: How then does it cease? — he says 'through the depositing' and so forth:

body.text: śūnyatāvāsanādhānāddhīyate bhāvavāsanā /
body.translated_text: Through the depositing of the impression of emptiness, the impression of [real] existence diminishes.

body.text: śūnyatāyā māyāsvabhāvaniḥsvabhāvatāyā vāsanā tasya ādhānam āvedhaḥ / abhyāsena dṛḍhīkaraṇamiti yāvat / tasmādvirūddhapratyayāt hīyate nivartate / vahnisaṃnidhānācchītasparśavat / kim? bhāvavāsanā anavarāgrasaṃsārābhyastavastusadrāhādhyavasānavāsanā / tasyā bhūtārthatvāt, vastunijasvabhāvatvācca / itarasyā alīkatvāt āgantukatvācca / nanu bhāvābhiniveśo vā śūnyatābhiniveśo vā iti nābhiniveśaṃ prati kaścidviśeṣaḥ, tasyāpi kalpanāsvabhāvānatikramāt / yadāha-
body.translated_text: The impression of emptiness — of the illusion-like lack of intrinsic nature; its depositing — its penetration, meaning its strengthening through practice. Through that opposing factor, [the impression of existence] diminishes — ceases. Like cold touch in the presence of fire. What [diminishes]? The impression of [real] existence — the impression of the conviction of substantial reality cultivated through beginningless, endless <s>saṃsāra</s>. [This impression diminishes] because the [impression of emptiness] is of a true nature, and because it is the intrinsic nature of things. The other [impression of existence is overcome] because it is false and adventitious. But surely, whether it is clinging to existence or clinging to emptiness, there is no distinction with regard to clinging, since even the latter does not transcend the nature of conceptual construction. As it is said:

children.translated_text: Emptiness has been declared by the wise to be the escape from all views;
but those for whom emptiness itself is a view — them they have declared to be incurable.

body.text: iti / [ma. śā.-13.8]
body.translated_text: [<s>Madhyamakaśāstra</s> 13.8]

body.text: etat parihartumāha kiṃcinnāstītyādi-
body.translated_text: To resolve this, he says 'nothing exists' and so forth:

body.text: kiṃcinnāstīti cābhyāsātsāpi paścātprahīyate // Bca_9.33 //
body.translated_text: And through the practice of 'nothing exists,' even that [impression of emptiness] is subsequently abandoned. // Bca_9.33 //

body.text: kiṃciditi bhāvo vā śūnyatā vā / nāsti na vidyate / caśabdaḥ pūrvāpekṣayā samuccaye / ityevaṃ cābhyāsāt bhāvavāsanāprahāṇasya paścāt sāpi śūnyavāsanāpi prahīyate nivartate / ayamabhiprāyaḥ- śūnyatāvedho hi bhāvābhiniveśasya pratipakṣatvāt prahāṇopāyabhūtaḥ / adhigate ca upeye paścāt kolopamatvāt upāyasyāpi prahāṇamanuṣṭhīyate / etadevāha-
body.translated_text: 'Something' (<s>kiṃcit</s>) means either existence or emptiness. 'Does not exist' — is not found. The particle 'ca' (and) indicates addition with reference to what precedes. Through the practice of 'thus [nothing exists],' after the abandonment of the impression of existence, even that — even the impression of emptiness — is subsequently abandoned, ceases. The intent is this: the penetration of emptiness, being the antidote to clinging to existence, serves as the means of abandonment. And when the goal has been attained, subsequently, by the principle of a raft, the abandonment of even the means is undertaken. This very [point] he states:

children.translated_text: The teaching of emptiness, the nectar, is for the abandonment of all conceptual constructions;
but one who grasps even at that [emptiness] — him you have declared to be lost.

body.text: iti // [catuḥ-2.21]
body.translated_text: [<s>Catuḥstava</s> 2.21]

body.text: syādetat- yadi nāma kiṃcinnāstīti manasikārābhyāsād bhavati śūnyatāvāsanāyāḥ prahāṇam, tathāpi tadabhyāsāt punarabhāvakalpanā pravartamānā nivartayitumaśakyā / tataśca gaṇḍapraveśe 'kṣitārānirgamo jāta iti tadavasthaṃ tava dauṣṭhayam, ityatrāha yadā na labhyate ityādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: even if the abandonment of the impression of emptiness occurs through the practice of the mental attention 'nothing exists,' still, the conceptual construction of non-existence that would proceed from that practice cannot be averted. And so, having entered the abscess, the extraction of the needle has become [a problem] — your predicament remains the same. To this he says 'when no entity' and so forth:

children.text: yadā na labhyate bhāvo yo nāstīti prakalpyate /
children.translated_text: When no entity is found that is conceptualized as 'it does not exist,'

children.text: tadā nirāśrayo 'bhāvaḥ kathaṃ tiṣṭhenmateḥ puraḥ // Bca_9.34 //
children.translated_text: then non-existence, being without basis, how could it stand before the mind? // Bca_9.34 //

body.text: iyamapi [abhāvakalpanā] vicāreṇa nāvatiṣṭhate iti / yo bhāvo nāstīti prakalpyate, yasya bhāvasya pratiṣedhaḥ kriyate, sa yadi vicāryamāṇo niḥsvabhāvatayā na labhyate na prāpyate taimirikopalabdhakeśastabakavat / tadā nirāśraya iti / yasyāsau parikalpito bhāvaḥ, tasya saṃbandhino 'bhāvāt nirālambaḥ abhāvaḥ kalpanāvidarśitamūrtiḥ kathaṃ tiṣṭhenmateḥ puraḥ, kathamasau vicāreṇa buddheragrataḥ pratibhāsate? svayameva bhāvaniḥsvabhāvatāyāṃ nivartate //
body.translated_text: This [conceptual construction of non-existence] too does not withstand examination. The entity that is conceptualized as 'it does not exist' — of which entity the negation is made — if, when examined, it is not found, not obtained, due to its lack of intrinsic nature — like the cluster of hair perceived by one with cataracts — then 'without basis': the conceptually imputed entity related to which [non-existence was posited] being absent, non-existence — a form projected by conceptual construction — being without support, without foundation — how could it stand before the mind? How could it appear before the intellect upon examination? It ceases on its own, through the very lack of intrinsic nature of entities.

body.text: athavā anyathāvatāryate- bhavatu nāma śūnyatābalādhānād bhāvavāsanāvinivṛttiḥ / tatpratiṣedhābhāvādabhāvābhiniveśastu kena vāryate ityata āha- yadā na labhyate ityādi / anyat sarvaṃ pūrvavat //
body.translated_text: Or alternatively, it is interpreted differently: granted, through the strengthening of emptiness, the impression of existence ceases. But since the negation of existence is not negated, who averts the clinging to non-existence? Therefore he says 'when no entity' and so forth. Everything else is as before.

body.text: ayamatra samudāyārthaḥ- sarvadharmaśūnyatā hi bhāvābhiniveśaprahāṇāya upādīyate / sāpi śūnyatā śūnyatābhimukhīkaraṇāt paścāt prahīyate / yāpi ca kathaṃcid bhāvakalpanā jāyate, sāpi samanantaravicāreṇa nivartate / ata eva etatsamastakalpanājālavinivartanāya bhagavatyāṃ prajñāpāramitāyāṃ vistareṇa adhyātmaśūnyatādayo 'ṣṭādaśa śūnyatāḥ proktāḥ / na ca śūnyatā bhāvād vyatiriktā, bhāvasyaiva tatsvabhāvatvāt / anyathā śūnyatāyā bhāvād vyatireke dharmāṇāṃ niḥsvabhāvatā na syāt / niḥsvabhāvatā tatsvabhāva iti prasādhitaṃ prāk / etadapi prajñāpāramitāyāmuktam-
body.translated_text: Here the cumulative meaning is this: the emptiness of all <s>dharmas</s> is adopted for the purpose of abandoning clinging to existence. That very emptiness too, after one turns toward emptiness, is subsequently abandoned. And whatever conceptual construction of existence somehow arises, that too ceases through immediate examination. For this very reason, in order to avert this entire net of conceptual constructions, in the <s>Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā</s>, eighteen emptinesses beginning with the emptiness of the internal are taught in detail. And emptiness is not distinct from entities, since it is the very nature of entities. Otherwise, if emptiness were distinct from entities, <s>dharmas</s> would not lack intrinsic nature. That the lack of intrinsic nature is their very nature has been established before. This too is stated in the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>:

body.text: punaraparaṃ subhūte bodhisattvo mahāsattvaḥ prajñāpāramitāyāṃ caran sarvākārajñatāpratisaṃyuktairmanasikārairevaṃ pratyavekṣate- na rūpaśūnyatayā rūpaṃ śūnyam, rūpameva śūnyam, śūnyataiva rūpam / na vedanāśūnyatayā vedanā śūnyā, vedanaiva śūnyā, śūnyataiva vedanā / na saṃjñāśūnyatayā saṃjñā śūnyā, saṃjñaiva śūnyā, śūnyataiva saṃjñā / na saṃskāraśūnyatayā saṃskārāḥ śūnyāḥ, saṃskārā eva śūnyāḥ, śūnyataiva saṃskārāḥ / na vijñānaśūnyatayā vijñānaṃ śūnyam, vijñānameva śūnyam, śūnyataiva vijñānam // iti vistaraḥ / uktaṃ ca-
body.translated_text: 'Furthermore, <s>Subhūti</s>, a <s>Bodhisattva</s> <s>Mahāsattva</s>, practicing the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>, reflects with mental applications connected with knowledge of all aspects thus: "Form is not empty by the emptiness of form; form itself is empty, emptiness itself is form. Feeling is not empty by the emptiness of feeling; feeling itself is empty, emptiness itself is feeling. Perception is not empty by the emptiness of perception; perception itself is empty, emptiness itself is perception. Formations are not empty by the emptiness of formations; formations themselves are empty, emptiness itself is formations. Consciousness is not empty by the emptiness of consciousness; consciousness itself is empty, emptiness itself is consciousness."' Thus in detail. And it is said:

children.text: yaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ śūnyatā saiva te matā /
children.translated_text: That which is dependent origination — that you consider to be emptiness;
there is no independently existing entity — this is your incomparable lion's roar!

body.text: iti / [catuḥ-2.20]
body.translated_text: [<s>Catuḥstava</s> 2.20]

body.text: iti na śūnyatā dharmād vyatiriktā / tasmācchūnyatāyāmapi nābhiniveśaḥ kartavyaḥ iti //
body.translated_text: Thus emptiness is not distinct from <s>dharmas</s>. Therefore, even in emptiness, no fixation should be made.

body.text: evaṃ sarvavikalpapratyastamayāt samastāvaraṇanirmuktirupajāyate ityupadarśayannāha yadā na bhāva ityādi-
body.translated_text: Showing that from the subsiding of all conceptual constructions, liberation from all obscurations arises, he says 'when neither entity' and so forth:

children.text: yadā na bhāvo nābhāvo mateḥ saṃtiṣṭhate puraḥ /
children.translated_text: When neither entity nor non-entity stands before the mind,
then, there being no other course, [the mind], without support, is pacified. // Bca_9.35 //

body.text: yadā na bhāvaḥ paramārthasatsvabhāvo materbuddheḥ saṃtiṣṭhate puro 'grataḥ, na abhāvaḥ, nāpi bhāvavirahitalakṣaṇo 'bhāvaḥ yadā mateḥ saṃtiṣṭhate puraḥ, tadā anyagatyabhāvena vidhipratiṣedhābhyāṃ gatyantarābhāvāt, ubhayānubhayapakṣayoretaddūyavidhipratiṣedhātmakatvāt, ābhyāmavyatiriktatayā anayoḥ saṃgrahe tāvapi saṃgṛhītāviti nirāśrayā, sadasatorālambanayorayogāt buddhiḥ praśāmyati upaśāmyati / sarvavikalpopaśamānnirindhanavahnivat nirvṛtimupayātītyarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: When no entity — no ultimately real intrinsic nature — stands before the intellect, and when no non-entity — nothing characterized by the absence of existence — stands before the mind, then, 'there being no other course' — because there is no alternative through either affirmation or negation, since the positions of both [existence and non-existence] and of neither [existence nor non-existence] are by nature composed of these very two [viz. affirmation and negation of existence], and since these [remaining two positions] are included when these two [are included], being inseparable from them — the intellect, 'without support,' since the objects of existence and non-existence are not tenable, is pacified — subsides. Through the subsiding of all conceptual constructions, like a fire whose fuel is exhausted, it attains <s>nirvṛti</s> (cessation) — this is the meaning.

body.text: kathaṃ tarhi sakalakalpanāvirahādanekakalpāsaṃkhyeyābhilaṣitaṃ parārthasaṃpadupāyabhūtaṃ buddhatvamadhigamya parārthamabhisaṃpādayati bhagavānityatrāha cintāmaṇiriti-
body.translated_text: But then, how, when bereft of all conceptual construction, having attained <s>Buddhahood</s> — which is the means for the accomplishment of others' welfare, wished for through innumerable <s>kalpa</s>-<s>asaṃkhyeyas</s> — does the Blessed One accomplish the welfare of others? To this he says '<s>cintāmaṇi</s>' and so forth:

children.translated_text: Just as a wish-fulfilling gem and a wish-granting tree fulfill desires,
so too the image of the <s>Jina</s> is seen, through [the power of] those to be trained and [his former] aspirations. // Bca_9.36 //

body.text: cintāmaṇiriti cintitaphaladātā ratnaviśeṣaḥ / kalpataruriti kalpitaphaladātā vṛkṣaviśeṣaḥ / sa yathā vikalpamantareṇāpi lokānāṃ yathābhavyamicchāyāḥ paripūraṇaḥ abhilāṣasya saṃpādakaḥ / jinabimbaṃ tathekṣyate iti saṃbandhaḥ / caturmārajayājjino bhagavān, pāpakadharmajayādvā / jinasya buddhasya bhagavataḥ bimbaṃ dvātriṃśatā mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇairvirājitaṃ śarīram / tathā tena prakāreṇa īkṣyate sarvakalpanābhāve 'pi parahitasukhasaṃpādanasamarthaṃ pratīyate / kathaṃ punaretadiṣṭamātreṇa bhaviṣyatītyāha- vineyapraṇidhānābhyāmiti / vineyavaśāt ye buddhasya bhagavato vineyāḥ, tadupādhiphalaviśeṣapratilambhahetukuśalakarmaparipākāt, tadvaśāt / praṇidhānavaśācca, yatpūrvaṃ bodhisattvāvasthāyāmanekaprakāraṃ bhagavatā sattvārthasaṃpādanaṃ praṇihitaṃ tasyākṣepavaśāt, kulālacakrabhramaṇākṣepanyāyena anābhogena pravartanāt sarvasattvahitasukhasaṃpādanamupapadyate / yaduktam-
body.translated_text: '<s>Cintāmaṇi</s>' — a special jewel that grants wished-for results. 'Wish-granting tree' (<s>kalpataru</s>) — a special tree that grants desired results. Just as it, even without conceptual construction, fulfills — accomplishes — the desires, the aspirations — of beings as befits each. 'The image of the <s>Jina</s> is thus seen' — this is the connection. '<s>Jina</s>' — the Blessed One, the conqueror of the four <s>Māras</s>, or the conqueror of evil <s>dharmas</s>. The 'image' of the <s>Jina</s>, of the <s>Buddha</s>, of the Blessed One — the body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being. 'Thus' — in that manner — 'is seen' — even in the absence of all conceptual construction, it is understood to be capable of accomplishing the benefit and happiness of others. How then will this come about merely through wish? He says: 'through those to be trained and [his] aspirations.' Through the power of those to be trained — those who are the Blessed <s>Buddha</s>'s disciples — through the ripening of their wholesome <s>karma</s> that is the cause for obtaining the particular fruits of that condition; through that [power]. And through the power of aspirations — the manifold aspirations for the accomplishment of beings' welfare that the Blessed One formerly made in the <s>Bodhisattva</s> stage — through the impelling force of those, by the principle of the spinning of a potter's wheel, through functioning without deliberate effort, the accomplishment of the benefit and happiness of all beings takes place. As it is stated:

body.text: yasyāṃ rātrau tathāgato 'bhisaṃbuddho yasyāṃ ca parinirvṛtaḥ, atrāntare tathāgatena ekamapyakṣaraṃ nodāhṛtam / tat kasya hetoḥ? nityaṃ samāhito bhagavān / ye ca akṣarasvararutavaineyāḥ sattvāḥ, te tathāgatamukhādūrṇākośāduṣṇīṣāt dhvaniṃ niścarantaṃ śṛṇvantītyādi /
body.translated_text: 'In the night in which the <s>Tathāgata</s> became fully awakened, and [the night] in which he entered <s>parinirvāṇa</s> — in the interval between these, the <s>Tathāgata</s> did not utter even a single syllable. For what reason? The Blessed One is always in <s>samādhi</s>. And those beings who are to be trained by syllables, sounds, and utterances — they hear the sound issuing from the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s mouth, from the <s>ūrṇākośa</s>, from the <s>uṣṇīṣa</s>.' And so forth.

body.text: uktaṃ ca-
body.translated_text: And it is said:

children.translated_text: When he is established in meditative absorption, like a wish-fulfilling gem,
teachings issue even from walls and such, as wished for.
Through those [teachings], people come to know all the matters they wished to learn,
and they quickly attain what is beneficial, each as befits them.

body.text: iti / [tattvasaṃgraha 3241-42]
body.translated_text: [<s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 3241-42]

body.text: catuḥstave 'pyuktam-
body.translated_text: And in the <s>Catuḥstava</s> too it is said —

children.translated_text: 'Not even a single syllable was uttered by you, O Lord,
yet the entire assembly of those to be trained was satisfied by the rain of <s>Dharma</s>.'

body.text: iti // [catuḥ-1.7]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Catuḥstava</s> 1.7]

body.text: evamasādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇamākhyāya punaranyathā hetvavasthāyā eva sa tādṛśaḥ prabhāvāti- śayaviśeṣo yadanābhogena parārthasaṃpādanasamarthaphalamupajāyate iti vṛttadvayenopadarśayannāha yathā gāruḍika ityādi-
body.translated_text: Having thus stated this uncommon cause, he shows through two examples, in yet another way, that the very state of the cause is such that there is a surpassing excellence of power whereby the fruit — capable of accomplishing the welfare of others without deliberate effort — arises. He says 'just as a <s>Gāruḍika</s>' and so forth —

children.translated_text: Just as a <s>Gāruḍika</s> (snake-charm specialist), having empowered a pillar, passes away,
that [pillar], even long after he has passed, would pacify poisons and such. // <s>Bca</s> 9.37 //

body.text: yathā gāruḍiko viṣatatvavit labdhamantrasāmarthyaḥ stambhaṃ kāṣṭhamayaṃ vā anyadvā sādhayitvā mantreṇābhisaṃskṛtya mamābhāvādayameva sarvaviṣāpahāracaturo bhaviṣyatīti vinaśyati, svayamuparatavyāpāro bhavati / sa stambhaḥ tenābhimantritaḥ tasmin gāruḍike ciranaṣṭe 'pi prabhūtakālamuparate 'pi viṣādīnupaśāmayet, ādiśabdāt grahādivikāramapaharet / chāndasasamayaṃ paripālayatā mito 'pi upadhāyā ṇici hrasvo na kṛtaḥ / saṃjñāpūrvakasya vidheranityatvādvā //
body.translated_text: Just as a <s>Gāruḍika</s> — one who knows the science of poisons, who has obtained the power of mantras — having empowered a pillar, whether made of wood or something else — having consecrated it with mantras — thinking 'In my absence, this very [pillar] will be skillful in removing all poisons' — passes away, his own activity having ceased. That pillar, consecrated by him, even long after that <s>Gāruḍika</s> has passed away — even after a long time has elapsed — would pacify poisons and such; by the word 'and such,' it would also remove the effects of planetary spirits and such.
