children.translated_text: Teeth, hair, and nails are not I; I am not bone, nor am I blood;

children.text: na siṃghāṇaṃ na ca śleṣmā na pūyaṃ lasikāpi vā // Bca_9.58 //
children.translated_text: I am not mucus, nor phlegm, nor pus, nor lymph either. // Bca_9.58 //

body.text: dantakeśanakhā nāham / pratyekamamī ahaṃpratyayaviṣayā na bhavanti / nāsthi nāpyasmi śoṇitam / asthi haṭṭam / śoṇitaṃ rudhiram / etaddūyamapi nāsmi nāham / siṃghāṇaṃ na ca śleṣmā na pūyam / siṃghāṇaṃ nāsikāvivaraniryātaḥ kledaḥ / śleṣmā mukhavivaravinirgataḥ / pūyaṃ vraṇe pakvarudhiram / etānyapi nāhaṃ bhavanti / lasikāpi vā, lasikā vraṇakledaḥ, sāpi nāham //
body.translated_text: "Teeth, hair, and nails are not I" — each of these individually is not the object of the I-notion. "I am not bone, nor am I blood" — bone is skeletal structure; blood is gore — these two also are not I. "I am not mucus, nor phlegm, nor pus" — mucus is the moisture discharged from the nasal cavity; phlegm is what comes out of the oral cavity; pus is putrefied blood in a wound — these too are not I. "Nor lymph either" — lymph is the moisture of a wound; that too is not I.

children.text: nāhaṃ vasā na ca svedo na medo 'strāṇi nāpyaham /
children.translated_text: I am not fat, nor sweat, nor marrow; the viscera too are not I;

children.text: na cāhamantranirguṇḍī gūthamūtramahaṃ na ca // Bca_9.59 //
children.translated_text: nor am I the intestinal membrane; feces and urine are not I either. // Bca_9.59 //

body.text: nāhaṃ vasā na ca svedo na meda iti / vasā śarīrasnehaḥ / svedaḥ prasvedaḥ / medaścaturtho dhātuḥ / imānyapi nāham / antrāṇi nāpyahamiti / antrāṇi prasiddhāni, tānyapi
body.translated_text: "I am not fat, nor sweat, nor marrow" — fat is the oily substance of the body; sweat is perspiration; marrow is the fourth bodily constituent — these too are not I. "The viscera too are not I" — the viscera are well known; those too

body.text: nāham / na cāhamantranirguṇḍī antranirguṇḍī sūkṣmātmikā, sāpi naivāham / gūthamūtramahaṃ na ca, gūthaṃ viṣṭhā / etadapi dvayaṃ nāhaṃ na bhavāmi //
body.translated_text: are not I. "Nor am I the intestinal membrane" — the intestinal membrane is of subtle nature; that too is definitely not I. "Feces and urine are not I either" — feces is excrement; this pair too is not what I am.

children.text: nāhaṃ māṃsaṃ na ca strāyu noṣmā vāyurahaṃ na ca /
children.translated_text: I am not flesh, nor sinew; I am not heat, nor am I wind;

children.text: na ca cchidrāṇyahaṃ nāpi ṣaḍ vijñānāni sarvathā // Bca_9.60 //
children.translated_text: nor am I the orifices; nor am I the six consciousnesses in any way. // Bca_9.60 //

body.text: nāhaṃ māṃsaṃ na ca snāyu noṣmā / snāyu sirā / ūṣmā śarīratejodhātuḥ / ime 'pi nāham / vāyurahaṃ na ca, vāyurāśvāsapraśvāsādilakṣaṇaḥ, so 'pi naivāham / na ca cchidrāṇi cakṣurādīni, tānyapi nāham / nāpi ṣaḍ vijñānāni sarvathā, ṣaṭ cakṣuḥśrotraghrāṇajihvākāyamanovijñānāni, tānyapi nāhaṃ bhavanti / sarvathā sarvaprakāreṇa pratyekaṃ samuditāni vā / tathā hi dantādisamudāyātmakameva vicāryamāṇaṃ śarīramupalabhyate / tacca pratyekamahaṃpratyayavedyaṃ na bhavati, pratyekamahaṃpratyayasya teṣu abhāvāt / na hi pareṣāmapi ekaikaśaḥ keśādayo 'haṃ pratyayavedyā bhavanti / samuditā api te eva kevalāḥ pūrvavat / na ca samuditeṣu teṣu kaścidekaḥ saṃbhavati, tasya pratiṣetsyamānatvāt / nāpyaneke samuditā api ekapratyayaviṣayā bhavitumarhanti / na ca anekeṣu ekapratyayo bhrānto yuktaḥ / na ca bhrāntestattvavyavasthā / tasmāt kalpanāmātrametadahamityarthaśūnyamābhātīti niścitam / uktaṃ caitadaśubhabhāvanāprastāve śikṣāsamuccaye-
body.translated_text: 'I am not the flesh, nor the sinews, nor the bodily heat.' Sinews are the veins. Bodily heat is the fire-element of the body. These too are not I. 'Nor am I the wind' — the wind characterized by inhalation, exhalation, and such — that too is indeed not I. 'Nor the apertures' — the eyes and such — those too are not I. 'Nor indeed the six consciousnesses in any way' — the six consciousnesses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — those too are not I. 'In any way' — in every manner — individually or collectively. For the body, when examined, is found to be nothing but a collection of teeth and such. And that [body] is not cognizable by the I-notion individually, since the I-notion is absent in each [component] individually. For others too do not experience hair and such as individually cognizable by the I-notion. And those same [components], even when gathered together, are just as before [— not the I]. Nor when they are gathered does some single [entity] come into being, since that [entity] will be refuted. Nor can many [components], even when gathered, be the object of a single cognition. Nor is a mistaken single cognition regarding many [things] justified. Nor can there be a determination of reality from what is mistaken. Therefore it is certain that this 'I' is a mere conceptualization that appears empty of [real] referent. And this has been stated in the context of the contemplation of impurity in the <s>Śikṣāsamuccaya</s> —

body.text: santi asmin kāye keśā romāṇi nakhā dantā rajo malaṃ tvakū māṃsāsthi snāyu śirā bukkā hṛdayaṃ plīhakaḥ klomakaḥ antrāṇi antraguṇāḥ āmāśayaḥ pakkāśayaḥ audarīyakaṃ yakṛt purīṣam aśru svedaḥ kheṭaḥ siṃghāṇakaṃ vasā lasikā majjā medaḥ pittaṃ śliṣmapūyaśoṇitaṃ mastakaluṅgaṃ prasrāvaḥ / eṣu ca vastuṣu bodhisattvaḥ upaparīkṣaṇajātīyo bhavati / etat punaḥ paścāt kāyasmṛtyupasthānaparyante nirdekṣyāmaḥ / iti / evaṃ nirviṣaya evāhaṃpratyayaviśeṣaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'In this body there are: head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, dust, grime, skin, flesh, bones, sinews, veins, lungs, heart, spleen, pleura, intestines, mesentery, undigested stomach contents, digested stomach contents, stomach contents, liver, feces, tears, sweat, phlegm, nasal mucus, fat, synovial fluid, marrow, adipose tissue, bile, mucus-pus-blood, brain, and urine. Regarding these constituents, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> becomes one who investigates. We shall explain this further later, at the conclusion of the section on mindfulness of the body.' Thus. In this way, the particular I-notion is indeed without an object.

body.text: syādetat- yadi nāma keśādayo 'haṃpratyayavedyā na bhavanti, tathāpi nāyaṃ nirviṣayaḥ sidhyati / yataḥ antarvyāpārapuruṣagocara eva ahaṃpratyayo 'smābhiriṣyate iti naiyāyikādayaḥ / naitadapi yuktam / yasmāt- ahaṃ gauraḥ kṛśo dīrgho gacchāmītyādyākāraparāmarśātmaka eva ayamahaṃpratyayaḥ pratibhāsate / na ca ātmana etadrūpamiṣyate paraiḥ / na ca anyākāreṇa jñānena anyasya grahaṇaṃ yuktam, atiprasaṅgāt / tathā hi tadvān, idamidaṃ tasya lakṣaṇamupavarṇayanti pare / tatra naiyāyikāstāvat nityaṃ sarvagataṃ pratiprāṇibhinnamacetanaṃ cetanāyogāttu cetanaṃ sukhādiguṇādhāraṃ śubhāśubhakarmakartāraṃ tatphalopabhoktāraṃ paralokinaṃ ca ātmānamicchanti / naiyāyikavadvaiśeṣikā api / taduktam-
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Even if hair and such are not cognizable by the I-notion, still this does not prove it is without an object, since we the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others accept that the I-notion has as its domain the inner-functioning <s>puruṣa</s> (self). This too is not justified. Because the I-notion manifestly appears with the character of apprehending [forms] such as 'I am fair, I am thin, I am tall, I walk' and so on. And such a form is not accepted by others as belonging to the self. Nor is it justified that a cognition of one form would grasp another [object], since there would be an overextension. For they — the opponents — describe the self as possessing such-and-such, and such-and-such are its characteristics. Among them, the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> hold the self to be permanent, all-pervading, distinct in each living being, non-conscious [by nature], but conscious through conjunction with consciousness, the substratum of qualities such as pleasure and such, the agent of meritorious and non-meritorious <s>karma</s>, the experiencer of its fruit, and one who transmigrates to the next world. The <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> hold likewise. As stated —

children.translated_text: 'Others hold the self to be the substratum of desire and such,
intrinsically non-conscious, yet permanent and all-pervading;
the agent of meritorious and non-meritorious actions,
and the experiencer of their fruit — conscious through conjunction with consciousness, not by its own nature.'

body.text: iti / [tattvasaṃgraha-171-172]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 171-172]

body.text: jaiminīyāstuvyāvṛttyanugamātmakaṃ buddhirūpeṇa pariṇāminaṃ caitanyarūpamātmānamicchanti / tacca caitanyaṃ buddhisvabhāvam / na ca tasya pravṛttinivṛttī bhavataḥ, tasyobhayatrānugatarūpatvāt / tadyathā- sarpasya kuṇḍalāvasthānivṛttau ṛjutvāvasthāpravṛttau ca sarpatvasyobhayatrāpyavṛttiḥ / yathoktam-

children.translated_text: 'Others hold the self to be characterized by persistence and change,
of the nature of consciousness — and consciousness has the characteristic of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect).

body.translated_text: The <s>Jaiminīyas</s> (Mīmāṃsakas) hold the self to be of the nature of consciousness, which transforms in the form of cognition, characterized by persistence and change. And that consciousness has the nature of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect). But it does not have activity or cessation, since its form persists in both [states]. Just as: when a snake's coiled state ceases and its straight state commences, the serpent-nature persists in both [states]. As stated —

children.translated_text: Just as a snake's coiled state ceases and thereupon
the straight state arises, yet the serpent-nature does not cease —
so too, for the self whose nature is eternal consciousness,
there is no complete disappearance of all forms, yet persistence of all [its nature].'

body.text: iti / [tattvasaṃgraha-222-224]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 222-224]

body.text: iti viśeṣaḥ / anyat sarvaṃ pūrvavat //
body.translated_text: This is the distinction. Everything else is as before.

body.text: jaināstu jaiminīyavaccetanamātmānamicchanti dravyaparyāyarūpeṇa yathāyogamanugamavyāvṛttyātmakam / tathā coktam-
body.translated_text: The <s>Jainas</s> hold the self to be conscious like the <s>Jaiminīyas</s>, characterized by persistence and change in the form of substance and mode, as applicable. And so it is stated —

children.translated_text: 'The <s>Jainas</s> speak like the <s>Jaiminīyas</s>, with the difference in the characteristic of consciousness,
[holding the self to be] characterized by persistence and change in the form of substance and mode.'

body.text: tattvasaṃgraha-311
body.translated_text: <s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 311

body.text: kāpilāstu nityaṃ vyāpakaṃ nirguṇaṃ svayameva caitanyātmakamātmānamicchanti, na tu buddhisaṃbandhāt / buddheḥ svayamacitsvabhāvatvāt / caitanyaṃ puruṣasya svarūpamiti vacanāt / nāpi sa kasyacit kāryasya kartā, svayaṃ tatphalopabhoktā vā, niṣkriyatvāt / prakṛtireva tatkartrī tasya, tatphalopanetrī ca / viparyāsavaśādasau svātmani tat samāropayati / tathā hi- yadā puruṣasya śabdādiviṣayopabhogākāramautsukyamupajāyate, tadā prakṛtiḥ parijñātapuruṣautsukyā puruṣeṇa yujyate, tataḥ śabdādisargaṃ karoti / śabdādiṣu śrotrādivṛttibhirmanasādhiṣṭhitābhiḥ parigṛhīteṣu viṣayeṣu buddhiradhyavasāyaṃ karoti / tato buddhyavasitamarthaṃ puruṣaścetayate iti / evaṃ caitanyasvarūpatvānnirguṇatvam, vyāpitvānniṣkriyatvamiti sāṃkhyapuruṣasya viśeṣaḥ / uktaṃ ca-
body.translated_text: The <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> (followers of <s>Kapila</s>) hold the self to be permanent, all-pervading, without qualities, and of the nature of consciousness in itself — not through conjunction with <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), since <s>buddhi</s> is itself non-conscious by nature. Because of the statement: 'Consciousness is the self's own form.' Nor is [the self] the agent of any effect, nor itself the experiencer of its fruit, since it is inactive. It is <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) alone that is the agent of that, and the one that procures its fruit. Through the force of delusion, [the self] superimposes that [agency and enjoyment] upon itself. For when the eagerness arises in the <s>puruṣa</s> for the enjoyment of objects such as sound and such, then <s>Prakṛti</s>, having understood the <s>puruṣa</s>'s eagerness, unites with the <s>puruṣa</s> and creates the manifestation of sound and such. When the objects — sound and such — are grasped by the activities of the ear and such, presided over by the mind, <s>buddhi</s> makes a determination. Then the <s>puruṣa</s> cognizes the object determined by <s>buddhi</s>. Thus, because of being of the nature of consciousness, it is without qualities; because of being all-pervading, it is inactive — this is the distinctive [teaching] of the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> <s>puruṣa</s>. And it is said —

children.translated_text: 'Others consider consciousness to be distinct from the nature of <s>buddhi</s>;

children.text: ātmanaśca nijaṃ rūpaṃ caitanyaṃ kalpayanti te //
children.translated_text: and they conceive consciousness as the self's own form.

children.text: pradhānenopanītaṃ ca phalaṃ bhuṅkte sa kevalam /
children.translated_text: It merely enjoys the fruit brought forth by <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter);
agency does not belong to it — that is held to belong to <s>Prakṛti</s> alone.'

body.text: tattvasaṃgraha-285-86
body.translated_text: <s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 285-286

children.translated_text: 'Enveloped in darkness, with perverted consciousness, the foolish one
falsely conceives "I am doing" regarding these qualities of <s>Prakṛti</s> that are in motion — [he] who is unable even to bend a blade of grass.'

body.text: iti / [sāṃkhyakramadīpikā-43]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Sāṃkhyakramadīpikā</s> 43]

body.text: upaniṣadvādinastu samastaprāṇisaṃtānāntargatamekameva vyāpi nityaṃ ca jñānamicchanti / tadvivartarūpatayā sakalamidaṃ kṣitijalapavanahutāśanādikaṃ jagadavabhāsate / tatsvabhāva eva cātmā / na bāhyaṃ kimapyavayavi paramāṇvādikaṃ grāhyaṃ pramāṇaprasiddhamasti / āha ca-
body.translated_text: The <s>Upaniṣadvādins</s> (Vedāntins) hold that a single, all-pervading, and eternal consciousness exists within the continua of all living beings. In the form of its transformation, this entire world — earth, water, wind, fire, and such — appears. And the self is of that very nature. There is no external composite made of atoms and such, established by valid cognition, that is an object of apprehension. And it is said —

children.translated_text: 'This world of earth, fire, water, and such is an eternal transformation of consciousness;
the self is of that nature — thus others declare.'
'Nothing whatsoever that possesses the characteristic of being an object of apprehension exists here;
all this is a transformation of consciousness — therefore everything is to be examined.'

body.text: iti / [tattvasaṃgraha-328-29]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 328-329]

body.text: pudgalavādinastu punarantaścaratīrthikāḥ / skandhebhyastattvānyatvābhyāmavācyaṃ pudgalanāmānamātmānamicchanti / anyathā tīrthikasiddhāntābhiniveśadarśanaṃ syāt / āha ca-
body.translated_text: The <s>Pudgalavādins</s>, however, are crypto-<s>Tīrthikas</s> within [Buddhism]. They hold a self called <s>pudgala</s> (person) that is inexpressible as either identical with or different from the aggregates. Otherwise there would be the appearance of clinging to a <s>Tīrthika</s> tenet. And it is said —

body.text: kecicca saugataṃmanyā apyātmānaṃ pracakṣate /

children.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 336]

body.translated_text: 'Some who consider themselves followers of the <s>Sugata</s> also assert a self.'

body.text: kathamātmano 'haṃpratyayaviṣayatā syāt? svasvarūpeṇa tatrāpratibhāsanāt / tatkathamātmā ahaṃpratyayatayā pratibhāsate ityucyate? tasmād vikalpamātrametat / nirviṣayamutpadyate iti sthitam //
body.translated_text: How could the self be the object of the I-notion? Because it does not appear there in its own form. How then is the self said to appear as the I-notion? Therefore this is mere conceptualization. It arises without an object — this is established.

body.text: saṃprati citsvabhāvātmavādinaḥ sāṃkhyādayaḥ ṣaḍvijñānānāmātmaniṣedhamasahiṣṇavaḥ prāhuḥ- śabdādijñānaṃ cidātmakamātmaivāsmābhirabhidhīyate / tatkathamasyātmatāpratiṣedha ucyate? iti parābhiprāyamākalayya siddhāntavādī prasaṅgamāsañjayannāha-
body.translated_text: Now, the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> and others who assert the self as being of the nature of consciousness, unable to bear the denial that the six consciousnesses are the self, say: 'What we call the self is cognition of sound and such, which is of the nature of consciousness. How then can the denial of its selfhood be stated?' Gauging the opponent's intention, the proponent of the system, pressing the consequentialist [argument], says —

body.text: śabdajñānaṃ yadi tadā śabdo gṛhyeta sarvadā /
body.translated_text: If [the self were identical with] cognition of sound, then sound would be grasped at all times.

body.text: nanu yadi śabdajñānātmaka ātmā, tasya ca nityatvāt śabdajñānaṃ nityaṃ syāt, tadā śabdo 'pi sadā nityameva tadbhāvābhāvakālayorgrahītavyaḥ syāt, śabdagrahaṇasvabhāvasya tasya tatsadasattākāle sarvadānuvartanāt / anyathā nityatvameva tasya hīyeta / bhavatu, evameveti cet, āha-
body.translated_text: If the self were of the nature of cognition of sound, and since it is permanent, cognition of sound would be permanent — then sound too would always have to be grasped permanently, at the times of both its presence and absence, since [the self's] nature of grasping sound would persist at all times of the [sound's] existence and non-existence. Otherwise, its very permanence would be impaired. [If you say:] granted, let it be exactly so — he says —

body.text: jñeyaṃ vinā tu kiṃ vetti yena jñānaṃ nirucyate // Bca_9.61 //
body.translated_text: But without something to be known, what does it know — by virtue of which it is called 'knowledge'? // <s>Bca</s> 9.61 //

body.text: jñānameva nityamupasthitam, śabdasya tu kādācitkatvāt na sarvadā sattābhivyaktiḥ / tataśca tadasattākāle jñeyaṃ vinā viṣayamantareṇa kiuṃ vetti kiṃ jānāti tad jñānam? tuśabdo 'sattākālapraśnaviśeṣe vartate / yena jñeyena śūnyamapi jñānaṃ nirucyate abhidhīyate / jñeyaṃ jānātīti jñānamākhyāyate, tadabhāvāt kathaṃ jñānamityāśayaḥ //
body.translated_text: Knowledge itself is permanently present, but since sound is occasional, there is not always a manifestation of its existence. Therefore, at the time of [sound's] non-existence, without something to be known — without an object — what does that knowledge know? The word 'tu' (but) refers to the specific question about the time of non-existence. 'By virtue of which' — even when devoid of the knowable, it is called, is designated as, 'knowledge.' Since it is called 'knowledge' because it knows the knowable — in the absence of that [knowable], how can it be knowledge? This is the intention.

body.text: etadevāha-
body.translated_text: This very point he states —

body.text: ajānānaṃ yadi jñānaṃ kāṣṭhaṃ jñānaṃ prasajyate /
body.translated_text: If what does not know is knowledge, then a piece of wood would be knowledge.

body.text: yadapi viṣayaṃ na jānāti, tadapi yadi jñānamucyate, tadā kāṣṭhamajñānasvabhāvaṃ jñānaṃ prasajyate / na hi tena kiṃcidaparāddhaṃ yena na vijñānaṃ syāt / na caivam / tasmādviṣayaparijñānābhāvāt yathā kāṣṭhaṃ jñānaṃ na bhavati, tathā anyadapi na syādityāha-
body.translated_text: If even what does not know an object is called knowledge, then a piece of wood — of non-knowing nature — would absurdly be knowledge. For it has done nothing wrong that it should not be consciousness. But this is not so. Therefore, just as a piece of wood is not knowledge due to the absence of cognition of an object, so too nothing else would be either — he says —

body.text: tenāsaṃnihitajñeyaṃ jñānaṃ nāstīti niścayaḥ // Bca_9.62 //
body.translated_text: Therefore, it is certain that there is no knowledge when there is no proximate knowable. // <s>Bca</s> 9.62 //

body.text: yena nirviṣayaṃ na jñānam, tena kāraṇena asaṃnihitajñeyaṃ asaṃnihitamayogyadeśasthaṃ jñeyaṃ grāhyo viṣayo yasya tattathoktaṃ jñānaṃ nāsti na vidyate iti niścayaḥ ekānta eṣaḥ / sāpekṣatvāt //
body.translated_text: Since there is no knowledge without an object — for this reason, knowledge for which no proximate, appropriately situated knowable — an object to be grasped — exists: such [so-called] knowledge does not exist — this is the definitive conclusion. Because of its dependent nature.

body.text: syādetat- śabdasya sadāvidyamānatvāt nāsaṃnihitaviṣayaṃ śabdajñānam / agrahaṇaṃ tu kadācit kādācitkābhivyaktitvāditi noktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ / naitadasti / yato yadasya jñānasya paricchedyaṃ rūpaṃ vyaktamityucyate, tasya sadāsaṃnihitaviṣayatayā grāhakamajñānamabhidhīyate / śabdasya tu sadā sattvamasattvaṃ vā na vivakṣitam / jñānaṃ tu kadācidagrāhakamityetāvataiva sādhyasiddheḥ / tasmādasaṃnihitajñeyamityanena jñānasyaiva agrāhakatvaṃ sādhyate / yena rūpeṇa jñānasya grāhyo viṣayaḥ, tasya na sarvadā saṃnidhānamastīti kṛtvā iti kathaṃ noktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ? śabdasya yathā sarvadā sattvaṃ nāsti, tadvistarabhayānnocyate //
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Since sound does not always exist, the cognition of sound does not have a non-proximate object. The non-grasping at times is due to the occasional manifestation [of sound] — therefore the stated fault does not apply. This is not so. Because with respect to that form of this knowledge that is to be discerned — that which is called 'manifest' — that is called non-knowing precisely because its object is not always proximate. But whether sound always exists or not is not what is at issue. Rather, the fact that knowledge sometimes does not grasp — this alone suffices to prove the thesis. Therefore, by 'when there is no proximate knowable,' what is proven is precisely knowledge's non-grasping. The form in which knowledge has a graspable object — that [object] does not always have proximity: this being so, how does the stated fault not apply? Just as sound does not always exist — this is not elaborated for fear of prolixity.

body.text: api ca / yadi śabdajñānamevātmā, tadā tadgrahaṇātmakatvāttasya rūpagrahaṇaṃ na syāt / naitadasti / yataḥ tadeva rūpagrāhakamiṣyate iti cedatrāha tadevetyādi-
body.translated_text: Moreover, if cognition of sound alone is the self, then since it has the nature of grasping that [sound], it would not be able to grasp form. But this is not so, since that very [self] is accepted as grasping form. To this he says 'that very' and so forth —

body.text: tadeva rūpaṃ jānāti tadā kiṃ na śṛṇotyapi /
body.translated_text: If that very [knowledge] knows form, why then does it not also hear [sound]?

body.text: tadeva śabdajñānameva yadi rūpaṃ jānātīti matam, tadā kiṃ na śṛṇotyapi, tadā rūpagrahaṇakāle kimiti na śṛṇotyapi, śabdamapi kiṃ na gṛhṇāti? śabdajñānatvāt / atha gṛhṇātyeva, yadi saṃnihitaṃ syāt / kevalamasaṃnidhānāt na doṣa iti parasyottaramāśaṅkayāha śabdasyetyādi-
body.translated_text: If it is held that that very cognition of sound knows form, then why does it not also hear — at the time of grasping form, why does it not also hear, why does it not also grasp sound? — since it is [supposed to be] cognition of sound. But [if you say:] it does indeed grasp [sound], if it is proximate; but there is no fault merely because of non-proximity — anticipating the opponent's reply, he says 'because of the non-proximity of sound' and so forth —

body.text: śabdasyāsaṃnidhānāccettatastajjñānamapyasat // Bca_9.63 //
body.translated_text: If because of the non-proximity of sound, then from that, the cognition of sound too does not exist. // <s>Bca</s> 9.63 //

body.text: śabdasya viṣayatāmāpannasya asaṃnidhānādayogyadeśāt grahaṇaṃ na syāt- yadi, evamabhidhīyate, tatastat jñānamapyasat / tat tasmāt tarhi śabdasyāsaṃnidhānāt tat jñānamapi śabdajñānam asadavidyamānam / śabdajñānameva tarhi tanna bhavatītyarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: If — because sound, having become an object, is absent from an unfit location — apprehension [of it] would not occur: if this is what is claimed, then that cognition too would be non-existent. Therefore, from the absence of sound, that cognition too — the cognition of sound — would be non-existent, would not exist. The meaning is: it would simply not be a cognition of sound.

body.text: kiṃ ca / yadi śabdajñānaṃ tadā rūpagrahaṇādyātmakaṃ tanna yujyate ityāha śabdagrahaṇetyādi-
body.translated_text: Moreover, if it is a cognition of sound, then its being of the nature of apprehending form is not justified — he says with 'that which has the form of apprehending sound' and so forth —

body.text: śabdagrahaṇarūpaṃ yattadrūpagrahaṇaṃ katham /
body.translated_text: That which has the form of apprehending sound — how can it be an apprehension of form?

body.text: śabdasya grahaṇarūpaṃ śabdasya grahaṇasvabhāvam / śabdagrāhakamiti yāvat / yat jñānaṃ tad rūpagrahaṇaṃ rūpagrahaṇātmakaṃ katham? na kathaṃcidapi syāt / ekasya niraṃśasya rūpadvayāyogāt / nanu yathā kaścideka eva kasyacidapekṣayā pitā, kasyacidapekṣayā ca sa eva putraḥ syāt, tathā prakṛte 'pi rūpadvayamekasya bhaviṣyatītyāha ekaḥ pitetyādi-
body.translated_text: 'Having the form of apprehending sound' — having the nature of apprehending sound — being an apprehender of sound. That cognition — how could it be an apprehension of form, of the nature of apprehending form? In no way could it be so, because dual form is impossible for a single, partless [entity]. 'But just as a single person may be a father in relation to one and that same person a son in relation to another, so too in the present case, the single [cognition] will have dual form' — to this he says with 'one person is a father' and so forth —

body.text: ekaḥ pitā ca putraśca kalpyate na tu tattvataḥ // Bca_9.64 //
body.translated_text: One person is conceived as both father and son — but not in truth. // <s>Bca</s> 9.64 //

body.text: ekaḥ pitā eva janakaḥ putraśca janyaḥ sa eveti kalpyate, sa tu tadapekṣayā kalpanayā vyavasthāpyate / na tu tattvataḥ, na punaḥ paramārthataḥ / eka eva svabhāvaḥ ubhayātmakaḥ kalpanāsamāropitavyapadeśāt [rūpabhedena] punareka eva tathā nānābhidhānena naivābhidhīyate / ubhayavāstavarūpadvayamekasya ghaṭanīyam, tacca kathaṃcidapi na saṃgacchate, rūpadvayavyatibhinnatayā vastuno 'pi dvitvaprasaṅgāt / tasmāt yathā vāstavamekasya dvirūpatvaṃ tanna dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇyasti, yaccāsti kālpanikam, tat prakṛtānupayogīti yatkiṃcidetat //
body.translated_text: One and the same person is conceived as both father — generator — and son — the generated. But he is determined thus through conceptual designation in relation to those [respective persons]. 'Not in truth' — not, however, in the ultimate sense. One single nature is spoken of as having both characters through designation superimposed by conceptualization [upon it] through [apparent] difference of form; but one single [thing] is never truly spoken of by multiple designations [as having genuinely different natures]. The genuine dual form of both [father and son] must be reconciled in a single [entity], and that is in no way possible, since through the bifurcation of two forms, even the thing itself would entail duality. Therefore, just as the genuine dual-formedness of a single [thing] does not exist in the illustration, and what does exist [there] is merely conceptual and is not useful for the subject at hand — this [argument] amounts to nothing.

body.text: ito 'pi na pāramārthiko 'yaṃ vyapadeśa ityāha sattvaṃ raja iti-
body.translated_text: Furthermore, showing that this designation is not ultimate, he says with '<s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>' and so forth —

body.text: sattvaṃ rajastamo vāpi na putro na pitā yataḥ /
body.translated_text: Since <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> are neither son nor father,

body.text: etacca avaśyaṃ tvayāpi svīkartavyam- sāṃkhyamate hi triguṇamekaṃ jagat, tataḥ sattvaṃ rajastamo vāpīti samudāyaḥ samuccayārthaḥ / yato yasmādete guṇāḥ svasvabhāvāvasthitāḥ pratyekaṃ samuditā vā / tasmānna pitā na putraḥ paramārthataḥ / sarvadā guṇā eva kevalāḥ santi / ayamarthaḥ- putrāvasthāyāṃ ye sattvarajastamolakṣaṇā guṇāḥ, te eva prāptajanakabhāvā api tena pūrvāparakālayoraviśiṣṭasvabhāvā eva / te tatastadapekṣya pitā putraścābhidhīyante, na tu tatra kaścidviśeṣaḥ / tataḥ kālpanika evāyaṃ vyavahāraḥ / yadi ca rūpagrahaṇakāle 'pi śabdagrahaṇātmakamekameva tajjñānam, tadā tatsvabhāvamupalabhyeta, na copalabhyate / tato na tadgrahaṇātmakamityāha śabdagrahaṇetyādi-
body.translated_text: And this must necessarily be accepted even by you: for in the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> view, the world consists of the single [principle] of the three <s>guṇas</s>. Therefore '<s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>' — the word 'and' is in the sense of conjunction. 'Since' — because — these <s>guṇas</s>, whether abiding in their own nature individually or taken together — therefore [one is] neither father nor son in the ultimate sense. At all times, only the <s>guṇas</s> alone exist. This is the meaning: the very <s>guṇas</s> characterized as <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> that [exist] in the state of being a son — those same [<s>guṇas</s>], even when they have attained the state of being a generator, are of undifferentiated nature in the prior and subsequent periods. They are called 'father' and 'son' merely in relation to those [respective states], but there is no real distinction therein. Therefore this designation is merely conceptual. And if at the time of apprehending form too, that cognition is one single thing whose nature is apprehension of sound, then that nature should be perceived — but it is not perceived. Therefore it is not of that nature — he says with 'the nature connected with apprehension of sound' and so forth —

body.text: śabdagrahaṇayuktastu svabhāvastasya nekṣyate // Bca_9.65 //
body.translated_text: The nature connected with apprehension of sound is not perceived in it. // <s>Bca</s> 9.65 //

body.text: śabdagrahaṇena yuktaḥ saṃbaddhaḥ / tuśabdo viśeṣābhidhāne / svabhāvastasya rūpagrāhakasya jñānasya nekṣyate na pratīyate / atastadā tasya śabdagrahaṇatā nāstīti niścīyate //
body.translated_text: 'Connected with apprehension of sound' — joined, related. The word 'but' indicates a specific point. The nature of that cognition — which apprehends form — 'is not perceived,' is not experienced. Therefore, at that time, it is determined that it does not have the character of apprehending sound.

body.text: syādetat- yadi nāma na pratīyate, tathāpi tadeva tat / kathaṃ tarhi rūpagrahaṇamityāha tadevetyādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: even if it is not perceived, still it is that very same [cognition]. How then does it apprehend form? He says with 'that same thing' and so forth —

body.text: tadevānyena rūpeṇa naṭavatso 'pyaśāśvataḥ /
body.translated_text: That same [cognition], in another form, like an actor — but even he is impermanent.

body.text: tadeva śabdajñānam / anyena rūpeṇa svabhāvena rūpagrahaṇātmakena rūpaṃ gṛhṇātīti śeṣaḥ / kathamiva tasyānurūpatā? naṭavat / yathā nāṭyasamaye raṅgabhūmigato naṭaḥ eka eva
body.translated_text: 'That same' — that very cognition of sound — 'in another form' — in another nature, one having the nature of apprehending form — apprehends form: this is to be supplied. How does the analogy apply? 'Like an actor.' Just as at the time of performance, an actor who has come to the stage, being one single [person],

body.text: nānārūpeṇāvatarati, tathā prakṛte 'pīti na doṣaḥ / atrāha- so 'pyaśāśvataḥ iti anityaḥ pūrvasvabhāvaparityāgena rūpāntaramāviśati / na ca pūrvāparakālayorekasvabhāva eva naṭo nānārūpasaṃbandhāt, anyathā tasya rūpadvayamekadeti bhāṣeta / iti sādhyavikalo dṛṣṭāntaḥ / athāpi syāt- bhāvaḥ sa eva / svabhāvaḥ punarasya aparāpara utpadyate nirudhyate ca / tataḥ ayamadoṣa ityatrāha sa evānyetyādi-
body.translated_text: takes on various forms — so too in the present case, there is no fault. To this he says: 'but even he is impermanent' — he is impermanent, abandoning his former nature and assuming another form. And the actor is not of one single nature in the prior and subsequent periods, because of his connection with different forms; otherwise, one would have to say that his two forms exist simultaneously. Thus the illustration lacks the property to be proved. But one might think: the entity is the same, but its nature arises and ceases in different ways. Therefore this is not a fault — to this he says with 'if that same' and so forth —

body.text: sa evānyasvabhāvaścedapūrveyaṃ tadekatā // Bca_9.66 //
body.translated_text: If it is the same yet of different natures, then this unity is unprecedented! // <s>Bca</s> 9.66 //

body.text: sa evātmā naṭo vā / anyasvabhāvaḥ aparasvabhāvaḥ / ced yadi ucyate, tadā apūrveyaṃ tadekatā, apūrveyamadṛṣṭapūrveyamīdṛśī tadekatā / tasya bhāvasya aparasvabhāvotpattāvapi ekatā abhinnātmatā / tathā hi- sa eveti tattvamākhyāyate, punaranyasvabhāva iti tasyaiva anyatvam / na caitat parasparaviruddhadharmadvayamekasya yuktam / na hi bhāvo nāma anya eva svabhāvāt, yena tasyotpādanirodhayorapi bhāvasya tau na syātām / nāpi tadabhinnasya svabhāvasya utpādanirodhayorbhāvasya tādavasthyaṃ yuktamabhedābhāvaprasaṅgāt / bhede vā saṃbandhāsiddhiriti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'The same' — that very self or actor. 'Of different nature' — of another nature. 'If' — if this is claimed, then this unity is unprecedented — this unity, such an identity, of that entity with the arising of another nature, is unprecedented — never seen before. For 'it is the same' declares the identity, while 'of different nature' declares its otherness. And these two mutually contradictory properties cannot belong to a single [thing]. For an entity is not something entirely different from its nature, such that even when that [nature] arises and ceases, those [changes] would not belong to the entity. Nor is it justified that the entity — which is non-different from its nature — remains in the same state when [its nature] arises and ceases, since there would be the absurd consequence of no difference [between the states]. Or, if there were [genuine] difference, the [claimed] relation would be unestablished — this is the meaning.

body.text: syādetat- bhavatveva eṣa prasaṅgaḥ yadi rūpadvayamasyātmanaḥ satyaṃ syāt / kiṃ tarhi nijamasya rūpamapahāya aparaṃ rūpamatāttvikam, tena noktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ, ityāśayamāśaṅkayannāha anyadrūpamityādi-
body.translated_text: One might think: let this consequence stand if the dual form of this self is real. But rather, abandoning its own form, it [takes on] another form that is unreal. Therefore the stated fault does not follow — anticipating this intention, he says with 'the other form' and so forth —

body.text: anyadrūpamasatyaṃ cennijaṃ tadrūpamucyatām /
body.translated_text: If the other form is unreal, then state its own form!

body.text: anyadrūpaṃ tadviṣayopādhikaṃ sphaṭikopalasyeva asatyamasvābhāvikam, iti cedyadi, tarhi nijaṃ tadrūpamucyatām nijaṃ svābhāvikaṃ tasyātmano rūpaṃ tattvamucyatām / astyevānyadrūpaṃ tasya / kiṃ tat? jñānatā cet-
body.translated_text: 'The other form' — that pertaining to the particular object — like [the appearance of] a crystal — 'is unreal,' not of its own nature — if this is claimed, then state its own form, its intrinsic form, its true nature! There does exist another form of it. What is that? If [you say] it is the nature of cognition —

body.text: jñānatā cettataḥ sarvapuṃsāmaikyaṃ prasajyate // Bca_9.67 //
body.translated_text: If it is the nature of cognition, then the unity of all persons would follow. // <s>Bca</s> 9.67 //

body.text: jñānātmataiva tasya pūrvāparakālānugāminī nijaṃ rūpam / kimanyadvaktavyam? [tadrūpeṇa pūrvāparānyarūpasaṃbandhe 'pi sphaṭikavad yadi eko 'stītyucyate, evaṃ sarvapuṃsāmaikyaṃ prasajyate, evaṃ jñānatvena tatsādhāraṇarūpatvāt / tadyathā pūrvaparakālikayoḥ śabdarūpajñānayorbhinnākāratvād bhinnayorapyekatvameva, tathā sarvasattvānāṃ prāṇigatigatānāmekātmatā prasajyate] āpadyate, vastuto bhede 'pi viśeṣābhāvāt //
body.translated_text: The very nature of cognition, which persists through prior and subsequent periods, is its own form. What else is there to say? [If one says that despite the connection with different forms in prior and subsequent periods, like a crystal, there is still a single entity, then] the unity of all persons would follow — would result — since that form [cognition] is the common nature [of all]. Just as two cognitions at different times — of sound and of form — though of different aspects, though different, are still identical [on this view], so the identity of all beings in all modes of rebirth would follow, since even despite real difference, there is no distinguishing feature [on this account].

body.text: itthaṃ ca punaridamatiprasajyate ityāha cetanetyādi-
body.translated_text: Furthermore, this too would additionally follow — he says with 'sentient and insentient' and so forth —

body.text: cetanācetane caikyaṃ tayoryenāstitā samā /
body.translated_text: And sentient and insentient would be one, since their existence is equal.

body.text: yadi vā avāntaraṃ bhedanibandhanaṃ viśeṣamapāsya kiṃcidākārakamāśritya ekatvamucyate tadā cetanā puruṣadharmaḥ, acetanā prakṛtyādidharmaḥ / cakāro doṣāntarasamuccaye / te 'pi ekamabhinnaṃ vastu syātām / katham? tayoścetanācetanayoḥ yena kāraṇena astitā samā / sāpi bhāvānāṃ nijaṃ rūpam / samā dvayorapi tulyā /
body.translated_text: Or, if unity is claimed on the basis of some aspect, setting aside the particular distinguishing feature that grounds the difference — then sentience is a property of <s>puruṣa</s>, and insentience is a property of <s>prakṛti</s> and such. The word 'and' is for conjoining another fault. Even those two would be one undifferentiated thing. How? Because their 'existence' — of the sentient and the insentient — is equal, since that [existence] too is the own form of things, and is equal, the same, for both.

body.text: nanu ca / atrāpi sādṛśyanibandhanamiṣyate eva ekatvaṃ vastubhede 'pi / tato 'yamiṣṭaprasādhanādadoṣa ityāha viśeṣaścetyādi-
body.translated_text: But here too the unity based on similarity is precisely what is intended, even when there is a real difference in things. Therefore this is not a fault, since it is merely [affirming what is] already accepted — he says with 'and when the distinction' and so forth —

body.text: viśeṣaśca yadā mithyā kaḥ sādṛśyāśrayastadā // Bca_9.68 //
body.translated_text: And when the distinction is false, what then is the basis for similarity? // <s>Bca</s> 9.68 //

body.text: dūṣaṇāntaradyotane cakāraḥ / viśeṣo bhedaḥ sarvabhāvānāmaniyamena yadā mithyā asatyam [tyaḥ?], nijameva rūpaṃ satyam, tadā kaḥ sādṛśyāśrayaḥ syāt? kimāśritya sādṛśyaṃ vyavasthāpyate? viśeṣasadbhāve hi kiṃcinmātrasādharmyeṇa sādṛśyaṃ syāt / viśeṣābhāve ca tadeva tat syānna sadṛśam / na hi gogavayayorgoviśeṣamananubhavan na gavayo gosadṛśo bhavet, api tu gaureva syāt / ato viśeṣa eva sādṛśyāśrayaḥ / sa ca yadā pāramārthiko na bhavati, tadā kaḥ sādṛśyasya samānākāratāyāḥ puṃsāmanyasya vā āśrayo nibandhanaṃ vā bhavet? naiva kaścidityarthaḥ / ato vastuta eva ekatvamāpatitaṃ bhavataḥ, na sādṛśyakṛtam / tat kathaṃ siddhasādhanādadoṣa ityucyate?
body.translated_text: The word 'and' is for introducing another objection. 'Distinction' — difference — of all things without restriction — 'when' it is 'false,' unreal — while the own form alone is real — then what would be the basis for similarity? On the basis of what would similarity be established? For when distinction really exists, similarity could be [based] on some partial commonality. But in the absence of distinction, that would simply be that very thing — not something similar. For a cow and a <s>gavaya</s> — one who does not experience the specific [difference of the] cow does not become [merely] 'cow-like' but would simply be a cow. Therefore distinction itself is the basis for similarity. And when that [distinction] is not ultimately real, then what basis — what ground — would there be for similarity, for having a common aspect, among persons or anything else? None whatsoever — this is the meaning. Therefore, an actual unity would result for you, not one based on similarity. How then can one say 'there is no fault since it merely [affirms what is] already accepted'?

body.text: evaṃ kāpila [jaina]jaiminīyaparikalpitasya citsvabhāvasyātmanaḥ sattvamasiddham / upaniṣadvādiparikalpite 'pi yathāsaṃbhavaṃ dūṣaṇamabhidheyamiti //
body.translated_text: Thus, the reality of the self postulated by the <s>Kāpilas</s> [<s>Sāṃkhyas</s>], <s>Jainas</s>, and <s>Jaiminīyas</s> as being of the nature of consciousness has been shown to be unestablished. Against the self postulated by the <s>Upaniṣad</s>-proponents too, the objection should be stated as applicable.

body.text: sāṃpratamacetanasya naiyāyikādiparikalpitasyātmanaḥ sadvayavahārapratiṣedhāyāha acetanaścetyādi-
body.translated_text: Now, to negate the conventional [designation of] the insentient self postulated by the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others, he says with 'and the insentient' and so forth —

body.text: acetanaśca naivāhamācaitanyātpaṭādivat /
body.translated_text: And the insentient [ātman] is certainly not the self, because of insentience — like cloth and such.

body.text: cetanastāvadātmā uktakrameṇa na yujyate / acetano 'pi naivāhamātmā yukta iti cakārārthaḥ / kutaḥ? ācaitanyāt caitanyābhāvāt / na vidyate cetanā asyetyacetanaḥ / tasya bhāvaḥ ācaitanyam / ubhayapadavṛddhiḥ pāralaukikādivat / tasmāt / acetanatvādityarthaḥ / kathamiva? paṭādivat / yathā paṭavṛkṣaparvatādayaḥ caitanyavirahādātmā na bhavanti, tathā abhimato 'pi / karmakartṛtvāderasyābhyupagamāt / anyathā na kiṃcit prayojanaṃ tena / na ca acetanasya tadyuktam, yathā paṭādeḥ / yadi nāma svayamasāvacetanaḥ, tathāpi buddheścetanā cetayate, tenāyamadoṣaḥ iti parābhiprāyaṃ saṃbhāvayannāha atha jña ityādi-
body.translated_text: The conscious self has already been shown to be unjustified in the manner stated. And the insentient [self] too is certainly not the self — the meaning of the word 'and.' Why? Because of insentience — because of the absence of sentience. 'That which has no sentience is insentient.' Its state is 'insentience.' Both words undergo <s>vṛddhi</s> [vowel strengthening], as in '<s>pāralaukika</s>' and such. Therefore — because of insentience — this is the meaning. Like what? 'Like cloth and such.' Just as cloth, tree, mountain, and such, due to the absence of sentience, are not the self — so too this postulated [self]. Because agency, experiencership, and such are accepted for it. Otherwise, there is no purpose whatsoever for it. Nor are those [properties] justified for what is insentient, as with cloth and such. 'But even if it is itself insentient, still, through the connection with <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), it becomes sentient; thereby this is not a fault' — entertaining the opponent's intent, he says with 'if it is a knower' and so forth —

body.text: atha jñaścetanāyogādajño naṣṭaḥ prasajyate // Bca_9.69 //
body.translated_text: If it becomes a knower through connection with sentience, then when unknowing, its destruction would follow. // <s>Bca</s> 9.69 //

body.text: atheti pṛcchāyām / athāyamātmā cetanāyogād buddhisamavāyāt svayamacetano 'pi jño bhavati / jānātīti jñaḥ iti kapratyayāntasya rūpam / evamupagamyamāne ajño naṣṭaḥ prasajyate / yadā tarhi madamūrcchāvasthāyāṃ cetanānivṛttau ayamātmā ajño na kiṃcidapi jānāti, tadā naṣṭaḥ prāktanacaitanyasaṃbaddhasvabhāvaparityāgādvinaṣṭaḥ prasajyate //
body.translated_text: 'If' (<s>atha</s>) — in a question. If this self, through connection with sentience — through conjunction with <s>buddhi</s> — though itself insentient, becomes a knower — 'one who knows': thus the form with the <s>ka</s>-suffix — if this is accepted, then when unknowing — when, in a state of intoxication, fainting, and such, sentience ceases — this self is unknowing, does not know anything at all — then its destruction would follow — its destruction, loss of its previous nature connected with sentience, would result.

body.text: caitanyasaṃbandhāsaṃbandhakālayorekasvabhāvatvānnāyaṃ doṣa iti paramāśaṅkayannāha athāvikṛta ityādi-
body.translated_text: Anticipating the opponent's objection — 'this is not a fault, since it is of one nature in both periods of connection and non-connection with sentience' — he says with 'if it is unmodified' and so forth —

body.text: athāvikṛta evātmā caitanyenāsya kiṃ kṛtam /
body.translated_text: If the self is unmodified, then what has sentience done for it?

body.text: atha caitanyotpādanirodhayoravikṛta eva anutpannāniruddhasvabhāva evātmā / yadyevam, tarhi caitanyenāsya kiṃ kṛtam, acetanasya sarvakālamavikṛtasya sataḥ asyātmanaḥ caitanyena buddhisamavāyena kiṃ kṛtam, kimatiśayādhānamanuṣṭhitam? na kiṃcit / buddhisamavāye 'pi tathaivāpracyutaprācyasvabhāvasya avasthānādacetana evātmā / tathā ca sati kimanuṣṭhitaṃ bhavadbhirityāha-
body.translated_text: If the self is unmodified — of unborn, undestroyed nature — during the arising and ceasing of sentience, then what has sentience done for it? For this self — which is insentient at all times, unmodified — what has sentience, the conjunction with <s>buddhi</s>, done — what superiority has it conferred? Nothing at all. Since even when there is conjunction with <s>buddhi</s>, the self, remaining in the same state with its previous nature unaltered, is simply insentient. This being the case, what have you accomplished? He says —

body.text: ajñasya niṣkriyasyaivamākāśasyātmatā matā // Bca_9.70 //
body.translated_text: Thus, for one that is unknowing and inactive, [it would have] the selfhood of space! // <s>Bca</s> 9.70 //

body.text: ajñasya kiṃcidapi hitāhitaṃ jñātumaśaktasya niṣkriyasya nirgato bahirbhūtaḥ kriyāyā iti niṣkriyaḥ / tasya sarvapratīkārarahitasya anādheyātiśayatayā asaṃskartavyasya / athavā sarvakarmaṇi śaktivikalasya gamanādhikriyāśūnyasya vā ākāśasya prakṛtānupayogitvādākāśakalpasya / evaṃ sati ātmatā ātmasvabhāvavyavasthā vyavasthāpitā / etacca svamatenodāharaṇam / yathā niḥsvabhāvatayā sarvakriyāśūnyaṃ prajñaptisanmātramākāśam, tathā ātmāpītyarthaḥ / paramatenāpi vā / yathā ca na karmakartrādirūpamākāśamacetanatvādakriyatvācca, tathā ātmapīti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Of one who is ignorant' — incapable of knowing anything beneficial or harmful — 'inactive' — having gone outside, become external to activity, hence 'inactive.' Of such a one, devoid of all remedy, who cannot receive any enhancement, who cannot be conditioned. Or alternatively, one who is devoid of capacity for all action, or who is void of the operation of movement and such. Like space, which by nature is useless — 'like space.' This being so, 'selfhood' — the determination of the nature of the self — has been established. And this is an illustration from one's own [i.e. the Buddhist] position: just as space, being devoid of intrinsic nature, void of all activity, is merely a designation — so too is the self, is the meaning. Or from the opponent's own position as well: just as space is not of the nature of agent, action, and such, due to being non-conscious and inactive, so too is the self — this is the purport.

body.text: idānīṃ punaranyathā ātmapratiṣedhabādhakaṃ paramatenotthāpayannāha na karmetyādi-
body.translated_text: Now, raising in another way an objection from the opponent's position that undermines the refutation of the self, he says 'the connection of action' and so forth:

body.text: na karmaphalasaṃbandho yuktaścedātmanā vinā /
body.translated_text: If the connection of action and result is not justified without a self —

body.text: yadi na kaścidekaḥ paralokī syāt, tadā tenātmanā paralokagāminā vinā antareṇa karmaphalasaṃbandho 'yuktaḥ / karma śubhāśubham, phalaṃ ca tasyaiva iṣṭāniṣṭalakṣaṇam, tayoḥ saṃbandhaḥ / karmaṇaḥ kṛtasya phalena vā saṃbandhaḥ / yenaiva kṛtaṃ karma, tasyaiva tatphalapratilambho nānyasyeti / na yukto na ghaṭate / iṣyate ca paraloke karmaphalasaṃbandhaḥ / tatra ca saugatānāmapyavivādaḥ / tathā ca sūtram-
body.translated_text: If there were not some single entity that transmigrates to the next world, then without that self — that transmigrator to the next world — the connection of action and result would be 'unjustified.' <s>Karma</s> — wholesome and unwholesome — and its result, characterized by the desired and undesired, of that very [self]; the connection of those two — of the <s>karma</s> that was done, with its result. Only the very one by whom the <s>karma</s> was done obtains its result, not another. It is not justified, does not cohere. And the connection of action and result in the next world is accepted. And therein even the <s>Saugatas</s> (Buddhists) have no dispute. Thus the <s>sūtra</s> states:

body.text: anenaiva kṛtaṃ karma, ko 'nyaḥ pratyanubhaviṣyati? na hi bhikṣavaḥ kṛtopacitāni karmāṇi pṛthivīdhātau vipacyante nābdhātau na tejodhātau na vāyudhātau / upātteṣveva skandhadhātvāyataneṣu............ iti vistaraḥ /
body.translated_text: 'The <s>karma</s> done by this very one — who else will experience it? For, monks, <s>karmas</s> that have been done and accumulated do not ripen in the earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element. They ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases...' Thus in detail.

body.text: uktaṃ ca-
body.translated_text: And it is said:

children.translated_text: Actions do not perish even in hundreds of crores of <s>kalpas</s>;

children.text: sāmagrīṃ prāpya kālaṃ ca phalanti khalu dehinām //
children.translated_text: having met with the assemblage [of conditions] and the [right] time, they assuredly bear fruit for embodied beings.

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: tataḥ karmaphalasaṃbandho 'nivārito bhavatāmapi / tasmādavaśyamaṅgīkartavya ātmā / anyathā sarvametadasaṃgataṃ syāt / kathamasati ātmani karmaphalasaṃbandho ghaṭate ityāha karma kṛtvetyādi-
body.translated_text: Therefore, the connection of action and result is unobstructed even for you. Hence a self must necessarily be accepted. Otherwise, all this would be incoherent. How, in the absence of a self, does the connection of action and result cohere? — he says 'having done the action' and so forth:

body.text: karma kṛtvā vinaṣṭe hi phalaṃ kasya bhaviṣyati // Bca_9.71 //
body.translated_text: For when the doer of the action has perished, whose will the result be? // Bca_9.71 //

body.text: hi yasmāt karma kṛtvā karmotpādya śubhāśubhalakṣaṇam / vinaṣṭe niruddhe sati karmakartari / phalaṃ kasya bhaviṣyati / ātmano 'sattve paralokagāminaḥ kasyacidabhāvāt / yena cittakṣaṇena kṛtaṃ karma, tasya kṣaṇikatayā tatkarmakriyākāle nivṛttatvāt, kṛtasya karmaṇaḥ phalaṃ sugatau durgatau vā sukhaduḥkhātmakaṃ kasya bhaviṣyati utpatsyate? naiva kasyacit syāt / paraloke ca kṛtakarmaṇa eva phalayogino 'nyasya kasyacidutpādāt, iti kṛtavipraṇāśo 'kṛtābhyāgamaśca syāt //
body.translated_text: 'For' (<s>hi</s>) — because. Having done, having produced <s>karma</s> characterized as wholesome or unwholesome — when the doer of that <s>karma</s> has perished, has ceased — whose will the result be? In the absence of a self, because there is no one who transmigrates to the next world. The mental moment by which the <s>karma</s> was done, since it is momentary and has ceased at the time of the action of that <s>karma</s> — the result of the <s>karma</s> that was done, whether happiness or suffering in fortunate or unfortunate destinies — whose will it arise? It would not be anyone's. And since in the next world, [the one who experiences the fruit] is someone other than the very doer of the <s>karma</s> and enjoyer of the fruit, there would be the fault of loss of what was done and the encountering of what was not done.

body.text: upalakṣaṇaṃ caitat / smṛtipratyabhijñānasaṃśayanirṇayasvayaṃnihitapratyanumārgaṇadṛṣṭārthakutūhalaviramaṇakāryakāraṇabhāvatadadhigatapramāṇabandhamokṣādayo 'pi na syuḥ cedyadi matam, tanna yuktamityāha dvayorityādi-
body.translated_text: And this is illustrative [of further implications]. Memory, recognition, doubt, determination, the retrieval of what was self-deposited, curiosity about what was previously seen, cessation, causality, the valid cognition that ascertains them, bondage, liberation, and such would also not exist. If this is your view, that it is not justified — he says 'for both of us' and so forth:

body.text: dvayorapyāvayoḥ siddhe bhinnādhāre kriyāphale /
body.translated_text: Since for both of us it is established that the basis of action and result is different —

body.text: dvayorapyāvayoḥ / ātmavādino bhavataḥ, mama ca nairātmyavādinaḥ / siddhe niścite / ke siddhe? āhabhinnādhāre kriyāphale karma kriyā asmin bhave, tasyāḥ phalaṃ paraloke / te bhinnādhāre nānādhikaraṇe siddhe / tathāhi- na yenaiva śarīreṇa tasmin janmani karma karoti, tenaiva pretya phalamupabhuṅkte / ataḥ anyadeva karmakartṛ, tadanyacca phalabhoktṛ / ato bhinnādhāre kriyāphale bhavataḥ / atra ca avipratipattirāvayoḥ / syādetat- ātmavyāpāramantareṇa te eva kartṛtvopabhoktṛtve na syātāmityatrāha-
body.translated_text: 'For both of us' — for you, the proponent of the self, and for me, the proponent of selflessness. 'Established' — ascertained. What is established? — he says: 'the basis of action and result is different.' <s>Karma</s>, action, in this life; the result of that, in the next world. Their basis is different — of different locus. This is established. For indeed, one does not perform <s>karma</s> with the very body in that life with which one experiences the result after dying. Therefore, the doer of <s>karma</s> is one, and the enjoyer of the result is another. Thus, the basis of action and result is different for you. And in this, there is no disagreement between us. One might think: without the operation of a self, those very agencies of doing and experiencing would not exist — to this he says:

body.text: nirvyāpāraśca tatrātmetyatra vādo vṛthā nanu // Bca_9.72 //
body.translated_text: And since the self is inactive therein, is not the dispute futile? // Bca_9.72 //

body.text: nirvyāpāro vyāpārarahitaḥ / tatra tayoḥ karmakriyāphalopabhogayoḥ ātmā niṣkriyatvādacetanatvāt / nityatvānna kvacidapi kriyāyāṃ samarthaḥ / yadapyuktam-
body.translated_text: 'Inactive' — devoid of operation. 'Therein' — in those two: the performance of <s>karma</s> and the enjoyment of its result. The self [is inactive] due to its being devoid of activity and non-conscious. Being eternal, it is not capable of any action whatsoever. And what was stated:

children.translated_text: 'The connection with mere cognition and such is declared to be its agency;
the conjunction with the experience of pleasure, suffering, and such is its enjoyer-ship.'

body.text: iti / [tattvasaṃgraha-176]
body.translated_text: [<s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 176]

body.text: tadapi pūrvāparakālayoravicalitasvabhāvasya uktakrameṇa na saṃgacchate / iti hetoratrātmani nirvyāpāre vādo vivādo vṛthā niṣphalaḥ / yadarthamasāvaṅgīkṛtaḥ, tatra tasyānupayogitvāt / nanviti parasaṃbodhane //
body.translated_text: That too does not cohere in the manner stated for [a self] whose nature is unchanged in the earlier and later periods. Therefore, for this reason — when the self is inactive therein — the dispute, the debate, is futile, fruitless; since for the purpose for which it was accepted, it is useless therein. 'Nanu' is for addressing the other [party].

body.text: nanu yadi ātmā na bhavet, kathaṃ tarhi kṛtavipraṇāśādidoṣo na syāt? tato na vṛthā tadvāda ityāha hetumānityādi-
body.translated_text: But if the self does not exist, then how would the fault of loss of what was done and such not arise? Therefore the dispute about it is not futile — he says 'connected with cause' and so forth:

body.text: hetumān phalayogīti dṛśyate naiṣa saṃbhavaḥ /
body.translated_text: 'The one connected with cause is the enjoyer of result' — this is not seen to be possible.

body.text: yo hetumān karmaṇā yuktaḥ, sa eva phālayogī phalasaṃbaddhaḥ iti evameṣa saṃbhavo na dṛśyate, nopalabhyate / yasmāt-
body.translated_text: The very one who is connected with <s>karma</s>, connected with cause, is the enjoyer of result, connected with the fruit — this possibility is not seen, is not found. Because:

body.text: anya eva mṛto loke jāyate anya eva hi /
body.translated_text: Indeed, the one who dies in this world, and the one who is born — they are different.

body.text: tato hetumataḥ phalayogo na dṛśyate / etattarhi kathaṃ nīyate yaduktam- anenaiva kṛtaṃ karma, ko 'nyaḥ pratyanubhaviṣyatīti? atrāha saṃtānasyetyādi-
body.translated_text: Therefore, the connection of the one possessing cause with its result is not observed. Well then, how is it to be understood, what was stated: 'the <s>karma</s> done by this very one — who else will experience it?' To this he says 'relying on the unity' and so forth:

body.text: saṃtānasyaikyamāśritya kartā bhokteti deśitam // Bca_9.73 //
body.translated_text: Relying on the unity of the continuum, it is taught that the doer is the enjoyer. // Bca_9.73 //

body.text: saṃtānasya uttarottarānekakṣaṇaparaṃparālakṣaṇasya kāryakāraṇabhāve na pravartamānasya aikyamāśritya anekeṣu ekatvaṃ lokādhyavasāyavaśādāropitameva nimittīkṛtya kartā bhoktā iti deśitam- ya eva karmaṇaḥ kartā sa eva tatphalasyopabhoktā ca / ityetaddeśitatve 'pi neyābhiprāyavaśāt bhagavatā prakāśitam / anyathā karmaphalocchedaṃ manyeta janaḥ / na tu tāvatā ubhayalokānugāminaḥ sattvamākhyātam / ata eva ca tatraivoktam- upātteṣveva skandhadhātvāyataneṣu vipacyante iti / tathā cetanā karma, cetayitvā karma iti vacanācca / taduktam-
body.translated_text: 'Of the continuum' — characterized by an unbroken succession of numerous successive moments, not operating through causality [of a permanent entity] — 'relying on its unity' — taking as the basis a oneness that is merely superimposed through the force of worldly determination upon what is in fact many — it is taught: 'the doer is the enjoyer' — 'the very one who is the agent of <s>karma</s> is also the enjoyer of its fruit.' Even in this being taught, it was disclosed by the Blessed One with a provisional intent. Otherwise, people would think that <s>karma</s> and its fruit are annihilated. But for that much, no entity that continues through both worlds has been declared. For this very reason it was stated there: 'they ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.' And also because of the statement: '<s>Cetanā</s> (volition) is <s>karma</s>; having willed, there is <s>karma</s>.' As it is said:

children.text: karmajaṃ lokavaicitryaṃ cetanā tatkṛtaṃ ca tat /
children.translated_text: The diversity of the world is born from <s>karma</s>; <s>cetanā</s> (volition) and what is produced by it — that is <s>karma</s>;
<s>cetanā</s> is mental <s>karma</s>; from it arise verbal and bodily actions.

body.text: iti / [abhi. ko. 4.1]
body.translated_text: [<s>Abhidharmakośa</s> 4.1]

body.text: anyatrāpyuktam-
body.translated_text: It is also said elsewhere:

children.translated_text: Mind alone creates the sentient world and the world-vessel, supremely marvelous;

children.text: karmajaṃ hi jagaduktamaśeṣaṃ karma cittamavadhūya na cāsti //
children.translated_text: for the entire world is said to be born from <s>karma</s>, and <s>karma</s>, setting aside mind, does not exist.

body.text: iti / [ma. a. 6.89]
body.translated_text: [<s>Madhyamakāvatāra</s> 6.89]

body.text: tasmānna cittavinirmuktamanyat karmāsti / tacca kuśalākuśalaṃ cittamutpadya nirudhyamānaṃ svopādeyacittakṣaṇe kuśalākuśalādisaṃskāraviśeṣavāsanāmādadhāti / tadapi tadāhitavāsanamuttarottaratadabhisaṃskṛtakṣaṇaparaṃparāvicchedataḥ saṃtānapravartamānaṃ pariṇativiśeṣamupagacchat karmaviśeṣānurūpaṃ tathāvidhaṃ sukhādisvabhāvaṃ cittātmakameva phalamabhinirvartayati paraloke / tadyathā kṣitibījādayaḥ parasparopasarpaṇapratyayaviśeṣāt samadhigatātiśayatayā prathamakṣaṇopanipātinaḥ svopādeyabhūtadvitīyakṣaṇakalāpe kāryotpādānuguṇaviśeṣotpādanadvāreṇa taduttarottaratāratamyamupajanayantaḥ saṃtatipariṇāmaviśeṣādantyakṣaṇalakṣaṇaṃ prakarṣaparyantamāsādayanto bījānurūpaśālikodravāṅkuramutpādayanti / yathā ca lākṣārasaparibhāvitaṃ mātuluṅgādibījamuptaṃ tatsaṃskāraparaṃparāpravṛtteḥ tatpuṣpādiṣu raktatāmutpādayati, na ca tatra kaścit pūrvāparakālayoreko 'nugāmī samasti / tacca kuśalākuśalasamānasyāpi (?) kalpanopasthāpitatvāt nopanyāso yuktaḥ / taduktam-
body.translated_text: Therefore, no <s>karma</s> exists apart from mind. And that wholesome or unwholesome mind, arising and ceasing, deposits in the immediately succeeding mental moment a particular impression of wholesome, unwholesome, and such formations. That too, bearing the deposited impression, through the unbroken succession of successive moments conditioned by it, proceeding as a continuum, undergoing particular transformations, produces — in the next world — a result that is of the nature of mind alone, characterized by happiness and such, in accordance with the particular <s>karma</s>. Just as earth, seeds, and such, through the particular condition of their mutual proximity, having attained enhancement, in the immediately succeeding second moment-aggregate — which is their product — through producing the particular [qualities] conducive to the production of the effect, and generating increasing degrees of intensification in successive [moments], from the particular transformation of the continuum reaching the culmination of development characterized by the final moment, produce a sprout of rice or millet in accordance with the seed. And just as a citron seed and such, permeated by lac juice, when sown, through the continuation of that conditioning, produces redness in its flowers and such — yet in none of this is there a single entity that persists through the earlier and later periods. Nor is it appropriate to adduce the equal applicability [of this argument] to the other [position, i.e. the self], since that [self] is merely set up by conceptual construction (?). As it is said:

children.translated_text: In the very continuum in which the impression of <s>karma</s> was deposited,

children.text: phalaṃ tatraiva badhnāti karpāse raktatā yathā //
children.translated_text: the fruit manifests there alone — just as redness [manifests] in cotton.

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: tasmādyathā bījādiṣu ātmānamantareṇāpi pratiniyamena kāryaṃ tadutpattiśca krameṇa bhavati, tathā prakṛte 'pi paralokagāminamekaṃ vināpi kāryakāraṇabhāvasya niyāmakatvāt pratiniyatameva phalam, kleśakarmābhisaṃskṛtasya saṃtānasya avicchedena pravartanāt paraloke phalapratilambho 'bhidhīyate, iti nākṛtābhyāgamo na kṛtavipraṇāśo bādhakam / tato nātmānamantareṇa karmaphalasaṃbandho na yujyate / yathā ca satyevātmani sa na ghaṭate, tathā sapracayamucyamānamativistaraṃ syāditi neha pratanyate // āha ca-
body.translated_text: Therefore, just as in seeds and such, even without a self, effect-production and its arising occur determinately in regular sequence, so too in the present case, even without a single transmigrator to the next world, since the causal relation itself is the determinant, the result is perfectly determinate — because the continuum conditioned by afflictions and <s>karma</s> proceeds without interruption, the obtaining of the result in the next world is stated. Thus, neither the encountering of what was not done nor the loss of what was done constitutes an objection. Hence it is not the case that the connection of action and result is not justified without a self. And how, even when a self does exist, that [connection] does not cohere — that, if stated with [all its] ramifications, would be excessively lengthy, and so is not extended here.

children.translated_text: There is no self; there are merely aggregates, conditioned by afflictions and <s>karma</s>;
through the continuum of the intermediate existence, [the being] enters the womb, like a lamp.

body.text: iti // [abhi. ko.]
body.translated_text: [<s>Abhidharmakośa</s>]

body.text: pudgalatadvādibhistattvānyatvapratiṣedhapakṣābhyupagamāt svayameva vastutvaṃ pratiṣiddham / vastuno hi tattvānyatvaprakārānatikramāt, parasparaparihāravatorekapratiṣedhāparavidhināntarīyakatvāt / bhārahārādisūtramapi samarthitamatrārthe / tasmādābhiprāyikīṃ bhagavato deśanāmajānadbhiḥ parikalpito 'sau, na vastusat / vastutvābhyupagame nānyatvam, ityātmano nirākaraṇenaiva nirastaḥ, iti na punarviśeṣeṇa pratiṣedhitaḥ / uktaṃ caitadbhagavatā-
body.translated_text: By the <s>Pudgalavādins</s> and their followers, through accepting the position of neither identity nor difference, the real existence [of the <s>pudgala</s>] has been refuted by themselves. For since a real thing cannot transcend the modes of identity and difference, the denial of one being necessarily entailed by the affirmation of the other — and vice versa. The <s>Bhārahāra</s> (Burden-Bearer) <s>sūtra</s> and such have also been interpreted in this sense. Therefore, that [<s>pudgala</s>] was conceptually constructed by those who do not understand the intentional teaching of the Blessed One — it is not a real thing. If its real existence were accepted, there could be no difference [from the self] — therefore, by the very refutation of the self, it is refuted. Thus it has not been specifically refuted again. And the Blessed One stated this:

body.text: iti hi bhikṣavaḥ asti karma, asti phalam / kārakastu nopalabhyate ya imān skandhān vijahāti, anyāṃśca skandhānupādatte, anyatra dharmasaṃketāt / atrāyaṃ dharmasaṃketaḥ, yadasmin sati idaṃ bhavati, asyotpādādidamutpadyate iti //
body.translated_text: 'Indeed, monks, there is <s>karma</s>, there is result. But no agent is found who abandons these aggregates and takes up other aggregates — except through the convention of <s>dharmas</s>. Herein, this is the convention of <s>dharmas</s>: when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises.'

body.text: etena bhagavataiva idaṃpratyayatāmātralakṣaṇaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvo 'pi darśita eva / ayamapi ca saṃtānasyetyanena [saṃtāna eka ityanena] yathāvyavahāramanirūpitasvarūpaḥ sūcita eva, saṃtānavacanena idaṃpratyayatāmātrasyābhyupagamāt / anyathā saṃtāna eva na syāt / tena vāstavakāryakāraṇabhāvabhāvino doṣā nāvalīyante / idameva ācāryapādairapyuktam-
body.translated_text: By this, the Blessed One himself has shown that the causal relation too is characterized merely by conditionality. Moreover, by this [verse] 'relying on the unity of the continuum,' it is indicated that [the continuum's unity] is of unexamined nature, [posited] in accordance with convention — since by the word 'continuum,' mere conditionality alone is accepted. Otherwise, there would be no continuum at all. Therefore, the faults that attend upon real causal efficacy do not attach [to our position]. This very point was stated by the Master as well:

children.translated_text: 'If everything is powerless' — if [one objects:] regarding seeds and such in relation to sprouts and such,

children.text: dṛṣṭā śaktirmatā sā cetsaṃvṛtyāstu yathā tathā //
children.translated_text: power is observed; if that [power] is accepted, let it be conventionally, just as it is.

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: kāryakāraṇabhāvapratiniyamādeva smṛtyabhāvo 'pi nirastaḥ / ekasyānugamātmano 'bhāvāt na smartā kaścidiha vidyate, kiṃ tarhi smaraṇameva kevalamāropavaśāt smaryamāṇavastuviṣayam / na ca atra smarturabhāve 'pi kaścid vyāghātaḥ / anubhūte hi vastuni vijñānasaṃtāne smṛtibījādhānāt kālāntareṇa saṃtatiparipākahetoḥ smaraṇaṃ nāma kāryamutpadyate / evaṃ pratyabhijñānādayo 'pi draṣṭavyāḥ / ativistarabhayāt pratyekamiha na pratividhīyante iti tatsamarthanamanyatraiva vistareṇāvadhāryamiti //
body.translated_text: Through the very determinacy of causal relation, the absence of memory [as an objection] is also refuted. Since there is no single persisting self, there is no 'rememberer' here; but rather, there is merely remembering alone, through the force of superimposition, having as its object the thing remembered. Nor is there any contradiction in the absence of a rememberer. For when an impression that is the seed of memory has been deposited in the cognitive continuum regarding a thing that was experienced, after some time, through the cause of the maturation of the continuum, the effect called 'remembering' arises. Thus recognition and such should also be viewed. Due to fear of excessive length, each is not individually addressed here; therefore their justification should be ascertained in detail elsewhere.

body.text: sarvametat saṃvṛtisatyamupādāya samarthitam / paramārthe tu sarvadharmāṇāṃ niḥsvabhāvatvāt sarvavikalpoparamācca na kiṃcidutpadyate vā nirudhyate vā sātmakamanātmakaṃ vā / nāpi vicāryamāṇaṃ karma tatphalaṃ vā, nāpi ihaloko na paraloko vā na kaścidasti, kalpanāviṭhapitatvāt / tasmāt sarvametat pratibimbasaṃnibhaṃ niḥsvabhāvamutpadyate nirudhyate ca / kāryakāraṇaṃ ca sātmakaṃ nirātmakaṃ ca nityamanityaṃ cābhidhīyate / svapnavat karmakartṛtvam, tatphalopabhogaḥ, ihalokaḥ, paralokaḥ, sugatidurgatigamanaṃ ca kalpanānāmaprahāṇāt / iti sarvatra sustham / yadvakṣyati-
body.translated_text: All this has been established relying upon <s>saṃvṛtisatya</s> (conventional truth). But in the ultimate sense, since all <s>dharmas</s> are devoid of intrinsic nature and all conceptualization has ceased, nothing arises or ceases, nothing is with self or without self. Nor is <s>karma</s> or its fruit to be analyzed; nor does this world or the next world exist, nor does anyone exist — because all is fabricated by conceptualization. Therefore, all this, resembling a reflection, devoid of intrinsic nature, arises and ceases. Cause and effect are called 'with self' and 'without self,' 'permanent' and 'impermanent.' Like a dream: agency of action, the enjoyment of its fruit, this world, the next world, and going to good or bad destinies — [all persist] from the non-abandonment of conceptualization. Thus all is well-established. As will be stated —

children.text: evaṃ na ca nirodho 'sti na ca bhāvo 'sti tattvataḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Thus, in reality, there is neither cessation nor existence;
unborn and unceased — therefore is this entire world.'

body.text: svapnopamāstu gatayo vicāre kadalīsamāḥ /

children.translated_text: And so forth. [Bodhi. 9.151-52]

body.translated_text: 'The states of existence are like a dream; upon analysis, like a plantain tree.'

body.text: uktaṃ ca-
body.translated_text: And it is said —

children.translated_text: 'The agent is autonomous, and action too — you have stated [these] conventionally;
but their establishment depends mutually upon each other, according to your accepted [system].'

children.text: na kartāsti na bhoktāsti puṇyāpuṇyaṃ pratītyajam /
children.translated_text: 'There is no agent, no experiencer — merit and demerit arise dependently;

children.text: yatpratītya na tajjātaṃ proktaṃ vācaspate tvayā //
children.translated_text: what arises dependently is not [truly] born — thus have You, Lord of Speech, declared.'

body.text: iti / [catuḥ 2.8-9]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Catuḥstava</s> 2.8-9]

body.text: yathā nirātmānaśca sarve dharmāḥ karmaphalasaṃbandhāvirodhaśca, niḥsvabhāvatā ca, yathā dṛṣṭasarvadharmāvirodhaśca, tathā pitāputrasamāgame deśitam / taduktam-
body.translated_text: How all <s>dharmas</s> are without self, yet the connection of <s>karma</s> and its fruit is unimpeded; and how [there is] absence of intrinsic nature, yet non-contradiction with all seen <s>dharmas</s> — all this has been taught in the <s>Pitāputrasamāgama</s>. As stated —

body.text: bhagavānāha- evameva mahārāja bālo 'śrutavān pṛthagjanaścakṣuṣā rūpāṇi dṛṣṭvā saumanasyasthānīyāni abhiniviśate / so 'bhiniviṣṭaḥ samanunīyate / samanunītaḥ saṃrajyate / saṃrakto rāgajaṃ karmābhisaṃskaroti trividhaṃ kāyena, caturvidhaṃ vācā, [trividhaṃ manasā] / tacca karmābhisaṃskṛtamādita eva kṣīṇaṃ niruddhaṃ vigataṃ vipariṇataṃ na pūrvāṃ diśaṃ niśritya tiṣṭhati, na dakṣiṇām, na paścimām, nottarām, nordhvam, nādhaḥ, nānuvidiśam, neha, na tiryak, nobhayamantarā / tat punaḥ kālāntareṇa maraṇakālasamaye pratyupasthite jīvitendriyanirodhe āyuṣaḥ parikṣayāt tatsabhāgasya karmaṇaḥ kṣīṇatvāt caramavijñānasya nirudhyamānasya manasa ārambaṇībhavati / tadyathāpi nāma śayitavibuddhasya janapadakalyāṇī / iti hi mahārāja caramavijñānenādhipatinā tena ca karmārambaṇena aupapattyaṃśikaṃ dvayapratyayaṃ prathamaṃ vijñānamutpadyate / yadi vā nārakeṣu, yadi vā tiryagyonau, yadi vā yamaloke, yadi vā āsurakāye, yadi vā manuṣyeṣu, yadi vā deveṣu / tasya ca prathamavijñānasya aupapattyaṃśikasya samanantaraniruddhasya anantaraṃ sabhāgā cittasaṃtatiḥ pravartate, yatra vipākasya
body.translated_text: The Blessed One said: 'Just so, Great King, a foolish, unlearned ordinary person, having seen forms with the eye — forms that are a basis for pleasant feeling — clings to them. Having clung, he is gratified. Being gratified, he becomes attached. Being attached, he produces <s>karma</s> born of attachment — threefold by body, fourfold by speech, [threefold by mind]. And that <s>karma</s>, once produced, is from the very start exhausted, ceased, gone, transformed; it does not abide depending on the eastern direction, nor the southern, nor the western, nor the northern, nor above, nor below, nor in the intermediate directions, nor here, nor transversely, nor in between the two. But then, at the time of death, when the end of life has arrived, through the exhaustion of life-force, through the exhaustion of <s>karma</s> of similar class, as the final consciousness is ceasing, it becomes the object of the mind. Just as a beautiful woman of the countryside [appears] to one who has awakened from sleep. Thus, Great King, with the final consciousness as the dominant [factor] and that <s>karma</s> as the object, the first consciousness that belongs to the rebirth-moment, conditioned by both, arises — whether among hell-beings, or in the animal realm, or in the world of <s>Yama</s>, or in the <s>Asura</s> body, or among humans, or among gods. And immediately after the cessation of that first consciousness belonging to the rebirth-moment, a homogeneous mental continuum proceeds, in which the ripening [of karma]

body.text:
pratisaṃvidā prajñāyate / tatra yaścaramavijñānasya nirodhaḥ, tatra cyutiriti saṃkhyā bhavati, yaḥ prathamavijñānasya prādurbhāvaḥ, tatropapattiriti / iti mahārāja na kaściddharmo 'smāllokāt paralokaṃ gacchati, cyutyupapattī prajñāyete / tacca mahārāja caramavijñānamutpadyamānaṃ na kutaścidāgacchati, nirudhyamānaṃ na kvacidgacchati / karmāpyutpadyamānaṃ na kutaścidāgacchati, nirudhyamānaṃ na kvacidgacchati / [prathamavijñānamapyutpadyamānaṃ na kutaścidāgacchati, nirudhyamānaṃ na kvacidgacchati] / tat kasya hetoḥ? svabhāvavirahitatvāt / caramavijñānaṃ caramavijñānena śūnyam, karma karmaṇā śūnyam, prathamavijñānaṃ prathamavijñānena śūnyam, cyutiścyutyā śūnyā, upapattirupapattyā śūnyā / karmaṇāṃ ca avandhyatā prajñāyate, vipākasya ca pratisaṃvedanā
/ na tatra kaścit kartā, na bhoktā, anyatra nāmasaṃketāt // iti vistaraḥ //
body.translated_text:
is discerned through discriminative knowledge. Therein, the cessation of the final consciousness — that is reckoned as 'death'; the manifestation of the first consciousness — that is [reckoned as] 'rebirth.' Thus, Great King, no <s>dharma</s> whatsoever goes from this world to the next world, yet death and rebirth are discerned. And, Great King, that final consciousness, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go anywhere. <s>Karma</s> too, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, does not go anywhere. [The first consciousness too, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, does not go anywhere.] Why? Because of being devoid of intrinsic nature. The final consciousness is empty of the final consciousness; <s>karma</s> is empty of <s>karma</s>; the first consciousness is empty of the first consciousness; death is empty of death; rebirth is empty of rebirth. Yet the non-barrenness of <s>karmas</s> is discerned, and the experiencing of the ripening [is discerned].
There is no agent, no experiencer — except for [mere] conventional designation.' Thus in detail. //

body.text: evaṃ dveṣamohābhyāmapi karmābhisaṃskaraṇaṃ yathāyogyaṃ vācyamiti //
body.translated_text: Thus, the production of <s>karma</s> through hatred and delusion too should be stated as appropriate. //

body.text: śālistambasūtre 'pyuktam-
body.translated_text: In the <s>Śālistambasūtra</s> too it is said —

body.text: punaraparaṃ tattve 'pratipattirmithyāpratipattirajñānamavidyā / evamavidyāyāṃ satyāṃ trividhāḥ saṃskārā abhinirvartante puṇyopagāḥ, apuṇyopagāḥ ānañjayopagāśca / ime ucyante avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārā iti / puṇyopagānāṃ saṃskārāṇāṃ puṇyopagameva vijñānaṃ bhavati, apuṇyopagānāṃ saṃskārāṇāmapuṇyopagameva vijñānaṃ bhavati, ānañjyopagānāṃ saṃskārāṇāmānañjyopagameva vijñānaṃ bhavati / idamucyate saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānamiti / tadeva vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam / nāmarūpavivṛddhyā ṣaḍbhirāyatanadvāraiḥ kṛtyakriyāḥ pravartante, tannāmarūpapratyayaṃ ṣaḍāyatanamucyate / ṣaḍbhya āyatanebhyaḥ ṣaṭ sparśakāyāḥ pravartante / ayaṃ ṣaḍāyatanapratyayaḥ sparśa ityucyate / yajjātīyaḥ sparśo bhavati tajjātīyā vedanā pravartate / iyaṃ sparśapratyayā vedanetyucyate / yastāṃ vedayati, viśeṣeṇāsvādayati, abhinandayati, adhyavasyati, adhitiṣṭhati, sā vedanāpratyayā tṛṣṇetyucyate / āsvadanā, abhinandanā, adhyavasāyasthānam, ātmapriyarūpasātarūpairviyogo mā bhavatviti aparityāgo bhūyo bhūyaśca prārthanā, idaṃ tṛṣṇāpratyayamupādānamityucyate / evaṃ prārthayamānaḥ punarbhavajanakaṃ karma samutthāpayatti kāyena vācā manasā, sa upādānapratyayo bhava ityucyate / tatkarmanirjātānāṃ pañcaskandhānāmabhinirvṛttiryā, sā bhavapratyayā jātirityucyate / yā (yo) jātyabhinirvṛttānāṃ skandhānāmupacayaparipākādvināśo bhavati, tadidaṃ jātipratyayaṃ jarāmaraṇamityucyate / peyālaṃ / tatra vijñānaṃ bījasvabhāvatvena hetuḥ / karma kṣetrasvabhāvatvena hetuḥ / avidyā tṛṣṇā ca kleśasvabhāvatvena hetuḥ / karmakleśā vijñānabījaṃ saṃjanayanti / tatra karma vijñānabījasya kṣetrakāryaṃ karoti / tṛṣṇā vijñānabījaṃ snehayati / avidyā vijñānabījamavakirati / asatāmeṣāṃ pratyayānāṃ vijñānabījasyābhinirvṛttirna bhavati / tatra karmaṇāṃ naivaṃ bhavati- ahaṃ vijñānabījasya kṣetrakāryaṃ karomi /
body.translated_text: 'Furthermore, non-comprehension of reality, wrong comprehension, and unknowing — this is ignorance. When ignorance exists, three kinds of formations are produced: those tending toward merit, those tending toward demerit, and those tending toward the imperturbable. These are called formations conditioned by ignorance. The consciousness of meritorious formations is meritorious; the consciousness of demeritorious formations is demeritorious; the consciousness of imperturbable formations is imperturbable. This is called consciousness conditioned by formations. That consciousness itself conditions name-and-form. Through the development of name-and-form, activities proceed through six sense-door faculties — that is called the six sense-bases conditioned by name-and-form. From the six sense-bases, six classes of contact proceed — this is called contact conditioned by the six sense-bases. Whatever kind the contact is, that kind of feeling proceeds — this is called feeling conditioned by contact. One who experiences that [feeling], relishes it particularly, delights in it, determines it, abides in it — that is called craving conditioned by feeling. Relishing, delighting, the ground of determination, [the wish that] there be no separation from what is dear and pleasant to oneself — non-relinquishment, repeated longing — this is called appropriation conditioned by craving. Thus longing, one produces <s>karma</s> that generates rebirth through body, speech, and mind — that is called existence conditioned by appropriation.
