The full production of the five aggregates born from that <s>karma</s> — that is called birth conditioned by existence. The destruction that occurs from the growth and maturation of the aggregates produced by birth — that is called aging-and-death conditioned by birth.' And so forth. 'Therein, consciousness has the nature of a seed — it is a cause. <s>Karma</s> has the nature of a field — it is a cause. Ignorance and craving have the nature of afflictions — they are causes. Afflictions and <s>karma</s> generate the seed of consciousness. <s>Karma</s> performs the function of a field for the seed of consciousness. Craving moistens the seed of consciousness. Ignorance scatters the seed of consciousness. In the absence of these conditions, the production of the seed of consciousness does not occur. The <s>karmas</s> do not think thus: "I perform the function of a field for the seed of consciousness."

body.text:
tṛṣṇāyāṃ api naivaṃ bhavati- ahaṃ vijñānabījaṃ snehayāmīti / avidyāyā api naivaṃ bhavati- ahaṃ vijñānabījamavakirāmīti / vijñānabījasyāpi naivaṃ bhavati- ahamebhiḥ pratyayairjanitamiti / api tu vijñānabījaṃ karmakṣetrapratiṣṭhitaṃ tṛṣṇāsnehābhisyanditam avidyāvakīrṇaṃ virohati,
nāmarūpāṅkurasyābhinirvṛttirbhavati / sa ca nāmarūpāṅkuro na svayaṃkṛto na parakṛto nobhayakṛto neśvaranirmito na kālapariṇāmito na caikakāraṇādhīno nāpyahetusamutpannaḥ / atha ca mātāpitṛsaṃyogādṛtusamavāyādanyeṣāṃ ca pratyayānāṃ samavāyādāsvādanānuprabaddhaṃ vijñānabījaṃ tatratatropapattyāyatanapratisaṃdhau mātuḥ kukṣau nāmarūpāṅkuramabhinirvartayati asvāmikeṣu dharmeṣu amameṣu aparigraheṣu apratyarthikeṣu ākāśasameṣu māyālakṣaṇasvabhāveṣu hetupratyayānāmavaikalyāt / peyālaṃ / na tatra kaściddharmo 'smāllokāt paralokaṃ saṃkrāmati / asti ca karmaphalam, asti ca vijñaptiḥ, hetupratyayānā mavaikalyāt / peyālaṃ / yathā agnirupādānavaikalyānna jvalati, upādānāvaikalyācca jvalati, evameva karmakleśajanitaṃ vijñānabījaṃ tatratatropapattyāyatanapratisaṃdhau mātuḥ kukṣau nāmarūpāṅkuramabhinirvartayati asvāmikeṣu dharmeṣu amameṣu aparigraheṣu apratyarthikeṣu ākāśasameṣu māyālakṣaṇasvabhāveṣu hetupratyayānāmavaikalyāt / evamādhyātmikasya pratītyasamutpādasya pratyayopanibandho draṣṭavyaḥ //
body.translated_text:
Craving too does not think thus: "I moisten the seed of consciousness." Ignorance too does not think thus: "I scatter the seed of consciousness." The seed of consciousness too does not think thus: "I am generated by these conditions." Rather, the seed of consciousness — established in the field of <s>karma</s>, moistened by the moisture of craving, scattered by ignorance — sprouts,
and the production of the sprout of name-and-form occurs. And that sprout of name-and-form is not self-made, not other-made, not made by both, not created by God, not transformed by time, not dependent on a single cause, nor arisen without a cause. Rather, from the conjunction of mother and father, from the conjunction of the season, and from the conjunction of other conditions, the seed of consciousness — bound by relishing — at this or that place of rebirth, in the mother's womb, produces the sprout of name-and-form, among <s>dharmas</s> that are ownerless, without possessor, unappropriated, without adversary, equal to space, of a nature whose characteristic is illusion, due to the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.' And so forth. 'No <s>dharma</s> whatsoever transmigrates from this world to the next world. Yet there is the fruit of action, and there is manifestation, due to the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.' And so forth. 'Just as fire does not burn when fuel is deficient, and burns when fuel is not deficient — just so, the seed of consciousness, generated by <s>karma</s> and afflictions, at this or that place of rebirth, in the mother's womb, produces the sprout of name-and-form, among <s>dharmas</s> that are ownerless, without possessor, unappropriated, without adversary, equal to space, of a nature whose characteristic is illusion, due to the non-deficiency of causes and conditions. Thus should the conditioning of internal dependent origination be seen.' //

body.text: tatra ādhyātmikaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ pañcabhiḥ kāraṇairdraṣṭavyaḥ / katamaiḥ pañcabhiḥ? na śāśvatataḥ, nocchedataḥ, na saṃkrāntitaḥ, parīttahetuto vipulaphalābhinirvṛttitaḥ, tatsadṛśānuprabandhataśceti / kathaṃ na śāśvatataḥ? yasmādanye māraṇāntikāḥ skandhāḥ, anye aupapattyaṃśikāḥ skandhāḥ prādurbhavanti / na tu ya eva māraṇāntikāḥ skandhāḥ, ta eva aupapattyaṃśikāḥ prādurbhavanti / ato na śāśvatataḥ / kathaṃ nocchedataḥ? na ca pūrvaniruddheṣu māraṇāntikeṣu skandheṣu aupapattyaṃśikāḥ skandhāḥ prādurbhavanti, nāpyaniruddheṣu / api tu māraṇāntikāḥ skandhā nirudhyante, tasminneva ca samaye aupapattyaṃśikāḥ skandhāḥ prādurbhavanti, tulādaṇḍonnāmāvanāmavat / ato nocchedataḥ / kathaṃ na saṃkrāntitaḥ? visadṛśāt sattvanikāyādvisabhāgāḥ skandhā jātyantare 'bhinirvartante / ato na saṃkrāntitaḥ / kathaṃ parīttahetuto vipulaphalābhinirvṛttitaḥ? parīttaṃ karma kriyate, vipulaphalavipāko 'nubhūyate / ataḥ parīttahetuto vipulaphalābhinirvṛttitaḥ / kathaṃ tatsadṛśānuprabandhataḥ? yathāvedanīyaṃ karma kriyate, tathāvedanīyo vipāko 'nubhūyate / atastatsadṛśānuprabandhataḥ / evamādhyātmikaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ pañcabhiḥ [kāraṇaiḥ-ākāraiḥ] draṣṭavyaḥ // iti vistaraḥ //
body.translated_text: Therein, internal dependent origination should be seen through five aspects. Which five? Not through eternalism, not through annihilationism, not through transmigration, through the production of abundant fruit from a small cause, and through the continuity of what is similar. How not through eternalism? Because the aggregates at the moment of death are different, and different aggregates belonging to the rebirth-moment manifest. It is not the case that the very aggregates at the moment of death are the ones that manifest as belonging to the rebirth-moment — therefore not through eternalism. How not through annihilationism? The aggregates belonging to the rebirth-moment do not manifest when the aggregates at the moment of death have previously ceased, nor when they have not ceased. Rather, the aggregates at the moment of death cease, and at that very moment the aggregates belonging to the rebirth-moment manifest — like the rising and falling of the beam of a balance. Therefore not through annihilationism. How not through transmigration? Dissimilar aggregates are produced in a new birth from a dissimilar class of beings — therefore not through transmigration. How through the production of abundant fruit from a small cause? Small <s>karma</s> is performed, yet its ripening into abundant fruit is experienced — therefore through the production of abundant fruit from a small cause. How through the continuity of what is similar? As <s>karma</s> is performed to be experienced [in a certain way], so its ripening is experienced — therefore through the continuity of what is similar. Thus should internal dependent origination be seen through five [aspects].' Thus in detail. //

body.text: tadevamātmādivirahe 'pi karmaphalasaṃbandho 'vikalaḥ sūtreṣu bhagavatā svayamupadarśita ityupadarśitaṃ bhavati / iti naikasyobhayānuvartino 'bhāve 'pi kiṃcidvirudhyate iti //
body.translated_text: Thus it has been shown that even in the absence of a self and such, the connection of <s>karma</s> and its fruit is unimpeded — this was demonstrated by the Blessed One himself in the <s>sūtras</s>. Therefore, even though no single entity persists through both [lives], nothing whatsoever is contradicted. //

body.text: yadi kathaṃcidapi nāstyevātmā, kathaṃ tarhi-
body.translated_text: If a self does not exist in any way whatsoever, how then [is it said] —

children.text: ātmā hi ātmano nāthaḥ ko nu nāthaḥ paro bhavet /
children.translated_text: 'The self is the lord of the self; who else could be lord?

children.text: ātmanā hi sudāntena svargaṃ prāpnoti paṇḍitaḥ //
children.translated_text: Through a well-tamed self, the wise one attains heaven.'

body.text: =dhammapada
body.translated_text: = <s>Dhammapada</s>

body.text:
iti gāthāyāmuktam? cittameva ahaṃkārasaṃniśrayatayā asyāmātmaśabdenoktam /
anyatra sūtre-
body.translated_text:
— as stated in this verse? It is the mind itself that is called by the word 'self' (<s>ātman</s>) in this [verse], because it serves as the basis for the sense of 'I.'
In another <s>sūtra</s> —

body.text:
cittasya damanaṃ sādhu cittaṃ dāntaṃ sukhāvaham /
[=dhammapada]
body.translated_text:
'The taming of the mind is good; a tamed mind brings happiness.'
[= <s>Dhammapada</s>]

body.text: iti cittasya damanavacanāt / tadapi ca ātmadṛṣṭayabhiniviṣṭānāmanyatrātmagrāhaparikalpavicchedārthaṃ neyārthatayā saṃvṛtyā cittamātmeti prakāśitaṃ na tu paramārthataḥ / etena yaduktamāryalaṅkāvatāre-
body.translated_text: Thus, from the statement about the taming of the mind. And even that too, for those who are attached to the view of self, for the purpose of cutting off the conceptual elaboration of grasping a self elsewhere [than in mind], has been revealed as "the mind is the self" provisionally, by convention — not ultimately. By this, what is stated in the <s>Āryalaṅkāvatāra</s> —

children.translated_text: "Person, continuum, aggregates, conditions, atoms,
<s>Pradhāna</s>, God, agent — I teach mind-only."

body.translated_text: <s>Laṅkāvatāra</s> 2.139, 10.133

body.text: iti, tadapi vyākhyātaṃ bhavati / yataḥ tadapi ca anyatra pudgalādyabhiniveśabādhanāya vacanam / na tu tāvatā cittasya paramārthasattvamuktam / evamanyatrāpi skandhādiṣvātmadeśanā neyārthā / ataścittamapi vastuto nāhaṃpratyayasya viṣayaḥ //
body.translated_text: — that too has been explained. For that too is a statement for the purpose of undermining attachment to person and such elsewhere. But that much does not declare the ultimate reality of mind. Likewise, elsewhere too, the teaching of self in the aggregates and such is of provisional meaning. Therefore, even mind is not in reality the object of the I-notion.

body.text: bhavatu vā cittaṃ paramārthasat / tathāpi na vastutaḥ tadahaṃkāragocara ityupadarśayannāha atītetyādi-
body.translated_text: Or let mind be ultimately real; even so, it is not in reality the domain of the ego-sense — showing this, he says with "past" and so forth —

body.text: atītānāgataṃ cittaṃ nāhaṃ taddhi na vidyate /
body.translated_text: The past and future mind is not I, for it does not exist.

body.text: tridhā hi cittaṃ saṃbhavati parikalpamupādāya atītamanāgataṃ pratyutpannaṃ ca / tatra / atītānāgataṃ naṣṭājātaṃ cittaṃ nāhaṃ na ahaṃdarśanaviṣayaḥ / kutaḥ? hiryasmāt / tadatītā nāgataṃ cittaṃ na vidyate, na saṃpratyasti, naṣṭājātatvāt / yadatītaṃ tat kṣīṇaṃ niruddhaṃ vigataṃ vipariṇāmitam / yadanāgatam, tadapyasaṃprāptamiti / pratyutpannaṃ tarhi cittamahaṃ bhaviṣya tītyata āha-
body.translated_text: For mind occurs in three ways, based on conceptual division: past, future, and present. There, the past and future — what has perished and what has not yet arisen — that mind is not I, is not the object of the I-view. Why? "For" — because. That past and future mind does not exist, does not presently exist, since it has perished or not yet arisen. What is past — that has been exhausted, ceased, gone, transformed. What is future — that too has not yet arrived. "Then let the present mind be I" — to this he says —

body.text: athotpannamahaṃ cittaṃ naṣṭe 'sminnāstyahaṃ punaḥ // Bca_9.74 //
body.translated_text: If the arisen [mind] is I, then when it perishes, I no longer exist. // Bca_9.74 //

body.text: yathā utpannaṃ vartamānaṃ cittamahamastu, tadapi na yuktam / yato naṣṭe 'sminnāstyahaṃ punaḥ, asmin pratyutpanne citte naṣṭe dvitīyakṣaṇe atīte sati nāstyahaṃ punaḥ, paścādahaṃpratyayasya viṣayo neṣṭaḥ syāt / pratyutpannasya sthitirnopalabhyate / tat kutaścittamālambyatāṃ yena ālambanaṃ syāt? ato na cittālambano 'pīti nirālambana evāyamahaṃpratyaya utpadyate //
body.translated_text: Let the arisen, present mind be I — even that is not justified. Because "when it perishes, I no longer exist" — when this present mind perishes, at the second moment, having become past, I no longer exist; afterward, no desired object of the I-notion would exist. The abiding of the present is not found. So from what [ground] should mind be taken as a support, such that it would be a basis? Therefore, even one whose support is mind [has no valid support] — thus this I-notion arises utterly without basis.

body.text: evamātmano 'sattvāt nātmā, tryadhvavartināścittasya ca tadviṣayatvāt / nāpi cittamahaṃkārasya viṣaya iti prasādhyopasaṃharannāha yathaivetyādi-
body.translated_text: Thus, due to the non-existence of a self — there is no self — and because the mind existing in the three times is its [alleged] domain — nor is mind the domain of the ego-sense — concluding the proof and summarizing, he says with "just as" and so forth —

children.translated_text: Just as the plantain trunk, when broken apart piece by piece, is nothing,
so too the I, when sought through analysis, is found to be non-existent. // Bca_9.75 //

body.text: yathaiva kadalīstambho rambhādaṇḍakhaṇḍam, bhāgaśaḥ pratyavayavaśaḥ kṛto 'vadhūto na kaścit na vastusan prāpyate, tathā ahamapyasadbhūtaḥ kadalīstambhavat / ahamapi ahaṃpratyayasya viṣayo 'pi asadbhūtaḥ avastubhūtaḥ, vandhyātanayavat / na kaścidviṣayo 'syāstīti bhāvaḥ / katham? mṛgyamāṇo vicārataḥ nirūpaṇataḥ //
body.translated_text: Just as the plantain trunk — the stalk of the banana plant — when "broken apart piece by piece," limb by limb, is "nothing" — nothing of substantial reality is found — so too the I is non-existent, like the plantain trunk. The I, even as the object of the I-notion, is "non-existent" — devoid of real substance, like the son of a barren woman. There is no object of it whatsoever — this is the meaning. How? "When sought" — "through analysis," through examination.

body.text: punaranyadbādhakamātmapratiṣedhe prasañjayannāha yadītyādi-
body.translated_text: Again, raising another objection as an obstacle to the negation of self, he says with "if" and so forth —

body.text: yadi sattvo na vidyeta kasyopari kṛpeti cet /
body.translated_text: "If a being does not exist, toward whom is there compassion?" — if this is asked,

body.text: yadi sarvathaiva sattvaḥ ātmā pudgalo vā vicāryamāṇo na vidyeta, na syāt, tadā kasyopari kṛpā karuṇā bodhisattvānāṃ bhavet, sattvamantareṇa kimālambya pravarteta? karuṇā ca samyaksaṃbodhisādhanam, tatpūrvakameva saṃbhāranidāneṣu dānādiṣu pravartanāt / ataḥ karuṇāpuraḥsarāḥ sarve buddhadharmāḥ pravartante / tathā coktamāryadharmasaṃgītau-
body.translated_text: If a being — a self, a person — upon examination does not exist in any way, would not exist, then toward whom would <s>Bodhisattvas</s> have compassion, <s>kṛpā</s>? Without a being, relying on what would [compassion] operate? And compassion is a means to perfect awakening, since engagement in giving and such — the foundations of the accumulations — proceeds on the basis of compassion. Therefore, all <s>Buddha</s>-qualities proceed preceded by compassion. As stated in the <s>Āryadharmasaṃgīti</s> —

body.text: atha khalu āryāvalokiteśvaro bodhisattvo mahāsattvo bhagavantametadavocat- na bhagavan bodhisattvena atibahuṣu dharmeṣu śikṣitavyam / eka eva dharmo bodhisattvena svārādhitaḥ kartavyaḥ supratibiddhaḥ / tasya karatalagatāḥ sarve buddhadharmā bhavanti / tadyathā- yena rājñaścakravartinaścakraratnaṃ gacchati, tena sarvabalakāyo gacchati / evameva bhagavan yena bodhisattvasya mahākaruṇā gacchati, tena sarve buddhadharmā gacchanti / tadyathā bhagavan jīvitendriye sati anyeṣāmindriyāṇāṃ pravṛttirbhavati, evameva bhagavan mahākaruṇāyāṃ satyāṃ bodhikārakāṇāṃ dharmāṇāṃ pravṛttirbhavatīti //
body.translated_text: "Then the noble <s>Avalokiteśvara</s>, <s>Bodhisattva</s> <s>Mahāsattva</s>, said this to the Blessed One: 'A <s>Bodhisattva</s>, Blessed One, need not train in exceedingly many <s>dharmas</s>. Just one <s>dharma</s> should be well attended to, well penetrated by a <s>Bodhisattva</s>. Then all <s>Buddha</s>-qualities become available in the palm of his hand. Just as wherever the wheel-jewel of a <s>Cakravartin</s> king goes, there the entire army goes — just so, Blessed One, wherever the great compassion of a <s>Bodhisattva</s> goes, there all <s>Buddha</s>-qualities go. Just as, Blessed One, when the life-faculty exists, the other faculties function — just so, Blessed One, when great compassion exists, the <s>dharmas</s> that produce awakening function.'"

body.text: āryagayāśīrṣe coktam-
body.translated_text: And it is said in the <s>Āryagayāśīrṣa</s> —

body.text: kimārambhā mañjuśrīḥ bodhisattvānāṃ caryā, kimadhiṣṭhānā? mañjuśrīrāha- mahākaruṇārambhā devaputra bodhisattvānāṃ caryā sattvādhiṣṭhānā // iti vistaraḥ //
body.translated_text: "What is the beginning of the <s>Bodhisattvas</s>' practice, <s>Mañjuśrī</s>? What is its foundation? <s>Mañjuśrī</s> said: Great compassion is the beginning of the <s>Bodhisattvas</s>' practice, O <s>devaputra</s>; beings are its foundation." Thus in detail.

body.text: tasmādavaśyaṃ prathamataḥ sattvālambanā karuṇābhyupagantavyāḥ duḥkhitasattvādhiṣṭhānena samutpatteḥ / sattvābhāve ca sā na syāditi cet, evaṃ manyase yadi, tadā naitadvaktavyamityāha kāryārthamityādi-
body.translated_text: Therefore, first of all, compassion with beings as its object must necessarily be accepted, since it arises on the basis of suffering beings. "And if beings do not exist, [compassion] would not [arise]" — if you think thus, then this should not be said — he says with "for the purpose of the goal" and so forth —

body.text: kāryārthamabhyupetena yo mohena prakalpitaḥ // Bca_9.76 //
body.translated_text: That [being] who is conceptually constructed through the delusion undertaken for the purpose of the goal — // Bca_9.76 //

body.text: kāryamabhimatasādhyaṃ puruṣārtha ityucyate / tadarthamabhyupetena svīkṛtena mohena saṃvṛtyā yaḥ prakalpitaḥ samāropitaḥ sattvaḥ, tasyoparītyarthaḥ / tathāhi sakalakalpanājālarahitaṃ sarvāvaraṇavinirmuktaṃ paramapuruṣārthatayā buddhatvamiha sādhyam / tacca sarvadharmānupalambhamantareṇa nādhigamyate / sa ca prajñāprakarṣagamanāt saṃpadyate / tacca sādaranirantaradīrghakālābhyāsādupajāyate / tadārambhaśca karuṇāvaśādutpadyate / sā ca prathamato duḥkhitasattveṣu pravartamānā saṃbhārārambhanidānamupapadyate iti kāryārthaṃ mohasya saṃvṛtisatyarūpasyābhyupagamaḥ / tataḥ prathamataḥ sattvālambanaiva karuṇā, tataḥ paraṃ dharmālambanā, anālambanā ca / ayamabhiprāyaḥ- na sarvathā sattvasyābhāvaḥ / skandhādayo hi saṃvṛttyā ātmaśabdenocyante / yathoktaṃ bhagavatā-
body.translated_text: The "goal" — the desired objective — is called the highest human aim. For the purpose of that, "through the delusion undertaken" — accepted — "through delusion," by convention, the being who is "conceptually constructed" — superimposed — toward him [compassion is directed]: this is the meaning. For the <s>Buddhahood</s> that is free from all nets of conceptualization and liberated from all obscurations, being the supreme human goal, is what is to be accomplished here. And that is not attained without the non-apprehension of all <s>dharmas</s>. And that [non-apprehension] is accomplished through the culmination of <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom). And that [prajñā] arises from respectful, uninterrupted, and long-term practice. And the commencement of that [practice] arises from the power of compassion. And that [compassion], operating initially toward suffering beings, becomes the foundation for commencing the accumulations — thus, the acceptance of delusion of the nature of conventional truth is for the purpose of the goal. Therefore, compassion is first with beings as its object, then with <s>dharmas</s> as its object, and finally objectless. This is the intent: it is not the case that a being is entirely non-existent. For the aggregates and such are conventionally referred to by the word "self." As stated by the Blessed One —

body.text: ye kecidbhikṣavaḥ śramaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ātmeti samanupaśyantaḥ samanupaśyanti imānete (tān?) pañcopādānaskandhān / iti /
body.translated_text: "Whatever ascetics or <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, monks, perceive a self when they perceive — they perceive these five aggregates of clinging."

body.text: tato yadi nāma prajñayā nirūpayataḥ paramārthataḥ sattvānupalambhaḥ, tathāpi saṃvṛtyā na niṣidhyate iti / taduktam-
body.translated_text: Therefore, even though for one who examines with wisdom there is ultimately no apprehension of a being, conventionally it is not denied. As stated —

children.text: yataḥ prajñā tattvaṃ bhajati karuṇā saṃvṛtimataḥ
children.translated_text: "Since wisdom attends to reality, while compassion attends to convention —
as you correctly analyzed that the world is without beings;
yet when you were possessed by compassion, mother of the Ten-Powered Ones,

children.text: tadā te 'bhūdārte suta iva pituḥ prema jagati //
children.translated_text: then your love for the world was like a father's for his child."

body.text: iti / [ratnadāsaviracitaṃ guṇaparyantastotram-33]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Guṇaparyantastotra</s> by <s>Ratnadāsa</s>, v. 33]

body.text: catuḥstave 'pi-
body.translated_text: In the <s>Catuḥstava</s> too —

children.text: sattvasaṃjñā ca te nātha sarvathā na pravartate /
children.translated_text: "O Lord, the perception of "being" does not at all operate for You,
yet toward beings afflicted with suffering, You are supremely compassionate."

body.text: iti / [catuḥ-1.9]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Catuḥstava</s> 1.9]

body.text: tasmādamī rūpādaya eva saṃvṛtyā sattvaśabdenocyante / iti na karuṇā nirviṣayā //
body.translated_text: Therefore, these very [things] — form and such — are conventionally referred to by the word "being." Thus compassion is not without an object.

body.text: nanu paramārthataḥ sattvābhāve kasya tat kāryam, iti kathaṃ tatsādhanāya kasyacit pravṛttirityabhisaṃdhāya āha kāryamityādi-
body.translated_text: Now, in the ultimate absence of a being, whose is that goal? Hence how could anyone's engagement toward its accomplishment [be justified]? With this in mind, he says with "the goal" and so forth —

body.text: kāryaṃ kasya na cetsattvaḥ satyamīhā tu mohataḥ /
body.translated_text: "Whose is the goal if there is no being?" True — but the striving is through delusion.

body.text: na cet sattva iti / yadi sattvo nāsti, tadā ekasyānuyāyino 'bhāvāt rūpādīnāṃ ca utpannavināśitvāt kāryaṃ kasya? na kasyacit syādityarthaḥ / satyamityabhyupagame iti / evameva etanmatameva asmākam- naiva kasyacit paramārthataḥ kāryam, asvāmikatvāt sarvadharmāṇām / yadyevam, kathaṃ tarhi tatsādhanāya prathamataḥ pravṛttiriti cet, īhā tu mohataḥ / īhā ceṣṭā punastatkāryārthitayā vyāpāraḥ mohāt / mamaiva tat kāryaṃ bhaviṣyatītyekatvādhyavasāyena sattvābhāve 'pi saṃvṛtyā māyāsvabhāvatayā / vastuto nirīhatvāt sarvadharmāṇāmanyatra pratītyasamutpādāt / taduktam-
body.translated_text: "If there is no being" — if a being does not exist, then since no single follower exists, and since form and such arise and perish, whose is the goal? No one's — this is the meaning. "True" — in granting this: this is indeed our position — for no one ultimately has a goal, since all <s>dharmas</s> are ownerless. If so, how then does engagement toward its accomplishment [occur] initially? "The striving is through delusion" — the "striving," the activity, the engagement for the purpose of that goal, is "through delusion" — "that goal will be mine" — through the determination of unity, even in the absence of a being, conventionally, through a nature that is like an illusion. In reality, since all <s>dharmas</s> are without striving [of their own], there is nothing apart from dependent origination. As stated —

children.translated_text: "Without striving, subject to conditions, empty, arising from conditions like illusions —
all <s>dharmas</s>, O Lord, have been revealed by You as devoid of intrinsic nature."

body.text: iti / [catuḥ-2.22]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Catuḥstava</s> 2.22]

body.text: tasmāt saṃvṛtereva kāryārthavyāpāraḥ / nanu ca moho nāma avidyāsvabhāvatayā sarvathaiva anupādeyaḥ / tat kathaṃ punastasyaiva svīkāraḥ ityata āha duḥkhetyādi-
body.translated_text: Therefore, the engagement for the purpose of the goal belongs to convention alone. "But delusion, being of the nature of ignorance, is entirely unacceptable. So how can it be accepted?" — to this he says with "suffering" and so forth —

body.text: duḥkhavyupaśamārthaṃ tu kāryamoho na vāryate // Bca_9.77 //
body.translated_text: But delusion for the purpose of accomplishing the cessation of suffering is not prevented. // Bca_9.77 //

body.text: dvividho hi mohaḥ- saṃsārapravṛttihetuḥ tatpraśamahetuśca / tatra yaḥ saṃsāranidānam, sa prahātavya eva / anyastu yaḥ paraṃparayā duḥkhavyupaśamārthaṃ sarvasattvajātyādivyasananimittaṃ
body.translated_text: For delusion is of two kinds: that which is the cause of the perpetuation of <s>saṃsāra</s>, and that which is the cause of its pacification. There, that which is the root of <s>saṃsāra</s> — that should certainly be abandoned. But the other, which indirectly, for the purpose of the cessation of suffering — on account of the calamity of birth and such of all beings —

body.text: kāryamohaḥ kāryasya paramārthasatyalakṣaṇasyādhigamāya mohaḥ, sa punarna vāryate, na pratiṣidhyate / upādīyate eva, paramārthopayogitvāt / idamihādhikṛtam, tadapi kāryaṃ nātmasukhābhilāṣeṇa mahadbhirupādīyate, api tu sarvasattvānāmātyantikasarvaduḥkhavyupaśamārtham / tatra ca upeyabhūtaḥ paramārthādhigama eva / tasyāpyupāyabhūtaṃ [saṃvṛtisatyam] / saṃvṛtisatyamantareṇa paramārthānadhigamāt / iti duḥkhapraśamārthatā kāryamohasya / etat kāryārthamavicārataḥ [9.4] ityasmin prastāve pratipāditameva pūrvam / punarvipañcayitumuktam //
body.translated_text: is the "goal-directed delusion" — the delusion for the attainment of the goal characterized by ultimate truth — that is not prevented, is not prohibited. Rather, it is adopted, since it serves the ultimate purpose. This is the subject here: even that goal is not adopted by the great ones through desire for one's own happiness, but for the purpose of the absolute cessation of all suffering of all beings. And therein, the ultimate attainment is what is to be achieved. And the means for that is [conventional truth]. Since without conventional truth there is no attainment of the ultimate. Thus, the goal-directed delusion serves the cessation of suffering. This was already established in the context of "the goal should not be examined" [9.4]. It is stated again for the purpose of elaboration.

body.text: syādetat- yathā duḥkhopaśamahetutvāt kāryamoho 'vidyāsvabhāvo 'bhyupagamyate, tathaiva ātmamoho 'pi taddhetutvādastu / tat kimātmā yatnena niṣidhyate? tatsadbhāve 'pi ātmabhāvanayā ahaṃkāraparikṣayāt bhaviṣyati saṃsāranivṛttiḥ / tataḥ kiṃ nairātmyabhāvanayetyatrāha duḥkhaheturityādi-
body.translated_text: One might think: just as goal-directed delusion, though of the nature of ignorance, is accepted because it causes the cessation of suffering, so too let self-delusion be accepted as a cause of that. Why then is the self so strenuously negated? Even in its existence, through the cultivation of self, with the exhaustion of ego-sense, there will be the cessation of <s>saṃsāra</s>. So what use is the cultivation of selflessness? — to this he says with "cause of suffering" and so forth —

body.text: duḥkhaheturahaṃkāra ātmamohāttu vardhate /
body.translated_text: The ego-sense, the cause of suffering, increases through the delusion of self.

body.text: yathā kāryamoho duḥkhopaśamahetuḥ, na tathā dvitīya ātmamohaḥ, tasmin sati ahaṃkārakṣayābhāvāt / ātmamohāttu anātmani ātmaviparyāsadarśanāt punarahaṃkāro vardhate, vṛddha upajāyate / kiṃbhūtaḥ? duḥkhahetuḥ duḥkhasya sāṃsārikasya triduḥkhatālakṣaṇasya hetuḥ kāraṇam / ahaṃkārakṣayācca duḥkhopaśama iṣyate / sati ca ātmadarśane kathamasau nivarteta? kāraṇe 'vikalasāmarthye kāryasya nivṛttyayogāt / tato duḥkhamapi na nivartate / tathāhi ātmānaṃ paśyataḥ saṃskṛteṣu skandhadhātvāyataneṣu ahamiti dṛḍhataramutpadyate snehaḥ / tatastadduḥkhapratīkārecchayā sukhābhilāṣo doṣān pracchādya tadarthitayā guṇādhyāropāt tatsādhaneṣu pravartate / svopakāriṇi vayamiti buddhirupajāyate / ahaṃ mameti ca darśanāt paripanthini vidveṣaḥ / tataḥ samastaduḥkhanidānaṃ sarva eva kleśopakleśā labdhaprasarāḥ pravartante / iti ātmamohapravartito duḥkhaheturahaṃkāro bhavati / taduktamācāryapādaiḥ-
body.translated_text: Just as goal-directed delusion is the cause of the cessation of suffering, the second — the delusion of self — is not like that, since in its presence the exhaustion of ego-sense does not occur. Rather, through the delusion of self — from seeing a self in what is not-self, a distorted view — the ego-sense increases, arises intensified. Of what kind? Being the cause of suffering — the cause of <s>saṃsāric</s> suffering characterized by the three kinds of suffering. And it is accepted that from the exhaustion of ego-sense comes the cessation of suffering. But when the view of self exists, how could it cease? Because when the cause is of undiminished power, the cessation of the effect is impossible. Therefore suffering too does not cease. For one who sees a self: in conditioned [things] — the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases — the attachment of "I" arises even more firmly. Then, from the desire to remedy that suffering, from the desire for happiness, concealing faults, through the superimposition of qualities on their objects, one engages in the means [to obtain them]. The thought "we are on the side of what benefits oneself" arises. From the view of "I" and "mine," hatred [arises] toward what obstructs. Then, as the root of all suffering, all afflictions and secondary afflictions, having gained free course, operate. Thus the ego-sense, set in motion by the delusion of self, becomes the cause of suffering. As stated by the venerable master —

children.translated_text: One who sees a self — in him the perpetual affection of 'I' [arises].
From affection he craves for pleasures; craving conceals faults.
Seeing qualities, craving ardently, he appropriates the means [to obtain] 'mine.'
As long as there is clinging to self, for so long there is <s>saṃsāra</s>.
When the self exists, the notion of 'other' [arises]; from the distinction of self and other, appropriation and hatred [arise].
Bound to these two, all faults are produced.

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: itthamātmasnehānnivartayitumaśakyo 'haṃkāraḥ /
body.translated_text: In this way, the ego-sense, being inseparable from the attachment to self, cannot be averted.

body.text: tato 'pi na nivartyaścet
body.translated_text: If it cannot be averted even from that [self-view] —

body.text: tato 'pi ātmadarśanādapi na nivartyo nivartayitumaśakyo 'haṃkāraśced yadi, tadā-
body.translated_text: 'Even from that' — if the ego-sense cannot be averted, cannot be removed, even from the perception of self — if so, then:

body.text: varaṃ nairātmyabhāvanā // Bca_9.78 //
body.translated_text: better is the meditation on selflessness. // Bca_9.78 //

body.text: nairātmyasya pudgalādivirahasya bhāvanā abhyāsaḥ / varamuttamam / ātmadarśanapravṛttāhaṃkāranivṛttihetutvāt / tāvatkālamastu, paścāt punariyamapi prahāsyate, upalambhadṛṣṭitvāditi bhāvaḥ / tathāhi tadbhāvanāprakarṣaparyantagamanāt sākṣānnairātmyadarśanāt virodhi satkāyadarśanaṃ nivartate / tannivṛttau ca ekasyānugāmino darśanābhāvāt pūrvāpararūpavikalasya kṣaṇamātrasya darśanam / tataḥ pūrvāparasamāropābhāvāt na anāgatasukhasādhanaṃ kiṃcidātmanaḥ paśyati / tato na tasya kvacidviṣaye rāgo jāyate, nāpi tatprativirodhini dveṣaḥ, āsaṅgābhāvādeva / nāpyakāriṇaṃ prati apakārasthānaṃ paśyati / yena yasmin kṛto 'pakāraḥ, tayordvayorapi dvitīyakṣaṇe 'bhāvāt / na ca anyena kṛte 'pakāre prekṣāvataḥ anyatra vairaniryātanamucitam, nāpi yasya kṛtastenāpi / evaṃ rāgādinivṛttau anye 'pi tatprabhavāḥ kleśopakleśā notpadyante / nāpi vastutaḥ kaścit kasyacidapakārī, idaṃ pratītya idamutpadyate iti pratītyasamutpādadarśanādvā / evaṃ hi pudgalaśūnyatāyāṃ satkāyadarśananivṛttau chinnamūlatvāt kleśā na samudācaranti / yathoktamāryatathāgataguhyasūtre-
body.translated_text: The meditation — the practice — of selflessness, the absence of a person and such. It is 'better' — supreme — because it is the cause for the cessation of the ego-sense that operates through the perception of self. Let it persist for some time; later this [meditation on selflessness] too will be abandoned, since it is a view of apprehension — this is the purport. For through reaching the culmination of that meditation, from the direct seeing of selflessness, the opposing <s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s> (view of the composite of self) ceases. And upon its cessation, since there is no perception of a single persisting entity, there is merely the seeing of a momentary [entity] that is devoid of [both] earlier and later forms. Consequently, from the absence of a superimposition of earlier and later [continuity], one does not see anything of the self as a means to future happiness. Therefore, no attachment arises in him toward any object, nor hatred toward what opposes it, due to the very absence of clinging. Nor does he see any ground for causing harm toward one who is not an agent. For both — the one by whom and the one to whom the harm was done — are absent in the second moment. And in a harm done by another, retaliation directed elsewhere is not appropriate for a discerning person, nor [is it appropriate to direct it] at the very one by whom it was done. Thus, when attachment and such have ceased, the other <s>kleśas</s> and subsidiary afflictions that arise from them also do not arise. Nor is anyone in reality a harmer of anyone, either from the understanding that 'dependent on this, that arises' — through the seeing of dependent origination. For in this way, when the <s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s> ceases through the emptiness of persons, the afflictions, their root being cut, do not operate. As stated in the <s>Āryatathāgataguhyasūtra</s>:

body.text: tadyathāpi nāma śāntamate vṛkṣasya mūlacchinnasya sarvaśākhāpatrapalāśaṃ śuṣyati, evameva śāntamate satkāyadṛṣṭipraśamāt sarvakleśā upaśāmyantīti //
body.translated_text: 'Just as, <s>Śāntamati</s>, when the root of a tree is cut, all its branches, leaves, and foliage dry up — even so, <s>Śāntamati</s>, through the pacification of <s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>, all afflictions are pacified.'

body.text: tasmādvaraṃ nairātmyabhāvanā //
body.translated_text: Therefore, better is the meditation on selflessness.

body.text: gatamidamānuṣaṅgikam / saṃprati punarahaṃkāraviṣayaṃ nirūpayitumupakramate / syādetatyadi nāma ātmā vicāreṇa kharaviṣāṇasadṛśatvānnāhaṃkārasya viṣayaḥ, tathāpi kāyāvayavī tadviṣayo bhaviṣyatītyatrāha kāyo neti-
body.translated_text: This incidental [discussion] is concluded. Now he undertakes to examine the object of the ego-sense. It might be said: even if the self, through examination, is like a horn of a donkey and is not an object of the ego-sense, still, the body as a composite whole will be its object — to this he says 'the body is not' and so forth:

children.text: kāyo na pādau na jaṅghā norū kāyaḥ kaṭirna ca /
children.translated_text: The body is not the feet, nor are the legs the body; the thighs are not the body, nor is the hip;

children.text: nodaraṃ nāpyayaṃ pṛṣṭhaṃ noro bāhū na cāpi saḥ // Bca_9.79 //
children.translated_text: nor the abdomen, nor this the back; nor the chest, nor the arms — none is the body. // Bca_9.79 //

children.text: na hastau nāpyayaṃ pārśvau na kakṣau nāṃsalakṣaṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: Nor are the hands, nor is this the flanks; nor the armpits, nor is it characterized as the shoulders;

children.text: na grīvā na śiraḥ kāyaḥ kāyo 'tra kataraḥ punaḥ // Bca_9.80 //
children.translated_text: nor the neck, nor the head — so which among these is the body? // Bca_9.80 //

body.text: kāyo 'pi vicāreṇaiko naiva kaścidastītyupadarśayati- tathā hi karacaraṇādayo bhāgā evaṃ paraṃ dṛśyante, na tvekaḥ kāyo nāma pratibhāsate / na ca teṣvanyatamaḥ kāyo yujyate / yataḥ kāyo na pādau, na caraṇau, na jaṅghā / jaṅghā ca kāyo na bhavati / norū jaṅghaikadeśaviśeṣau na kāyaḥ / kaṭirna ca, śroṇirapi naiva kāyaḥ / nodaram, jaṭharamapi kāyo na bhavati / nāpyayaṃ pṛṣṭham, ayaṃ kāyaḥ pṛṣṭhamapi naiva / noraḥ, noro vakṣo 'pi na kāyaḥ / bāhū na cāpi saḥ, sa kāyo bhujāvapi na bhavati / na hastau, karāvapi na kāyaḥ / nāpyayaṃ pārśvau,
body.translated_text: He shows that even the body, upon examination, is simply not one thing: for hands, feet, and other parts are seen as separate, but no single 'body' appears. Nor is any one of them justified as the body. For the body is not the feet — not the soles; the legs are not [the body]. The shanks are not the body either. The thighs — specific portions adjacent to the shanks — are not the body. Nor the hip — the waist too is not the body. Nor the abdomen — the belly too is not the body. 'Nor this the back' — this body is not the back either. Nor the chest — the thorax too is not the body. 'The arms are not it either' — that body is not the upper limbs. The hands — the palms too are not the body. 'Nor is this the flanks' —

body.text: ayaṃ kāyaḥ pārśvāvapi na bhavati / na kakṣau, bhujamūle api na kāyaḥ / nāṃsalakṣaṇaḥ, nāpi skandhasvabhāvaḥ kāyaḥ / na grīvā, na kaṃdharā kāyaḥ / na śiraḥ kāyaḥ, mastako 'pi kāyo na bhavati / caraṇādīnāṃ vakṣyamāṇavicāreṇa paramāṇuśo 'pyanavasthānāt, karacaraṇādīnāmanyatamacchede kāyavināśena maraṇaprasaṅgāt, parābhyupagamābhāvācca naiṣu pratyekaṃ kāyātmatā / evaṃ yadā na pratyekamete kāyasvabhāvāḥ, etatsamudāyamātraṃ ca śarīram, tat kāyo 'tra kataraḥ punaḥ, atra eṣu pādādibhāgeṣu purovartiṣu śarīrakalpanānimitteṣu kataraḥ kāyo bhavatu? naiva kaścideko 'pi nirūpyamāṇaḥ kāyātmaka upalabhyate iti yāvat //
body.translated_text: this body is not the sides either. Nor the armpits — the roots of the arms too are not the body. 'Not characterized as the shoulders' — nor is the body of the nature of the shoulder-blades. Nor the neck — the cervical region is not the body. Nor the head — the cranium too is not the body. Since by the examination to be stated, even feet and such do not abide down to their atoms, since the destruction of any one of the limbs — hands, feet, and such — would entail the destruction of the body and thus the absurd consequence of death, and since no one else accepts [any particular limb as the body] — [therefore] in none of these individually is there a bodyhood. Thus, when none of these individually are of the nature of the body, and the physical frame is merely the aggregate of these — then 'which among these is the body?' — among these parts such as feet and such, present before one, which serve as the basis for the conceptual construction of a body — which would be the body? Not even a single [part], when examined, is found to be of the nature of the body — this is the purport.

body.text: athāpi syāt- naivamabhidhīyate pratyekaṃ karādayaḥ kāyaḥ, kiṃ tarhi sarvāvayavavyāpakatvādavayavinaḥ sarvāvayaveṣu vartate ityatrāha yadītyādi-
body.translated_text: But one might say: it is not asserted that hands and such individually are the body; rather, since the composite whole pervades all its parts, it exists in all parts — to this he says 'if' and so forth:

body.text: yadi sarveṣu kāyo 'yamekadeśena vartate /
body.translated_text: If this body exists in all [parts] by a portion —

body.text: sarvāvayaveṣu vartamāno 'yamekadeśena vartate, yugapat sarvātmanā vā? tatra yadi sarveṣu karacaraṇādiṣu avayaveṣu kāyo 'vayavī, ekadeśena vartate, kenacid bhāgena kaṃcidavayavaṃ vyāpnoti / na sarvātmanā sarvamityarthaḥ / tadā etanna vaktavyam / yataḥ yairekadeśairavayaveṣu vartate, teṣvapi kimekadeśeṣu aparaiḥ ekadeśena vartate, sarvātmanā veti vikalpo na nivartate / tatrāpi punarekadeśena vṛttikalpanāyāmanavasthānivṛttirna syāt / api ca / tasya avakāśābhāvādeva avayaveṣu na vṛttirityāha aṃśā ityādi-
body.translated_text: Existing in all parts, does this [body] exist by a portion, or simultaneously in its entirety? If this body, the composite whole, exists in all parts — hands, feet, and such — by a portion, pervading each part by some fraction — not in its entirety — this is the meaning. Then this should not be said. Because:

body.text: aṃśā aṃśeṣu vartante sa ca kutra svayaṃ sthitaḥ // Bca_9.81 //
body.translated_text: The portions exist in [their own] portions — so where is it itself established? // Bca_9.81 //

body.text: aṃśā bhāgāḥ aṃśeṣu svasvabhāgeṣu vartante vyavatiṣṭhante, svasvabhāgavyavasthitatvāt sarvabhāvānām / sa ca kutra svayaṃ sthitaḥ? svayaṃ punarasau kāyo 'vayavī kva nu nāma vyavasthitaḥ iti na vidmaḥ //
body.translated_text: The portions — the parts — exist in, abide in, their own respective parts — because all entities are established in their own respective parts. So where is it itself — that body, the composite whole — established? We do not know where indeed it is situated.

body.text: atha dvitīyo vikalpaḥ, tatrāha sarvātmaneti-
body.translated_text: Now, regarding the second alternative, he says 'in its entirety' and so forth:

children.translated_text: If the body exists in its entirety everywhere — in the hands and such —
then there would be as many bodies as there are hands and such. // Bca_9.82 //

body.text: sarvātmanāpi vṛttisaṃbhāvanāyām / avayaveṣu anavakāśatvāt sa ca kutra svayaṃ sthitaḥ iti prasaṅgo nādyāpi nivartate / tathāpi punaraparamucyate- sarvātmanā sarvabhāvena naikadeśena / sarvatra sarveṣu karādiṣvavayaveṣu / ādiśabdāccaraṇādiṣu sthitaḥ samavetaḥ kāyāvayavī cet yadi, tadā punarayaṃ doṣaḥ syādityāha- kāyā iti / kāyāvayavinaḥ tāvanta eva syuḥ, tatsaṃkhyāparicchinnā eva prāpnuyuḥ / kiyantaḥ? yāvantaste karādayaḥ, te karacaraṇādayo 'vayavāyāvantaḥ yatsaṃkhyāparicchinnāḥ, tatsamavetā avayavino 'pi tāvanta eva bhaveyuḥ / tasya niraṃśatayā sarvātmanā teṣu parisamāptatvāt / tadanekasaṃbandhādanekatvāt / nānyathā ekavṛttiḥ syāt / ayaṃ ca prasaṅgaḥ anekatra ekadeśena vṛttipakṣe 'pi yojayitavyaḥ / yathā raktāraktapihitāpihitakampādayo 'pi yathāyogaṃ vaktavyā iti //
body.translated_text: Even when considering the possibility of existing in entirety — because there is no room [for the whole] in the parts, the absurd consequence 'where is it itself established?' is still not averted. Nevertheless, further it is said: if the body exists in its entirety — in its complete nature, not by a portion — everywhere, in all parts such as hands and such — the word '<s>ādi</s>' includes feet and such — if it is conjoined [with them], then this fault would follow — he says: 'bodies' and so forth. The composite bodies would be just as many — they would amount to exactly that number. How many? As many as those hands and such — those parts such as hands, feet, and such — whatever their number — the composite wholes conjoined with them would be exactly that many. Because, being without parts, [the whole] is completely exhausted in each of them, being present in its entirety. Through its conjunction with many, it becomes many. There could be no other [explanation of] existing as one [in many]. And this absurd consequence should also be applied to the position of existing by a portion in multiple [parts]. Just as [the arguments about] being colored and uncolored, covered and uncovered, moving, and such should be stated as appropriate.

body.text: evaṃ pratyakṣādipramāṇasamadhigamyaḥ kāyo nāsti / bādhakaṃ punarasya anantaramuktamastīti prasādhitamityupadarśayannāha naivāntarityādi-
body.translated_text: Thus, a body cognizable through valid means of knowledge such as direct perception does not exist. And that which refutes it has just been stated — showing that it is established — he says 'neither within' and so forth:

body.text: naivāntarna bahiḥ kāyaḥ kathaṃ kāyaḥ karādiṣu /
body.translated_text: The body is neither within nor without — how then is the body in the hands and such?

body.text: pūrvamantarvyāpārapuruṣapratiṣedhāt māṃsaśoṇitādīnāṃ vicāritatvāt naivāntarmadhye kāyaḥ / adhunā punaravayavinaḥ pratiṣedhāt na bahiḥ na bāhyaḥ pratyakṣādigocaraḥ kāyaḥ, iti kathaṃ kāyaḥ karādiṣu vyavasthāpyate? atha karādivyatirikto bhaviṣyatītyāha karādibhya ityādi-
body.translated_text: Previously, through the refutation of an inner operating person, [and] because flesh, blood, and such have been examined — the body is not within, not in the middle. And now, through the refutation of the composite whole — the body is 'not without,' not external, not an object of direct perception and such. So how is the body established in the hands and such? If it might be separate from the hands and such — he says 'separate from the hands' and so forth:

body.text: karādibhyaḥ pṛthaṅ nāsti kathaṃ nu khalu vidyate // Bca_9.83 //
body.translated_text: It does not exist separate from the hands and such — how indeed then does it exist? // Bca_9.83 //

body.text: karādibhyo 'vayavebhyaḥ pṛthag bhinnaḥ upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptaḥ kāyo nāsti, na pratibhāsate / karādaya eva hi kevalāḥ pratibhāsante / evaṃ yo na karādisvabhāvaḥ, nāpi tadādheyaḥ samaveto nāpyantargataḥ, na cāpi tadvayatiriktaḥ, sa kāyaḥ kathaṃ nu khalu vidyate? kathaṃ nviti kathaṃcidapi kāyamanupalabhamānaḥ tatsattvamasaṃbhāvayan pṛcchati- kathaṃ nu kena prakāreṇa / nviti vimarśe / vidyate, tatsattā vyavasthāpyate?
body.translated_text: The body does not exist — does not appear — separate from the parts such as hands and such, possessing the mark of being perceivable as distinct. For only hands and such alone, in isolation, appear. Thus, something that is not of the nature of hands and such, nor conjoined with them as their substratum, nor contained within them, nor separate from them — how indeed does that body exist? 'How indeed' — being utterly unable to find a body, unable to conceive of its existence, he asks: in what way, by what mode — 'indeed' is for deliberation — does it exist, does its existence get established?

body.text: yadā caivaṃ vicāreṇa kāyo vyavasthāpayitumaśakyaḥ, tadā asanneva vyavahartavya ityupasaṃharannāha tannāstītyādi-
body.translated_text: And when thus, through examination, the body cannot be established, then it should be dealt with as simply non-existent — concluding, he says 'therefore it does not exist' and so forth:

body.text: tannāsti kāyo mohāttu kāyabuddhiḥ karādiṣu /
body.translated_text: Therefore the body does not exist; but through delusion there is the notion of 'body' in the hands and such.

body.text: tannāsti kāya iti, yasmāduktavicāreṇa nopalabhyate, tasmādupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpto 'nupalabhyamāno nāsti kāyaḥ yadi nāsti, kathaṃ tarhi karādiṣu kāyabuddhirityāha- mohāttu ityādi / mohādavidyāvaśāt tu punaḥ kāyabuddhiḥ karādiṣu ekadravyarahiteṣu, na tu paramārthataḥ / avadhāraṇe vā tuśabdaḥ / tathāhi anavarāgrasaṃsārapravṛttijanmaparaṃparāparicitamithyābhyāsavāsanāvaśāt yathāvasthitavastutattvapratipattāvapi tadviparītasamāropakalpanā upajāyate / tadupanibaddho 'yaṃ kāyādivyavahāro loke pravartate, na tu pāramārthika iti //
body.translated_text: 'Therefore the body does not exist' — since through the examination described it is not found, therefore the body — being unfound despite possessing the mark of perceivability — does not exist. If it does not exist, how then is there the notion of 'body' regarding the hands and such? He says: 'through delusion' and so forth. Through delusion — through the power of ignorance — there is the notion of 'body' regarding the hands and such, which are devoid of a single substance — but not in ultimate reality. Or the word 'tu' is for emphasis. For through the power of the latent impressions of false habituation cultivated through the beginningless succession of <s>saṃsāric</s> births, even when the true nature of things as they actually stand is recognized, the conceptual construction of a false superimposition opposite to that arises. The conventional discourse of 'body' and such, dependent on that [false superimposition], operates in the world — but it is not ultimately [real].

body.text: kathamanyatra sā na bhavati ityatrāha saṃniveśeti-
body.translated_text: Why does that [notion] not arise elsewhere? To this he says 'due to the particular configuration' and so forth:

body.text: saṃniveśaviśeṣeṇa sthāṇau puruṣabuddhivat // Bca_9.84 //
body.translated_text: Due to the particular configuration, like the notion of a person in a tree-stump. // Bca_9.84 //

body.text: karacaraṇādisaṃniveśaḥ saṃsthānam, tadeva viśeṣo bheda itarasmāt, tena vibhramahetunā karādiṣveva, na sarvatra sā bhavati / pratiniyataviṣayā hi bhrāntaya iṣyante / kathamiva? sthāṇau puruṣabuddhivat / yathā sthāṇau puruṣasvabhāvarahite 'pi puruṣasādhāraṇordhvatādisaṃniveśaviśeṣamupalabdhavato dūrādavivecitaparaviśeṣasya kasyacit vibhramāt puruṣabuddhirupajāyate, tathā prakṛte 'pītyarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: The configuration of hands, feet, and such — the arrangement — that very thing as a particular distinction from other [configurations] — through that cause of error, [the notion arises] only regarding the hands and such, not everywhere. For errors are accepted as having determinate objects. Like what? 'Like the notion of a person in a tree-stump.' Just as in a tree-stump that is devoid of the nature of a person, for someone who, from a distance, having perceived a particular configuration of uprightness and such that is common to a person, has not discriminated the specific differences of another [thing] — through that error, the notion of a person arises — so too in the present case, is the meaning.

body.text: syādetat- kathaṃ punaretadavasitaṃ mohāt kāyabuddhiḥ, na tu punarvastutaḥ ityatrāha yāvadityādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: how is this concluded — that the notion of 'body' is from delusion, and not from reality? To this he says 'as long as' and so forth:

body.text: yāvatpratyayasāmagrī tāvatkāyaḥ pumāniva /
body.translated_text: As long as the assemblage of conditions [persists], for so long the body [appears] — like a person [in a stump].

body.text: yāvat yāvatkālāvadhiparicchinnā pratyayānāṃ kāraṇānāṃ pṛthivyādiṣaḍdhātuṣaṭsparśāyatanāṣṭādaśamanopavicārātmakānāṃ karmāyattavṛttīnāṃ sāmagrī samavadhānam, tāvatkālāvadhireva kāyaḥ pumāniva / yathā puruṣasvabhāvavirahito 'pi paramārthataḥ parikalpitarūpatayā puruṣa iva pratibhāsate vyavahriyate / upalakṣaṇaṃ caitat / strī vetyapi draṣṭavyam / na pūrvaṃ kalalādyavasthāyāṃ na paścādvikalitatvād bhasmādyavasthāyāṃ nijasvabhāvābhāvāt / idamatrāpi sāmānyamityupadarśayannāha evamityādi-
body.translated_text: As long as — for the time-duration defined by — the assemblage, the convergence, of conditions, of causes — consisting of the six elements of earth and such, the six contact-bases, and the eighteen mental examinations — whose operation depends on <s>karma</s> — for that time-duration alone is there a body, 'like a person [in a stump].' Just as [something] that is devoid of the nature of a person in the ultimate sense, through its conceptually constructed form, appears like a person and is treated as such. And this is illustrative: 'or a woman' should also be considered. Not before, in the <s>kalala</s> (embryonic) and other [early] stages; not after, due to being dismembered, in the state of ashes and such — because of the absence of an intrinsic nature [of its own]. Showing that this same [principle] applies here too, he says 'likewise' and so forth:

body.text: evaṃ karādau sā yāvattāvatkāyo 'tra dṛśyate // Bca_9.85 //
body.translated_text: Likewise, as long as hands and such [exist], for so long a body is seen therein. // Bca_9.85 //

body.text: yathā pratyayasāmagrīsadbhāve kāyaḥ pumāniva pratibhāsate, sadbhāvena pratibhāsate, evaṃ tathā karādau yāvat sā pratyayasāmagrī, tāvat kāyo 'tra karādau dṛśyate, kalpanāvaśāt pratibhāsate, na tu paramārthataḥ / tasmāt sāmagrīsākalye bhavati, tadabhāve ca na bhavati kāyabuddhiḥ / ato mohādeva karādiṣu kāyabuddhiriti niścitam / ayamatra samudāyārthaḥtattatpratyayasāmagrīsadbhāve tattadvastusvabhāvamantareṇāpi abhūtaṃ tattvamādarśayantī bhrāntivaśādasau kalpanā upajāyate / tadvaśāt saṃniveśaviśeṣeṣu strīpuruṣakāyādivyavahāraḥ pravartate / ata eva bhasmādyavasthāyāṃ sāmagrīvaikalyānnivartate / ato nāyaṃ kāyādivyavahāro vāstava iti vakṣyati / taduktam-
body.translated_text: Just as when the assemblage of conditions is present, the body appears like a person — appears as existing — so too, as long as that assemblage of conditions [persists] in the hands and such, the body is seen here in the hands and such — it appears through the force of conceptualization, but not in the ultimate sense. Therefore, in the completeness of the assemblage, the cognition of 'body' arises; in its absence, it does not arise. Hence it is certain that the cognition of 'body' in the hands and such is from delusion alone. Here, the collective meaning is this: in the presence of the assemblage of respective conditions, that conceptualization — which reveals an unreal reality even without the intrinsic nature of the respective thing — arises through the force of error. On account of that [conceptualization], in particular arrangements [of parts], the conventions of 'woman,' 'man,' 'body,' and such operate. For this very reason, in the state of ashes and such, [these conventions] cease through the deficiency of the assemblage. Therefore, this convention of 'body' and such is not real — as will be stated. As it is said —

children.translated_text: 'The intrinsic nature of the body should be stated — that which abides devoid of [change of] states.
If the body has the form of a statue, it does not exist in flesh or ashes.'
'If it abides there in subtle form, having abandoned grossness,

children.text: anirdeśyaḥ svataḥ prāptaḥ kāya ityucyate katham //
children.translated_text: it is inexpressible, self-obtained — how can it be called "body"?'

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: uktaṃ ca-
body.translated_text: And it is said —

children.translated_text: 'That whose arising is from causes, whose abiding is not without conditions,
and whose cessation is from the absence of conditions — how is it understood as "existing"?'

body.text: iti / [yuktiṣaṣṭikā-]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Yuktiṣaṣṭikā</s>]

body.text: kvacit pāṭhaḥ-
body.translated_text: In some readings —

body.text: yāvatpratyayasāmagrī tāvatkāṣṭhaṃ pumāniva //
body.translated_text: 'As long as the assemblage of conditions [persists], so long a post [appears] like a person.'

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: tatredaṃ vyākhyeyam- yāvadviparyāsapratyayasāmagrī sthāṇau puruṣapratītiḥ, tāvat kāṣṭhaṃ sthāṇusvabhāvaṃ pumāniva pratīyate, na tadabhāve / evameva karādau yāvat sā pratyayasāmagrī, tāvat kāyo 'tra karādau dṛśyate, na paścāt / ato mohādeva kāyabuddhiriti niścayaḥ //
body.translated_text: There, this should be explained thus: as long as the assemblage of conditions for the perversion [persists] — the perception of a person in a post — so long the post, being of the nature of a post, is perceived as if it were a person, not in the absence of that [assemblage]. In the same way, as long as that assemblage of conditions [persists] in the hands and such, the body is seen here in the hands and such — not afterward. Therefore, it is certain that the cognition of 'body' is from delusion alone.

body.text: nanu yadi nāma kāyo nāsti, karacaraṇādayaḥ punaravayavāḥ pratyakśopalabdhatvāt pratiṣeddhumaśakyāḥ ityāśaṅkaya karādayo 'pi parikalpitasvabhāvā evetyupadarśayitumāha evamaṅgulītyādi-
body.translated_text: But even if the body does not exist, the parts — hands, feet, and such — being directly perceived, cannot be denied — anticipating this, to show that the hands and such too are of a conceptually constructed nature, he says with 'likewise, the toe-clusters' and so forth —

body.text: evamaṅgulipuñjatvātpādo 'pi kataro bhavet /
body.translated_text: Likewise, by being a cluster of toes, which one would a foot be?

body.text: yathaiva vicāryamāṇaḥ kāyo nāsti, evaṃ karacaraṇādayo 'pi na santi / yataḥ aṅgulīnāṃ puñjaḥ samudāyaḥ / aṅgulīnāmityupalakṣaṇam / pārṣṇiprabhṛtīnāmapi draṣṭavyaḥ / tasya bhāvastattvam, tasmāt tatsvabhāvādityarthaḥ / pādo 'pi caraṇo 'pi kataro bhavet? tatsamudāyamantareṇa vicāryamāṇo naiva kaściditi bhāvaḥ / aṅgulipuñjo 'pi naikasvabhāva ityāha so 'pītyādi-
body.translated_text: Just as the body does not exist when analyzed, likewise the hands, feet, and such also do not exist. Because a foot too is a cluster — an aggregate — of toes. 'Toes' is illustrative; it should be seen as applying to heels and such as well. Its state is its nature — therefore, 'from that nature' — this is the meaning. 'Which one would a foot be?' — a foot too, when analyzed apart from that aggregate, is simply nothing — this is the meaning. The toe-cluster too is not of a single nature — he says with 'that too' and so forth —

body.text: so 'pi parvasamūhatvāt parvāpi svāṃśabhedataḥ // Bca_9.86 //
body.translated_text: That too, by being an assemblage of joints; and joints too, by the division of their own parts. // <s>Bca</s> 9.86 //

body.text: so 'pi aṅgulipuñjo 'pi vicārato na vastusan / kutaḥ? parvasamūhatvāt, parvaṇāmaṅgulibhāgānāṃ samūhatvāt saṃghātatvāt kataro bhavediti prakṛtena saṃbandhaḥ / parvaṇāmapi pratyekamavastutvamityata āha- parvāpi na vastu / kasmāt? svāṃśabhedataḥ, svasya ātmanaḥ aṃśānāmavayavānāṃ bhedato 'pi vibhāgāt //
body.translated_text: That — even the toe-cluster — when examined, is not a real thing. Why? Because of being an assemblage of joints — of finger-segments — because of being an aggregate: 'which one would it be?' — this is the connection with the main [sentence]. Even the joints, individually, are not real things — therefore he says: joints too are not real. Why? Because of the division of their own parts — the parts, the portions, of themselves — from their division too, from their separation.

body.text: aṃśā api tattvato na santītyāha-
body.translated_text: The parts too do not exist in truth — he says —

body.text: aṃśā apyaṇubhedena
body.translated_text: The parts too, by the division into atoms,

body.text: iti / aṃśāḥ parvabhāgāḥ api aṇubhedena paramāṇuśo vibhāgena bhidyamānatvāt kalpitā eva / aṇavo 'pi na pratyekaṃ paramārthasantaḥ ityāha-
body.translated_text: thus — the parts, the portions of the joints, too, by the division into atoms — by being divided into individual atoms — are merely conceptually constructed. And even atoms do not individually exist in the ultimate sense — he says —

body.text: so 'pyaṇurdigvibhāgataḥ /
body.translated_text: that atom too, by the division of [its] directional parts.

body.text: diśāṃ pūrvāparadakṣiṇottarādharordhvasvabhāvānāṃ saṃbandhena vibhāgato nānātvāt / tadvibhāgabhedādbhidyamānasya paramāṇoḥ ṣaḍaṃśatā syāt / dikṣu vā vibhāgāḥ nānādigavasthitā nānārūpāṃśāḥ paramāṇoḥ, tato bhedena na tasya svabhāvo 'vatiṣṭhate //
body.translated_text: Through the connection with the [six] directions — east, west, south, north, below, and above — by the division [into parts facing each direction], because of multiplicity. Through the division of those directional parts, the atom, being divided, would have six parts. Or, the divisions — the portions of different aspects situated in different directions — belong to the atom; by their division, its intrinsic nature does not withstand [analysis].

body.text:
digbhāgabhedo yasyāsti tasyaikatvaṃ na yujyate /
[viṃśakārikā-14]
body.translated_text: 'That which has division into directional parts — its unity is not justified.'

body.text: iti nyāyāt / tathāhi- pūrvāparādidigavasthitaparamāṇvabhimukhaṃ yat tat paramāṇormadhyavartino rūpam, tat kimekameva, aparāparaṃ vā? yadi ekameveti pakṣaḥ, tadā sarvaparamāṇūnāṃ parivāryāvasthitānāmekadeśatāprasaṅgaḥ / yataḥ pūrvādidigavasthitaparamāṇusamānadeśatāmantareṇa aparadigādyavasthitaparamāṇunā na prāgdeśāvasthitaparamāṇvabhimukharūpābhimukhaṃ syāt, anyathā rūpabhedaprasaṅgāt / tatsamānadeśatā ca na tatsvarūpāntarbhāvamantareṇa, tasyāpi pūrvadigavasthitasya paramāṇoraparaparamāṇunā sarvātmanā saṃbandhena tatsvarūpāntarbhāvāt paramāṇumātraṃ dravyaṃ syāt / tathā ca sati pracayarūpā bhūdharādayo na syuḥ / ato bhavanādīnāṃ pracayamicchatā dvitīya eva pakṣaḥ samabhyupeyaḥ / tadā ca ṣaḍbhiraparāpararūpeṇa yugapat saṃbandhāt ṣaḍbhāgo madhyaparamāṇuḥ syāt, tattaddeśāvasthitāparāparaparamāṇusaṃbandhena tatparamāṇurūpasya bhedāt / iti paramāṇurapi naikasvabhāvo yuktaḥ / yaduktamācāryapādaiḥ-
body.translated_text: [<s>Viṃśatikā</s> 14] — by this logic. For: what is the form of the central atom that faces the atom situated in the eastern direction and such? Is it one single [form], or different [forms]? If the first position — that it is one single [form] — then the absurd consequence follows that all the surrounding atoms would occupy the same place. Because, without occupying the same place as the atom situated in the eastern direction, the atom situated in another direction and such could not face the form facing the eastern atom; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of a division of forms. And that co-location is impossible without the inclusion within the form of the other [atom]. And since that [eastern] atom too has its entire [surface] in contact with the other atom, the result would be a material substance of only atomic size. And in that case, aggregated forms such as mountains and such would not exist. Therefore, one who wishes for the aggregation of buildings and such must accept only the second position. And then, because of being simultaneously connected with six different forms, the central atom would have six parts — because the form of each atom differs through its connection with the different atoms situated in each respective location. Thus, even an atom is not justified as being of a single nature. As was stated by the Master [<s>Vasubandhu</s>] —

children.translated_text: 'Through simultaneous connection with six [atoms], the atom would have six parts;
if the six occupied the same place, the aggregate would be of merely atomic size.'

body.text: iti / [viṃśakārikā-12]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Viṃśatikā</s> 12]

body.text: te 'pi punaraṇīyāṃso bhāgāḥ tathaiva nirūpyamāṇāḥ nirātmatayā nabhaḥsvabhāvatāṃ pratipadyante ityāha digvibhāgo 'pītyādi-
body.translated_text: Those still finer parts too, when similarly analyzed, arrive at the nature of space through being selfless — he says with 'the directional division too' and so forth —

body.text: digvibhāgo niraṃśatvādākāśaṃ tena nāstyaṇuḥ // Bca_9.87 //
body.translated_text: The directional division too, being partless — is space; therefore the atom does not exist. // <s>Bca</s> 9.87 //

body.text: digvibhāgo 'pi digbhedena paramāṇorvibhāgo 'pi pūrvavat ṣaḍaṃśatayā bhidyamānaḥ kataro bhavet? na kiṃcidvastu syāt / etat sarvatra pūrveṣu yojanīyam / kutaḥ? anaṃśatvāt / ato 'bhinikṛṣyamāṇo niḥsvabhāvatayā ākāśaṃ śūnyameva / tena kāraṇena nāstyaṇuḥ, na vidyate paramāṇuriti / evaṃ karādayo 'pi vicārato niḥsvabhāvā draṣṭavyā iti / tataḥ kāyo 'pi na paramārthataḥ kaścidasti, ekānekasvabhāvaviyogasya pratipādanāt / itthaṃ na keśādayaḥ, na cātmā, nāpi cittam, na ca kāyaḥ ahaṃkārasya viṣayo vastutaḥ / tasmādavidyāsamutthāpitātmatayā ātmādisattvamantareṇāpi pravartamāno 'yamahamiti pratyayo nirviṣaya eva samutpadyate / tena yaduktam-
body.translated_text: 'The directional division too' — even the division of the atom by directional parts — being divided, like before, into six parts — which one would it be? It would be no real thing whatsoever. This should be construed with all the preceding [levels of analysis]. Why? Because of being partless. Therefore, being drawn out [in analysis], through its lack of intrinsic nature, it is space — simply empty. For that reason, the atom does not exist — the <s>paramāṇu</s> is not found to exist. Thus the hands and such too, when analyzed, should be seen as devoid of intrinsic nature. From this, the body too does not exist in any way in the ultimate sense, since the separation from the natures of unity and multiplicity has been demonstrated. In this way, there are no hairs and such, no self, no mind, and no body [as objects of] the sense of 'I' in reality. Therefore, even though it operates with a selfhood projected by ignorance — even without the existence of a self and such — this cognition 'I' arises as entirely without an object. Therefore, what was stated —

body.text: ahameva na kiṃciccedbhayaṃ kasya bhaviṣyati /
body.translated_text: 'If the self is simply nothing, whose could fear be?'

body.text: iti, tat samarthitam / sarveṇa caitena kāyasmṛtyupasthānamupadarśitaṃ bhavati / yaduktaṃ dharmasaṃgītisūtre-
body.translated_text: — that has been established. And by all of this, the mindful establishment regarding the body (<s>kāyasmṛtyupasthāna</s>) has been shown. As stated in the <s>Dharmasaṃgītisūtra</s> —

body.text: punaraparaṃ kulaputra bodhisattva evaṃ kāyasmṛtimupasthāpayati- ayaṃ kāyaḥ pādapādāṅulijaṅghorutrikodaranābhīpṛṣṭhavaṃśahṛdayapārśvapārśukāhastakalācībāhvaṅgagrīvāhanulalāṭaśiraḥkapālamātrasamūhaḥ karmabhavakārakopacitaḥ nānākleśopakleśasaṃkalpavikalpaśatasahasrāṇāmāvāsaḥ / bahūni cātra dravyāṇi samavahitāni yaduta keśaromanakhadantāsthicarmapiśitavapāsnāyumedovasālasikāyakṛnmūtrapurīṣāmāśayapakkāśayarudhirakheṭapittapūyasiṃghāṇakamastiṣkamastakaluṅgāni / evaṃ bahudravyasamūhaḥ / tat ko 'tra kāyaḥ? tasya pratyavekṣamāṇasya evaṃ bhavati- ākāśasamo 'yaṃ kāyaḥ / sa ākāśavat kāye smṛtimupasthāpayati / sarvametadākāśamiti paśyati / tasya kāyaparijñānahetorna bhūyaḥ kvacit smṛtiḥ prasarati, na visarati, na pratisaratīti //
body.translated_text: 'Furthermore, <s>kulaputra</s>, a <s>Bodhisattva</s> establishes mindfulness of the body thus: this body is merely an assemblage of feet, toes, legs, thighs, belly, abdomen, navel, back, spine, heart, ribs, sides, hands, forearms, arms, shoulders, neck, jaw, forehead, head, and skull — accumulated through <s>karma</s>, becoming, and action — the dwelling of hundreds of thousands of afflictions, secondary afflictions, intentions, and conceptualizations. And herein many substances are contained, namely: hair of the head, body-hair, nails, teeth, bones, skin, flesh, fat, sinews, marrow, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, mucus, brain, cerebellum. Thus it is an assemblage of many substances. What then is the "body" here? For one who thus examines, this thought arises: this body is like space. He establishes mindfulness of the body as like space. He sees: all this is space. For one whose cause is the full understanding of the body, mindfulness no longer spreads further, does not diffuse, does not counter-flow.'

body.text: punaruktam-
body.translated_text: It is further stated —

body.text: ayaṃ kāyo na pūrvāntādāgato nāparānte saṃkrānto na pūrvāntāparāntāvasthito 'nyatrāsadviparyāsasaṃbhūtaḥ kārakavedakarahito nādyantamadhye pratiṣṭhitamūlaḥ, asvāmiko 'mamo 'parigrahaḥ / āgantukairvyavahārairvyavahriyate kāya iti deha iti bhoga iti āśraya iti kuṇapa iti āyatanamiti / asārako 'yaṃ kāyaḥ mātāpitṛśukraśoṇitasaṃbhūtaḥ aśucipūtidurgandhisvabhāvaḥ
body.translated_text: 'This body does not come from the prior limit, does not transmigrate to the posterior limit, does not abide in between the prior and posterior limits — except as arisen from the perversion of what does not exist — devoid of agent and experiencer, without a foundation established in beginning, end, or middle, ownerless, not "mine," not possessed. It is spoken of through adventitious conventions as "body," "physical form," "object of enjoyment," "basis," "corpse," "sense-base." This body is without essence, arisen from the mother's and father's semen and blood, of the nature of impurity, putrefaction, and foul odor,

body.text: rāgadoṣamohaviṣādataskarākulaḥ nityaṃ śatanapatanabhedanavikiraṇaviṃdhvaṃsanadharmā nānāvyādhiśatasahasranīḍa iti //
body.translated_text: beset by the thieves of desire, hatred, and delusion, always subject to the nature of crumbling, falling, breaking, scattering, and disintegrating — a nest for hundreds of thousands of various diseases.'

body.text: evaṃ yadā vicāryamāṇo vastutaḥ śūnyasvabhāvatayā ākāśasaṃkāśaḥ sarvathā kāyaḥ, tadā mithyaiva vastutattvamāropya rāgādikamutpādayantaḥ saṃsāramupabṛṃhayanti bālāḥ ityāhaevamityādi-
body.translated_text: Thus, when the body, upon analysis, is in every way of the nature of emptiness, resembling space — then those childish ones who, falsely superimposing a real nature upon things, give rise to desire and such, [thereby] nourish <s>saṃsāra</s> — he says with 'thus' and so forth —

body.text: evaṃ svapnopame rūpe ko rajyeta vicārakaḥ /
body.translated_text: In form thus like a dream, who with discernment would be attached?

body.text: evamityuktakrameṇa svapnopame svapnopalabdhe iva rūpe 'saumanasyasthānīye ko rajyeta, ka āsajyeta? asya ca upalakṣaṇatvāt ko dviṣyāt, ko muhyet, ityapi veditavyam / tadyathā- saumanasyasthānīyāni cakṣuṣā rūpāṇi dṛṣṭvā rāgo jāyate / daurmanasyasthānīyāni cakṣuṣā rūpāṇi dṛṣṭvā dveṣo jāyate / upekṣāsthānīyāni cakṣuṣā rūpāṇi dṛṣṭvā moho jāyate iti / yadetanmanopratikūleṣu rūpeṣvanunītaṃ carati, tenāsya rāga utpadyate / pratikūleṣu rūpeṣu pratihataṃ carati, tenāsya dveṣa utpadyate / naivānukūleṣu na pratikūleṣu saṃmūḍhaṃ carati, tenāsya moha utpadyate / evaṃ śabdādiṣu trividhamālambanamanubhavati pūrvavat / tatra yaḥ paṇḍitajātīyaḥ, iti hi atyantayā cakṣurāyatanaṃ śūnyaṃ cakṣurāyatanasvabhāvena tat pūrvāntato 'pi nopalabhyate, aparāntato 'pi nopalabhyate, madhyato nopalabhyate svabhāvarahitatvāt / evamanyeṣu śrotrādiṣu vaktavyam / evamatyantatayā rūpāyatanaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ rūpāyatanasvabhāvenetyādi pūrvavat / evaṃ śabdādiṣu vācyam //
body.translated_text: 'Thus' — in the manner stated. 'In form like a dream' — in form that is as if perceived in a dream — which is an occasion for pleasure — who would be attached, who would cling? And since this is illustrative, 'who would hate, who would be deluded?' — this too should be understood. Namely: seeing with the eyes forms that are occasions for pleasure, desire arises. Seeing with the eyes forms that are occasions for displeasure, hatred arises. Seeing with the eyes forms that are occasions for equanimity, delusion arises. When, regarding forms that are agreeable to the mind, [the mind] moves along compliantly — from that, desire arises in it. Regarding forms that are disagreeable, [the mind] moves along in opposition — from that, hatred arises in it. Regarding [forms] that are neither agreeable nor disagreeable, [the mind] moves along in confusion — from that, delusion arises in it. Likewise with sound and such, it experiences the threefold object, as before. There, one who belongs to the wise: 'for ultimately, the eye sense-base is empty of the nature of the eye sense-base — it is not found from the prior limit, not found from the posterior limit, not found in the middle — because it is devoid of intrinsic nature.' Likewise for the others — the ear and such — this should be stated. 'Likewise, ultimately, the form sense-base [is empty of the nature of the form sense-base]' and so forth, as before. Likewise with sound and such, this should be stated.

body.text: iti hi māyopamānīndriyāṇi svapnopamān viṣayān paśyati, tasya kathaṃ rāgādikamutpadyate? ata evāha- vicāraka iti / vicārako vicakśaṇaḥ / evametadyathābhūtaṃ samyak prajñayā paśyan ko rajyeta dveṣṭi muhyati vā? atra ca svapnopalabdhajanapadakalyāṇīprabhṛti bhagavatoktaṃ nidarśanamupadarśitavyam / kāyābhāve ca strāyādikalpanayāpi rāgo na yukta ityāha kāyaścetyādi-

children.text: kāyaścaivaṃ yadā nāsti tadā kā strī pumāṃśca kaḥ // Bca_9.88 //
children.translated_text: And when the body thus does not exist, then what is a woman, and what is a man? // <s>Bca</s> 9.88 //

body.translated_text: Thus, when illusion-like senses perceive dream-like objects, how can desire and such arise for one [who understands this]? For this very reason he says: '<s>vicāraka</s>' — one who examines, one who is discerning. Thus, seeing this correctly, as it truly is, with wisdom — who would be attached, hate, or be deluded? And here, the illustration spoken by the Blessed One — beginning with a woman of the countryside perceived in a dream — should be cited. And in the absence of a [real] body, desire through the conceptualization of 'woman' and such is also not justified — he says with 'and when the body' and so forth —

body.text: hetusamuccye cakāraḥ / yasmāt stryādikalpanayā rāgo na bhavati / kāyo yadā evamuditanayena nāsti, niḥsvabhāvaḥ, tadā kāyābhāvāt kā strī kāminī yasyāḥ kamanīyatayā puruṣe rāgo bhavet? kaśca pumān kāmukaḥ yasya rañjanīyatayā striyāṃ rāgo bhavet? strī hi svātmani strīti saṃkalpya bahirdhā puruṣe puruṣa iti rāgaṃ janayati / evaṃ puruṣo 'pi svātmani puruṣa iti saṃkalpya bahirdhā striyāṃ strīti rāgaṃ janayati / kāyābhāve tu striyāṃ strīti na saṃvidyate, puruṣe puruṣo na saṃvidyate / yacca svabhāvena na saṃvidyate, na tat strī na puruṣa iti / tasmādasati kāye stryādikalpanākṛto 'pi na yujyate rāgaḥ / tatkasya hetoḥ? manyanāpagatā hi sarvadharmā iti / yathāpradhānamayaṃ nirdeśaḥ / evameva strakcandanādayo 'pi svabhāvarahitā veditavyāḥ / tathā dveṣamohaviṣayā apīti / uktaṃ caitadbhagavatā pitāputrasamāgame-
body.translated_text: The particle 'and' (<s>ca</s>) is for accumulating reasons. Because through conceptualizations such as 'woman' and such, desire does not arise [in reality]. When the body, in the manner explained by the stated reasoning, does not exist — is devoid of intrinsic nature — then, due to the non-existence of the body, what is 'woman,' a desirable one, through whose attractiveness desire in a man would arise? And who is the 'man,' the desirous one, through whose susceptibility desire for a woman would arise? For a woman, having conceptualized 'I am a woman' with regard to herself, externally generates desire for a man, [conceptualizing] 'man.' Likewise, a man too, having conceptualized 'I am a man' with regard to himself, externally generates desire for a woman, [conceptualizing] 'woman.' But in the absence of the body, 'woman' is not found in a woman, 'man' is not found in a man. And what does not exist by its own nature is neither woman nor man. Therefore, in the absence of the body, desire produced by the conceptualization of woman and such is not justified. For what reason? Because 'all <s>dharmas</s> are free from conceit.' This statement is primarily [relevant] here. Likewise, garlands, sandalwood, and such too should be understood as devoid of intrinsic nature. And similarly, the objects of hatred and delusion too. And this was stated by the Blessed One in the <s>Pitāputrasamāgama</s> —

body.text:
ṣaḍdhāturayaṃ mahārāja puruṣaḥ, ṣaṭsparśāyatanaḥ, aṣṭādaśamanopavicāraḥ / ṣaḍdhāturayaṃ mahārāja puruṣa iti khalu punaretad yuktam / kiṃ caitat pratītya kam? ṣaḍime mahārāja dhātavaḥ / katame ṣaṭ? tadyathā- pṛthvīdhātuḥ, abdhātuḥ, tejodhātuḥ, vāyudhātuḥ, ākāśadhātuḥ, vijñānadhātuśca / ime mahārāja ṣaḍ dhātavaḥ / yāvat ṣaḍimāni mahārāja sparśāyatanāni / katamāni ṣaṭ? cakṣuḥsparśāyatanaṃ rūpāṇāṃ darśanāya yāvanmanaḥsparśāyatanaṃ dharmāṇāṃ vijñānāya / imāni mahārāja ṣaṭ sparśāyatanāni / peyālaṃ / aṣṭādaśa ime mahārāja manaupacārāḥ / katame aṣṭādaśa? iha puruṣaḥ cakṣuṣā rūpāṇi dṛṣṭvā saumanasyadaurmanasyopekṣāsthānīyāni rūpāṇyupavicarati / evaṃ śrotrādiṣu vācyam / tena pratyekamindriyaṣaṭkena saumanasyāditrayabhedādaṣṭādaśa manaupavicārā bhavanti / peyālaṃ / katamaśca mahārāja ādhyātmikaḥ pṛthvīdhātuḥ? yat kiṃcidasmin kāye 'dhyātmaṃ kakkhaṭatvaṃ kharagatamupāttam / tat punaḥ katamat? tadyathā- keśā romāṇi nakhā dantā ityādi / katamaśca mahārāja bāhyaḥ pṛthvīdhātuḥ? yat kiṃcid bāhyaṃ kakkhaṭatvaṃ kharagatamupāttam / ayamucyate bāhyaḥ pṛthvīdhātuḥ / tatra mahārāja ādhyātmikaḥ pṛthvīdhātuḥ utpadyamāno na kutaścidāgacchati, nirudhyamāno na kvacit saṃnicayaṃ gacchati / bhavati mahārāja samayo 'yaṃ yat strī adhyātmaṃ [ahaṃ] strīti kalpayati / sā adhyātmamahaṃ strīti kalpayitvā bahirdhā puruṣaṃ puruṣa iti kalpayati / sā bahirdhā puruṣaṃ puruṣa iti kalpayitvā saṃraktā satī bahirdhā puruṣeṇa sārdhaṃ saṃyogamākāṅkṣate / puruṣo 'pi adhyātmaṃ puruṣo 'smīti kalpayatīti purvavat / tayoḥ saṃyogākāṅkṣāyāṃ saṃyogo bhavati / saṃyogapratyayāt kalalaṃ jāyate / tatra mahārāja yaśca saṃkalpyate, yaśca saṃkalpayitā, ubhayametanna saṃvidyate / striyāṃ strī na saṃvidyate / puruṣe puruṣo na saṃvidyate / iti hi asannasadbhūtaḥ saṃkalpo jāyate / so 'pi saṃkalpaḥ sadbhāvena na saṃvidyate / yathā saṃkalpaḥ, tathā saṃyogo 'pi / kalalamapi svabhāvena na saṃvidyate / yacca svabhāvato na saṃvidyate, tat kathaṃ kakkhaṭatvaṃ janayiṣyati? iti hi mahārāja saṃkalpaṃ jñātvā kakkhaṭatvaṃ veditavyaṃ yathā kakkhaṭatvamutpadyamānaṃ na kutaścidāgacchatīti / bhavati mahāraja samayaḥ, yadayaṃ kāyaḥ śmaśānaparyavasāno bhavati / tasya tat kakkhaṭatvaṃ saṃklidyamānaṃ saṃnirudhyamānaṃ na pūrvāṃ diśaṃ gacchati, na dakṣiṇām, na paścimām, nottarām, nordhvam, nādhaḥ, nānuvidiśaṃ gacchati
/ evaṃ mahārāja ādhyātmikaḥ pṛthivīdhāturdraṣṭavyaḥ / peyālaṃ / tatra mahārāja pṛthivīdhātorutpādo 'pi śūnyaḥ, vyayo 'pi śūnyaḥ, utpanno 'pi pṛthivīdhātuḥ svabhāvaśūnyaḥ / iti hi mahārāja pṛthivīdhātuḥ pṛthivīdhātutvena nopalabhyate, anyatra vyavahārāt / so 'pi vyavahāro na strī na puruṣaḥ / evaṃ mahārāja yathābhūtaṃ samyak prajñayā draṣṭavyamiti / tena kā manyanā? manyanā māragocaraḥ / tat kasya hetoḥ? manyanāpagatā hi sarvadharmāḥ // iti //
body.translated_text:
'This person, Great King, consists of six elements, six contact sense-bases, and eighteen mental examinations. This person consists of six elements, Great King — this indeed is fitting. What are these, and in dependence on what? These, Great King, are six elements. Which six? Namely: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element. These, Great King, are the six elements. Up to: these, Great King, are the six contact sense-bases. Which six? The eye-contact sense-base for seeing forms, up to the mind-contact sense-base for cognizing <s>dharmas</s>. These, Great King, are the six contact sense-bases.' And so forth. 'These, Great King, are eighteen mental examinations. Which eighteen? Here a person, having seen forms with the eye, examines forms that are a basis for pleasant feeling, unpleasant feeling, or neutral feeling. Likewise for the ear and the rest.' Thus, through the sixfold division of each faculty and the threefold division of pleasant feeling and such, eighteen mental examinations arise. And so forth. 'And what, Great King, is the internal earth element? Whatever in this body is internal, hard, solid, and appropriated. And what is that? Namely: hairs of the head, bodily hairs, nails, teeth,' and so forth. 'And what, Great King, is the external earth element? Whatever external is hard, solid, and appropriated. This is called the external earth element. Therein, Great King, the internal earth element, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go to any repository. There is a time, Great King, when a woman conceives internally [the thought] "I am a woman." Having conceived internally "I am a woman," she conceives externally of a man as "man." Having conceived of a man externally as "man," being attached, she desires union with the man externally. A man too conceives internally "I am a man"' — and so forth as before. 'When the two desire union, union occurs. From the condition of union, <s>kalala</s> (embryonic matter) is born. Therein, Great King, both what is conceived and the conceiver — neither is found. In a woman, "woman" is not found. In a man, "man" is not found. Thus a conception that is neither existent nor non-existent is born. That conception too is not found as having real existence. Just as the conception, so too the union. The <s>kalala</s> too is not found by its own nature. And what is not found by its own nature — how will it generate hardness?
