Thus, Great King, having known the conception, hardness should be understood — how hardness, when arising, does not come from anywhere. There is a time, Great King, when this body comes to its end in the charnel ground. That hardness of it, as it decays and ceases, does not go to the eastern direction, nor to the southern, nor the western, nor the northern, nor above, nor below, nor to the intermediate directions.
Thus, Great King, should the internal earth element be seen.' And so forth. 'Therein, Great King, even the arising of the earth element is empty; even its destruction is empty; even the earth element when arisen is empty of intrinsic nature. Thus, Great King, the earth element is not apprehended as the earth element, except through convention. And that convention too is neither woman nor man. Thus, Great King, one should see with correct wisdom as it really is.' Therefore, what is conceit? Conceit is the domain of <s>Māra</s>. For what reason? Because all <s>dharmas</s> are free from conceit.' //

body.text: evaṃ kāyasmṛtyupasthānaṃ pratipādya vedanāsmṛtyupasthānamupadarśayituṃ vedanāṃ vicārayannāha yadyastītyādi-
body.translated_text: Having thus taught the mindfulness of the body (<s>kāyasmṛtyupasthāna</s>), in order to show the mindfulness of feelings (<s>vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna</s>), analyzing feeling, he says 'if there is' and so forth —

children.text: yadyasti duḥkhaṃ tattvena prahṛṣṭān kiṃ na vādhate /
children.translated_text: If suffering exists in reality, why does it not afflict the joyful?

children.text: śokādyārtāya mṛṣṭādi sukhaṃ cetkiṃ na rocate // Bca_9.89 //
children.translated_text: If pleasure [exists in reality], why is delicious [food] and such not pleasing to one afflicted by grief and such? // Bca_9.89 //

body.text: trividhā hi vedanāsukhā vedanā, duḥkhā vedanā, aduḥkhāsukhā ceti / tatra rūpavadvedanāpi nāsti paramārthataḥ / kathamiti cet / yadyasti duḥkham, asātaṃ veditam / tattvena paramārthataḥ / tadā prahṛṣṭān kiṃ na bādhate, saṃtoṣayuktān kiṃ na duḥkhayati? sukhamapi yadyasti tattvena, tadā śokādyārtāya / ādiśabdāt kāmabhayonmādārtāya / mṛṣṭādi sukhaṃ cet, mṛṣṭādi surasamāhārapānādi / ādiśabdāt strakūcandanādi sukhaṃ sukhahetutvāt / sukhaṃ cedyadi, kiṃ na rocate? na hi vastu satsvabhāvaṃ kadācidapi nivartitumutsahate / tasmāt kalpanopasthāpitameva sukhaduḥkhaṃ vedanīyamiti //
body.translated_text: Feeling is threefold: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant. Therein, like form, feeling too does not exist in the ultimate sense. How so? If suffering — an unpleasant sensation — exists in reality — in the ultimate sense — then why does it not afflict the joyful, why does it not cause pain to those endowed with satisfaction? And if pleasure exists in reality, then, for one afflicted by grief and such — by the word 'such,' for one afflicted by desire, fear, or madness — if delicious [food] and such [is pleasure] — delicious, well-prepared food, drink, and such — by the word 'such,' garlands, sandalwood, and such — [if it is] pleasure, since it is a cause of happiness — if it is indeed pleasure, why is it not pleasing? For a thing possessing a real intrinsic nature is never capable of being averted. Therefore, pleasure and pain that are experienced are set up by conceptualization alone. //

body.text: yaduktaṃ prahṛṣṭān kiṃ na bādhate iti, tatra parasya samādhānamāha balīyasetyādi-
body.translated_text: To what was said — 'why does it not afflict the joyful?' — he presents the opponent's resolution, saying 'because overpowered by something stronger' and so forth —

body.text: balīyasābhibhūtatvādyadi tannānubhūyate /
body.translated_text: If it is not experienced because overpowered by something stronger,

body.text: na hi prahṛṣṭāvasthāyāṃ sarvathaiva duḥkhamasat / kiṃ tarhi samudbhūtavartinā sukhena tiraskṛtatvāt vidyamānamapi nānubhūyate, balīyasā atibalavatā sukhena abhibhūtatvādupahatatvāt / sadapi yadi tadduḥkhaṃ nānubhūyate na vedyate ityucyate, tadā na yuktametadityāha vedanātvamityādi-
body.translated_text: It is not the case that in the state of joy, suffering is entirely non-existent. Rather, because it is eclipsed by the pleasure that has arisen and is operative, it is not experienced even though present — because overpowered, overcome by something stronger, by exceedingly powerful pleasure. If that suffering, even though present, is said not to be experienced, not to be felt — then this is not justified — he says 'how can it be a feeling?' and so forth —

body.text: vedanātvaṃ kathaṃ tasya yasya nānubhavātmatā // Bca_9.90 //
body.translated_text: How can that be a feeling whose nature is not to be experienced? // Bca_9.90 //

body.text: vedanātvaṃ vedanāsvabhāvatvaṃ kathaṃ kena prakāreṇa tasyāvyaktasya sukhasya yasya nānubhavātmatā nānubhūyamānasvabhāvatā / vedyate iti hi vedanocyate, vedanānubhava iti vacanāt / yadi ca avedyamānāpi vedanā syāt, tadā na kiṃcinna vedanā syādityatiprasaṅgaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Being a feeling' — having the intrinsic nature of feeling — how, in what way, [can this be the case] for that unmanifest pleasure whose nature is not to be experienced — whose own nature is one of not being experienced? For it is called 'feeling' (<s>vedanā</s>) because it is felt — from the statement 'feeling is experience.' If there could be feeling even when not being felt, then nothing would not be a feeling — this is the absurd overextension. //

body.text: athāpi syāt- na sarvathā nānubhūyate, kiṃ tu sūkṣmatayā anubhūtamapi ananubhūtakalpamityatrāha astītyādi-
body.translated_text: But one might say: it is not entirely unexperienced; rather, due to subtlety, even though experienced, it is as if unexperienced — to this he says 'there is' and so forth —

children.text: asti sūkṣmatayā duḥkhaṃ sthaulyaṃ tasya hṛtaṃ nanu /
children.translated_text: If suffering exists in subtle form, has not its grossness been removed?
And if the remainder is merely a satisfaction, then that too is merely a subtle [form] of it. // Bca_9.91 //

body.text: asti vidyate sūkṣmatayā anupalakśyamāṇatayā duḥkham, tarhi balīyasā sukhena kiṃ kṛtamasya? sthaulyameva hṛtaṃ nanu, prahṛṣṭāvasthāyāṃ pravṛttena balavatā sukhena sthaulyaṃ prābalyamasya duḥkhasya hatamabhibhūtam / nanu, nanviti parasya saṃbodhane / iti mataṃ bho tava, na hi sūkṣmatā nāma duḥkhasya sātānubhavakāle kācidupalabhyate / tat kathaṃ sūkṣmatā tasyeti vaktavyam / atha tuṣṭimātrā aparā tasmādeva udbhūtavṛtteḥ sukhāt, aparā tuṣṭimātrā dvitīyā sukhamātrā alpīyasī sukhakaṇikā syāt, duḥkhasya sūkṣmatā bhavet, ced yadi abhipretam, nanu sāpyasya sūkṣmatā sāpi tuṣṭimātrā aparā, asya sukhasyaiva sūkṣmatā, na tu duḥkhasya, tuṣṭeḥ sukhajātitvāt / iti duḥkhasya sūkṣmatā avedyasvabhāvā sukhānubhavakāle nāstyeveti niścitam //
body.translated_text: 'There exists' — there is — suffering 'in subtle form' — in an imperceptible way — then what has been done to it by the stronger pleasure? Its grossness alone has been removed — by the powerful pleasure operative in the state of joy, the grossness, the predominance of this suffering has been overpowered. '<s>Nanu</s>' — [used for] addressing the opponent. This is your view — but subtlety of suffering at the time of the experience of pleasure is in no way apprehended. So how can it be said that there is subtlety of that [suffering]? But if 'another' — a second — 'mere satisfaction' — a mere pleasure, a lesser particle of happiness — different from that very arisen, operative pleasure — if that would be the subtlety of suffering — if this is intended — surely 'that too is the subtlety of this' — that other mere satisfaction is the subtlety of this pleasure itself, not of suffering, since satisfaction is of the genus of pleasure. Thus, the subtlety of suffering — of unfelt nature — does not exist at all at the time of experiencing pleasure: this is established. //

body.text: syādetat- na duḥkhaṃ kālpanikatayā kādācitkam, kiṃ tarhi kāraṇavaikalyāt kadācinnopalabhyate ityatrāha viruddhetyādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: suffering is not occasional due to being fabricated; rather, it is sometimes not apprehended due to the deficiency of its cause — to this he says 'opposed' and so forth —

body.text: viruddhapratyayotpattau duḥkhasyānudayo yadi /
body.translated_text: If suffering does not arise when the opposing condition arises,

body.text: duḥkhena viruddhasya sukhasya yaḥ pratyayo hetuḥ sparśaḥ, tasyotpattau ābhimukhye sati / atha vā / viruddhasya pratyayasya sukhahetorutpattau janmani, viruddhaḥ pratyayo 'syeti vā / duḥkhenetyapekṣāyāmapi gamakatvādbhavati samāsaḥ / tasyotpattau satyāṃ prahṛṣṭāvasthāyāṃ hetuvaikalyāt duḥkhasyānudayo duḥkhasyānutpattiśceducyate, tadā-
body.translated_text: The 'opposing condition' of suffering is the cause of pleasure, [namely] contact. 'When it arises' — when it is present. Or alternatively: 'when the opposing condition' — the cause of pleasure — arises, is born; the 'opposing condition' means: that whose condition is opposed. Or: the condition that is opposed to suffering. Even with the dependence on 'to suffering,' the compound works because it conveys the meaning. When this arises — in the state of joy — if it is said that suffering does not arise, does not originate, due to the deficiency of its cause — then —

body.text: kalpanābhiniveśo hi vedanetyāgataṃ nanu // Bca_9.92 //
body.translated_text: Does it not follow that feeling is a clinging produced by conceptualization? // Bca_9.92 //

body.text: nanu yadeva asmābhirabhihitaṃ tadeva sāṃpratamāgatamāyātam / kiṃ tat? kalpanayā abhiniveśaḥ, kalpanayā kṛto yo 'bhiniveśaḥ, hiravadhāraṇe / sa eva vedanā sukhā duḥkhā taditarā vā / nānyat vāstavaṃ sukhādyasukhādiheturvāsti, iti / tathāhi nijasvabhāvarahitamapi yat sukhasādhanatvena parikalpitam, tadabhiniveśātsukhaṃ veditamutpadyate, itarasmāditarat / kathamanyathā yadeva anyasya duḥkhasādhanam, tadeva aparasya kasyacit sukhasādhanaṃ syāt? tasyaivaikasya yasya śabdaśravaṇādapi duḥkhamāsīt, punaḥ kālāntareṇa tasya darśanāt prītirupajāyate / tasmāt kālpanikameva sukhādikaṃ tatsādhanaṃ vā, na vāstavam / āha ca-
body.translated_text: '<s>Nanu</s>' — what we ourselves have stated has now arrived, has been reached. What is that? The clinging made by conceptualization — the clinging produced through conceptualization — '<s>hi</s>' is for emphasis — that itself is feeling — pleasant, painful, or otherwise. There is no other real [thing] that is the cause of pleasure or displeasure. For even what is devoid of its own intrinsic nature, when conceptualized as a means of pleasure, from the clinging to it, a pleasant sensation arises; and from the other [conceptualization], the other [sensation]. How else would the very same thing that is a cause of suffering for one person be a cause of pleasure for another? For the very same one whose hearing of a sound [once] caused pain — at a later time, from seeing that [person], delight arises. Therefore, pleasure and such, and their causes, are merely fabricated — not real. And it is said —

children.text: ahirmayūrasya sukhāya jāyate viṣaṃ viṣābhyāsavato rasāyanam /
children.translated_text: 'A serpent is born to the delight of a peacock; poison is a tonic for one habituated to poison;

children.text: bhavanti cānandaviśeṣahetavo mukhaṃ tudantaḥ karabhasya kaṇṭakāḥ //
children.translated_text: and thorns that prick the face of a young elephant become causes of special delight.'

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: vedanā abhiniveśasvabhāvatvādeva ca vicāreṇa nivartayituṃ śakyate ityāha ata evetyādi-
body.translated_text: And because feeling is of the nature of clinging, it can be averted through analysis — he says 'for this very reason' and so forth —

body.text: ata eva vicāro 'yaṃ pratipakṣo 'sya bhāvyate /
body.translated_text: For this very reason, this analysis is the antidote to be cultivated.

body.text: ata eveti / yata eva abhiniveśasvabhāvā vedanā, ata eva vicāro 'yaṃ vimarśo 'yaṃ pratipakṣo virodhī, nirākṛtikāraṇatvāt asyābhiniveśasya sukhādirūpasya bhāvyate vicintyate / tatsādhanābhāve tadabhiniveśābhāvāt / api ca / itthamapyabhiniveśo vedanetyāha vikalpetyādi-
body.translated_text: 'For this very reason' — precisely because feeling is of the nature of clinging, 'for this very reason, this analysis' — this examination — 'is the antidote,' the opponent — because it is the cause of refutation — 'of this clinging in the form of pleasure and such' — 'is to be cultivated,' is to be reflected upon. Because in the absence of the establishment [of the object], the clinging to it is absent. Moreover, showing that clinging too is feeling, he says 'conceptualization' and so forth —

body.text: vikalpakṣetrasaṃbhūtadhyānāhārā hi yoginaḥ // Bca_9.93 //
body.translated_text: For yogins feed on the <s>dhyāna</s> born from the field of conceptualization. // Bca_9.93 //

body.text: ata eveti vartate / vikalpa eva kṣetraṃ janmabhūmitvāt / tasmin saṃbhūtaṃ jātaṃ dhyānaṃ viviktaṃ kāmaiḥ, viviktaṃ pāpakairakuśalairdharmaiḥ savitarkaṃ savicāraṃ samādhijaṃ prītisukhamityādi / dhyānādibhāvanā samādhisamāpattervikalpabhavatvāt, tadeva āhāraḥ śarīrayāpanāhetutvāt, yeṣāṃ te tathoktāḥ / ke te? yoginaḥ / hiryasmāt kalpanānirmitaprītisukhāhārasaṃdhāritaśarīrā yoginaḥ, tasmāt kalpanābhiniveśo vedaneti pratipāditam //
body.translated_text: 'For this reason' carries over [from the previous]. Conceptualization itself is the field, being the birthplace [of feeling]. Born — arisen — in that [field of conceptualization] is meditation — secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome <s>dharmas</s>, endowed with applied thought and sustained thought, born of concentration, accompanied by joy and happiness — and so forth. The cultivation of meditation and such, because it is born of conceptualization — of the attainment of <s>samādhi</s> — that very [meditation] is food, being the cause of sustaining the body — those [yogins] for whom this is so are described thus. Who are they? Yogins. 'For' — since yogins have their bodies sustained by food consisting of joy and happiness constructed by conceptualization, therefore it has been demonstrated that clinging to conceptualization is feeling.

body.text: sāṃprataṃ hetvanabhisaṃbhavādeva na vedanā vastusatī yuktetyāha sāntarāvityādi-
body.translated_text: Now, showing that even from the impossibility of the cause, feeling is not justified as a real entity, he says 'with an interval' and so forth —

body.text: sāntarāvindriyārthau cetsaṃsargaḥ kuta etayoḥ /
body.translated_text: If sense-faculty and object are with an interval, how could there be contact between the two?

body.text: ayamatra samudāyārthaḥ- sparśapratyayā vedanā / viṣayendriyavijñānānāṃ trayāṇāṃ saṃnipātaśca sparśaḥ / sparśāḥ ṣaṭ saṃnipātajāḥ [abhi. ko.-3.30] iti vacanāt / sa trikasaṃnipātajaḥ sparśa eva na ghaṭate, kutastatpratyayā vedanā bhaviṣyatīti / tathāhiindriyārthayoḥ sāntarayorvā syānnirantarayorvā? tatra indriyārthāvakṣaviṣayau sāntarau savyavadhānau yadi, tadā saṃsargaḥ saṃnipāto melanaṃ kutaḥ kasmāt etayorindriyārthayoḥ? naiva yujyate / sparśo hi saṃparka ucyate / vyavadhāne sati sa kathaṃ bhavet iti bhāvaḥ / atha dvitīyaḥ prakāraḥ, so 'pi na yujyate ityāha nirantaratve ityādi-
body.translated_text: Here the combined meaning is: feeling is conditioned by contact. And contact is the conjunction of the three — object, sense-faculty, and consciousness. Because of the statement: 'the six contacts arise from conjunction' [<s>Abhidharmakośa</s> 3.30]. That very contact born of the conjunction of three simply does not work — so how could feeling conditioned by it come about? For the sense-faculty and object would either have an interval between them or be without interval. In the first case: if the sense-faculty and object — the eye and visual object [for example] — are with interval, with a gap between them, then how could there be contact — conjunction, meeting — between the two, between the sense-faculty and object? It is simply not justified. For contact is said to be a coming together. When there is a gap, how could that occur? — this is the meaning. But the second alternative also does not work — he says 'even in the absence of interval' and so forth —

body.text: nirantaratve 'pyekatvaṃ kasya kenāstu saṃgatiḥ // Bca_9.94 //
body.translated_text: Even without interval, there would be identity — whose meeting with what could there be? // <s>Bca</s> 9.94 //

body.text: nirantaratve 'pi vyavadhānābhāve 'pi sati ekatvaṃ tādātmyamindriyārthayoḥ / evaṃ hi tayoḥ sarvātmanā nairantaryaṃ bhavet yadi aṇīyasāpi nāṃśena vyavadhānaṃ syāt sadharmatā ca / tatrāntarbhāve tattvameva / evaṃ ca kasya kenāstu saṃgatiḥ? ekatve sati bhedābhāvāt kiṃ kena saṃgataṃ syāt? na hi ātmanaiva ātmanaḥ saṃgatiryuktāḥ /
body.translated_text: Even without interval — even in the absence of a gap — there would be identity, complete oneness, between the sense-faculty and object. For their complete lack of interval would only obtain if there were no gap whatsoever, even by the most minute part — and [if there were] also sameness of characteristics. When they are absorbed into each other — that is identity itself. And thus, whose meeting with what could there be? In the presence of identity, since there is no differentiation, what could be in contact with what? For the meeting of oneself with oneself is not justified.

body.text: syādetat- niraṃśānāmeva paramāṇūnāṃ saṃsargo vastutaḥ / na ca tatra aṃśāṃśivyavahāro yuktaḥ, sthūlarūpāṇāmeva tatsaṃbhavāt / tatra ca saṃsargadūṣaṇe na kiṃciddūṣyate ityāha nāṇorityādi-
body.translated_text: [Objection:] It is the partless atoms themselves that come into contact in reality. And there, the discourse of parts and wholes is not justified, since it occurs only for gross forms. And in the refutation of contact [at the gross level], nothing is refuted. He says 'there is no entry' and so forth —

body.text: nāṇoraṇau praveśo 'sti nirākāśaḥ samaśca saḥ /
body.translated_text: There is no entry of one atom into another atom; it is spaceless and equal [on all sides].

body.text: paramāṇūnāmapi naiva saṃparko yuktaḥ / yataḥ ekasyāpyaṇoranyasminnaṇau na praveśo 'sti, nāntarbhāvo 'sti / kutaḥ? co yasmāt / nirākāśaḥ saḥ nīrandhraḥ paramāṇuḥ / samaḥ sa tulyaḥ, nimnonnatābhāvāt / iti kathaṃ niraṃśasya saṃgatirastu? athāpi syāt- mā bhūdaṇoraṇau praveśaḥ, saṃgatimātraṃ kevalamastu, tāvatā siddhaṃ naḥ sādhyamityāha apraveśa iti-
body.translated_text: Even the contact of atoms is not justified. Because there is no entry — no interpenetration — of even one atom into another atom. Why? The word 'and' [means] 'because.' That atom is spaceless — without interstices. It is equal — the same [on all sides], due to the absence of indentations and protrusions. So how could there be contact for something partless? One might say: let there be no entry of one atom into another; let there be mere contact alone — with that much our thesis is established. He says 'without entry' —

body.text: apraveśe na miśratvamamiśratve na saṃgatiḥ // Bca_9.95 //
body.translated_text: Without entry there is no intermixture; without intermixture there is no contact. // <s>Bca</s> 9.95 //

body.text: sarvātmanā hi saṃparkaḥ saṃgatiraṇoḥ, anyathā sāṃśatvaprasaṅgāt / tathā ca tatsvarūpaṃ svātmanā vyāpnuvata eva tena saṃgatiḥ / evaṃ tatsvarūpamiśratvābhāve saṃgatirna syāt / tacca miśratvaṃ tatra praveśamantareṇa na bhavet / itthamapraveśe praveśābhāve sati na miśratvaṃ nāsaṃbhinnarūpatvam / amiśratve miśratvābhāve ca na saṃgatiḥ nāsaṅgaḥ //
body.translated_text: For the contact of an atom must be with its entire being — otherwise there would be the absurd consequence of it having parts. And thus, contact would only occur when its own form pervades [the other] with its entire self. In the absence of such intermixture with that [other] form, there could be no contact. And that intermixture would not occur without entry [into the other]. Thus, without entry — in the absence of entry — there is no intermixture, no unseparated state of forms. And without intermixture — in the absence of intermixture — there is no contact, no conjunction.

body.text: niraṃśasya sarvathaiva saṃsargo na yujyate ityāha niraṃśasya cetyādi-
body.translated_text: Showing that the contact of something partless is in no way justified, he says 'for something partless' and so forth —

body.text: niraṃśasya ca saṃsargaḥ kathaṃ nāmopapadyate /
body.translated_text: How indeed could contact of something partless ever be possible?

body.text: niraṃśasya aṃśaśūnyasya ca padārthasya / co dūṣaṇasamuccaye / saṃsargo mīlanaṃ kathaṃ nāmopapadyate? nāmeti saṃbhāvayānām / kathaṃ saṃsargaḥ saṃbhāvyate? sarvālpasyāpi avaśyamekenāṃśena bhavitavyam / yasya punaraṃśa eva nāsti, tasya amūrtasya aṃśābhāve asattvameva prāptamiti bhāvaḥ / na caitad bhavato 'pi pramāṇapratītaṃ kvacidastītyāha saṃsarga ityādi-
body.translated_text: 'For something partless' — for a thing devoid of parts. The word 'and' is for accumulation of objections. 'Contact' — meeting — how indeed could it be possible? 'Indeed' is for deliberation. How could contact be conceived? For even the smallest thing must necessarily have at least one part. And for that which has no part at all — for that which is formless — in the absence of parts, its very non-existence would follow. This is the meaning. And this has not been established for you either by any valid cognition — he says 'in contact' and so forth —

body.text: saṃsarge ca niraṃśatvaṃ yadi dṛṣṭaṃ nidarśaya // Bca_9.96 //
body.translated_text: If you have seen partlessness in contact, please show [us] an example. // <s>Bca</s> 9.96 //

body.text: .........................āha vijñānasya tvityādi-
body.translated_text: ........................... He says 'as for consciousness' and so forth —

body.text: vijñānasya tvamūrtasya saṃsargo naiva yujyate /
body.translated_text: As for consciousness, which is formless, contact is simply not justified.

body.text: turatiśayābhidhāne / vijñānasya viṣayavijñapteḥ / punaḥsaṃsargo naiva yujyate, na saṃgacchate / kutaḥ? amūrtasyeti hetupadametat / mūrtiśūnyasya vijñānasya / amūrtatvādityarthaḥ / parasparasaṃparko hi saṃsargaḥ / sa ca mūrtimatāmeva vidyate / yasya tu mūrtireva nāsti, tasya kathaṃ saṃsargaḥ syāt? iti trayāṇāmapi saṃsargamavadhūya saṃprati samūha eva vastusan nāsti iti pratipādayannāha samūhasyāpītyādi-
body.translated_text: The word 'tu' is in the sense of emphasis. 'Of consciousness' — of the representation of objects. Again, 'contact is simply not justified,' does not cohere. Why? 'Because of being formless' — this is the causal clause. For consciousness, which is devoid of form. Because of being formless — this is the meaning. For mutual contact is contact, and that exists only for things with form. But for that which has no form at all — how could there be contact for it? Thus, having rejected the contact of all three [components], now showing that the aggregate too is not a real entity, he says 'even of the aggregate' and so forth —

body.text: samūhasyāpyavastutvādyathā pūrvaṃ vicāritam // Bca_9.97 //
body.translated_text: Even the aggregate is not a real entity, as was previously analyzed. // <s>Bca</s> 9.97 //

body.text: api dūṣaṇasamuccaye / samūhasyāpi saṃghātasyāpi / avastutvāt vasturahitatvāt aśvaviuṣāṇavat saṃsargo naiva yujyate iti prakṛtena saṃbandhaḥ / samūhasyaivābhāvāt / kathaṃ punaravastukatvam? yathā pūrvaṃ vicāritam, yathā prāṅ nirūpitam, evamaṅgulipuñjatvādityādinā //
body.translated_text: The word 'also' is for accumulation of objections. 'Even of the aggregate' — even of the composite. 'Because of not being a real entity' — because of being devoid of reality, like a hare's horn — 'contact is simply not justified': this connects with the main [statement]. Because the aggregate itself does not exist. How then is it non-real? 'As was previously analyzed' — as was examined before — thus, through [the analysis] 'being a collection of fingers' and so forth.

body.text: hetvasaṃbhavameva upasaṃharannāha tadevamityādinā-
body.translated_text: Concluding the very impossibility of the cause, he says 'thus' and so forth —

body.text: tadevaṃ sparśanābhāve vedanāsaṃbhavaḥ kutaḥ /
body.translated_text: Thus, in the absence of contact, from where could feeling arise?

body.text: tasmādevaṃ pratipāditakrameṇa sparśanābhāve trikasaṃparkābhāve vedanāsaṃbhavaḥ kutaḥ, vedanāyāḥ sukhādirūpāyāḥ saṃbhava utpādaḥ kutaḥ, naiva yujyate / kāraṇābhāve kāryasya saṃbhavāyogāt / iti paramārthato vedanābhāve hitāhitaviṣayasyāsaṃbhavāt /
body.translated_text: Therefore, in the manner thus demonstrated, in the absence of contact — in the absence of the conjunction of the three — from where could feeling arise? The arising — the production — of feeling in the form of pleasure and such: from where [could it come]? It is simply not justified — because in the absence of a cause, the arising of an effect is impossible. Thus, in the ultimate non-existence of feeling, since the object of what is beneficial or harmful is impossible —

body.text: kimarthamayamāyāsaḥ
body.translated_text: What is the purpose of this exertion?

body.text: sukhaduḥkhasādhanaprāptiparihārāya yo 'yamāyāsaḥ kriyate sa kimarthaḥ? ākāśacarvaṇārthamiva naivocita iti bhāvaḥ / mā bhūt sukhasādhanāya, duḥkhasyābhiṣoḍhumaśakyatvāt tatparihārāya bhavatu cedāha-
body.translated_text: This exertion that is made for the purpose of obtaining the means of happiness and avoiding [suffering] — what is its purpose? It is simply not fitting — like chewing space, as it were. This is the meaning. Let it not be for the sake of happiness; since suffering cannot be endured, let it be for its avoidance — if [one says] so, he says —

body.text: bādhā kasya kuto bhavet // Bca_9.98 //
body.translated_text: Whose affliction, and from what, could arise? // <s>Bca</s> 9.98 //

body.text: vedanāyā vicāreṇa niḥsvabhāvatvād bādhā avicārataḥ ātmādeḥ pūrvanirastatvādvedakābhāvaḥ / upaghātahetorapi vikalpakalpitatvāt na paramārthataḥ sattvam / ityevaṃ bādhā pīḍāvedanābhāvāt kasya vedakābhāvādbhavet, kuta upaghātahetorabhāvācca bhavet? naiva paramārthataḥ kasyacit kutaścit syāt / tasmādveditrabhāvādapi vedanā na yuktā //
body.translated_text: Through the analysis of feeling, because of its lack of intrinsic nature, affliction — without analysis, the self and such having been previously refuted — the experiencer is absent. The cause of harm too, being constructed by conceptualization — is not ultimately real. Thus, affliction — pain-feeling — because of the absence [of feeling]: whose [could it be], because of the absence of an experiencer? And from what could it arise, because of the absence of a cause of harm? There is simply, in the ultimate sense, no [affliction] for anyone from anything. Therefore, even from the absence of an experiencer, feeling is not justified.

body.text: saṃprati vedanābhāvāt tatpratyayā tṛṣṇāpi kāraṇavirahāt paramārthato notpādamarhatītyupadarśayitumāha yadā netyādi-
body.translated_text: Now, showing that since feeling does not exist, craving conditioned by it too does not deserve to arise ultimately, being devoid of its cause, he says 'when' and so forth —

children.text: yadā na vedakaḥ kaścidvedanā ca na vidyate /
children.translated_text: When there is no experiencer whatsoever, and feeling does not exist,

children.text: tadāvasthāmimāṃ dṛṣṭvā tṛṣṇe kiṃ na vidīryase // Bca_9.99 //
children.translated_text: then, O craving, seeing this state of affairs, why do you not disintegrate? // <s>Bca</s> 9.99 //

body.text: yo vedanāṃ vedayate sa vedakaḥ / yadā kaścidātmādirnāsti, tadabhāvātsamanantaranirūpaṇācca vedanā na vidyate / tadā avasthāmimāṃ evaṃvidhāṃ svajanmavikalāṃ dṛṣṭvā upalabhya tṛṣṇe kiṃ na vidīryase, tadduḥkhaduḥkhitāpi satī kiṃ na viśīryase, yadadyāpi tadviyogavidhurā tvamātmānaṃ na muñcasi //
body.translated_text: The one who experiences feeling is the experiencer. When no self or such exists — because of its absence, and because of the immediately preceding analysis — feeling does not exist. Then, seeing this state of affairs — this condition of such a kind, in which your own birth is impaired — O craving, why do you not disintegrate? Even you, who suffer from the suffering of that [futile craving], why do you not fall apart? — [the point being:] even now, bereft of that [feeling], you do not release yourself.

body.text: syādetat- yadi vedako na syāt, vedanā ca nāsti, kenāyaṃ tarhi sukhasādhanatvādinā bhāveṣu dṛṣṭādivyavahāraḥ pravartate ityatrāha dṛśyate ityādi-
body.translated_text: [Objection:] If there is no experiencer and no feeling, then by what does this conventional discourse of seeing beneficial properties and such in things proceed? To this he says 'it is seen' and so forth —

children.translated_text: It is seen and touched by a mind whose nature is like a dream and an illusion;
because feeling is co-arisen with mind, it is not [truly] perceived by it. // <s>Bca</s> 9.100 //

body.text: dṛśyate cakṣurindriyajena / spṛśyate kāyendriyajātena cittena jñānena / evaṃ tarhi cittameva vedakaṃ vastusadastīti cedāha svapnamāyopamātmanā / svapnopamasvabhāvena māyopamasvabhāvena ca / pratītyasamutpannena cittena, na tu paramārthasatā / kathaṃ cittād vyatiriktaṃ cittena dṛśyate? sahajātatvāt, cittena sahotpannatvāt cittena saha janma yasya tasya darśanam, ekasāmagrīpratibaddhatvāt pratītyasamutpādasyācintyatvācca / na tu paramārthato darśanamasti yenaivaṃ dṛṣṭādivyavahāraḥ / vedanā tena nekṣyate, yena dṛṣṭasukhasādhanādivyavahāro 'pyanyata eva, tena kāraṇena vedanā nekṣyate, na dṛśyate vastutaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'It is seen' — by that born from the eye-faculty. 'It is touched' — by that born from the body-faculty, by mind, by cognition. If so, then mind is the experiencer and exists as a real entity — if [one says] so, he says: 'whose nature is like a dream and an illusion.' With a nature like a dream, with a nature like an illusion — by a mind that has arisen dependently, not by an ultimately real [mind]. How is something distinct from mind seen by mind? Because it is co-arisen — because it is born simultaneously with mind; because its birth is together with mind — the seeing of that [feeling]. Because [they are] bound by a single causal assemblage, and because dependent origination is inconceivable. But there is no seeing in the ultimate sense such that the conventional discourse of seeing and such would [be established]. 'Feeling is not perceived by it' — by this reason, feeling is not perceived, is not seen as real — because even the conventional discourse of seeing beneficial means and such [proceeds] from something else [than ultimate reality].

body.text: athāpi syāt- na sahajaṃ dṛśyate, api tu jñānaṃ viṣayākāratayā tata utpadyamānamuttarakālaṃ tasya grāhakamucyate, ityetadapahastayitumāha pūrvamityādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: it is not that what is co-arisen is seen; rather, cognition, arising in the form of the object and thus produced from it, is called the grasper of that [object] at a subsequent moment. To refute this, he says 'by what is born before or after' and so forth —

body.text: pūrvaṃ paścācca jātena smaryate nānubhūyate /
body.translated_text: What is born before or after is remembered, not experienced.

body.text: avaśyaṃ sahajātasya vedanam, anyathā pūrvaṃ prāgbhāvi paścāduttarakālaṃ jātena utpannena jñānena smaryate nānubhūyate smṛtirūpeṇa viṣayīkriyate, na sākṣādvidyate / tajjñānakāle tasyātītatvāt / na ca atītasya svarūpeṇa vedanamucitam, avidyamānatvāt / svarūpavedanaṃ cānubhavaḥ / tasmāt smaraṇamātrametat / tatra yuktaṃ na svarūpavedanam / vedanāyāḥ svabhāvavyavasthāpakaṃ lakṣaṇameva ayuktamityāha svātmānamityādi-
body.translated_text: The experience of what is co-arisen is necessary; otherwise, what is born before, or arisen afterward — by cognition that has arisen [at a later time] — it is remembered, not experienced. It is made into an object in the form of memory, not directly known — because at the time of that cognition, it [the feeling] has already passed. And the experience of what has passed, in its own form, is not fitting, since it does not exist. And experience in its own form is what constitutes direct experience. Therefore this is mere remembering. In that case, experience in the proper sense is not justified. He says that the very defining characteristic that establishes the nature of feeling is unjustified — 'itself' and so forth —

body.text: svātmānaṃ nānubhavati
body.translated_text: It does not experience itself,

body.text: svātmānaṃ svaṃ svarūpaṃ nānubhavati, na vedayate, svasaṃvedanasya pūrvaṃ nirastatvāt / anyena tarhi sā jñānenānubhūyate vedanā? āha-
body.translated_text: [Feeling] does not experience itself — its own form, its own nature — it does not cognize [itself], since self-cognition has been previously refuted. Is that feeling then experienced by another cognition? He says —

body.text: na cānyenānubhūyate // Bca_9.101 //
body.translated_text: nor is it experienced by another. // <s>Bca</s> 9.101 //

body.text: na ca naiva / anyena tatsamānakālabhāvinā jñānenānubhūyate, vedyate, jñānasya jñānāntareṇa avedanāt //
body.translated_text: 'Nor' — indeed not. It is not experienced — not cognized — by another, by a cognition existing at the same time, since one cognition is not cognized by another cognition.

body.text: na cāsti vedakaḥ kaścidvedanāto na tattvataḥ /
body.translated_text: And there is no experiencer; therefore feeling does not exist in reality.

body.text: na ca naivāsti vedakaḥ kaścit, yo vedanāṃ vedayate, cittamanyadvā / ataḥ asmāt kāraṇāt vedanā anubhava iti vedanālakṣaṇaśūnyatvādvedanā na tattvataḥ na paramārthataḥ, anyatrābhiniveśāt tatsvarūpapratipādakasya kasyacidabhāvāt / etaduktamāryākṣayamatisūtre-
body.translated_text: And indeed there is no experiencer — no one who experiences feeling — whether mind or anything else. Therefore — for this reason — feeling, being empty of the defining characteristic of feeling — namely 'experience' — does not exist in reality, does not exist ultimately — because of the absence of anything that would establish its own nature, due to [its nature being posited only] through clinging from elsewhere. This was stated in the <s>Āryākṣayamatisūtra</s> —

body.text: api tu khalu punarabhiniveśo vedanā, parigraho vedanā, upādānaṃ vedanā, upalambho vedanā, viparyāso vedanā, vikalpo vedanetyādi //
body.translated_text: 'But rather, clinging is feeling, grasping is feeling, appropriation is feeling, apprehension is feeling, perversion is feeling, conceptualization is feeling,' and so forth.

body.text: dharmasaṃgītisūtre 'pyuktam-
body.translated_text: In the <s>Dharmasaṃgītisūtra</s> too it is said —

children.translated_text: 'Feeling is said to be experience — by whom is it experienced?

children.text: vedako vedanā vedyaḥ pṛthagbhūto na vidyate //
children.translated_text: The experiencer, the feeling, and the experienced — these do not exist as separate entities.'
'Thus should mindfulness be established regarding feeling by the discerning;

children.text: yathā bodhistathā hyeṣā śāntā śuddhā prabhāsvarā //
children.translated_text: for it is like awakening itself — peaceful, pure, and luminous.'

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: tasmādvedakavedanāsvabhāvaśūnyaṃ pratītyasamutpannamātraṃ nirvyāpāramasvāmikaṃ māyāprapañcavadupalambhagocaratāmupagatamidaṃ kalevaramavabhāsate, iti na kasyacit sukhaṃ vā duḥkhaṃ vā svakīyaṃ bhavatītyāha nirātmaka ityādi-
body.translated_text: Therefore, this body — empty of the nature of experiencer and feeling, merely dependently arisen, without activity, without owner, coming within the range of apprehension like an illusory display — appears thus. Therefore, neither happiness nor suffering belongs to anyone — he says 'selfless' and so forth —

body.text: nirātmake kalāpe 'smin ka evaṃ bādhyate 'nayā // Bca_9.102 //
body.translated_text: In this selfless assemblage, who is afflicted by it [feeling]? // <s>Bca</s> 9.102 //

body.text: nirātmake kasyacidātmādervedakasyābhāvādasvāmike kalāpe ekasyānuyāyino 'bhāvāt pratītyasamutpannamātre 'smin māyāsvabhāvavadupalambhagocaratāmupagate / evamindrajālavat paśyan saṃjātavismayo brūte- ka evaṃ bādhyate 'nayā / evamuktakrameṇa kasyacidvedayiturabhāvāt vedanāyāśca, kaḥ paramārthato 'nayā vedanayā bādhyate pīḍayate? vicārato naiva kaścit / tasmāt vikalpa evāyaṃ sukhādisādhanādhyavasāyaḥ / tadetadvedanāsmṛtyupasthānaṃ darśitam //
body.translated_text: In this [collection of aggregates] that is without a self, ownerless — due to the absence of any experiencer such as a self — without a single follower, being merely dependently arisen, having come within the range of apprehension as if of the nature of an illusion — seeing thus, as if a magical illusion, one who has become astonished says: "Who is thus afflicted by this?" Thus, in the manner stated, due to the absence of any experiencer and of feeling itself, who is ultimately afflicted, pained, by this feeling? Upon analysis, no one at all. Therefore, this determination to produce happiness and such is merely conceptual. Thus the foundation of mindfulness of feeling has been demonstrated.

body.text: sāṃprataṃ cittasmṛtyupasthānamupadarśayitumāha nendriyeṣvityādi-
body.translated_text: Now, in order to demonstrate the foundation of mindfulness of mind, he says with "not in the sense-faculties" and so forth —

children.text: nendriyeṣu na rūpādau nāntarāle manaḥ sthitam /
children.translated_text: Mind is not established in the sense-faculties, nor in form and such, nor in between;
nor is mind found inside or outside, nor anywhere else. // Bca_9.103 //

body.text: tatra ṣaṣṭhaṃ tāvanmanovijñānaṃ nirūpayati- tathā kva punaridaṃ manovijñānaṃ svayamupasthitam? tatra na tāvadindriyeṣu cakṣurādiṣu manaḥ sthitaṃ sthitimupagatam / na rūpādau viṣaye manaḥ sthitam / nāntarāle, nāpīndriyaviṣayayorantarāle madhye manaḥ sthitam / ekatrāpyaniścitasvarūpatvāt / nāpyantarna bahiścittam / nāpyantarna madhye kāyasya cittaṃ nāpi bahiḥ na bāhyeṣu śarīrāvayaveṣu cittaṃ labhyate / anyatrāpi na labhyate, uktebhyaḥ sthānebhyaḥ anyatrāpi kkaciddeśāntare yatra tatra vā na labhyate, na prāpyate vicārataḥ //
body.translated_text: There, he first examines the sixth, the mental consciousness: where then is this mental consciousness itself established? There, first, mind is not established, has not taken up abiding, in the sense-faculties — the eye and such. Mind is not established in the objects — form and such. Not in between — nor is mind established in between, in the middle, between sense-faculty and object. Because even in a single [location], its nature is not determined. Nor is mind inside or outside — nor in the interior, the middle of the body, nor outside, in the external parts of the body, is mind found. Nor is it found anywhere else — in any other region beyond the stated locations, here or there, it is not found, not obtained, upon analysis.

body.text: tathā kkacit kathaṃcidbhavati, tataḥ kathaṃ tasya niṣedha ityatrāha yanna kāye ityādi-
body.translated_text: If it exists somehow somewhere, then how can it be negated? — to this he says with "what is not in the body" and so forth —

children.text: yanna kāye na cānyatra na miśraṃ na pṛthak kvacit /
children.translated_text: What is not in the body, nor elsewhere, neither mixed nor separate, anywhere —

children.text: tanna kiṃcidataḥ sattvāḥ prakṛtyā parinirvṛtāḥ // Bca_9.104 //
children.translated_text: that is nothing; therefore, beings are by nature in <s>parinirvāṇa</s>. // Bca_9.104 //

body.text: yaccittaṃ na kāye bāhyābhyantare śarīre / na cānyatra, naiva kāyādanyatra bāhye vastuni / na miśram / kriyāviśeṣaṇametat / dvayorādhyātmikabāhyayormiśramapi na sthitam / yaccittaṃ na pṛthak kāyāt, nāpi pṛthak svātantryeṇa ca kvacidavasthitaṃ yaccittam, tat paramārthato na
body.translated_text: The mind that is not in the body — in the body whether internal or external. "Nor elsewhere" — not at all in any external object other than the body. "Not mixed" — this is a qualification of the action; not established even as mixed in the two, the internal and external. The mind that is not separate from the body, nor established separately and independently anywhere — that, ultimately, is

body.text: kiṃcit na vastusat / kalpanopadarśitameva tat / āsaṃsāraṃ cittaṃ māyāvatpratibhāso niḥsvabhāvatvāt / ataḥ asmāt kāraṇāt sattvāḥ prāṇinaḥ prakṛtyā svabhāvena parinirvṛtāḥ parimuktasvabhāvāḥ / niḥsvabhāvatālakṣaṇasya prakṛtinirvāṇasya sarvasattvasaṃtāneṣu sadā vidyamānatvāt / svayameva tu abhūtaparikalpavaśādasatyapi satyamāropya kleśavāsanopahatacittasaṃtatayaḥ saṃsāracārakāvarodhaniṣiddhasvātantryavṛttayo 'parimuktā ityucyante na tu paramārthataḥ //
body.translated_text: nothing, not a real entity. It is merely shown by conceptualization. Throughout <s>saṃsāra</s>, mind is an appearance like an illusion, due to its lack of intrinsic nature. Therefore — for this reason — beings, living creatures, are by nature, by their own nature, in <s>parinirvāṇa</s>, of a nature that is liberated. Because the natural <s>nirvāṇa</s> characterized by the lack of intrinsic nature is always present in the continua of all beings. But by themselves, through the force of false conceptualization, superimposing reality upon what is unreal, their mental continua impaired by the impressions of afflictions, their autonomous conduct obstructed by the imprisonment of <s>saṃsāra</s> — they are said to be "unliberated," but not ultimately.

body.text: iti mano vicārya cakṣurādivijñānaṃ vicārayannāha jñeyādityādi-
body.translated_text: Having thus examined the mental [consciousness], he examines the visual and other consciousnesses — with "before the knowable" and so forth —

children.translated_text: If cognition [arises] before the knowable, relying on what does it arise?

children.text: jñeyena saha cejjñānaṃ kimālambyāsya saṃbhavaḥ // Bca_9.105 //
children.translated_text: And if cognition [arises] simultaneously with the knowable, relying on what does it arise? // Bca_9.105 //

body.text: tathā hi na kvacit sadā sadrūpamavasthitaṃ jñānam, kiṃ tu cakṣurādisāmagrīṃ pratītya utpadyamānaṃ rūpādijñeyagrāhakamityucyate, iti parasyāśayamāśaṅkaya vikalpayati- tat punarjñeyāt pūrvaṃ vā syāt, jñeyasamānakālaṃ vā, jñeyasya paścādvā iti / tatra yadi prācīno vikalpaḥ, tatrāha- jñeyāt grāhyaviṣayāt pūrvaṃ prāgeva, anutpanne eva jñeye yadi jñānamutpannamabhidhīyate, tadā kimālambya asya saṃbhavaḥ? pūrvaṃ jñeyamālambanamantareṇa kimālambya kimāśritya asya saṃbhava utpādaḥ? dvitīyapakṣamāśrityāha- jñeyena grāhyaviṣayeṇa saha samānakālaṃ cedyadi jñānam, kimālambya asya saṃbhavaḥ? samānakālasya jñeyasya akāraṇatayā anālambanatvāt / nākāraṇaṃ viṣayaḥ iti vacanāt //
body.translated_text: For indeed, cognition does not exist anywhere, always, in a permanent form; rather, it arises depending on the assemblage of the eye and such, and is said to grasp the knowable such as form — thus, anticipating the opponent's position, he analyzes: does it [arise] before the knowable, simultaneously with the knowable, or after the knowable? There, if the first alternative [is considered], he says: if cognition is said to have arisen before the knowable, the graspable object — before it, even before the knowable has arisen — then relying on what does it arise? Without the knowable as its object-support, relying on what, depending on what, does it arise? Taking up the second alternative, he says: if cognition [arises] simultaneously with the knowable, the graspable object — then relying on what does it arise? Because a knowable that is simultaneous, not being a cause, is not an object-support, as stated: "what is not a cause is not an object."

body.text: atha tṛtīyaḥ prakāraḥ svīkriyate, athetyādi-
body.translated_text: Now, if the third alternative is accepted — with "if" and so forth —

body.text: atha jñeyādbhavet paścāt tadā jñānaṃ kuto bhavet /
body.translated_text: If [cognition] arises after the knowable, then from what would cognition come?

body.text: atheti pṛcchāyām / jñeyāditi / pūrvaṃ jñeyam, paścāt tadanantaraṃ nivṛtte jñeye bhavet utpadyeta jñānam, tadā jñānaṃ kuto bhavet, jñānakāle jñeyasya nivṛttatvāt, kuta ālambanāt jñānaṃ bhavet, kimāśritya utpadyeta? tasmādviṣayādisāmagrīto 'pi paramārthato na sidhyati jñānam / idaṃ cittasmṛtyupasthānamāryaratnakūṭādiṣvabhihitam-
body.translated_text: "If" — in a question. "From the knowable" — the knowable first [arises], and afterward — immediately after — when the knowable has ceased, if cognition were to arise, then from what would cognition come? Since the knowable has ceased at the time of cognition, from what object-support would cognition come, depending on what would it arise? Therefore, even from the assemblage of objects and such, cognition is not ultimately established. This foundation of mindfulness of mind has been stated in the <s>Āryaratnakūṭa</s> and such —

body.text: sa evaṃ cittaṃ parigaveṣate- katarat taccittaṃ rajyati vā duṣyati vā muhyati vā? kimatītamanāgataṃ pratyutpannaṃ vā? iti / tatra yadatītam, tat kṣīṇam / yadanāgatam, tadasaṃprāptam / pratyutpannasya sthitirnāsti / cittaṃ hi kāśyapa nādhyātmaṃ na bahirdhā nobhayamantareṇopalabhyate / cittaṃ hi kāśyapa arūpyanidarśanamapratighamavijñaptikamapratiṣṭhamaniketam / cittaṃ hi kāśyapa sarvabuddhairna dṛṣṭam, na paśyanti, na drakṣyanti / [yat sarvabuddhairna dṛṣṭam], na paśyanti, na drakṣyanti, kīdṛśastasya pracāro draṣṭavyaḥ? anyatra vitathapatitayā saṃjñayā dharmāḥ pravartante / cittaṃ hi kāśyapa māyāsadṛśamabhūtakalpanatayā vividhāmupapattiṃ parigṛhṇāti / peyālaṃ / cittaṃ hi kāśyapa nadīstrotaḥsadṛśamanavasthitamutpannabhagnavilīnam / cittaṃ hi kāśyapa dīpārciḥsadṛśaṃ hetupratyayatayā pravartate / cittaṃ hi kāśyapa vidyutsadṛśaṃ
body.translated_text: "He thus investigates the mind: 'Which is that mind that is attached, or hates, or is deluded? Is it past, future, or present?' There, what is past — that has been exhausted. What is future — that has not yet arrived. The present has no abiding. For mind, <s>Kāśyapa</s>, is not found internally, nor externally, nor in both, nor in between. For mind, <s>Kāśyapa</s>, is formless, invisible, non-resistant, without information, without foundation, without abode. For mind, <s>Kāśyapa</s>, has not been seen by all <s>Buddhas</s>, is not seen, will not be seen. [What has not been seen] by all <s>Buddhas</s>, is not seen, will not be seen — how should its activity be seen? Except that <s>dharmas</s> proceed through a perception that has fallen into falsity. For mind, <s>Kāśyapa</s>, is like an illusion — through false conceptualization it grasps various modes of rebirth. In abbreviated form. For mind, <s>Kāśyapa</s>, is like a river's current — unstable, arising, breaking, and dissolving. For mind, <s>Kāśyapa</s>, is like a lamp's flame — it functions through causes and conditions. For mind, <s>Kāśyapa</s>, is like lightning —

body.text: kṣaṇabhaṅgayanavasthitam / cittaṃ hi kāśyapa ākāśasadṛśam, āgantukaiḥ kleśopakleśairupakliśyate / peyālaṃ / yāvat cittaṃ hi kāśyapa parigaveṣyamāṇaṃ na labhyate / yanna labhyate, tannopalabhyate / tannaivātītaṃ nānāgataṃ na pratyutpannam / tat tryadhvasamatikrāntam / yat tryadhvasamatikrāntaṃ tannaivāsti na nasti ityādi //
body.translated_text: momentarily perishing and unstable. For mind, <s>Kāśyapa</s>, is like space — it is afflicted by adventitious afflictions and secondary afflictions. In abbreviated form. Up to: for mind, <s>Kāśyapa</s>, when searched for, is not found. What is not found is not apprehended. That is neither past, nor future, nor present. That has transcended the three times. What has transcended the three times neither exists nor does not exist." And so forth.

body.text: evaṃ cittasmṛtyupasthānaṃ pratipādya dharmasmṛtyupasthānaṃ pratipādayitumuktameva kramaṃ yojayannāha evaṃ cetyādi-
body.translated_text: Having thus established the foundation of mindfulness of mind, in order to establish the foundation of mindfulness of <s>dharmas</s>, connecting the sequence already stated, he says with "thus" and so forth —

body.text: evaṃ ca sarvadharmāṇāmutpattirnāvasīyate // Bca_9.106 //
body.translated_text: And thus, the arising of all <s>dharmas</s> is not ascertained. // Bca_9.106 //

body.text: cakāra evakārārthaḥ / evameva yathoditanyāyena sarvadharmāṇāṃ sarvabhāvānāmutpattirutpādo nāvasīyate na pratīyate / teṣāmapi svahetutaḥ pūrvaṃ samānakālaṃ paścādvā utpattau idameva dūṣaṇaṃ yathāsaṃbhavaṃ vācyam / utpādābhāvānnirodho 'pi na yujyate / anutpannasya nirodhāyogāt / ata eva ca anutpannāniruddhasvabhāvatayā niṣprapañcatvāt sarvadharmā vimokśābhimukhā dharmadhātuniryātā ākāśadhātuparyavasānā aprajñaptikā avyavahārā anabhilāpyā anabhilapanīyā ityucyante / evaṃ dharmasmṛtyupasthānenāvirahitaṃ sarvadharmeṣvanāsaṅgajñānamutpadyate / dharmasmṛtyupasthānabhāvanā ca āryākṣayamatisūtre darśitā / yaduktam-
body.translated_text: The "and" has the meaning of "indeed." In just this way, by the reasoning stated, the arising, the origination, of all <s>dharmas</s>, of all entities, is not ascertained, is not found. For their arising too — whether before, simultaneously with, or after their own cause — this very objection should be stated as applicable. Due to the absence of arising, cessation too is not justified, since the cessation of what has not arisen is impossible. For this very reason, being of un-arisen and un-ceased nature, being free from conceptual elaboration, all <s>dharmas</s> are said to be directed toward liberation, issued from the <s>dharmadhātu</s>, culminating in the space-element, beyond designation, beyond convention, inexpressible, and unspeakable. Thus, through non-separation from the foundation of mindfulness of <s>dharmas</s>, non-clinging knowledge regarding all <s>dharmas</s> arises. And the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness of <s>dharmas</s> is shown in the <s>Āryākṣayamatisūtra</s>. As stated —

body.text: dharme dharmānupaśyī viharan bodhisattvo na kaṃciddharmaṃ samanupaśyati / yato na buddhadharmāḥ, yato na bodhiḥ, yato na mārgaḥ, yato na niḥsaraṇam, sarvadharmā niḥsaraṇamiti viditvā anāvaraṇamahākaruṇāsamādhiṃ samāpadyate / sa sarvadharmeṣu sarvakleśeṣu ca kṛtrimasaṃjñāṃ pratilabhate- niṣkleśā ete dharmā naite sakleśāḥ / tatkasya hetoḥ? tathāhi ete nītārthe 'rthaṃ samavasaranti / nāsti kleśānāṃ saṃnicayo rāśībhāvaḥ, na rāgabhāvaḥ, na dveṣabhāvaḥ, na mohabhāvaḥ / eṣāmevānubodhād bodhiḥ / yatsvabhāvāśca kleśāḥ, tatsvabhāvā bodhiḥ, ityevaṃ smṛtimupasthāpayati / iti //
body.translated_text: "A <s>Bodhisattva</s> dwelling in contemplation of <s>dharmas</s> in <s>dharmas</s> does not perceive any <s>dharma</s>. Since there are no <s>Buddha</s>-qualities, since there is no awakening, since there is no path, since there is no deliverance — knowing that all <s>dharmas</s> are deliverance, he enters the <s>samādhi</s> of unobstructed great compassion. He obtains the perception of artificiality regarding all <s>dharmas</s> and all afflictions: 'These <s>dharmas</s> are free from affliction; they are not afflicted. For what reason? For they converge upon meaning in the definitive sense. There is no accumulation, no heaping up of afflictions; there is no state of desire, no state of hatred, no state of delusion. From the awakening to these very [afflictions], there is awakening. The afflictions are of the same nature as awakening.' — thus he establishes mindfulness."

body.text: uktaṃ ca-
body.translated_text: And it is said —

children.translated_text: "For that which has no arising whatsoever — what cessation could there be for it?
Through being of the nature of an illusory elephant, it is primordially peaceful, effortlessly."

children.text: yaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ śūnyatā saiva te matā /
children.translated_text: "That which is dependent origination — that itself is emptiness, in Your view;
and of that same nature is the true <s>Dharma</s>, and equal to it is the <s>Tathāgata</s>."
"That is reality, also the ultimate, <s>tathatā</s> (suchness), accepted as substance;
that is the real, that is non-deceptive — from the awakening to that, one is called <s>Buddha</s>."

body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Catuḥstava</s> 3.27, 39, 20]

body.text: evaṃ dharmasmṛtyupasthānaṃ darśayatā sarvadharmā anutpannāniruddhāḥ prakāśitāḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus, in demonstrating the foundation of mindfulness of <s>dharmas</s>, all <s>dharmas</s> have been revealed as un-arisen and un-ceased.

body.text: tathā sati saṃvṛtisatyamayuktamityuktaṃ syāt / tataḥ satyadvayavyavasthāpanaṃ na ghaṭate iti parihartuṃ codyamutthāpayannāha yadyevamityādi-
body.translated_text: This being so, it would be said that conventional truth is unjustified. Therefore, the establishment of the two truths would not hold together — raising this objection in order to resolve it, he says with "if this is so" and so forth —

body.text: yadyevaṃ saṃvṛtirnāsti tataḥ satyadvayaṃ kutaḥ /
body.translated_text: If this is so, convention does not exist; then from where are the two truths?

body.text: yadi paramārthataḥ sarvadharmā anutpannāniruddhasvabhāvāḥ, evaṃ sati saṃvṛtirnāsti, vyavahāro na syāt, paramārthasatyamevaikaṃ syāt / tataḥ saṃvṛterabhāvāt satyadvayaṃ saṃvṛtisatyaṃ paramārthasatyaṃ ceti yaduktam-
body.translated_text: If ultimately all <s>dharmas</s> are of un-arisen and un-ceased nature, then convention does not exist, discourse would not exist, and there would be only the single ultimate truth. Therefore, since convention does not exist, the two truths — conventional truth and ultimate truth — as stated —

body.text:
saṃvṛtiḥ paramārthaśca satyadvayamidaṃ matam /
[9.2]
body.translated_text:
"Convention and the ultimate — these two truths are accepted."
[9.2]

body.text: iti, tadetat satyadvayaṃ kutaḥ? naiva syāt / tadabhāvācca paralokagamanakarmakriyāphalasaṃbandhasvabhāvopārjanādi na syāt, sarvavyavahārābhāvāt / athāpi syāt- yadi nāma nāsti, tathā marīcikādiṣu jalakalpanayeva saṃvṛtisvabhāvayā kalpanayā buddhyā vyavasthāpyate, tataḥ satyadvayamupapadyate ityāśaṅkayannāha atha seti-
body.translated_text: — these two truths, from where? They would simply not exist. And in their absence, there would be no going to the next world, no connection of action and fruit, no acquisition of inherent nature and such — since all discourse would be absent. One might further think: even if it does not exist, just as in mirages and such, through the conceptualization of water and such, it is established through the conceptualization of conventional nature, through cognition — therefore the two truths are tenable — anticipating this, he says with "even that" and so forth —

body.text: atha sāpyanyasaṃvṛtyā
body.translated_text: But even that [convention] is [established] by another convention.

body.text: atheti praśne / sāpīti saṃvṛtiḥ / na kevalaṃ paramārthasatyamityaperarthaḥ / anyayā saṃvṛtyā kalpanābuddhirūpayā vyavasthāpyate / athavā / apiravadhāraṇe bhinnakrame ca / anyayaiva saṃvṛtyeti yojanīyam / evamekaṃ saṃdhitsato 'nyat pracyavate ityupadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: "But" — in a question. "Even that" — convention. "Not only ultimate truth" — this is the meaning of "even." It is established by another convention, one in the form of conceptual cognition. Alternatively: "even" is for emphasis and separate sequence — it should be construed as "by another convention itself." Showing that in trying to establish one, the other slips away, he says —

body.text: syātsattvo nirvṛtaḥ kutaḥ // Bca_9.107 //
body.translated_text: From where then would a being be liberated? // Bca_9.107 //

body.text: yadi paramārthatastatsvabhāvaśūnyamapi kalpanābuddhiviṣayīkaraṇāt sāṃvṛtamucyate, yo 'pi tarhi sarvadharmaniḥsvabhāvatālakṣaṇaṃ paramārthasatyamadhigamya anupalambhayogena sarvaprapañcavirahāt parinirvṛtimupayātaḥ, so 'pi sattvaḥ parinirvṛto vinirmuktaḥ kuto bhavet? naiva syāt / tasyāpi buddhayā viṣayīkaraṇāt / buddhiśca sarvaiva saṃvṛtiḥ kalpanāsvabhāvatvāt / buddhiḥ saṃvṛtirucyate iti vacanāt nirvṛtirapi saṃvṛtiḥ syāt //
body.translated_text: If even what is ultimately empty of that nature is called conventional because of being made an object by conceptual cognition, then even one who, having realized the ultimate truth characterized by the lack of intrinsic nature of all <s>dharmas</s>, has attained <s>parinirvāṇa</s> through the yoga of non-apprehension, free from all conceptual elaboration — even that being, liberated, in <s>parinirvāṇa</s> — from where would he come? He would simply not exist, since even he is made an object by cognition. And all cognition is convention, since it is of the nature of conceptualization. Since it is stated that "cognition is called convention" — even liberation would be convention.

body.text: atra parihāramāha paracittetyādi-
body.translated_text: Here he states the resolution — with "the conceptualization of another's mind" and so forth —

body.text: paracittavikalpo 'sau
body.translated_text: That is the conceptualization of another's mind.

body.text: parasya nirvṛtasattvādanyasya sattvasya cittaṃ tasyāsau vikalpaḥ, yo 'yaṃ nirvṛtasyāpi buddhayā viṣayīkaraṇam / na hi paracittavikalpena anyasya saṃvṛtiryuktā / tato 'nyabuddhayā viṣayīkriyamāṇo 'pi nirvṛta evāsau / kutaḥ? yataḥ-
body.translated_text: The mind of another being — different from the being that has attained <s>nirvāṇa</s> — that is conceptualization regarding that [nirvāṇa-attainer], which is the making of even one who has attained <s>nirvāṇa</s> into an object by [another's] cognition. For it is not justified that one [being]'s conventional [existence] arises through another mind's conceptualization. Therefore, even though made an object by another's cognition, that one has still attained <s>nirvāṇa</s>. Why? Because —

body.text: svasaṃvṛtyā tu nāsti saḥ /
body.translated_text: By his own convention, however, he does not exist.

body.text: tuḥ pūrvasmādviśeṣamabhidhatte / svasaṃvṛtyā nijasaṃvṛtyā svakalpanayā sa iti parinirvṛto nāsti, na vidyate / parinirvṛta eva saḥ iti svayamasya sarvavikalpoparamāt / anyatrāpi tarhi kathamanyasaṃvṛtiḥ syādityatrāha sa paścādityādi-
body.translated_text: The word 'however' (<s>tu</s>) expresses a distinction from the foregoing. 'By his own convention' — by his own convention, by his own conceptualization — 'he' — the one who has attained <s>parinirvāṇa</s> — 'does not exist,' is not found. He has attained <s>parinirvāṇa</s> precisely [because] in him all conceptualization has ceased. But then how could another's convention exist even elsewhere? — to this he says 'he, subsequently' and so forth —

body.text: sa paścānniyataḥ so 'sti na cennāstyeva saṃvṛtiḥ // Bca_9.108 //
body.translated_text: If he is subsequently determined to exist, then convention exists; if not, convention simply does not exist. // Bca_9.108 //

body.text:
asmin sati idaṃ bhavati, asyotpādādidamutpadyate iti idaṃpratyayatāmātrameva saṃvṛtiḥ /
iti dharmebhyo dharma utpadyamānaḥ paścādbhāvī bhavet / tataḥ sa paścānniyato dharmaḥ, so 'sti yadi, tadā astyeva saṃvṛtiḥ / na cedyadi sa nāsti, tadā nāstyeva saṃvṛtiḥ /
body.translated_text:
'When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises' — mere conditionality alone is convention.
Thus, a <s>dharma</s> arising from [other] <s>dharmas</s> would be a subsequent existent. If that subsequently determined <s>dharma</s> exists, then convention does exist. But if that does not exist, then convention simply does not exist.

body.text: gaganendīvarādiṣu idaṃpratyayatāyā abhāvāt / etaduktaṃ bhavati- yadi nāma parinirvṛto buddhyā viṣayīkṛtaḥ, naiva tāvatā paracittavikalpamātreṇa tasyāparinirvṛtiḥ / svayamasya sarvavikalpaprapañcopaśamāt / na raktacittenālambitaḥ svayaṃ prahīṇasarvakleśāvaraṇo vītarāgo 'pyavītarāgo bhavet / tasmāt sarvakalpanāvirahādanyasaṃvṛtyālambito 'pi svayaṃ parinirvṛta evāsau paramārthataḥ / ata eva sarvadharmāḥ sarvakalpanāśūnyatvādanutpannāniruddhasvabhāvatvācca prakṛtiparinirvṛtā ādiśāntā ityucyante / tathāpi tathāvidhebhya eva tathāvidhā anye dharmā utpadyante nirudhyante ca / māyāsvabhāvavat / tena ca rūpeṇa parikalpavaśāt punarālambyamānāḥ sāṃvṛtāḥ, vāstavarūpābhāvācca anutpannāniruddhā ityucyante kharaviṣāṇavat / yaduktam-
body.translated_text: Because in [the case of] a sky-lotus and such, conditionality is absent. What is stated here is this: even if one who has attained <s>parinirvāṇa</s> is made an object by cognition, his non-attainment of <s>parinirvāṇa</s> does not follow merely from the conceptualization of another's mind. Because in him, all conceptual elaboration has ceased. One who is grasped by a mind of attachment does not, simply because of that, become un-dispassioned — though he has himself abandoned all the obscurations of the afflictions — he would not become one with attachment. Therefore, due to the absence of all conceptualization, even though grasped by another's convention, he has attained <s>parinirvāṇa</s> in the ultimate sense. For this very reason, all <s>dharmas</s> — being empty of all conceptualization and of the nature of the unborn and unceased — are said to be primordially in <s>nirvāṇa</s>, quiescent from the beginning. Nevertheless, from just such [<s>dharmas</s>], other such <s>dharmas</s> arise and cease — like things of the nature of illusion. And in that form, through the power of conceptual construction, being grasped again, they are conventional; and due to the absence of a real form, they are called unborn and unceased, like the horn of a donkey. As is said —

children.text: śūnyebhya eva śūnyā dharmāḥ prabhavanti dharmebhyaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'From <s>dharmas</s> that are empty, [other] <s>dharmas</s> that are empty arise.'
Thus. //

body.text: āryalalitavistare 'pyuktam-
body.translated_text: In the <s>Āryalalitavistara</s> too it is said —

children.translated_text: 'Formations are like the flame of a lamp, quickly subject to arising and cessation;
unstable like the wind, weak and without essence like a mass of foam.'
'Formations are without effort, empty, like a plantain tree-trunk upon examination;
like an illusion, deluding the mind, like showing an empty fist to beguile a child.'
* * * * And so forth.

children.text: yatha muñca pratītya balvajaṃ rajju vyāyāmabalena vartitā /
children.translated_text: 'Just as a rope, made by twisting with the strength of arms, depending on <s>muñja</s> grass and <s>balvaja</s>,

children.text: ghaṭiyantra sacakra vartate teṣu ekaikaśa nāsti vartanā //
children.translated_text: turns the wheel of a water-machine — in each one individually, there is no turning.'
'So too, the turning that operates through all the links of existence, supported by mutual accumulation —
the turning in each one individually is not found from beginning to end.'

children.text: mudrāt pratimudra dṛśyate mudrasaṃkrānti na copalabhyate /
children.translated_text: 'From a seal, a counter-seal is seen, but no transference of the seal is found;

children.text: na ca tatra na caiva sānyato eva saṃskāra anuchedaśāśvatāḥ //
children.translated_text: it is neither there nor from elsewhere — just so are formations, neither annihilated nor eternal.'

children.text: araṇiṃ yatha cottarāraṇiṃ hastavyāyāma trayebhi saṃgati /
children.translated_text: 'Just as the lower fire-stick and the upper fire-stick and the effort of hands — through the conjunction of these three,

children.text: iti pratyayato 'gni jāyate jātu kṛtārthu laghu nirudhyate //
children.translated_text: from that condition fire is born; having accomplished its purpose, it quickly ceases.'

children.text: atha paṇḍitu kaści mārgate kutayaṃ āgatu kutra yāti vā /
children.translated_text: 'Then a wise person investigates: from where did this come, and where does it go?

children.text: vidiśo diśi sarvi mārgato nāgati nāsya gatiśca labhyate //
children.translated_text: Searching in all directions and intermediate directions — neither its coming nor its going is found.'

children.text: skandhāyatanāni dhātavaḥ tṛṣṇa avidyā iti karmapratyayā /
children.translated_text: 'The aggregates, sense-bases, and elements — craving and ignorance — these are the conditions of <s>karma</s>;

children.text: sāmagri tu sattvasucanā sa ca paramārthatu nopalabhyate //
children.translated_text: the assemblage is designated as a "being," but in the ultimate sense it is not found.'

body.text: catuḥstave 'pyuktam-
body.translated_text: In the <s>Catuḥstava</s> too it is said —

children.translated_text: 'Neither from what has ceased nor from what has not ceased does a sprout arise from a seed;
all arising is like the arising of an illusion — this was declared by You.'
'Therefore, this world, arisen from conceptual construction, has been fully understood by You
as non-existent — unborn, it does not perish.'
'There is no <s>saṃsāra</s> of what is permanent, nor is there <s>saṃsāra</s> of what is impermanent;

children.text: svapnavat saṃsṛtiḥ proktā tvayā tattvavidāṃ vara //
children.translated_text: <s>saṃsāra</s> is said to be like a dream — thus You, O best of knowers of reality, declared.'

body.text: iti / [catuḥ-1.16-18]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Catuḥstava</s> 1.16-18]

body.text: tasmāt paramārthata utpādanirodhābhāve 'pi na saṃvṛtisatyavirodha iti sarvaṃ samañjasam //
body.translated_text: Therefore, even though arising and cessation are absent in the ultimate sense, there is no contradiction with <s>saṃvṛtisatya</s> (conventional truth) — thus everything is consistent. //

body.text: nanu yadi paramārthato 'nutpannāniruddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ, tadā na jñānaṃ na ca jñeyaṃ vastutaḥ saṃbhavati / tat kimiha kena vicāryate iti vicāro 'pi na syāt / atastūṣṇīmeva sthātavyamityata āha kalpanetyādi-
body.translated_text: But if ultimately all <s>dharmas</s> are unborn and unceased, then neither knowledge nor the knowable exists in reality. So what is being analyzed here by whom? — thus even analysis would not be possible. Therefore one should simply remain silent — to this he says 'conceptualization' and so forth —

children.translated_text: Conceptualization and the conceptualized — these two are mutually dependent;
relying upon what is commonly accepted, all analysis is conducted. // Bca_9.109 //

body.text: kalpanā āropikā buddhiḥ / kalpitaṃ tayā samāropitam / cetyuktasamuccaye / ityevaṃ dvayamubhayamanyonyasya niśritaṃ parasparasamāśritam, kalpanāpekṣayā kalpitam, kalpitāpekṣayā kalpaneti / yathāprasiddhaṃ lokavyavahārato niścitamāśritya gṛhītvā vicāro vimarśaḥ sarva ucyate abhidhīyate / sarva iti na kaścideva vicāro 'pi saṃvṛtimāśritya pratanyate, na tu paramārthasatyam, tasya sarvavyavahārātikrāntatvādityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: 'Conceptualization' — the superimposing cognition. 'The conceptualized' — what is superimposed by it. 'And' (<s>ca</s>) is for accumulating what was stated. 'Thus' — in this way — 'the two,' both, are mutually dependent — resting upon each other; the conceptualized in dependence on conceptualization, and conceptualization in dependence on the conceptualized. 'Relying upon what is commonly accepted' — having taken up what is established through worldly discourse — 'all analysis' — all examination — 'is conducted,' is stated. 'All' — [meaning] even analysis itself proceeds relying upon convention, not upon <s>paramārthasatya</s> (ultimate truth), since that transcends all discourse: this is the meaning. //

body.text: vicāro 'pi bahirvicāravat kālpanikasvabhāvatvādvicārayitavya iti cet, vicārasyāśakyavicāratvādityabhisaṃdhāyāha vicāritenetyādi-
body.translated_text: If even analysis, like external analysis, is of fabricated nature and should itself be analyzed — since analysis cannot be analyzed [further] — with this in mind, he says 'when analyzed' and so forth —

children.translated_text: But when the analyzed is analyzed by [yet another] analysis,
then there would be an infinite regress, since that analysis too would require analysis. // Bca_9.110 //

body.text: vicāritena tu parīkṣitena punaryadā vicāreṇa vicāryate nirūpyate, tadā anavasthā apratiṣṭhānaṃ syāt / kutaḥ? tasyāpi vicārasya vicāraṇāt / yo 'sau vicārasya vicāraṇārthaṃ vicāra upādīyate, tasyāpi vicārasya vicāraṇāddhetoḥ //
body.translated_text: When 'the analyzed' — what has been examined — is again 'analyzed by analysis' — is investigated — then there would be 'an infinite regress' — a lack of firm ground. Why? Because of the analysis of that analysis too. That analysis which is employed for the purpose of analyzing the [first] analysis — from the analysis of that analysis too, [there would be the fault]. //

body.text: vicārye tarhi vicāryamāṇe kathamiyamanavasthā na syādityatrāha vicārite ityādi-
body.translated_text: But if it is the analyzed that is being analyzed, how would this infinite regress not arise? — to this he says 'when the analyzed' and so forth —

children.translated_text: But when the analyzed has been analyzed, there is no further basis for analysis;
being without basis, it does not arise — and that is called <s>nirvāṇa</s>. // Bca_9.111 //

body.text: vicārye tu parīkṣye punarvastuni vicārite nirṇīte sati vicārasya nirṇayasya punaruttarakālaṃ kartavyasya āśrayo nāsti, yamāśritya punarvicārānusaraṇenānavasthānaṃ syāt / vicāryasya vicāraṇe caritārthatayā punarākāṅkṣābhāvāt / ata eva nirāśrayatvānnodeti, āśrayābhāvānna punarvicāraḥ pravartate / sarvasamāropaniṣedhaṃ vidhāya vastutattvaparijñānāt kṛtakṛtyatvāt pravṛttinivṛttyabhāvāt
body.translated_text: When the analyzed — the object of examination — the very thing [to be investigated] — has been analyzed, has been determined, then there is no basis for analysis — for the determination — to be conducted at a subsequent time, on the basis of which an infinite regress would follow through the pursuit of further analysis. Because the analysis of the analyzed has fulfilled its purpose, there is no further expectation [of analysis]. For this very reason, 'being without basis, it does not arise' — due to the absence of a basis, analysis does not operate further. Having accomplished the negation of all superimposition and established the complete knowledge of the reality of things — being one whose task is accomplished — due to the absence of both engagement and withdrawal

body.text: na kkacit sajyate, nāpi virajyate / tacca nirvāṇamucyate, sarvavyavahāranivṛtteḥ sarvatra nirvyāpāratayā praśāntatvāt tadeva nirvāṇamabhidhīyate //
body.translated_text: one does not cling anywhere, nor is one averse. And that is called <s>nirvāṇa</s> — since all conventional discourse has ceased and there is complete quiescence everywhere through the absence of any activity, that itself is called <s>nirvāṇa</s>. //

body.text: kalpitaviṣaye 'vaśyameva sarvatra vicāraḥ satyo na tu paramārthata ityāha yasya tvityādi-
body.translated_text: Analysis must necessarily be true everywhere regarding fabricated objects, but not from the standpoint of ultimate reality — he says 'for one for whom, however' and so forth —

body.text: yasya tvetaddūyaṃ satyaṃ sa evātyantaduḥsthitaḥ /
body.translated_text: But for one for whom this pair is true — he alone is in an extremely difficult position.

body.text: yasya punaḥ paramārthasadbhāvavādinaḥ etaddūyaṃ vicāro vicāryaṃ ceti etadubhayamapi satyaṃ paramārthasat, sa eva bhāvasvabhāvavādī atyantaduḥsthitaḥ atyantamatiśayena duḥkhena sthito duḥsthitaḥ duṣkaraṇīyatvāt / etadevopadarśayannāha yadītyādi-
body.translated_text: For one who asserts the real existence [of things] — for whom this pair, analysis and the analyzed, both have real, ultimate existence — he alone, the proponent of the intrinsic nature of entities, is in an extremely difficult position — established in extremely intense difficulty — because [his position] is extremely hard to maintain. Showing just this, he says 'if' and so forth —

body.text: yadi jñānavaśādartho jñānāstitve tu kā gatiḥ // Bca_9.112 //
body.translated_text: If the object [is established] through the power of knowledge, what is the recourse for the existence of knowledge? // Bca_9.112 //

body.text: yadi jñānavaśāt jñānasya pramāṇasya vaśāt sāmarthyāt arthaḥ prameyaṃ vyavasthāpyate, tadā bhavatu nāma pramāṇāt prameyavyavasthā, ko nāma nivārayati? kevalamidamiha nirūpaṇīyam-jñānāstitve tu kā gatiḥ? jñānasya pramāṇasya punarastitvaṃ kuto niścitamiti vaktavyam / svasaṃvedanasyābhāvāt pramāṇāntarānveṣaṇe anavasthānaṃ syāditi kā gatirāśrayaṇīyā?
body.translated_text: If through the power of knowledge — through the power of valid cognition — the object, the knowable, is established, then let there indeed be the establishment of the knowable through valid cognition — who would prevent it? But this alone must be examined: what is the recourse for the existence of knowledge? Whence is the existence of knowledge — of valid cognition — determined? — this must be stated. Since self-cognition does not exist, in the search for another valid cognition there would be an infinite regress — what recourse is to be relied upon?

body.text: syādetat- syādeva anavasthānam, yadi jñānastitve pramāṇaṃ mṛgyate / yāvatā prameyādeva pramāṇavyavasthā, tat kuto 'navasthānaṃ syādityāśaṅkayannāha athetyādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: there would indeed be an infinite regress if a valid cognition were sought for the existence of knowledge. But the establishment of valid cognition comes from the knowable itself — so whence the infinite regress? — anticipating this, he says 'but if' and so forth —

body.text: atha jñeyavaśājjñānaṃ jñeyāstitve tu kā gatiḥ /
body.translated_text: But if knowledge [is established] through the power of the knowable, what is the recourse for the existence of the knowable?

body.text: atheti parābhiprāyaprakāśane / atha jñeyasya prameyasya vaśāt jñānaṃ vyavasthāpyate, tarhi jñeyāstitve tu kā gatiḥ? yadi jñeyavaśāt jñānaṃ vyavasthāpyate, tadā svayameva jñeyaṃ jñānāstitve vyavasthānibandhanaṃ syāt, tacca kutaḥ pramāṇāt siddhamiti pṛcchati- jñeyāstitve punaḥ kā gatiriti / prameyasiddhaye jñānāntarānusaraṇe tadapi jñānāntaraṃ kutaḥ siddhamiti vaktavyam / tasmādeva jñeyāditi cet, jñeyaṃ kutaḥ siddham? tatsiddhau jñānāntarānusaraṇe punaranavasthānamaparyavasānaṃ syāt / syādetat- bhavedetat yadi jñānasya jñeyasya vā siddhaye jñānāntarāpekṣā syāt, api tu parasparamitaretarasya siddhiḥ / ato noktadoṣaprasaṅga iti parasyāśayamāvirbhāvayannāha athānyonyetyādi-
body.translated_text: '<s>Atha</s>' (but if) reveals the opponent's intent. If knowledge is established through the power of the knowable — the object of knowledge — then what is the recourse for the existence of the knowable? If knowledge is established through the power of the knowable, then the knowable itself would be the ground of establishing the existence of knowledge — but whence is that [knowable] itself established by what valid cognition? — he asks: what is the recourse for the existence of the knowable? In pursuing another cognition for the establishment of the object of knowledge, one must also say whence that other cognition too is established. If from that very knowable — then whence is the knowable established? In pursuing yet another cognition for its establishment, there would again be an infinite regress, without conclusion. One might say: this would be the case if the establishment of either knowledge or the knowable required another cognition; but each is established through the other, mutually. Therefore the stated fault does not follow — revealing the opponent's intent, he says 'but if mutually' and so forth —

body.text: athānyonyavaśātsattvamabhāvaḥ syāddūyorapi // Bca_9.113 //
body.translated_text: If [their] existence depends on each other, both would be non-existent. // Bca_9.113 //

body.text: atha punarevamabhidhīyate- anyonyasya jñānasya jñeyasya parasparasya vaśāt sāmarthyāt jñānajñeyayorapi sattvamastitvaṃ niścīyate jñānavaśājjñeyasya jñeyavaśācca jñānasyeti yāvat / tadevaṃ sati abhāvaḥ syād dvayorapi / dvayorapi jñānajñeyayorabhāvaḥ syāt, ekasyāpi sattvasiddhirna bhavet / itaretarāśrayatvādekasyāsiddhau dvitīyasyāpyasiddhiḥ //
body.translated_text: But if it is stated thus: through each other's power — the power of knowledge and the knowable, mutually — the existence of both knowledge and the knowable is determined: knowledge through the power of the knowable, and the knowable through the power of knowledge. If this is the case, then both would be non-existent. Both — knowledge and the knowable — would be non-existent; the existence of even one would not be established. Due to mutual dependence, when one is unestablished, the second too is unestablished. //

body.text: atra prakṛtānurūpadṛṣṭāntamāha pitā cedityādi-
body.translated_text: Here, he gives an example suited to the topic, saying 'if the father' and so forth —

body.text:
pitā cenna vinā putrātkutaḥ putrasya saṃbhavaḥ /
putrābhāve pitā nāsti
body.translated_text:
If the father does not exist without the son, whence is the son's arising?
Without the son, there is no father —

body.text: pitā janakaḥ yadi putraṃ vinā putramantareṇa na syāt, putrajananasāpekṣatvādasya vyapadeśasya, tarhi kutaḥ putrasya saṃbhavaḥ, kutaḥ kasmāt piturabhāvāt putrasya janyasya saṃbhavaḥ janma astu? kimiti cet, putrābhāve pitā nāsti / hetupadametat / yataḥ putrasya abhāve asattve pitā nāsti na bhavati / pitrā hi putro janayitavyaḥ / sa ca na putraṃ yāvajjanayati, tāvat pitaiva na bhavati / yāvacca pitā na bhavati, tāvat putrasya tasmāt saṃbhavo nāsti / ataḥ itaretarāśrayaṇādekābhāvādanyatarābhāvaḥ syāditi dvayorapyanayorabhāva iti samudāyārthaḥ / amumarthaṃ dārṣṭāntike yojayannāha tatheti-
body.translated_text: 'Father' — the begetter. If without the son — in the absence of a son — he would not exist, since this designation depends on having begotten a son — then whence is the arising of the son? Whence, from what, since the father does not exist, would the birth of the son — the one to be begotten — come about? If one asks why — 'without the son, there is no father.' This is the causal statement. Because in the absence of the son, in the non-existence [of the son], 'the father does not exist,' does not come into being. For a son is to be begotten by a father. And as long as he has not yet begotten a son, for that long he is not yet a father. And as long as he is not a father, for that long the arising of a son from him does not exist. Therefore, through mutual dependence, from the non-existence of one, the non-existence of the other would follow — thus both of these would be non-existent: this is the combined meaning. Applying this meaning to the subject at hand, he says 'likewise' —

body.text: tathāsattvaṃ tayordvayoḥ // Bca_9.114 //
body.translated_text: Likewise, both of those are non-existent. // Bca_9.114 //

body.text: yathātra pitāputrodāharaṇe, tathā asattvaṃ tathaiva abhāvaḥ tayordvayorjñānajñeyayoḥ / tathāhi- jñeyajananājjñānamucyate, jñānaparicchedyatayā ca jñeyamiti yāvat jñānaṃ na sidhyati, yāvat parijñānaṃ na sidhyati, tāvat paricchedyatayā ca jñeyaṃ na sidhyati / itaretarāśrayaṇādubhayābhāvaḥ syāditi bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: Just as in the illustration of father and son here, so too the non-being, the non-existence, of those two — knowledge and the knowable — is just the same. For knowledge is so called because it is produced from the knowable, and the knowable [is so called] because it is determined by knowledge. As long as knowledge is not established, as long as comprehensive knowledge is not established, the knowable too is not established as what is to be determined. From their mutual dependence, the non-existence of both would follow — this is the purport.

body.text: syādetat- na brūmaḥ- anyonyavaśāt siddhiranayoḥ api tu jñeyakāryaṃ jñānam, tato jñānādaṅkurād bījamiva jñeyaṃ setsyati / iti parāśayamudbhāvayannāha aṅkura ityādi-
body.translated_text: One might say: we do not claim that these two are established through mutual dependence; rather, knowledge is the effect of the knowable — from that, the knowable will be established from knowledge just as a seed is [inferred] from a sprout.
