Presenting the opponent's intention, he says 'a sprout' and so forth:

children.translated_text: A sprout is born from a seed; by that very [sprout] the seed is indicated;

children.text: jñeyājjñānena jātena tatsattā kiṃ na gamyate // Bca_9.115 //
children.translated_text: from knowledge born from the knowable, why is its [the knowable's] existence not understood? // Bca_9.115 //

body.text: aṅkuro jāyate utpadyate bījāt khalabilāntargatāt / bījaṃ tenaiva bījājjātena aṅkureṇa sūcyate gamyate yathā, tathā atra jñeyāt prameyāt jñānena jātena utpannena tatsattā tasya jñeyasya sattā sadbhāvaḥ kiṃ na gamyate, kiṃ na pratipadyate? atrāpi bījāṅkuravat kāryakāraṇabhāvasya vidyamānatvāt //
body.translated_text: A sprout is born, arises, from a seed contained within the husk. The seed is indicated, understood, by that very [thing] — by the sprout born from the seed — in the same way. Here, from the knowable — the object of valid cognition — by knowledge that has been born, that has arisen, its existence — the existence, the real being, of that knowable — why is it not understood, why is it not recognized? Since here too, as in the case of the seed and sprout, a causal relation exists.

body.text: nāyaṃ sadṛśo dṛṣṭānta ityāha aṅkurādityādi-
body.translated_text: This is not an apt illustration — he says 'from something other than the sprout' and so forth:

children.translated_text: It is from knowledge other than the sprout that the seed is understood to exist;

children.text: jñānāstitvaṃ kuto jñātaṃ jñeyaṃ yattena gamyate // Bca_9.116 //
children.translated_text: from what is the existence of knowledge known — the knowledge by which the knowable is understood? // Bca_9.116 //

body.text: aṅkurāt kāryāt bījamastīti yadgamyate, tannāyamasyaiva kevalasya prabhāvaḥ, kiṃ tarhi anyato jñānādaṅkuravyatiriktāt tadastīti gamyate / tathā hi- na yogyatāmātreṇa kāryaṃ kāraṇasya gamakam, bījasyaiva aṅkurajananamapratipannasyāpi gamakatvaṃ syāt / nāpi svarūpapratītimātreṇa apratipannakāryakāraṇabhāvasyāpi tatpratipattiprasaṅgāt, api tu avinābhāvitvena niścitam / ataḥ prākpratipannakāryakāraṇabhāvasya punaḥ paścāt kkacid bījāvinābhāvinamaṅkuramupalabdhavataḥ aṅkurādadhyavasāyātmakamanumānamutpadyate, tato bījamastītyavasīyate / ato jñānaviṣayīkṛta eva aṅkuro bījapratipattihetuḥ / jñānāstitvaṃ jñānasya sadbhāvaḥ kuto jñātaṃ kasmāt pratītam? svasaṃvedanābhāvādanavasthānabhayena jñānāntarānanusaraṇācca, jñeyaṃ yattena gamyate, yad yasmāt jñeyaṃ tena jñānena jñeyakāryeṇa gamyate avasīyate / na hi svayamaniścitaṃ liṅgaṃ
body.translated_text: That the seed is understood to exist from the sprout — the effect — this is not the result of the sprout's power alone; rather, it is understood from knowledge other than the sprout — distinct from it. For a mere capacity does not make the effect an indicator of the cause; otherwise, even without the causal relation of the seed with the sprout being recognized, there would be indication. Nor is it through mere perception of the [sprout's] own form, since even for something whose causal relation is not recognized, there would be the absurd consequence of that recognition. Rather, it must be ascertained through invariable concomitance. Therefore, for one who has previously recognized the causal relation and subsequently, somewhere, perceives a sprout that is invariably concomitant with a seed — from the sprout an inferential cognition of the nature of determination arises, and thereby the seed is determined to exist. Thus it is the sprout as made an object of knowledge that is the cause of recognizing the seed. The existence of knowledge — the real being of knowledge — from what is it known, from what is it recognized? Due to the absence of self-cognition and out of fear of infinite regress from not following yet another knowledge — the knowable that is understood by that knowledge — from that, the knowable is understood, determined, by that knowledge, which is the effect of the knowable. For a mark that is not itself ascertained

body.text: sādhyasya gamakamupapadyate / jñāpakahetutvādasya jñeyagamakatvam / tasmādvāstavapakṣe jñānajñeyāsiddhervicāraḥ kartumaśakyaḥ, kālpanikapakṣe tu yathāprasiddhavyavahāramāśritya śakyate iti niścitam //
body.translated_text: cannot serve as an indicator of what is to be proven. Its being an indicator of the knowable is due to its being a cognitive cause. Therefore, on the realist position, the inquiry cannot be made since knowledge and the knowable are unestablished; on the conventionalist position, however, it can be made by relying on established conventional discourse — this is determined.

children.text: na svato nāpi parato na dvābhyāṃ nāpyahetutaḥ /
children.translated_text: Not from self, not from other, not from both, and not from no cause —

children.text: utpannā jātu vidyante bhāvāḥ kvacana kecana //
children.translated_text: things are never found to have arisen anywhere whatsoever.

body.text: ma. śā. 1.3
body.translated_text: <s>Madhyamakaśāstra</s> 1.3

body.text: ityasyārthasya samarthanārthaṃ nāpyahetuta iti turīyakoṭiprasādhanāya tāvat svabhāvavādimatamapākartumāha loka ityādi-
body.translated_text: In order to establish the meaning of this [verse], and specifically to prove the fourth extreme — 'not from no cause' — he undertakes to refute the view of the <s>Svabhāvavādins</s> (proponents of intrinsic nature / naturalists), saying 'the world' and so forth:

body.text: lokaḥ pratyakṣatastāvatsarvaṃ hetumudīkṣate /
body.translated_text: The world, from direct perception itself, observes everything to have a cause. // Bca_9.117 [first half] //

body.text: tathā hi te svaparasvabhāvasarvahetunirapekṣameva bhāvagrāmavaicitryamutpadyate iti varṇayanti / yataḥ na paṅkajādīnāṃ nālapatradalakesarādikamanekaprakārabhedabhinnavaicitryamacetanā jalapaṅkādayo nirvartayitumalam / na ca cetano 'pi kaścidanyaḥ karmaṇā tādṛśanirmāṇapravīṇa upalabhyate, nāpi cādriyate, tatkarmaṇo 'paryavasānāt yugapadaparyantaviśeṣeṣu vyāpārāyogācca / tasmāt kiṃcitkāraṇamantareṇaiva sarvamidaṃ jagadvaicitryamutpadyate iti teṣāṃ matam, taduktam-
body.translated_text: For they maintain that the diversity of the world of entities arises quite independently of any cause — whether self, other, or all [causes]. Since neither the insentient water, mud, and such are capable of producing the diverse variety of many different kinds such as the stalk, petals, petal-divisions, and filaments of a lotus; nor is any sentient other [being] found who is skilled at such construction through [its] activity; nor does one even regard such [a being], since that activity would have no terminus and since there would be the impossibility of engaging simultaneously in unlimited particular [tasks] — therefore, their view is that all this diversity of the world arises without any cause whatsoever. As it is said:

children.translated_text: The birth of entities is described by the <s>Svabhāvavādins</s> as devoid of all causes;
they do not even call themselves [i.e. their own nature] a cause.
'Who creates the diversity of lotus filaments and such?
Or the eye-spots of a peacock — by whom is their variety fashioned?'
'Just as the sharpness and such of thorns is causeless,
so too, through their occasional nature, suffering and such are causeless.'

body.text: tattvasaṃgraha-110-112
body.translated_text: <s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 110-112

body.text: tadevaṃvādino lokapratītādeva hetusāmarthyādbādhā syādityupadarśayati / lokaḥ sarvo janaḥ / pratyakṣataḥ indriyāśritājjñānāt / pratyakṣata ityupalakṣaṇādanumānato 'pi tatpratītibhāvāt / pratyakṣānumānābhyāmiti yāvat / sarvamanekaprakāraṃ hetuṃ jagadvaicitryakāraṇam, udīkṣate tadanvayavyatirekānuvidhāyi kāryamupajanayantaṃ paśyati / yat kāryaṃ yasya sadbhāve bhavati, tadabhāve ca na bhavatīti pratīyate, sa tasya heturiti niścīyate / iti lokapratītādeva hetuvyāpārādasya ahetukatvapratijñā bādhyate / tadevopadarśayannāha padmanālādītyādi-
body.translated_text: He shows that the one who speaks thus is refuted by the very power of causes perceived by the world. 'The world' — all people. 'From direct perception' — from cognition dependent on the senses. The word 'from direct perception' is illustrative: also from inference, since their recognition [of causes] exists through that too. Meaning: from direct perception and inference. 'Everything' — of many kinds — 'a cause' — the reason for the world's diversity — '[the world] observes' — sees it producing effects that conform to its agreement [with the cause] and difference [in its absence]. That whose effect comes to be when it exists, and does not come to be when it does not exist — this is recognized — that is determined to be its cause. Thus, from the very worldly perception of causal operation, the claim of causelessness is refuted. Showing just that, he says 'the diversity of the lotus stalk' and so forth:

body.text: padmanālādibhedo hi hetubhedena jāyate // Bca_9.117 //
body.translated_text: For the diversity of the lotus stalk and such arises from the diversity of causes. // Bca_9.117 [second half] //

body.text: padmasya rājīvasya nālamādi yeṣāṃ padmadalakesarādīnāṃ te tathoktāḥ, teṣāṃ bhedo nānātvam / hiryasmāt / hetubhedena hetoḥ kāraṇasya bhedena viśeṣeṇa jāyate utpadyate, nānyathā / aniyamena sarvatra sadbhāvaprasaṅgāt / ataḥ yad yasyānvayavyatirekānuvidhānaṃ kurvat pratīyate, tat tasyaiva kāryaṃ nānyasyetyabhyupagamanīyam / yasmāt pratiniyatakāraṇādeva pratiniyataviśeṣotpattiḥ, tadbhedena tadbhedāditi na ahetumatī //
body.translated_text: 'Of the lotus' — of the <s>rājīva</s> (lotus) — 'the stalk and such' — of the lotus petals, petal-divisions, filaments, and such — thus they are so called; their 'diversity' — variety. 'For' — because. 'From the diversity of causes' — from the difference, the specificity, of causes — it 'arises,' is produced — and not otherwise. Because [otherwise] there would be the absurd consequence of its existence everywhere without restriction. Therefore, what is perceived as following the agreement and difference of something — that must be accepted as the effect of that very thing and not of another. Since the specific production arises only from a specific cause, the diversity [of effects arises] from the diversity of that [cause] — thus it is not without cause.

body.text: nanu bhavedeṣa viśeṣaḥ yadi hetoreva svayamasau viśeṣaḥ siddhaḥ syāt / kiṃ tu tasyaiva kutaḥ sa bhavatīti vaktavyam / na ca nirviśeṣādviśeṣotpattiḥ, punarahetutvaprasaṅgāt / ityāśaṅkāṃ pariharannāha kiṃkṛta ityādi-
body.translated_text: But this specificity would hold only if the specificity of the cause itself were independently established. But what gives rise to its [specificity]? And from something without specificity, no specific production [can arise], since that would again be [tantamount to] causelessness. Resolving this doubt, he says 'produced by what' and so forth:

body.text: kiṃkṛto hetubhedaścet pūrvahetuprabhedataḥ /
body.translated_text: If [you ask] what produces the diversity of causes — from the diversity of the prior cause.

body.text: kiṃkṛtaḥ kena kṛtaḥ kuto yātaḥ hetubhedaścet, hetorbhedo viśeṣaśceducyate / pūrvahetuprabhedataḥ pūrvasya prāktanasya tajjanakasya hetoḥ prabhedataḥ prabhedādviśeṣāt / tasyāpi tatpūrvasya hetoḥ kuto viśeṣa iti cet, punastatrāpi pūrvahetuviśeṣāditi vaktavyam, iti uttarottarasya viśeṣākāṅkṣāyāṃ pūrvapūrvasya viśeṣādityuttaraṃ vācyam / na caivamanavasthānamaniṣṭaṃ kiṃcidāpādayati- anavarāgrasya saṃsārasya pūrvakoṭirna prajñāyate ityabhyupagamāt / ata eva phalāviparyayo 'pi na svato bhavatītyāha kasmāccedityādi-
body.translated_text: 'Produced by what' — made by what, arising from what — 'is the diversity of causes?' — if you ask about the diversity, the specificity, of causes — it is answered: 'from the diversity of the prior cause' — from the diversity, the specificity, of the prior, the preceding cause that generates it. And if [one asks] what gives that [prior cause] too its specificity — again, from the specificity of the [yet] prior cause — this must be said. Thus, when the demand for specificity of each successive [cause arises], the answer 'from the specificity of each preceding [cause]' is to be given. And this infinite regress does not entail anything undesirable, since it is accepted that the prior limit of beginningless and endless <s>saṃsāra</s> is not known. For this very reason, the non-reversal of results too does not occur of its own accord — he says 'why' and so forth:

body.text: kasmāccetphalado hetuḥ pūrvahetuprabhāvataḥ // Bca_9.118 //
body.translated_text: Why is the cause productive of results? Through the power of the prior cause. // Bca_9.118 //

body.text: kasmāt kāraṇāt phalado viśiṣṭaphaladānasamartho hetuścet, pūrvahetuprabhāvataḥ pūrvasya tajjanakasya hetoḥ sāmarthyāt svahetunā sa tādṛśastatsvabhāvo 'jani yena sahakāriviśeṣopahitakāryotpādānuguṇaviśeṣaparaṃparāpariṇatimadhigacchan asati pratibandhavaikalyayoḥ saṃbhave tathāvidhameva phalamutpādayati / ataḥ aviparītaphaladānamapi svahetusāmarthyopajanitameva / tena abhyudayaniḥśreyasasādhanahetoryathāsaṃkhyamabhyudayaniḥśreyasameva phalaṃ jāyate, tadviparītādviparītamiti na kathaṃcidapi viparyayaḥ //
body.translated_text: Why — for what reason — 'is the cause productive of results' — capable of granting a specific result — if [you ask this, it is] through the power of the prior cause — through the capacity of the prior cause that generates it. Its own cause made it such, of such a nature, whereby — endowed with the particular specialization conducive to effect-production through specific auxiliary conditions — when there is the occurrence [of conditions] without obstruction or deficiency — it produces just such a result. Therefore, the non-reversal of results too is produced by the power of its own cause. Thus, for the cause of higher rebirth and the highest good, respectively, the result is precisely higher rebirth and the highest good; from its opposite, the opposite — and there is no reversal whatsoever.

body.text: etacca avaśyaṃ svabhāvavādinā sahetukatvamakāmakenāpi svīkartavyam / kathamanyathā hetumantareṇa pratijñātamahetukatvaṃ bhāvānāṃ setsyati? pratijñāmātreṇa tasya kenacidagrahaṇāt / hetuvyāpāreṇa tat prasādhayataḥ svayameva punaḥ sahetukatvābhyupagamāt vandhyā me māteti bruvataḥ iva pratijñāyāḥ svavacanena bādhanaṃ syāt ityubhayataḥpāśā rajjuriti saṃkaṭaprāpto batāyaṃ tapasvī / taduktam-
body.translated_text: And the <s>Svabhāvavādin</s> must necessarily accept causality, however unwillingly. How else, without a cause, could the claimed causelessness of entities be established? Since through mere assertion alone, it would not be accepted by anyone. And in establishing it through the operation of a reason — [the <s>Svabhāvavādin</s>] himself accepts causality, which would be a contradiction of his own thesis by his own words — like one who says 'my mother is barren.' Thus [he is] caught by a rope with a noose at both ends — alas, this wretched one is trapped! As it is said:

children.text: na heturastīti vadan sahetukaṃ nanu pratijñāṃ svayameva śātayet /
children.translated_text: 'In saying "there is no cause," would he not himself shatter his own thesis of causality?

children.text: athāpi hetupraṇayālaso bhavet pratijñayā kevalayāsya kiṃ bhavet //
children.translated_text: And if he is too lazy for reasoning, what use would his mere thesis be?'

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: tasmāt kudṛṣṭivijṛmbhitamevaitat pramāṇabādhitatvāt //
body.translated_text: Therefore, this is merely the sport of a wrong view, since it is contradicted by valid means of knowledge.

body.text: evaṃ svabhāvavādinaṃ nirākṛtya caturthaprakāraprasādhanārthameva īśvarakāraṇatāṃ jagataḥ pratyākhyātuṃ tadupakṣepaṃ kurvannāha īśvara ityādi-
body.translated_text: Having thus refuted the <s>Svabhāvavādin</s>, in order to prove the fourth extreme as well, and to reject [the claim of] God as the cause of the world, introducing [the topic], he says '<s>Īśvara</s>' and so forth:

body.text: īśvaro jagato hetuḥ
body.translated_text: <s>Īśvara</s> is the cause of the world —

body.text: īśvarakāraṇavādino hi svabhāvavādimataniṣedhamākarṇya viśeṣamabhidhātumardhamavasitaṃ bhārasyeti manyamānāḥ prāhuḥ- sāhāyyameva anuṣṭhitamevaṃ bhavadbhiḥ / na hi kāraṇamantareṇaiva
body.translated_text: For the proponents of God as cause, having heard the refutation of the <s>Svabhāvavādin</s>'s position, thinking that half their burden has already been accomplished and wishing to state the distinguishing point, say: assistance has indeed been rendered by you. For without a cause

body.text: jagadvaicitryamupapadyate deśādyaniyamaprasaṅgāt / kevalamacetanāḥ punaramī jalapaṅkādayo vaicitryāsāmarthyā iti yuktamanenoktam / tatra astyeva sa bhagavān viśvavaicitryanirmāṇapravīṇaḥ jagadekasūtradhāraḥ sakalajagadādibhūtaḥ nityātmatayā sarvadānupahataśaktiprabhāvaḥ sarvabhāvānāṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvāditattvavedī samastārvācīnadarśanāgocaramāhātmya īśvaraḥ / tena hetunā sahetukaṃ sakalamidaṃ sacarācaraṃ jagaditi kaḥ sacetanaḥ anyathā vaktumutsahate? iti naiyāyikādiveśmakathāmabhidhāya pratyācaṣṭe- īśvaro jagato hetuḥ / īśvara iti śaṃkarasyākhyā / sa eva jagato viśvasya hetuḥ sṛṣṭisthitipralayakāraṇam / tasmādevaitadviśvamaśeṣamutpadyate / anyathā punaracetanopādānatvāt kathamamī girisaridavanisāgarādaya utpattibhājo bhaveyuḥ? cetanāva dadhiṣṭhānāt punarime samutpattumutsahante, tadvayāpāreṇaiva pravartanāt / taduktam-
body.translated_text: the diversity of the world is not justified, since there would be the absurd consequence of non-restriction by place, time, and such. Only, these insentient water, mud, and such are incapable of [producing] diversity — this has rightly been said. There, there does indeed exist the Blessed One who is skilled in fashioning the world's variety, who holds the single thread of the universe, who is the primordial being of the entire world, who by virtue of eternal selfhood has power and majesty forever unimpaired, who knows the reality of causal relations and such of all entities, whose greatness is beyond the scope of all modern philosophies — <s>Īśvara</s>! Through him as cause, all this world with its moving and non-moving [beings] is caused — what sentient being could venture to say otherwise? — thus having related the tale told in the house of the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and such, he replies: '<s>Īśvara</s> is the cause of the world.' '<s>Īśvara</s>' is the name of <s>Śaṃkara</s>. He alone is the cause of the world, the universe — the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. From him alone this entire universe arises. Otherwise, since the material cause is insentient, how could these mountains, rivers, earth, oceans, and such be subject to arising? Only through being presided over by a conscious [being] can these come into being, since they function through his operation alone. As it is said:

children.translated_text: Some declare <s>Īśvara</s> to be the cause of all that is subject to arising;
an insentient [thing] surely does not initiate its own effects by itself.
'This <s>Meru</s> would not exist, nor this earth, nor this ocean,
nor these eyes of the world — the sun and moon — beautiful in their placement,
if <s>Īśāna</s> were not, like a potter, the creator of the universe —
thus someone indeed declares that this world is created by <s>Īśvara</s>, because of its being a product.'

body.text: iti / [tattvasaṃgraha-46-47]
body.translated_text: [<s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 46-47]

body.text: tasmājjagadevamacetanaviśvasvabhāvamīśvarakāraṇatāmātmano brūte / atrocyate- kimanayā svagṛhītopakalpitayā prameyaracanayā vacanaracanāprapañcamālayā? naitaducyamānamapi svasamayābhiniveśināṃ jaḍadhiyāṃ prītikaraṃ pramāṇaśūnyaṃ viduṣāṃ saṃtoṣamutpādayati / tathā hi- yadyasau kāruṇikaḥ, kimarthaṃ punarimān narakādiduḥkhapīḍitān prāṇinaḥ karoti? tathā ca sati kāruṇikatvaṃ tasya śraddhāsamadhigamyameva syāt / svakṛtāsatkarmaphalopabhogena tatkṣepāpanayane yasya pravṛttiḥ, kathamakāruṇiko nāmeti cet, na / tat karma kāruṇikaḥ kimiti kārayati yenāniṣṭaṃ phalamupabhujyate, tatrāpi tasya vyāpārāt, sarvotpattimatāṃ nimittakāraṇatvāt / api ca kiṃ tasminnavyāpriyamāṇe tat karmaphalamupabhujyate na vā? yadi prathamaḥ pakṣaḥ, tadā kathametat-
body.translated_text: Therefore, the world, being thus of the nature of an insentient universe, declares <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) as its own cause. Here it is said: what is the use of this fabricated arrangement of proofs, a garland of verbal elaborations, constructed from one's own preconceptions? Even when spoken, this, being devoid of valid cognition, does not produce delight for those of dull intellect who cling to their own doctrines, nor does it generate satisfaction for the wise. For indeed — if he is compassionate, why then does he create these beings who are tormented by the sufferings of hell and such? And that being the case, his compassionateness would be accessible only through faith. 'If one objects: his activity consists in removing the censure through the experience of the fruits of one's own bad actions — how can he be called uncompassionate?' — No. Why does the compassionate one cause that <s>karma</s> by which undesirable fruit is experienced, since even there his activity is involved, because he is the efficient cause of all that comes into being? Moreover, when he is not involved, is the fruit of that <s>karma</s> experienced or not? If the first position, then how does this [verse apply] —

children.translated_text: This ignorant creature, powerless regarding its own pleasure and pain,
impelled by <s>Īśvara</s>, goes to heaven or to a dog's pit.

body.text: iti / [mahābhā.-3.30.28]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Mahābhārata</s> 3.30.28]

body.text: sarvakāryeṣveva tadvayāpārābhyupagamasya anenaiva anaikāntikatāprasaṅgāt / atha dvitīyaḥ, tadā kṛpālurasau tatropekṣāṃ kimiti nādhivāsayati, yad yatnena sāhāyyameva tatropakalpayati / atha kṛtasya karmaṇo 'vipraṇāśādavaśyaṃ tena tatphalamanubhavitavyamiti tadupabhogāya vyāpriyate iti cet, kathaṃ punaretasminnavyāpriyamāṇe 'vaśyaṃ tenānubhavitavyaṃ sāmagrīvaikalyāt / kaḥ punarevaṃ
body.translated_text: Because of the absurd consequence that, by accepting his involvement in absolutely all effects, through this very [argument] the inconclusiveness [of the proof would follow]. If the second [position], then why does the merciful one not tolerate indifference toward that, instead devoting effort to providing assistance? If one objects: because performed <s>karma</s> does not perish, [the being] must necessarily experience its fruit, and so [<s>Īśvara</s>] acts for that experience — then how, when he is not involved, must it necessarily be experienced, given the deficiency of the assemblage [of conditions]? Furthermore, what

body.text: vipraṇāśe 'pi doṣaḥ?
body.translated_text: fault is there even in the perishing [of karma]?

body.text: prayatnata eva tato nivartitumucitaṃ kāruṇikasya / evaṃ hi tadicchāyattavṛttitayā tasyāparipākāt tena svamaiśvaryamupadarśitaṃ tatra bhavet / atra sattvānāṃ tatkarmasaṃcodito 'sau dayālurapi sthātumaśaktaḥ, mahad bata anena svamaiśvaryamitthaṃ dyotitamanyatra syāt / tat parakarmaṇāpi samākṛṣṭo nāma nātmani vaśitvamadhigacchati, īśvarataḥ karmaṇa eva mahat sāmarthyamevaṃ prakāśitaṃ syāt / tadvaraṃ karmaiva paryupāsyaṃ yatsāmarthyena samākṛṣyamāṇo maheśvaro 'pi sthātumasamarthaḥ / tasmādidamavyāhatameva-
body.translated_text: It would be proper for the compassionate one to exert effort precisely to prevent that. For thus, since [the being's] activity depends on his will, through his lack of maturity [in that will], his own sovereignty would be demonstrated therein. Here, 'this compassionate one, even though merciful, is unable to stand still when impelled by the <s>karma</s> of beings — alas, how his own sovereignty has been displayed!' — this reasoning would apply elsewhere. Thus, being drawn even by another's <s>karma</s>, he does not achieve mastery over himself; compared to <s>Īśvara</s>, <s>karma</s> itself would have greater power thus displayed. Then it would be better to worship <s>karma</s> itself, by whose power even the great Lord is unable to stand still. Therefore, this [verse] stands unrefuted —

body.text: namaḥ satkarmabhyo vidhirapi na yebhyaḥ prabhavati //
body.translated_text: Homage to good deeds, over which even fate has no power!

body.text: iti / [bhartṛhari-vairāgya-92]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Bhartṛhari</s>, <s>Vairāgya</s> 92]

body.text: atha na kāruṇikaḥ, tadāsau vītarāgaḥ sarāgo vā? yadi ādyo vikalpaḥ, tadā yadi nāma dayāvirahāt sukhaṃ nopanayati, duḥkhaṃ tu janasya kasmādutpādayatīti vaktavyam / duḥkhaṃ hi rāgādivaśena kasyacidupanīyate / te cāsya na santi / kathamakāraṇameva janaṃ duḥkhayati? krīḍārthaṃ duḥkhayatīti cet, krīḍārthaṃ vītarāgasya pravṛttiriti cet, niścitamasau na vītarāgaḥ / rāgādimatāmapi tāvajjitendriyāṇāṃ na krīḍārthaṃ dṛśyate pravṛttiḥ, kiṃ punarvītarāgāṇāṃ tathā bhaviṣyati / na rakṣaḥpiśācādimantareṇa anyasya paraduḥkhena krīḍā saṃbhāvyate //
body.translated_text: Now, if he is not compassionate, then is he dispassionate or passionate? If the first alternative — if, due to the absence of compassion, he does not bring about happiness, then it must be stated why he produces suffering for people. For suffering is inflicted upon someone through the force of desire and such, and those [passions] do not belong to him. How does he cause suffering to people without cause? If one objects that he causes suffering for sport — if one claims that a dispassionate being acts for sport, then it is certain that he is not dispassionate. For even among passionate beings who have conquered their senses, activity for sport is not observed — how much less will it be so for the dispassionate? Sport in others' suffering is not conceivable for anyone other than <s>rākṣasas</s>, <s>piśācas</s>, and such.

body.text: atha avītarāga iti pakṣaḥ, tadā kathamayamitarajanasādhāraṇaḥ sannīśvaro bhavitumarhati? rāgādikleśapāśāyattavṛtterjagadaiśvaryāyogāt / anyathā tadanyasyāpi tathāvidhasya tatprasaṅgāt / nāpi saṃsāracārakoparuddhasvātantryasya viśvavaicitryaracanācāturyaṃ tadanyasyeva yujyate / tadevamastitvameva bhavantaṃ vipralambhayati yadevaṃvidhasyāpi yāvadaiśvaryamabhyupagamyate / bhavatu vā tathāvidhasyāpi kartṛtvam / tathāpi kimasau svasthātmā [asvasthātmā vā]? yadi svasthātmā, tadā kimiti janamakāṇḍameva duḥkhayati? na hi svasthātmā niraparādhaṃ janaṃ pīḍayan dṛṣṭaḥ / atha vimārgagāminameva kṛtāparādhaṃ pīḍayatīti cet, vimārgagāminamapi ayameva kārayati / tathābhūtamapi kārayitvā punaḥ pīḍayatīti sa laukikeśvarāṇāmapi jaghanyatayā vṛttimatiśete / te hi svayaṃkṛtāparādhameva aparādhinamanuśāsati / ayaṃ punarātmanaiva kārayitveti mahānasya viśeṣaḥ / atha asvasthātmā, tadā asādhu tadārādhane svargāpavargārthināṃ prekṣāvatāṃ pravṛttiḥ / na hi unmattasyārādhanamunmattakādanyaḥ kartumutsahate / tathā hi svargādilipsayā tadārādhanāya pravartante prekṣāvantaḥ / tacca apariniścitasvabhāvatayā tato na saṃbhāvyate, viparyayo 'pi vā tadārādhanaphalasya saṃbhāvyate / tadārādhanapravṛttāstu gāḍhataraśraddhāvaśena tamunmattamācakṣāṇā ātmānamevonmattakamācakṣīran / kathamanyathā tadārādhane pravartante? tadaparonmattakairvā kimaparāddhaṃ yataste na paryupāsyante? teṣāṃ prabhāvātiśayavikalatvāditi cet, na vai prakṛte 'pi kaṃcit prabhāvātiśayamutpaśyāmaḥ / unmattakaḥ sakalajagadatiśāyiśaktiriti ko 'nya unmattakādvaktumarhati? tadayamabhivicāryamāṇo na kvacidavasānaṃ labhate iti alaṃ durmativiṣyanditeṣu ādareṇeti / tasmāt sūktametadū yaduktam-
body.translated_text: Now, if the position is that he is not dispassionate — then how can this one, being on par with ordinary people, deserve to be <s>Īśvara</s>? Because one whose activity is subject to the bonds of afflictions such as desire cannot have sovereignty over the world. Otherwise, anyone else of such a nature would equally qualify. Nor is the skill in fashioning the variety of the world justified for one whose independence is obstructed by wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s>, any more than for anyone else. Thus, it is his very existence that deceives you, since sovereignty is attributed even to one of such a nature. Or let there be creatorship even for one of such a nature. Even so — is he of sound mind or unsound mind? If of sound mind, then why does he cause suffering to people for no reason whatsoever? For one of sound mind is never seen causing pain to an unoffending people. Now, if one objects that he punishes only one who has gone astray and committed an offense — even one who goes astray is made to do so by this very [Lord] himself. Having caused [the being] to act thus and then punishing it — this surpasses even the conduct of the most contemptible among worldly rulers. For they punish only one who has himself committed an offense. But this one [punishes] after having himself caused [the offense] — that is his great distinction. Now, if he is of unsound mind, then it is improper for discerning people seeking heaven and liberation to devote themselves to his worship. For no one other than a madman would undertake the worship of a madman. For the discerning engage in his worship out of desire for heaven and such. But since his nature is unascertained, [the desired results] are not to be expected from him — or even the opposite of the fruit of his worship is conceivable. And those who engage in his worship, attributing madness to this madman due to the force of deeply entrenched faith, would be proclaiming themselves as madmen. How else would they engage in his worship? And what offense have the other madmen committed that they are not worshipped? If one says it is because they lack an excess of power — indeed, even in the present case, we do not perceive any excess of power. 'A madman surpasses the entire world in power' — who other than a madman is fit to say this? Thus, when examined, this [doctrine] finds no resting place anywhere. Enough then of respect for the outpourings of faulty reasoning! Therefore, it is well said what was stated —

children.text: sukhasya duḥkhasya na ko 'pi dātā paro dadātīti kubuddhireṣā /
children.translated_text: No one is a giver of happiness or suffering; the notion that another gives is erroneous thinking.
For the world is strung on the thread of its own <s>karma</s>; the conceit 'I am the doer' is vain.

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: tasmādakartṛkameva idaṃ jagadaśeṣamiti na paridṛṣṭakāraṇādanyaḥ svatantraścetano vā tasya kartā kaścidasti / idameva vistareṇa pratipādayituṃ siddhāntavādī prāha-
body.translated_text: Therefore, this entire world is indeed without a creator — there is no independent, conscious agent of it other than the observed causes. To establish this very point at length, the proponent of the system says —

body.text: vada kastāvadīśvaraḥ /
body.translated_text: Tell me then, who is <s>Īśvara</s>?

body.text: īśvarakāraṇavādinaṃ pṛcchati- vada brūhi ko 'yamīśvaro bhavato 'bhimataḥ? tāvacchabdenedamabhidhatte- yeṣāṃ kṣityādīnāmanvayavyatirekānuvidhāyi kāryamupalabhyate, tatra katamadīśvaraṃ bhavānācaṣṭe? na ca anupalabdhānvayavyatirekavyāpārasya kāraṇatā prakalpayituṃ yuktā, atiprasaṅgāt / tasmāt tatkāraṇatāmicchatā dṛṣṭānvayavyatirekavyāpāra eva aṅgīkartavyaḥ / na cānyasya kṣitibījādivyatiriktasya anvayavyatirekānuvidhānaṃ kurvat dṛśyate kāryam / tat kathaṃ tasya kāryopayogitvaṃ vyavasthāpyate? yaduktam-
body.translated_text: He asks the proponent of <s>Īśvara</s> as cause: Tell me, speak — who is this <s>Īśvara</s> accepted by you? By the word 'then' (<s>tāvat</s>), he indicates this: among those [things] whose effects are observed as conforming to the presence and absence [of their causes] — such as earth and such — which one do you declare to be <s>Īśvara</s>? And it is not proper to posit causality for one whose operations of presence and absence are not observed, because of overextension. Therefore, one who wishes to assert its causality must accept only that whose operations of presence and absence are observed. And no effect is seen conforming to the presence and absence of anything other than earth, seeds, and such. So how is its usefulness for effects to be established? As was stated —

children.translated_text: When those [causes] are present, [the effect] indeed arises; [yet] for that, another [cause] is fabricated.
As its cause everywhere, there would be no end to [the postulation of additional] causes.

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: atha pṛthivyādīni bhūtānyeva īśvaro bhavatviti parābhiprāyamāśaṅkayāha bhūtāni cedityādi-
body.translated_text: Now, anticipating the opponent's intent — 'let the elements such as earth themselves be <s>Īśvara</s>' — he says with 'if the elements' and so forth —

body.text: bhūtāni cedbhavatvevaṃ nāmamātre 'pi kiṃ śramaḥ // Bca_9.119 //
body.translated_text: If the elements — let it be so; then why the trouble even over a mere name? // <s>Bca</s> 9.119 //

body.text: yadi bhūtāni pṛthivyādīni īśvara ucyate, tadā abhyupagamyate eva / bhavatvevam, evamastu, na vayamatra vipratipadyāmahe / kṣityādyanvayavyatirekānuvidhānavataḥ kāryasya darśanāt / kevalaṃ nāmamātre 'pi kiṃ śramaḥ? nāmaiva kevalamarthabhedaśūnyaṃ nāmamātrakam / apiravadhāraṇe / nāmamātre eva kimiha mahāsamārambheṇa tatprasādhanāya śramaḥ āyāsaḥ kriyate? mayā kṣityādaya ucyante, tvayā punastānyeva bhūtāni īśvaraḥ iti nārthataḥ kaścidviśeṣaḥ? na cātra vipratipattāvarthaśūnyāyāṃ kiṃcit phalamupalabhyate //
body.translated_text: If the elements — earth and such — are called <s>Īśvara</s>, then it is indeed accepted. Let it be so, let it be thus — we do not disagree about this, since effects are observed as conforming to the presence and absence of earth and such. Only, 'why the trouble even over a mere name?' 'Name alone' (<s>nāmamātram</s>) is a mere name devoid of any difference in meaning. The particle '<s>api</s>' is for emphasis. Why is effort, exertion, undertaken with such great endeavor to establish this, merely over a name? I call them earth and such; you call those very elements '<s>Īśvara</s>' — there is no difference in substance. And in this dispute, devoid of [any real] content, no fruit is obtained.

body.text: atha astyeva arthaviśeṣaḥ, tadā naiṣāmīśvaratvaṃ yuktamityāha api tvityādi-
body.translated_text: Now, if there is indeed a difference in meaning, then their being <s>Īśvara</s> is not justified — he says with 'but rather' and so forth —

children.text: api tvaneke 'nityāśca niśceṣṭā na ca devatāḥ /
children.translated_text: But rather, they are many, impermanent, inert, and not divine,

children.text: laṅghayāścāśucayaścaiva kṣmādayo na sa īśvaraḥ // Bca_9.120 //
children.translated_text: they can be trodden upon, and they are impure — earth and such are not that <s>Īśvara</s>. // <s>Bca</s> 9.120 //

body.text: apituśabdena adhikamāha / naite kṣityādayo bhavatāmīśvaratvena kalpayituṃ yujyante, tallakṣaṇāyogāt / kathaṃ kṛtvā? aneke nānāsvabhāvāḥ, anityāśca vinaśvarasvabhāvāḥ, niśceṣṭāḥ, acetanatayā nirvyāpārāḥ / na ca devatāḥ, nāpi ca ārādhyarūpāḥ / laṅghayāśca atikramaṇīyāḥ anaghṛṣyatvāt / aśucayaścaiva apavitrāḥ / amedhyādiṣvapi pṛthivyādisadbhāvāt /
body.translated_text: By the word 'but rather' (<s>api tu</s>), he states something additional. These — earth and such — are not fit to be posited by you as <s>Īśvara</s>, because of the inapplicability of his defining characteristics. How so? They are 'many' — of various natures; 'impermanent' — of perishable nature; 'inert' — inactive, due to being insentient; 'not divine' — nor are they objects of worship; 'they can be trodden upon' — they can be transgressed, because they cannot resist; 'and impure' — unclean, because earth and such exist even in excrement and such.

body.text: kṣmādayaḥ kṣmā pṛthivī ādiryeṣāmaptejovāyūnāṃ te tathoktāḥ / na sa īśvaraḥ, sa īśvaraḥ tādṛkkhabhāvo na bhavati, tatṣaṭprakāraviparītatvāt //
body.translated_text: '<s>Kṣmā</s> and such' — <s>kṣmā</s> is earth; those of which it is the first — water, fire, and wind — are thus designated. 'Not that <s>Īśvara</s>' — 'that <s>Īśvara</s>' — a nature of that kind — does not exist, because of being contrary to those six characteristics.

body.text: yadi kṣmādayo neśvaraḥ, ākāśaṃ tarhi bhaviṣyatītyāha nākāśamityādi-
body.translated_text: If earth and such are not <s>Īśvara</s>, then perhaps space will be — he says with 'not space' and so forth —

body.text: nākāśamīśo 'ceṣṭatvāt
body.translated_text: Space is not the Lord, because of inactivity.

body.text: ākāśamapi īśaḥ īśvaro na bhavati / kutaḥ? aceṣṭatvāt, svabhāvavikalatayā nirvyāpāratvāt, paramate 'pi niṣkriyatvāt / ātmā tarhi bhavatu-
body.translated_text: Space too is not <s>Īśa</s>, the Lord. Why? Because of inactivity — because of being inactive due to lack of intrinsic capacity; even in the opponent's own view, because of actionlessness. Then let it be the self —

body.text: nātmā pūrvaniṣedhataḥ /
body.translated_text: Not the self, because of its prior refutation.

body.text: pūrvameva vistareṇa ātmanaḥ pratiṣiddhatvāt niḥsvabhāvaḥ śaśaviṣāṇavadasau / athāpi syāt- avitarkyamāhātmyatvādasya nārvāgdarśanairidamitthamiti tatsvarūpaṃ vivecayituṃ śakyamityāha acintyasyetyādi-
body.translated_text: Because the self has already been refuted at length, it is without intrinsic nature, like a hare's horn. Now one might think: because his greatness is beyond reasoning, those of limited vision cannot determine his true nature as 'this is thus' — he says with 'of the inconceivable' and so forth —

body.text: acintyasya ca kartṛtvamapyacintyaṃ kimucyate // Bca_9.121 //
body.translated_text: And as for the inconceivable — its creatorship too is inconceivable; what then can be said? // <s>Bca</s> 9.121 //

body.text: yadi asau cintātikrāntamāhātmyaḥ, tadā acintyasya ca cintāpathamatikrāntasya īśvarasya kartṛtvaṃ yugapatkāraṇatvamapi acintyamatarkyaṃ kimucyate, kimabhidhīyate? kartṛtvamapyasya acintyatvānna vaktumucitamityarthaḥ //
body.translated_text: If he is one whose greatness transcends thought, then 'of the inconceivable' — of <s>Īśvara</s> who transcends the path of thought — 'creatorship' — simultaneous causality — is also 'inconceivable,' beyond reasoning. What then 'can be said,' what can be stated? The meaning is: his creatorship too, being inconceivable, is not fit to be asserted.

body.text: syādetat- atidurlakṣyasvabhāvatayā cintayitumaśakyo 'sau, kāryaṃ tu tasya sarvajanapratītisādhāraṇatvāt cintyameva, iti bruvāṇaṃ pratyāha tena kimityādi-
body.translated_text: There might be this [objection]: he is incapable of being thought about because of his nature being exceedingly difficult to discern; but his effect, being common to the experience of all people, is indeed thinkable. To the one who speaks thus, he replies with 'what then by that' and so forth —

body.text: tena kiṃ straṣṭumiṣṭaṃ ca
body.translated_text: What then does he wish to create?

body.text: bhavatu nāma tasya kāryaṃ cintyam, tathāpi tena kiṃ straṣṭumiṣṭuṃ ca / tena īśvareṇa acintyamāhātmyena kiṃ kāryaṃ straṣṭuṃ nirmātumiṣṭamabhipretaṃ ca, iti parasyottaramāśaṅkayannāha-
body.translated_text: Let his effect indeed be thinkable; even so, 'what then does he wish to create?' By that — by <s>Īśvara</s> of inconceivable greatness — what effect does he wish 'to create,' to fashion? 'And' — anticipating the opponent's reply, he says —

body.text: ātmā cet
body.translated_text: If [you say] the self —

body.text:
atra pūrvapadasyākāreṇa cchandonurodhāt saṃdhirna kṛtaḥ /
ātmā tena straṣṭumiṣṭaṃ cenmatam, etat pratiṣedhayati-
body.translated_text: Here, for the first word, the <s>sandhi</s> is not made with the vowel '<s>ā</s>' due to metrical requirements. If the view is that <s>Īśvara</s> wishes to create the self — he refutes this —

body.text: nanvasau dhruvaḥ /
body.translated_text: Is it not the case that it is eternal?

body.text: nanu bhoḥ, asāvātmā dhruvo nityo 'bhimato bhavatām / tat kathamasau kriyate? anyathā nitya eva sa na syāt / sadakāraṇavannityamiti nityalakṣaṇābhāvaprasaṅgāt / anyatrāpi na tasya sṛṣṭivyāpāra upalakśyate ityāha kṣmādītyādi-
body.translated_text: Sir, that self is accepted by you as eternal, permanent. So how is it created? Otherwise, it would simply not be eternal. Because 'what is eternal exists without cause' — there would be the absurd consequence of the absence of the defining characteristic of eternality. Elsewhere too, his creative activity is not observed — he says with '<s>kṣmā</s> and such' and so forth —

body.text: kṣmādisvabhāva īśaśca jñānaṃ jñeyādanādi ca // Bca_9.122 //
body.translated_text: The nature of earth and such, <s>Īśa</s>, and cognition from the cognizable are beginningless. // <s>Bca</s> 9.122 //

body.text: karmaṇaḥ sukhaduḥkhe ca
body.translated_text: And pleasure and pain from <s>karma</s> —

body.text: ādiśabdena aptejovāyvākāśakāladiṅmanāṃsi gṛhyante / teṣāṃ svabhāvo dhruvaḥ / so 'pi na tena kriyate, pṛthivyādīnāṃ paramāṇūnāṃ nityatvābhyupagamāt / sthūlarūpe ca tadvayāpārasya niṣetsyamānatvāt / ākāśādīnāmapi nityatvāt / īśaśceti / īśvaro 'pi dhruvaḥ iti ātmānamasau na karoti / jñānaṃ jñeyādanādi ceti / jñānamapi jñeyādutpadyamānamanādi
body.translated_text: By the word '<s>ādi</s>' (and such), water, fire, wind, space, time, direction, and minds are included. Their nature is permanent. Even that is not created by him, since the atoms of earth and such are accepted as eternal. And because his activity regarding gross forms will be denied. And because space and such are also eternal. 'And <s>Īśa</s>' — <s>Īśvara</s> too is permanent; thus he does not create himself. 'Knowledge, being beginningless, from the knowable, and...' — knowledge too, arising from the knowable and being beginningless

body.text: ca, āsaṃsāraṃ jñeyāmālambya pravartanāt, tadapi na tena kriyate / tatkarmaṇaḥ sukhaduḥkhe ca, karmaṇaḥ śubhāśubhāt yathāsaṃbhavaṃ sukhaduḥkhe ca bhavataḥ iṣṭāniṣṭavipākaje, tatrāpi na tasya vyāpāraḥ / evaṃ sati-
body.translated_text: — since it operates throughout <s>saṃsāra</s> by taking the knowable as its object — that too is not created by him. 'And pleasure and suffering from <s>karma</s>' — from wholesome and unwholesome <s>karma</s>, pleasure and suffering respectively arise, born as the ripening of the desired and undesired — there too he has no operation. This being so —

body.text: vada kiṃ tena nirmitam /
body.translated_text: Say, what has been created by him?

body.text: brūhi kimidānīṃ teneśvareṇa nirmitaṃ racitam, iti na kvacit tasya sāmarthyamupalabhyate / tat kathamasya jagatkartṛtvamucyate? adhunā sarvatra sādhāraṇaṃ dūṣaṇamāha hetorityādi-
body.translated_text: Tell us: what, then, has <s>Īśvara</s> created, fashioned? — thus his power is not found in any domain. Then how can his creatorship of the world be asserted? Now he states a refutation common to all [views], saying 'if the cause' and so forth:

body.text: hetorādirna cedasti phalasyādiḥ kuto bhavet // Bca_9.123 //
body.translated_text: If the cause has no beginning, how could the result have a beginning? // Bca_9.123 //

body.text: tathāhi asau nityo vā jagato hetuḥ syādanityo vā? nitya eva tadvādibhirasau parikalpitaḥ / tatra nityatve sati hetoḥ kāraṇasya ādirnāsti, yadi, tadā phalasyādiḥ kuto bhavet? naiva syādityarthaḥ / nityamupasthite samarthasvabhāve hetau kāryamapi tajjanyamajastrameva jāyeta / iti tatsāmarthyapratibaddhaṃ kāryaṃ sadā prāpnoti / tat-
body.translated_text: For [we ask:] is he an eternal or non-eternal cause of the world? He has been conceived as eternal by his proponents. In that case, if the cause — the reason — has no beginning — if it does, then how could the result have a beginning? It would not — this is the meaning. When the cause is eternally present with a nature capable [of producing], the effect too, being produced by it, would arise incessantly. Thus the effect, being bound to its power, would always obtain. Therefore —

body.text: kasmātsadā na kurute
body.translated_text: Why does he not always create?

body.text: kasmāt kāraṇāt sadā sarvakālaṃ na kurute? na sarvaṃ kāryaṃ janayatīti kathaṃ kasyacit kāryasya kadācit kriyāvirāmaḥ //
body.translated_text: For what reason does he not always, at all times, create? Why does he not produce all effects? — so how could there be cessation of activity regarding any effect at any time?

body.text: athavā / anyathāvatāryate- yadi ca neśvaro jagataḥ kartā syāt, kathamidaṃ pralayānantaramāditaḥ sargabhāg bhavet, ityatrāha hetorityādi- anavarāgro hi jātisaṃsāraḥ / tataśca hetoḥ kleśakarmādilakṣaṇasya ādiḥ pūrvakoṭiḥ na cedasti, phalasya sattvabhājanalokavivartādilakṣaṇasya ādiḥ prathamārambhaḥ kuto bhavet? naiva vidyate ityarthaḥ / anādau saṃsāre hi sattvānāṃ karmādhipatyena sthitisaṃvartavivartānāṃ pravartanāt / etacca uktameva "karmaṇaḥ sukhaduḥkhe ca" [9.123] ityanena //
body.translated_text: Or alternatively, it is introduced differently: if <s>Īśvara</s> were not the creator of the world, how would this [world] come into being as a creation anew after dissolution? To this he says 'if the cause' and so forth. For the succession of births in <s>saṃsāra</s> is without beginning or end. And so, if the cause — characterized as afflictions, <s>karma</s>, and such — has no beginning, no prior limit, then how could the result — characterized as the evolution of the sentient and material worlds — have a beginning, a first inception? It simply does not exist — this is the meaning. For in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, through the dominion of beings' <s>karma</s>, the processes of maintenance, dissolution, and evolution proceed. And this has already been stated by the [verse] 'and pleasure and suffering from <s>karma</s>' [9.123].

body.text: athavā / atrāpi īśvaramevābhisaṃdhāyoktaṃ hetoriti / hetorīśvarasya ādirna cedasti, pralayakāle 'pi tasyānupahatatayā māhātmyasyābhyupagamāt phalasya tatkṛtasya sargādilakṣaṇasya ādiḥ kuto bhavet? nityatayā tatkāraṇasya sadā samarthatvāt sargādikamapi nityameva syāt / ato nityasamarthe tasmin sargāderādireva na syāt / tataḥ kathaṃ sargasyādāvapi tadvayāpāro bhavet? api ca / yadi asau kartā syāt, tadā nityatvāt-
body.translated_text: Or alternatively, even here, with reference to <s>Īśvara</s> himself, it is said 'if the cause' — if the cause, <s>Īśvara</s>, has no beginning — since even at the time of dissolution, his greatness is accepted as unimpaired — then how could the result — characterized as creation and such, produced by him — have a beginning? Since its cause, being eternal, is always capable, creation and such too would be eternal. Therefore, when he is eternally capable, there would be no beginning of creation at all. Then how could his activity exist even at the beginning of creation? Moreover, if he were the creator, then since he is eternal —

body.text: kasmātsadā na kurute
body.translated_text: Why does he not always create

body.text: sargādikamiti śeṣaḥ / tathāhi yadi kadācit sargaṃ karoti, tadā tatkāraṇasvabhāvatayā sadā tameva kuryāt / evaṃ sthitisaṃhārayorapi vaktavyam / yugapadvā tasya sargādikriyā syāt / ata eva ca hetoruparamābhāvāt / na phalasyāpi virāmaḥ / anyat pūrvavat //
body.translated_text: creation and such — this is to be supplied. For if he creates at some time, then being of the nature of that cause, he would always create that very thing. Likewise for maintenance and destruction, the same should be said. Or his activity of creation and such would be simultaneous. And for this very reason — because the cause does not cease — the result too does not cease. The rest is as before.

body.text: athāpi syāt- yadi nāma asau sadā samarthasvabhāvaḥ, tathāpi kadācit sahakārivaikalyānna karotītyāha-
body.translated_text: But one might say: even if he is always of a capable nature, still, sometimes, due to the deficiency of auxiliary conditions, he does not create — he says:

body.text: na hi so 'nyamapekṣate /
body.translated_text: For he does not depend on another.

body.text: iti / samarthasvabhāvo heturīśvaraḥ / hiryasmāt / nānyaṃ sahakāriṇamapekṣate / nityasya samarthasvabhāvasya sataḥ tadapekṣāyogāt / na hi nityatayā anādheyātiśayasya kācidapekṣā nāma / viśeṣotpattau vā tadavyatiriktasvabhāvasya tasyāpyutpattiprasaṅgāt / vyatireke vā viśeṣādeva kāryotpattiḥ, tasya akārakatvaṃ syāt / taduktam-
body.translated_text: Thus: the cause, <s>Īśvara</s>, is of a capable nature. 'For' — because. He does not depend on another, on an auxiliary condition. For an eternal being of capable nature, such dependence is not tenable. For one who is eternal and cannot receive any enhancement, there is simply no such dependence. Or, in the arising of a specific [effect], since his nature is not distinct [from the auxiliary], its arising too would follow. Or in the case of [its being] distinct, the effect would arise from the specific [auxiliary] alone, and he would be a non-agent. As it is said:

children.translated_text: 'If one needs something else to produce something,
then a thing that can produce nothing — why would anything need it?'

body.text: iti / [catuḥ -3.12]
body.translated_text: [<s>Catuḥśataka</s> 3.12]

body.text: bhavantu vā tasya sahakāriṇaḥ / tathāpi te nityā vā syuranityā vā? ye tāvannityāḥ paramāṇvādayaḥ, teṣāṃ na sadbhāvavaikalyaṃ saṃbhavati, nāpi tadāyattasaṃnidhīnāṃ saṃnidhānavaikalyam / anityānāmapi tadāyattodayasaṃnidhīnāṃ kuto vaikalyaṃ nāma, yena sahakārivaikalyānna karotītyucyate? tato nāyamatra parihāraḥ / ata evāha tenākṛta ityādi-
body.translated_text: Or let there be auxiliary conditions for him. Even so, are they eternal or non-eternal? Those that are eternal — atoms and such — their non-existence is impossible, nor is the non-presence of things whose proximity depends on them [impossible]. And of non-eternal [auxiliaries] too, whose arising and proximity depend on him — how could there be deficiency, such that it could be said 'due to deficiency of auxiliaries, he does not create'? Therefore, this is no resolution. For this very reason he says 'nothing not created by him' and so forth:

body.text: tenākṛto 'nyo nāstyeva tenāsau kimapekṣatām // Bca_9.124 //
body.translated_text: There is simply nothing else not created by him — so what would he depend on? // Bca_9.124 //

body.text: tena īśvareṇa akṛtaḥ, yaḥ utpattimāṃstena akṛtaḥ, sa nāstyeva, na vidyate anyo 'paro jagati / tena kāraṇena tadāyattavṛttīnāṃ sahakāriṇāṃ sadāsaṃnihitatvādasau nityaḥ kartā kimapekṣatām? kimapekṣamāṇaḥ kadācit kāryaṃ na kuryāt? itthaṃ na kācidapi tasyāpekśāstīti sadā kāryaṃ kurvīta //
body.translated_text: 'Not created by him' — by <s>Īśvara</s> — that which is subject to arising and not created by him — simply does not exist, is not found — 'another' thing in the world. For this reason — since the auxiliary conditions, whose operation depends on him, are always present — what would this eternal creator depend on? Depending on what would he sometimes not produce the effect? Thus, since there is no dependence whatsoever for him, he would always create.

body.text: athāpi syāt- samavāyikāraṇam, asamavāyikāraṇam, nimittakāraṇaṃ ceti kāraṇatritayāt kāryamutpadyate / tadasya nimittakāraṇatvāt sāmagrīmapekṣya kāryaṃ kurvato noktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ iti parāśayamāśaṅkayāha apekṣata ityādi-
body.translated_text: But one might say: since a material cause, an inherent cause, and an efficient cause — from these three causes the effect arises — since he is the efficient cause, there is no absurd consequence of the stated faults when he creates in dependence on the assemblage. Anticipating the opponent's intention, he says 'if he depends on the assemblage' and so forth:

body.text: apekṣate cetsāmagrīṃ
body.translated_text: If he depends on the assemblage —

body.text: yadi nāma asau sadā sarvakāryāṇi kartuṃ samarthaḥ, tathāpi apekṣate sāmagrīm / na hi sāmagrīmantareṇa satyapi samarthe kartari kāryamutpadyate / yathā kila paṭotpādanasamarthe 'pi kvaciddhetau turītantuvemādikamantareṇa na paṭa utpadyate, tathā prakṛte 'pi cedyadi, āha-
body.translated_text: Even if he is always capable of producing all effects, still, he depends on the assemblage. For without the assemblage, even though the capable agent exists, no effect arises. Just as even for a cause capable of producing cloth, without the shuttle, threads, loom, and such, no cloth is produced — if the same applies in the present case, he says —

body.text: heturna punarīśvaraḥ /
body.translated_text: <s>Īśvara</s> is no longer the cause.

body.text: yadi sāmagrīsadbhāve karoti, tadabhāve ca na karotītyabhyupagabhyate, tadā punarīśvaro heturna syāt / sāmagryā eva kāryotpatteḥ, tataścānutpatteḥ / tasyā bhāvābhāvayoḥ kāryasya bhāvābhāvadarśanāt, na tu punarīśvarabhāvābhāvayoriti / na sāmagrīkāle 'pi sa pararūpeṇa kartā, svarūpaṃ cāsya prāgapi samarthaṃ tadeveti kathaṃ kadācit kriyāvirāmaḥ? yadapyuktam- kuvindādivat kadācit karotīti, tadapi na yuktam / yataḥ kuvindādayaḥ prāgasamarthā eva / punaḥ paścāt turyādisāmagrīpratilambhādapūrvasāmarthyādhigamāt paṭādikāryaṃ kurvanti / anyathāpi teṣāmapi pūrvaṃ tatsāmarthyasadbhāve tatkriyāprasaṅgo na nivartate iti sādhyavikalo
body.translated_text: If it is accepted that he creates when the assemblage exists and does not create when it does not, then <s>Īśvara</s> would no longer be the cause. Since the effect arises from the assemblage alone, and does not arise from that [<s>Īśvara</s> alone]. Because the existence and non-existence of the effect is observed [to follow] the existence and non-existence of the assemblage, but not the existence and non-existence of <s>Īśvara</s>. Nor even at the time of the assemblage is he a creator in a form other than his own, and his own form was capable even before — so how could there be cessation of activity at any time? And what was said — 'like a weaver, he creates at some time' — that too is not justified. Because weavers and such are previously incapable themselves. Subsequently, through obtaining the assemblage of shuttle and such, having gained new capability, they produce cloth and such effects. Otherwise, if their capability existed even before, the absurd consequence of their activity [at that prior time] would not be averted — thus the illustration is defective.

body.text: dṛṣṭāntaḥ / kiṃ ca / sāmagrījanane 'pi sa eva kāraṇam, sa ca sarvadā saṃnihitasvabhāva iti kathaṃ kadācit sāmagrīvaikalyamapyasya? ata evopadarśayannāha-
body.translated_text: Moreover, even in producing the assemblage, he alone is the cause, and he is always present by nature — so how could there ever be deficiency of the assemblage for him? For this very reason, showing [this], he says:

body.text: nākartumīśaḥ sāmagryāṃ
body.translated_text: He is not able not to create regarding the assemblage —

body.text: iti / nākartumīśaḥ, na akriyāyāṃ samarthaḥ / sāmagryāṃ sāmagrīviṣaye / sarvakāryakriyāyāṃ samarthatvāt sāmagrījanmanyapi nodāsituṃ śaknoti / janayatu tarhi sāmagrīmiti cedāha-
body.translated_text: Thus: 'not able not to create' — not capable of inaction — 'regarding the assemblage' — with respect to the assemblage. Being capable of creating all effects, he cannot be idle even regarding the production of the assemblage. 'Then let him produce the assemblage' — if so, he says:

body.text: na kartuṃ tadabhāvataḥ
body.translated_text: Nor is he able to create it in its absence.

body.text: na kartumapi sāmagryāmīśaḥ / kutaḥ? tadabhāvataḥ, tasyāḥ sāmagryā abhāvataḥ avidyamānatvāt / na ca avidyamānasvabhāve vandhyāsuta iva kiṃcit kartuṃ śakyate nīrūpatvāt / yadvakṣyati-
body.translated_text: Nor is he able to create [it] even regarding the assemblage. Why? 'In its absence' — because of the non-existence of that assemblage, because it is not present. And one cannot do anything regarding what is of non-existent nature — like the son of a barren woman — since it has no form. As will be stated:

children.translated_text: 'There is no transformation of non-existence, even in hundreds of crores of <s>kalpas</s>.'

body.text: bhavatu nāma sāmagrīsadbhāve satyeva kartā / tathāpi kiṃ sāmagrībalākṛṣṭaḥ svayamanicchanneva karoti, āhosvidicchan iti vikalpau / tatra ādyaṃ vikalpamāśaṅkayannāha karotītyādi-
body.translated_text: Granted, when the assemblage exists, he is the creator. Even so, does he create involuntarily, compelled by the power of the assemblage, or does he create voluntarily? — these are the two alternatives. Regarding the first alternative, he says 'if he creates' and so forth:

body.text: karotyanicchannīśaścetparāyattaḥ prasajyate /
body.translated_text: If <s>Īśvara</s> creates unwillingly, the absurd consequence follows that he is subject to another.

body.text: karoti kāryamabhinirvartayati anicchan anabhilaṣan / īśa īśvaraḥ / cenmatam, parāyattaḥ prasajyate, parāyattaḥ paratantraḥ prasajyate āsajyate / sāmagrīvaśena anicchato 'pi kurvataḥ tadvaśavartitvaprasaṅgāt / na ca pāratantryamanubhavataḥ īśvaratvaṃ yuktam, atiprasaṅgāt / dvitīyaṃ vikalpamadhikṛtyāha-
body.translated_text: 'Creates' — brings about the effect — 'unwillingly' — without desiring. '<s>Īśa</s>' — <s>Īśvara</s>. 'If' — if this is the view, then — 'the absurd consequence follows that he is subject to another' — the absurd consequence attaches that he is dependent, subject to another's power. Because, when he creates even without wishing, being subject to the power of the assemblage, dependence on it follows. And for one who experiences dependence, lordship is not justified, since there would be over-extension. Regarding the second alternative, he says:

body.text: icchannapīcchāyattaḥ syāt
body.translated_text: Even if he wills, he would be dependent on desire —

body.text: atha icchan karotīti pakṣaḥ svīkriyate, tadāpi icchāyattaḥ syāt / icchāsadbhāve kāryavyāpārāt, tadabhāve ca avyāpārāt / tadapekṣāsadbhāvāt-
body.translated_text: If the position 'he creates willingly' is accepted, then too he would be 'dependent on desire.' Since his engagement in productive activity occurs when desire exists, and non-engagement when it does not — since the existence of dependence on it [is established] —

body.text: kurvataḥ kuta īśatā // Bca_9.126 //
body.translated_text: Where then is the lordship of one who creates [thus]? // Bca_9.126 //

body.text: evaṃ kurvataḥ kāryamabhinirvartayataḥ sataḥ tasya kuta īśatā, kutaḥ eśvaryam? etena yaduktaṃ kenacit- buddhimattvādīśvarasya naiṣa doṣaḥ / buddhiśūnyo hi svasattāmātrajanyamakrameṇaiva kāryaṃ kuryāt, buddhimāṃstu kartumīśāno 'pyanicchanna karoti, iti kastasyopālambha iti, tadapi nirastam / tathā hi tā api icchāḥ svasattāmātranibandhanāḥ kiṃ na karotīti sa eva tasyopālambhaḥ / api ca / yadi tā na sahakāriṇyaḥ, kiṃ tāsāṃ viyoge 'pi na karoti atha asahakārivaikalye 'pi kāryākaraṇe sarvadā tadāyattaḥ? sahakāriṇyaścet, tathā tadbhāve 'pi sarvakāryaṃ kiṃ na karoti? sahakāriṇāṃ sākalye śaktatvāt / kevalasya aśaktasya na kārakatvamiti cet, tat kimayaṃ pararūpeṇa kārakaḥ? tathā cedakāraka eva / na hi svarūpeṇa
body.translated_text: For one who thus creates — who is in the process of bringing about effects — where then is his lordship, where is his sovereignty? By this, what was said by someone — 'since <s>Īśvara</s> possesses intelligence, this fault does not apply; for an unintelligent [cause] would produce effects generated merely from its own existence, without order; but an intelligent one, though capable of creating, does not create when unwilling — so what reproach can be made against him?' — that too is refuted. For those very desires, being based on his mere existence alone — why does he not [always desire to] create? — this very reproach applies to him. Moreover, if those [desires] are not auxiliaries, why does he not create even in their absence? Or, even in the absence of auxiliaries, if he always depends on them for non-production of effects? And if they are auxiliaries, why then, even in their presence, does he not create all effects — since when auxiliaries are complete, he is capable? If it is said that he alone, being incapable, is not an agent — then is this one an agent through another's form? If so, he is simply not an agent at all. For one who is not an agent by his own nature

body.text: akārakaḥ kārako nāma / svarūpamapi asya nijaśaktiśabdavācyaṃ kāryopayogīti cet, alamidānīmāgantukaśaktiṣvapekṣayā / samartho 'pyeṣa prakṛtyā sahakāriṇāmasaṃnidhau nava kāraka iti cet, mātāpi satī prakṛtyā bandhyā ityetadapi tarhi devānāṃ priyeṇa vaktavyamityāstāṃ tāvat / anityastu tadvādināṃ nābhimataḥ / tathā ca sati anyasādhāraṇasvabhāvasya kathamīśatvamiti neśvarakāryaṃ jagadvaicitryamiti siddham //
body.translated_text: is not called an agent. If it is said that his own form too, denoted by the word 'own capacity,' is useful for the effect — then enough with the dependence on adventitious capacities! [If it is said that] even though he is capable by nature, in the non-proximity of auxiliaries he is not an agent — then even a woman who exists [as a mother] is by nature barren! — this too should be said with the approval of the gods. But enough of this. A non-eternal [<s>Īśvara</s>], however, is not accepted by his proponents. And in that case [of non-eternality], since his nature would be shared with others, how could there be lordship? — thus it is established that the diversity of the world is not the product of <s>Īśvara</s>.

body.text: yadi na buddhimatkartṛkaṃ jagat, tarhi nityaparamāṇupuñjamayaṃ dvayaṇukādikrameṇotthaṃ kṣititaruparvatādikaṃ bhavatvityāha ye 'pītyādi-
body.translated_text: If the world is not created by an intelligent creator, then let it be composed of eternal atoms, arising through the sequence of dyads and such, [constituting] earth, trees, mountains, and such — he says 'those who' and so forth:

body.text: ye 'pi nityānaṇūnāhuste 'pi pūrvaṃ nivāritāḥ /
body.translated_text: Those too who speak of eternal atoms — they too have been refuted earlier.

body.text: ye 'pi mīmāṃsakādivādino nityānaṇūn paramāṇunāhuḥ jagadvaicitryakāraṇatvena bruvate, te 'pi vādinaḥ pūrvam "aṃśā apyaṇubhedena" [9.87]ityādinā paramāṇuvicārasamaye tatpratiṣedhānnivāritā nirākṛtāḥ ato nityaparamāṇumayamapi nedaṃ jagat //
body.translated_text: Those too — proponents such as <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> and others — who speak of eternal atoms, who assert them as the cause of the world's diversity — those proponents too have been refuted earlier, at the time of examining atoms, by the [verse] 'the parts too, by the division of the atom' [9.87] and such — refuted through the negation of those [atoms]. Therefore, this world is not composed of eternal atoms either.

body.text: evamīśvarakāraṇatāṃ ślokārdhena antarāle eva nityaparamāṇusvabhāvatāṃ ca jagato nirasya tasyaiva turyaprakārasya samarthanāya pradhānapariṇāmarūpatāṃ nirākartuṃ sāṃkhyamatamudbhāvayannāha sāṃkhyā ityādi-
body.translated_text: Having thus rejected in half a verse the nature of the world as caused by <s>Īśvara</s>, and in the interim [rejected] the nature of eternal atoms as well, in order to establish that very fourth alternative, and to reject [the claim of] the transformation of <s>Pradhāna</s> [as the world's form], he introduces the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine, saying '<s>Sāṃkhyas</s>' and so forth:

body.text: sāṃkhyāḥ pradhānamicchanti nityaṃ lokasya kāraṇam // Bca_9.127 //
body.translated_text: The <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> hold <s>Pradhāna</s> (primal matter) to be the eternal cause of the world. // <s>Bca</s> 9.127 //

body.text: sāṃkhyāḥ kāpilāḥ pradhānaṃ prakṛtirityaparanāmadheyam icchanti manyante nityaṃ lokasya kāraṇam / tacca nityamavinaśvarasvabhāvaṃ lokasya sarvasya carācarasya jagataḥ kāraṇaṃ pariṇāmarūpeṇa hetumicchanti //
body.translated_text: The <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> — the followers of <s>Kapila</s> — hold, that is, maintain, that <s>Pradhāna</s>, whose other name is <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), is the eternal cause of the world. And that [<s>Pradhāna</s>] is eternal, of imperishable nature, and they hold it to be the cause of the entire world, of all that is moving and non-moving, in the form of transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>).

body.text: kimidaṃ pradhānaṃ nāmeti cedāha sattvamityādi-
body.translated_text: If one asks 'What is this so-called <s>Pradhāna</s>?' — he says beginning with '<s>Sattva</s>' —

children.translated_text: <s>Sattva</s>, <s>Rajas</s>, and <s>Tamas</s> — the <s>guṇas</s> in equipoise —
are called <s>Pradhāna</s>; in disequilibrium, the world is said [to arise]. // <s>Bca</s> 9.128 //

body.text: sattvaṃ rajastamaśceti ete trayo guṇā aviṣamaṃ sthitāḥ sāmyāvasthāṃ prāptāḥ pradhānamiti kathyante, pradhānamityucyante / eṣāṃ tāvat prakṛtyavasthā / viṣamairjagaducyate, viṣamāvasthāṃ prāptaiḥ punarebhireva guṇairjagaducyate, viśvavaicitryapariṇāmaḥ kathyate / tathāhi teṣāṃ prakriyāyadā puruṣasya viṣayopabhogākāramautsukyamupajāyate, tadā prakṛtiḥ parijñātapuruṣautsukyā puruṣeṇa yujyate / tadā punaḥ śabdādisargarūpeṇa pariṇatimupajanayati / tadā ayaṃ kramaḥ-
body.translated_text: <s>Sattva</s>, <s>Rajas</s>, and <s>Tamas</s> — these three <s>guṇas</s>, when situated in equipoise, having reached the state of equilibrium, are called <s>Pradhāna</s>, are designated as <s>Pradhāna</s>. This, then, is their state as <s>Prakṛti</s>. 'In disequilibrium, the world is said [to arise]' — when these very <s>guṇas</s> have reached a state of disequilibrium, the world is said [to arise], that is, the transformation into the diversity of the universe is described. For the process of their evolution is as follows: when an eagerness in the form of desire for sense-experience arises in the <s>Puruṣa</s> (spirit), then <s>Prakṛti</s>, having discerned the eagerness of <s>Puruṣa</s>, is joined with <s>Puruṣa</s>. Then she generates transformation in the form of the creation of sound and other [sense objects]. Then the sequence is as follows —

children.translated_text: From <s>Prakṛti</s> [arises] <s>Mahat</s> (the Great), from that <s>Ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-sense), and from that the group of sixteen;
from five of those sixteen, the five gross elements. //

body.text: sāṃkhyakārikā-22
body.translated_text: <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 22

body.text: asyāyamarthaḥ- prakṛtermahān, pradhānānmahān / mahāniti buddherākhyā / tato mahato 'haṃkāraḥ, ahamiti pratyayaḥ / tasmādahaṃkārādgaṇaśca ṣoḍaśakaḥ, ṣoḍaśaka iti ekādaśendriyāṇi pañca ca tanmātrāṇi / tatra pañca karmendriyāṇi vākpāṇipādapāyūpasthalakṣaṇāni / pañca buddhīndriyāṇi
body.translated_text: The meaning of this is: from <s>Prakṛti</s> [arises] <s>Mahat</s>, from <s>Pradhāna</s> [arises] <s>Mahat</s>. '<s>Mahat</s>' is a designation for <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect). From that <s>Mahat</s>, <s>Ahaṃkāra</s> — the notion of 'I.' From that <s>Ahaṃkāra</s>, the group of sixteen: 'sixteen' means the eleven <s>indriyas</s> (faculties) and the five <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements). Among these, the five organs of action (<s>karmendriyas</s>) are characterized as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. The five organs of cognition (<s>buddhīndriyas</s>) are

body.text: śrotraṃ tvakū cakṣū rasanaṃ ghrāṇaṃ ceti / ubhayātmakaṃ tu manaḥ ityekādaśa bhavanti / pañca tanmātrāṇi punaḥ śabdasparśarūparasagandhāḥ / pañcabhyaḥ pañca bhūtāni / pañcabhyaḥ śabdādibhyaḥ pañca bhūtāni bhavanti pañca bhūtāni ca ākāśavāyutejojalapṛthivyākhyāni / ādyaprakṛtistu kāraṇameva na kāryam / mahadahaṃkārau śabdādayaśca pañca kāryaṃ kāraṇaṃ ca / ekādaśendriyāṇi ākāśādayaśca pañca kāryameva na kāraṇam / puruṣaḥ punarubhayasvabhāvavarjita iti / yadāha-
body.translated_text: ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose. And <s>Manas</s> (mind), being of both natures, [makes] eleven. The five <s>tanmātras</s> are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. 'From the five, the five gross elements' — from the five [<s>tanmātras</s>] beginning with sound, the five gross elements come to be, and the five gross elements are designated as <s>Ākāśa</s> (space), <s>Vāyu</s> (air), <s>Tejas</s> (fire), <s>Jala</s> (water), and <s>Pṛthivī</s> (earth). The original <s>Prakṛti</s> is cause only, not effect. <s>Mahat</s>, <s>Ahaṃkāra</s>, and the five beginning with sound are both effect and cause. The eleven <s>indriyas</s> and the five beginning with <s>Ākāśa</s> are effect only, not cause. <s>Puruṣa</s>, moreover, is devoid of both natures. As is stated —

children.translated_text: The root <s>Prakṛti</s> is not a modification; the seven beginning with <s>Mahat</s> are both <s>prakṛtis</s> and modifications;

children.text: ṣoḍaśakastu vikāro na prakṛtirna vikṛtiḥ puruṣaḥ //
children.translated_text: the group of sixteen is modification only; <s>Puruṣa</s> is neither <s>prakṛti</s> nor modification. //

body.text: iti / [sāṃkhyakārikā-3]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 3]

body.text: tacca pradhānamaśeṣakāryaśaktimayameva triguṇātmakameva kāryamabhinirvartayati / kathamanyathā tatrāvidyamānaṃ kāryaṃ vaiśvarūpyamutpadyate? tathā coktam-
body.translated_text: And that <s>Pradhāna</s>, being replete with the capacity for all effects, being of the nature of the three <s>guṇas</s>, produces effects. For how otherwise would the effect — the diversity of the universe — which is not present in it, arise? And thus it has been stated —

children.translated_text: From <s>Pradhāna</s> alone, which is endowed with all powers,
the differentiations of effects proceed, being in truth of that very nature. //
But if the effect were non-existent in the essence of the cause by way of its power,
then it could not be produced at all — like a sky-lotus, due to its formlessness. //

body.text: iti / [tattvasaṃgraha-7-8]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 7-8]

body.text: evaṃ kila pradhānāt kāryarūpeṇa jagadvivartaḥ pravartate iti kāpilāḥ / tadevaṃ tat sarvamākāśe viracitacitramiva pratibhāsate iti manyamānaḥ siddhāntavādī dūṣayitumāha ekasyeti-
body.translated_text: Thus, according to the <s>Kāpilas</s>, from <s>Pradhāna</s> the evolution of the world proceeds in the form of effects. Now, the proponent of the [Buddhist] doctrine (<s>siddhāntavādī</s>), considering that all this appears like a painting drawn in space, begins to refute [them] with 'of one' —

body.text: ekasya trisvabhāvatvamayuktaṃ tena nāsti tat /
body.translated_text: The three-natured-ness of one is illogical; therefore, that does not exist.

body.text: ekasya sataḥ pradhānasya trisvabhāvatvaṃ sattvarajastamobhedena tryātmakatvamayuktamasaṃgatam / tena kāraṇena nāsti tat, na vidyate tat triguṇātmakaṃ pradhānam / ekamanekasvabhāvamiti parasparāhatametat / ataḥ tasminnapahastite sarvaṃ tatkāryamapākṛtaṃ bhavet / mā bhūnnāma tadekasvabhāvaṃ triguṇātmakam, guṇāstāvat svarūpataḥ santītyāha evamityādi-
body.translated_text: The three-natured-ness of the one existent <s>Pradhāna</s> — its threefold nature through the division of <s>Sattva</s>, <s>Rajas</s>, and <s>Tamas</s> — is illogical, inconsistent. For that reason, 'that does not exist' — that <s>Pradhāna</s> of three-<s>guṇa</s> nature does not exist. That something is one yet of multiple natures — this is mutually contradictory. Therefore, when that is set aside, all its effects would also be eliminated. 'Let it not be of one nature, [but] of three-<s>guṇa</s> nature; still, the <s>guṇas</s> at least exist in their own form' — to this he says beginning with 'likewise' —

body.text: evaṃ guṇā na vidyante pratyekaṃ te 'pi hi tridhā // Bca_9.129 //
body.translated_text: Likewise, the <s>guṇas</s> do not exist, for they too are each threefold. // <s>Bca</s> 9.129 //

body.text: evameva pradhānavat guṇāḥ sattvarajastamorūpā na vidyante / te 'pi hi tridhā / hiryasmāt / te 'pi guṇāḥ pratyekamekaikaśaḥ tridhā triprakārāḥ / tathā hi sarvaṃ triguṇātmakaṃ bruvatāṃ pratyekaṃ guṇā api svarūpeṇa triguṇātmakāḥ prāpnuvanti / tathā tadguṇā api triguṇātmakatayā naikasvabhāvā vidyante //
body.translated_text: In just the same way as <s>Pradhāna</s>, the <s>guṇas</s> — of the form of <s>Sattva</s>, <s>Rajas</s>, and <s>Tamas</s> — do not exist. 'For they too are threefold' — '<s>hi</s>' means 'because.' Those <s>guṇas</s> too are each individually threefold, of three kinds. For indeed, for those who assert that everything is of three-<s>guṇa</s> nature, each individual <s>guṇa</s> too, by its own nature, must be of three-<s>guṇa</s> nature. Likewise, those <s>guṇas</s> of <s>guṇas</s> too, being of three-<s>guṇa</s> nature, do not exist as being of one nature.

body.text: yadā caivaṃ vicārayato guṇā na santi, tadā tadvivartarūpāḥ śabdādayo 'pi na yujyante ityāha guṇābhāve ityādi-
body.translated_text: And when, upon such investigation, the <s>guṇas</s> do not exist, then sound and such, which are transformations of those [<s>guṇas</s>], are also not justified — he says beginning with 'in the absence of the <s>guṇas</s>' —

body.text: guṇābhāve ca śabdāderastitvamatidūrataḥ /
body.translated_text: And in the absence of the <s>guṇas</s>, the existence of sound and such is extremely remote.

body.text: guṇānāṃ sattvādīnām abhāve asattve ca / dūṣaṇāntarasamuccaye cakāraḥ / śabdāderādigrahaṇāt sparśādiparigrahaḥ / astitvaṃ sadbhāvaḥ atidūrataḥ, sarvathaiva na yujyate / kāraṇābhāve kāryasya sattvāyogāt / yadapyuktam-
body.translated_text: 'In the absence' — in the non-existence — 'of the <s>guṇas</s>,' of <s>Sattva</s> and such. The word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) is for the accumulation of further refutations. By the word 'beginning with' (<s>ādi</s>) after 'sound,' touch and such are included. 'Existence' — real being — 'is extremely remote,' is in no way justified, because in the absence of the cause, the existence of the effect is unjustified. As for what was also stated —

children.translated_text: 'This manifest [world] is observed to be accompanied by pleasure and such,
because of the single apprehension of the form of serenity, agitation, and dullness.' //

body.text: iti / [tattvasaṃgraha-14]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Tattvasaṃgraha</s> 14]

body.text: tadapi na yuktam / yaśca sattvādīnāṃ sukhādirūpatāmupapādayituṃ tatpariṇāmasya rūpādino vyaktasya sukhādyanvayo heturuktaḥ, so 'pi nāstītyāha acetana ityādi-
body.translated_text: That too is not correct. And the argument that was adduced as a reason — that the connection of the manifest, whose nature is form and such, with pleasure and such, and which is a transformation of <s>Sattva</s> and such, establishes the nature of <s>Sattva</s> and such as being pleasure and such — that too does not hold. He says beginning with 'in the non-sentient' —

body.text: acetane ca vastrādau sukhāderapyasaṃbhavaḥ // Bca_9.130 //
body.translated_text: And in the non-sentient — cloth and such — the occurrence of pleasure and such is also impossible. // <s>Bca</s> 9.130 //

body.text: acetane jaḍarūpe ca / pūrvavaccakāraḥ / vastrādau acitsvabhāve paṭādau sukhāderapi cidātmakasya tādātmyenāsaṃbhavaḥ abhāvaḥ / yataḥ sattvarajastamāṃsyeva sukhaduḥkhamohā ucyante / te ca guṇā na hi santi / tat kathaṃ tatra sukhādayo bhaveyuḥ?
body.translated_text: 'In the non-sentient' — in what is of inert nature. The word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) is as before [for accumulating refutations]. 'In cloth and such' — in what is of non-conscious nature, such as cloth — there is 'impossibility,' absence, 'of pleasure and such' as identical with what is of conscious nature. Because <s>Sattva</s>, <s>Rajas</s>, and <s>Tamas</s> themselves are said to be pleasure, pain, and delusion. And those <s>guṇas</s> do not exist. So how could pleasure and such exist in them?

body.text: athāpi syāt- na sukhādyātmakatayā parādayaḥ sukhādisvabhāvā ucyante, api tu sukhādestadutpatterityāśaṅkayannāha taddhetvityādi-
body.translated_text: Now there might be this [objection]: cloth and such are not said to be of the nature of pleasure and such in the sense of being identical with pleasure and such, but rather because pleasure and such are produced from them — anticipating this, he says beginning with 'having that as cause' —

body.text: taddheturūpā bhāvāścennanu bhāvā vicāritāḥ /
body.translated_text: If things have the nature of being the cause of that — well, things have [already] been examined!

body.text: tasya sukhāderheturūpāḥ kāraṇasvabhāvā bhāvā bāhyāḥ paṭādayaścenmatam, nanu bhāvā vicāritāḥ / nāmī paṭādayaḥ avayavirūpāḥ, nāpi paramāṇusvarūpā nāpi triguṇātmakāḥ / evaṃ bhāvā vicāritāḥ nirūpitāḥ yuktitaḥ, pratibhāsamānānāṃ māyāvanniḥsvabhāvatvācca / tat ke ime bhāvāḥ sukhādiheturūpā bhaviṣyanti? api ca / vyaktasya sukhādisvabhāvatve paṭādaya eva sukhādijanyāḥ syurityāha sukhādyevetyādi-
body.translated_text: If the view is that external things such as cloth are of the nature of being the cause of that — of pleasure and such — well, 'things have been examined!' Those things — in the form of wholes like cloth — are neither [established as] wholes, nor as atoms, nor as being of three-<s>guṇa</s> nature. Thus 'things have been examined,' investigated through reasoning, and because they are without intrinsic nature like an illusion, despite appearing. Then what are these things that would be of the nature of being the cause of pleasure and such? Moreover, if the manifest were of the nature of pleasure and such, then cloth and such themselves would be produced by pleasure and such — he says beginning with 'pleasure and such alone' —

body.text: sukhādyeva ca te hetuḥ
body.translated_text: Pleasure and such alone would be their cause,

body.text: paṭasyāpi sukhādyeva ca / te tava sāṃkhyasya / hetuḥ syāt / vyaktasya sukhādyātmakatvāt / tathāpi-
body.translated_text: and for cloth too, pleasure and such alone would be — for you, the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> — the cause, because the manifest is of the nature of pleasure and such. Even so —

body.text: na ca tasmātpaṭādayaḥ // Bca_9.131 //
body.translated_text: but cloth and such do not [arise] from that. // <s>Bca</s> 9.131 //

body.text: ādiśabdāccandanamālādayaḥ //
body.translated_text: By the word 'and such' (<s>ādi</s>), sandalwood, garlands, and such [are included].

body.text: viparyayaḥ punarihopalabhyate ityāha paṭādestvityādi-
body.translated_text: But the reverse is observed here — he says beginning with 'from cloth and such' —

body.text: paṭādestu sukhādi syāttadabhāvātsukhādyasat /
body.translated_text: Rather, from cloth and such, pleasure and such would arise; in their absence, pleasure and such are non-existent.

body.text: paṭādestu / ādiśabdānmālādeḥ / punaḥ sukhādi syāt / ādiśabdādduḥkhādi bhavet / tadabhāvāt, teṣāṃ paṭādīnāmabhāvāt / sukhādyasat, paṭādikāryatvāt sukhādyapi na syāditi tadanvayavyatirekānuvidhānāt sukhādestatkāryatvam / sattvādiguṇātmakatayā yadapi sukhādīnāṃ nityatvamiṣṭam, tadapi na samyagityāha sukhādikānāṃ cetyādi-
body.translated_text: 'From cloth and such' — by the word 'and such,' from garlands and such. 'Pleasure and such would arise' — by the word 'and such,' pain and such would arise. 'In their absence' — in the absence of those things such as cloth — 'pleasure and such are non-existent.' Because pleasure and such are effects of cloth and such, pleasure and such also would not exist [without them] — thus, since pleasure and such follow their presence and absence, pleasure and such are their effects. As for the eternality of pleasure and such that is maintained on the grounds of their being of the nature of the <s>guṇas</s> <s>Sattva</s> and such — that too is not correct. He says beginning with 'of pleasure and such' —

body.text: sukhādīnāṃ ca nityatvaṃ kadācinnopalabhyate // Bca_9.132 //
body.translated_text: And the eternality of pleasure and such is never observed. // <s>Bca</s> 9.132 //

body.text: sukhaduḥkhamohānāṃ ca / cakāro 'dhikadoṣavivakṣāyām / nityatvaṃ dhruvasvabhāvatvaṃ kadācinnopalabhyate, na dṛśyate / guṇānāmeva asattvāt teṣāṃ nityatvādyayogāt //
body.translated_text: Of pleasure, pain, and delusion. The word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) is for indicating additional faults. 'Eternality' — permanent nature — 'is never observed,' is not seen. Because of the very non-existence of the <s>guṇas</s>, and because their eternality and such are unjustified.

body.text: yadi ca sukhādīnāṃ nityatvaṃ syāt, tadā nityamupalabhyerannityāha satyāmityādi-
