body.translated_text: And if pleasure and such were eternal, then they would be perceived at all times — he says beginning with 'when there truly is' —

body.text: satyāmeva sukhavyaktau saṃvittiḥ kiṃ na gṛhyate /
body.translated_text: When the manifestation of pleasure truly exists, why is awareness not apprehended?

body.text: yadi satyamavasthitarūpāḥ sukhādayaḥ, tathā sarvadeti sadā tatsaṃvedanaṃ syāt, tatsvabhāvāparityāgāditi samudāyārthaḥ / satyāmeva sukhavyaktau, ekadā bhūtāyāṃ sukhavyaktau sukhasya nityatve sati / saṃvittiḥ kiṃ na gṛhyate, sukhasya saṃvedanaṃ sarvadā kiṃ na syāt? na ca sarvadā saṃvedanamasti / tasmāt kadācidanupalabhyamānaṃ tat tadā nāstīti niścitamiti kathaṃ nityatvam? syādetat- sarvadā vyaktirūpatāyāṃ syādeṣa doṣaḥ / yadā punastadeva śaktirūpatayā layagataṃ bhavati, tadā na doṣa ityāha tadevetyādi-
body.translated_text: If pleasure and such are real, of established nature, then they should always be experienced, because their own nature is never abandoned — this is the combined meaning. 'When the manifestation of pleasure truly exists' — when the manifestation of pleasure, having once occurred, [is maintained, then] given the eternality of pleasure — 'why is awareness not apprehended?' — why would there not always be the experience of pleasure? And indeed there is not always experience. Therefore, since it is sometimes not perceived, it is certain that at that time it does not exist — so how can there be eternality? There might be this [reply]: this fault would apply if it always had the form of manifestation; but when that very [pleasure], in the form of a latent power, has gone into dissolution, then there is no fault — he says beginning with 'that very' —

body.text: tadeva sūkṣmatāṃ yāti sthūlaṃ sūkṣmaṃ ca tatkatham // Bca_9.133 //
body.translated_text: That very thing becomes subtle — how can what is gross be subtle? // <s>Bca</s> 9.133 //

body.text: tadeva vyaktāvavasthitiṃ kṛtvā bhāvasamāśrayāt, paścādanupalambhakāle sūkṣmatāṃ yāti, divā nakṣatrāṇīva anupalabdhasvabhāvatāṃ samāśrayate, tadetadasaṃgatam / kutaḥ? yad yasmāt sthūlaṃ vyaktasvabhāvaṃ sat, sūkṣmaṃ tat katham? avyaktasvabhāvaṃ tat sukhādi katham? nitya tayā nānāsvabhāvatā ekasya na yukteti bhāvaḥ //
body.translated_text: That very thing, having remained in the state of manifestation due to dependence on objects, afterward, at the time of non-perception, 'becomes subtle' — assumes the nature of non-perception, like stars in the daytime. This is inconsistent. Why? Because 'that which is gross' — being of manifest nature — 'how can it be subtle?' — how can that pleasure and such be of unmanifest nature? Due to eternality, multiplicity of natures in one thing is not justified — this is the purport.

body.text: athāpi syāt- ekadā parasparaviruddhayorekasminnayogaḥ pūrvadharmanivṛttau tu dharmāntarotpatterna doṣa ityāha sthaulyamityādi-
body.translated_text: Now there might be this [reply]: granted that the simultaneous presence of mutually contradictory [properties] in one thing is unjustified, but upon the cessation of the prior property, the arising of another property is not a fault — he says beginning with 'grossness' —

body.text: sthaulyaṃ tyaktvā bhavetsūkṣmamanitye sthaulyasūkṣmate /
body.translated_text: Having abandoned grossness, it becomes subtle — [then] grossness and subtlety are impermanent.

body.text: sthaulyamāvirbhāvarūpatāṃ tyaktvā parityajya bhavet sūkṣmaṃ tirohitarūpaṃ syāt / evamabhyupagame sati anitye sthaulyasūkṣmate utpādavināśālīḍhatvādadhruve sthaulyasūkṣmate syātām / bhavatāṃ nāma anitye, kā kṣatirityāha sarvasyetyādi-
body.translated_text: Having 'abandoned grossness' — having given up the form of manifestation — 'it becomes subtle' — it would be of hidden form. Given such an acceptance, 'grossness and subtlety are impermanent' — since they are subject to arising and destruction, grossness and subtlety would be impermanent. 'Let them be impermanent — what harm is there?' — he says beginning with 'of everything' —

body.text: sarvasya vastunastadvatkiṃ nānityatvamiṣyate // Bca_9.134 //
body.translated_text: Why is the impermanence of every thing not similarly accepted? // <s>Bca</s> 9.134 //

body.text: sarvasya vastunaḥ pañcaviṃśatitattvalakṣaṇasya / tadvat sthaulyasūkṣmatāvat kiṃ nānityatvamiṣyate? kimiti niranvayavināśaḥ na svīkriyate? ayamabhiprāyaḥ- sthaulyasūkṣmatayorapi niranvayavināśāsadutpādamantareṇa nāvirbhāvatirobhāvau yuktau / anyathā kathaṃcit kenacidrūpeṇa avasthānāt pūrvavat punarupalabdheḥ prasaṅgaḥ / tadvat sukhādīnāmapi / tasmādavaśyaṃ tayorniranvayavināśāsadutpādau ca aṅgīkartavyau / yathā ca tayoretau bhavataḥ, tathā anyeṣāmapi viśeṣābhāvāt syātāmiti //
body.translated_text: 'Of every thing' — of the twenty-five <s>tattvas</s> (principles). 'Similarly' — like grossness and subtlety — 'why is impermanence not accepted?' Why is destruction without residue not acknowledged? The purport is this: without accepting destruction without residue and origination from non-existence for grossness and subtlety as well, manifestation and concealment are not justified. Otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence of re-perception at some time in some form, as before. Similarly for pleasure and such. Therefore, destruction without residue and origination from non-existence must necessarily be acknowledged for both of them. And just as these hold for them, so too they would hold for other things as well, since there is no distinction.

body.text: kiṃ ca / yadi sthaulyasūkṣmatayorvināśotpattī iṣyete, tadā sukhādīnāmanityatāprasaṅgaḥ syāt / tathā hi tat sthaulyaṃ sukhādbhinnamabhinnaṃ vā syāt / tatra yadi bhinnam, tadā tasmin nivṛtte 'pi pūrvavat sukhasaṃvedanaṃ syāt / na hi paṭe nivṛtte 'pi ghaṭasyānupalabdhiryuktā / tasya taditi saṃbandhakalpanāyāmanavasthānaprasaṅgāt / na ca satyapi saṃbandhe akāraṇasya nivṛttau anyasya nivṛttiryujyate, gonivṛttāviva tatsvāminaḥ / nāpi sukhasya tat kāraṇam, paṭādereva sukhotpatteḥ / nāpi tadapi kāraṇam, sukhādisamānakālatvāttasya //
body.translated_text: Moreover — if the arising and destruction of grossness and subtlety are accepted, then there would be the absurd consequence of the impermanence of pleasure and such. For that grossness would be either different from or non-different from pleasure. In the first case, if it is different, then even when that [grossness] has ceased, the experience of pleasure would continue as before. For it is not proper that a pot should not be perceived even when a cloth has ceased [to exist]. Because in the supposition of a relation between them as 'that [belongs to] that,' there would be an infinite regress. And even when a relation exists, the cessation of one that is not the cause does not justify the cessation of another — just as the cessation of a cow does not [justify the cessation] of its owner. Nor is that [grossness] the cause of pleasure, since pleasure arises from cloth and such alone. Nor is it [pleasure] also a cause [of grossness], since that [grossness] is simultaneous with pleasure and such.

body.text: atha abhinnamiti pakṣaḥ, atrocyate-
body.translated_text: Now, [consider] the alternative that [grossness] is non-different [from pleasure] — to this he replies —

body.text: na sthaulyaṃ cetsukhādanyat
body.translated_text: If grossness is not other than pleasure,

body.text: yadi sthaulyaṃ sukhādanyat bhinnaṃ na bhavati, tadā syāt sukhameva tat / tadā-
body.translated_text: If grossness is not other than, not different from pleasure, then it would simply be pleasure itself. Then —

body.text: sukhasyānityatā sphuṭam /
body.translated_text: the impermanence of pleasure is evident.

body.text: tatsvabhāvatayā sthaulyasya nivṛttau sukhasya vinivṛtteḥ sukhasya anityatā vinaśvaratā sphuṭaṃ niścitam //
body.translated_text: Since grossness is of that very nature [as pleasure], upon the cessation of grossness, pleasure ceases — thus the impermanence, the perishability of pleasure, is evident, certain.

body.text: syādetat- yadi sarvathā vināśaḥ syāt, tadā sukhasya punarutpattirna syāt / atyantāsato gaganotpalavadutpādāyogāt, iti paramatamupadarśayannāha nāsadityādi-
body.translated_text: There might be this [objection]: if there is destruction in every respect, then the re-arising of pleasure would not occur, because there is no possibility of the arising of what is absolutely non-existent, like a sky-lotus. Presenting the opponent's view, he says with '<s>nāsat</s>' and so forth —

body.text: nāsadutpadyate kiṃcidasattvāditi cenmatam /
body.translated_text: Nothing non-existent arises — if this is the view, because of non-existence.

body.text: yat sarvathā kāraṇātmani avidyamānaṃ tannotpadyate, yathā gaganāmbhoruham / tathā ca anyadapi yadi syāt, tadā notpadyate / ato nāsadutpadyate kiṃcit, nātyantāsatsvabhāvamutpadyate kiṃcit / kutaḥ? asattvāt / abhāvāt, iti cenmatam, evaṃ yadi saṃmatam, tadā naitadvaktavyamityāha vyaktasyetyādi-
body.translated_text: That which is in no way present in the causal substrate does not arise — like a sky-lotus. And if something else were likewise [non-existent], it too would not arise. Therefore, nothing non-existent arises; nothing of absolutely non-existent nature arises. Why? Because of non-existence, because of absence — if this is the view, if this is accepted, then this should not be stated — he says with '<s>vyaktasya</s>' and so forth —

body.text: vyaktasyāsata utpattirakāmasyāpi te sthitā // Bca_9.135 //
body.translated_text: The arising of a manifest [entity] from non-existence is established even for you who are unwilling. // <s>Bca</s> 9.135 //

body.text: vyaktasyāsataḥ prāk śaktayavasthāyāmavidyamānasya vyaktasya paścādutpattirutpādaḥ / anabhilāṣiṇo 'pi te tava sadutpattivādinaḥ sthitā āpannā / anyathā prāgapi tasya sadbhāve paścādvat pūrvamapi tadupalabdhiprasaṅgaḥ / yathā vyaktasyāsata utpattiḥ, tathā yadi anyasyāpi syāt, tadā na virudhyate kiṃcit //
body.translated_text: The arising, the origination of a manifest [entity] — of what was previously non-existent in the state of potentiality — of a manifest [entity] that subsequently [appears]. Even for you, the proponent of existent-origination (<s>sadutpattivādin</s>), who are unwilling, it is established, entailed. Otherwise, if it existed even before, then as in the later [state], there would be the absurd consequence of its being perceived even previously. Just as the arising of a manifest [entity] from non-existence [occurs], so too if it were the case for another — nothing would be contradicted.

body.text: api ca / satkāryavādinaḥ kāraṇāvasthāyāṃ kāryasadbhāvāt idamapi dūṣaṇamaparamāśaṅkayate ityāha annāda ityādi-
body.translated_text: Furthermore — the proponent of <s>satkāryavāda</s> (pre-existence of the effect in the cause) anticipates yet another objection due to the existence of the effect in the causal state, and he says with '<s>annāda</s>' and so forth —

body.text: annādo 'medhyabhakṣaḥ syāt
body.translated_text: An eater of food would be an eater of excrement,

body.text: annamattītyannādaḥ annabhakṣakaḥ amedhyabhakṣaḥ syāt aśucibhoktā bhavet / katham?
body.translated_text: An eater of food — one who eats food — would be an eater of excrement, would become a consumer of impurity. How?

body.text: phalaṃ hetau yadi sthitam /
body.translated_text: if the effect exists in the cause.

body.text: kāryaṃ yadi kāraṇe satsvabhāvam / tathāhi- kāryamamedhyamannasya, tacca annāvasthāyāmeva satkāryavādino vidyate, iti annabhakṣaṇāt tadbhakṣaṇamāśaṅkayate bhavataḥ / kiṃ ca idamapi satkāryavādinaḥ prasaṅgāntaramāsañjayannāha paṭārgheṇetyādi-
body.translated_text: If the effect has real existence in its cause. For excrement is the effect of food, and according to the <s>satkāryavādin</s>, it exists even in the state of food — thus, from the eating of food, the eating of that [excrement] is to be apprehended. Moreover, raising yet another absurd consequence for the <s>satkāryavādin</s>, he says with '<s>paṭārgheṇa</s>' and so forth —

body.text: paṭārgheṇaiva karpāsabījaṃ krītvā nivasyatām // Bca_9.136 //
body.translated_text: Let one buy cotton seeds at the price of cloth and wear them! // <s>Bca</s> 9.136 //

body.text: phalaṃ hetau yadi sthitamiti saṃbandhaḥ / karpāsabīje kāraṇe bhaviṣyataḥ paṭasya kāryasya sadbhāvāt paṭasyārgheṇa mūlyena karpāsabījaṃ krītvā gṛhītvā nivasyatāṃ paridhīyatām //
body.translated_text: 'If the effect exists in the cause' — this connects [with the previous]. Since the future cloth, which is the effect, exists in the cotton seed, which is the cause, let one buy the cotton seed at the price, the cost, of cloth, and having acquired it, wear it, put it on!

body.text: athāpi syāt- yadi nāma paramārthataḥ kāraṇe kāryamasti, tathāpi nāyaṃ saṃvṛtyavidyātimiropahatalocanaḥ sāṃvyavahāriko lokaḥ paśyatītyāśaṅkayannāha mohādityādi-
body.translated_text: Now there might be [this objection]: even if in ultimate reality the effect exists in the cause, nevertheless the worldly person — whose eyes are afflicted by the cataract of <s>saṃvṛti</s> (conventional ignorance) — does not see it. Anticipating this, he says with '<s>mohāt</s>' and so forth —

body.text: mohāccennekṣate lokaḥ
body.translated_text: If, due to delusion, the world does not see,

body.text: mohādajñānāt sadapi vastutattvaṃ nekṣate na paśyati lokaḥ / tato noktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ / cedyadi / nanu-
body.translated_text: due to delusion, due to ignorance, the world does not see, does not perceive the real nature of things even though they exist — and therefore there is no absurd consequence of the stated defects. If — but then —

body.text: tattvajñasyāpi sā sthitiḥ // Bca_9.137 //
body.translated_text: that same condition holds for the knower of reality as well. // <s>Bca</s> 9.137 //

body.text: yadi nāma na loko 'paśyaṃstathā vyavahāraṃ karoti, tattvajñasya tu yujyate / na caivam / yataḥ tattvajñasyāpi kāraṇe kāryamastīti paramārthavedino 'pi sāṃkhyasya sā sthitiḥ, saiva sarvasāṃvyavahārikajanasādhāraṇī vyavasthitiḥ / te 'pi dṛśyante annabhakṣaṇādiṣu pravartamānāḥ karpāsabījaṃ paṭārthinaḥ pariharantaḥ //
body.translated_text: Even if the world, not seeing [the effect in the cause], conducts its transactions accordingly, for the knower of reality it should be appropriate [to see it]. But this is not the case. Because for the knower of reality too — even for the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> who claims to know ultimate truth — 'that same condition' holds, that very same ordinary practice common to all conventional people. They too are seen engaging in the eating of food and such, and avoiding cotton seeds when they desire cloth!

body.text: nāpyayamatra parihāro yujyate ityāha lokasyetyādi-
body.translated_text: Nor is this defense justified in this case — he says with '<s>lokasya</s>' and so forth —

body.text: lokasyāpi ca tajjñānamasti kasmānna paśyati /
body.translated_text: The world too has that knowledge — why then does it not see?

body.text: lokasya sāṃvyavahārikajanasyāpi tajjñānamasti, yena kāryaṃ kāraṇe 'stīti pratipadyate, na tattvajñasyaiva / tathāhi- kāryaṃ dṛṣṭvā kāraṇe astīti niścayaḥ ubhayorapi tattvajñasya lokasya ca sādhāraṇaḥ / ato lokaḥ kasmāddhetorna paśyati? tatra lokasyādarśanakāraṇaṃ vaktavyam / lokasya darśanamapramāṇamiti cedatrāha loketyādi-
body.translated_text: The world, the conventional people too, have 'that knowledge' by which one understands that the effect exists in the cause — it is not the exclusive possession of the knower of reality alone. For the certainty 'the effect exists in the cause,' arrived at by seeing the effect, is common to both — to the knower of reality and to the world. Therefore, why, for what reason, does the world not see? A reason must be given for the world's not seeing. If [you say] the world's seeing is not a valid means of knowledge — to this he says with '<s>loka</s>' and so forth —

body.text: lokāpramāṇatāyāṃ cet
body.translated_text: If the world is not a valid authority,

body.text: lokasya sāṃvyavahārikajanasya apramāṇatāyāṃ tajjñānasyāprāmāṇye-
body.translated_text: if there is invalidity of the knowledge of the world, of conventional people —

body.text: vyaktadarśanamapyasat // Bca_9.138 //
body.translated_text: then even the seeing of the manifest is unreal. // <s>Bca</s> 9.138 //

body.text: vyaktasya āvirbhūtasvarūpasya saṃdarśanam / tadapyasat apramāṇaṃ syāt / na tasmād vastutattvavyavasthā prāpnoti / etacca asmābhiriṣyate eva / sarvasāṃvyavahārikapramāṇānāṃ paramārthato 'pramāṇatvāt / tathā ca bhavato 'pi asmatpakṣanikṣepaḥ //
body.translated_text: The perception of the manifest — of what has its nature clearly revealed. Even that would be unreal, would not be a valid means of knowledge. Therefore, the determination of the real nature of things would not be obtained. And this is indeed accepted by us — since all conventional means of knowledge are ultimately not valid means of knowledge. Thus, there is a casting of your position into our own position as well.

body.text: evaṃ ca pariniṣṭhitaḥ kāpilaḥ siddhāntavādino 'pi sādhāraṇadūṣaṇamāsañjayannāha pramāṇamityādi-
body.translated_text: And thus, raising a common objection even against the established <s>Kāpila</s> [i.e., <s>Sāṃkhya</s>] doctrinal proponent, he says with '<s>pramāṇam</s>' and so forth —

body.text: pramāṇamapramāṇaṃ cennanu tatpramitaṃ mṛṣā /
body.translated_text: If even a valid means of knowledge is not a valid means of knowledge, then is not what is ascertained by it false?

body.text: yadi pramāṇamapi paramārthataḥ pramāṇaṃ na bhavatīti bhavatāṃ pakṣaḥ, nanu tatpramitaṃ mṛṣā, pramāṇasyāprāmāṇye tatpramitaṃ tena pramāṇena paricchinnaṃ mṛṣā alīkaṃ prāpnoti / kimataḥ syāt?
body.translated_text: If your position is that even a valid means of knowledge is ultimately not a valid means of knowledge, then is not 'what is ascertained by it false' — when the valid means of knowledge is invalid, what is 'ascertained by it,' what is determined by that means of knowledge, becomes false, unreal. What follows from this?

body.text: tattvataḥ śūnyatā tasmādbhāvānāṃ nopapadyate // Bca_9.139 //
body.translated_text: Therefore, the emptiness of entities is not established in reality. // <s>Bca</s> 9.139 //

body.text: yadi pramāṇasyāprāmāṇye tatpramitaṃ mṛṣā, tadā yeyaṃ bhāvānāṃ dharmāṇāṃ tattvataḥ paramārthataḥ śūnyatā sarvadharmaniḥsvabhāvatā tasmāt pramāṇānniścitā, sāpi nopapadyate, na saṃgacchate / sarvapramāṇopadarśitasya mṛṣārthatvāt sāpi sarvadharmaniḥsvabhāvatā tadvicārakapramāṇopadarśitaiva iti samāno nyāyaḥ //
body.translated_text: If, when the valid means of knowledge is invalid, what is ascertained by it is false, then this emptiness of entities — this absence of intrinsic nature of all <s>dharmas</s> — which is determined in reality, in the ultimate sense, through that valid means of knowledge, it too 'is not established,' does not hold. Because everything presented by all valid means of knowledge would be of false import, that absence of intrinsic nature of all <s>dharmas</s> too, being itself presented by the valid means of knowledge that investigates it — the same reasoning applies.

body.text: atra parihāramāha kalpitamityādi-
body.translated_text: To this he offers a reply, saying with '<s>kalpitam</s>' and so forth —

body.text: kalpitaṃ bhāvamaspṛṣṭvā tadabhāvo na gṛhyate /
body.translated_text: Without grasping a conceptually constructed entity, its absence is not apprehended.

body.text: kalpanākalpitaṃ samāropitaṃ bhāvamaspṛṣṭvā kalpanābuddhayā agṛhītvā tadabhāvo na gṛhyate nālambyate / tathāhi ghaṭamāropitarūpeṇa parikalpya tatsaṃbandhitayā ghaṭābhāvaṃ pratipadyate lokaḥ / ghaṭasya vicāreṇa lokaprasiddhenaiva yadā na kiṃcit svarūpamavatiṣṭhate, tadā tadabhāvaḥ tadviparyayarūpaḥ sutarāṃ na kaścit / tadevopadarśayannāha tasmādityādi-
body.translated_text: Without grasping, without apprehending through conceptual cognition, a conceptually constructed, superimposed entity, its absence is not apprehended, not grasped. For the world, having conceptualized a pot in its superimposed form, understands the absence of the pot as related to that [conceptualization]. When, through analysis, by the commonly known [investigation] of a pot, no intrinsic form whatsoever remains, then its absence — which has the nature of being the opposite of that — is all the more nothing whatsoever. Making this very point explicit, he says with '<s>tasmāt</s>' and so forth —

body.text: tasmādbhāvo mṛṣā yo hi tasyābhāvaḥ sphuṭaṃ mṛṣā // Bca_9.140 //
body.translated_text: Therefore, the entity that is false — its absence is clearly false. // <s>Bca</s> 9.140 //

body.text: yasmāt kalpitabhāvavivekena abhāvo gṛhyate, tasmādbhāvo mṛṣā asatsvabhāvo yaḥ, tasyābhāvaḥ sphuṭaṃ mṛṣā, tasya niḥsvabhāvasya bhāvasya abhāvo virahaḥ sphuṭaṃ niścitaṃ mṛṣā asatyaḥ / tasyāpi parikalpitarūpatvāt / evaṃ ca bhāvābhāvayoḥ parikalpitarūpatve sarvadharmaniḥsvabhāvataiva avatiṣṭhate //
body.translated_text: Since absence is apprehended through discrimination of the conceptually constructed entity, therefore the entity that is false, that has unreal nature — its absence is 'clearly false': the absence, the non-existence, of that entity which has no intrinsic nature is certainly, assuredly false, unreal — because that [absence] too is of a conceptually constructed nature. And thus, when both entity and absence are of conceptually constructed nature, the absence of intrinsic nature of all <s>dharmas</s> alone remains established.

body.text: punaridameva upasaṃhāravyājena vispaṣṭayannāha tasmāt svapne ityādi-
body.translated_text: Again, making this very point clear by way of a summation, he says with 'therefore, in a dream' and so forth —

body.text: tasmātsvapne sute naṣṭe sa nāstīti vikalpanā /
body.translated_text: Therefore, in a dream, when a son has perished, the thought 'he does not exist' —

body.text: yasmādbhāvābhāvau kalpanopasthāpitatvānmṛṣārthau, tasmāt svapne middhākrāntacittāvasthāyāmutpannavinaṣṭe sute putre sati sa putro nāstīti vikalpanā tadabhāvavikalpaḥ / kiṃ karoti?
body.translated_text: Since entity and absence are of false import because they are presented through conceptualization, therefore, in a dream — in the state of a mind overcome by sleep — when a son, a child, has arisen and perished, the thought 'that son does not exist' is the conceptualization of his absence. What does it do?

body.text: tadbhāvakalpanotpādaṃ vibadhnāti
body.translated_text: obstructs the arising of the conceptualization of his existence.

body.text: tasya sutasya bhāvaḥ tasyāstitvaṃ tasya kalpanā sattvasamāropaḥ tasyotpādaḥ unmajjanaṃ taṃ ni[vi?]badhnāti / niṣedhayati- tathaiva tarhi seti cenna mṛṣā ca sā // Bca_9.141 //
body.translated_text: The existence of that son — the conceptualization of superimposing his reality — the arising, the emergence of that [conceptualization] — it obstructs, it blocks. [Response to objection:] 'Then that [absence-thought] is equally [unreal]' — if so, [the reply is:] no, it too is false. // <s>Bca</s> 9.141 //

body.text: sā kalpanā tadbhāvakalpanāṃ vibadhnāti api mṛṣā / alīkasutasya svapne anutpannāniruddhatvāt / athavā satyābhimate eva sute svapne naṣṭe sarvametadyojanīyam / evaṃ sarvadharmāṇāmutpādanirodhau kalpanopadarśitau draṣṭavyau / etaduktaṃ bhavati- yathā svapnopalabdhasya vastuno 'nutpannāniruddhasyāpi kalpanopadarśitau bhāvābhāvau na paramārthasantau, atha ca kalpanayā vyavahāragocaramupagatau pratibhātaḥ, na ca sā kalpanā asatyārthaviṣayatayā apramāṇam, tadviṣayasya paramārthato niḥsvabhāvatvāt, tathaiva jāgraddaśāyāmupalabdhayorapi bhāvābhāvayorvyavahārapathamupagatayoḥ kalpanāpratipāditayorvyavasthā / iti tasyā aprāmāṇye 'pi na sarvadharmaniḥsvabhāvatā vighaṭate / yadāha [nāgārjunaḥ catuḥstave]-
body.translated_text: That conceptualization obstructs the conceptualization of his existence, and yet is [itself] false — because the unreal son in the dream has neither truly arisen nor truly ceased. Alternatively, all this should be construed with reference to a son that is believed to be real, who has perished in a dream. Thus, the arising and cessation of all <s>dharmas</s> should be seen as presented through conceptualization. This is what is stated: just as the entity and absence of a thing perceived in a dream — which has neither truly arisen nor ceased — are not ultimately real, yet through conceptualization have entered the domain of conventional usage and appear so; and that conceptualization is not an invalid means of knowledge merely because it has an unreal object, since its object is ultimately without intrinsic nature — just so is the status of entity and absence that are perceived in the waking state too, which have entered the path of conventional usage and are presented through conceptualization. Therefore, even if that [conceptualization] is not a valid means of knowledge [ultimately], the absence of intrinsic nature of all <s>dharmas</s> is not undermined. As [<s>Nāgārjuna</s>] said in the [<s>Catuḥstava</s>] —

children.translated_text: The world — arisen, abiding, and destroyed — has been declared by You to be, in reality,
mere conceptualization — thus all <s>dharmas</s> have been illuminated.

body.text: kalpanāpyasatī proktā yayā śūnyaṃ vikalpyate //
body.translated_text: Even the conceptualization by which emptiness is conceptualized has been declared to be unreal.

body.text: catuḥ-3.34
body.translated_text: <s>Catuḥstava</s> 3.34

body.text: iti sarvaṃ samañjasam //
body.translated_text: Thus, everything is consistent.

body.text: evamahetubhūtasvabhāveśvarapradhānakartṛtvaṃ jagato nirākṛtya nāpyahetutaḥ ityasyārthaṃ prasādhya upasaṃharannāha tasmādevamityādi-
body.translated_text: Having thus refuted the creatorship of intrinsic nature, <s>Īśvara</s>, <s>Pradhāna</s>, and such — which are not [true] causes — of the world, and having established the meaning of 'nor from no cause,' he sums up saying with 'therefore, in this way' and so forth —

body.text: tasmādevaṃ vicāreṇa nāsti kiṃcidahetutaḥ /
body.translated_text: Therefore, through such analysis, nothing exists without a cause.

body.text: yataḥ svabhāvādisaṃbhūtaṃ na kiṃcit kāryamupapadyate, tasmādevaṃ vicāreṇa samanantaranirūpaṇena nāsti kiṃcidahetutaḥ, svabhāvāderahetuto 'kāraṇājjātaṃ kiṃcit kāryaṃ nāsti na vidyate / upalakśaṇaṃ caitat / puruṣakālādikṛtatvamapi nāsti, teṣāmapyahetutvāt / ato nāpyahetuta iti siddham / nanu yadi nāma svabhāveśvarapradhānāderahetuto na kiṃcidasti, tathāpi paridṛṣṭakāraṇādeva paramārthataḥ utpatsyate / tat kathaṃ sarvadharmāṇāṃ niḥsvabhāvatā setsyatīti parāśayamāśaṅkaya na svato nāpi parato na dvābhyām iti koṭitrayaṃ samarthayannāha na ca vyastetyādi-
body.translated_text: Since no effect whatsoever is established as having arisen from intrinsic nature and such, therefore, through such analysis — through the examination just conducted — nothing exists without a cause; nothing born from no cause, from a non-cause such as intrinsic nature, exists, is found. And this is merely indicative; neither is creatorship by <s>Puruṣa</s>, time, and such established, since those too are non-causes. Thus 'nor from no cause' is proven. Now, even if nothing exists from intrinsic nature, <s>Īśvara</s>, <s>Pradhāna</s>, or from no cause, still it will arise ultimately from observed [empirical] causes alone — 'then how will the absence of intrinsic nature of all <s>dharmas</s> be established?' Anticipating the opponent's thought, and establishing the three alternatives — not from self, not from other, not from both — he says with 'nor in the separate' and so forth —

body.text: na ca vyastasamasteṣu pratyayeṣu vyavasthitam // Bca_9.142 //
body.translated_text: Nor is [an effect] established in conditions, whether separate or combined. // <s>Bca</s> 9.142 //

body.text: na ca naiva / vyastasamasteṣviti vyasteṣu samastesu ca / tatra na ca vyasteṣu, ekaikaśaḥ svataḥ parataśceti / nāpi samasteṣu dvābhyāṃ svaparābhyām / pratyayeṣu kāraṇeṣu / vyavasthitam utpādarūpatayā pratiṣṭhitaṃ kiṃcit //
body.translated_text: 'Nor' — indeed not. 'In the separate and combined' means: in the separate and in the combined. Among these, 'not in the separate' — individually, [meaning] not from self and not from other. 'Nor in the combined' — not from both, from self and other together. 'In conditions' — in causes. '[Nothing is] established' — nothing is grounded as having the form of origination.

body.text: tatra na tāvat svataḥ svabhāvādbhāvā utpadyante / utpādāt pūrvaṃ tasya svabhāvasyāvidyamānatvāt kuta utpadyantām? utpanne ca tasmin satyapi svarūpe tasyāpi niṣpannatvāt kimutpadyantām? api ca / svata eva janmani jātasyaiva punarjanma syāt / na ca tadyuktam / kṛtasya karaṇayogāt / jātasya punarjanmani bījadīnāmeva āsaṃsāraṃ pravṛtteḥ nāṅkurādayaḥ kadācidutpattumavasaraṃ labheran / na ca etadabhyupagacchato 'pi lokata eva bādhāmanubhavat siddhipathamupayāti, bījāderaṅkurādyutpattidarśanāt / na ca bījāṅkurayoraikyam, ubhayorapi bhinnarūparasavīryavipākatvāt / svasvabhāvajanyatve ca kasyacidutpattireva na syāt, itaretarāśrayatvāt / tathā hi yāvat svabhāvo na bhavati, tāvadutpattirna syāt, yāvacca utpattirna bhavati, tāvat svabhāvo na syāt / tasmānna svataḥ kiṃcidutpadyate //
body.translated_text: In this regard, first, entities do not arise from themselves — from their own nature. Since prior to arising, that intrinsic nature does not exist, from what would they arise? And when it has arisen, even though its own form exists, since that too is already accomplished, what would arise? Moreover: if there were arising from itself, there would be the re-arising of what has already arisen. But this is not proper, because it would entail the doing of what is already done. If there were re-arising of what has already arisen, then seeds and such would continue operating throughout <s>saṃsāra</s>, and sprouts and such would never find an occasion to arise. Nor does one who accepts this attain the path of success, since one experiences obstruction from the world itself, given that the arising of sprouts and such from seeds and such is observed. And there is no identity between seed and sprout, since both differ in form, taste, potency, and maturation. And if each were produced from its own intrinsic nature, nothing whatsoever could arise, because of mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>). For as long as the intrinsic nature does not exist, so long there would be no arising; and as long as there is no arising, so long the intrinsic nature would not exist. Therefore, nothing arises from itself.

body.text: nāpi parataḥ / parato hi janmani iṣyamāṇe śālibījādapi kodravāṅkurasyotpattiprasaṅgaḥ / śālikodravayorapi ca kodravāṅkurāpekṣayā paratvamaviśiṣṭam, sarvasya vā janma sarvato bhavet / sarveṣāṃ parasparaṃ paratvāviśeṣāt / atha yadi nāma paratvamaviśiṣṭam, tathāpi kāryakāraṇayoranyonyajanyajanakabhāvasya niyāmakatvāt na sarvasyotpattiriti cet, na / anutpanne hi kārye kasmin punarasya śaktiriti vaktavyam / na ca kāryakāraṇayorasamānakālatayā janyajanakabhāvapratiniyamo 'pi kaścit / ata eva ekasaṃtatipratiniyamo 'pi na yuktaḥ, kāryakāraṇamantareṇa saṃtaterabhāvāt / tasya ca ekakṣaṇānavasthānāt keyaṃ saṃtatirnāma? pūrvāparakṣaṇapravāhasya ca kalpanāsamāropitatvāt nāsti saṃtatirvāstavī / etena sādṛśyamapi niyāmakamiha nirastam / iti na kiṃcit kenacidekasaṃtatipatitaṃ sadṛśaṃ vā janyajanakabhāvaniyataṃ vā asti, janyajanakabhāvasyaiva cātra cintyatvāt, kathaṃ tenaiva parihāraḥ? tasmāt parato 'pi na kasyacit saṃbhavaḥ //
body.translated_text: Nor from another. For if arising from another were accepted, there would be the absurd consequence that even from a rice-seed a millet-sprout could arise. For the otherness of rice and millet with respect to a millet-sprout is undifferentiated — or else everything would be born from everything, since there is no distinction of otherness among all things mutually. But if it is said that although otherness is undifferentiated, still, because of the determining relation of cause and effect as mutually produced and producer, not everything arises from everything — no. For when the effect has not yet arisen, with respect to what is its capacity to be stated? And since cause and effect are not simultaneous, there is no determination whatsoever of the relation of produced and producer. For this very reason, determination within a single continuum (<s>saṃtati</s>) is also not justified, since without cause and effect there is no continuum. And since that [entity] does not remain for a single moment, what is this so-called continuum? And since the stream of prior and subsequent moments is superimposed by conceptual construction, there is no real continuum. By this, similarity too as a determining factor is refuted here. Thus, nothing whatsoever — whether falling within a single continuum or similar, whether determined by the relation of produced and producer — exists, and since the very relation of produced and producer is what is being questioned here, how can the answer consist of that very thing? Therefore, from another too, nothing whatsoever comes into being.

body.text: nāpi dvābhyām, pratyekapakṣoktasarvadoṣaprasaṅgāt / pratyekaṃ ca dvayoraśaktayormilitayorapyasāmarthyāt / na hi ekenāndhenādṛṣṭamārgo bahubhirapi draṣṭuṃ śakyate / pratyekaṃ vā sikatāstailadānāsamarthā militā api tatsamarthā bhavanti / tasmādubhayapakṣapratipāditadoṣaprasaṅgāt dvābhyāmapi na kasyacidutpattisaṃbhavaḥ //
body.translated_text: Nor from both, because of the absurd consequence of all the defects stated in each individual position. And because two [factors] that are each individually incapable are also powerless when combined. For just as a road not seen by one blind person cannot be seen even by many [blind persons], or just as grains of sand individually incapable of yielding oil are not capable of it even when combined — therefore, because of the absurd consequence of the defects demonstrated in both positions, arising from both is also not possible for anything.

body.text: iti svaparobhayajanitamahetujanitaṃ vā tattvato na kiṃcidasti / tasmāt paramārthato 'nutpannāniruddhasvabhāvaṃ māyāmarīcipratibimbapratiśrutkāsamaṃ pratītyasamutpannaṃ svabhāvaśūnyameva sarvaṃ viśvamābhāsate / na tu punaridaṃpratyayatāmātraṃ sāṃvṛtamiha niṣidhyate / yaduktamatra bhagavatā śālistambasūtre-
body.translated_text: Thus, nothing whatsoever exists in reality as produced from self, other, both, or without cause. Therefore, in the ultimate sense, everything — the entire universe — which is unborn and of unceasing nature, equal to an illusion, a mirage, a reflection, and an echo, dependently arisen, and empty of intrinsic nature, merely appears. But this mere conditionality, which is conventional, is not denied here. As the Blessed One stated in the <s>Śālistamba Sūtra</s> —

body.text: tatra kathaṃ pratītyasamutpādaṃ paśyati? ihoktaṃ bhagavatā- ya imaṃ pratītyasamutpādaṃ satatasamitaṃ nirjīvaṃ yathāvadaviparītamajīvamajātamabhūtamakṛtamasaṃskṛtamapratighamanālambanaṃ śivamabhayamanāhāryamavyayamavyupaśamasvabhāvaṃ paśyati, sa dharmaṃ paśyati / yastu evaṃ satatasamitaṃ nirjīvam- ityādi pūrvavat yāvat- avyupaśamasvabhāvaṃ paśyati so 'nuttaradharmaśarīraṃ buddhaṃ paśyati / [āryadharmābhisamaye samyagjñānādupanayenaiva?] / pratītyasamutpāda iti kasmāducyate? sahetukaḥ sapratyayo nāhetuko nāpratyaya ityucyate / peyālaṃ / atha ca punarayaṃ pratītyasamutpādo dvābhyāṃ kāraṇābhyāmutpadyate / katamābhyāṃ dvābhyāṃ kāraṇābhyāmutpadyate? hetūpanibandhataḥ pratyayopanibandhataśca / so 'pi dvividho draṣṭavyaḥ- bāhyaścādhyātmikaśca / tatra bāhyasya pratītyasamutpādasya hetūpanibandhaḥ katamaḥ? yadidaṃ bījādaṅkuraḥ, aṅkurāt patram, patrāt kāṇḍam, kāṇḍānnālam, nālādgaṇḍaḥ, gaṇḍādgarbham, garbhācchūkaḥ, śūkāt puṣpam, puṣpāt phalamiti / asati bīje 'ṅkuro na bhavati, yāvadasati puṣpe phalaṃ na bhavati / sati tu bīje aṅkurasyābhinirvṛttirbhavati / evaṃ yāvat sati puṣpe phalasyābhinirvṛttirbhavati / tatra bījasya naivaṃ bhavati- ahamaṅkuramabhinirvartayāmīti / aṅkurasyāpi naivaṃ bhavati- ahaṃ bījenābhinirvartita iti / evaṃ yāvat puṣpasya naivaṃ bhavati- ahaṃ phalamabhinirvartayāmīti, phalasyāpi naivaṃ bhavati- ahaṃ puṣpeṇābhinirvartitamiti / atha punarbīje sati aṅkurasyābhinirvṛttirbhavati prādurbhāvaḥ / evaṃ yāvat puṣpe sati phalasyābhinirvṛttirbhavati prādurbhāvaḥ / evaṃ bāhyasya pratītyasamutpādasya hetūpanibandho draṣṭavyaḥ //
body.translated_text: Therein, how does one see dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>)? Here the Blessed One has said: 'Whoever sees this dependent origination as constant, continuous, lifeless, as it truly is without distortion, without a living principle, unborn, not having become, unmade, unconditioned, unobstructed, without support, auspicious, fearless, not to be taken away, undecaying, and of the nature of non-cessation — that one sees the <s>Dharma</s>. And whoever thus sees it as constant, continuous, lifeless — and so on as before up to — of the nature of non-cessation, that one sees the <s>Buddha</s>, the unsurpassed <s>Dharma</s>-body.' [By way of approach through right knowledge in the realization of noble <s>Dharma</s>?] Why is it called dependent origination? Because it is said to have causes and conditions, not to be without cause and not without conditions. Abbreviated. And further, this dependent origination arises from two types of causes. From which two types of causes does it arise? From the ground of primary causes (<s>hetu</s>) and from the ground of conditions (<s>pratyaya</s>). And it should be viewed as twofold — external and internal. Therein, what is the ground of primary causes for external dependent origination? Namely: from the seed comes the sprout, from the sprout the leaf, from the leaf the stalk, from the stalk the stem, from the stem the bud, from the bud the ovary, from the ovary the awn, from the awn the flower, from the flower the fruit. When there is no seed, the sprout does not come to be, and so on up to: when there is no flower, the fruit does not come to be. But when there is a seed, the production of the sprout occurs. Thus, up to: when there is a flower, the production of the fruit occurs. Therein, the seed does not think: 'I produce the sprout.' Nor does the sprout think: 'I am produced by the seed.' Thus, up to: the flower does not think: 'I produce the fruit,' nor does the fruit think: 'I am produced by the flower.' But rather, when there is a seed, the production, the manifestation, of the sprout occurs. Thus, up to: when there is a flower, the production, the manifestation, of the fruit occurs. Thus should the ground of primary causes for external dependent origination be viewed.

body.text: kathaṃ bāhyasya pratītyasamutpādasya pratyayopanibandho draṣṭavyaḥ? ṣaṇṇāṃ dhātūnāṃ samavāyāt / katameṣāṃ ṣaṇṇāṃ dhātūnāṃ samavāyāt? yadidaṃ pṛthivyaptejovāyvākāśaṛtusamavāyāt bāhyasya pratītyasamutpādasya pratyayopanibandho draṣṭavyaḥ / tatra pṛthivīdhāturbījasya saṃdhāraṇakṛtyaṃ karoti / abdhāturbījaṃ snehayati / tejodhāturbījaṃ paripācayati / vāyudhāturbījamabhinirharati / ākāśadhāturbījasyānāvaraṇakṛtyaṃ karoti / ṛturapi bījasya pariṇāmanākṛtyaṃ karoti / asatsu eṣu pratyayeṣu bījādaṅkurasyābhinirvṛttirna bhavati / yadā bāhyaśca pṛthivīdhāturavikalo bhavati, evamaptejovāyvākāśaṛtudhātavaśca avikalā bhavanti, tadā sarveṣāṃ
body.translated_text: How should the ground of conditions for external dependent origination be viewed? Through the conjunction of six elements (<s>dhātu</s>). Through the conjunction of which six elements? Namely, through the conjunction of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and season — thus should the ground of conditions for external dependent origination be viewed. Therein, the earth element performs the function of supporting the seed. The water element moistens the seed. The fire element ripens the seed. The wind element draws out the seed. The space element performs the function of non-obstruction for the seed. Season too performs the function of transformation for the seed. When these conditions are absent, the production of the sprout from the seed does not occur. When the external earth element is complete, and likewise the water, fire, wind, space, and season elements are complete, then through the conjunction of all of them

body.text: samavāyāt bīje nirudhyamāne aṅkurasyābhinirvṛttirbhavati / tatra pṛthivīdhātornaivaṃ bhavati- ahaṃ bījasya saṃdhāraṇākṛtyaṃ karomīti / evaṃ yāvadṛtorapi naivaṃ bhavati- ahaṃ bījasya pariṇāmanākṛtyaṃ karomīti / aṅkurasyāpi naivaṃ bhavati- ahamebhiḥ pratyayairjanita iti / atha punaḥ satsu eteṣu bīje nirudhyamāne aṅkurasyābhinirvṛttirbhavati / sa cāyamaṅkuro na svayaṃkṛto na parakṛto nobhayakṛto neśvaranirmito na kālapariṇāmito na prakṛtisaṃbhūto na caikakāraṇādhīno nāpyahetusamutpannaḥ / pṛthivyaptejovāyvākāśaṛtusamavāyāt bīje nirudhyamāne aṅkurasyābhinirvṛttirbhavati / evaṃ bāhyasya pratītyasamutpādasya pratyayopanibandho draṣṭavyaḥ //
body.translated_text: when the seed is ceasing, the production of the sprout occurs. Therein, the earth element does not think: 'I perform the function of supporting the seed.' Likewise, up to: season too does not think: 'I perform the function of transforming the seed.' Nor does the sprout think: 'I am produced by these conditions.' But rather, when these are present, when the seed is ceasing, the production of the sprout occurs. And this sprout is not self-made, nor made by another, nor made by both, nor created by <s>Īśvara</s> (God), nor transformed by time, nor born from <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), nor dependent on a single cause, nor arisen without cause. Through the conjunction of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and season, when the seed is ceasing, the production of the sprout occurs. Thus should the ground of conditions for external dependent origination be viewed.

body.text: tatra bāhyaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ pañcabhiḥ kāraṇairdraṣṭavyaḥ / katamaiḥ pañcabhiḥ? na śāśvatato nocchedato na saṃkrāntitaḥ parīttahetuto vipulaphalābhinirvṛttitaḥ tatsadṛśānuprabandhataśceti / kathaṃ na śāśvatat iti? yasmādanyo 'ṅkuro 'nyadvījam, na ca yadeva bījaṃ sa evāṅkuraḥ / athavā punaḥ- bījaṃ nirudhyate, aṅkuraścotpadyate / ato na śāśvatataḥ / kathaṃ nocchedataḥ? na ca pūrvaniruddhādbījādaṅkuro niṣpadyate, nāpyaniruddhādbījāt, api ca, bījaṃ ca nirudhyate, tasminneva samaye 'ṅkura utpadyate, tulādaṇḍonnāmāvanāmavat / ato nocchedataḥ / kathaṃ na saṃkrāntitaḥ? visadṛśo bījādaṅkura iti / ato na saṃkrāntitaḥ / kathaṃ parīttahetuto vipulaphalābhinirvṛttitaḥ? parīttabījamupyate, vipulaphalānyabhinirvartayatīti / ataḥ parīttahetuto vipulaphalābhinirvṛttitaḥ / kathaṃ tatsadṛśānuprabandhataḥ? yādṛśaṃ bījamupyate tādṛśaṃ phalamabhinirvartayatīti / atastatsadṛśānuprabandhataśceti / evaṃ bāhyaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ pañcabhiḥ kāraṇairdraṣṭavyaḥ // iti /
body.translated_text: Therein, external dependent origination should be viewed through five characteristics. Through which five? Not from permanence, not from annihilation, not from transmigration, from a small cause the production of abundant fruit occurs, and through the continuation of what is similar to it. How 'not from permanence'? Because the sprout is one thing and the seed another — it is not the case that the seed itself is the sprout. Or alternatively: the seed ceases and the sprout arises — therefore not from permanence. How 'not from annihilation'? The sprout is not produced from a seed that has previously ceased, nor from a seed that has not ceased; rather, the seed ceases and, at that very moment, the sprout arises — like the rising and falling of the arms of a balance. Therefore not from annihilation. How 'not from transmigration'? Because the sprout is dissimilar from the seed. Therefore not from transmigration. How 'from a small cause the production of abundant fruit occurs'? A small seed is sown and it produces abundant fruits. Therefore, from a small cause the production of abundant fruit occurs. How 'through the continuation of what is similar to it'? Whatever kind of seed is sown, that kind of fruit it produces. Therefore, through the continuation of what is similar to it. Thus, external dependent origination should be viewed through five characteristics. So it is.

body.text: ādhyātmikastu pratītyasamutpādaḥ pūrvameva vistareṇa pratipāditaḥ / ihāpi yojayitavyaḥ / evaṃ paramārthavicāre sāṃvṛtamapratiṣiddhameva //
body.translated_text: As for internal dependent origination, it has already been explained in detail previously. It should be applied here as well. Thus, in the investigation of ultimate reality, the conventional is not denied at all.

body.text: nanu bhāvā nātyantāsaṃbhavino bhavanti / api tu hetupratyayabalādanāgatādadhvanovartamānamadhvānamāgacchanti, vartamānāt punaranityatābalādatītamadhvānaṃ gacchanti / ityevamutpādasthitivināśavyapadeśaḥ / pratītyasamutpādo 'pi yathāvadevaṃ saṃgacchate iti traikālyavādimatamāśaṅkayāha anyata ityādi-
body.translated_text: Now, [the opponent says:] entities are not utterly impossible. Rather, by the power of causes and conditions, they come from the future time-period to the present time-period; and from the present, by the power of impermanence, they go to the past time-period. Thus there is the designation of arising, abiding, and destruction. Dependent origination too is consistent in just this way. Anticipating this view of the three-times theorists (<s>traikālyavādin</s>), he says with 'from another' and so forth —

body.text: anyato nāpi cāyātaṃ na tiṣṭhati na gacchati /
body.translated_text: Nor has it come from another [place or time]; it neither abides nor departs.

body.text: anyato deśakālāt / nāyātaṃ nāgataṃ kiṃcit / nāpyāgataṃ sat vartamānādadhvanaḥ kvacidgacchati / nāpi tenaikasvabhāvena kvacittiṣṭhati / tathāhi- yadi anāgatādadhvano vartamānamāgacchet, vartamānādvā atitam, tadā saṃskṛtamapi nityaṃ syāt, sarvadā vidyamānatvāt / nānityaṃ nāmāsti, sa ca dharmo na ca nityaḥ iti kathametat setsyati?
body.translated_text: 'From another' — from another place or time. Nothing whatsoever 'has come,' has arrived. 'Nor' does what has arrived go anywhere from the present time-period. 'Nor does it abide' anywhere with that single intrinsic nature. For if it were to come from the future time-period to the present, or from the present to the past, then even the conditioned would be permanent, since it would exist at all times. How could it be maintained that 'there is impermanence,' and 'that <s>dharma</s> is not permanent'?

body.text: atha pūrvāparakālayoḥ kāritraśūnyatayā dharmasya adhvasu viśeṣaḥ / tathā hi yadā asaṃprāptakāritraḥ kṛtyaṃ na karoti, tadā anāgato 'bhidhīyate, yadā karoti tadā pratyutpannaḥ, yadā tu kṛtyānnivṛttaḥ tadā atīta iti viśeṣaḥ / etadapi na kiṃcit / tenaivātmanā tasyaiva
body.translated_text: Alternatively, the distinction of a <s>dharma</s> across the time-periods is through the absence of function in the earlier and later times. That is to say: when it has not attained its function and does not perform its activity, then it is called 'future'; when it performs [its activity], then it is 'present'; and when it has ceased from its activity, then it is 'past' — this is the distinction. This too amounts to nothing. For by that very nature, of that very [<s>dharma</s>]

body.text: tadāpi sadbhāvāt kāritramapi kathaṃ na syāditi vaktavyam / pratyayāntarāpekṣāpi nityamavasthitarūpasya na saṃbhavati / kāritraśūnyasya ca vastutve aśvaviṣāṇādīnāmapi tattvaprasaṅgaḥ / kāritraṃ vā kathamatītamanāgataṃ pratyutpannaṃ ca ucyate? kiṃ tadaparakāritrasadbhāvāt svayameva vā? pūrvatra anavasthānam, pāścātye ca dharmasyāpi svayamatītatvādivyavasthāyāṃ na kiṃcit kṣīyate / yadi ca / yathā vartamānaṃ dravyato 'sti, tathā atītamanāgataṃ cāsti, tadā naivam / svabhāvena sato dharmasya kathamanutpannavinaṣṭasvabhāvatā? kimasya pūrvaṃ nāsīt yasyābhāvādajāta ityucyate? kiṃ ca paścānnāsti yasyābhāvādvinaṣṭa iti? tenaiva cātmanā pūrvāparakālayoravasthāne vartamānavadupalabdhyādiprasaṅgaḥ / tasmādabhūtatvādabhavanadharmato na saṃgacchate kathaṃcidapi adhvatrayayogaḥ, tattvābhyupagamato nātītādisadbhāvaḥ / tadayamatra saṃgrahaślokaḥ-
body.translated_text: even then, since it exists, it must be stated how it could not also have causal efficacy. And the dependence on another condition is not possible for what is of permanently established form. And if what is devoid of causal efficacy were a real thing, then even hare's horns and such would have the absurd consequence of being real. Or, how is causal efficacy said to be past, future, and present? Is it so because of the existence of another causal efficacy, or by itself? In the first case, there is an infinite regress; in the second, even for the <s>dharma</s> itself, nothing is lost in the determination of being past and such by itself. And if, just as the present exists as a substance, so too the past and future exist — then it is not so. How can a <s>dharma</s> that exists by its own nature have the nature of being unarisen or destroyed? What was it that did not previously exist, such that due to its absence it is called 'unarisen'? And what does not exist later, such that due to its absence it is called 'destroyed'? And if it persists in the prior and subsequent periods with that very nature, there would be the absurd consequence of being perceived and such, like the present. Therefore, being unreal — of the nature of non-becoming — the connection with the three times is in no way consistent; from the acceptance of [their] reality, the existence of past and such [as real entities] does not follow. Here is the summary verse —

children.text: svabhāvaḥ sarvadā nāsti bhāvo nityaśca neṣyate /
children.translated_text: Intrinsic nature never exists, and a [permanent] entity is not accepted.
And an entity is not different from its intrinsic nature — clearly this is the play of <s>Īśvara</s>!

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: yadapyucyate- astyatītaṃ karma, astyanāgataṃ phalam, iti sūtravacanādastyatītādibhāvaḥ, tadapi hetuphalāpavāde tadduṣṭipratiṣedhārthamuktaṃ bhagavatā- astyatītam, astyanāgatam, iti / atītaṃ tu yadabhūtapūrvamutpadya vinaṣṭam, anāgataṃ yat sati hetau bhaviṣyati / evaṃ hi hetvādyastītyucyate, astiśabdasya nipātatvāt kālatrayavṛttitvam / itthaṃ ca etadevaṃ yatparamārthaśūnyatāyāmuktaṃ bhagavatā-
body.translated_text: As for what is said — 'past <s>karma</s> exists, future fruit exists' — from this <s>sūtra</s>-statement, the past and such exist — this too was stated by the Blessed One for the purpose of preventing the false view that would result from the denial of cause and fruit: 'the past exists, the future exists.' But 'past' is what, having previously arisen, has been destroyed; 'future' is what will come to be when its cause is present. For thus, cause and such are said to 'exist' — since the word '<s>asti</s>' (exists), being a particle, functions across the three times. And in this manner, it is this very thing that was stated by the Blessed One in the context of ultimate emptiness —

body.text: cakṣurbhikṣava utpadyamānaṃ na kutaścidāgacchati, nirudhyamānaṃ na kvacit saṃnicayaṃ gacchati / iti hi bhikṣavaḥ cakṣurabhūtvā bhavati, bhūtvā ca prativigacchatīti //
body.translated_text: 'Monks, the eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go to any repository. Thus, monks, the eye, not having been, comes to be; having been, it passes away.'

body.text: yadi ca anāgataṃ cakṣuḥ syāt, noktaṃ syādabhūtvā bhavatīti / tasmānnādhvasaṃkrāntirasti / yadi caivam, na kutaścidāgamanam, kvacid gamanaṃ vā prajñāyate, pratibhāsamānasya ca pratyutpannasya na rūpaṃ kiṃcidvicāreṇāvatiṣṭhate, tadā-
body.translated_text: And if the eye were future [i.e., pre-existent], it would not have been said 'not having been, it comes to be.' Therefore, there is no transition across the three times. And if this is so — neither coming from anywhere nor going anywhere is discerned — and even for the present that appears, no form whatsoever withstands analysis — then —

body.text: māyātaḥ ko viśeṣo 'sya yanmūḍhaiḥ satyataḥ kṛtam // Bca_9.143 //
body.translated_text: What is the difference of this from an illusion, that which the deluded take as real? // <s>Bca</s> 9.143 //

body.text: māyātaḥ aindrajālikanirmitahastyādirūpāyā api niḥsvabhāvatayā viśeṣo naiva kaścit asya hetupratyayopajanitasya vasturūpasya paridṛśyamānasya //
body.translated_text: From an illusion — from the form of elephants and such conjured by a magician — through its lack of intrinsic nature, there is simply no difference whatsoever of this apparent thing-form produced by causes and conditions.

body.text: kathaṃ na viśeṣaḥ? punaridameva vyaktīkurvannāha māyayetyādi-
body.translated_text: How is there no difference? Making this very point explicit, he says with 'by illusion' and so forth —

children.translated_text: That which is produced by illusion, and that which is produced by causes —

children.text: āyāti tatkutaḥ kutra yāti ceti nirūpyatām // Bca_9.144 //
children.translated_text: where does it come from, and where does it go? Let this be examined! // <s>Bca</s> 9.144 //

body.text: māyāśabdenātra māyānirmāṇahetuvijñānādiviśeṣa ucyate kāraṇe kāryopacārāt, hetorapi māyāsvabhāvatāpratipādanārtham / tayā nirmitam, yacca vasturūpaṃ māyāhetunā māyāsvabhāvena yadviracitamiti yāvat / yacca anyadvasturūpaṃ hetubhiḥ lokaprasiddhaiḥ kāraṇairjanitam / parasparasamuccayārthaṃ cakāradvayam / āyāti āgacchati / tanmāyānimirtaṃ hetunirmitaṃ vā vasturūpaṃ
body.translated_text: By the word 'illusion' (<s>māyā</s>), here is meant the particular consciousness and such that is the cause of the magical creation — by the figurative application of the effect-term to the cause, and for the purpose of showing that even the cause is of the nature of illusion. 'Produced by that' — whatever thing-form is created by the illusion-cause, by what is of the nature of illusion — this is the meaning. 'And' whatever other thing-form is generated 'by causes' — by the commonly known conditions. The two instances of the word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) are for mutual conjunction. 'Comes' — arrives. That thing-form — whether illusion-produced or cause-produced —

body.text: kutaḥ kasmāt? kutra yāti ca, vinaṣṭaṃ sat kva punaretad gacchati? ityevaṃ nirūpyatāṃ sūkṣmekṣikayā vicāryatām, yadi tasya kutaścidāgacchati kvacid gacchati vā upalabhyate //
body.translated_text: from where, from what? 'And where does it go?' — when destroyed, where then does it go? 'Let this be examined' — let it be investigated with subtle discernment — whether it is found to come from anywhere or go anywhere.

body.text: nanu ca / yadi hetupratyayasāmarthyopajanitaṃ vasturūpam, tadā kathamiva alīkaṃ syāt? ata eva alīkamityāha yadanyetyādi-
body.translated_text: But if the thing-form is produced by the power of causes and conditions, then how can it be unreal? For this very reason it is unreal — he says with 'that which, by the proximity of another' and so forth —

children.translated_text: That which is seen in the proximity of another is not [seen] in its absence.

children.text: pratibimbasame tasmin kṛtrime satyatā katham // Bca_9.145 //
children.translated_text: In that which is like a reflection — in that which is artificial — how can there be reality? // <s>Bca</s> 9.145 //

body.text: yad vasturūpamanyasya hetupratyayasya saṃnidhānena dṛṣṭamupalabdham, na tadabhāvataḥ, tasya anyasya abhāvataḥ na dṛṣṭam, tatparādhīnavṛttitvāt / pratibimbasame pratibimbena ādarśamaṇḍalapratibhāsinā mukhādisādṛśyena tulye / yathā mukhādibimbādarśamaṇḍalādisaṃnidhānena pratibimbaṃ pratibhāsate, tathā vasturūpamapi hetupratyayasaṃnidhānayoriti / evaṃbhūte vasturūpe kṛtrime parāyattavṛttitayā asvābhāvike satyatā amṛṣārthatā kutaḥ? naiva yujyate / na hi paropanidhisvabhāvānāmakṛtrimatā yuktā / taduktam-
body.translated_text: Whatever thing-form is seen, perceived, 'in the proximity of another' — of another cause or condition — 'is not' [seen] 'in its absence' — in the absence of that other, it is not seen, because its activity depends on another. 'Like a reflection' — comparable to a reflection, which is a likeness of a face and such appearing in the surface of a mirror. Just as a reflection appears through the proximity of the face-image, mirror-surface, and such — so too a thing-form [appears] through the proximity of causes and conditions. In such a thing-form — 'in that which is artificial' — in what functions through dependence on another, lacking intrinsic nature — 'how can there be reality?' — how can there be non-falsity? It is in no way justified. For it is not justified that what is of the nature of depending on another's proximity should be non-artificial. As was stated —

children.text: hetutaḥ saṃbhavo yeṣāṃ tadabhāvānna santi ye /
children.translated_text: Those whose arising is from a cause, and which do not exist in its absence —

children.text: kathaṃ nāma na te spaṣṭaṃ pratibimbasamā matāḥ //
children.translated_text: how are they not clearly regarded as similar to a reflection?

body.text: iti / [yuktiṣaṣṭikā-]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Yuktiṣaṣṭikā</s>]

body.text: tasmānna hetupratyayopajanitaṃ kiṃcit paramārthasadasti / na ca hetupratyayānāṃ sāmarthyaṃ kvacidapi paramārthataḥ saṃbhavati //
body.translated_text: Therefore, nothing produced by causes and conditions exists as ultimately real. And the power of causes and conditions is nowhere ultimately possible.

body.text: tathāhi- svaparobhayātmakairhetubhirvidyamāno vā bhāvaḥ kriyeta, avidyamāno vā, ubhayasvabhāvo vā? tatra na vidyamānaḥ kriyate ityāha vidyamānasyetyādi-
body.translated_text: For indeed — would an entity be produced by causes that are of the nature of self, other, both, or neither? Among these, an existent [entity] is not produced — he says with 'of an existent' and so forth —

body.text: vidyamānasya bhāvasya hetunā kiṃ prayojanam /
body.translated_text: What is the purpose of a cause for an entity that [already] exists?

body.text: vidyamānasya kāraṇavyāpārāt prāgeva satsvabhāvasya hetunā kāraṇena kiṃ prayojanam? kāryasya niṣpannātmakatayā nirvartyasvabhāvābhāvāt hetuvyāpārasyānupayogāt / dvitīyaṃ vikalpamadhikṛtyāha athāpītyādi-
body.translated_text: For an existent — for what has real nature even prior to the activity of a cause — what is 'the purpose of a cause,' of a causal agent? Because, since the effect is already of an accomplished nature, due to the absence of anything to be accomplished, the activity of the cause is useless. Regarding the second alternative, he says with 'or even if' and so forth —

body.text: athāpyavidyamāno 'sau hetunā kiṃ prayojanam // Bca_9.146 //
body.translated_text: Or even if it is non-existent — what is the purpose of a cause? // <s>Bca</s> 9.146 //

body.text: athāpīti prakārāntaradyotane / avidyamāno 'sau na satsvabhāvaḥ / tarhi hetunā kiṃ prayojanam? tadāpi na hetunā kimapi prayojanamasti, tatrāpyasatsvabhāvatvāt hetuvyāpārābhāvāt //
body.translated_text: 'Or even if' (<s>athāpi</s>) is for indicating another possibility. 'Non-existent' — not of real nature. Then what is 'the purpose of a cause'? Even then, there is no purpose whatsoever for a cause, because even there, due to its being of unreal nature, the activity of a cause is absent.

body.text: syādetat- yadi nāma vidyamānasya niṣpannatvāt kartavyābhāvāt na hetunā kimapi prayojanam, avidyamānasya tu kiṃ na bhavatītyāha nābhāvasyetyādi-
body.translated_text: There might be this [objection]: granted that for an existent [entity], because it is already accomplished and there is nothing to be done, there is no purpose for a cause; but why should this not hold for a non-existent [entity]? He says with 'of a non-existent' and so forth —

body.text: nābhāvasya vikāro 'sti hetukoṭiśatairapi /
body.translated_text: There is no transformation of a non-existent, even by hundreds of <s>koṭis</s> of causes.

body.text: na abhāvasya avidyamānasvabhāvasya vikāro 'sti, anyathātvaṃ bhāvasvabhāvatā asti, nīrūpatayā tasyāpi kartavyābhāvāt / hetukoṭiśatairapi, āstāṃ tāvad hetuśatairhetusahasraiḥ,
body.translated_text: 'Of a non-existent' — of what is of unreal nature — there is no 'transformation,' no alteration into the nature of an existent, because for that too, being formless, there is nothing to be done. 'Even by hundreds of <s>koṭis</s> of causes' — let alone by hundreds of causes or thousands of causes,

body.text: hetūnāṃ koṭiśatairapi, tasya niḥsvabhāvatayā kenacidapi vikārayitumaśakyatvāt / mā bhavatu vikāraḥ, bhāvasvabhāvatā kevalamasyāstu cedatrāha tadavastha iti-
body.translated_text: even by hundreds of <s>koṭis</s> of causes, because it, being without intrinsic nature, cannot be transformed by anything whatsoever. 'Let there be no transformation; let it merely have the nature of an existent' — if this is intended, he says with 'remaining in that state' —

body.text: tadavastha kathaṃ bhāvaḥ
body.translated_text: Remaining in that state, how can it be an entity?

body.text: tadavastho 'parityaktābhāvasvabhāvaḥ naiva bhāvaḥ syāt, nābhāva eva bhāvo bhavati, kevalamabhāvasvabhāvatānivṛttau bhāvasvabhāvo bhavati / atrāha-
body.translated_text: 'Remaining in that state' — not having abandoned the nature of non-existence — it would simply not be an entity. Non-existence does not become an entity; only upon the cessation of the nature of non-existence does the nature of an entity come about. To this he says —

body.text: ko vānyo bhāvatāṃ gataḥ // Bca_9.147 //
body.translated_text: Or what other [thing] has come to the state of being an entity? // <s>Bca</s> 9.147 //

body.text: yadi na prāgabhāvo bhāvasvabhāvo bhavati, ko vā tarhi abhāvādanyaḥ aparaḥ bhāvatām, abhāvasvabhāvatāṃ parityajya bhāvarūpatāṃ gataḥ? nānyaḥ kaścit pratīyate, kāraṇasya kāryasvabhāvatāyāḥ pūrvameva pratiṣiddhatvāt //
body.translated_text: If the prior non-existence does not become the nature of an entity, then what other, different from the non-existence, having abandoned the nature of non-existence, has 'come to the state of being an entity,' has attained the form of an entity? No other is discerned, since the cause's having the nature of the effect has already been refuted.

body.text: syādetat- nānyaḥ kaścidbhāvo bhavati, kiṃ tarhi prāgabhāvasya bhāvavirodhinaḥ sadbhāvāttadā bhāvo na bhavati, paścāt punastasminnapagate bhavatyevetyāha-
body.translated_text: There might be this [objection]: no other entity comes to be; rather, since the prior non-existence, which is opposed to the entity, exists at that time, the entity does not come to be then; but later, when that [non-existence] has departed, it does indeed come to be — he says —

body.text: nābhāvakāle bhāvaścetkadā bhāvo bhaviṣyati /
body.translated_text: If there is no entity at the time of non-existence, then when will the entity come to be?

body.text: nābhāvakāle abhāvasattāsamaye na bhāvaścet, yadi bhāvo na bhavati, kadā bhāvo bhaviṣyati? abhāvakāle bhāvasyānutpattiścet, na kadācidbhāvasyonmajjanaṃ syāt, abhāvena virodhinā sadā kroḍīkṛtatvāt / tenaivotpadyamānena bhāvena abhāvasya vināśo bhaviṣyatīti cedāha-
body.translated_text: 'At the time of non-existence' — at the time when non-existence prevails — 'if there is no entity' — if the entity does not come to be — then 'when will the entity come to be?' If the entity does not arise at the time of non-existence, then the entity would never emerge, because it is always enveloped by the opposing non-existence. 'The non-existence will be destroyed by the very entity that is arising' — if this is claimed, he says —

body.text: nājātena hi bhāvena so 'bhāvo 'pagamiṣyati // Bca_9.148 //
body.translated_text: For the non-existence will not be removed by an entity that has not been born. // <s>Bca</s> 9.148 //

body.text: yāvadasau bhāvo na jāyate, tāvadabhāvasya vināśo nāstyeva / hiryasmāt / tasmāt na ajātena anutpannena bhāvena so 'bhāvaḥ prāgabhāvarūpaḥ apagamiṣyati nivartayiṣyate //
body.translated_text: As long as that entity is not born, so long the destruction of non-existence simply does not occur. '<s>Hi</s>' — because. Therefore, by an entity that has not been born, that has not arisen, 'that non-existence' — the prior non-existence — 'will not be removed,' will not be averted.

body.text: athāpi syāt- mā apagacchatu nāma abhāvaḥ, tasminnanapagate eva bhāva utpadyate / utpanne ca bhāve bhāvābhāvayoḥ parasparaparihārāt paścādabhāvaḥ svayameva apagamiṣyatītyāha na cetyādi-
body.translated_text: Now one might think: let non-existence not depart; even while it has not departed, the entity arises. And once the entity has arisen, since entity and non-existence mutually exclude each other, afterward the non-existence will depart of its own accord — he says with 'and not' and so forth —

body.text: na cānapagate 'bhāve bhāvāvasarasaṃbhavaḥ /
body.translated_text: And when non-existence has not departed, there is no possibility for the occasion of the entity.

body.text: bhavatyeva kramaḥ, yadi pūrvaṃ bhāva eva bhavet / na caitadasti / co yasmāt / na caiva anapagate anivṛtte abhāve bhāvasyāvasaraḥ avakāśaḥ, tasya saṃbhavaḥ / bhāvotpattivirodhinaḥ abhāvasyaiva bhāvāt / kāraṇenaiva tadabhāvo nivartayiṣyate cet, na / kāraṇasya kāryotpattāveva vyāpārāt / kāryamutpādayadeva tadabhāvamapi nirvartayatīti cet, utpādayatyeva kāryam, yadi tadvirodhino 'bhāvādutpādayituṃ kṣamate / na ca tasminnapratihatasāmarthye tatkāryamutpādayituṃ kṣamate / na ca kāraṇena tadabhāvasya virodhaḥ, kāraṇakāle 'pi tatprāgabhāvasya bhāvāt sattāvasthānāt / tasmādbhāvātmani abhāvātmani vā kārye na kāraṇasya vyāpāro yujyate / ubhayānubhayapakṣe ca pratyekapakṣaniṣedhādeva kāraṇavyāpārasya niṣedhaḥ kṛto bhavatīti draṣṭavyam / nāpi tayoḥ saṃbhavo 'sti / virodhinorekatra ekadā vidhipratiṣedhayorbhāvāyogāt / taduktam-
body.translated_text: The sequence works only if the entity comes to be first. But this is not the case. 'And' — because. And indeed, when non-existence has not departed, has not ceased, there is no 'possibility for the occasion' — the opportunity — 'of the entity.' Because non-existence itself, which opposes the arising of the entity, prevails. 'The cause itself will remove that non-existence' — if so, no. Because the cause's activity is only for the production of the effect. 'While producing the effect, it also removes that non-existence' — if so, it produces the effect only if it is able to produce it from the non-existence that opposes it. And when that [non-existence] has unimpeded power, it is not able to produce that effect. And the cause has no opposition to that non-existence, since even at the time of the cause, the prior non-existence of that [effect] prevails — remains in existence. Therefore, the activity of a cause is not justified with respect to an effect that is of the nature of either entity or non-entity. And in the case of both and neither, the negation of the activity of the cause has already been accomplished by the negation of each individual position — this should be understood. Nor is there the arising of both, since the simultaneous presence of affirmation and negation — of entity and non-entity — in one place at one time is impossible. As was stated —

children.text: na sannutpadyate bhāvo nāpyasan sadasanna ca /
children.translated_text: An existent entity does not arise, nor does a non-existent, nor one both existent and non-existent.

children.text: na svato nāpi parato na dvābhyāṃ jāyate katham //
children.translated_text: Not from itself, not from another, not from both — how is it born?

body.text: iti / [catuḥ-2.13; 3.9]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Catuḥśataka</s> 2.13; 3.9]

body.text: evaṃ tāvadbhāvasyotpattiḥ paramārthato na kathaṃcidapi saṃgacchate / nāpi kathaṃcidutpannasya satsvabhāvasya nivṛttiryujyate ityāha bhāvaścetyādi-
body.translated_text: Thus, so far, the arising of an entity is in no way consistent in the ultimate sense. Nor is the cessation of what has arisen and has real nature justified — he says with 'and an entity' and so forth —

body.text: bhāvaścābhāvatāṃ naiti dvisvabhāvaprasaṅgataḥ // Bca_9.149 //
body.translated_text: And an entity does not pass into non-existence, because of the absurd consequence of dual nature. // <s>Bca</s> 9.149 //

body.text: pūrvāpekṣaścakāraḥ / yathā abhāvo bhāvatāṃ naiti, tathā bhāvaśca abhāvatāṃ naiti, gacchati / kutaḥ? dvisvabhāvaprasaṅgataḥ / bhāvasya sataḥ yadā abhāvasvabhāvatā bhavati, tadā ca ekasyaiva vastunaḥ dvayoḥ svabhāvayoḥ prasaṅgaḥ syāt, ekasyaiva bhāvābhāvarūpatvāt / na ca bhāvatāṃ parityajya abhāvarūpatāṃ yātīti vaktumucitam / tadā ca bhāvasyaivābhāvāt ko 'bhāvarūpatāṃ yātīti na vidmaḥ / na ca satsvabhāvasya pāramārthikatve nivṛttiryuktā, pāramārthikatvasya abhāvaprasaṅgāt //
body.translated_text: The word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) connects with what precedes. Just as non-existence does not pass into the state of an entity, so too 'an entity does not pass into non-existence,' does not go [into it]. Why? 'Because of the absurd consequence of dual nature.' When an entity that exists takes on the nature of non-existence, then for one and the same thing there would be the absurd consequence of two natures, since one and the same thing would have the form of both entity and non-entity. And it is not proper to say that it abandons the nature of entity and goes to the form of non-entity. For then, since the entity itself would be absent, we do not know who has gone to the form of non-entity. And for what has real nature, if it is ultimately real, cessation is not justified, since there would be the absurd consequence of the absence of ultimate reality.

body.text: itthaṃ bhāvasyotpādavināśayoḥ paramārthato 'bhāvaṃ prasādhya upasaṃharannāha evamityādi-
body.translated_text: Having thus established the absence, in the ultimate sense, of both the arising and cessation of entities, he sums up saying with 'thus' and so forth —

body.text: evaṃ na ca nirodho 'sti na ca bhāvo 'sti sarvadā /
body.translated_text: Thus, there is neither cessation, nor is there ever an entity.

body.text: evamuktakrameṇa utpādavināśāyogāt / co hetau / yasmānna nirodho 'sti, na vināśo 'sti, [na ca bhāvo 'sti,] na vastusattvamasti / caḥ samuccaye / sarvadā sarvasmin kāle / "utpādādvā tathāgatānāmanutpādādvā tathāgatānāṃ sthitaivaiṣā dharmāṇāṃ dharmatā dharmasamatā dharmasthititā dharmaniyāmatā dharmadhātuḥ tathatā avitathatā" / ityādivacanāt / yata evam-
body.translated_text: Thus, by the stated sequence, since arising and destruction are impossible — 'and' regarding the reason: since there is no cessation, no destruction, [no entity,] no real existence of things. The word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) is for accumulation. 'Always' — at all times. 'Whether <s>Tathāgatas</s> arise or whether <s>Tathāgatas</s> do not arise, this <s>dharmatā</s> (nature of things) of <s>dharmas</s> is established — <s>dharmasamatā</s> (equality of dharmas), <s>dharmasthititā</s> (stability of dharmas), <s>dharmaniyāmatā</s> (certainty of dharmas), <s>dharmadhātu</s> (realm of dharmas), <s>tathatā</s> (suchness), <s>avitathatā</s> (non-deviation)' — because of such statements. Since it is thus —

body.text: ajātamaniruddhaṃ ca tasmātsarvamidaṃ jagat // Bca_9.150 //
body.translated_text: Unborn and unceased — therefore all this world. // <s>Bca</s> 9.150 //

body.text: ajātamanutpannam / aniruddhaṃ ca avinaṣṭaṃ paramārthataḥ / tasmādutpādavināśābhāvāt pūrvoktāt / sarvamaśeṣam / idaṃ niḥsvabhāvatāsamānādhikaraṇaṃ jagadviścaṃ sattvabhājanalokasaṃjñitaṃ sacarācaraṃ vā / māyotpādanirodhavad vyavahāravaśāt punarutpādanirodhau staḥ / etena saṃvṛtisatyasyāpratiṣedha uktaḥ / dharmasaṃgītau caitaduktam-
body.translated_text: 'Unborn' — unarisen. 'And unceased' — not destroyed, in the ultimate sense. 'Therefore' — because of the aforementioned absence of arising and destruction. 'All' — without remainder. 'This' — having the same substrate as essencelessness — the world, designated as the world of sentient beings and the receptacle-world, or [the world] of the moving and non-moving. Like the arising and cessation of an illusion, arising and cessation exist by the force of convention. By this, the non-negation of conventional truth is stated. And in the <s>Dharmasaṃgīti</s> this was said —

body.text: tathatā tathateti kulaputra śūnyatāyā etadadhivacanam / sā ca śūnyatā notpadyate na nirudhyate āha- yadi evaṃ sarvadharmāḥ śūnyā uktā bhagavatā, tat sarvadharmā notpatsyante, na nirotsyante / nirārambho bodhisattvaḥ / āha- evametat kulaputra, yathābhisaṃbudhyase / sarvadharmā notpadyante, na nirudhyante / āha- yadetaduktaṃ bhagavatā saṃskṛtā dharmā utpadyante nirudhyante ca ityasya tathāgatabhāṣitasya ko 'bhiprāyaḥ? āha- utpādanirodhābhiniviṣṭaḥ kulaputra lokasaṃniveśaḥ / tatra tathāgato mahākārūṇiko lokasya trāsapadaparihārārthaṃ vyavahāravaśāduktavān utpadyante nirudhyante ca / na cātra kasyaciddharmasya utpādo na nirodhaḥ // iti //
body.translated_text: '<s>Tathatā</s> (suchness), <s>tathatā</s> — O son of good family, this is a designation for <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness). And that <s>śūnyatā</s> neither arises nor ceases.' He said — 'If thus all <s>dharmas</s> are declared empty by the Blessed One, then all <s>dharmas</s> will not arise and will not cease. The <s>Bodhisattva</s> is without undertaking.' He said — 'Just so, O son of good family, as you understand it. All <s>dharmas</s> do not arise and do not cease.' He said — 'As for what was stated by the Blessed One — "conditioned <s>dharmas</s> arise and cease" — what is the intention of that statement of the <s>Tathāgata</s>?' He said — 'O son of good family, the world-convention is attached to arising and cessation. Therein, the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the greatly compassionate one, for the purpose of averting the ground of terror for the world, has spoken by the force of convention: "they arise and they cease." But herein, there is no arising of any <s>dharma</s> whatsoever, nor cessation.' Thus.

body.text: tasmāt sarvadharmā anutpannāniruddhasvabhāvatayā ādiśāntāḥ prakṛtiparinirvṛtāḥ, iti jagato niḥsvabhāvatāyāṃ tadantargatānāṃ narakādigatīnāmapi niḥsvabhāvataivetyupadarśayannāha svapnetyādi-
body.translated_text: Therefore, since all <s>dharmas</s> are primordially quiescent and naturally in <s>parinirvāṇa</s> by virtue of having the nature of non-arising and non-cessation — showing that since the world is without intrinsic nature, the destinies of hell and such included within it are also without intrinsic nature — he says with 'like a dream' and so forth —

body.text: svapnopamāstu gatayo vicāre kadalīsamāḥ /
body.translated_text: The destinies are like a dream; upon examination, they are like a plantain tree.

body.text: svapnena upamā tulyaṃ yāsāṃ tāḥ tathoktāḥ / turavadhāraṇe / svapnopalabdhasvabhāvagatayaḥ narakapretatiryaṅyanuṣyadevānāṃ sabhāgatāviśeṣāḥ / yathā svapne deśāntarādigamanāgamanaṃ sukhaduḥkhādyanubhavanaṃ ca, tathā anadhigataparamārthatattvasya narakādiṣu veditavyam, na tu tattvataḥ / katham? vicāre kadalīsamāḥ / hetupadametat / sarvadharmāṇāṃ niḥsvabhāvatayā vicāre vimarśe sati yasmāt kadalīsamāḥ kadalīvanniḥsārāḥ gatayaḥ, tasmādityarthaḥ / etena yathoktaṃ prāk[4.47]
body.translated_text: 'Like a dream' — those whose likeness is to a dream, they are so called. The word '<s>tu</s>' is for emphasis. The destinies obtained in the nature of a dream — the specific existences (<s>nikāyasabhāgatā</s>) of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. Just as in a dream there is traveling to other lands and such, and experiencing pleasure and pain — so too should it be understood for one who has not realized the ultimate truth, regarding hell and the rest — but not in reality. How so? 'Upon examination, they are like a plantain tree' — this is a statement of the reason. Since upon examination, upon investigation, all <s>dharmas</s>, being without intrinsic nature, the destinies are like a plantain tree — coreless like a plantain tree — therefore, this is the meaning. By this, what was stated earlier [4.47] —

body.text: māyaiveyamato vimuñca hṛdaya trāsam
body.translated_text: 'This is but an illusion — therefore release your heart from fear'

body.text: ityādi, tadapi prasādhyopadarśitaṃ bhavati / yataśca anutpannāniruddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ, ata āha nirvṛtetyādi-
body.translated_text: — and so forth, that too is shown to be established. And since all <s>dharmas</s> are unborn and unceased, therefore he says with 'of the liberated' and so forth —

body.text: nirvṛtānirvṛtānāṃ na viśeṣo nāsti vastutaḥ // Bca_9.151 //
body.translated_text: Between the liberated and the unliberated, there is no difference in reality. // <s>Bca</s> 9.151 //

body.text: nirvṛtāḥ ye sarvāvaraṇaprahāṇādvinirmuktasarvabandhanā / anirvṛtāḥ ye rāgādikleśapāśāyattacittasaṃtatayaḥ saṃsāracārakāntargatāḥ / teṣāmubhayeṣāmapi viśeṣo bhedo nāsti, na saṃbhavati / kutaḥ? vastutaḥ paramārthataḥ sarvadharmāṇāṃ niḥsvabhāvatayā prakṛtiparinirvṛtatvāt / saṃvṛtyā punarasti eva viśeṣaḥ, ityanekadhā pratipāditam / ata evāha-
body.translated_text: 'The liberated' — those who are released from all bonds through the abandonment of all obscurations. 'The unliberated' — those whose mind-streams are subject to the bonds of the afflictions of desire and such, who are within the round of <s>saṃsāra</s>. Of both of these, 'there is no difference,' no distinction. Why? 'In reality' — in the ultimate sense, because all <s>dharmas</s>, being without intrinsic nature, are naturally in <s>parinirvāṇa</s>. Conventionally, however, there indeed is a difference — this has been established in many ways. For this very reason he says —

children.translated_text: Since there is, in reality, non-difference between <s>Buddhas</s> and the realm of sentient beings,

children.text: ātmanaśca pareṣāṃ ca samatā tena te matā //
children.translated_text: the equality of self and others is accordingly maintained by them.

body.text: iti // [catuḥ-3.40]
body.translated_text: Thus. [<s>Catuḥśataka</s> 3.40]

body.text: iti paramārthatattvāparijñānānmithyābhiniveśādāropitajagajjālamupakalpya ātmanaiva ātmānamākulayati bālajanaḥ ityupadarśayannāha evamityādi-
body.translated_text: Thus, through the failure to comprehend ultimate reality, by imagining the fabricated net of the world through false attachment, the childish person torments himself by himself — showing this, he says with 'thus' and so forth —

children.text: evaṃ śūnyeṣu dharmeṣu kiṃ labdhaṃ kiṃ hṛtaṃ bhavet /
children.translated_text: When <s>dharmas</s> are thus empty, what is gained and what is taken away?

children.text: satkṛtaḥ paribhūto vā kena kaḥ saṃbhaviṣyati // Bca_9.152 //
children.translated_text: By whom will anyone be honored or despised? // <s>Bca</s> 9.152 //

children.text: kutaḥ sukhaṃ vā duḥkhaṃ vā kiṃ priyaṃ vā kimapriyam /
children.translated_text: From where comes pleasure or pain? What is dear, and what is not dear?

children.text: kā tṛṣṇā kutra sā tṛṣṇā mṛgyamāṇā svabhāvataḥ // Bca_9.153 //
children.translated_text: What is craving, and where is that craving, when sought in terms of its intrinsic nature? // <s>Bca</s> 9.153 //

children.text: vicāre jīvalokaḥ kaḥ ko nāmātra mariṣyati /
children.translated_text: Upon examination, what is the world of the living? Who will die here?

children.text: ko bhaviṣyati ko bhūtaḥ ko bandhuḥ kasya kaḥ suhṛt // Bca_9.154 //
children.translated_text: Who will come to be? Who has been? Who is a relative? Who is a friend to whom? // <s>Bca</s> 9.154 //

body.text: evaṃ pratipāditanyāyena śūnyeṣu niḥsvabhāveṣu dharmeṣu kiṃ labdham, kiṃ kutaścit prāptaṃ yallābheṣu prahṛṣyanti? kiṃ hṛtam, kimapahṛtaṃ kena kasyacit bhavet, yallābhāpahāreṇa prakupyanti?
body.translated_text: When <s>dharmas</s> are empty — without intrinsic nature — according to the reasoning thus established, 'what is gained' — what has been obtained from anywhere, over which people rejoice in gains? 'What is taken away' — what has been taken away from anyone by anyone — over which people become angry at loss and theft?

body.text: satkṛtaḥ pūjitaḥ, paribhūtaḥ apakṛto vā kena kaḥ saṃbhaviṣyati? vastusvabhāvābhāve na kaścit kenacidityarthaḥ //
